Monitoring and evaluation make the difference between a program that works and a program that believes it works. Coverage is measured by household surveys that count nets, their condition, and their use, not by the number of nets distributed. Entomological monitoring measures vector density, species composition, infection rates, insecticide susceptibility, and the proportion of vectors resting indoors. Human outcome monitoring tracks cases, test positivity, and location, which can reveal that transmission persists in a pocket the program never reached. Because any of these measures can improve for reasons unrelated to the intervention, programs compare areas and time periods rather than crediting themselves for a seasonal decline. Programs also fail for structural reasons that have little to do with biology, because a campaign that cannot reach the last village when the road floods each year leaves a pocket that reseeds the surrounding area, and a spraying program that depends on one donor's annual budget cannot sustain the pressure that elimination requires.

Every vector control measure and every antiparasitic drug has adverse effects, and a nurse who names them honestly protects both the patient and the program. Insecticides applied indoors can cause eye and skin irritation, headache, and respiratory symptoms, particularly when rooms are not ventilated or when residents return too soon after spraying. Nets treated with insecticide can cause skin irritation and, rarely, a burning sensation in the eyes. Mass treatment with preventive chemotherapy can produce nausea, abdominal pain, dizziness, and rash, and people who feel unwell after a tablet are less likely to accept the next round. Ivermectin used against onchocerciasis can provoke a reaction in people who harbor microfilariae, with fever, itching, rash, and sometimes more severe inflammation, and this reaction is a predictable consequence of killing the parasite rather than an allergy to the drug. Praziquantel can cause abdominal discomfort, headache, and dizziness that are usually mild and brief, and explaining that these reactions are expected and not a sign that the medicine is harming the person is part of the treatment itself.

The nurse's role in vector-borne disease begins before any program exists, in the recognition of an exposure that no one has named. The questions that matter are specific: where the patient sleeps, whether the house has screens or nets, what time of day the patient is outdoors, whether water stands near the home, whether animals are kept inside, and what the patient was doing in the weeks before the fever began. A patient with an eschar, a swollen lymph node, a painless skin ulcer that has not healed in months, or an unexplained eosinophilia may be carrying a vector-borne diagnosis that has been overlooked. Nurses see these findings first because they see the patient's skin, review the medication list, and take the history in a room where the patient is willing to talk. Recording the answers in the chart makes the next clinician's work possible, and repeating the exposure question when a fever persists is one of the highest-yield habits in tropical practice.

At the community level the nurse turns vector biology into instructions that people can follow. Nets should be tucked under the mattress, used every night of the year rather than only in the wettest months, and repaired when torn. Water containers should be covered and emptied on a weekly schedule so that larvae cannot complete their development. Standing water around the compound should be removed, which is often a task for a neighborhood rather than for a single household. Anyone with fever should be tested rather than treated blindly, and anyone with bleeding, confusion, or difficulty breathing should be referred immediately. Advice must acknowledge what families can actually do, because telling a household to eliminate standing water when it has no reliable water supply is not advice. The nurse who pairs a message with a realistic solution is far more likely to be heard.

Clinicians working in endemic areas also need personal protection that matches the vector, and this is a planning task rather than a formality. Repellents applied to exposed skin and permethrin-treated clothing reduce bites from mosquitoes and ticks. Long sleeves and trousers during the hours of peak biting are simple and effective where the heat allows them. Aerosol insecticides and window screens reduce indoor exposure, and a bed net is essential where Anopheles is active at night. For Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever and other infections that spread in hospitals, gloves, gowns, eye protection, and safe handling of sharps and body fluids are the measures that prevent transmission to staff, and ticks should be removed with fine forceps, pulled steadily close to the skin without crushing the body. Post-exposure planning, including whom to call and where to obtain evaluation, should be settled before deployment rather than during an illness.

Where treatment or prevention is prescribed for a vector-borne disease, the regimen must be verified against current guidance rather than recalled from memory. The World Health Organization publishes treatment guidelines for malaria, leishmaniasis, trypanosomiasis, Chagas disease, and the helminth infections, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention publishes recommendations for clinicians in the United States. Doses and durations are revised as resistance emerges and as new evidence accumulates, and recommendations differ between countries even for the same disease. Current guidance for onchocerciasis, for example, gives ivermectin at 150 micrograms per kilogram by mouth, repeated according to the national program protocol rather than by individual preference. Treatment for Chagas disease with benznidazole or nifurtimox, treatment for leishmaniasis with liposomal amphotericin B or pentavalent antimonials, and treatment for plague with gentamicin or doxycycline all carry age-specific and weight-specific considerations that vary among guidelines. The current national guideline and the current World Health Organization recommendation must be checked before prescribing, and a pediatric dose calculated from a table that has since been revised is a preventable error.

Vector ecology is being reshaped by human activity at a pace that outstrips most programs' ability to adapt. Irrigation schemes, dams, and rice cultivation create year-round larval habitat where transmission was previously seasonal, and deforestation moves vectors and their hosts closer to settlements. Unplanned urban growth creates the containers, the standing water, and the dense human population that Aedes aegypti requires. Warming extends the range where the extrinsic incubation period is short enough for transmission, and shifting rainfall makes the timing of seasons less predictable. Extreme weather compresses all of this into sudden events, when flooding displaces people, disrupts sanitation, and concentrates vectors and hosts together. Because so many vector-borne diseases are zoonoses first and human diseases second, the human, veterinary, and environmental sectors have to work from the same map, since a human case may be the first sign of an animal outbreak.

When you arrive in a new setting, the fastest way to understand the vector-borne risk is to read the place in a fixed order. Identify the water, because water determines which larvae can develop and where. Identify the housing, because wall construction, roofing, screens, and eaves determine which vectors rest and feed indoors. Identify the animals, because they determine which zoonotic cycles are running, and identify the working and sleeping hours of the people, because those determine when exposure occurs. Identify the season, because the same village is a different risk in the dry months and in the wet months. Then ask which of those features can be changed and which cannot, and build the plan around the ones that can, because that sequence is what converts vector biology into a nursing assessment.

To summarize, a vector is a living link whose competence depends on the pairing of a pathogen, an arthropod, and an environment, and whose efficiency depends far more on how long it lives and how often it bites people than on how many of them exist. Mosquitoes of the genus Anopheles transmit malaria at night, Aedes mosquitoes transmit dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever by day, and Culex mosquitoes carry lymphatic filariasis and several encephalitis viruses in between. Sandflies carry leishmaniasis, tsetse flies carry African trypanosomiasis, triatomine bugs carry Chagas disease, ticks carry the rickettsioses, the borrelioses, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, snails support schistosomiasis, blackflies carry onchocerciasis, and fleas carry plague. Biological transmission requires the pathogen to develop inside the vector, which is why the extrinsic incubation period and vector survival govern so much of what control can achieve, while mechanical transmission requires only a contaminated surface and is answered by sanitation. Endophilic and exophilic behavior, breeding site ecology, and the water-borne and soil-borne routes of the helminths each point to a specific intervention, and every link in a transmission cycle is a place where a program can act. The insecticide-treated bed net works through biology rather than obedience, because it kills as well as blocks, and its community benefit depends on coverage, condition, and timing rather than on the virtue of the sleeper. Logistics, monitoring, resistance surveillance, and honest reporting of adverse effects decide whether any of this reaches the people who need it, and the nurse stands at the point where the biology becomes care. Verify every regimen against the current national and World Health Organization guidance before you prescribe, and let the ecology of the place tell you what to look for in the patient in front of you.

# Chapter 4 — The Advanced Practice Nurse in Tropical Medicine: Scope, Task-Sharing, and Ethics

The advanced practice nurse who works in tropical medicine practices at the outer edge of what any single clinician can safely hold. You are asked to recognize diseases you may see once a year, to run a clinic on intermittent electricity, to make referral decisions across hours of difficult road, and to do all of it while the patient in front of you speaks a language you learned as an adult. This chapter is about the frame that holds that work together. It is about your scope of practice, the arrangements that allow you to act safely beyond the traditional nursing role, the logistics that determine whether your knowledge ever reaches the patient, and the ethical commitments that should govern your conduct when nobody is watching. The clinical chapters that follow assume this frame, and none of them will make sense if you imagine yourself practicing inside a well-supplied hospital with a physician in the next room. Read this chapter as the foundation on which every later decision rests.

Scope of advanced nursing practice differs across countries far more than most clinicians expect. In some countries the advanced practice nurse holds independent authority to assess, diagnose, prescribe, and refer, and may run a clinic without physician oversight. In others the same clinician works under delegated authority, governed by a written agreement that names the tasks permitted and the physician who carries ultimate responsibility. In still others the title does not exist at all, and experienced nurses perform advanced tasks through informal arrangements that have never been written down and are therefore invisible to the regulator. Regulation, not competence, decides what you may legally do. A procedure you performed without hesitation in one health system can be a disciplinary offense in another, and an assumption of authority is a poor defense. Before you accept a post, read the law and the regulations that govern nursing practice in that jurisdiction, and confirm exactly what standing orders, prescribing rights, and diagnostic privileges you hold. Ask for those documents in writing, and keep them with you.

The role grew out of several historical streams that are worth knowing because they explain its contradictions. Missionary and colonial nursing in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries placed nurses in settings with no physician at all, and the tasks they absorbed were never formally recognized in the laws of the time. The primary health care movement that followed the declaration at Alma-Ata in 1978 made the nurse the intended backbone of first-contact care for populations that had none. The later scale-up of treatment for HIV and AIDS, and the response to drug-resistant tuberculosis, forced ministries of health to authorize nurses to initiate and manage treatment because there were simply not enough physicians to do it. Each of these moments expanded practice first and wrote the rules afterward. The result is that advanced nursing practice in tropical settings is very often more capable than its legal description suggests. That gap is a source of both pride and risk.

Task-shifting and task-sharing describe two ways of organizing that expansion, and the words carry different meanings. Task-shifting is the deliberate movement of a defined clinical task from a more highly trained cadre to a less highly trained one, usually with the goal of extending coverage to people who currently receive nothing. Task-sharing is the same redistribution of work described as a collaboration, in which responsibility is genuinely shared and the more specialized clinician remains available for consultation rather than handing the task away and disappearing. The distinction is not merely semantic. Shifting can suggest that the nurse is a cheaper substitute for a physician, while sharing implies that the nurse is a colleague with a defined and respected domain of practice. The word you choose shapes how your work is valued, how you are supervised, and whether the arrangement survives the next budget reduction. In practice, the most durable programs combine both ideas, with clear protocols, measured competence, and an explicit route back to the physician when the case falls outside the protocol.

The evidence that nurses can deliver comparable outcomes for defined conditions is substantial and should be known by anyone who has to defend the arrangement. Trials and systematic reviews across several settings have compared nurse-led care with physician-led care for uncomplicated malaria, uncomplicated respiratory infection, first-line treatment of tuberculosis, hypertension, contraception, immunization, and the initiation and monitoring of antiretroviral therapy. For these defined tasks, the outcomes measured, including correct prescribing, treatment completion, viral suppression, blood pressure control, and patient satisfaction, have generally been comparable, and in several studies adherence and follow-up were better under nurse-led care. The World Health Organization has endorsed task-sharing as a strategy for expanding access to essential services in countries with severe shortages of health workers. That endorsement rests on conditions that are easy to overlook. The tasks must be genuinely defined, the training must be adequate, the supervision must be real, and the supply of medicines must be dependable.

Equivalence has boundaries, and an honest account of task-sharing names them rather than pretending they do not exist. The evidence is strongest for protocol-driven tasks with clear decision rules and measurable outcomes. It is weaker for tasks that depend on pattern recognition across large volumes of experience, such as reading a subtle chest radiograph or managing an undifferentiated acutely ill adult without a working diagnosis. Nothing in the evidence base suggests that task-sharing removes the need for physicians; it redistributes specific and bounded pieces of work. A useful discipline is to ask, for each task, whether a validated protocol exists, whether competence can actually be measured, and whether there is a defined referral path for the cases that fall outside it. When all three answers are yes, the task is a reasonable candidate for sharing. When any answer is no, the task needs a physician, a consultation, or a different plan altogether.

The instruments that make task-sharing safe are ordinary and unglamorous, and nurses often underestimate how much depends on them. A standing order is a written authorization, signed by the responsible physician or medical director, that permits a nurse to take a defined action without a case-by-case order. A protocol is the fuller document that describes the clinical reasoning behind the action, its indications, its contraindications, and the monitoring that must accompany it. A clinical algorithm is a decision tree that turns a complex assessment into a sequence with branch points and explicit stop rules. None of these replace judgment, and none of them should be used as a shield for not thinking about the person in front of you. Their purpose is to make the correct action the default action when the clinician is tired, interrupted, or working alone at the end of a long night.

Standing orders remain safe only if they are current, and currency is a nursing responsibility rather than a clerical one. An algorithm printed five years ago may now direct you to a medicine that has been withdrawn, a dose that has been reduced, or a test that has been replaced by something better. Regimens are revised, guidance differs between countries, and the current national guideline and the recommendation of the World Health Organization must be checked before you prescribe or administer any dose. Consider a familiar example: a child with acute watery diarrhea and no signs of severe dehydration is treated with oral rehydration salts and zinc, with zinc given at 20 milligrams each day for 10 to 14 days, and the child is reassessed for hydration at defined intervals. Consider another. A child with fast breathing and no danger signs receives amoxicillin at 40 milligrams per kilogram for each dose, twice a day, for 5 days. Those figures describe what current guidance recommends, but the weight band tables that accompany them, especially the tables for antimalarials such as artemether with lumefantrine, have been revised more than once. Verification against the current guideline is part of the task itself, not an insult to your competence.

The nurse who works where there is no physician carries a particular kind of authority and a particular kind of loneliness. In many rural districts the most senior clinical decision-maker is a nurse, and the district hospital may be 3 hours away by road in the dry season and effectively unreachable in the wet season. Your threshold for referral must therefore be lower than it would be in a city, and your threshold for holding a patient must be higher, because a delay in referral is a real clinical intervention with real consequences. Know your routes, your vehicles, your river crossings, and the hour at which travel becomes unsafe. Know which consultant can be reached by telephone, at what hour, and for what kind of question. The decision to hold or to move a deteriorating patient is one of the most consequential judgments in tropical nursing, and it is a judgment you will often make alone.

Logistics begin with electricity, because almost everything else depends on it. Vaccines, some medicines, laboratory reagents, and blood products require controlled temperatures, and a cold chain fails silently when the power does. Check and record refrigerator temperatures at least twice a day, once in the morning and once in the afternoon, and keep that record where a supervisor can see it. Know which items in your refrigerator are freeze-sensitive, because a vaccine that has been frozen may look perfectly normal and be useless. Learn the shake test for adsorbed vaccines and use it whenever you suspect a freeze event. Keep an alternative power source for the refrigerator, whether solar, generator, or a well-managed ice pack system, and rehearse what you will do in the first 30 minutes of an outage. A cold chain is not a piece of equipment; it is a daily habit carried out by a named person.

Supplies and reagents decide whether your knowledge can be used at all. Stock-outs are the ordinary condition of many rural facilities rather than an exceptional emergency, and the nurse is often the only person who can anticipate them. Know your consumption, know your lead times, and order against the season rather than against the shelf. Rotate stock so that the earliest expiry is used first, record every batch and expiry date, and protect diagnostic tests from heat and moisture in the way the manufacturer requires. Build a small buffer of the items whose absence would stop your clinic entirely, and know which items have no alternative. When the rapid diagnostic tests for malaria run out, the consequence is not administrative; it is that febrile patients are treated blind, with all the waste and delay that implies. Quantification, ordering, and storage are clinical skills in this setting, and they deserve the same attention you give to a physical examination.

Transport and referral logistics deserve the same seriousness as any diagnostic question. An ambulance may be a motorcycle, a bicycle trailer, a boat, or a shared pickup, and its availability at 2 in the morning is a genuine clinical variable. Prepare a referral pack before you need it, containing a letter that states the working diagnosis, the treatment already given with times and doses, the allergies, the relevant observations, and the name and contact of the person sending the patient. Send a copy of the chart with the patient and keep a copy for your own records. Where possible, send an escort, and make sure the receiving facility knows the patient is coming. Confirm that blood for transfusion is available before you transfer a patient with severe anemia, because a referral that ends at an empty blood bank is a wasted and dangerous journey.

Staffing is the quiet determinant of safety, and it is an ethical subject rather than an administrative one. A nurse responsible for 40 inpatients, several of them children and several of them acutely ill, cannot provide the monitoring that any protocol assumes. Skill mix matters as much as raw numbers, and a ward staffed by one experienced nurse and several untrained assistants is a different clinical environment from a ward staffed by three trained nurses. Community health workers can extend reach enormously when they are trained, supervised, and paid, and they can become a source of harm when they are given tasks without support. Ratios are not a bureaucratic obsession. They are an expression of how much attention each patient can receive, and attention is the substance of nursing care. When staffing falls below what safe practice requires, say so in writing, and keep saying it.

Monitoring is where nursing contributes something that no algorithm can replace. The physician may make the diagnosis, but the nurse is the one who observes the patient across time, and deterioration usually announces itself in trends rather than in single measurements. Record respiratory rate, mental status, capillary refill, urine output, and temperature at the intervals your protocol requires, and look at the pattern rather than at the most recent number. A child whose respiratory rate has risen from 30 to 50 breaths per minute over 4 hours is deteriorating even if the latest value still falls within the range quoted for that age. Use a structured early warning score where one exists, because it converts scattered observations into a single number that forces a response. Escalate on the trend, and document the escalation together with the reply you received.

Adverse effects belong to the same discipline of attentive watching. Every medicine you give can cause harm, and the medicines used in tropical medicine include several with narrow margins and dangerous reactions. Some antimalarials cause the breakdown of red blood cells in people with an inherited enzyme deficiency, and that deficiency must be considered before certain courses are given, particularly the 14 day course of primaquine used against the dormant liver stage of malaria. Many antibiotics cause rash, and a few cause a sudden severe reaction within minutes of the first dose. Antituberculosis medicines can injure the liver, and the nurse who notices jaundice, nausea, or dark urine and stops to ask a question may prevent a death. In patients starting treatment for HIV, a paradoxical worsening of symptoms can occur as the immune system recovers, and recognizing it early changes management. Report every suspected reaction to the national pharmacovigilance system, which feeds the World Health Organization program for international drug monitoring, because a reaction that is never reported can never be counted.

Documentation is the only witness when no supervisor is present, and it is also the instrument of your own accountability. Write what you observed, what you did, when you did it, and why, in a note that another clinician could act on without speaking to you. Record the time of every dose and every observation, because the interval between them is often the clinical finding. Write down the advice you received by telephone and the name of the person who gave it. Record refusals, delays, and the reasons for them, including the ones caused by the system rather than by the patient. Good documentation protects the patient, protects you, and becomes the data from which your facility learns what is actually happening. When nobody reviews your charts, review them yourself, and invite a colleague to review them with you.

Supervision in these settings has to be supportive rather than punitive if it is to work at all. A supervisor who arrives to inspect and blame will be told what is convenient, and the information that matters will disappear. A supervisor who arrives with a checklist, observes practice, discusses the difficult cases, and helps solve the supply problem will learn what is really going on. Where no external supervisor exists, build a local version. Regular case discussions, a monthly review of deaths and referrals, a shared logbook of complications, and a standing arrangement to telephone a distant colleague about a hard case are all forms of supervision. These practices are what keep a lone clinician honest and current. They are also the mechanism by which a system discovers that a protocol no longer fits reality.

Ethics begin with the duty to care, which is a genuine professional obligation and also a limited one. You have a duty to treat patients, including during outbreaks, and that duty has historically been honored by nurses at great personal cost. You do not have an unlimited duty to die. The limits are set by the availability of protection, the proportionality of the risk, and the reciprocal obligations of your employer, who owes you training, functioning personal protective equipment, vaccination and prophylaxis where they exist, insurance, and support if you become ill or must be isolated. A nurse who is asked to care for patients with a highly transmissible infection using a cloth mask and a plastic apron is not being tested for courage; she is being exposed by an institution that has failed to prepare. Name that failure clearly, in writing, and refuse what is genuinely unsafe.

Resource allocation is an ethical problem you will meet at the bedside rather than in a committee room. When there is one functioning ventilator, one unit of blood, or one place in the referral vehicle, someone must decide, and in practice that decision often falls to the nurse. Implicit rationing, in which the choice is made by habit, social standing, or who speaks the loudest, is both unjust and invisible. Explicit criteria, agreed in advance and applied consistently, are fairer even when they are painful. Use triage protocols, document the criteria you applied, and be transparent with families about what is scarce and why. Where you disagree with a decision, raise it through the proper channel rather than quietly working around it. Consistency is the safeguard that protects the next patient as much as the present one.

Dual loyalty names the conflict between obligations to your patient and obligations to an employer, a state, or another third party. You may be required to report a diagnosis to a public health authority, to test a patient without consent under a legal order, to provide care in a detention facility, or to disclose information to an immigration officer. Some of these obligations are lawful and ethically defensible, because reporting certain infections protects the community. Others place you in the position of harming the person in front of you. Know in advance which reporting duties are legally required in your jurisdiction and which are merely requested, because the difference matters. Tell the patient what you must report and why, before you report it, whenever that is possible. Where a legal duty conflicts with your professional conscience, use the available channels, seek advice, and put your objection in writing.

Research participation raises a different set of obligations, and nurses are usually closer to it than they expect to be. You may be the person who explains a study, obtains consent, collects samples, records outcomes, or notices that a participant is being pressed to enroll. Consent is valid only when it is informed, voluntary, and genuinely understood, and understanding cannot be assumed when the information is delivered in a second language, at speed, to someone who cannot read. Undue inducement is a real risk where a small payment is a large sum in the local economy. Ask what happens to participants after the study ends, whether the community receives any benefit, and who will treat a complication caused by the research itself. Where the standard of care in the study falls below what you can accept, raise it with the ethics committee rather than carrying it out quietly. The nurse is often the last person in the chain with the standing to protect the participant.

Cultural humility is more useful than cultural competence, and the difference repays careful thought. Competence suggests that a group can be mastered through a list of traits, and a list becomes a stereotype the moment it meets a person who does not match it. Humility is a stance rather than a body of knowledge. It means accepting that you do not yet understand this patient's world, asking rather than assuming, being willing to be corrected, and holding your own explanations with a degree of doubt. Ask what the patient believes is causing the illness, what they fear most, and what they have already tried. The answers change the plan more often than any cultural fact sheet ever will. Humility also means recognizing that your presence carries power, because you control medicines, referrals, and paperwork that the patient needs.

Interpreters are clinical instruments, and using them badly produces bad medicine. Never use a child to interpret a serious conversation, and avoid using a family member when the subject is sensitive, because the relative may soften, edit, or withhold what is said. Brief the interpreter before the encounter and tell them what you need to ask, then speak to the patient and not to the interpreter, in short sentences that a listener can carry. Allow silence for the interpretation and resist the urge to fill it. Check understanding by asking the patient to repeat the plan in their own words rather than by asking whether they understood. Afterward, acknowledge with the interpreter what was difficult in the conversation, because they carry the material too. Record that an interpreter was used and who it was, so that the next clinician can rely on the note.

Traditional healers are collaborators in most tropical settings, not obstacles to be cleared away. For a large share of the population they are the first and sometimes the only source of care, and they are trusted, affordable, and permanent residents of the community in a way that a rotating nurse is not. Condemning them wholesale does not protect patients; it drives care underground and removes any chance of influencing it. Collaboration usually works better when it is specific and practical. Teach the danger signs that require immediate referral, agree on a referral pathway with a named contact, supply simple materials such as insecticide-treated bed nets, and invite healers to bring patients themselves. Be clear about practices that cause harm, such as deep scarification, forceful enemas, or the use of toxic preparations, and negotiate rather than threaten. Where a traditional practice is harmless and meaningful, allowing the patient to continue it alongside treatment often buys the adherence you need.

Personal safety and security are part of professional practice, not a private worry to be managed after hours. The single largest threat to a nurse working in many tropical settings is a road traffic crash, followed by infectious exposure and then by violence or civil unrest. Use a seat belt in every vehicle, avoid traveling at night where the roads or the checkpoints make it hazardous, and agree on a check-in schedule with someone who will raise the alarm if you miss it. Know the security plan for your area, including curfew hours, safe routes, and the trigger for evacuation. Practice safe injection technique and dispose of sharps immediately, because a needle injury at the end of a long shift is a foreseeable event rather than a freak accident. Report every exposure at once, because the window for prophylaxis against HIV and other infections is short. Security is a shared responsibility, and the organization that sends you also owes you a plan.

Burnout and moral distress are occupational hazards that require an organizational response rather than a private one. Burnout has three recognizable dimensions, an exhausting depletion of energy, a growing cynicism or detachment from the work, and a sense that you are no longer effective. Moral distress is a distinct experience in which you know what the patient needs and are prevented from providing it by shortages, policy, or hierarchy. Repeated moral distress can become moral injury, a lasting damage to your sense of yourself as a good clinician. The consequences include attrition, medical error, depression, and suicide, and they are common enough that you should treat them as expected rather than shameful. What helps is concrete and includes adequate staffing, manageable workloads, real clinical autonomy, peer support, structured debriefing after critical incidents, regular supervision, protected sleep, and access to mental health care. What does not help is resilience training delivered as a substitute for fixing the conditions that made you unwell in the first place.

Mentoring local staff is the difference between a visit and a contribution. If your skills leave when you leave, the program has not been strengthened; it has been borrowed. Teach at the bedside, in the language of the ward, using the patients already in front of you, and let the learner perform the task under observation rather than watching you perform it. Use low-fidelity simulation and checklists for rare emergencies, keep a logbook of competencies, and assess performance against a defined standard rather than against your memory of your own practice. Build the teaching capacity of the most experienced local nurse, so that she becomes the trainer of the next cohort. Learn the local system, its constraints, and its history from your colleagues before you propose changes, and give credit publicly for the work they do.

Mentoring runs in both directions, and the outsider usually has as much to learn as to teach. The local nurse knows which families will not accept a referral, which medicines actually arrive, and which traditional practice will be continued whether or not you approve of it. Treat that knowledge as expertise rather than as folklore. Ask what has been tried before, because programs that failed leave lessons that are written down nowhere. Be careful with the posture of the rescuer, which flatters the visitor and diminishes the resident. The most durable improvements in a district usually come from local leaders who stay, and your task is to support them rather than to become them. The measure of your work is what remains after you have gone.

Legal and professional protection matters a great deal when you cross a border to practice. Licensure is specific to a jurisdiction, and a qualification that permits independent practice at home may permit nothing at all elsewhere. Confirm your registration status, your indemnity insurance, the scope defined by the local regulator, and the standing orders that apply to your post, and keep copies of those documents with you. In emergencies, several countries grant temporary registration to visiting clinicians, but that registration still carries a defined and limited scope. Practicing outside it exposes you and your patients to avoidable risk and can end your ability to work in the country. When an instruction from an employer conflicts with the law or with your scope, get the conflict resolved in writing before you act.

To summarize, the advanced practice nurse in tropical medicine works within a scope that is set by law and by local regulation, and that scope differs sharply from country to country. Task-sharing extends safe care to people who would otherwise receive none, but only when the tasks are defined, the training is adequate, the supervision is real, and the protocols are current. The unglamorous infrastructure of electricity, cold chain, reagents, transport, staffing, and documentation decides whether knowledge becomes treatment. Monitoring, recognition of adverse effects, and honest reporting are core nursing contributions rather than secondary duties. The ethics of duty to care, resource allocation, dual loyalty, and research participation require you to act with transparency even when nobody checks. Cultural humility, skilled interpretation, and genuine partnership with traditional healers and local colleagues make the care acceptable as well as correct. Personal safety, recognized moral distress, and mentorship are what allow this work to continue without consuming the people who do it.

# Chapter 5 — Travel and Migration History: The Structured Exposure History

In tropical medicine the history is not the preliminary to the diagnosis. It decides which diagnosis is even possible. A patient can be examined from head to foot, and the examination will offer fever, perhaps a rash, perhaps an enlarged spleen, and none of that will distinguish dengue from scrub typhus, leptospirosis, acute HIV infection, or malaria. The exposure history is what separates them, because it tells you which organisms the patient could have met and when. Where the laboratory is a microscope and a refrigerator that works most days, the history carries even more of the weight.

Take the history in a fixed sequence, because the same order every time is the only reliable way to avoid leaving out the decisive question. Begin with the itinerary rather than the symptoms, since the itinerary is neutral ground and the patient can answer it without feeling accused. Ask the patient to walk you from departure to return, then close the gaps place by place, asking for towns, districts, islands, and villages rather than countries alone. Only then move to behaviors, then food and water, then animals and insects, then blood, needles, and sex, and finally to prevention. Save the intimate questions for the end and ask them in the same matter of fact voice you used for the flight schedule.

Destination is where geographic risk mapping begins, and the map is a clinical instrument. A country name is too blunt, because Brazil contains both a dengue epidemic in a coastal city and a rural Amazon basin where malaria and cutaneous leishmaniasis are ordinary events. Ask for specific places, then place them on the maps you carry, the malaria transmission maps, the distribution of dengue and chikungunya, the belt of schistosomiasis, and the range of Chagas disease. Then ask what the patient did there, because the same district carries different risks for a rice farmer and a conference attendee. The map tells you what is possible and the activity tells you what is probable.

Dates matter more than most clinicians expect, so write them down exactly. Record the day of departure, the day of return, and the day of onset, then calculate the interval between return and onset, because duration shapes the differential. Season determines which vectors were active and which water sources were contaminated, so ask about the rainy or dry season, about flooding, and about sleeping under a roof or outdoors. Altitude belongs here too, because the malaria line sits at roughly 1500 to 2000 meters and above it the risk falls away, while altitude illness becomes a diagnosis in its own right. Ask about headache, breathlessness, or confusion at height.

The return date anchors the whole differential, because every infection has an incubation window and the window tells you what the patient could not have acquired. The short group, measured in days, includes dengue, chikungunya, influenza, cholera, shigellosis, and the rickettsial diseases. The middle group, measured in one to three weeks, includes malaria, typhoid fever, leptospirosis, hepatitis A and E, acute HIV infection, brucellosis, Q fever, and yaws, the busiest window in a returning traveler clinic. The long group, measured in months, includes tuberculosis, leishmaniasis, filariasis, rabies, schistosomiasis, amoebic liver abscess, hepatitis B, Chagas disease, and echinococcosis. A fever that begins eight months after a trip cannot be acute dengue, and a fever that begins three days after a trip is not tuberculosis. Say the interval aloud and let it order the differential before anyone orders a test.

Two refinements of the incubation idea keep you out of trouble. The first is that the relevant interval is often measured from the last possible exposure rather than from the return date, so ask when the patient was last in a rural area, a freshwater lake, a market, or a household with animals. The second is the difference between the incubation period and the time a test becomes positive, because a patient with malaria can have a negative blood film on the first day of fever and a positive one on the third. When the interval does not fit the diagnosis you are considering, do not force it. Reconsider the exposure history and let the timing reopen the question.

Rural or urban is the next fork in the road, and accommodation is its practical form. The mosquito that transmits malaria, Anopheles, bites between dusk and dawn and breeds in rural and periurban water, so unscreened housing near standing water and the absence of an insecticide-treated bed net raise the risk. The mosquito that transmits dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever, Aedes aegypti, bites during the day and breeds in domestic containers, so that risk follows the patient into the center of a city. Ask where the patient slept and whether there was air conditioning, screens, a net, a fan, a thatched roof, or a tent. Ask about running water, a flush toilet, a latrine, or open defecation, because that answer moves the enteric and helminth diseases up or down the list.

Food and water questions should name specific foods and practices, because general questions produce general answers. Ask about tap water, ice, unboiled water, bottled water, and whether the seal was intact, and about salads washed in tap water. Ask about raw or undercooked freshwater fish, which carries the liver flukes Clonorchis and Opisthorchis, raw crab, which carries Paragonimus, and water plants such as watercress, which carry Fasciola. Ask about unpasteurized milk and soft cheese, which carry Brucella, and undercooked pork, which carries the tapeworm Taenia solium, and about raw meat and bushmeat in general. Ask about street food, market food, and food from a wedding or a funeral, because shared meals explain shared illness.

Animal contact is a short set of questions with a long reach. Ask about dogs, cats, monkeys, bats, rodents, cattle, goats, sheep, and wild animals, and ask about the circumstances, a bite, a scratch, a lick on broken skin, a slaughter, a butchering, or a visit to a cave. A dog bite abroad raises rabies and tetanus, unpasteurized milk raises brucellosis, contact with rodents and their urine raises leptospirosis, contact with sheep and goats around a birth raises Q fever, and a cave full of bird or bat droppings raises histoplasmosis. Ask whether the patient cleaned a barn or a chicken coop, and whether they waded in water that animals could have contaminated. Ask about bites the patient dismissed, because a small bite from a bat may not be noticed and still requires attention.

Insect avoidance is where you learn how seriously the patient took the risk, and where you must not moralize. Ask what repellent was used, how often, whether a bed net was used and whether it was treated with insecticide, whether the net had holes, and whether the room was screened or air conditioned. Ask about bites, because a patient who remembers being bitten repeatedly is giving you useful information, while a patient who noticed no bites gives almost nothing, since many vectors bite painlessly or at night. Ask separately about day biting and night biting, which tells you whether to think about Aedes or Anopheles, and ask about the sandfly, the tsetse fly, the triatomine bug, the blackfly, and ticks. Ask whether the patient walked in tall grass, sat on logs, slept on the ground, or kept livestock. Ask whether malaria chemoprophylaxis was taken at all, and whether the decision not to take it was the patient's, a clinician's, or an accident of a late appointment.

Then move to the exposures that travel through blood and skin, and ask them plainly. Ask about new sexual partners during travel or after return, about condom use, and about partners whose infection status is unknown, because HIV and AIDS, syphilis, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C all belong in the differential of a fever after travel. Ask about tattoos, piercings, scarification, traditional circumcision, cupping, and any procedure that broke the skin, and ask where it was done and with what instruments. Ask about injections for any reason, including vitamins, pain relief, and cosmetic treatments, and about dental work, dialysis, surgery, and blood transfusion, because the safety of the blood supply and the sterility of needles vary between countries and between clinics within a country. Ask about needle sharing and drug use without a lecture.

Prevention is the last section of the itinerary and often the most revealing. Ask which vaccines the patient received before travel, how many doses, and when the last dose was given, and ask to see the yellow fever certificate and the vaccination card if the patient carries them. Then ask about malaria chemoprophylaxis by name, because brand names and generic names are remembered differently, and by schedule, because the schedule is where adherence fails. Doxycycline is usually taken as 100 milligrams once daily, mefloquine as 250 milligrams once weekly, and atovaquone with proguanil as one tablet once daily, each with its own rules about when to start, when to stop, and whether to take it with food. Ask whether the patient started before travel, continued after leaving the area, missed days, or stopped early, and whether any tablets remain in the bottle, because the bottle is a more honest witness than memory. Ask what happened when they took it, and treat the answer as clinical data rather than as a confession.

Before you act on any of this, remember how the guidance is made. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control all publish recommendations for chemoprophylaxis and vaccination, and those recommendations are revised as resistance patterns, drug availability, and safety data change. Countries adapt the guidance to their own epidemiology, so national programs differ. Doses and schedules quoted in any course, including this one, describe what guidance said at the time of writing and not what it says today. Check the current guideline, and the current national guideline for the place where you are prescribing, before you write the prescription. The same discipline applies to the treatment decisions that this history will later support.

The single most important category in travel medicine is the traveler who is visiting friends and relatives, and it deserves its own paragraph because it is so often missed. These travelers are usually members of a diaspora returning to a country of origin or to their parents' country, and the chart often records only the words visiting family, which hides everything that matters. They stay longer than tourists, stay in private homes, travel to rural districts, drink the local water, eat the local food, and sleep without nets when the household has none. They frequently travel with children who may never have had a consultation before departure, and those children are the least likely to have received chemoprophylaxis or routine vaccines. They often delay seeking care, because they do not think of themselves as travelers, and they are less likely to have taken chemoprophylaxis at all. They may also have partial immunity that makes malaria present atypically, so when you hear visiting family, raise your suspicion rather than lowering it.

The migrant and refugee history follows a different structure, because it is a history of movement over years rather than of one trip. Ask about the country of origin, the specific region and language, the route of transit and every country crossed, the duration of each stage, the camps, the settlements, and the time since arrival. The stage of migration changes the differential, because the first weeks bring acute infections and untreated conditions from the journey, the first months bring diseases with long incubation periods and the consequences of crowding and poor sanitation, and the years afterward bring latent tuberculosis, chronic hepatitis, schistosomiasis, and Chagas disease. Ask about the conditions of the journey, including detention, camps with shared water and latrines, boats, and crowded apartments. Remember the healthy migrant effect, the tendency for people well enough to travel to look healthier than the population they left, so a normal examination early after arrival proves very little.

There is a difference between what a chart asks and what a person will tell you, and closing that gap is a clinical skill. An intake form asks for country of origin and produces a word, and the word is then treated as though it were a history. A patient may not disclose migration status, may fear consequences for themselves or for family members, may have been instructed not to discuss the journey, or may simply not consider the past relevant to a present fever. Trust is built by explaining why the question is asked, by asking it in privacy, by using a professional interpreter rather than a family member or a child, and by making clear that the answer will be used for care. Ask about the past in the patient's own chronology and let them decide how much detail to give. If a person declines to answer, document the refusal without judgment and make it easy to answer at the next visit.

Adherence questions fail when they sound like an accusation and succeed when they sound like a request for information about a difficult task. Do not ask whether the patient took the tablets as prescribed, but ask which tablets were taken yesterday and which were missed in the last two weeks. Ask what got in the way, and be prepared for the real answers, including cost, a side effect the patient did not want to mention, vomiting, forgetfulness, a broken routine, a belief that the tablets were no longer needed, advice from a relative, or a pregnancy that changed the calculation. Ask whether the patient stopped early because the trip ended, because the tablets ran out, or because someone said the medicine was dangerous, and ask about traditional remedies and antibiotics bought without a prescription. Then say clearly that the answer changes the interpretation of every test you are about to order, because this is not a moral question but a pharmacological one.

Certain exposures are almost never volunteered, and you must ask for them by name. Sexual contacts, needle use, tattoos, piercings, scarification, traditional healing practices that break the skin, injections from unlicensed practitioners, and terminations of pregnancy are all in this category. So are less obvious ones, such as drinking water from a stream, swimming in a lake where schistosomiasis is transmitted, walking barefoot in soil where hookworm is common, handling a dead animal, and nursing a sick relative at home without protection. Patients omit these things because they are ashamed, because they think the detail is trivial, because no one asked before, because the memory is painful, or because they do not know that a freshwater lake is a route of infection. Ask in a way that normalizes the answer, and explain the link to the illness in one sentence, because a patient who understands why you are asking will answer more truthfully.

Prophylaxis has adverse effects, and knowing them serves two purposes, because it explains why adherence failed and it tells you what to watch for in a patient who did take the drug. Mefloquine can cause vivid dreams, anxiety, insomnia, dizziness, and rarely neuropsychiatric symptoms severe enough to stop the drug, and those effects explain many of the quiet discontinuations you will uncover. Doxycycline commonly causes nausea, heartburn, and sensitivity of the skin to sunlight, and it can irritate the esophagus if it is swallowed with too little water or taken while lying down, so the counseling detail matters as much as the dose. Atovaquone with proguanil is generally well tolerated but can cause abdominal discomfort, and it is taken with food so that it is absorbed. Ask what the patient actually experienced rather than what they were warned about, and write the answer in the record. In a patient who took the drug correctly and still became ill, the exposure history rather than the adherence becomes the focus.

Document the exposure history so that the next clinician can use it without repeating the interview. Use a consistent sequence in the note, the dates, the places, the accommodation, the food and water, the animals, the insects, the blood and skin exposures, the sexual history, and the prevention taken. Write the negatives as deliberately as the positives, because the absence of freshwater contact or of a dog bite changes the differential, and a negative that was never recorded will be repeated as an unknown. Record the exact interval between the last exposure and the onset of illness, and note who provided the information, whether the patient, a relative, or a document. Many patients carry vaccination cards, prophylaxis boxes, and laboratory reports in another language, so ask to copy these documents and reconcile them with the account, noting any discrepancy rather than choosing one version. Avoid vague phrases such as unwell after travel, because the next clinician must be able to act on what you write.

The emergency department is where tropical diagnoses are most often missed, and the misses follow a small number of patterns. The first is the failure to ask about travel at all, or the failure to ask in a way that produces the truth, so the patient who says no because they live locally is never asked where they were born or when they last visited family. The second is anchoring, the moment a plausible common diagnosis such as influenza, a urinary infection, or gastroenteritis is accepted and the exposure history is never taken. The third is the single negative malaria test, treated as a final answer when the blood film needs to be repeated over 48 to 72 hours. The fourth is discharge before the laboratory result returns, and the fifth is the absence of triage criteria that would move a febrile returning traveler into a rapid assessment pathway.

There are traps on the other side as well, and they are just as costly. The clinician who has just read about an exotic disease may pursue it while the common local illness goes untreated. The patient who took chemoprophylaxis may be assumed not to have malaria, although prophylaxis reduces risk without abolishing it, and the patient with partial immunity may present with a mild illness that is nevertheless severe malaria. The patient with a fever and a rash may be seated next to others before anyone considers measles, dengue, or a viral hemorrhagic fever, when infection control should have begun at triage. The person whose chart lists a chronic condition may have their fever attributed to that condition when it deserves its own assessment. The antidote is the same in every case, which is to ask the structured questions early, write the answers down, and repeat the assessment when the picture does not fit.

Once the history is on the table, the examination becomes efficient because you know what to look for. Undress the patient enough to see the skin, and look for an eschar, a rash, a burrow, a nodule, a migrating swelling, a wound, or a scar the patient did not mention, and look at the palms, the soles, the scalp, and the genital area, which are the places examinations miss. Examine the eyes for conjunctival suffusion, jaundice, and pallor, feel the neck, the axillae, and the groin for lymph nodes, and palpate the abdomen for the spleen and the liver, which are the two organs that change the differential in a febrile patient. Assess mental status, respiratory rate, hydration, capillary refill, and urine output, because these decide how quickly the patient must be treated regardless of the eventual diagnosis. Examine the nervous system when the history suggests trypanosomiasis, leprosy, or a neurological complication, and examine the joints when it suggests chikungunya or brucellosis. Let the history choose the examination rather than performing the same routine on every patient.

From the history you should be able to build a short chain that runs from exposure to organism to test to treatment. A patient who waded in fresh water where Schistosoma haematobium is transmitted and who now has blood in the urine needs urine filtration, and a patient who swam in a lake where Schistosoma mansoni is transmitted and who now has bloody diarrhea needs stool examination in addition. A patient who walked barefoot in soil where hookworm is common and who now has iron deficiency anemia needs stool examination rather than iron alone, because treating the anemia without treating the worm is only a temporary fix. A patient who handled a sick animal and now has an undulant fever needs blood cultures and serology, and a prolonged combination treatment is the eventual decision. A patient with a painless ulcer and contact with a person who had a similar ulcer should have yaws and syphilis considered together. The chain is what converts an interesting history into a clinical plan.

Adapt the history to the person in front of you, because the same questions carry different weight in different bodies. In pregnancy, ask about the trimester, the antenatal care received, and the timing of travel relative to conception, because malaria in pregnancy, dengue in pregnancy, Zika, and congenital Chagas disease have their own windows and consequences, and because many drugs are avoided or adjusted. In children, ask who traveled with the child, what the child ate and drank, whether the child was breastfed throughout, what vaccinations were given, and whether the child played in soil or water, and remember that a child born abroad may have been exposed to infections the parents never considered. In the immunocompromised patient, ask about the degree and duration of immunosuppression and any planned transplantation or chemotherapy, because the exposure history must be completed before suppression begins. In older adults, ask about medicines and chronic illnesses, because the risk of severe disease and of drug interaction both rise.

The exposure history is not a single event. Take it early, write it down, and return to it as the illness declares itself, because a detail that seemed irrelevant on the first day can become the whole answer on the fourth. Patients remember things between visits, and family members who were not present at the first interview often supply the crucial fact about a lake, a dog, a funeral, or a course of tablets. When the working diagnosis is not fitting, the productive move is usually to repeat the exposure history rather than to order a broader panel of tests. Ask about illness in the household or the travel group, since a shared exposure can explain two cases at once, and document each revision with its date.

The nursing role in all of this is larger than it may appear. In many clinics the nurse takes the history, and in many settings the nurse runs the consultation before travel and the one after return, teaches the patient what to record, administers the vaccines, and explains the tablets. That position carries the responsibility to ask the structured questions well, to make privacy and interpretation possible, to write the record so that it survives the shift change, and to speak the exposure findings to the team in a way that changes the plan. It also carries the responsibility to notice when a patient is deteriorating between rounds, because a history that predicts severe disease helps only if someone is watching closely enough to act. The nurse is often the only person who asks about cost, about a tablet that was stopped, and about the child who was not vaccinated.

There is an unglamorous logistics layer that decides whether any of this works in practice. The vaccination card exists because the record of doses must travel with the patient, and the cold chain fails where power is unreliable, which is why a vaccine given abroad may not have produced protection. The prophylaxis bottle exists because the tablet must be taken on a schedule nobody is watching, which is why the bottle is better evidence than the memory. The clinic record exists because the next clinician needs the itinerary, and the record fails when there is no form to hold the itinerary and no time to fill it in. The interpreter exists because the history is conducted in language, and the consultation fails when the interpreter is a child or a neighbor with their own agenda. Designing these small systems is as much a part of tropical nursing as recognizing an eschar.

Monitoring after the history is taken is where nursing attention converts assessment into safety. If malaria is possible, the blood film must be repeated over 48 to 72 hours while the patient is observed, and the nurse is the person who notices that the second and third samples were never sent. If a patient is started on treatment before the diagnosis is confirmed, the nurse watches for the response, for the rash that suggests a drug reaction, for the diarrhea that follows broad spectrum antibiotics, and for the deterioration that means the working diagnosis is wrong. If a patient is discharged, the nurse ensures that the instructions name the symptom that should bring the patient back, the fever that persists, the bleeding, the drowsiness, the reduced urine output, or the breathlessness. Document the monitoring plan and the threshold for escalation, because a plan that is not written depends on a particular person being on shift.

To summarize, the structured exposure history is the diagnostic instrument of tropical medicine, and everything else supports it. Take it in the same sequence every time, covering destination with enough geographic detail to place the patient on a risk map, exact dates and duration and season and altitude, rural or urban location and type of accommodation, food and water, animal contact, insect avoidance, sexual and blood borne exposures, and the vaccinations and chemoprophylaxis actually taken. Use the interval between the last exposure and the onset of illness to order the differential, and let the incubation window tell you which diagnoses are possible before you test for any of them. Notice the traveler who is visiting friends and relatives, and take the migrant and refugee history as a history of years rather than days, asking in privacy with a professional interpreter. Ask about adherence and about adverse effects without accusation, document the positives and the negatives so that the next clinician can act on them, and include the dose verification discipline that current guidance demands. Watch for the emergency department traps, and remember that the history belongs to the patient and to the public health system at the same time.

# Chapter 6 — The Febrile Returning Traveler

Fever is the most frequent reason a returning traveler seeks medical care, and it is the reason that most often conceals real danger. A traveler comes back from a trip with a temperature, a story, and a set of assumptions, and the clinician has one urgent task before every other: to decide whether this is malaria, and specifically whether it is falciparum malaria, because that is the diagnosis that can kill a healthy adult within a day or 2. The parasite Plasmodium falciparum, the species responsible for the most severe form of malaria, is the organism to exclude first, not because it is always the most likely diagnosis but because it is the most lethal and the most time-sensitive. Nearly every other febrile illness can wait an hour while that question is answered. This chapter walks through the first encounter, the triage decisions, the differential organized by incubation period, the physical findings that shift probability, the actions that belong to the first hour, and the nursing work that holds the process together. It follows the framework set out by the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and it treats every regimen it mentions as a moving target rather than a settled fact.

The word returning does important work in that title, because the returning traveler is not the same patient as the person who became ill in a village with no laboratory and no pharmacy. The returning traveler usually arrives in a setting where blood films, blood cultures, serology, imaging, and intensive care are available, and that changes the calculus in both directions. It means you can afford to wait for a diagnosis in a stable patient, and it means you have no excuse for failing to obtain one. It also means the differential is broader, because a patient who has been in 3 countries in 3 weeks may have carried 3 different exposures home in the same body. The clinician who treats a returning traveler must therefore hold 2 ideas at once: the possibility of a tropical infection that is rare locally, and the possibility of an ordinary infection that is common everywhere. Influenza, urinary infection, pneumonia, and infectious mononucleosis occur in travelers too, and the exotic diagnosis is not automatically the right one.

Triage begins before the patient is fully undressed, and it begins with a decision about how sick this person is right now. You are looking for the patient who cannot wait, the one whose mental status has changed, whose breathing is fast, whose hands are cold, whose skin is mottled, or whose urine output has fallen. The first minute should establish whether the airway is open, whether the patient is breathing comfortably, and whether there is a palpable pulse and adequate circulation. If any of those are in doubt, the patient moves to resuscitation and the history waits. If the patient is stable and talking, you have bought yourself a few minutes to ask where they have been, when they returned, and whether they took any medication to prevent malaria.

Mental status is the single most important bedside observation in a febrile returning traveler because it converts a routine fever into a neurological emergency. A patient who is confused, drowsy, agitated, or difficult to rouse may have cerebral malaria, bacterial meningitis, encephalitis, typhoid encephalopathy, a metabolic derangement such as hypoglycemia, or sepsis with poor cerebral perfusion. Ask the patient's companion whether this is different from the patient's normal self, because a quiet person may look quiet rather than confused. Document a formal level of consciousness rather than the word alert, so the next clinician can compare. A change in mental status in the context of fever from the tropics is a red flag until proven otherwise.

The respiratory rate is the vital sign that is most often recorded inaccurately and most often ignored, and in this population it is a powerful signal. A rate above the expected range for the patient's age suggests pneumonia, pulmonary edema, severe anemia, acidosis, or the beginning of acute respiratory distress. Count it for a full 60 seconds with the patient at rest and without announcing what you are doing, because breathing changes when it is watched. A rising respiratory rate in a patient who looked stable an hour ago is often the first sign of deterioration, and it frequently appears before the blood pressure falls. Treat a rising rate as an urgent finding, not as anxiety.

Capillary refill, skin temperature, and the character of the pulse tell you about perfusion in a way that a single blood pressure reading cannot. Press the fingertip or the sternum for 5 seconds and count until color returns, remembering that the finding is unreliable in a cold room and in the elderly. Cold peripheries with a normal blood pressure suggest compensated shock, and compensated shock can decompensate quickly in a patient with severe malaria or dengue. Mottling of the knees, a thready radial pulse, and a narrow pulse pressure all belong to the same story. When you find them, you have found a patient who needs intravenous access and fluid now.

The skin and the urine output complete the picture, and both are easy to overlook in a busy triage area. Look at the whole skin surface, including the palms, soles, trunk, and any area the patient cannot easily see, and ask whether the rash is new. Look for petechiae, purpura, bruising, bleeding gums, epistaxis, blood in the stool, and any puncture or bite mark. Urine output is the most honest measure of end-organ perfusion available at the bedside, so ask when the patient last passed urine, how much, and what color, and catheterize or measure if the patient is unwell. A patient who has not passed urine for 12 hours is a patient in trouble, whatever the blood pressure says.

The red flags that demand immediate action can be spoken as a short litany, and every nurse who works with returning travelers should be able to recite it. Impaired consciousness, a seizure, a respiratory rate above the expected range, oxygen saturation below the expected range, systolic blood pressure below the expected range, capillary refill greater than 3 seconds, cold and mottled skin, urine output below the expected volume, any bleeding, jaundice with abdominal pain, severe anemia, and a blood glucose below the expected range all require action within minutes. Add to that list a patient who looks worse than the numbers suggest, because experienced clinicians recognize severe illness before the monitor does. Any one of these findings should trigger a call to the responsible clinician and a move to a monitored area. None of them should wait for the laboratory result that will explain them.

When a red flag is present, the response is a sequence rather than a single act. Establish intravenous access, draw blood for the tests that will matter, measure the glucose immediately, and begin fluid resuscitation if the circulation is compromised. Give oxygen if the saturation is low, position the patient to protect the airway if consciousness is impaired, and treat a seizure with the locally approved anticonvulsant. Start empirical treatment for the most dangerous plausible diagnosis rather than waiting for confirmation, because in severe malaria and in bacterial sepsis the delay itself harms the patient. The nurse who begins this sequence is not exceeding the scope of practice; the nurse who begins it is the reason the patient survives.

The differential diagnosis of fever in a returning traveler is most usefully organized by incubation period, because the interval between exposure and illness eliminates whole categories of disease. Ask when the patient was away and when the fever began, and count the days carefully, because a fever that started 4 days after return has a different differential from one that started 6 months after return. The exposure history from the previous chapter supplies the other half of the equation, since the place, the season, the insects, the water, the food, and the sexual contacts all modify probability. Incubation period and exposure together narrow the field far more than either does alone. Write the interval down, because memory drifts and the arithmetic matters.

Illnesses with an incubation of days, roughly up to 10 days, include dengue, chikungunya, influenza, and a group of acute viral and bacterial infections that arrive fast. Dengue is the classic example, with fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, and sometimes a rash, and it is important to remember that the fever of dengue typically breaks just as the dangerous phase begins. Chikungunya produces fever with disabling joint pain, often in the small joints of the hands and feet, and it rarely causes the plasma leakage of dengue. Influenza is common in travelers and easy to forget, and it can be severe in the elderly, in pregnancy, and in those with chronic disease. A fever that begins within 2 days of return, before any tropical incubation could have elapsed, is usually not a tropical disease at all.

The same short window contains enteric fever, meaning typhoid and paratyphoid fever, which usually appears 7 to 14 days after exposure but can appear as early as 3 days. Rickettsial disease, including scrub typhus and the spotted fever group, commonly appears 6 to 20 days after a bite, so it straddles the boundary between the day group and the week group. Measles and meningococcal disease belong in this window as well, and both are public health events that require notification and infection control measures. Zika virus usually produces a mild illness with rash, conjunctivitis, and joint pain, and its importance lies in congenital infection rather than in the acute fever itself. When the interval is short, think in terms of these fast-moving infections and do not anchor on the most exotic name in the travel history.

A fever with an incubation of days also raises the possibility of a viral hemorrhagic fever, and although these diseases are rare, the consequences of missing one are severe. Lassa fever, Ebola disease, Marburg disease, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever can all present initially as an undifferentiated fever, and the early symptoms overlap with malaria and with typhoid. The clues that should raise suspicion include a history of travel to an area where such transmission occurs, contact with a person who had a similar illness, work in a health facility or with animals, and the appearance of bleeding, a rash, or unexplained deterioration. If suspicion is real, do not wait for the diagnosis to act on infection control, because the safety of the staff and of the other patients depends on early precautions. Notify the responsible public health authority at the moment of suspicion, not after confirmation.

Illnesses with an incubation of weeks include malaria, which remains the diagnosis to exclude first for reasons of both frequency and lethality. Falciparum malaria usually appears 7 to 30 days after infection, but it can appear within a week or be delayed for months, especially in a patient who took incomplete or ineffective prevention. Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale can present many months after exposure because they leave dormant liver forms that reactivate, and this late presentation is a common reason for a missed diagnosis. Plasmodium malariae can cause fever years after exposure, and Plasmodium knowlesi, found in Southeast Asia, can progress rapidly. Any fever in a patient with a compatible travel history is malaria until the films say otherwise.

The week group also contains leptospirosis, hepatitis, and acute HIV infection, each of which has a characteristic pattern that helps. Leptospirosis appears 5 to 14 days after contact with water or soil contaminated by rodent urine, and it produces fever, severe headache, muscle pain in the calves, and red eyes from conjunctival suffusion. Hepatitis A and hepatitis E appear 2 to 6 weeks after exposure and produce fever, nausea, malaise, dark urine, and jaundice, with the fever often fading as the jaundice deepens. Acute HIV infection appears 2 to 4 weeks after exposure with fever, sore throat, rash, lymphadenopathy, and a flu-like illness that is dismissed as a flu. None of these three is rare in a returning traveler, and each has a specific test that should be sent when the story fits.

Brucellosis and the rickettsial infections complete the week group, and both reward a careful exposure history. Brucellosis follows the consumption of unpasteurized milk or cheese or contact with livestock, appears 1 to 4 weeks later, and produces fever that is often drenching and nocturnal, with sweats, weakness, and joint pain. The rickettsial diseases follow a bite from a tick, a mite, or a flea, and they produce fever with headache, muscle pain, and often a rash or an eschar. Acute schistosomiasis, also called Katayama syndrome, appears 2 to 8 weeks after freshwater contact with fever, cough, abdominal pain, and eosinophilia. These are diagnoses that depend on the clinician asking the right question, because the patient will not volunteer the answer.

Illnesses with an incubation of months form the last group, and they behave differently because they are usually chronic rather than acute. Tuberculosis appears weeks to years after exposure, and it should be considered in any traveler with fever, night sweats, weight loss, and cough, especially if they have lived or worked in a high-burden setting or have HIV. Visceral leishmaniasis produces months of fever, splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and wasting, and it is often mistaken for a hematological malignancy. Lymphatic filariasis and other filarial infections can produce fever with lymphangitis and swelling, though fever is less prominent than the swelling itself. Amebic liver abscess appears weeks to months after exposure with fever and right upper quadrant pain, and it is frequently misdiagnosed as a bacterial abscess or a malignancy.
