The chronic group also includes schistosomiasis, which may produce intermittent fever with abdominal or urinary symptoms months after freshwater exposure, and subacute infective endocarditis, which is not tropical at all but is easily missed in a patient with fever and a heart murmur. Chronic brucellosis, chronic Q fever, and tuberculosis of the abdomen or the spine all belong to the same long list. A fever that has lasted more than 2 weeks without an explanation deserves a systematic second evaluation, with repeated cultures, imaging, and a deliberate return to the exposure history. The most common error in this group is to stop after the first negative test. The second most common error is to give a course of antibiotics that blunts the fever without producing a diagnosis.

Physical findings shift probability in ways that are worth learning by heart, because they can be found in a 5 minute examination and can change the entire plan. An eschar, which is a black crusted lesion at the site of a bite, is one of the most useful findings in tropical medicine. It is characteristic of scrub typhus, of African tick bite fever, and of several other rickettsial infections, and it is often hidden in the axilla, the groin, the belt line, or under the breast. Search for it deliberately, because a patient with fever, headache, and an eschar should receive doxycycline immediately rather than after the serology returns. The presence of an eschar converts a broad differential into a narrow one.

Conjunctival suffusion, which is redness of the eyes without discharge, is a signature finding of leptospirosis and is also seen in some viral illnesses. It differs from the watery discharge of a common cold and from the crusting of bacterial conjunctivitis, and it is often accompanied by severe muscle pain in the calves and by a headache that does not respond to ordinary analgesia. A patient with fever, red eyes, calf pain, and a history of freshwater contact or rodent exposure should be treated for leptospirosis while the test is pending. The finding is subtle and it is missed when the eyes are not examined in daylight. Ask the patient to look up and down while you retract the lids, and record what you see.

Splenomegaly is found by palpation and percussion, and it is a clue to a specific set of diseases. An enlarged spleen in a febrile traveler suggests malaria, enteric fever, visceral leishmaniasis, brucellosis, infective endocarditis, leptospirosis, or a hematological condition. Palpate from the right lower quadrant toward the left costal margin, and use percussion to confirm what your hand cannot feel, because a soft spleen in a muscular patient is easily missed. Remember that a tender enlarged spleen can rupture, so avoid vigorous deep palpation in a patient with suspected enteric fever or infectious mononucleosis. Document the finding in terms of how many centimeters below the costal margin, so that others can track it.

Relative bradycardia, sometimes called the Faget sign, means a pulse rate that is slower than expected for the degree of fever, and it is a classic clue in enteric fever, brucellosis, leptospirosis, yellow fever, and some rickettsial infections. It is a pattern rather than a diagnosis, and it should prompt you to consider those illnesses rather than to exclude them. The finding is easiest to appreciate when you record the temperature and the pulse together and compare them with the expected relationship. Do not let a normal pulse reassure you in a patient with a high fever and a compatible history. The bedside observation of a slow pulse with a high fever is worth more than many laboratory results.

Jaundice in a febrile returning traveler has a short but important differential that includes hepatitis A and hepatitis E, leptospirosis, severe malaria, yellow fever, and biliary sepsis. Jaundice with anemia and hemoglobinuria suggests severe falciparum malaria, and jaundice with renal failure and hemorrhage suggests leptospirosis in its severe form. Jaundice with a tender enlarged liver and a high fever suggests ascending cholangitis, which is a surgical emergency rather than a tropical one. Jaundice with a slow pulse and bleeding in a patient returning from an area where yellow fever occurs is a diagnosis that must be notified. In every case, jaundice in a febrile patient is a marker of severity and a reason to move the patient to a monitored setting.

Lymphadenopathy is a finding that should be described precisely, because its location and character carry meaning. Tender enlarged nodes in the neck and the axillae occur in acute HIV infection, in dengue, in chikungunya, and in many viral illnesses. Firm matted nodes, especially in the neck with a discharging sinus, occur in tuberculosis, and the nodes may need aspiration rather than excision. Generalized lymphadenopathy with fever and weight loss is a reason to consider HIV, tuberculosis, and lymphoma. A single inflamed node with a bite history in a patient returning from an area where plague or tularemia occurs is an urgent finding that requires prompt treatment. Always ask how long the nodes have been present and whether they are painful.

The rash deserves its own systematic approach, because the timing, the distribution, and the character together narrow the differential more than any single feature. A blanching maculopapular rash on the trunk suggests typhoid, dengue, or a viral exanthem, while petechiae and purpura suggest a bleeding disorder, meningococcal disease, or severe dengue. A rash that starts on the face and spreads downward suggests measles, and a rash with a slapped cheek appearance suggests parvovirus. An eschar with a surrounding rash suggests a rickettsial infection, and a rash on the palms and soles suggests secondary syphilis or a rickettsial disease. Ask whether the rash appeared before or after the fever, because that sequence matters. Photograph or describe the rash in the record so that the next examiner can compare.

What must happen in the first hour is a list of actions rather than a single decision, and it should be rehearsed until it is automatic. Measure the vital signs including the temperature, the respiratory rate, the blood pressure, the oxygen saturation, and the level of consciousness. Measure the blood glucose, because hypoglycemia is common in severe malaria, in sepsis, and in children, and because it is immediately reversible. Obtain intravenous access and draw blood cultures from 2 separate sites before antibiotics are given. Send a thick and thin blood film for malaria, a complete blood count, a renal profile, liver enzymes, a coagulation screen, and lactate, and if the patient could be pregnant, send a pregnancy test. Give fluid and antibiotics as indicated by the clinical picture rather than waiting for results.

The malaria film is the single most important early test, and it should be ordered and repeated in a way that accounts for its limitations. A single negative film does not exclude malaria, because parasite density fluctuates and may be below the detection threshold early in the illness. Repeat the film every 12 to 24 hours for at least 3 sets, and in a patient who has taken prophylaxis or partial treatment, expect the density to be low and tell the laboratory to look carefully. Ask for a thick film for detection and a thin film for species identification and parasite density, because the density guides management. If the first films are negative and the patient is severely ill with a compatible history, treat for severe malaria anyway while continuing to investigate.

Rapid diagnostic tests for malaria detect parasite antigens and provide a result within minutes, but the nurse must understand what they cannot do. The most common test detects a protein produced by Plasmodium falciparum, and it can give a false negative when the parasite does not produce that protein, a situation seen in some regions. The test also remains positive for weeks after successful treatment, so a positive result in a patient who was treated recently does not prove current infection. Use the rapid test to speed up the decision in an emergency, but always send microscopy as well. A negative rapid test in a seriously ill patient with a compatible exposure must not close the question.

Empirical treatment before the diagnosis is certain is sometimes the right choice, and the decision rests on the severity of the illness and the danger of the disease being treated. In a patient with fever and an eschar, or with a compatible exposure and a severe headache, give doxycycline immediately because rickettsial disease responds quickly and delays are costly. In a patient with impaired consciousness and a travel history that includes an area where malaria occurs, treat as severe malaria without waiting for the film. In a patient with suspected bacterial meningitis, begin antibiotics before the lumbar puncture if the patient is unstable or if imaging must come first. The principle is to treat the disease that will kill the patient fastest, then to refine the diagnosis as the results arrive.

Severe malaria is treated with intravenous artesunate, and the current guidance is a dose of 2.4 milligrams per kilogram given intravenously at the start of treatment and again 12 hours and 24 hours later, then once every 24 hours until the patient can take oral treatment. Children receive the same weight-based dose, and the dose should be calculated on the actual weight rather than estimated. If artesunate is unavailable, alternative parenteral treatments include artemether given intramuscularly and quinine given intravenously, but these are less preferred. Rectal artesunate can be given as a pre-referral treatment when a patient with severe malaria cannot reach definitive care quickly. In every case, the nurse should verify the weight, the dose, and the route against the current guideline before the drug is given.

Rickettsial disease is treated with doxycycline, and the usual adult dose is 100 milligrams given by mouth or intravenously every 12 hours. Children are treated with 2.2 milligrams per kilogram by mouth or intravenously every 12 hours, and current guidance favors treating children rather than withholding the drug, because the risk of the infection exceeds the risk of the short course. Pregnant patients are a more difficult group, and the decision should follow the local guideline and the severity of the illness. Treatment is usually continued for 5 to 7 days and until the patient has been afebrile for at least 48 hours. The clinical response is often rapid, and a patient who improves within 48 hours of the first dose probably has the diagnosis right.

Enteric fever and suspected bacterial meningitis are treated with a third-generation cephalosporin, most often ceftriaxone, and the dose depends on the syndrome rather than on the fever alone. For enteric fever, the usual adult dose is 1 to 2 grams given intravenously every 24 hours, and for meningitis it is 2 grams given intravenously every 12 hours, with dose adjustment for children by weight. Antibiotic resistance has removed fluoroquinolones from use in many parts of the world, so the choice must follow the local resistance pattern and the travel destination. Blood cultures should be drawn before the first dose whenever this can be done without delaying treatment. Do not treat a fever with an antibiotic simply because the patient is anxious, because an unnecessary course obscures the diagnosis and drives resistance.

Every regimen in this chapter is a snapshot of guidance that changes, and the listener must hear that clearly. Doses and regimens are revised as resistance emerges, as new drugs are licensed, and as trials report new results, and guidance differs between countries and between agencies. Before prescribing or administering any drug named here, check the current guideline from the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and check the local formulary as well. Confirm the dose against the patient's weight, renal function, pregnancy status, and allergies rather than relying on memory or on this text. When 2 clinicians disagree about a dose, the correct response is to open the guideline, not to split the difference.

Adverse effects deserve anticipation rather than reaction, because the drugs used here are powerful and the patients are often unstable. Intravenous artesunate can cause delayed hemolysis, with falling hemoglobin and rising bilirubin appearing 1 to 3 weeks after treatment, so arrange a blood count at 1 week and again at 2 and 4 weeks. Quinine can cause hypoglycemia and can prolong the interval between the Q and T waves on the electrocardiogram, so monitor the glucose closely and watch the cardiac rhythm. Doxycycline causes nausea, heartburn, and photosensitivity, and it should be taken with a full glass of water while sitting upright to prevent irritation of the esophagus. Ceftriaxone can cause rash, diarrhea, and biliary sludge, and any new rash during an infusion should be treated as a possible hypersensitivity reaction until proven otherwise.

Monitoring in the hours after admission is where most of the preventable harm is avoided, and it is nursing work from beginning to end. Record the vital signs at a frequency that matches the severity of the illness, which may mean every 15 minutes in a patient with severe malaria and every 4 hours in a stable patient with a mild febrile illness. Measure the blood glucose every 4 to 6 hours in any patient with severe malaria, impaired consciousness, or poor oral intake, and more often if the patient is receiving quinine. Record the fluid balance hourly in a patient receiving intravenous fluids, and record the urine output as a volume rather than as a word. Track the temperature trend, because a fever that is not responding to treatment is information, and a fever that has resolved followed by a return is also information.

Neurological monitoring belongs in every serious febrile illness, because the brain is the organ that tells you the treatment is failing. Check the level of consciousness at every set of observations, and check the pupils, the limb strength, and the ability to speak clearly. Watch for a seizure, for a new focal deficit, for abnormal posturing, and for a headache that is worsening despite analgesia. In a patient with cerebral malaria, the return of consciousness usually follows the fall in parasite density, and its absence after 48 hours should prompt a search for another cause. Document each neurological observation so that a subtle decline becomes visible across shifts. The nurse who notices that the patient answered questions yesterday and does not today has made a diagnosis before the laboratory has.

The nurse's role between rounds is not a passive one, and it is often the difference between a good outcome and a catastrophe. Deterioration rarely announces itself as a single dramatic event; it announces itself as a rising respiratory rate, a fall in urine output, a change in the character of the pulse, a new confusion, or a cooler periphery. Because the nurse is the person who is actually present, the nurse is the person most likely to see these changes first. Escalate on the basis of a trend rather than waiting for a threshold, because thresholds are crossed only at the end of a process. A brief, structured handover that names the trend and the concern is more useful than a complete recitation of numbers.

Pregnancy changes both the differential and the management, and it requires a lower threshold for admission and for investigation. Malaria in pregnancy is more severe, more likely to cause hypoglycemia and pulmonary edema, and more likely to cause fetal loss, premature delivery, and low birth weight. Current guidance supports the use of intravenous artesunate in all trimesters for severe malaria, and oral artemisinin-based combination therapy for uncomplicated disease, with the specific choice made in consultation with the current guideline. Doxycycline and tetracyclines are generally avoided in pregnancy, so an alternative must be chosen when a rickettsial infection is suspected, and the decision should involve a clinician experienced in the field. Document the pregnancy test result before giving any drug, because the result changes which drug is safe.

Children deteriorate faster than adults and compensate longer before they decompensate, so the thresholds for concern are different. A child with fever from the tropics should be weighed accurately, because both fluid and drug doses depend on the weight and estimated weights are often wrong. Hypoglycemia is common in children with severe malaria, seizures are common, and severe anemia develops quickly. Dehydration and shock present differently in children, and the signs include a prolonged capillary refill, cool peripheries, a weak fast pulse, and reduced skin turgor. Monitor the glucose, the level of consciousness, and the urine output closely, and involve the caregiver in watching the child between observations. A child who is playing again after fluids is telling you the resuscitation worked.

Immunocompromised patients and those without a spleen need a broader differential and a lower threshold for empirical treatment. A patient with advanced HIV may present with tuberculosis, with a fungal infection, with a bacterial sepsis, or with one of the opportunistic infections, and the fever may be blunted by the underlying immune state. A patient who has had a splenectomy or who has sickle cell disease is at high risk from encapsulated organisms and from malaria, and a fever in such a patient is an emergency by itself. Patients taking corticosteroids, chemotherapy, or biologic drugs may be febrile from an infection that would otherwise be mild, including strongyloidiasis with hyperinfection. Ask about immunosuppressive drugs and about the spleen, because neither question appears on a standard travel form.

Migrants and travelers who are visiting friends and relatives deserve specific attention, because they often fall through the gaps in both prevention and care. They may travel for months, they may stay in rural areas rather than in hotels, they may not seek pre-travel advice, and they may delay care after return because they assume they have immunity or because they fear the cost. They may have partial immunity to malaria, which means they can carry parasites with few symptoms while remaining capable of transmitting the infection to mosquitoes in the destination country. They may also be reluctant to disclose the full travel history, so the history must be taken with respect, without judgment, and with an explanation of why it matters. A fever in this group deserves the same urgency as a fever in a tourist, and sometimes more.

Logistics decide whether good clinical thinking becomes good care, and the nurse manages most of the logistics. Find out when the laboratory can process a blood film, whether the thick film is read on site, and how long the result takes, because the answer shapes the timing of treatment. Arrange transport for specimens that must travel, protect them from heat and delay, and label them with the time of collection. Keep the cold chain intact for tests that require it, and do not leave a specimen on a bench while waiting for a form to be completed. Confirm that the laboratory has received the specimen and that a result is expected, because a specimen that is never processed is worse than no specimen at all.

Infection control and notification are part of the first hour when a dangerous transmissible infection is possible. If a viral hemorrhagic fever is suspected, place the patient in a single room, use the personal protective equipment that the local protocol requires, restrict visitors and staff, and use dedicated equipment where it exists. Notify the responsible public health authority immediately, because the notification pathway is what brings the reference laboratory and the specialist advice. Handle sharps and waste according to the protocol, and clean spills with the approved disinfectant. Document the precautions that were used and the time they began, because the record protects both the patient and the staff. Never wait for a laboratory confirmation before beginning these measures.

Communication with the patient and the family is clinical work, not an afterthought, and it determines whether the patient returns for follow-up. Explain in plain language why the malaria films are being repeated, why a negative result does not end the investigation, and why admission is sometimes advised even when the patient feels able to go home. Give written and spoken instructions about the warning signs that should bring the patient back immediately, including confusion, bleeding, difficulty breathing, inability to drink, and a fall in urine output. Provide the follow-up appointment and the contact number before discharge, and confirm that the patient has understood. Where language is a barrier, use an interpreter rather than a family member for the clinical conversation.

Discharge advice must also address the unfinished business of the returning traveler, because the diagnosis may not be complete at the moment of discharge. A patient discharged with an undiagnosed fever needs a clear plan for repeat testing, a named person to contact, and an appointment within a defined interval. A patient treated for malaria needs a blood count after treatment to detect delayed hemolysis, and a patient treated for enteric fever needs to know that relapse can occur. A patient with a chronic exposure risk needs the next travel consultation arranged before the next trip rather than after it. Record the plan in the discharge summary in terms that the next clinician can act on, and make sure the patient has a copy.

Referral thresholds should be agreed before the shift becomes busy, because decisions made in advance are clearer than decisions made in a crisis. A patient who needs a level of care that your facility cannot provide should be transferred early, and the transfer should be arranged while the patient is still stable enough to travel. Discuss the case with the receiving clinician by telephone, and send a written summary with the patient that includes the exposure history, the vital sign trends, the treatment given, and the tests pending. Never send a patient with unexplained confusion, shock, or a bleeding tendency without a clinician accompanying the transfer or an agreed monitoring plan. The most dangerous moment in the care of a severely ill traveler is the gap between 2 facilities.

Quality improvement belongs in this chapter because the same errors recur in every setting. The most common failures are a single negative malaria film that is treated as final, a rickettsial infection that is missed because the skin was never fully examined, an enteric fever that is diagnosed too late because no blood culture was drawn, and a deteriorating patient whose trend was not escalated. Review the cases in which the diagnosis was delayed, and ask whether the delay came from knowledge, from process, or from staffing. Feed the answer back into the triage protocol, the admission checklist, and the handover format. A unit that reviews its own delays is a unit that will recognize the next dangerous traveler faster.

To summarize, fever in a returning traveler is a time-sensitive problem in which malaria, and especially falciparum malaria, must be excluded first because it is the diagnosis most likely to kill quickly. Triage begins with mental status, respiratory rate, capillary refill, skin, bleeding, and urine output, and the red flags among those findings demand immediate action rather than observation. Organize the differential by incubation period, with dengue, chikungunya, typhoid, and rickettsial disease in the first days, malaria, leptospirosis, hepatitis, acute HIV infection, and brucellosis in the following weeks, and tuberculosis, leishmaniasis, filariasis, amebic liver abscess, and schistosomiasis in the following months. Let the physical findings, including the eschar, conjunctival suffusion, splenomegaly, relative bradycardia, jaundice, and lymphadenopathy, refine that probability. In the first hour, measure the vital signs and the glucose, obtain cultures before antibiotics, send and repeat the malaria films, and treat the most dangerous diagnosis when the evidence supports it. Verify every dose against the current guideline from the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control before you give it, because regimens change and guidance differs between countries. Anticipate the adverse effects of the drugs you administer, monitor the trends rather than the thresholds, and remember that the nurse who watches the patient between rounds is frequently the first person to know that the illness is turning. Carry the logistics, the infection control, the notification, the communication, and the follow-up with the same care you give the clinical assessment, because in this disease the details are the treatment.

# Chapter 7 — The Syndromic Approach to Tropical Fever

A syndrome is a cluster of findings that occur together often enough to be useful before a diagnosis is known, and in tropical medicine it is the only honest starting point when the laboratory is a day away. You take the presenting pattern, name the small group of organisms that produce it, and arrange that group by what will kill the patient first. Fever itself is a regulated elevation of the body's thermal set point, driven by cytokines released when the immune system recognizes a pathogen, and the shape of the curve is far less reliable than most teaching suggests. Sustained fever, intermittent fever and the stepwise ascent all occur with the same organism, so what matters more than the curve are the associated findings: the rash, the yellow eyes, the altered consciousness, the falling blood pressure, the falling urine output.

Four syndromes carry most of the weight in a febrile patient: fever with rash, fever with jaundice, fever with neurological signs, and fever with an abnormal blood count, of which eosinophilia most often changes the plan. Diarrhea, skin lesions, enlarged lymph nodes and an enlarged spleen are modifiers that narrow the list inside one of the four. A patient may present inside two syndromes at once, and the overlap is itself diagnostic information rather than a problem to be resolved first. The aim is not to name a disease from the doorway but to decide the next hour, the next day, and what finding would make you change your mind.

A rash in a febrile patient usually arises by one of three mechanisms, each with its own appearance and tempo. Direct viral injury to skin cells produces a widespread eruption that follows the viremia, while immune complexes deposited in small dermal vessels produce a maculopapular rash that may later become petechial. Injury to the vessel wall produces lesions that do not fade when pressed, and that bedside test separates the dangerous from the ordinary. The timing of the rash against the fever is your best discriminator, because a rash with or before the fever suggests dengue, chikungunya or measles, while a rash after several days suggests rickettsial disease, typhoid fever or meningococcal infection. Examine the whole skin in good light, including the scalp, palms, soles, mouth and perineum, because distribution is often the diagnosis.

Dengue is the first consideration in a returning traveler with fever and rash, and it is caused by four related viruses transmitted by day-biting mosquitoes of the genus Aedes. The illness begins abruptly with high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, and a rash that may flush early and become maculopapular later. The dangerous transition usually occurs as the fever settles, between the third and the seventh day, when plasma leaks from the smallest vessels into the tissues. Warning signs include abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose, lethargy, restlessness and fluid accumulation in the chest or abdomen. A rising hematocrit with a falling platelet count during this window signals that the patient has entered the critical phase.

Current guidance from the World Health Organization recommends crystalloid solutions, given by mouth when the patient can drink and intravenously when they cannot, with the rate adjusted to urine output, hematocrit and clinical signs rather than fixed in advance. Aspirin and the nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided because they increase bleeding risk. Acetaminophen is used for fever, commonly 10 to 15 milligrams per kilogram every six hours in a child and 500 to 1000 milligrams every six hours in an adult, never exceeding the daily maximum in the current guideline. Verify every dose against the patient's weight and the current national guideline before it is given, and record the urine output hourly during the critical phase.

Chikungunya is carried by the same mosquitoes and begins in a similar way, but its signature is joint pain so severe that patients often cannot walk or grip. The fever is usually shorter than in dengue, and the rash is more often itchy. Most people recover, yet a substantial minority continue to have joint pain for months, and the nurse's role in that phase is realistic counseling, pain relief and referral for rehabilitation rather than repeated courses of antibiotics. Neonates and older adults are at higher risk of severe disease, and infection around the time of birth can produce serious neonatal illness.

Measles remains a major cause of fever with rash in unvaccinated populations, and its pattern is one of the most reliable in medicine. After an incubation of roughly 10 to 14 days comes a prodrome of high fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes, often with small white spots on the inside of the cheek called Koplik spots. The rash then begins behind the ears and along the hairline and spreads downward over the face, trunk and limbs, fading in the same order. Pneumonia, diarrhea, ear infection and encephalitis are the complications that kill, and malnutrition magnifies every one of them. Current guidance from the World Health Organization supports vitamin A, given as 200,000 international units on two consecutive days for a child older than one year, with the schedule confirmed against the current guideline because the dose differs by age.

Rickettsial disease belongs on the list for any febrile patient with a rash and a history of insect or mite exposure, and its mechanism explains its danger. These organisms multiply in the cells lining small blood vessels, producing a vasculitis that leaks fluid, consumes platelets and can injure brain, lungs and kidneys. The rash may be maculopapular, may become petechial, and may involve the palms and soles, and an eschar at the bite site strongly suggests scrub typhus or a tick-borne spotted fever. Because serology returns too late to guide the first decision, current guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention supports beginning doxycycline, commonly 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day in an adult, on suspicion rather than waiting for confirmation.

Typhoid fever, caused by the bacterium Salmonella Typhi, produces a stepwise fever that climbs over the first week, a relatively slow pulse for the height of the fever, and a faint rash of rose-colored spots on the trunk that is easily missed in dark skin or poor light. Constipation often precedes diarrhea, and the patient may look deceptively well before deteriorating suddenly. The intestinal lymphoid tissue can ulcerate and perforate, which is the complication that kills, and the diagnosis rests on blood culture taken before antibiotics. Resistance has removed fluoroquinolones from most of the world, and current guidance favors ceftriaxone or azithromycin, with the exact dose and duration confirmed against the national guideline before prescribing.

The organism invades the bloodstream, releases endotoxin and damages the vessel wall, so the rash begins as tiny petechiae and can progress to large purpuric areas with skin necrosis, a picture called purpura fulminans. The patient may have fever, headache, neck stiffness, vomiting and drowsiness, or may present with shock and a rash alone. Immediate treatment is ceftriaxone, commonly 1 gram intravenously every 12 hours in an adult and 100 milligrams per kilogram per day in a child, together with fluid resuscitation and urgent referral. Close contacts need prophylaxis, usually rifampicin or a single dose of ciprofloxacin according to local guidance, and the case must be notified to public health authorities.

Jaundice is yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes caused by bilirubin accumulation, and it helps to sort the mechanism before sorting the diseases. Prehepatic jaundice comes from excessive breakdown of red cells, hepatic jaundice from injured liver cells that cannot process or excrete bilirubin, and posthepatic jaundice from obstruction of the bile ducts. In obstruction the urine is dark, the stool is pale and the patient often itches, while in liver injury the liver may be tender and the enzymes are raised. Naming the mechanism tells you what to look for next, and in a limited setting a urine dipstick and a careful history can separate red cell destruction from obstruction before any laboratory result arrives. Where malaria is endemic, a rapid diagnostic test or a blood film takes priority, because treatable severe malaria is common and fast.

Hepatitis A and hepatitis E spread by the fecal-oral route, usually through contaminated water or food, and they produce an acute illness with fever, nausea, poor appetite, abdominal discomfort and then jaundice. Hepatitis A is usually self-limiting in children, who may have no symptoms at all, while adults tend to be sicker. Hepatitis E is particularly dangerous in pregnancy, where it can cause fulminant hepatic failure and high mortality in the third trimester. Treatment is supportive, with attention to hydration, nutrition and drugs that burden the liver, and the nurse also teaches household hygiene and traces a common water source when several cases appear together.

Leptospirosis is caused by spirochetes of the genus Leptospira, shed in the urine of rodents and other animals and entering the body through cuts, mucous membranes or waterlogged skin. The illness begins with fever, headache and muscle pain, but two signs matter: conjunctival suffusion, a reddening of the whites of the eyes without discharge, and severe calf tenderness. In its severe form, called Weil's disease, jaundice appears with kidney failure and bleeding, and the jaundice has a distinctive orange tint. Current guidance supports treatment with doxycycline or a penicillin, and the dose and route must be checked against the current guideline.

Severe malaria from Plasmodium falciparum is a leading cause of fever with jaundice in endemic areas, and it arises when a heavy parasite load destroys red cells, obstructs small vessels and consumes glucose. The patient may be jaundiced from red cell destruction and liver injury, and the urine may turn dark from hemoglobin, a picture historically called blackwater fever. Hypoglycemia is common, especially in children and in pregnancy, and it can mimic worsening cerebral malaria, so glucose belongs at the bedside within minutes of arrival. Current guidance from the World Health Organization treats severe malaria with intravenous artesunate, commonly 2.4 milligrams per kilogram at the start and again 12 hours and 24 hours later, then once a day, and pre-referral rectal artesunate is recommended for young children who cannot reach a treatment center quickly.

Yellow fever is a viral hemorrhagic illness carried by mosquitoes in parts of Africa and South America, and it produces a biphasic illness in which an initial febrile phase may be followed by a brief remission and then a severe phase with jaundice, bleeding, kidney failure and shock. The diagnosis is confirmed by laboratory testing, and there is no specific antiviral treatment, so care is supportive and rapid referral matters more than any drug. Ascending cholangitis, an infection of an obstructed biliary tree, can present in a similar way, with fever, jaundice and right upper abdominal pain, sometimes with confusion and low blood pressure. The obstruction is usually a stone or, in some regions, a parasite or a tumor pressing on the duct, and the laboratory shows a cholestatic pattern with a raised white cell count. Antibiotics are given promptly, but the definitive treatment is drainage of the obstruction, by endoscopy or surgery, and antibiotics alone will not cure an obstructed duct.

Fever with neurological signs most often requires immediate action, and the first steps are always the same: secure the airway, check the glucose, and look for a treatable cause before assuming the worst. Assess consciousness with a simple scale, examine the pupils, look for neck stiffness, test for focal weakness, and ask the family when the change began. A seizure is common in this group and must be stopped and its cause investigated. Hypoglycemia, low sodium, high fever and drug effects can all mimic encephalitis, so they are excluded at the bedside first. Only then does the differential move to cerebral malaria, meningitis, encephalitis and the slower infections that invade the nervous system.

Cerebral malaria is a diffuse brain dysfunction caused by Plasmodium falciparum, and it occurs when infected red cells stick to the lining of small cerebral vessels, obstructing flow and provoking inflammation. The patient, most often a child in an endemic area, becomes drowsy and then unrousable, sometimes after a seizure, and may have abnormal posturing. A normal cerebrospinal fluid with a positive malaria test and no other explanation defines it, and retinal changes on examination support the diagnosis. Treatment is intravenous artesunate as described earlier, with close attention to glucose, fluid balance, temperature and seizures. Mortality remains high, and survivors may carry neurological sequelae, so monitoring and rehabilitation planning begin on the first day.

Bacterial meningitis produces fever, headache, neck stiffness, vomiting and a change in consciousness, and early on it may look like any other febrile illness. The organism is linked to the patient's age, with different bacteria dominating in neonates, older children and adults. A lumbar puncture gives the answer, but it must not delay antibiotics when the patient is unstable or has signs of raised pressure, because treatment within the first hour changes the outcome. Current guidance recommends ceftriaxone, with or without vancomycin depending on local resistance, and dexamethasone in certain age groups, with every dose checked against the guideline and the patient's weight. The nurse watches for seizures, unequal pupils, falling consciousness and shock, and reports each change at once.

Japanese encephalitis is a mosquito-borne viral infection of the brain that occurs mainly in rural Asia, where it affects children and can leave severe neurological damage. It begins like a nonspecific febrile illness and may progress to headache, vomiting, drowsiness, seizures and coma. There is no specific antiviral treatment, so care is supportive, with attention to the airway, seizures, fluids and nutrition, and vaccination remains the main preventive measure in affected countries. Survivors may have movement disorders, weakness or cognitive change, so the nurse's long-term work is rehabilitation and support for the family.

Human African trypanosomiasis, also called sleeping sickness, is caused by the parasite Trypanosoma brucei and spread by the tsetse fly in parts of sub-Saharan Africa. A painless chancre may appear at the bite site, followed by fever, enlarged lymph nodes and a rash. Later the parasite enters the central nervous system, producing sleep disturbance, behavioral change, tremor and progressive neurological decline. The stage of disease is determined by examination of the cerebrospinal fluid, because the drugs that reach the brain differ from those that do not, and using the wrong one leaves the patient untreated. Current guidance includes oral fexinidazole and combinations such as eflornithine with nifurtimox, and the regimen must be confirmed with the current guideline and the national program.

Typhoid fever can produce an encephalopathy that looks like meningitis but is not, with drowsiness, confusion, tremors and sometimes rigidity, while the cerebrospinal fluid is usually unremarkable. The mechanism is thought to involve systemic inflammation and toxin effects rather than direct invasion of the brain, so it responds to treatment of the underlying typhoid rather than to a separate neurological regimen. In every neurological case the nursing work is observation repeated often enough to catch deterioration before it becomes irreversible. Record consciousness, pupils, breathing pattern, temperature and seizure activity at every round, and use the same scale each time so the trend is visible. Keep the airway clear, position the patient to protect it, and have oxygen and suction ready, and measure glucose whenever consciousness falls.

Eosinophilia is a rise in the number of eosinophils, the white cells that defend against parasites and also drive allergic inflammation, and it is usually defined as a count above 500 cells per microliter. The mechanism is a response to signals released by immune cells when they meet a parasite they cannot easily kill, so it marks chronic tissue invasion more than acute bloodstream infection. The count rises slowly and falls slowly, so a measurement taken on the first day may be normal even in a disease that will later produce a high count. Steroids, severe acute illness and some infections suppress the count as well. Repeat the count after a week or two when the clinical picture suggests a helminth, because a normal value never excludes a parasite.

The organisms that most often raise the eosinophil count in tropical practice are the soil-transmitted helminths, including Ascaris lumbricoides, the large roundworm, and the hookworms Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, which cause chronic blood loss as well as eosinophilia. Schistosomiasis raises the count while the parasite migrates through the body and may be normal later in established bladder or intestinal disease. Filarial infection, especially lymphatic filariasis from Wuchereria bancrofti and onchocerciasis from Onchocerca volvulus, raises the count particularly in its acute phases. Strongyloidiasis matters because its autoinfection cycle can persist for decades, and trichinellosis from undercooked meat produces marked eosinophilia with muscle pain and edema.

Strongyloides stercoralis deserves special attention because of its autoinfection cycle, in which larvae mature within the same host and reinvade the bowel or the skin, allowing infection to persist silently for decades after a person leaves an endemic area. When the immune system is suppressed, particularly by corticosteroids, the parasite multiplies without restraint, producing hyperinfection with severe diarrhea, abdominal pain, lung symptoms, sepsis and high mortality. This is why screening for strongyloidiasis before starting corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive treatment is a rule rather than a preference, even in a patient with no symptoms now. Current guidance treats it with ivermectin, commonly 200 micrograms per kilogram by mouth once a day for 2 days, with the guideline and the patient's weight checked before administration.

The evaluation of eosinophilia begins with a careful exposure and travel history, followed by stool examination using methods that will actually find the organism. A single stool sample is unreliable, so current guidance calls for repeated samples, and for the Baermann method or agar plate culture when strongyloidiasis is suspected. Serology helps for some parasites, and imaging helps when liver, lungs or bowel are involved, while empirical treatment without examination is sometimes justified in endemic settings according to national guidance. Explain to the patient why several samples are needed, because the delay feels like indifference unless it is explained.

Diarrhea in a febrile patient is classified by duration and character, and the classification points directly at the mechanism. Acute watery diarrhea lasts less than 14 days and is usually caused by a toxin or by an organism that does not invade the bowel wall, which is why there is no blood and why dehydration is the main threat. Dysentery means diarrhea with visible blood and indicates invasion and inflammation of the bowel lining, most often by Shigella and sometimes by Entamoeba histolytica, Campylobacter or a nontyphoidal Salmonella. Persistent diarrhea lasts 14 days or more and usually reflects malabsorption, repeated infection or an underlying condition such as HIV or tuberculosis, and it is a major cause of malnutrition in children.

The most important measurement in any diarrheal illness is the degree of dehydration, assessed from the patient's general condition, the eyes, the mouth, the skin, the pulse and the urine output rather than from a single number. Current guidance from the World Health Organization classifies dehydration as none, some or severe, and treatment follows directly: oral rehydration salts by mouth in small frequent sips for some dehydration, and rapid intravenous fluid with Ringer's lactate for severe dehydration until pulse and perfusion improve. The standard low-osmolarity oral rehydration salts mixture contains sodium chloride 2.6 grams, glucose 13.5 grams, potassium chloride 1.5 grams and trisodium citrate 2.9 grams dissolved in 1 liter of clean water, and the nurse should confirm the sachet instructions before mixing. Zinc, commonly 20 milligrams by mouth once a day for 10 to 14 days in a child, shortens the episode. Verify the dose against the current guideline and the child's weight, and record the urine output as the measure of success.

Bloody diarrhea changes management because the target is the invasive organism rather than the fluid loss alone, and current guidance supports antibiotics for shigellosis, usually ciprofloxacin or azithromycin depending on local resistance, and metronidazole for amoebic dysentery followed by a luminal agent to clear the cysts. Antimotility drugs are avoided in bloody diarrhea because slowing the bowel can worsen invasion and, with Shiga toxin, increase the risk of kidney injury. When diarrhea persists beyond 14 days, the approach shifts to nutrition, weight monitoring and the search for HIV, tuberculosis or another chronic infection. The nurse monitors stool frequency, abdominal pain, temperature and urine output.

An ulcer is a break in the skin with loss of the surface, and its edge, base, tenderness and discharge all carry information. A nodule is a solid raised lesion deeper than a centimeter, a plaque is a broader raised area, and a migratory swelling moves from place to place over days. The eschar is a black, crusted, painless lesion with a rim of redness that marks the site where an arthropod fed. Certain lesions narrow the diagnosis immediately: an eschar with fever suggests scrub typhus from Orientia tsutsugamushi or a tick-borne spotted fever and justifies empirical doxycycline, while a chronic painless ulcer with a raised edge on an exposed limb suggests cutaneous leishmaniasis and a painless swelling with sinuses discharging grains suggests mycetoma. A migratory swelling under the skin, sometimes with a worm visible in the eye, suggests loiasis from Loa loa, and a serpiginous itchy track suggests cutaneous larva migrans. A painless ulcer with a rolled edge and sensory loss suggests leprosy, and multiple ulcers in a child in the tropics should raise the question of yaws, so read these patterns against the exposure history and confirm them with an appropriate test when available.

Enlarged lymph nodes and an enlarged spleen are general clues that become specific when read with the syndrome. Tender matted nodes suggest infection with a spreading organism, while a single fluctuant node suggests a bubo, as in plague or lymphogranuloma venereum. Generalized lymphadenopathy with fever and weight loss requires consideration of HIV, tuberculosis and lymphoma, so the nurse examines the neck, axillae, groin and abdomen rather than only the symptomatic site. An enlarged spleen accompanies malaria, visceral leishmaniasis, typhoid fever, brucellosis and schistosomiasis, and it is found by careful palpation rather than by imaging when imaging is unavailable.

The chain from syndrome to organism to test to treatment is the spine of this chapter and should become a habit. The syndrome gives you a list, the exposure history reorders it, the examination looks for the discriminating sign, and the test confirms what you have begun to treat. Choose the test that changes your management, not the test that is easiest to send, and understand its window of positivity so a negative result is read correctly. The greatest danger here is anchoring on the first plausible diagnosis and bending every later finding to fit it, because a patient with a positive malaria film may also have meningitis. Protect yourself with a written differential, a scheduled re-examination and a deliberate question at every round: what have I not explained, and would a colleague see something I have missed?

The syndromic approach depends on logistics as much as on knowledge, and a brilliant diagnosis is worthless if the drug or the sample cannot move. Know what your clinic holds, including antibiotics, antimalarials, intravenous fluids, oral rehydration salts, testing supplies and personal protective equipment, and know the expiry dates and cold chain requirements. Plan how a specimen reaches the laboratory, how long it takes, and what you will do with the result when it arrives after the patient has gone home. Decide in advance where a patient with suspected meningitis or a viral hemorrhagic fever will be isolated, and who will be notified. Standing orders and clinical algorithms written for your setting are the instruments that make this safe when no physician is present.

Monitoring a febrile patient is a scheduled activity, not a reaction to a crisis. Record temperature, pulse, breathing rate, blood pressure, consciousness and urine output at intervals set by the severity of the illness, and use an early warning score if your setting has one. Look at the patient between measurements, because the nurse who notices the change in breathing or the new confusion is often the one who saves the life. Repeat the malaria film over 48 to 72 hours when the first is negative and suspicion remains, and repeat the hematocrit in dengue as the fever settles. Write down what you see when you see it, because memory is a poor record and the trend is the diagnosis.

Doxycycline causes nausea, irritation of the esophagus and sensitivity to sunlight, so it is given with water and the patient is warned about the sun. Ceftriaxone can cause rash, diarrhea and, rarely, a serious allergic reaction, so the first dose is given where resuscitation is possible. Artesunate can be followed by delayed destruction of red cells several days after treatment, so a falling hemoglobin after apparent recovery requires attention rather than reassurance. Document every suspected reaction and report it through the pharmacovigilance system. Your role is wider than the drug, because you take the exposure history, decide who is seen first, isolate the infectious, teach the family what to watch for at home, and explain in plain words why treatment continues after the fever settles.

Pregnancy, infancy, advanced age and immunosuppression each change the probabilities and the thresholds for action in every syndrome. Malaria in pregnancy is more severe and threatens the fetus, and the choice of treatment depends on the trimester, so the current guideline must be consulted rather than recalled. A neonate with fever may have a serious bacterial infection with almost no localizing signs, so the threshold for investigation and treatment is low, and an older adult may have a blunted fever response and still be gravely ill. The regimens named here are the ones current guidance supports today, and they will not remain unchanged, because recommendations are revised as evidence appears and national programs adapt them to local resistance patterns and to the drugs they can obtain. Before you prescribe, verify the dose, the interval and the duration against the current national guideline and the patient's weight, and have a second clinician check the arithmetic when a child is involved.

To summarize, the syndromic approach to tropical fever is a disciplined way of acting before certainty arrives. You recognize the pattern, whether rash, jaundice, neurological change, eosinophilia, diarrhea or a skin lesion, and you let the pattern name the small group of organisms that matter. You use the exposure history and the examination to reorder that group, you choose the test that will change what you do, and you treat when waiting would be more dangerous than the drug. You monitor on a schedule, you watch for adverse effects, and you keep supply, specimen transport and isolation working in the background. Above all, you hold your first diagnosis loosely, because the patient who does not fit it is telling you something, and the next observation may be the one that saves a life.

# Chapter 8 — Diagnostics Where Resources Are Limited

In tropical medicine the diagnosis is often made or lost in the hour before the laboratory sees the specimen. A clinic may have a working microscope and no incubator, a refrigerator that fails when the generator runs out of fuel, and a courier who comes once a week. The clinician who knows what each test can and cannot do, and what each specimen needs to stay valid, can still practice well inside those limits. This chapter follows that chain from collection to understanding, and it keeps returning to the nursing work that holds it together.

Everything begins with the specimen, and a specimen is only as good as the minute in which it was taken. Blood for a malaria film drawn after a dose of antimalarial medicine may be clear when it should have been full of parasites, and blood for a culture drawn after antibiotics may grow nothing. A stool left warm overnight loses the fragile motile forms that would have made the diagnosis, and urine collected at the wrong hour may hold too few eggs to find. Timing is not a detail of technique; it is part of the test itself, and the nurse who controls the timing controls much of the result.

The practical sequence is easiest to remember as four questions. What does this test need in order to work, and does this patient meet that condition? Has the patient already been treated, and how long ago? Is the specimen the right one, at the right volume, labeled at the bedside with the name and the time? Will it reach the laboratory inside the window the test allows, and if not, how will it be stored until it does? Each question has a failure mode that produces a result which looks like an answer and is not one.

Behind those questions lies a biological clock that no amount of care can hurry. Every infection has a prepatent period, the interval between infection and the moment the organism becomes detectable, and a test done before that interval closes is negative in a person who is genuinely infected. A malaria film may be negative on the first day of fever and positive 12 hours later, while a blood culture in typhoid fever is most often positive in the first week. Serology runs on its own clock, since antibodies take days to weeks to appear and then persist long after recovery, so the date of the specimen must always be read with the date the illness began.

Some organisms appear in the blood or the skin only at particular hours, and a specimen taken at the wrong time is read as normal. The microfilariae of Wuchereria bancrofti, the worm of lymphatic filariasis, circulate mainly at night, so a midday sample may show nothing while one taken after ten in the evening shows many. The microfilariae of Loa loa do the opposite and are easier to find during the day. Urine for the eggs of Schistosoma haematobium is best collected around midday, when the bladder releases the eggs that accumulated overnight. Skin snips for Onchocerca volvulus ignore the clock but must be incubated in saline before they yield their microfilariae.

The malaria film remains the foundation of tropical parasitology, and it is two tests in one. The thick film is a drop of blood spread over a small area and stained without fixation, so the red cells burst and release their parasites into a dense layer that can be scanned quickly, which makes it the more sensitive test. The thin film is a single layer of intact red cells, fixed and stained, and it preserves the shape of the parasite, which is how the species is identified. Giemsa stain is the standard, and its quality depends on the pH of the buffer and the freshness of the stain, both of which fail quietly in a hot clinic. A film too thick is unreadable, one too thin misses a low density, and one not fully dry before staining washes away the cells.

Quantifying the parasites matters as much as finding them, because the density changes what the clinician does. The usual approach is to count parasites while counting a fixed number of white blood cells, commonly 200, and then to express the result against an assumed count of 8,000 per microliter. A density above 100,000 per microliter in a non-immune patient, or above 250,000 in a patient living in a transmission area, marks severe disease and demands parenteral treatment and close observation. The count is also a baseline for judging the response, since a density that has not fallen after 24 to 48 hours of effective therapy suggests resistance or a failure of absorption from vomiting. Density belongs in the nursing assessment beside the temperature and the level of consciousness.

One negative film is never enough to exclude malaria, because parasite density fluctuates through the day and can fall below the threshold of the microscope. The standard practice is a film every 12 to 24 hours, three films over 48 to 72 hours, before malaria is set aside, with the patient observed rather than sent home. The same rule applies to a patient who has already taken antimalarial treatment, since a partially treated infection can be suppressed without being cured. The slides should be kept, because a second reader can settle a difficult species call and a slide outlasts the electronic record. Where the laboratory can do it, a polymerase chain reaction test detects very low densities, but it rarely answers in time to change the first decision.

The rapid diagnostic test for malaria changed what a rural clinic could do, because it needs no microscope, no electricity, and no stain, and it answers in 15 to 20 minutes. Most of these tests detect a parasite antigen in the blood, and the antigen most commonly used is histidine-rich protein 2, which is produced by Plasmodium falciparum. A test that detects only histidine-rich protein 2 will not reliably detect Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium ovale, Plasmodium malariae, or Plasmodium knowlesi, so infection with one of those species can be missed. Antigen can persist for days to weeks after successful treatment, so a positive result in a patient treated last month does not prove that the present fever is malaria. The test is not interchangeable with a film, and the differences decide how a result may be used.

Some parasites carry deletions in the gene for histidine-rich protein 2, produce no antigen at all, and give a negative test while the film is positive. Those deletions were first described in South America and have since been reported in parts of Africa and Asia, and a negative rapid test in a severely ill patient must never overrule the clinical picture. A test combining histidine-rich protein 2 with an enzyme called lactate dehydrogenase, or with aldolase, detects more species and is less affected by deletions, at a higher cost. Where both a rapid test and a microscope exist, the film should confirm and quantify what the rapid test suggests. Where only the rapid test exists, the negative result must be carried with an honest awareness of what it cannot exclude.

Blood cultures remain the reference method for typhoid fever, brucellosis, and bacterial sepsis, and they are among the first casualties of a resource-limited setting. A culture needs enriched medium, a clean venipuncture site, an adequate volume of blood, an incubator that holds a steady temperature for days, and a laboratory that can identify whatever grows. Volume is the strongest determinant of yield, and many systems ask for 10 milliliters per bottle in an adult, more than a hurried collector usually draws. Cultures taken before the first antibiotic dose are far more likely to be positive, and the two or three sets that would raise the yield are rarely affordable. Without an incubator, the honest response is to draw cultures only where the result will be acted upon, and to treat empirically.

Contamination is the other constraint, because a culture that grows an organism from the skin tells the clinician something false but persuasive. Coagulase-negative staphylococci, diphtheroids, and other skin organisms appear when the site was not properly disinfected or the bottle was handled carelessly, and each such result may lead to unnecessary antibiotics and unnecessary cost. The nurse controls the antiseptic, the drying time before puncture, and the transfer of the specimen, and these steps sit within nursing practice in a way that laboratory quality control does not. A culture is only as clean as the moment of collection, and that moment is a nursing moment.

Serology detects the immune response rather than the organism, and that single fact determines both its usefulness and its traps. Because antibodies appear only after the organism has been present for days, a specimen taken early in an illness is often negative and means only that the body has not yet answered. The reliable approach is paired sera, one in the acute phase and a second two to four weeks later, with a fourfold rise between them accepted as evidence of recent infection. A single high level cannot separate a current infection from one acquired years ago, so a positive result on one specimen in a person from an endemic area proves very little, and where paired sera are impossible the clinician must reason from the clinical picture.

Cross-reactivity is the second trap, and it is nowhere more consequential than among the flaviviruses. Dengue, Zika, yellow fever, West Nile, and Japanese encephalitis are closely related, and antibodies against one frequently react in a test designed for another. The problem is acute in a person who has had dengue before, because a second infection with a different serotype produces a rapid and very high antibody response that several flavivirus tests will detect at once. This means a single positive dengue antibody test in a previously infected person may reflect the old infection, the new one, or a cross-reaction, and a high level makes secondary dengue more likely, which is the infection that carries the greatest risk of severe disease. Where only antibody testing exists, the timing of the specimen relative to the day of illness is what makes the result interpretable.

Similar caution applies elsewhere. Rickettsial infections cross-react with one another and with some other bacteria, so a positive test may identify the group without the species. Leptospirosis serology can react with syphilis and other spirochetes, and the microscopic agglutination test, the reference method, is performed in very few laboratories. Brucellosis serology can react with other gram-negative organisms, and antibody tests for tuberculosis have performed so poorly that they should not replace sputum examination and culture. The World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention both caution against basing treatment on a single serological result, and that caution is worth carrying into every clinic.

Stool examination is the workhorse of intestinal parasitology, and it is done in three different ways for three different purposes. The Kato-Katz method uses a measured template and cellophane soaked in glycerol and malachite green, producing a thick smear in which the eggs of Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, hookworm, and Schistosoma mansoni can be counted. Because the volume of stool under the template is known, the count converts into eggs per gram, which is how the intensity of infection is graded and how a program measures its effect over time. The method is cheap, needs only a microscope, and is the standard for surveys and mass treatment programs. Its weakness is that it samples very little stool, so light infections are missed and sensitivity falls when a specimen sits at room temperature.

The formol-ether concentration method exists to offset that weakness. A portion of stool is emulsified in formalin, strained, shaken with ether or ethyl acetate, and centrifuged, which separates the fatty debris and leaves the eggs and cysts in a small sediment examined in a few fields. It recovers more eggs and cysts than a direct smear and is the better test for light infections, for protozoan cysts, and for specimens that must travel before examination, though it needs a centrifuge and cannot measure intensity. Neither method performs well on a single specimen, so at least two or three stool specimens collected on different days should be examined before a negative result is accepted.

Strongyloides stercoralis, the threadworm that causes strongyloidiasis, needs a method of its own, because it sheds larvae rather than eggs and those larvae are easily missed. The Baermann method places fresh stool on gauze over a funnel of warm water, so the larvae migrate down and can be collected from the bottom after an hour or two. A single Baermann examination detects perhaps one half of infections, and the yield rises with repetition, which is why a patient with a compatible history and a negative test may still need treatment. An agar plate culture is more sensitive in experienced hands. Because strongyloidiasis can persist for decades and can produce overwhelming hyperinfection when the patient later receives corticosteroids, the screening question matters as much as the test.

Urine filtration is the standard method for Schistosoma haematobium, the species that settles in the veins around the bladder. A measured volume of urine, usually 10 milliliters, is drawn through a membrane filter, and the filter is examined under the microscope where the terminal-spined eggs are counted. Collecting the specimen around midday raises the yield, because eggs accumulate in the bladder overnight and are released during the day, so a first-morning specimen may be misleadingly empty. The count is reported as eggs per 10 milliliters and grades the intensity of infection just as the stool egg count grades intestinal schistosomiasis. Visible blood in the urine, or a positive dipstick for blood, is a useful clue in a high-prevalence setting and can guide which children to examine when laboratory time is scarce.

Onchocerciasis, the infection caused by Onchocerca volvulus, is diagnosed by finding microfilariae in the skin. A skin snip is taken with a small punch or a razor, usually from the shoulder, the buttock, or the calf, and a bloodless piece of skin is placed in saline and incubated for several hours so the microfilariae emerge and can be seen moving under the microscope. The procedure must be clean and explained to the patient, because it leaves a small scar. Two snips from different sites raise the yield, though the test cannot detect infection before the adult worms release microfilariae and is unhelpful after ivermectin. Palpating for subcutaneous nodules is a complementary skill, and the nurse who finds a nodule has found the adult worms themselves.

Lymph node aspiration is a small procedure that answers several tropical questions at once. In human African trypanosomiasis, fluid aspirated from an enlarged cervical node can be examined directly for trypanosomes moving among the cells, and a positive result is diagnostic without further tests. In leishmaniasis, aspirate from a node or from the edge of a skin lesion can show amastigotes inside the cells, and the same material serves for culture or a polymerase chain reaction test where available. In tuberculosis, a node aspirate sent for microscopy, culture, or a molecular test can confirm a diagnosis that sputum examination would never reach. Aspiration is also part of the assessment of suspected plague, and the nurse prepares the patient, labels the slides at the bedside, and makes sure the material reaches the laboratory fresh.

The polymerase chain reaction, which everyone calls PCR, detects the genetic material of an organism rather than the organism itself, and it can find a pathogen when very few copies are present. In tropical medicine it can identify a malaria species from a dried blood spot, confirm a dengue or chikungunya diagnosis in the first days of illness, detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis, and distinguish the subspecies that cause human African trypanosomiasis. Its strength is also its demand, because it needs a clean laboratory, a stable supply of reagents, reliable electricity, trained staff, and a specimen that arrives before the nucleic acid has degraded. Dried blood spots on filter paper help, since they can be stored and shipped at room temperature and processed much later. Where PCR exists it is usually at a provincial or national laboratory and answers questions asked days earlier.

When no molecular test exists, the clinician is not without options, but the options change shape. The syndromic approach replaces the organism-specific diagnosis, so a patient with fever and an eschar is treated for a rickettsial infection without waiting for serology, and a patient with bloody diarrhea and tenesmus is treated for shigellosis on the strength of the clinical picture. Empirical treatment becomes a deliberate and documented decision, with a reason recorded, a review date set, and a plan for what to do if the patient does not improve. Specimens that can be sent should still be sent, because the result may guide the next patient even when it is too late for this one. What must never happen is that the absence of a laboratory becomes the absence of a decision.

Point-of-care testing moves part of the laboratory to the bedside, and its value is measured by how quickly an answer changes management. The best-known example in tuberculosis is the GeneXpert system, a cartridge-based molecular test that takes a sputum specimen and reports within about two hours whether Mycobacterium tuberculosis is present and whether the gene conferring resistance to rifampicin is mutated. That second result is why the test has been so widely adopted, because it turns a diagnosis and a drug-susceptibility signal into a single morning's work instead of a wait of weeks. The cartridge has a shelf life and a temperature range, and the machine needs stable power and occasional calibration. A negative result does not exclude tuberculosis when the clinical picture is convincing, particularly in a child who cannot produce good sputum, and a positive result does not say whether the disease is active or merely old scarring.

Other point-of-care tests are so familiar that they are easy to take for granted. A glucose meter answers in seconds and is essential in severe malaria, in the malnourished child, and in any patient with impaired consciousness, but strips expire, the meter must be coded to the strip, and a reading from a cold or wet finger can be wrong. A hemoglobin measurement, from a portable device or a centrifuge, guides transfusion and detects the anemia of hookworm and malaria. A urine dipstick detects blood, protein, glucose, ketones, nitrite, and leukocyte esterase, and it is one of the most useful and least expensive tests in a tropical clinic, provided the strip is read at the correct time. A pregnancy test changes treatment choices in malaria and in leishmaniasis, and rapid tests for HIV, for hepatitis B, and for syphilis extend the same principle to the bedside.

Understanding sensitivity and specificity is the arithmetic that turns a result into a decision. Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease who test positive, so a highly sensitive test misses few cases and is used when missing a diagnosis is costly. Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease who test negative, so a highly specific test produces few false positives and is used when a false diagnosis would be harmful. No test is perfect, and the two properties trade against each other when the threshold moves, so a test with 95 per cent sensitivity and 95 per cent specificity is excellent yet still depends entirely on who was tested. The missing piece is prevalence, the share of the tested group who actually have the disease, so a positive rapid test is usually true where malaria is common and mostly false where it is rare.

Every diagnostic procedure carries its own risk, and the nurse who performs or supports it must know what to watch for. A skin snip bleeds and can become infected, so the site is cleaned and the patient is told how to care for it. A lumbar puncture, performed to stage human African trypanosomiasis or diagnose meningitis, can be followed by a headache worse on sitting up, and rarely by bleeding or infection, so the patient is observed and hydrated afterward. Venipuncture can cause a hematoma, and a patient with a bleeding disorder or a low platelet count may bleed far more than expected, which is a particular concern in dengue and in viral hemorrhagic fevers. The monitoring is not incidental to the diagnosis; it is part of the care that makes the diagnosis possible.

Testing and treating are intertwined where the result may not return in time. A patient treated empirically for a rickettsial infection might receive doxycycline 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day, a patient treated empirically for strongyloidiasis might receive ivermectin 200 micrograms per kilogram by mouth once, and a patient treated empirically for schistosomiasis might receive praziquantel 40 milligrams per kilogram by mouth in divided doses. Those figures are what current guidance from the World Health Organization says at the time of writing, and regimens are revised, guidance differs between countries, and you must check the current national guideline before you prescribe. The nurse's part is to verify the dose against the guideline in hand, to check the weight, the kidney function, the pregnancy status, and the interacting medicines, and to know the adverse effects that require a call. Doxycycline can cause sensitivity to sunlight, ivermectin a reaction when microfilariae die in large numbers, and praziquantel dizziness and abdominal discomfort.

Quality control is the discipline that keeps a laboratory honest, and in a low-resource setting it is mostly about temperature, dates, and records. Reagents have expiry dates and storage temperatures, and a box of rapid tests left in a metal cabinet in the sun may fail long before the date printed on it. A refrigerator used for specimens, reagents, and vaccines must have a thermometer inside, and the temperature must be read and written down at least once a day, because a refrigerator that cycles between freezing and warm destroys some reagents and preserves others imperfectly. Blood culture media, serology kits, and assay plates all have their own requirements, and a night without power can undo a month of careful storage. Where a cold chain cannot be guaranteed, the test that does not need cold storage is often the better choice.

Supply chains decide which tests a clinic can offer, and a test that is unavailable leaves a gap nobody has planned for. Stockouts happen for reasons that have nothing to do with the patient, because a national tender is delayed, a shipment is held at a border, or a road washes out in the rainy season. The practical responses are to keep a buffer stock of the tests that change management most, to record consumption honestly, and to know the lead time for each item. Expiry dates must be checked on receipt and again on use, and stock must be rotated so the oldest is used first. Transport is the quiet half of the same problem, because a specimen bound for a district laboratory may travel by motorcycle, bicycle, boat, or on foot, packaged in a leakproof primary container, a leakproof secondary container with absorbent material, and a rigid outer container with the paperwork.

All of this comes back to the nurse, because the nurse usually decides that a test is needed, prepares the patient, takes or supervises the specimen, labels it, stores it, and sends it. At the front of that chain the nurse asks whether the patient has already taken medicine, whether the timing is right, and whether the patient understands what is being collected. At the back of the chain the nurse protects the specimen from heat, labels it correctly, and hands it to the right courier at the right time. Documentation holds the process together, so the record should carry the date and time of collection, the site and method, the test requested, any treatment already given, and the result when it arrives. When a result is unexpected the record should show that it was noticed, questioned, and reconciled with the clinical picture, because a test nobody can find or interpret has achieved nothing.

Another discipline is choosing the tests that will change what happens and declining the ones that will not. Each specimen costs money, time, and the attention of the person who processes it, and where those are scarce the marginal test is expensive even when its price is low. A test whose result will not alter treatment, or will not reach the clinician in time, is better not requested. Results must then reach the patient, since a patient told only that the test was normal may not return for the repeat that was planned, while a patient told that a result is positive without explanation may stop treatment as soon as they feel better. The nurse should explain in concrete terms what was tested, what the result means, and what happens next, and where a result is uncertain, saying so honestly is better than offering false certainty.

The single most important idea in this chapter is that a negative test is not the same as the absence of disease. A test can be negative because the organism is present in numbers below the detection limit, because the specimen was taken at the wrong time in the illness, because it was handled badly, because the test itself is insensitive, or because the patient was treated before collection. Malaria is the classic example, since a single film can be negative in a patient who is genuinely infected and a rapid test can be negative in a patient whose parasite carries a histidine-rich protein 2 deletion.
