Tuberculosis is another, because a sputum smear may be negative in active disease, especially in a child or a person with HIV. The way to weigh such a result is to keep the pre-test probability in view and to decide in advance what a negative result will change, so that high suspicion with an insensitive test prompts a repeat, a different test, or a documented decision to treat on clinical grounds.

To summarize, diagnostics in a resource-limited setting are a chain of decisions in which the specimen, the timing, the technique, the storage, the transport, the arithmetic of the result, and the communication of that result each carry as much weight as the test itself. The thick and thin malaria films, the rapid test with its histidine-rich protein 2 deletions, the blood culture with its volume and its contamination, the paired sera with their cross-reactivity and their dengue problem, the Kato-Katz and formol-ether and Baermann methods, the urine filtration, the polymerase chain reaction where it exists, and the point-of-care cartridge for tuberculosis all answer different questions and fail in different ways. Sensitivity and specificity describe a test, but prevalence and the pre-test probability decide what a result means for this patient. Quality control, refrigeration, expiry dates, and supply chains are not administrative housekeeping but the conditions under which a result can be believed at all. The habit of asking what a result can prove, what a negative result could still hide, and what will be done differently either way is what makes a limited laboratory safe, and a negative test is never absence of disease but the absence of evidence.

# Chapter 9 — Malaria

Malaria is the disease that tropical medicine is built around, and it remains a leading cause of death from infection in African children. A protozoan parasite of the genus Plasmodium causes it, a female Anopheles mosquito transmits it, and it can move from headache to coma within 24 hours. It is preventable, diagnosable, and curable, yet it still kills hundreds of thousands of people every year. This chapter follows the parasite from the salivary gland to the bedside, using guidance from the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and treating every dose as current guidance rather than permanent truth.

Five species of Plasmodium cause almost all human malaria, and each has its own habits, geography, and clinical signature. Plasmodium falciparum is the most dangerous and the most common in Africa, and it causes nearly every death. Plasmodium vivax is the most widespread, dominant across much of Asia and Latin America, and able to hide in the liver and cause repeated relapses. Plasmodium ovale is uncommon and rarely severe, and Plasmodium malariae is the rarest and can persist in the blood for years. Plasmodium knowlesi comes from macaque monkeys in Southeast Asia and can multiply fast enough to become severe.

Plasmodium falciparum dominates the mortality figures because of what it does to the blood vessel rather than at first contact. Its infected red cells grow sticky knobs that make them adhere to the lining of small vessels in the brain, the gut, the kidney, the lung, and the placenta. This process, called sequestration, hides the parasites from the spleen and lets them consume the local oxygen, so the microcirculation is obstructed and the tissue becomes acidotic. The other species mostly stay in circulation and cause disease by destroying red cells, which is why falciparum produces cerebral malaria and organ failure while the others rarely do.

The life cycle begins when a female Anopheles mosquito, feeding mostly between dusk and dawn, injects saliva containing sporozoites into the skin. The sporozoites reach the liver within minutes and enter liver cells, where the parasite grows into a schizont that divides without cell division. After roughly 1 to 2 weeks the schizont ruptures the liver cell and releases thousands of merozoites, and the interval between the bite and that release is the prepatent period. In Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale, a fraction of the sporozoites become hypnozoites, dormant liver forms that reactivate weeks to months later and cause a relapse without any new bite.

Once merozoites enter red cells, the parasite repeats a cycle of growth and division lasting about 48 hours for most species and 72 hours for Plasmodium malariae. The red cell becomes a trophozoite, then a schizont, and finally bursts, releasing a new generation of merozoites with fragments of parasite and red cell debris. That burst is what the body recognizes as a fever, which explains why the temperature may rise in a regular rhythm. Some merozoites become gametocytes, the sexual forms taken up by the next mosquito, and in falciparum malaria the infected cells may never circulate freely, so the peripheral count may understate the true burden.

Each antimalarial drug acts at one point in the life cycle and is blind to the others. Chloroquine concentrates in the parasite's digestive vacuole and blocks the detoxification of heme, so the parasite is poisoned by its own waste, but that mechanism fails wherever resistance has fixed itself. The antifolate drugs sulfadoxine with pyrimethamine block 2 steps in the parasite's folate pathway, atovaquone disrupts its mitochondrial electron transport, and doxycycline acts on its residual plastid, which is why antibiotics are slow and useful mainly for prevention. Primaquine and tafenoquine act on the dormant liver forms and the gametocytes, so a complete treatment is often 2 drugs rather than 1.

The incubation period from an infective bite to the first fever is usually 7 to 30 days for Plasmodium falciparum, and it can be much longer after partial prevention or infection with a species that has dormant liver forms. The classic teaching that malaria produces a fever every 48 or 72 hours is true only in the minority of patients with synchronized cycles and no prior immunity. In practice the fever is often continuous, irregular, or absent, and a patient may present with headache, malaise, nausea, and body aches rather than a dramatic rigor. Anyone who waits for the textbook pattern will miss cases, so fever after exposure in a malarious area is malaria until the films prove otherwise.

Uncomplicated malaria is defined by what it lacks rather than by what it has. The patient has fever or a history of fever, often with chills, sweats, headache, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, and the illness may be indistinguishable from influenza. The examination may show pallor, a palpable spleen, mild jaundice, or nothing at all, and there is no impaired consciousness, no respiratory distress, no bleeding, no shock, and no evidence of organ dysfunction. Because the patient can take medication by mouth, outpatient treatment is possible when someone reliable can observe the doses and the patient can return if things worsen.

The nonspecific nature of uncomplicated malaria is why clinicians in areas of high transmission no longer treat every fever as malaria without a test. Decades of presumptive treatment produced wasted drugs, missed diagnoses of pneumonia and meningitis, and pressure that selected for resistance. The World Health Organization now asks for confirmation by a rapid diagnostic test or by microscopy before treatment, except where no test is possible and suspicion is high. A returning traveler with fever presents the opposite problem, because there the test is always available and the clinician must still remember that malaria can be present.

Severe malaria is a medical emergency, and it is defined by criteria that describe what the parasite has already done to the body. Children and adults fail differently, so a child may present with convulsions, profound anemia, hypoglycemia, and acidosis, while an adult may present with renal failure, pulmonary edema, jaundice, and impaired consciousness. Any 1 of the criteria is enough to make the diagnosis and to change treatment from a tablet by mouth to a drug given intravenously. Several criteria together raise the risk of death sharply, and the trajectory over the first hours matters more than the initial number.

Impaired consciousness is the criterion most people associate with severe malaria, and cerebral malaria is its most feared expression. A patient who cannot localize a painful stimulus, who is drowsy and difficult to rouse, or who has had a generalized seizure may have parasites sequestered in the cerebral microcirculation. In children the diagnosis is supported by a Blantyre coma score below the normal range, and in adults by a Glasgow coma scale score below it, together with a blood film that shows the parasite. Seizures may appear only as twitching of a limb or deviation of the eyes, and reversible causes such as hypoglycemia and meningitis must be excluded at the bedside.

Acidosis is a powerful predictor of death in severe malaria, and it usually signals impaired tissue perfusion and increased anaerobic metabolism rather than a single organ failure. The patient breathes deeply and rapidly, often without obvious lung disease, and the bicarbonate and lactate measurements confirm the picture. In children, deep breathing is one of the most reliable bedside signs of severe disease and one of the easiest to overlook as anxiety or pneumonia. The acidosis is worsened by anemia, low blood volume, hypoglycemia, and the parasite's own consumption of glucose and oxygen, so the response is to correct those causes, give oxygen, and restore the circulation rather than to give bicarbonate.

Hypoglycemia is one of the most common and most reversible causes of deterioration in severe malaria. The parasite consumes glucose, the liver makes less of it, the patient may not be eating, and quinine stimulates the pancreas to release insulin, and young children and pregnant women are at particular risk. Sweating, tremor, and fast heart rate may be absent, so a low reading must be treated at once with an intravenous bolus of glucose followed by a continuous infusion and repeated measurement. A nurse who measures glucose on arrival, after any treatment that stimulates insulin, and at regular intervals prevents a large share of the deaths on the ward.

Severe anemia in malaria comes from the destruction of infected and uninfected red cells, from suppression of the bone marrow, and from repeated infection. The threshold differs by age and is more strict in young children, and a child below it may need a transfusion even before other criteria appear. Pallor of the conjunctivae, the palms, and the tongue is a useful bedside sign, and a rapid hemoglobin measurement should be obtained whenever it is available. The anemia develops over days, so the nurse watches the trend rather than a single number and weighs the severity against the real risks of blood that is not screened well.

Renal impairment in severe malaria ranges from a modest rise in creatinine to complete absence of urine, and it is more common in adults than in children. The mechanisms include reduced blood flow to the kidney, sequestration of parasites in the renal microcirculation, and the release of free hemoglobin when red cells are destroyed inside the vessels. Blackwater fever is the dramatic form, with massive destruction of red cells, dark urine, jaundice, and acute kidney injury, and it has been associated with quinine and with repeated infection. Dialysis is often needed when available, so the nurse watches the urine output hourly and reports a fall before the creatinine rises.

Pulmonary edema in severe malaria usually follows increased capillary permeability and fluid overload rather than heart failure, and it can appear even in a young patient. The patient becomes breathless and short of oxygen, the chest examination reveals crackles, and treatment is oxygen, careful fluid restriction, and ventilatory support where it exists. Bleeding from the gums, the nose, the gut, or the sites of venipuncture reflects disseminated intravascular coagulation and a low platelet count. Shock with cold peripheries and a prolonged capillary refill is a late and ominous finding, because too much fluid in severe malaria is as dangerous as too little.

A high parasite density is itself a criterion of severe disease, usually defined as more than 5 per cent of red cells parasitized or a count above the accepted threshold in each microliter, and it should be read with the clinical picture rather than in isolation. Prostration, meaning the patient cannot sit or walk unaided, counts as severe even when consciousness is preserved, and jaundice, hemoglobinuria, a high lactate level, and a low urine output each add weight. In pregnancy, severe malaria carries additional risk to the fetus, so any pregnant woman with malaria deserves rapid assessment and treatment. A patient who meets no criterion on arrival can still deteriorate, so the reassessment is as important as the initial classification.

The diagnosis rests on demonstrating the parasite in the blood, and the thick and thin films remain the reference method when they are done well. The thick film concentrates the parasites and is used to detect them and estimate the density, while the thin film shows the species and the stage. The films are stained with Giemsa, and the quality of the stain, the thickness of the smear, and the reader's experience matter more than the laboratory's equipment. A falling density over 24 to 48 hours is reassuring, while a rising density demands reassessment of the drug, the dose, and the diagnosis, and a single negative film does not exclude malaria, so films should be repeated over 48 to 72 hours when suspicion remains.

The rapid diagnostic test has changed malaria care where microscopy is not available, and it detects a parasite protein in a drop of blood within minutes. Most of these tests detect histidine-rich protein 2, which Plasmodium falciparum produces, and some detect a second enzyme that identifies the other species. The test is easy to use and needs no electricity, but it stays positive for days to weeks after a treated infection has cleared, so a positive result in someone treated recently does not prove a new episode. Some parasites have lost the ability to make histidine-rich protein 2, and these deletions produce a false negative in a patient who is genuinely infected, so a negative rapid test in a severely ill patient must be followed by microscopy.

The World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention publish guidance on classification and treatment, and that guidance is revised as resistance patterns and drug availability change. Regimens differ between countries and between age groups, and no chapter can substitute for the current national guideline, so the doses here are current guidance rather than a permanent standard. National programs adapt the recommendations of the World Health Organization to local resistance and local supply, so verify every dose against the current guideline and the product label before it is given. The nurse is often the last person who can catch a decimal error, a wrong weight, or a drug unsafe in pregnancy, and asking a second clinician to check unusual arithmetic is the standard of care.

Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is treated with an artemisinin-based combination therapy, meaning a fast-acting artemisinin derivative paired with a slower partner drug that clears the parasites the artemisinin leaves behind. The pairing is deliberate, because the short-acting component kills most parasites quickly while the partner eliminates the residual ones, which reduces the chance that resistant parasites survive. The common combinations include artemether with lumefantrine, artesunate with amodiaquine, dihydroartemisinin with piperaquine, and artesunate with mefloquine or with sulfadoxine and pyrimethamine, and every regimen is given for 3 days. Artemether with lumefantrine is the most widely used, given as 6 doses over 3 days, and an adult typically takes 4 tablets per dose, each containing 20 milligrams of artemether and 120 milligrams of lumefantrine, with the pediatric dose calculated by weight.

Two practical points determine whether the treatment works, and both belong to the nurse. The first is food, because artemether with lumefantrine is absorbed much better with fat, such as milk, breast milk, or a fatty meal, so tablets taken on an empty stomach may fail even with perfect adherence. The second is vomiting, because any dose vomited within 30 minutes should be repeated in full, and a dose vomited later may need repeating as well, since an unabsorbed dose equals no dose. The full 3 days must be completed even after the fever settles, because stopping early selects for the parasites that were hardest to kill.

Non-falciparum malaria is treated differently because the aim includes preventing relapse as well as curing the current illness. Chloroquine remains effective for Plasmodium vivax in most places, given as a total dose of 25 milligrams of base per kilogram over 3 days, although resistance rules it out in parts of Oceania and Southeast Asia, and Plasmodium ovale and Plasmodium malariae also respond. For Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale, primaquine is added to kill the dormant liver forms, usually 0.25 to 0.5 milligrams per kilogram by mouth once a day for 14 days, while tafenoquine offers a single dose of 300 milligrams for adults. Both drugs can destroy red cells dangerously in a person with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, so the enzyme status must be checked before either is given.

Severe malaria is treated with a drug given intravenously, and the drug of choice is artesunate. The World Health Organization recommends 2.4 milligrams per kilogram given intravenously at the start, again after 12 hours, again after 24 hours, and then once every 24 hours until the patient can take an oral artemisinin-based combination therapy. Quinine is the alternative where artesunate is not available, given as a loading dose of 20 milligrams per kilogram infused over 4 hours and then 10 milligrams per kilogram every 8 hours, and it demands close attention to hypoglycemia and the heart rhythm. For a child who cannot reach a clinic in time, a single rectal dose of artesunate at 10 milligrams per kilogram before referral reduces the risk of death and disability, and that pre-referral treatment is one of the most important practical advances in the field.

Once the patient can swallow and the parasite density is falling, treatment is completed with a full course of an artemisinin-based combination therapy by mouth. Artesunate is generally well tolerated, but it can cause a delayed destruction of red cells 1 to 3 weeks after treatment, when the cells that were once infected are removed by the recovering immune system. Any patient treated with artesunate who becomes anemic weeks later should have a hemoglobin measurement and a reticulocyte count, because the cause is often missed. The nurse also watches for the return of fever, a falling urine output, and fluid overload, and follow-up after discharge matters because the delayed complications declare themselves after the acute illness.

Resistance is the force that keeps rewriting malaria treatment, and its history is a lesson in why combination therapy matters. Chloroquine was the mainstay of treatment and prevention for decades, and it was lost first in Southeast Asia in the middle of the twentieth century and then across Africa in the last 2 decades of that century, while sulfadoxine with pyrimethamine followed the same path. Artemisinin partial resistance, seen first in the Greater Mekong region early in the present century, does not abolish the drug but slows the clearance of parasites, so the partner drug must finish the job. When the partner also fails, treatment failure becomes common, and partial resistance has now been detected in parts of East Africa.

Chemoprophylaxis is for people who are not immune and are going to a place where malaria is transmitted, and it works only when the right drug is chosen and taken as prescribed. The choice depends on the destination and its resistance pattern, the length of the trip, and the traveler's medical history, pregnancy status, and age. Mefloquine, 250 milligrams by mouth once a week, suits long stays but is avoided in people with a history of psychiatric illness or seizures. Doxycycline, 100 milligrams by mouth once a day, is effective and inexpensive but can cause sensitivity to sunlight, and it must be continued for 4 weeks after leaving the area. Atovaquone with proguanil, 1 tablet by mouth once a day, needs only 7 days of continuation but is expensive, and chloroquine is used only where the parasite remains fully sensitive.

The failure of chemoprophylaxis is almost always a failure of adherence rather than of the drug, because travelers forget doses, stop early when they leave the area where malaria is transmitted, or never start. The continuation after departure is the part most often abandoned, and it is exactly the part that prevents the illness appearing weeks later. Tafenoquine, taken as 200 milligrams by mouth once a day for 3 days before travel and then once a week, offers a simpler schedule for some adults, but it carries the same glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase caution as primaquine. Mefloquine has been linked to effects on mood and sleep, which are uncommon but serious, and the nurse's role in the pre-travel visit is to make the schedule concrete for the traveler.

Malaria control is not a single intervention but a package, and drugs alone will never eliminate it. Insecticide-treated bed nets reduce bites during the hours when Anopheles mosquitoes feed, through both a physical barrier and an insecticidal effect. Indoor residual spraying kills mosquitoes that rest on the walls of a dwelling after feeding, and larval source management removes or treats the standing water where the mosquito breeds. Seasonal chemoprevention in children during the months of highest transmission, and intermittent preventive treatment in pregnancy, reduce illness in the groups at greatest risk. The malaria vaccines now recommended for children in high transmission areas add a further layer, though they reduce illness rather than prevent infection.

Pregnancy changes malaria in both directions, and the guidance must be applied with the trimester in mind. The placenta concentrates parasites, and the result is maternal anemia, impaired fetal growth, premature delivery, and stillbirth, often without the fever that would bring a patient to care. In the first trimester, uncomplicated infection is usually treated with an artemisinin-based combination therapy, because the risk of untreated malaria outweighs the concern about the drug. In the second and third trimesters, the same combinations are used, and intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine and pyrimethamine is given at scheduled antenatal visits in areas of stable transmission. Severe malaria in pregnancy is treated with intravenous artesunate at the standard dose regardless of trimester, and prevention with an insecticide-treated bed net begins before conception where possible.

Infants and young children carry the greatest burden of severe malaria, and their treatment is a matter of arithmetic as much as pharmacology. Doses are calculated by weight, and the dispersible pediatric formulations of the artemisinin-based combinations have made accurate dosing much easier than splitting adult tablets. A child's dose of artemether with lumefantrine is based on a weight band and dispersed in a small amount of water, and children lose fluid and become hypoglycemic quickly and may convulse before any other sign appears. Malaria in the newborn is uncommon but occurs, transmitted from an infected mother, so a child who has been treated and remains febrile needs a repeat film, a glucose measurement, and a careful search for another cause.

Two words describe 2 different returns of malaria, and confusing them leads to the wrong treatment. Recrudescence is the reappearance of parasites from the same blood-stage infection that was never fully cleared, and it usually appears within weeks and reflects treatment failure, an inadequate dose, or resistance. Relapse is the reactivation of dormant liver forms, and it occurs only with Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale, often months after the original illness and after a period with no parasites at all. Recrudescence is managed by reviewing the dose and the drug, while relapse requires primaquine or tafenoquine to kill the hypnozoites, and reinfection is a third possibility that is common where transmission continues.

The nursing care of a patient with malaria is organized around a small number of things that determine survival, and they are glucose, fluid, drug timing, temperature, and neurological status. Each of them can deteriorate silently, and each can be corrected by a nurse who is watching. The ward may be crowded, the monitors few, and the laboratory far away, but these 5 observations need only a glucose meter, a clock, a thermometer, a fluid balance chart, and a working pen. Written down and handed over, they become the patient's continuity of care.

Glucose monitoring is the first nursing priority because hypoglycemia is common, dangerous, and reversible. Measure the blood glucose on arrival in every patient with severe malaria, then at intervals determined by the patient's condition, and always after a dose of quinine or a period without food. In children, check it whenever the child becomes drowsy, convulses, or stops feeding, because those signs may be hypoglycemia rather than cerebral malaria. Treat a low reading at once with an intravenous bolus of glucose, then start a continuous infusion and recheck within the interval your protocol specifies, and never assume a normal reading will stay normal.

Fluid balance in severe malaria is a narrow path between dehydration and overload, because the patient is often short of fluid from fever and poor intake while the capillary leak of severe infection means too much fluid collects in the lungs. Give fluids to restore the circulation, using a balanced crystalloid, then reassess the perfusion, the breathing rate, and the urine output before giving more. Measure the urine output hourly and report a fall below the expected rate at once, because the kidney is often the first organ to declare that the circulation is inadequate. Keep a strict intake and output chart, because the nurse who notices crackles at the lung bases after a bolus has prevented pulmonary edema.

Drug timing is a nursing responsibility in severe malaria, because the schedule for artesunate is based on hours and a missed dose is measured in parasite growth. Record the exact time of every dose, keep the intervals as prescribed, and prepare each dose freshly according to the instructions. Temperature control matters for comfort and metabolic demand, so use paracetamol for fever, avoid aspirin in children, and use tepid sponging when the temperature is high. Watch for the adverse effects of each drug, including delayed red cell destruction with artesunate, hypoglycemia and ringing in the ears with quinine, effects on mood and sleep with mefloquine, and sensitivity to sunlight with doxycycline, and report suspected reactions through the national system for monitoring drug safety.

Neurological checks turn the observation chart into an early warning system. Record the level of consciousness with a formal score, examine the pupils, check for stiffness of the neck, and look for weakness on one side at every shift and after every seizure. A seizure may be the only sign of cerebral malaria in a child, and it may be brief and easy to miss, so a nurse who is present when it happens has made the diagnosis. Protect the airway during a seizure, position the patient on the side, give oxygen, check the glucose, and give the prescribed anticonvulsant, then document the event because a patient whose consciousness deepens needs immediate reassessment.

The logistics of malaria care decide outcomes as much as the pharmacology does, and the nurse is usually the person who manages them. Stock must be counted, expiry dates checked, and a supply of artesunate and of the oral combination kept where severely ill patients arrive, because a stockout at the wrong moment is a clinical event. The cold chain matters for some products and not others, so know which drugs need refrigeration and protect them accordingly. Referral requires a plan covering who decides, who transports, what treatment is given before departure, and what documentation travels with the patient, and rectal artesunate given before referral is one of the most effective links in that chain.

Community work closes the loop, and it belongs to nursing practice as much as bedside care does. Teaching a household how to hang and use an insecticide-treated bed net, when to seek care for a fever, and why a full course of tablets must be finished prevents more malaria than any single prescription. Follow-up after treatment catches recrudescence and relapse, while campaigns of seasonal chemoprevention and visits for intermittent preventive treatment depend on nurses to screen and record the doses. Reporting cases to the surveillance system is a professional duty, because the national program cannot respond to a rise it cannot see, and these unglamorous tasks decide whether a program works.

To summarize, malaria is a protozoan infection transmitted by the female Anopheles mosquito and caused by 5 species of Plasmodium, of which Plasmodium falciparum causes nearly all the deaths. The life cycle moves from the salivary gland to the liver, then to the red cells, then to the gametocytes that return to the mosquito, and each class of drug acts at a different point in that sequence. Fever is unreliable in its pattern, so any compatible exposure requires a blood film or a rapid diagnostic test, and severe malaria is defined by impaired consciousness, acidosis, hypoglycemia, severe anemia, renal impairment, pulmonary edema, bleeding, shock, and high parasite density. Uncomplicated falciparum malaria is treated with an artemisinin-based combination therapy for 3 days, and severe malaria is treated with intravenous artesunate, with rectal artesunate given before referral when a child cannot reach care in time. Chloroquine has been lost across most of the world and artemisinin partial resistance is established in Southeast Asia, so regimens must be checked against current national guidance rather than remembered. Prevention rests on chemoprophylaxis for travelers, insecticide-treated bed nets, indoor residual spraying, and chemoprevention in the groups at highest risk, and the nursing priorities are glucose, fluids, drug timing, temperature, and neurological checks. The nurse who performs those checks is the reason most patients with severe malaria survive.

# Chapter 10 — Arboviral Diseases

Arboviral diseases are infections transmitted by arthropods, chiefly mosquitoes and ticks, and they form one of the largest and fastest changing groups in tropical medicine. The term arbovirus describes not a family but a strategy, in which unrelated viruses pass from one vertebrate host to another inside the body of a blood-feeding invertebrate. Dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, West Nile, Japanese encephalitis, tick-borne encephalitis, Rift Valley fever, Mayaro and Oropouche are the names to know, and they are not equally dangerous. What they share is a dependence on human behavior, because the water containers people keep, the houses they build and the journeys they take decide where these diseases appear. This chapter follows the guidance of the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and it treats every regimen as current guidance rather than permanent truth.

Aedes aegypti, the yellow fever mosquito, is the central character in the urban story, and Aedes albopictus, the Asian tiger mosquito, is its expanding understudy. Both breed in small collections of clean water close to people, including discarded tires, flower pots, water storage jars and roof gutters. Both bite during the day, so a bed net used at night gives little protection. Aedes aegypti is adapted to human settlements, feeds preferentially on people and can complete its life cycle within a few meters of the bed where a patient sleeps. Aedes albopictus tolerates cooler temperatures and has spread across much of Europe and North America, which is why the map of these diseases keeps redrawing itself.

These viruses enter a person through the saliva of a biting mosquito or tick, multiply in local tissues and spread through the blood, producing a period of viremia during which the patient can infect further mosquitoes. The incubation period is short, usually 3 to 14 days, and the illness that follows is often indistinguishable from many other febrile diseases. Most infections are silent or mild, and the proportion that becomes severe varies enormously. The first lesson of arboviral medicine is that the diagnosis is rarely obvious from the fever alone, and the clinician who waits for a textbook picture will miss the patients who matter most. The second lesson is that severity often announces itself as the fever settles, so the apparent improvement is exactly when your attention must sharpen.

Dengue is caused by 4 closely related viruses, called serotypes 1, 2, 3 and 4, and infection with one serotype produces lifelong protection against that serotype only. A second infection with a different serotype is the dangerous event, because antibodies left from the first infection can fail to neutralize the new virus and can instead help it enter the cells that amplify the immune response. This phenomenon, called antibody-dependent enhancement, explains why severe dengue is far more common in a second infection and why a patient reporting a previous dengue illness deserves caution. The useful rule is not to predict severity from the serotype but to watch every patient through the window in which severity appears.

Dengue passes through 3 phases, and the names of those phases are the backbone of nursing surveillance. The febrile phase lasts 2 to 7 days and brings high fever, severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain, nausea, vomiting and often a flushing rash. The critical phase begins as the fever subsides, usually between the third and the seventh day, and it lasts roughly 24 to 48 hours, during which the capillaries become leaky and fluid moves into the tissues. The trap for the unwary is that the patient often looks better at the very moment the critical phase begins, because the fever has broken and the pain has eased.

The warning signs of dengue tell you that the critical phase has arrived or is imminent, and the World Health Organization lists them explicitly so that they can be taught and remembered. They are abdominal pain or tenderness, persistent vomiting, bleeding from the gums or nose or into the gut, lethargy or restlessness, and fluid accumulation such as ascites or pleural effusion. Any one of these findings moves the patient from outpatient observation to inpatient care with intravenous fluids and close monitoring, and none should be dismissed as the ordinary misery of a viral illness. Persistent vomiting matters because it prevents oral rehydration, and lethargy is the sign most often missed when a quiet child is mistaken for an improving one.

Severe dengue is defined by shock, by significant bleeding, by severe organ impairment or by a combination of these, and it is an emergency that can kill within hours. Plasma leakage is the engine of the disease, because when the capillary wall becomes permeable, protein-rich fluid leaves the circulation, the hematocrit rises, the blood pressure falls and the organs are poorly perfused even though no blood has been lost. The shock of dengue is therefore distributive and hypovolemic at once, and it can remain compensated for a while before collapsing suddenly. Severe organ involvement can take the form of hepatitis, encephalitis, myocarditis or acute kidney injury, and it can occur with little obvious leakage, so a normal hematocrit does not exclude severe disease.

Fluid management in the critical phase saves lives, and it is also the intervention most easily done badly. Current World Health Organization guidance divides patients by the severity of leakage and by their ability to drink, giving oral rehydration salts to those who can take them and intravenous crystalloid, usually normal saline or a balanced solution, to those who cannot or who already show warning signs. A typical starting regimen for a patient with warning signs is 5 to 10 milliliters per kilogram of body weight per hour for the first 1 to 2 hours, followed by reassessment and stepwise reduction as the circulation improves, with the rate guided by urine output, hematocrit, blood pressure and perfusion. Colloid solutions are reserved for shock that does not respond to crystalloid, and blood transfusion is reserved for significant bleeding rather than for a low platelet count alone. These figures illustrate how the regimen is built rather than prescribe it, because guidance is revised as evidence accumulates, it differs between countries, and the current guideline must be checked before any fluid or drug is given. The nurse's most valuable contribution is not the choice of fluid but the frequency of reassessment, since a rate that was right 2 hours ago may be wrong now.

Aspirin and the other anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided in dengue for 2 reasons. They impair platelet function and irritate the stomach, so they increase the risk of bleeding in a patient whose platelets are already low. They can also mask the fever and malaise you are using to judge the phase of the illness, and they cause fluid retention that muddies the assessment of leakage. Acetaminophen, also called paracetamol, is the preferred antipyretic, and a common adult dose is 500 to 1000 milligrams by mouth every 6 hours, with the daily ceiling and the pediatric dose verified from the current guideline. Written instructions should name the medicines to avoid, because many over-the-counter preparations contain exactly the drugs that must not be used.

Recognizing the transition into the critical phase is the nursing skill this chapter exists to teach, and it is built on serial observation rather than on any single measurement. The transition usually occurs around the time the fever settles, so a patient who has been febrile for 4 days and now has a normal temperature is entering the window of greatest risk, not the window of safety. Record the temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, capillary refill, urine output and mental state at a fixed interval, and compare each set with the last, because a falling systolic pressure and a rising heart rate in a stable patient are the earliest signs of compensated shock. Measure the hematocrit frequently, since a rise of 20 per cent or more from the baseline suggests significant leakage, and remember that it can fall later when bleeding occurs. Ask about and look for the warning signs at every assessment, and document the answers, because the nurse who notices a narrowed pulse pressure and cool hands has recognized severe dengue before the laboratory does.

Chikungunya is transmitted by the same Aedes mosquitoes and produces an illness whose signature is pain rather than leakage. After an incubation of 2 to 7 days, the patient develops sudden high fever and severe joint pain, often in the small joints of the hands, wrists, ankles and feet, with headache, muscle pain, a rash and sometimes conjunctivitis. The fever usually settles within a week, but the joint pain can persist for months or years, and many patients report chronic arthralgia that limits work and sleep. Infection during pregnancy near the time of delivery can be transmitted to the newborn, who may develop fever, poor feeding, lethargy, rash and, in severe cases, neurological disease, so neonatal monitoring is required when a mother is viremic at delivery. Treatment is supportive, with rest, fluids and acetaminophen, and other analgesics are withheld until dengue has been excluded.

Zika virus produces the mildest of the acute illnesses in this group and the most devastating of the congenital ones, an uncomfortable combination for anyone who counsels pregnant women. Most infections cause a low fever, a rash, joint pain, conjunctivitis and fatigue, and many cause no symptoms at all, so the acute illness is a poor guide to who has been infected. The virus can cross the placenta and damage the developing brain, causing microcephaly, brain malformation, vision and hearing loss and developmental delay, and the risk is greatest in the first trimester, though it is not confined to it. Zika can also trigger Guillain-Barré syndrome, an acute inflammatory polyneuropathy that causes ascending weakness, loss of reflexes and, in severe cases, respiratory failure, appearing days to weeks after the acute illness. Unlike the other arboviruses here, Zika is transmitted sexually as well as by mosquitoes and can persist in semen for weeks or months, so barrier protection and the timing of conception belong in the conversation. Prevention in pregnancy is therefore a layered strategy of avoiding areas of active transmission, preventing bites by day and by night, and using condoms with partners who may have been exposed.

Yellow fever has the longest and most consequential history of any arboviral disease, and it remains a serious threat across tropical Africa and parts of South America. The virus circulates in a jungle cycle among primates and forest mosquitoes, in an intermediate cycle at the edge of settlements, and in an urban cycle in which Aedes aegypti carries it from person to person. Most infections are mild or silent, but roughly 1 in 7 patients enters a toxic phase after an apparent improvement, with returning fever, jaundice, abdominal pain, vomiting, bleeding from the gut, kidney failure and shock. There is no specific antiviral treatment, so care is supportive, with fluids, correction of coagulopathy where possible, management of kidney injury and intensive monitoring. Because the disease is notifiable, the public health response begins when the clinician suspects it, and any patient with jaundice, fever and bleeding after travel to an endemic area should be protected from mosquitoes and reported at once.

The yellow fever vaccine is one of the great successes of preventive medicine, and it is a live attenuated vaccine given as a single subcutaneous or intramuscular dose. A single dose is considered sufficient for lifelong protection in most people, although a booster may be advised for certain groups and some countries require a certificate for entry, so current guidance must be checked before travel. The vaccine is contraindicated in infants below a certain age, in pregnancy and breastfeeding in most circumstances, in people with severe immunosuppression including advanced HIV infection or AIDS, and in those with a history of disease of the thymus gland, because the live virus can cause fatal disease of the internal organs or of the nervous system in these groups. Mild reactions of fever, headache, muscle aches and soreness at the injection site are common, and serious reactions are rare but real, so pre-travel counseling must weigh the risk of the disease against the risk of the vaccine.

West Nile virus is transmitted by Culex mosquitoes and maintained in a cycle involving birds, which are the amplifying hosts, and it has spread widely across temperate and tropical regions. The feared complication is neuroinvasive disease, which takes the form of meningitis, encephalitis or acute flaccid paralysis and appears in a small minority of those infected, with the risk rising steeply with age and with immunosuppression. West Nile encephalitis causes confusion, tremor, weakness and sometimes parkinsonian features, and recovery is often incomplete, with fatigue and cognitive difficulty persisting for months. There is no human vaccine and no specific antiviral treatment, so care is supportive, and the nursing role centers on airway protection, prevention of pressure injury and early rehabilitation. Because the virus is carried by ordinary backyard mosquitoes, prevention means eliminating standing water, using repellent and screens, and reporting dead birds where local surveillance asks for it.

Japanese encephalitis is the leading cause of vaccine-preventable encephalitis in Asia, and it falls hardest on children in rural areas where rice paddies and pig pens bring Culex mosquitoes, birds and people into close contact. Infection is usually asymptomatic, but when it invades the central nervous system it produces fever, headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures and focal neurological deficits, and it can progress to coma. There is no specific antiviral treatment, so management is supportive, with attention to seizures, raised pressure inside the skull, airway protection, nutrition and prevention of the complications of immobility. Many survivors are left with intellectual disability, behavioral change, motor weakness, speech difficulty or epilepsy, so the burden outlasts the acute illness by decades and places a lifelong demand on families and health services. Effective vaccines exist in inactivated and live attenuated forms, and they are given in multi-dose schedules whose intervals, ages and boosters differ between countries, so the current national schedule and World Health Organization guidance must be verified before any dose is given.

Tick-borne encephalitis is transmitted by Ixodes ticks and, less commonly, by unpasteurized milk or cheese from infected animals, and it occurs across Europe and northern Asia. The illness is often biphasic, with a first phase of fever, fatigue, muscle aches and headache that settles after about a week, followed by apparent recovery and then a second phase in which the central nervous system is involved. The second phase can present as meningitis, as encephalitis with confusion, tremor, seizures and paralysis, or as inflammation of the spinal cord with weakness of the neck, shoulders and arms, and the neurological damage can be permanent. There is no specific antiviral treatment, so care is supportive and directed at seizures, breathing, pressure area care, bladder management and early rehabilitation. Vaccination is effective and is recommended for people living in or traveling to affected areas, with schedules and boosters that vary by product and by country and must be checked against current guidance.

Rift Valley fever is a zoonosis of sheep, cattle, goats and camels, transmitted to people by mosquitoes and by direct contact with the blood, tissues, abortion products and fluids of infected animals. It appears in explosive outbreaks after heavy rain and flooding, when mosquito populations expand and animals abort in large numbers, so it is a disease of veterinarians, farmers and abattoir workers. Most human infections cause a self-limited febrile illness with headache and muscle pain, but a minority develop hemorrhagic fever, encephalitis or ocular disease with damage to the retina and lasting visual loss. There is no specific antiviral treatment approved for human use, so management is supportive, with strict attention to barrier nursing when bleeding is present and to the safe handling of specimens. Control depends on animal vaccination, on protecting livestock from mosquitoes and on the use of gloves by anyone handling animals or their tissues. This is One Health in practice, because a human outbreak cannot be controlled without controlling the animal outbreak.

Mayaro virus and Oropouche virus are emerging names that clinicians in Latin America and the Caribbean should recognize, and they show how quickly the arboviral map can change. Mayaro virus is maintained in forest cycles involving primates and Haemagogus mosquitoes, and it causes a febrile illness with prominent, sometimes prolonged joint pain that closely resembles chikungunya and is easily mislabeled without laboratory testing. Oropouche virus is transmitted by biting midges and by some mosquitoes, and it has caused large urban outbreaks in the Amazon basin and, more recently, elsewhere in the Americas, with fever, headache, muscle pain, joint pain, nausea and sometimes recurrent symptoms. A recent and deeply concerning finding is the possibility of transmission of Oropouche virus from mother to fetus, with reports of fetal death, congenital malformation and neurological disease in newborns. Diagnosis depends on PCR and antibody testing in reference laboratories, and the practical message is to include these viruses when the presentation fits but dengue and chikungunya tests are negative.

Laboratory diagnosis is a matter of matching the test to the day of illness, because the wrong test at the wrong time produces a falsely reassuring answer. During the first days of fever, when the virus is still in the blood, PCR on serum is the most useful test, and for dengue there is also a test for the non-structural protein 1 antigen that is sensitive early in the illness. After about the fifth day the virus is usually cleared and diagnosis depends on antibodies, and a single positive antibody result can reflect an old infection in someone who has lived in an endemic area, so paired samples taken 2 to 4 weeks apart are far more informative. Cross-reactivity is a serious problem within this group of viruses, so a positive dengue antibody test in a patient previously vaccinated against yellow fever or infected with Zika may not mean dengue, and confirmation may require a neutralization assay in a reference laboratory. The nurse's role in diagnosis is largely logistical, and it consists of drawing the right specimen at the right time, labeling it accurately, transporting it correctly and recording the day of illness.

Infection control for arboviral disease rests on a simple principle, which is that these viruses are not spread from person to person by casual contact but can be spread by the mosquitoes that feed on a patient whose blood carries the virus. The practical measure is therefore to protect the patient from being bitten inside the health facility, especially during the first days of illness. Place the patient in a screened room or under a bed net, use repellent and long clothing, and eliminate standing water in the ward and the courtyard. Standard precautions, including hand hygiene, gloves and safe handling of sharps and body fluids, apply as they do for every patient. Zika is the exception, because it can be transmitted sexually and from mother to fetus, and notification requirements should be met promptly for dengue clusters, yellow fever, Rift Valley fever and any suspected viral hemorrhagic fever.

Vector control for Aedes-borne disease is different from the malaria model that many clinicians know. Because Aedes mosquitoes bite during the day, bed nets treated with insecticide and used at night do not protect against them, and indoor residual spraying has a limited effect on a mosquito that rests in cool, dark corners and feeds by day. The effective measures are removing the containers in which the mosquito breeds, covering or treating water storage vessels, cleaning gutters and drains, and eliminating discarded tires, bottles and plastic containers that collect rain. Personal protection includes repellents with approved active ingredients, long-sleeved clothing, screened windows and doors, and fans that reduce landing and biting, and it should be recommended to the whole household. The nurse who explains the life cycle of the mosquito plainly, and who shows a family the containers in their own compound, changes behavior more effectively than a leaflet.

Counseling before travel is where much arboviral disease is prevented, and it belongs in the same visit as malaria prophylaxis and routine vaccination. The traveler should be told which diseases occur at the destination, which vaccines are available, how long before departure they must be given and which are not available at all, so that the decision to travel rests on accurate information. Yellow fever and Japanese encephalitis have effective vaccines, dengue has a vaccine licensed in some countries for people with documented prior infection, and chikungunya has a vaccine available in certain settings, but each has eligibility criteria that must be checked against current guidance before it is offered. The traveler should also be advised on repellent use, the timing of outdoor activity, clothing, accommodation with screens or air conditioning, and the importance of seeking care promptly for fever after return. Pregnant women and women who may become pregnant need specific advice about Zika and about sexual transmission. The nurse providing this counseling should give a written summary, because a spoken plan is easily forgotten, and should record the advice in the notes.

Special populations require modified surveillance and modified thresholds. Infants and young children with dengue can deteriorate rapidly and may show lethargy, poor feeding, irritability and cold extremities rather than the classic warning signs, so parents must be taught to return immediately if any of these appear. Older adults and people with diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, kidney disease or obesity have a higher risk of severe dengue and less reserve for fluid shifts, so the balance of fluid is narrower and monitoring must be closer. Pregnant women with dengue are at higher risk of severe disease and of adverse pregnancy outcomes, and those with Zika face the additional burden of fetal risk that requires specialist referral and long-term follow-up. Monitoring should therefore be individualized, defining the observations to be recorded, the interval between them, the thresholds that trigger a call and the person responsible, because a monitoring plan that exists only in someone's intention is not a plan at all.

Adverse effects and complications in arboviral care arise as much from treatment as from the disease itself, and the nurse is the person most likely to detect them. Fluid overload is the classic complication of treating dengue, and it appears as puffy eyelids, swelling of the limbs, raised pressure in the neck veins, crackles at the lung bases, breathlessness and a fall in oxygen saturation, and it is more likely when the critical phase was treated with more fluid than the circulation needed. Too little fluid produces the opposite failure, with persistent shock, falling urine output, acid accumulation in the blood and organ injury, so the margin is narrow and assessment must be continuous. Bleeding can follow intramuscular injections, unnecessary punctures of veins, insertion of a urinary catheter and other procedures in a patient with a very low platelet count, so every intervention should be weighed against its bleeding risk. Patients recovering from dengue, chikungunya and West Nile infection may also have fatigue, depression, sleep disturbance and cognitive difficulty that persist after the acute illness, and these deserve assessment rather than dismissal.

The logistics of managing arboviral disease in a resource-limited setting determine what is actually possible, and they deserve as much planning as the clinical algorithm. The first requirement is a reliable way to measure what you are treating, with working thermometers, blood pressure cuffs in pediatric and adult sizes, scales for weight, containers to measure urine, and a functioning centrifuge for hematocrit or a dependable laboratory to which samples can be sent. The second is a secure supply of the relevant fluid, of oral rehydration salts, of acetaminophen in adult and pediatric formulations and of equipment for intravenous access, with a stock system that flags shortages before they become crises. The third is a plan for referral and transport, because some patients will need oxygen, transfusion, dialysis or intensive care that the facility cannot provide, and an honest discussion with the family before transfer is part of good care. Where the workforce is stretched, task-sharing with trained nurses and community health workers extends the reach of surveillance and early warning, provided that supervision and referral pathways are clear.

The nursing role in arboviral disease is continuous and cumulative, beginning before the diagnosis is made and continuing long after the fever has gone. At the bedside, the nurse performs the serial assessment that detects the transition into the critical phase, manages fluid balance with precision, watches for the complications of treatment, protects the patient from further mosquito bites and provides the reassurance frightened families need. In the clinic, the nurse teaches families the warning signs to watch for, the medicines to avoid, the importance of oral fluids and the circumstances that require an immediate return. In the community, the nurse takes part in vector control, outbreak investigation, vaccination campaigns and education about water storage and waste disposal. None of these roles requires permission from anyone else, and each depends on the same skill, which is the ability to observe carefully and to act on what you see.

Surveillance turns individual cases into usable knowledge, and it depends on clinicians and nurses who report rather than wait to be asked. Many countries require notification of dengue, chikungunya, Zika, yellow fever, Japanese encephalitis, West Nile virus infection and Rift Valley fever, and the requirement usually attaches to suspicion rather than confirmation, so a report should not be delayed for a laboratory result. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control all publish surveillance data and outbreak notices that guide clinical suspicion and travel advice. Laboratory confirmation, case definition and the systematic recording of place and date are what allow a cluster to be recognized as an outbreak and a response to begin. The nurse is often the person who notices the pattern first, simply because the nurse is the one taking the observations, and that observation should be passed upward without hesitation.

To summarize, arboviral diseases are infections carried by mosquitoes and ticks whose severity ranges from a mild fever to fatal shock, and they share a dependence on the vectors that live among us. Dengue demands the most disciplined nursing attention, because 4 serotypes, the enhancing effect of a second infection and the abrupt onset of plasma leakage make the transition from fever to shock the central event to detect. Watch for abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, bleeding, lethargy and fluid accumulation, remember that the critical phase often begins as the fever breaks, and treat fluid as a drug that must be adjusted against frequent reassessment. Chikungunya brings chronic joint pain and neonatal risk, Zika brings congenital infection and Guillain-Barré syndrome and can be transmitted sexually, yellow fever and Japanese encephalitis have effective vaccines but no specific treatment once disease begins, and West Nile, tick-borne encephalitis, Rift Valley fever, Mayaro and Oropouche each carry their own patterns of disease. Prevention is largely a matter of controlling Aedes mosquitoes, avoiding bites during the day, using barrier precautions with sick animals, vaccinating where a vaccine exists and counseling before travel. All regimens in this chapter are current guidance rather than settled truth, because they are revised as evidence accumulates, they differ between countries, and the current guideline must be checked before any drug, fluid or vaccine is given.

# Chapter 11 — Leishmaniasis

Leishmaniasis is caused by protozoan parasites of the genus Leishmania, transmitted by the bite of infected female sand flies, and it appears in three clinical forms so different that a listener may wonder why they share a chapter. The World Health Organization counts it among the neglected tropical diseases and estimates between 700,000 and 1 million new cases each year, with the visceral form alone causing an estimated 50,000 to 90,000 deaths annually when untreated. The parasites occur in more than 90 countries, and the burden falls hardest on people in poverty, in poor housing, and in conflict zones where the vector and the animal reservoir meet human beings. The three forms are visceral leishmaniasis, which attacks the internal organs and kills if untreated; cutaneous leishmaniasis, which produces skin ulcers that heal slowly and scar; and mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, which destroys the nose, the mouth, and the throat. Which form appears is determined above all by the species of parasite and secondarily by the immune response of the host. This chapter follows the parasite from the sand fly into the macrophage, through the three forms, through the medicines and their dangers, and finally to the nursing work that carries a patient through treatment and recovery.

The parasite has two forms, and the listener needs both to understand the diagnosis. In the gut of the sand fly it exists as a promastigote, an elongated cell with a free flagellum that propels it forward, and when the female takes a blood meal she injects these forms into the skin with saliva that dilates the small vessels and suppresses the local immune response. The promastigotes are taken up by macrophages, the cells whose ordinary work is to engulf and destroy invaders, and inside the macrophage they transform into amastigotes. The amastigote is round or oval, has no free flagellum, and divides until the macrophage bursts, and it is the amastigote that the microscopist looks for in a stained aspirate. More than 20 species are recognized, each with its own geography and host. Some are maintained in people, so that an infected person is the reservoir from which sand flies become infected, which is the pattern of Leishmania donovani in the Indian subcontinent, while others are maintained in animals, with dogs as the reservoir for Leishmania infantum around the Mediterranean and in Latin America. The distinction matters, because a parasite held in people can be interrupted by treating every human case, while one held in animals cannot.

The vector is a sand fly, an insect of the genus Phlebotomus in the Old World and of the genus Lutzomyia in the New World. Sand flies are small, 2 to 3 millimeters long, with hairy bodies and wings held in a shape like the letter V at rest. They fly silently, they are most active in the evening and through the night, and their bite is often not felt. The female, which needs blood for her eggs, breeds in moist organic material, in the cracks of mud walls, in animal sheds, in rodent burrows, and in leaf litter around houses. Sand flies are weak fliers that stay close to the breeding site, so the disease is intensely focal, sometimes appearing at one end of a village and not the other. They can pass through the mesh of a bed net that is untreated or coarsely woven, so the net that protects against malaria is not automatically enough. Control rests on the measures that reduce other vector-borne diseases, which are indoor residual spraying, insecticide-treated bed nets, screening of windows and doors, removal of organic waste and rubble, treatment of animal sheds, and repellents on exposed skin.

Which of the three diseases emerges depends on where the parasite can survive, and that is largely a property of the species. Species that multiply in the macrophages of the spleen, the liver, the bone marrow, and the lymph nodes produce visceral disease, and the two most important are Leishmania donovani, which causes human-maintained disease in the Indian subcontinent and East Africa, and Leishmania infantum, which causes animal-maintained disease around the Mediterranean, in the Middle East, and in Latin America. Species that remain in the skin produce cutaneous disease, including Leishmania major and Leishmania tropica in the Old World and Leishmania mexicana in the Americas. Species that leave the skin, travel through the lymph vessels, and settle in the mucosa of the upper airway produce mucocutaneous disease, and the leading species are Leishmania braziliensis, Leishmania panamensis, and Leishmania guyanensis. The host contributes as much as the parasite in some patients, because a person who is malnourished, who is infected with HIV, who takes corticosteroids, or who is otherwise immunosuppressed is more likely to develop severe and disseminated disease and less likely to respond to treatment. 

Visceral leishmaniasis, also called kala-azar, is the form that kills, and its course is insidious. The incubation period is usually 2 to 8 months, but it can be as short as 10 days or as long as several years, which makes the exposure history essential. The patient begins with fever, often twice in 24 hours, with drenching night sweats, progressive weakness, loss of appetite, and weight loss. The spleen enlarges steadily and is usually the most striking finding, followed by the liver, while in East Africa the lymph nodes may also enlarge and the classic Indian picture is fever with a large spleen and little else. The mechanism behind the fever and the wasting is a heavy parasite load in the network of macrophages that fills the spleen, the liver, and the bone marrow. The spleen removes blood cells faster than the marrow can replace them, the marrow itself is crowded with infected macrophages, and the result is pancytopenia, a fall in red cells, white cells, and platelets together. Untreated, the patient becomes profoundly anemic, bleeds easily, and cannot fight bacteria, and those three deficits rather than the parasite usually cause death within 2 years.

One complication of visceral disease is easy to miss and matters to whole communities. Months to years after apparently successful treatment, some patients develop post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, a skin condition of pale or hypopigmented macules, small papules, and nodules, most often on the face, the trunk, and the limbs. In the Indian subcontinent it appears most often 6 months to 3 years after treatment and is reported in perhaps 5 to 10 per cent of patients treated for visceral disease, while in East Africa it tends to appear earlier, sometimes while treatment is still being given, and it often resolves on its own. The lesions contain amastigotes, and the sand fly that feeds on them can become infected and then infect other people, so a person who looks cured and feels well can sustain transmission in a community that believes visceral leishmaniasis has been eliminated from its villages. Treating these lesions is not cosmetic care, and the nurse who notices new pale patches or nodules on the face of a former patient and reports them is closing a loop that vertical programs most often leave open.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis is the form that scars, and its natural history is measured in months. The lesion begins as a small papule at the site of a fly bite, usually on an exposed part of the body such as the face, the forearm, the wrist, or the calf, enlarges into a firm nodule, and after several weeks to months breaks down into an ulcer with a raised and indurated border and a crusted base. The lesion is painless, which allows patients to ignore it for a long time. In the Old World the wet ulcer of Leishmania major develops quickly and heals sooner, while the dry ulcer of Leishmania tropica enlarges slowly and lasts longer, and both have carried local names such as the Aleppo boil and the Baghdad boil. Most lesions heal on their own over 6 months to 2 years, leaving a depressed, pale, permanent scar, and the scar is the true burden of this form, because it falls on the face of a child or the hand of a young person and it carries stigma, exclusion from marriage, and interruption of schooling and work. The differential diagnosis includes cutaneous tuberculosis, sporotrichosis, squamous cell carcinoma, myiasis, and a foreign body reaction, so a lesion that does not heal must be sampled rather than watched indefinitely.

Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis is the most destructive form, and it is the reason that New World cutaneous lesions are treated more aggressively than Old World lesions. It is caused chiefly by Leishmania braziliensis and its close relatives, and it ordinarily appears months to years after a cutaneous lesion has healed, although the original ulcer may still be active or may never have been noticed. The parasite spreads through the lymph vessels from the skin to the mucosa of the nose, the pharynx, the larynx, and the mouth. The earliest symptoms are nasal stuffiness, crusting, and nosebleeds, which are easily mistaken for allergy or a common cold, and destruction follows. The nasal septum perforates, the palate erodes, the turbinates are consumed, and the collapse of the nasal bridge produces the characteristic tapir nose deformity. Laryngeal involvement can obstruct the airway, and the loss of the palate allows food and liquid to escape into the nose and the airway, which leads to aspiration and repeated pneumonia. The disfigurement is severe, progressive, and permanent, and the psychosocial damage is often worse than the physical damage, so every skin lesion acquired where Leishmania braziliensis circulates deserves serious consideration for systemic treatment.

Diagnosis depends on demonstrating the parasite, its genetic material, or a specific immune response. In visceral disease the specimen of choice is a bone marrow aspirate examined for amastigotes inside macrophages, while splenic aspiration gives a higher yield but risks hemorrhage and is reserved for centers that can manage it. Microscopy is the foundation, but its sensitivity ranges from about 50 to 85 per cent and depends on the skill of the microscopist, so a negative smear does not exclude the diagnosis. Testing for parasite DNA by PCR is the most sensitive method, it can be applied to blood, bone marrow, lymph node, skin, or mucosal tissue, and it can identify the species, which increasingly guides the choice of drug. The rK39 rapid test is an immunochromatographic strip that detects antibodies against a parasite antigen, with a sensitivity above 90 per cent in the Indian subcontinent and roughly 60 to 80 per cent in East Africa. The test remains positive for years after cure, so it cannot prove cure or confirm relapse, and it fails more often in patients with HIV, in whom the parasite must be found directly.

Treatment depends on the form of the disease, the species, the country, the immune status of the patient, and the medicines available, and no single regimen fits every setting. Four drugs carry most of the work, which are liposomal amphotericin B, miltefosine, sodium stibogluconate, and paromomycin, each with a different mechanism, route, and set of dangers. The World Health Organization publishes guidance for each region, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention publishes guidance for the United States, but the regimens differ between countries and change as new trials and resistance data appear. The nurse who gives any of these medicines must work from the current national protocol and product label rather than from memory or from a course such as this one, because a printed dose becomes outdated while a patient is still receiving it. The dose is calculated on the weight measured that day and adjusted for the renal and hepatic function measured that week.

Liposomal amphotericin B is the preferred treatment for visceral leishmaniasis in most settings where it can be afforded, because the medicine is packaged inside lipid spheres that concentrate in the liver, the spleen, and the bone marrow, exactly where the parasite lives. It binds to ergosterol in the parasite membrane and opens holes in it, which kills the amastigote. For visceral disease in the Indian subcontinent, current guidance supports a single intravenous dose of 10 milligrams per kilogram, which is remarkable for a disease that once required a month of injections. Around the Mediterranean and in South America a total dose of 3 milligrams per kilogram is often given as several doses over several days, and in patients with HIV co-infection the total dose is higher and the course longer. The infusion is given intravenously in a fluid volume over about 2 hours, and the nurse watches for fever, chills, shivering, and back pain during the infusion. The toxicities that matter are renal, with a rise in creatinine and a loss of potassium and magnesium, and the liposomal form is far gentler on the kidney than the older deoxycholate preparation. Infusion reactions are common and unpleasant but manageable with a slower infusion, hydration, and premedication.

Miltefosine is the only oral medicine for leishmaniasis in routine use, so a patient can complete treatment at home. It disrupts the phospholipid metabolism of the parasite membrane, and it is used for visceral, cutaneous, and post-kala-azar dermal disease. For visceral disease the dose is 2.5 milligrams per kilogram per day by mouth for 28 days, usually given as 50 milligrams twice a day for patients above 25 kilograms and 50 milligrams once a day for those below. The most important property of miltefosine is that it causes severe harm to a developing fetus. It is contraindicated in pregnancy, every woman of childbearing age must have a documented negative pregnancy test before the first dose, and contraception must continue for 5 months after the last dose because the drug remains in the body. The common adverse effects are vomiting, diarrhea, nausea, and loss of appetite, and treatment is often accompanied by a rise in creatinine and in liver enzymes. Adherence to a 28-day oral course is the central clinical challenge, and the nurse who explains why the full course matters, counts the remaining tablets at each visit, and treats vomiting as a threat to cure holds the difference between cure and relapse.

Sodium stibogluconate and meglumine antimoniate are pentavalent antimonials, long the standard treatment for leishmaniasis and still used in many countries, particularly for cutaneous and mucocutaneous disease, at 20 milligrams per kilogram per day given intravenously or intramuscularly for 28 days. Antimonials prolong the interval between the Q wave and the T wave on the electrocardiogram, and that prolongation can progress to a dangerous ventricular rhythm and to sudden death, which is rare but real. They cause pancreatitis with abdominal pain and a rise in amylase and lipase, and they cause liver injury, renal injury, joint pain, and reactions at the injection site. Risk factors for sudden death include increasing age, heart disease, and renal impairment, and the drug is avoided in patients with HIV because the pancreatic and cardiac risks are greater. Every patient receiving an antimonial needs a baseline electrocardiogram, repeated electrocardiograms during treatment, and periodic measurement of pancreatic enzymes, liver enzymes, renal function, and blood counts.

Paromomycin is an aminoglycoside antibiotic that is also active against Leishmania, and it is given intramuscularly at 15 milligrams per kilogram per day for 21 days. Its main dangers are damage to the ear and damage to the kidney, and hearing loss may begin with ringing in the ears or difficulty hearing high tones and may become permanent, so audiometry before and during treatment is the safeguard. The nurse must ask the patient directly about ringing or muffled hearing at every visit, because the damage can begin before the patient notices it. The World Health Organization supports combination regimens to shorten treatment and to protect the existing drugs from resistance, including paromomycin with sodium stibogluconate in East Africa and liposomal amphotericin B with miltefosine in the Indian subcontinent.

The treatment of cutaneous leishmaniasis depends on whether the lesion is likely to heal safely on its own or to leave unacceptable damage. A single small lesion caused by Leishmania major in the Old World will usually heal without treatment, and the decision may reasonably be to keep it clean and wait, while lesions that are multiple, large, on the face, over a joint, or caused by a species with the potential to spread to the mucosa are treated systemically. Local options include the injection of an antimonial directly into the lesion, heat therapy that raises the lesion to 50 degrees Celsius for about 30 seconds, and freezing with liquid nitrogen. Systemic options include miltefosine, sodium stibogluconate, and liposomal amphotericin B, and the choice is dictated by the species, the number and the site of the lesions, the pregnancy status of the patient, and the national protocol. Mucocutaneous disease requires systemic treatment, often with a higher cumulative dose of liposomal amphotericin B or with an antimonial, and it requires prolonged follow-up because relapse after apparent cure is common and because the destruction can resume quietly in the nose while the patient feels well.

Monitoring is where nursing practice carries the greatest weight, and it should be planned before the first dose rather than improvised afterward. The baseline assessment includes the weight, a complete blood count, liver enzymes, creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, electrolytes, pancreatic enzymes, an electrocardiogram for any patient who will receive an antimonial, a pregnancy test for every woman of childbearing age, and audiometry for any patient who will receive paromomycin. During treatment the nurse records the temperature, the symptoms, the weight, and the fluid intake and urine output, and ensures that the laboratory tests are drawn on schedule rather than when the patient becomes visibly ill. For antimonials the nurse watches for palpitations, dizziness, fainting, and chest discomfort and reports them immediately, because the first sign of a dangerous rhythm may also be the last. For miltefosine the nurse watches the gastrointestinal symptoms, tracks adherence by counting the tablets, and reminds the patient of the contraception rule at every visit. For any patient receiving a potentially nephrotoxic drug the nurse keeps the patient hydrated and watches the urine output, and for any patient receiving an aminoglycoside the nurse asks about hearing at every visit. None of these tasks is glamorous, and all of them are the reason a treatment which can kill a parasite can be given without killing the patient.

HIV infection and visceral leishmaniasis form one of the most difficult combinations in tropical medicine. HIV raises the risk that an infection with Leishmania will progress to visceral disease many times over, while visceral leishmaniasis accelerates the decline of the immune system. The central clinical problem is relapse. Without effective antiretroviral therapy, relapse occurs in a large proportion of patients, often within a year.
