The disease is not transmitted from person to person, but agricultural workers, soldiers and ecotourists who walk the same ground are all at risk.

The geography of scrub typhus was once drawn as a triangle covering Japan, Korea, China, Taiwan, Southeast Asia, India and northern Australia, and that region remains the core of the endemic area. In the last two decades it has been recognized far outside the triangle, in the Middle East, Africa, South America and islands of the Pacific and Indian Oceans. In much of Asia it is a leading cause of undifferentiated fever and a common reason for admission with fever of unknown origin. Outbreaks have followed floods, displaced populations, military operations and the clearing of land, so scrub typhus belongs in the differential for any febrile patient with a rural exposure almost anywhere in the tropics.

After an incubation of 6 to 21 days, scrub typhus begins with fever, headache, muscle pain and cough, and an eschar is present in roughly half of patients. Lymph nodes enlarge, the conjunctivae redden, and a flat spotted rash may appear on the trunk and spread outward. If treatment is delayed, the organism damages the pulmonary capillaries, the patient develops inflammation of the lung tissue and then acute respiratory distress syndrome, and respiratory failure becomes the most common cause of death. Inflammation of the brain, inflammation of the heart muscle, acute kidney injury, shock and bleeding from the gut also occur, and mortality without treatment ranges from about 6 per cent to 30 per cent or more when diagnosis is delayed.

Scrub typhus responds quickly to doxycycline, and current guidance describes 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 7 days for adults, with a single 200 milligram dose used in mild illness in some settings. Azithromycin at 500 milligrams once daily for 3 days is an accepted alternative and the preferred choice in pregnancy, while intravenous doxycycline at 100 milligrams every 12 hours is used when the patient cannot swallow. The fever typically falls within 24 to 48 hours of the first dose, and that rapid defervescence is itself a diagnostic clue. Read those numbers as an illustration rather than a prescription, because guidance is revised and the current World Health Organization and national guideline must be checked before treatment is ordered.

The question of doxycycline in children and in pregnancy comes up with every one of these diseases, and the concern is staining of developing teeth and effects on growing bone. That concern arose from repeated long courses given for acne, and short courses of the kind used for rickettsial disease have not been shown to cause clinically important staining. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the American Academy of Pediatrics both recommend doxycycline for suspected rickettsial illness in children of any age, because the risk of the disease outweighs the risk of the drug. In pregnancy the balance is harder, since the drug crosses the placenta, but a rickettsial infection can kill the mother, so azithromycin is often preferred for scrub typhus and specialist advice should be sought.

Rocky Mountain spotted fever is caused by Rickettsia rickettsii and transmitted by hard ticks, chiefly the American dog tick and the Rocky Mountain wood tick, with the brown dog tick responsible for outbreaks in the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. Despite its name, most cases in the United States occur in the south-Atlantic and south-central states, and the disease also occurs across Central and South America. The tick must remain attached for several hours to transmit the organism, and children, older adults and people with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency are at greater risk of severe disease. The illness begins abruptly after an incubation of 2 to 14 days with fever, severe headache, muscle pain and vomiting, and the patient often looks toxic from the first day.

The rash usually appears 2 to 5 days after the fever, starting as small pink spots on the wrists and ankles and spreading inward over the arms, legs and trunk. It often involves the palms and soles, and it later becomes spotted with bleeding as the vasculitis deepens. It may be faint, hard to see on deeply pigmented skin, or entirely absent in a minority of patients, so its absence never excludes the diagnosis. Severe disease brings gangrene of the limbs, inflammation of the brain, respiratory failure, kidney injury and shock, and without treatment reported case fatality reaches 20 to 30 per cent, most deaths following a delay in starting doxycycline.

Doxycycline is the treatment of choice at every age, and current guidance gives 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day for adults and 2.2 milligrams per kilogram of body weight twice a day for children, with a maximum of 100 milligrams per dose. Treatment continues for at least 3 days after the fever settles, usually 5 to 7 days in total and longer when the disease is severe. Here dose verification is not a formality, because the pediatric dose is calculated by weight, the maximum for each administration must be respected, and recommended durations differ between countries. Confirm the weight, confirm the concentration on the label, and confirm the current guideline before the first dose, because a delay while the team debates the diagnosis is more dangerous than the antibiotic itself.

Mediterranean spotted fever, also called boutonneuse fever, is caused by Rickettsia conorii and carried by the brown dog tick, Rhipicephalus sanguineus, which thrives in kennels and around human dwellings. It occurs around the Mediterranean basin, along the Black Sea, and in parts of Africa, the Middle East and India. A black eschar, sometimes called the tache noire, marks the bite site in most patients, and fever, headache and muscle pain follow, with a rash that often includes the palms and soles. Most cases are mild, but severe forms with involvement of several organs occur, particularly in people with diabetes, alcohol use disorder, glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency or advanced age, and doxycycline is the mainstay of treatment.

African tick bite fever is caused by Rickettsia africae and transmitted by Amblyomma ticks, which are aggressive, active by day and abundant in the game reserves and savanna of sub-Saharan Africa and the Caribbean. It is now one of the most common causes of fever in travelers returning from safari, and clusters occur in groups who travel together. Several eschars are common, often with enlarged regional lymph nodes, while the fever, headache and muscle pain are usually mild, and a rash is absent or sparse in many patients. Other organisms in the spotted fever group cause Indian tick typhus, Queensland tick typhus, Siberian tick typhus, Japanese spotted fever, and the infections due to Rickettsia parkeri and Rickettsia felis, and doxycycline treats all of them.

Murine typhus is caused by Rickettsia typhi and maintained in rats and their fleas, with the cat flea also playing a part, and it spreads when infected flea feces are scratched into a bite wound or inhaled as dust. It is a disease of ports, warehouses, grain stores, sewers and crowded urban neighborhoods, found worldwide in warm and coastal regions. Unlike scrub typhus and the spotted fevers it does not produce an eschar, and a rash appears in only about half of patients, usually on the trunk. Fever, headache and muscle pain dominate, severe cases with pneumonia, kidney injury and neurological involvement do occur, and doxycycline at 100 milligrams twice a day for 7 to 10 days is the standard treatment.

Epidemic typhus is caused by Rickettsia prowazekii and transmitted by the body louse, which lives in clothing and feeds on people who cannot wash or change their clothes. It appears where cold, crowding, poverty and displacement meet, in refugee camps, prisons and war zones, and it has shaped the outcome of armies and famines for centuries. Fever, headache, a rash beginning on the trunk and spreading outward, confusion and shock characterize the severe form, and mortality without treatment can reach 20 per cent or more. The organism can persist in lymph nodes for years and cause a returning illness known as Brill-Zinsser disease, which can seed a new outbreak wherever lice are present; doxycycline at 100 milligrams twice a day for 7 to 10 days is effective, and delousing interrupts transmission.

Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, which is not a rickettsia in the strict sense, and it is not transmitted by a bite at all. The organism forms a resistant spore-like structure that survives drying and is shed in the birth products, urine, feces and milk of infected sheep, goats and cattle. Infection follows inhalation of contaminated dust or aerosol, so the people at risk are farmers, shepherds, abattoir workers, veterinarians, laboratory staff, and anyone living downwind of a lambing or kidding shed. The incubation period is usually 1 to 3 weeks, and because a single infected placenta can contaminate a large area, the nurse should ask directly about animal contact and occupational exposure.

Acute Q fever is often silent or mild and settles on its own, but when it produces illness it usually takes the form of fever with severe headache, an atypical pneumonia, or inflammation of the liver. The chest radiograph may show patchy shadowing, and the patient may have a cough and breathlessness out of proportion to the physical findings. The dangerous consequence is chronic Q fever, which appears months to years later and most often infects the heart valves, particularly in people with pre-existing valve disease, vascular grafts, immunosuppression or pregnancy. It is difficult to diagnose because blood cultures are usually negative, so it requires PCR and serology together with careful clinical assessment, and a post-infectious fatigue syndrome can also leave the patient disabled.

Acute Q fever is treated with doxycycline at 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 14 days, one of the few regimens in this chapter that runs beyond a single week. Chronic Q fever, especially infection of the heart valves, requires prolonged combination treatment with doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine, often for 18 months to 3 years, under the care of an infectious disease specialist. Q fever in pregnancy carries a risk of miscarriage, stillbirth and preterm delivery and requires specialist care, while avoiding birth products, controlling dust and pasteurizing milk are the practical preventive measures. Confirm every regimen against the current national guideline, because the durations are long, the alternatives are few and the consequences of an error are serious.

Bartonellosis, also called Carrion disease, is caused by Bartonella bacilliformis and transmitted by sandflies of the genus Lutzomyia in the high Andean valleys of Peru, Ecuador and Colombia. It occurs at altitudes of roughly 500 to 3000 meters and has two distinct stages, which can appear in the same patient weeks apart. The first is Oroya fever, the acute and dangerous phase, and the second is verruga peruana, the eruptive phase with its crop of red nodules. The sandfly is small, bites at night and breeds in the sandy soil of these valleys, so the exposure history is unusually specific and unusually helpful.

Oroya fever begins after an incubation of about 2 to 3 weeks with fever, severe pallor, yellowing of the eyes, enlargement of the liver and spleen, and swollen lymph nodes. The organism invades the red blood cells and destroys them, producing a rapidly progressive anemia that the bone marrow cannot replace quickly enough. The greatest danger is secondary infection, particularly with Salmonella species and other organisms from the gut, which is a leading cause of death in the acute phase. Untreated mortality in the acute stage has historically been very high, and even with treatment the patient may need a blood transfusion, so watch for worsening anemia, falling blood pressure and any new infection.

Treatment of the acute stage uses doxycycline, ciprofloxacin or chloramphenicol, sometimes in combination, while the eruptive stage responds to azithromycin or rifampin. Chloramphenicol has been favored because it also covers the Salmonella co-infection, but its rare and serious effect on the bone marrow makes the choice a careful one. Fluoroquinolones are avoided in children and in pregnancy in most circumstances, and every dose and duration must be checked against the current World Health Organization and national guidance. Cat-scratch disease, caused by Bartonella henselae and transmitted by a kitten scratch or bite, is far more common and usually far milder, producing enlarged regional lymph nodes and fever that settle without treatment, though azithromycin shortens the course.

The Borrelia species cause two groups of disease, the Lyme group and the relapsing fevers, and both belong in the differential diagnosis for a febrile patient with the right exposure. Borrelia burgdorferi and its relatives are transmitted by Ixodes ticks, which are temperate-zone vectors maintained by rodents and deer rather than tropical ones, but travelers and migrants move the disease across borders. The early illness is marked by erythema migrans, a slowly expanding red ring at the bite site, with fever, headache and muscle aches. Untreated, it can spread to cause weakness of the facial nerve, inflammation of the coverings of the brain, inflammation of the heart and later arthritis, and a late skin change called acrodermatitis chronica atrophicans also occurs.

Early Lyme disease is treated with doxycycline at 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 10 to 14 days, or with amoxicillin at 500 milligrams three times a day, or with cefuroxime axetil at 500 milligrams twice a day. Pediatric doses are calculated by weight, and when the nervous system or the heart is significantly involved, intravenous therapy such as ceftriaxone is used for 14 to 28 days. In pregnancy amoxicillin is generally preferred, and some patients report persistent symptoms after adequate treatment, which is a real problem but does not respond to prolonged antibiotic courses. Verify the regimen and its duration against the current national guideline, and remember that prevention rests on repellent, permethrin-treated clothing and a full-body tick check.

The relapsing fevers are caused by several Borrelia species and transmitted either by body lice, in the case of Borrelia recurrentis, or by soft ticks of the genus Ornithodoros that live in rodent burrows and animal shelters. The hallmark is a fever that lasts several days, breaks, then returns after an interval, often for several cycles, as the organism changes its surface proteins and escapes the immune response. Louse-borne relapsing fever spreads when an infected louse is crushed on the skin, while the tick-borne form follows the bite of a soft tick that feeds quickly at night and is rarely noticed. During the febrile episodes the organisms are numerous in the blood and can sometimes be seen on an ordinary stained blood film, while complications include inflammation of the liver, inflammation of the brain, bleeding and loss of pregnancy.

Louse-borne relapsing fever responds to a single dose of doxycycline at 200 milligrams or a single dose of benzylpenicillin, while the tick-borne form is treated with doxycycline at 100 milligrams twice a day for 7 days. The first dose can trigger a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction, in which fever, shivering, a rise in heart rate, falling blood pressure and worsening of symptoms appear within a few hours as the organisms are killed and their contents released. This reaction is common and can be fatal if it is not anticipated, so the first dose should be given where the patient can be observed, with fluids and support for the circulation close at hand. Do not give the first dose at night and send the patient home, and tell the family that the reaction is expected; corticosteroids are sometimes used on specialist advice.

Anaplasmosis is caused by Anaplasma phagocytophilum, which infects a type of white blood cell called the neutrophil and is transmitted by Ixodes ticks, while ehrlichiosis is caused by Ehrlichia chaffeensis, which infects the monocyte and is transmitted chiefly by the lone star tick. Both produce a nonspecific febrile illness with headache, muscle pain and malaise, and both bring low white cell counts, low platelet counts and raised liver enzymes. A rash is uncommon in anaplasmosis and appears in only a minority of patients with ehrlichiosis, so these diseases usually present without any skin finding, which is the trap. Severe disease can bring respiratory failure, shock and neurological damage, and doxycycline at 100 milligrams twice a day, or the equivalent weight-based dose in children, is given for 7 to 14 days.

The diagnostic difficulty in this group is not that the tests are inaccurate but that they arrive too late to guide treatment. Serology by indirect immunofluorescence requires an acute sample taken in the first days of illness and a convalescent one taken 2 to 4 weeks later, and the diagnosis is supported by a fourfold rise between them. A single early sample is usually negative, so a negative result says nothing useful at the moment of decision, and the old Weil-Felix test has been abandoned because it is neither sensitive nor specific. PCR on blood, and on a swab or biopsy of an eschar, can give an answer early, but its sensitivity falls once antibiotics have been given, so take the sample with the first dose.

For all of these reasons the guiding principle is to treat on suspicion and not to wait for confirmation. The World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention both state that when the clinical picture and the exposure history suggest a rickettsial illness, effective antibiotic treatment should begin immediately, without awaiting laboratory results. In Rocky Mountain spotted fever the risk of death rises markedly when doxycycline is started after the fifth day of illness, and the same pattern is described in severe scrub typhus. Antibiotics given early can blunt the antibody response and complicate a later serological test, but that is a reason to record the treatment and interpret the result with care, not to withhold the drug from a deteriorating patient.

The differential diagnosis of these illnesses is the differential diagnosis of fever itself, and a few alternatives must be excluded alongside any rickettsial diagnosis. Malaria is the first, because it is common in the same places, it can kill within a day, and it is confirmed or excluded by a test available almost everywhere. Dengue and the other viral diseases carried by mosquitoes and ticks, leptospirosis, typhoid fever, meningococcal disease, viral hepatitis, measles and ordinary bacterial sepsis all overlap with the picture described here. Co-infection is not rare, so send the malaria test, the blood cultures and the rickettsial sample together and start empirical treatment for the most dangerous possibility.

The logistics of this chapter matter as much as the medicine, because the tests are slow to arrive while the drugs are simple. Doxycycline is inexpensive, stable and widely available as tablets and capsules, and it should be part of the essential stock of any clinic that sees febrile patients in an endemic area. The intravenous form may be unavailable, serology requires a reference laboratory and a cold chain, results may take weeks, and PCR requires the correct tube, prompt transport and a laboratory that offers the test. The nurse who manages the stock register, checks expiry dates, rotates supplies and arranges transport is doing work that directly determines whether a patient is treated on time, so never let a pending result or an empty shelf delay the first dose.

Monitoring in these illnesses is mostly the careful repetition of simple observations, and it is where the advanced practice nurse earns the title. Record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation at fixed intervals, increase the frequency when the patient is unstable, and assess mental state at every set of observations. Measure urine output and fluid balance, watch for the swelling and crackles that signal fluid overload or injury to the lung, and follow the hemoglobin, the platelet count, the liver enzymes and the kidney function. Compare each result with the last rather than with the normal range alone, because deterioration in scrub typhus and in Rocky Mountain spotted fever often occurs in the second week, and a patient who improves and then worsens must be reassessed from the beginning.

Doxycycline is well tolerated, but it has practical effects the nurse must anticipate and teach. Nausea, vomiting and abdominal discomfort are the most common, and they can be reduced by taking the medicine with food, although milk may reduce absorption in a patient whose treatment depends on adequate blood levels. Irritation and ulceration of the esophagus occur when the capsule is swallowed with too little water or when the patient lies down immediately afterward, so each dose should be taken with a full glass of water and the patient should remain upright for at least 30 minutes. Sensitivity to sunlight is a real risk in the tropics, yeast infections can follow a course of treatment, and antacids, calcium, iron and magnesium should be separated from the dose by about 2 hours.

Supportive care follows the same principles as in any severe febrile illness, and it sometimes saves the patient while the antibiotic is working. Give medicine to reduce fever for comfort, maintain hydration by mouth or intravenously, provide oxygen and breathing support for respiratory failure, and support the circulation in shock. Corticosteroids are used in some severe scrub typhus and in the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction only on specialist advice, because the evidence is limited and the risk of harm is real. Population prevention means controlling the vector that matters for each disease, with rodent and flea control for murine typhus, delousing for epidemic typhus, and repellents, permethrin-treated clothing and a tick check for the rest. An insecticide-treated bed net protects against mosquitoes at night and against lice not at all, so it should never be presented as protection against ticks, mites and chiggers.

The nursing role in this chapter can be stated in a few concrete habits. Take the exposure history with the same care you take in malaria, asking about farming, camping, safari, military service, displacement, animal contact and the kind of housing the patient lives in. Perform a complete skin survey for the eschar in good light, document it precisely, and prompt the team to start empirical doxycycline when the picture fits rather than accept a plan that waits for serology. Verify every dose against the current guideline, monitor for the complications and adverse effects described here, and educate the patient and the family about fever control, hydration and when to return. Recognize that pregnancy, childhood, older age, immunosuppression and absence of the spleen all raise the risk of severe disease, and let each lower your threshold for admission.

Consider a composite patient such as a 34 year old farmer from a rural district in northern Thailand who presents in the rainy season with 8 days of fever, severe headache, a dry cough and breathlessness. He has no rash, and the examination finds a black crusted lesion in the left groin that he had not noticed and which he attributes to a scratch. His chest radiograph shows patchy shadowing on both sides, his platelet count is low and his liver enzymes are raised, while malaria testing is negative. The correct response is not to wait for rickettsial serology, which will not return in time to help, but to start doxycycline on the basis of the exposure, the eschar and the lung involvement, and to support his breathing while the antibiotic takes effect.

To summarize, the rickettsioses and the other vector-borne bacteria gather many diseases under a single clinical habit, which is to think of them before the laboratory does. Scrub typhus, the spotted fever group, murine and epidemic typhus, Q fever, bartonellosis, the Borrelia infections, anaplasmosis and ehrlichiosis all present as fever with headache and often a rash or an eschar, and all can become severe when treatment is delayed. The tests that confirm them arrive after the decision point, so the decision rests on the exposure history, the physical examination and the deliberate search for the eschar. Doxycycline treats most of them, it is safe in short courses in children, and it is used in pregnancy when the illness is serious enough to threaten the mother. The nurse's contribution is to ask about the bite, to undress the patient and look, to insist on empirical treatment rather than watchful waiting, and to verify each dose against the current guideline.

# Chapter 15 — Soil-Transmitted Helminths

Soil-transmitted helminths are a group of parasitic worms whose eggs or larvae reach a new human host through soil contaminated with human feces, and they are among the most common infections of humankind. The group contains four worms that every advanced practice nurse in tropical medicine must know, and each one produces its own pattern of illness. They are the roundworm Ascaris lumbricoides, the two hookworms Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, the whipworm Trichuris trichiura, and the threadworm Strongyloides stercoralis. Together they infect an estimated 1.5 billion people, they are concentrated in the poorest communities of Africa, Asia, and Latin America, and they are a reason that children in those communities are shorter, lighter, and more anemic than they should be. None is transmitted by an insect, none requires an animal reservoir, and none is prevented by a vaccine. They are transmitted by poverty itself, by the absence of a latrine, by walking barefoot, and by the use of untreated human waste to fertilize crops. This chapter follows each worm in turn, then turns to the laboratory, the medicines, the campaigns that deliver those medicines to whole schools at once, and the nursing work that turns a deworming tablet into a lasting change.

Transmission is simple, and that simplicity makes these worms hard to eliminate. Ascaris and Trichuris are transmitted when a person swallows eggs that have matured in warm, moist soil, usually on unwashed hands, on raw vegetables, or on food prepared by someone whose hands carry the eggs. Hookworm and Strongyloides are transmitted when larvae that have hatched in the soil penetrate intact skin, most often the skin of bare feet, which is why these infections were once common among people who worked without shoes. The larvae wait in the soil for the warmth and moisture of a human foot, and they enter through hair follicles or small abrasions the person never noticed. Human waste used as fertilizer, a practice called night soil in some countries, concentrates the eggs and the larvae exactly where children play and where families grow food. The same sanitation failure that spreads these worms also spreads the bacteria and viruses that cause diarrhea, so a program that builds latrines and supplies clean water reduces several diseases at once. A latrine used consistently by every member of a household interrupts the cycle more effectively than any medicine, because a tablet treats the worms a person already carries, while a latrine prevents the next infection.

Ascaris lumbricoides is the largest intestinal worm that commonly infects people, and the adult female measures 20 to 35 centimeters in length. The adults live free in the lumen of the small intestine and do not attach to the wall. A fertilized female produces about 200,000 eggs a day, and those eggs pass in the stool and need 2 to 4 weeks in warm, shaded, moist soil before they become infective. The egg has a thick shell and is resistant, so it can survive in the environment for months or even years, which is why a household that stopped defecating in the yard may still be infected a year later. When a person swallows an infective egg, the larva hatches in the small intestine, penetrates the intestinal wall, and travels through the portal blood to the liver and then to the heart and the lungs. In the lungs the larva breaks into the air sacs, ascends the airway, is coughed up, and is swallowed, and it matures into an adult worm about 2 to 3 months after the egg was swallowed. This migration explains why the first illness a newly infected person notices is respiratory rather than intestinal.

The pulmonary phase of ascariasis appears 4 to 16 days after the eggs are ingested, and it produces cough, wheeze, breathlessness, low fever, and a patchy shadow on the chest radiograph that moves about as the larvae migrate. Sputum at this stage may contain eosinophils and occasionally larvae, and the blood shows a marked eosinophilia. The illness is usually mild and self-limited, and it is often mistaken for asthma or for a viral pneumonia, especially in a child who has never wheezed before. The intestinal phase is quieter but more dangerous, because a mass of adult worms can obstruct the bowel, and a bolus of worms in the terminal ileum produces colicky pain, vomiting, and distension that can progress to a complete obstruction needing surgery. The worms may also wander into the biliary tree or the pancreatic duct, causing biliary colic, infection of the bile ducts, or pancreatitis. Intestinal obstruction from Ascaris is a disease of young children, because a child's small intestine is narrow and because children carry the heaviest worm burdens. The classic patient is a child between 1 and 5 years of age with abdominal pain, vomiting, and a palpable mass, and the nurse must treat a reported worm in the stool or vomit as a diagnostic finding and ask about it directly. In a child who is passing worms and has a tender abdomen, the nurse should withhold food by mouth, secure intravenous access, and escalate promptly rather than giving another dose and waiting.

Hookworm infection begins with a step on contaminated soil, and the disease that follows is a study in slow blood loss. Two species cause it, Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, and Necator americanus is the commoner across much of the tropics, while Ancylostoma duodenale tolerates cooler climates and causes more blood loss per worm. Within minutes to hours after the larvae penetrate the skin, the person develops an itchy, raised, red rash at the site of entry, usually between the toes or on the sole, and this is called ground itch. The larvae then travel by the same route as Ascaris, through the blood to the lungs and up the airway, and they mature into adult worms in the small intestine, where each worm attaches to the lining and sucks blood every day for the several years that it lives. That daily loss is trivial in isolation and devastating in aggregate, because a child or a pregnant woman may carry hundreds of worms, and the result is iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss. The patient reports fatigue, breathlessness on exertion, and poor concentration, and the examination shows pallor, a rapid pulse, and in severe cases a murmur and swelling of the ankles. The laboratory shows a low hemoglobin, small red cells, a low ferritin level, and often a raised platelet count, with hidden blood in the stool. The differential diagnosis matters, because anemia in a tropical setting is not automatically hookworm disease, and the nurse who assumes so will miss malaria, tuberculosis, HIV, nutritional deficiency, and the anemia of chronic disease.

Trichuris trichiura, the whipworm, is a smaller worm whose shape explains its behavior. Its thin front end is threaded into the lining of the cecum and the colon, and its thicker back end lies free in the lumen, which gives it the look of a whip. The adult female lays eggs that pass in the stool, and the eggs need 2 to 4 weeks in moist soil before they become infective, so its cycle resembles that of Ascaris more than that of hookworm. Most infected people carry a light burden and have no symptoms at all, which is why the worm is often dismissed as a harmless finding on a stool report. Heavy infection, however, produces a distinctive syndrome of chronic bloody diarrhea, straining, and abdominal pain, and it is called Trichuris dysentery syndrome. Children with a heavy burden develop anemia, poor growth, and finger clubbing, and the chronic straining can cause rectal prolapse, one of the most treatable complications in tropical pediatrics. A rectal prolapse in a child in an endemic area should prompt a stool examination and a course of treatment, because the prolapse often resolves once the worms are cleared, and the nurse who assumes that surgery is the only answer has missed an infection that can be cured with a tablet.

Strongyloides stercoralis is the one worm in this chapter that can multiply inside a single human host, and that fact makes it the most dangerous. The infective larvae penetrate the skin as hookworm larvae do, travel through the lungs, and mature in the small intestine, but the female worms live embedded in the lining and produce eggs that hatch in the intestine itself. The resulting larvae are passed in the stool, but some of them mature within the bowel into infective larvae and penetrate the colonic wall or the skin around the anus, and this is autoinfection. Autoinfection allows a single exposure to establish a lifelong infection, and it explains why a person who walked barefoot once in a tropical village can still harbor the worm 40 years later. The worm is held at a low level by this internal cycle and by the immune system, and the person has few or no symptoms for decades. The larvae may also be found in the sputum, so a patient who is coughing and has a migrating rash may be told that the problem is asthma when the true cause is in the gut. An external cycle in the soil can also produce new infective larvae, so the organism can persist in a garden.

The hyperinfection syndrome is what happens when the balance between the worm and the immune system breaks, and the commonest trigger is a corticosteroid given for asthma, for an autoimmune disease, or as part of cancer treatment. The autoinfective cycle then accelerates out of control, the larval burden multiplies, and larvae migrate in enormous numbers through the lungs, the gut, and the bloodstream, carrying bacteria from the bowel with them. The result is a severe illness with cough, breathlessness, coughing of blood, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and septicemia, and the mortality is often greater than 50 per cent even with treatment. The tragedy is that the syndrome is preventable, because a blood test and a stool examination before the corticosteroid is started would have identified the infection. The rule is easiest to state as a question the nurse asks before any immunosuppressive plan begins. Has this patient ever lived, worked, or traveled for any length of time in a region where Strongyloides is endemic, and if so, has the infection been excluded? Screening consists of a stool examination by a method that detects larvae, a blood test for antibodies against the worm, and often more than one stool sample, because the sensitivity of a single test is low. A patient with a positive antibody test and a compatible exposure should be treated before the immunosuppressive drug is given, and the nurse's part is to make this screen visible in the record and to chase the result before the first dose.

Soil-transmitted helminths are distributed wherever poverty, poor sanitation, and warm moist soil coincide, and their burden falls most heavily on children. The World Health Organization estimates that about 1.5 billion people are infected with at least one of these worms, that more than 260 million preschool children and more than 600 million school-age children live in areas where the worms are transmitted, and that several hundred million women of reproductive age are also at risk. Infection is not evenly distributed within a community, because it is overdispersed, which means that a small proportion of people carry most of the worms and contribute most of the contamination. Heavy infection in childhood produces anemia, poor appetite, reduced absorption of nutrients, stunting, and impaired cognitive development, and the effect on school performance can be measured. In adults, hookworm infection reduces the capacity for physical work, which lowers agricultural productivity and household income, and hookworm anemia in pregnancy contributes to maternal death and to poor outcomes for the newborn. The World Health Organization measures this burden in disability-adjusted life years, a summary that combines years of life lost and years lived with disability, and the total remains large despite decades of control effort. The nurse who understands that the burden is concentrated in a minority of households will direct education and follow-up toward those households rather than toward the community as a whole.

Diagnosis begins at the bench, and the first tool is the stool examination. Direct microscopy of a wet preparation can show the eggs of Ascaris, Trichuris, and hookworm, but it is insensitive when the burden is light, so concentration and quantitative methods are used instead. The Kato-Katz technique is the standard quantitative method for these three worms. A measured amount of stool, usually about 41.7 milligrams, is pressed through a sieve, placed on a card with a template, covered with a strip of cellophane soaked in glycerine, and examined under the microscope, and the number of eggs counted is converted into eggs per gram of stool. That number is not merely a laboratory curiosity, because it classifies the intensity of infection as light, moderate, or heavy, and national programs use it to decide where to intervene and whether their interventions are working. The technique is inexpensive and needs only a microscope, a template, and cellophane strips, so it can be used in a district laboratory. Its weakness is that egg excretion varies from day to day, so a single sample can miss an infection or underestimate the burden, and the result must be read together with the clinical picture.

Strongyloides requires methods that look for larvae rather than eggs, and two such methods are standard. The Baermann method uses the warmth and moisture of a funnel of water. Fresh stool is placed on gauze inside a funnel, water at body temperature is added so that it just touches the sample, and the larvae, drawn to warmth and water, migrate downward through the gauze and collect in the stem of the funnel, where they can be drawn off and examined. The agar plate culture method places fresh stool on the surface of a nutrient agar plate, and the larvae that crawl across the plate carry bacteria with them, leaving visible tracks that can be seen the next day. Both methods need fresh stool and prompt processing, and both are more sensitive than a direct smear, but neither is perfectly sensitive. Serology detects antibodies against the worm and is useful for screening and for supporting a diagnosis when the stool is negative, but a positive result cannot distinguish a current infection from one treated years ago. The practical details are in the nurse's hands, because a specimen must be passed directly into a clean container, delivered the same day, and labeled with the exposures and the clinical question, and when the burden is light the nurse should arrange three samples on separate days rather than accept one result as final.

Treatment is simple, inexpensive, and highly effective, and three medicines carry almost the whole load. Albendazole is given by mouth at 400 milligrams as a single dose for Ascaris, for hookworm, and for light or moderate Trichuris infection. Mebendazole is given by mouth at 100 milligrams twice a day for 3 days, or as a single dose of 500 milligrams, and the 3-day course is preferred when the infection is heavy. For heavy Trichuris infection, which often coexists with heavy Ascaris infection, albendazole is given at 400 milligrams once a day for 3 days, and the longer course improves the cure rate substantially. Ivermectin is given by mouth at 200 micrograms per kilogram as a single dose for Strongyloides, and the dose is repeated after 2 weeks or after 1 month, because the autoinfective cycle may have released new larvae after the first dose. The two benzimidazoles, albendazole and mebendazole, are not interchangeable with ivermectin, and the choice depends on the worm that has been identified. For Strongyloides, ivermectin is the treatment of choice, and albendazole at 400 milligrams twice a day for 7 days is the alternative when ivermectin is unavailable or unsuitable. A patient treated with a single dose of albendazole who remains symptomatic should have the diagnosis and the species reconsidered rather than simply receiving another dose.

Strongyloides deserves one more warning, because the wrong management can kill. A patient with unrecognized strongyloidiasis who is treated with corticosteroids for an unrelated condition can develop hyperinfection within days, and the deterioration can be rapid. If the diagnosis is made in a patient who is already taking a corticosteroid, the corticosteroid should be reduced or stopped as quickly as the underlying condition allows, and treatment should start at once, often with ivermectin given daily until the stool is negative and then repeated. In disseminated disease, when larvae are found outside the gut and the lungs, treatment is prolonged, antibiotics are added, and the patient may need intensive care and mechanical ventilation. Pregnancy is the other situation that needs thought, because the first trimester is the period of organ formation and most guidance avoids deworming medicines during those weeks unless the need is urgent. Treatment is usually offered in the second and third trimesters, when the risk of the medicine is judged lower than the risk of untreated anemia, and albendazole and mebendazole are both used in that window in many national programs, while ivermectin is generally avoided. Lactation is less restrictive, because the amount of drug that passes into breast milk is small. A pregnant woman with hookworm infection and anemia should not be left untreated until after delivery simply because she is pregnant, because the anemia itself is dangerous to her and to the fetus.

All three medicines are well tolerated by the great majority of patients, and the common adverse effects are mild and brief. Abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, headache, and dizziness are reported after albendazole and mebendazole, and they usually appear within a day and settle without treatment. When a patient with a heavy worm burden is treated, the death of the worms can produce abdominal discomfort, and in heavy Ascaris infection the worms may be passed in the stool, which reassures the patient when it is explained in advance. Ivermectin may cause itching, a rash, joint pain, fever, and tender lymph nodes in patients who are co-infected with other parasites, and these reactions are usually mild. The serious adverse effects are uncommon but must be known. Ivermectin can cause severe neurological toxicity in a patient who is heavily infected with the parasite Loa loa, which is found in parts of Central and West Africa, which is why treatment in a co-endemic area must be planned with knowledge of the local guidance. Albendazole can raise the liver enzymes and, rarely, depress the bone marrow, so a patient given a prolonged or repeated course needs monitoring. Mebendazole is generally the safer of the two benzimidazoles for a long course, while albendazole is the more effective for a single-dose campaign.

None of the doses in this chapter should be given from memory. Antiparasitic regimens are revised as new trial evidence appears, guidance differs between countries, and the same infection may be managed with a single dose in one national program and a 3-day course in another. The World Health Organization publishes guidance on preventive chemotherapy for soil-transmitted helminths, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention publishes guidance for clinicians in the United States, and the two documents are updated on their own schedules and are written for different populations. The current national guideline, the current product label, and the local program protocol must all be checked before a medicine is prescribed, dispensed, or given. The dose of ivermectin is calculated from the weight measured on the day of treatment, not from the weight recorded at an earlier visit. The nurse verifies the weight, checks the medicine and the strength on the label, confirms that the child is above the minimum weight for the medicine, and asks about a history of allergy or of a previous reaction before the tablet is swallowed. A dose that was correct at the last campaign may be wrong at this one, and the guideline is the authority rather than the habit of the unit. The same discipline applies to the record, because the child treated twice in one round or missed altogether is usually a recording failure.

Mass drug administration is the strategy that has changed the epidemiology of these worms more than any clinical advance. The World Health Organization recommends periodic treatment of entire at-risk groups without individual diagnosis, and the groups targeted are preschool children, school-age children, and women of reproductive age. The medicine is usually albendazole at 400 milligrams or mebendazole at 500 milligrams as a single dose, repeated once or twice a year depending on the intensity of transmission, with the aim of keeping the worm burden low enough that illness does not develop. In areas where transmission is low and sanitation is improving, repeated rounds can interrupt transmission altogether, and several countries have reached the point where these worms are no longer a public health problem. Mass drug administration is necessary and it is not sufficient, because repeated treatment without improvement in water, sanitation and hygiene produces rapid reinfection. The World Health Organization therefore couples preventive chemotherapy with improvements in water supply, latrine construction, and hygiene education, and it treats these as one program rather than as separate activities. Coverage is uneven, and the children who are absent from school on the day of the campaign are often those who need treatment most, while hesitancy based on rumors about side effects or fertility is best answered by a nurse who listens and replies plainly. Programs must also guard against drug resistance, which has been documented in animal parasites and is watched for in human worms, and this is one more reason to keep the dose adequate and the coverage high.

The logistics of a deworming campaign are the part a nurse is most likely to be asked to manage, and they reward careful planning. The tablets are stable at room temperature, so no cold chain is needed, and the dose for school-age children is often decided by height rather than by weight, using a dosing pole marked in centimeters. The tablets are chewable, and a child who cannot chew may be given a crushed tablet mixed with water, while a child who is severely ill or below the minimum weight for the medicine should be referred rather than treated in the campaign. The team records the number of children treated, the number who were absent, and the number who refused, because coverage determines whether the campaign succeeds, and a campaign that reaches 60 per cent of children will not reduce transmission. A teacher or a community health worker can be trained to give the tablets under supervision, and adverse events are reported through the national system. The nurse teaches families why the worms are passed in the stool, why a latrine prevents the next infection, why shoes protect the feet, and why hands must be washed before food is eaten and after the toilet is used. The teaching must name the specific practice that matters in that community, so in a farming community the nurse may discuss the use of fresh human waste as fertilizer and suggest composting or storage before the crop is harvested. The nurse should also explain that a child may pass a worm after treatment and that this is expected, so that the sight does not become a reason to refuse the next round.

One of the most important nursing tasks in this chapter is the proper investigation of anemia, because the habit of giving iron alone hides diagnoses and delays treatment. Anemia in a person who lives where these worms are transmitted may be caused by hookworm, by Trichuris, by malaria, by tuberculosis, by HIV, by a nutritional deficiency, by a hemoglobin disorder, or by several of these at once. The workup begins with a complete blood count, a blood film, and a ferritin level, and it continues with a stool examination, a malaria test, and an assessment of the diet. A ferritin level can be falsely normal or high when there is inflammation or infection, so it must be interpreted with the clinical picture and, when the question is important, with a marker of inflammation. The nurse should ask about menstrual loss, pregnancy, the duration of symptoms, and any bleeding, because these answers change the differential diagnosis. Iron should be given when iron deficiency is documented or strongly suspected, but it should be given with a plan for follow-up and for rechecking the hemoglobin, not indefinitely. The nurse who treats anemia with iron alone in a patient who has hookworm disease will see a partial response and then a relapse, because the daily blood loss continues, and the true cause will have been missed.

Monitoring after treatment is what separates a campaign from a clinical program. After a course of treatment the stool should be re-examined to confirm that the eggs have cleared, and for Strongyloides the follow-up should use a larvae-specific method and should continue for months, because the autoinfective cycle can restart. The hemoglobin should be rechecked after 4 to 8 weeks in a patient treated for hookworm anemia, because the marrow needs time to respond, and growth should be measured in children, with weight and height plotted on a growth chart. In a mass drug administration program the indicators are coverage, meaning the proportion of the target group treated, and the egg reduction rate in a sample of the population, and a falling rate suggests poor adherence, reinfection, or the beginning of drug resistance. Some patients must be referred rather than managed in the clinic, and the nurse should recognize them quickly. A child with a distended, tender abdomen, vomiting, and absent stool or gas may have an intestinal obstruction from Ascaris, and a patient receiving a corticosteroid who develops fever, breathlessness, coughing of blood, or confusion may have hyperinfection syndrome, and each of these needs urgent escalation. A transplant recipient or a patient about to start chemotherapy needs a documented screen for Strongyloides before the immunosuppression begins, and a migrant from an endemic area may carry a worm silent for decades, so a history of exposure should be recorded at the first visit and kept in the chart. A patient with advanced HIV may have more severe diarrhea and more frequent reinfection, so strongyloidiasis should be considered in that population.

To summarize, soil-transmitted helminths are a small group of worms that infect more than a billion people and cause anemia, poor growth, and impaired development, and they are transmitted by fecal contamination of soil and by walking barefoot. Ascaris lumbricoides migrates through the lungs, can obstruct the bowel and block the biliary tree, and is diagnosed by the Kato-Katz method with its egg count. Hookworm, caused by Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, enters through the skin, causes ground itch, and produces chronic iron deficiency anemia through daily blood loss. Trichuris trichiura causes dysentery and rectal prolapse in heavy infection, and Strongyloides stercoralis can persist for decades through autoinfection and can cause fatal hyperinfection after corticosteroids, which is why screening before immunosuppression is a rule. Diagnosis rests on stool examination with the Kato-Katz method for eggs and the Baermann method or agar plate culture for larvae, supported by serology for strongyloidiasis. Treatment with albendazole, mebendazole, or ivermectin is simple and effective, but the dose must be verified against the current national guideline and product label every time, because regimens are revised and guidance differs between countries. The nurse's work is to run deworming campaigns, to teach the specific practices that prevent reinfection, to investigate anemia properly instead of treating it with iron alone, and to monitor the patients and the programs until the worms no longer return.

# Chapter 16 — Schistosomiasis and Food-Borne Trematodes

Schistosomiasis, also called bilharzia and snail fever, is caused by blood flukes of the genus Schistosoma. The worms do not multiply inside the human body, so disease severity depends on how many larvae entered the skin and how many eggs the surviving adults release each day. Roughly 200 million people are infected worldwide, and most live in sub-Saharan Africa, where the disease is a leading cause of chronic bladder and liver illness. It is a neglected tropical disease in the fullest sense, common, disabling, and treatable with one inexpensive drug, yet ignored because it kills slowly rather than dramatically.

Several species infect people, and they differ in where the adult worms live and therefore in what they do. Schistosoma haematobium settles in the veins around the bladder and causes urinary disease. Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum settle in the veins draining the intestines and cause intestinal and liver disease. Schistosoma mekongi, Schistosoma intercalatum, and Schistosoma guineensis are less common and follow the intestinal pattern. Schistosoma japonicum is the most zoonotic, because it also infects cattle, water buffalo, pigs, and dogs, which makes environmental control far harder.

Each species has a narrow, predictable geography, which is the most useful fact in the exposure history. Schistosoma haematobium is found throughout Africa, in the Nile valley, and in parts of the Middle East. Schistosoma mansoni occurs in much of Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, Brazil, Suriname, Venezuela, and a few Caribbean islands. Schistosoma japonicum occurs in China, the Philippines, and parts of Indonesia, while Schistosoma mekongi is limited to the Mekong basin in Laos and Cambodia. Transmission needs three things at once: fresh water, the snail that can host the parasite, and human waste reaching that water.

Eggs leave the body in urine or stool, and in fresh water they hatch into ciliated larvae called miracidia, which swim until they find the correct snail. Inside the snail the parasite multiplies asexually, and after 4 to 6 weeks the snail releases thousands of fork-tailed larvae called cercariae. Cercariae survive only 1 to 2 days, swimming toward shadows and turbulence, which is how they find a human body. They penetrate intact skin within minutes, lose their tails, and become schistosomulae, which travel through the lymphatics and bloodstream to the lungs and then the liver. There they mature, pair into male and female worms, and migrate to their final veins, where the female begins to lay eggs about 4 to 6 weeks after the skin was penetrated, and sometimes as late as 8 to 12 weeks for Schistosoma japonicum.

Schistosoma haematobium uses snails of the genus Bulinus, Schistosoma mansoni uses Biomphalaria, Schistosoma japonicum uses Oncomelania, and Schistosoma mekongi uses Neotricula. These snails thrive in warm, slow-moving fresh water enriched by human activity. The great water projects of the twentieth century created enormous new habitat, and the Aswan High Dam, Lake Volta, and the Senegal River valley all increased transmission. Lakes and rivers used for bathing, swimming, laundry, fishing, and rice farming are the places where infection is acquired, and children who play in shallow water are infected most heavily.

Not every freshwater contact produces infection, and not every rash after swimming is schistosomiasis, because repeated exposure is what builds the worm burden that causes chronic disease. Cercariae of bird and rodent schistosomes also penetrate human skin but die there, producing an itchy raised rash within hours called cercarial dermatitis, or swimmer's itch. That rash is an allergic reaction, not an established infection, and it resolves without treatment. A rash on the same day is not schistosomiasis, and fever several weeks later should not be dismissed as a rash.

Acute schistosomiasis, often called Katayama syndrome, appears 2 to 8 weeks after exposure, exactly when the maturing worms begin to release eggs. It causes fever, dry cough, urticaria, muscle aches, headache, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and an enlarged tender liver, with marked eosinophilia and sometimes transient infiltrates on chest imaging. The mechanism is an immune reaction to migrating larvae and newly deposited eggs rather than a direct effect of worm numbers, so the illness can be severe even in a light infection. Katayama syndrome is seen mostly in travelers and migrants without prior exposure, because people who grow up in endemic areas acquire their first infection in childhood and later infections smolder rather than erupt.

Chronic urinary schistosomiasis begins insidiously, and its earliest reliable symptom is terminal hematuria, blood at the end of the stream, often with burning, frequency, and suprapubic discomfort. Eggs lodged in the bladder wall provoke granulomas that become polyps or flat sandy patches, and the resulting fibrosis stiffens the bladder and narrows the ureters. Untreated, this leads to hydronephrosis, recurrent urinary infection, stones, and eventually kidney failure. Genital infection is common and often overlooked: in women it causes vulval and cervical lesions, vaginal bleeding, pain during intercourse, and infertility, and it roughly doubles the risk of acquiring HIV. Long-standing bladder infection is a recognized cause of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, appearing at a younger age than bladder cancer elsewhere.

Intestinal and hepatic schistosomiasis follows infection with Schistosoma mansoni and Schistosoma japonicum. The gut disease causes colicky abdominal pain, bloody diarrhea, tenesmus, and sometimes colonic polyps, and the chronic blood loss contributes to iron deficiency anemia. The liver disease is the more dangerous half. Eggs that cannot escape the intestinal wall are swept back into the portal venules, where each provokes a granuloma, and years of inflammation around the small portal veins lay down collagen that thickens the portal tracts without destroying the liver cells themselves. This periportal fibrosis, also called Symmers pipestem fibrosis, causes portal hypertension with splenomegaly and esophageal varices, and the patient may present with sudden vomiting of blood. Synthetic liver function is often preserved, so normal liver enzymes do not exclude advanced disease, and coexisting hepatitis B or hepatitis C worsens the outcome.

Eggs can also reach the central nervous system, producing neuroschistosomiasis, which is uncommon but devastating. They travel through the valveless venous plexus connecting the pelvic veins to the veins around the spinal cord and lodge there, causing an inflammatory mass rather than a simple obstruction. Spinal involvement is more frequent than brain involvement, especially with Schistosoma haematobium and Schistosoma mansoni, and it presents as acute transverse myelitis or a conus medullaris syndrome, with lower back pain, ascending numbness, weakness, and loss of bladder control. Cerebral disease presents with seizures, headache, focal weakness, or signs of raised intracranial pressure, and it can be mistaken for a brain tumor.

Diagnosis begins with the exposure history and the blood count, but it cannot stop there. Eosinophilia is a useful clue and not a specific one. Detecting eggs confirms active infection and identifies the species, while detecting antibodies only proves that exposure happened at some point in the patient's life. Antigen tests sit in between, because they reflect living adult worms and therefore active infection. Egg output varies from day to day and hour to hour, so a single negative sample never excludes the diagnosis when suspicion is real.

Urine filtration is the standard test for Schistosoma haematobium. Collect 10 milliliters of urine, ideally between noon and 2 in the afternoon, when egg excretion peaks, filter it through a fine nylon membrane, and examine the sediment under the microscope. Report the result as eggs per 10 milliliters of urine so that it can be compared over time, and because excretion fluctuates, collect samples on 2 or 3 different days. In field programs a reagent strip that detects blood in the urine is a cheap and reasonably sensitive screen, because almost everyone with heavy Schistosoma haematobium infection has microscopic blood in the urine.

For intestinal species, stool examination is the mainstay. The Kato-Katz technique uses a template holding about 41.7 milligrams of sieved stool, which is pressed onto a slide, cleared with glycerol, and examined under the microscope, and the count is multiplied to give eggs per gram of stool. The method is inexpensive and quantitative, which is what programs need to measure intensity and to monitor treatment. Its weakness is that light infections are easy to miss, so 2 to 3 samples on separate days are recommended before a patient is declared uninfected. Schistosoma mansoni eggs have a prominent lateral spine, Schistosoma japonicum eggs a small lateral knob, and Schistosoma haematobium eggs a terminal spine.

Several other tests extend what you can do when microscopy is unhelpful. The circulating cathodic antigen test is a urine cassette test for Schistosoma mansoni that gives a result in about 20 minutes and is widely used in surveys, although it is less reliable for Schistosoma haematobium. Rectal snip biopsy, in which a small piece of rectal mucosa is examined for eggs, remains useful for intestinal species when stool studies are negative, and bladder biopsy at cystoscopy can confirm urinary disease and exclude cancer. Serology is most useful in travelers and in the acute phase, when eggs are not yet being passed, but a positive antibody test alone can never prove active infection.

Ultrasound has become essential because it shows the damage eggs have already done, not merely the presence of worms. In urinary disease the bladder wall thickens, polyps appear, and the ureters and kidneys may dilate, and the standardized Niamey protocol allows comparable measurements between clinics. In intestinal and hepatic disease the Cairo protocol grades periportal fibrosis and can show an enlarged spleen and collateral veins. Portable machines now allow these measurements in district hospitals, and fibrosis may partially reverse after treatment while advanced changes persist. A normal ultrasound does not exclude infection, so imaging must be read alongside the epidemiology and the laboratory result.

Treatment rests on praziquantel, and understanding how it works explains why the timing of the dose matters. The drug increases the permeability of the worm's outer layer to calcium, causing violent contraction and damaging the tegument, which exposes worm antigens to the immune system, and the damaged worms move from the mesenteric veins into the liver, where they are trapped and killed. Praziquantel acts on adult worms and has little effect on the immature schistosomulae present in the first weeks after exposure. This is why a patient treated too early often remains infected, and why the standard advice is to wait until 4 to 6 weeks after the last freshwater exposure. If a traveler is diagnosed in the first weeks, many clinicians treat the acute illness supportively and give praziquantel once the worms have matured.

The dose depends on the species. For Schistosoma haematobium and Schistosoma mansoni, current guidance from the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention gives praziquantel at 40 milligrams per kilogram by mouth, usually as a single dose or divided into two doses taken 4 to 6 hours apart. For Schistosoma japonicum and Schistosoma mekongi the dose is 60 milligrams per kilogram, divided into two or three doses over one day. The tablets are 600 milligrams, so a dose is often three or four tablets, and in community campaigns the dose comes from a height pole rather than a measured weight. Praziquantel is taken with food and water, after a meal, because absorption improves and nausea is reduced.

Before you prescribe, verify. Dosing regimens are revised as new evidence appears, national programs adapt them to local species and supply, and guidance for pregnancy and young children has changed more than once in recent years. The World Health Organization now advises treating pregnant and lactating women in endemic areas rather than deferring treatment, and it supports treating children under 4 years of age after risk assessment, whereas older guidance restricted both groups. The current national guideline, the current product label, and the current program protocol must be checked before any dose is given, and a dose spoken from memory or copied from an old chart is not acceptable. Name the source of your regimen in your documentation so the next clinician can see what you followed.

Adverse effects of praziquantel are common, usually mild, and short-lived. Patients may report abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headache, dizziness, drowsiness, fever, or itching, generally within a few hours of the dose and settling within a day. The drowsiness matters practically, because a patient should not drive or operate machinery for the rest of that day, and sedatives and antihistamines should be used cautiously at the same time. Rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and dexamethasone lower the drug level and may reduce efficacy, while cimetidine raises it. Serious reactions are rare, but campaigns still need a plan for recording and referring them, and a nurse running a treatment day should have a clear route to a clinician and a vehicle.

After treatment, monitoring is where nursing follow-up earns its place. A test of cure is usually done about 4 to 6 weeks after treatment for antigen tests and about 3 months after treatment for egg counts, and the goal is a large fall in egg output rather than an absolute zero, because residual eggs and incomplete cure are both common. Eosinophilia should decline over several months. Reinfection is frequent wherever exposure continues, so a treated patient who returns to the same lake or canal may need repeated treatment, and the follow-up visit is the natural moment to teach prevention again. Patients with urinary disease need follow-up of blood in the urine, blood pressure, and kidney function, while those with hepatic disease may need endoscopy for varices. Children deserve growth and anemia monitoring, because chronic schistosomiasis blunts growth and worsens iron deficiency.

Praziquantel is also the backbone of public health control, delivered through mass drug administration to whole at-risk communities. Programs usually target school-age children and adults in high-prevalence areas, dose by height, and repeat treatment every year or every 2 years depending on measured prevalence. The tablet is 600 milligrams, and the height pole lets a team dose hundreds of people in a day without scales, though a nurse must supervise the pole, the quartering of tablets, and the recording. Coverage of at least 75 per cent of the target group is the benchmark that reduces transmission, and the World Health Organization coordinates a donation program that supplies the drug to eligible countries. Monitoring includes watching for vomiting soon after the dose, which may mean the drug was not absorbed and should be repeated.

Prevention is unglamorous, specific, and more durable than any single treatment. The first principle is to keep human waste out of fresh water, which means latrines people actually use, safe disposal of urine as well as stool, and sanitation that reaches schools and markets, not only households. The second is to reduce contact with contaminated water, which means a safe supply for drinking, bathing, and laundry so people are not forced into the canal or the lake. Snail control with molluscicides, drainage, and removal of aquatic vegetation can interrupt transmission at its source, and it works best combined with treatment rather than alone.

The food-borne trematodes are a different problem, and the nurse who understands the pattern can prevent them with a sentence. These flatworms have complex life cycles requiring a first intermediate host, usually a snail, and a second intermediate host, which may be a fish, a crab, a crayfish, or an aquatic plant. People become infected by eating that second host raw or undercooked, or by eating water plants carrying the encysted larvae, and the infection is never passed from person to person. The adults live for years in the bile ducts, the lungs, or the intestine, and the resulting disease is chronic, often silent, and occasionally malignant. Treatment is simple, but prevention is a matter of food preparation, which makes it a natural subject for nursing education.

The liver flukes are Clonorchis sinensis, the Chinese liver fluke, and the Opisthorchis species, chiefly Opisthorchis viverrini and Opisthorchis felineus. They occur in East and Southeast Asia, particularly China, Korea, Vietnam, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, and parts of Russia, and the Mekong region carries the heaviest burden. The adult worms live in the bile ducts and release eggs that pass in the stool, hatch in water, enter a snail, and develop into cercariae that encyst in freshwater fish, especially the carp family. A person is infected by eating those fish raw, and the dishes that transmit infection include koi pla, a raw minced fish dish from northeast Thailand, pla ra and pla som, and the salted or fermented fish preparations sold in many markets. The larvae mature in the bile duct in about 3 to 4 weeks, and the adults can live 20 to 30 years.

Most people with liver flukes have no symptoms, which is why the infection is found by screening rather than by complaint. When symptoms appear they are vague: pain in the right upper abdomen, indigestion, fatigue, and occasionally jaundice. Heavy and long-standing infection causes recurrent cholangitis, gallstones, biliary obstruction, and pancreatitis, and it produces a characteristic thickening and fibrosis around the bile ducts. The most serious consequence is cholangiocarcinoma, cancer of the bile ducts, and the link is strongest for Opisthorchis viverrini and Clonorchis sinensis, both classified as carcinogenic to humans. Any patient from an endemic area with unexplained eosinophilia, biliary symptoms, or a bile duct abnormality deserves stool examination and serology.

Diagnosis depends first on thinking of it, then on finding the eggs. Stool microscopy with the Kato-Katz method or a concentration technique reveals small oval eggs with an operculum and a small shoulder, though light infections may require several samples. Ultrasound can show dilated intrahepatic bile ducts and periductal fibrosis, and computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging may be needed when cancer is suspected. When cholangiocarcinoma is possible, imaging of the biliary tree and referral to a center with surgical and cancer services takes priority over the parasitological diagnosis, because delay changes the outcome.

Treatment of liver flukes is praziquantel at 25 milligrams per kilogram by mouth three times a day for 2 days, a higher total dose and longer course than the single dose used for schistosomiasis. An alternative is tribendimidine, shown to be effective against Opisthorchis viverrini in trials in the region. Cure rates are good, but the drug does not undo the damage already done to the bile ducts, and treated patients from high-risk areas remain at elevated risk of cholangiocarcinoma, so the nurse's role in long-term follow-up is real. After treatment, stool examination should be repeated at about 1 month, and persistent eggs mean the course either was not taken or did not work.

Paragonimiasis is caused by lung flukes, chiefly Paragonimus westermani, and it is acquired by eating raw or undercooked freshwater crab or crayfish. The larvae excyst in the small intestine, penetrate the gut wall, cross the abdominal cavity and the diaphragm, and mature in the lungs, where they form fibrous cysts. The classic illness is a chronic cough with blood-stained, rusty sputum, chest pain, and low-grade fever, and the chest radiograph shows nodules, cysts, or ring shadows easily mistaken for tuberculosis. Eggs are found in the sputum and stool, and serology is useful when the parasite burden is low. In some patients the worms migrate to the brain and cause cerebral paragonimiasis with seizures, headache, and focal deficits, one of the treatable causes of epilepsy in endemic areas. Treatment is praziquantel at 25 milligrams per kilogram three times a day for 2 days, and triclabendazole is an alternative.

Fascioliasis, caused by Fasciola hepatica and Fasciola gigantica, is the liver fluke people acquire from plants rather than fish. It is found worldwide, with important foci in the Andean highlands, in Egypt, and in Iran, and it is classically linked to eating watercress, water spinach, or water mint from a stream where infected sheep or cattle graze. The larvae encyst on the plants, and people swallow them with the plant or with untreated water, and occasionally immature worms come from eating the raw liver of an infected animal. There are two phases. In the acute hepatic phase, 2 to 4 months after ingestion, the migrating worms cause fever, pain in the right upper abdomen, an enlarged tender liver, and striking eosinophilia. In the biliary phase, the adult worms obstruct the bile ducts and cause cholangitis, gallstones, and anemia.

Diagnosis of fascioliasis differs from that of the other flukes, and the difference matters. In the acute phase, stool examination is usually negative, because the worms have not reached the bile ducts and are not laying eggs, so serology is the test of choice and it is highly sensitive. Once the biliary phase begins, eggs can be found in stool, and imaging may show tracks left by the migrating worms in the liver. The treatment is specific: triclabendazole at 10 milligrams per kilogram by mouth, given as a single dose in some guidelines and as two doses 12 hours apart in others, and it is the drug of choice because it is active against both immature and adult worms. Praziquantel does not work against Fasciola, and giving it wastes time while the patient remains ill. Where triclabendazole is unavailable, nitazoxanide is a less effective alternative, and the World Health Organization provides the drug through a donation program.

The intestinal flukes are the least dramatic members of the group and easy to overlook. Fasciolopsis buski, the giant intestinal fluke, is acquired from water caltrop, water chestnut, bamboo shoots, and lotus grown in contaminated water in South and Southeast Asia. Echinostoma species come from raw snails, clams, fish, and amphibians, and Heterophyes and Metagonimus species from raw or salted freshwater and brackish fish. The adult worms attach to the wall of the small intestine, and light infections cause only mild diarrhea and abdominal discomfort. Heavy infection with Fasciolopsis can cause ulceration, protein loss, and edema, particularly in children, and chronic infection contributes to poor growth. Praziquantel at 40 milligrams per kilogram by mouth as a single dose treats most of these infections, although some echinostomes need a higher dose, and repeat stool examination confirms cure.

This is where nursing education does its most valuable work, because a general instruction such as cook your food well changes nothing. The teaching has to name the specific food and the specific practice. Tell a family in northeast Thailand not to eat koi pla, and explain that the fish must be cooked until the flesh flakes; tell a family in the Andes not to eat watercress picked from the stream where the animals drink, and to cook the plants bought at market; tell a family on the Mekong not to drink the juice from crab shells and not to handle raw crab and then touch the mouth. Explain that lime juice, salt, and alcohol do not kill the larvae, and that only thorough cooking, or freezing at minus 20 degrees Celsius for at least 7 days, makes freshwater fish safe. Involve market vendors, food handlers, teachers, and community leaders, because the food is prepared in the household and sold in the market, not in the clinic.

Some practical logistics decide whether a program works, and the nurse usually manages them. Praziquantel tablets are 600 milligrams and are scored, but breaking them accurately still requires technique and a tablet cutter where one is available, and the height pole must be used consistently by everyone on the team. The drug does not need a cold chain, but it should be stored dry and below 30 degrees Celsius, and stock-outs are the commonest reason a treatment round fails. Record the name, age, height band, dose, and any adverse event for every person treated, because coverage and safety data justify the next round. Praziquantel is on the World Health Organization list of essential medicines, and mass distribution is donated, so supply arrives on a program timetable.

The nurse's assessment role is mostly a matter of asking the right questions. Ask where the patient has lived and traveled, whether they swam or waded in fresh water, whether they worked in irrigated fields, whether they eat raw freshwater fish, raw crab, or uncooked water plants, and whether anyone in the household has similar symptoms. Ask about blood in the urine, blood in the stool, and blood when coughing, because patients often do not volunteer these symptoms unless asked directly. Consider female genital schistosomiasis in any woman from an endemic area with pelvic pain, bleeding, or infertility, and consider neuroschistosomiasis in any patient with unexplained spinal cord disease or new seizures. Then connect the finding to the specimen: urine at midday, stool on more than one day, sputum when there is blood in the cough, and serology when the exposure was recent.

Special populations require deliberate thought rather than blanket rules. Pregnant and lactating women in endemic areas should be treated according to current World Health Organization guidance, which favors treatment rather than delay, and children under 4 years are also treated after risk assessment in most programs.
