People living with HIV need their antiretroviral therapy reviewed for interactions, and women with female genital schistosomiasis need treatment and counselling about their increased risk of acquiring HIV. Migrants and refugees from endemic countries should be screened for eosinophilia and for evidence of schistosomiasis and other helminths, because the late complications are preventable and the treatment is simple. Patients with advanced liver disease need variceal surveillance, and patients with bladder cancer need referral rather than repeated courses of antiparasitic drugs.

Surveillance and program monitoring close the loop between individual care and public health. Prevalence in school-age children is the standard indicator, measured by urine filtration or a rapid antigen test at sentinel schools, and it tells a program whether transmission is falling or returning. The egg reduction rate after treatment measures drug efficacy and can detect reduced susceptibility, which has been reported in a few settings and is watched closely. Schistosomiasis is not usually notifiable in the way cholera or viral hemorrhagic fever is, but laboratory confirmation belongs in the patient record, and unusual clusters or treatment failures should be reported to the local health authority.

A word about what not to do, because over-treatment has its own costs. Praziquantel is safe and cheap, but it is not a substitute for diagnosis where diagnosis is possible, and it does not treat Fasciola or the tapeworms, so a patient with eosinophilia who receives it blindly may remain ill and lose confidence in the clinic. Giving repeated doses to a patient whose blood in the urine comes from bladder cancer or a urinary stone delays the real diagnosis. Let the exposure history, the species, the specimen, and the current guideline decide the plan.

To summarize, schistosomiasis is caused by blood flukes whose adult worms live in the veins around the bladder or the intestine, and whose eggs produce the granulomatous damage that causes blood in the urine, intestinal bleeding, periportal fibrosis with portal hypertension, and, with Schistosoma haematobium, squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder. Diagnosis rests on the exposure history and on finding eggs in urine or stool, supported by antigen tests, serology, and ultrasound. Praziquantel is the treatment of choice, at 40 milligrams per kilogram for Schistosoma haematobium and Schistosoma mansoni and 60 milligrams per kilogram for Schistosoma japonicum and Schistosoma mekongi, and every regimen must be checked against current World Health Organization or national guidance before it is prescribed. The food-borne trematodes, including the liver flukes Clonorchis and Opisthorchis, the lung fluke Paragonimus, and Fasciola with its specific treatment triclabendazole, are acquired from raw fish, raw crab, and uncooked water plants, and they cause chronic biliary, pulmonary, and intestinal disease. Control depends on latrines, safe water, snail reduction, repeated community treatment, and food education that names the specific food and the specific practice. Your part is to ask the exposure questions, collect the right specimen at the right hour, verify every dose, monitor the response, and teach the household what to change.

# Chapter 17 — Cestodes: Neurocysticercosis and Echinococcosis

This chapter covers two tapeworm groups whose danger lies in the larval stage rather than the adult worm. Taenia solium, the pork tapeworm, causes two separate diseases in one person, and the genus Echinococcus builds a fluid-filled sac that grows silently for years and can kill within minutes if it ruptures. Both are neglected, both are preventable through latrines and meat inspection, and both require the nurse to think in years rather than days. You will meet them even in wealthy countries, because migration and travel carry them into neurology clinics and emergency departments everywhere.

A cestode is a flatworm with no gut of its own, absorbing nutrients through its outer surface. Taenia solium lives as a long ribbon in the human small intestine, its head bearing four suckers and a ring of hooks that grip the wall. Behind the head a neck produces a continuous chain of segments called proglottids, each a reproductive unit, and the chain can reach 2 to 7 meters. The terminal segments are gravid, packed with eggs, and they detach and pass out, and an untreated worm survives for years.

A gravid proglottid holds tens of thousands of eggs, and the thick shell lets each egg survive weeks to months in a cool, moist environment. A passed segment may crawl out of the anus and be found on the skin or clothing, sometimes the only complaint the patient makes. When a pig swallows eggs from human feces, the egg hatches and releases a six-hooked embryo called an oncosphere, which penetrates the gut wall, travels in the blood, and forms a larval cyst called a cysticercus in muscle. When a person eats undercooked pork containing those cysts, the scolex attaches and a new adult worm matures about 2 to 3 months later.

The far more dangerous route is swallowing the egg rather than the larva. When a human being swallows Taenia solium eggs, the oncosphere penetrates the intestinal wall and travels through the bloodstream exactly as it would in a pig, forming cysticerci in human tissue and most seriously in the brain. The eggs come from human feces, not from pork, so a person who eats no meat can still develop the disease. Eggs reach the mouth on contaminated hands, food, or water, and a carrier can contaminate himself or herself. Taeniasis is the adult worm in the intestine, while cysticercosis is the larval stage in human tissue, and their treatments differ completely.

Taeniasis is usually quiet. Most carriers have no symptoms and discover it only when they notice a moving segment in the stool or on the bedding. Others report mild abdominal discomfort, nausea, a change in appetite, loose stools, or itching around the anus. Weight loss is uncommon and the patient does not look ill, though the blood count may show mild eosinophilia.

A carrier sheds eggs for years, exposing every household member and neighbor who shares a latrine or water source. In endemic communities the person with the adult worm is the engine of neurocysticercosis, so finding and treating carriers interrupts transmission at its source. When you diagnose taeniasis, ask who else lives in the house and who prepares the food. Hygiene instruction given at that moment reaches the whole household at once.

Neurocysticercosis is the presence of larval cysts in the central nervous system, and it is one of the commonest causes of acquired epilepsy in the world. The World Health Organization counts it among the neglected tropical diseases, with the greatest burden in Latin America, sub-Saharan Africa, and parts of Asia where pigs roam freely and sanitation is incomplete. Nurses in wealthy countries now see it in migrants and long-term travelers. It is often missed because nobody thinks of a pork tapeworm when a patient arrives with a first seizure.

After penetrating the intestinal wall, the oncosphere is carried to the brain, meninges, ventricles, spinal cord, eye, muscle, and subcutaneous tissue. Cysts develop over weeks to months and may stay viable for years. How much disease they cause depends on where they land and on the host immune response rather than on how many eggs were swallowed. A single cyst in a quiet area of cortex may never announce itself, while a cluster at the base of the brain can be life-threatening.

A cyst passes through stages that explain both symptoms and treatment. In the vesicular stage the larva is alive and the fluid clear, and the surrounding brain shows little inflammation because the parasite suppresses the local immune response. In the colloidal stage the parasite is dying, the fluid turns turbid, and the immune system floods the area with edema and inflammation that cause symptoms. In the granular nodular stage the cyst collapses into a scar, and in the calcified stage it becomes a hard nodule that can remain for life. Most suffering comes from the middle stages, which is why killing the parasite can make a patient worse before better.

The location of the cysts determines the clinical picture. Parenchymal cysts cause seizures, headache, and focal weakness. Cysts in the subarachnoid space, especially the racemose form that grows like a cluster of grapes at the base of the brain, can become enormous, raise intracranial pressure, inflame blood vessels, and cause strokes. Cysts inside the ventricles obstruct the flow of cerebrospinal fluid and cause hydrocephalus, sometimes abruptly. Spinal cysts compress the cord, causing weakness, sensory loss, and loss of bladder control, and cysts in the eye can destroy vision and require surgery rather than drugs.

Seizures are the signature of the disease, because inflamed cortex, edema around a dying cyst, and old calcified scars all irritate the brain. A seizure may be focal, with twitching of one limb, unusual sensations, or impaired awareness, or it may generalize with loss of consciousness and convulsions. A first seizure in a person 20 to 40 years old who has lived in an endemic area should raise the question at once. Repeated untreated seizures can become a chronic epilepsy lasting decades, carrying stigma and loss of employment as well as medical risk.

Hydrocephalus turns a manageable illness into an emergency. A ventricular cyst can block the narrow channels through which cerebrospinal fluid circulates, and meningeal inflammation at the base of the brain can leave a scar that prevents fluid absorption. The patient develops headache that is worse on waking, vomiting, neck stiffness, blurred or double vision, and swelling of the optic discs, followed later by slow thinking, unsteadiness, and incontinence. These signs can build over days or weeks, so any patient with known cysticercosis who develops them needs urgent imaging and referral rather than a wait and see approach.

Imaging is the center of diagnosis. Computed tomography shows calcified lesions well, because calcium appears as bright dense dots, and it also shows cysts, edema, and hydrocephalus. Magnetic resonance imaging is better at distinguishing a living cyst from a dying one, at showing the scolex, and at finding cysts in the ventricles, the subarachnoid space, and the spinal cord. A viable cyst often appears as a rounded fluid collection with a bright dot inside, sometimes described as a hole with a dot, and the dot is the scolex.

Treatment begins with a principle that prevents harm: not every lesion requires an antiparasitic drug. A patient whose only finding is a calcified lesion with controlled seizures needs an anticonvulsant and nothing else, because there is no living parasite to kill. A patient with viable parenchymal cysts generally does benefit, but only with corticosteroids and usually with an anticonvulsant. Patients with cysts in the ventricles, the subarachnoid space, or the eye are managed individually and often surgically, because location, not mere presence, decides the approach.

When antiparasitic treatment is indicated, the choice lies between albendazole and praziquantel, and the dose must come from current guidance rather than memory. A widely used regimen is albendazole at 15 milligrams per kilogram per day by mouth divided into two doses for 10 to 14 days. An alternative is praziquantel at 50 milligrams per kilogram per day by mouth divided into three doses for 15 days, and some protocols use both drugs together. These regimens are revised as evidence accumulates, national recommendations differ, so the World Health Organization guidance, the current national guideline, and the product label must all be checked before the first dose. Name the source you followed in your documentation.

The reason corticosteroids are not optional is the most important safety concept in this chapter. The antiparasitic drug kills the cyst, and a dying cyst can no longer hide from the immune system, so the brain mounts an intense inflammatory response around it. That inflammation produces edema, raises pressure, causes headache, worsens seizures, and can be fatal when many cysts die at once. The treatment therefore causes the very complication it is meant to prevent, and corticosteroids suppress the response while the parasite is being killed. A patient given albendazole or praziquantel without corticosteroid cover, and without the ability to recognize and treat a flare, is exposed to avoidable danger.

Corticosteroids are started before or together with the antiparasitic drug and continued long enough to cover the period when cysts degenerate. Dexamethasone and prednisone are both used, with dexamethasone preferred when there is significant edema or raised intracranial pressure, given by mouth in divided doses and then tapered according to symptoms and imaging. In extensive subarachnoid disease, corticosteroids may be the main treatment and antiparasitic drugs withheld entirely. Dose and duration must be verified against current guidance, because practice varies with the burden and location of the cysts.

Anticonvulsant treatment is the other pillar, because seizures most threaten safety and social life. Many clinicians begin an anticonvulsant when a viable cyst is treated, since the treatment itself can provoke seizures. Levetiracetam is often preferred because it does not interact with the antiparasitic drugs, while carbamazepine and phenytoin lower the blood levels of albendazole and praziquantel and may reduce their effectiveness, and valproate is avoided in people who could become pregnant. How long to continue after lesions calcify is genuinely uncertain, so the decision must be individualized and reviewed with a neurologist where possible.

Monitoring during treatment is continuous nursing work rather than an occasional blood test. Before treatment, record a baseline neurologic examination, seizure history, blood pressure, blood glucose, and weight, and confirm that the corticosteroid has been prescribed rather than merely considered. During treatment, assess for worsening headache, vomiting, drowsiness, new weakness, visual change, and any increase in seizure frequency, because these may signal rising intracranial pressure from the inflammatory flare. Blood glucose must be checked when corticosteroids are used, and liver tests and blood counts followed during prolonged albendazole therapy. Document everything, because the next decision often depends on a trend rather than a single value.

Adverse effects must be anticipated and explained in advance. Albendazole commonly causes abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, headache, and dizziness, and it can raise liver enzymes, so liver tests are checked at baseline and during treatment. Rarely it suppresses the bone marrow, producing a fall in white cells or platelets, which is why blood counts are monitored, and it can cause temporary hair loss, so it is avoided in early pregnancy unless the illness justifies the risk. Praziquantel causes dizziness and drowsiness that make driving unsafe for the rest of the day, and its level falls with rifampicin, carbamazepine, phenytoin, and dexamethasone. Corticosteroids bring high blood sugar, high blood pressure, fluid retention, infection, and mood change, and must never be stopped abruptly after a long course.

Surgery and shunting are required for some patients and are not a failure of medical care. Ventricular cysts are often removed by neuroendoscopy, which can also restore the flow of cerebrospinal fluid. Hydrocephalus that cannot be relieved by removing the cyst is treated with a shunt that diverts fluid from the brain to the abdomen, or by a procedure that opens a channel at the floor of the third ventricle. Shunts fail, and failure presents with the return of headache, vomiting, drowsiness, or fever, so the patient and family must be taught these warning signs before discharge.

The logistics are as demanding as the medicine. Patients need imaging before treatment and again afterward, which may mean travel to a referral hospital and an overnight stay, so neurosurgical referral pathways must be identified in advance rather than improvised during a crisis. Albendazole, praziquantel, dexamethasone, and anticonvulsants must all be in stock at the same time, and the patient must be able to return for follow up, which depends on transport, work, and childcare. Cost is a barrier, and a nurse who knows the supply chain can prevent interruptions in treatment.

Treatment of the intestinal tapeworm is simpler but carries a trap. Niclosamide is given by mouth as a single dose of 2 grams for adults, with tablets chewed thoroughly or crushed and swallowed with water, and it kills the worm by preventing it from absorbing glucose. Praziquantel as a single dose of 5 to 10 milligrams per kilogram is an alternative and is highly effective, and albendazole at 400 milligrams per day for 3 days is a further option. Because niclosamide is poorly absorbed, it has the advantage of not acting on cysts elsewhere in the body.

That advantage matters because of the trap. If a patient has undiagnosed neurocysticercosis and is given praziquantel for the intestinal worm, the drug can attack the brain cysts and provoke seizures, headache, or raised intracranial pressure. In endemic areas, therefore, ask about seizures and chronic headache before treating taeniasis, and consider imaging first where it is available. Where imaging is not available, some programs prefer niclosamide for exactly this reason. This is one of the clearest examples of a drug that is safe for one disease being dangerous for another that the same patient may be hiding.

Prevention of cysticercosis rests on pig husbandry, sanitation, and meat safety, and each is a place where nursing education has measurable effect. Pigs must not roam freely and must not reach human feces, because a pig that eats infected stool becomes the next link in the chain. Keeping pigs in pens away from latrines and using manure as fertilizer rather than letting animals scavenge are changes communities can make. Meat inspection at slaughter identifies heavily infected carcasses, and pork must be cooked thoroughly until it is no longer pink and the juices run clear, while freezing at minus 10 degrees Celsius for 10 days also kills the larvae where cold storage exists.

Sanitation belongs to the same conversation. Latrines that are used consistently, kept clean, and sited away from wells and streams reduce the number of eggs reaching the environment, and hand hygiene with soap after defecation and before food preparation interrupts the route that carries eggs to the brain. Water sources should be protected from runoff, and produce grown in contaminated soil should be washed and cooked. Because the carrier is the source, finding and treating carriers in a community benefits everyone. This is the one health approach in practice, linking human health, pig health, and the environment through a single parasite.

Echinococcosis is caused by a different tapeworm with a different cycle, but it shares the theme of a larval stage that grows quietly in human tissue. Two species matter. Echinococcus granulosus causes cystic echinococcosis, in which the larva forms a well-defined fluid-filled sac called a hydatid cyst, most often in the liver or lung. Echinococcus multilocularis causes alveolar echinococcosis, in which the larva forms an infiltrating mass that behaves like a slow-growing cancer of the liver.

The adult worms are tiny, only a few millimeters long, and live in the intestine of the definitive host. In the cystic form the definitive host is the dog and the intermediate hosts are sheep, goats, cattle, and other grazing animals. The adult sheds eggs in dog feces, and the grazing animal swallows them while feeding on contaminated pasture. The oncosphere penetrates the gut wall, travels in the blood, and forms hydatid cysts in the animal's liver and lungs. The cycle closes when a dog eats the raw organs of an infected animal, which is exactly what happens when home slaughter leaves offal accessible to dogs, and human beings are infected by swallowing eggs from dog feces and are a dead end in the cycle.

The hydatid cyst grows slowly, which is why the disease presents late. A cyst may enlarge by only a few millimeters to a few centimeters in a year, so a person infected in childhood may not develop symptoms until middle age. About 60 to 70 per cent of cysts form in the liver and about 20 to 30 per cent in the lungs, with the remainder in kidney, spleen, bone, and brain. A cyst has an outer laminated layer, an inner germinal layer that produces brood capsules and microscopic protoscolices, and highly antigenic fluid, making it a self-contained parasite factory.

Many cysts cause no symptoms for years and are found incidentally. A liver cyst may produce a dull ache in the right upper abdomen, a sense of fullness after small meals, nausea, and a palpable mass, and a cyst pressing on a bile duct causes jaundice. A lung cyst causes cough, chest pain, and shortness of breath, and it may bleed into the airway. The most feared complication is rupture, because the fluid is intensely allergenic: rupture into the abdomen, bloodstream, or pleural space can cause anaphylaxis with low blood pressure, hives, airway swelling, wheezing, and collapse, which can be fatal within minutes. Spilled protoscolices can also seed the peritoneum and produce dozens of new cysts, a condition called secondary hydatidosis that is very difficult to treat.

Because rupture is both the danger and a possible consequence of our own interventions, the nurse must be prepared for anaphylaxis whenever a hydatid cyst is manipulated. Epinephrine must be drawn up and available, intravenous access established, airway equipment ready, and oxygen at hand before any aspiration or operation, and many teams insist that a clinician skilled in airway management and resuscitation be present. Elective puncture of a cyst for diagnosis alone is contraindicated. If fluid must be removed, it is done as a planned therapeutic procedure under imaging guidance, with albendazole cover and full resuscitation equipment in the room.

Diagnosis begins with imaging. Ultrasound is the first line for abdominal disease because it is portable, inexpensive, and informative, and it shows whether a cyst is a simple unilocular fluid collection, contains daughter cysts within itself, has a detached membrane floating inside, or has become solid and calcified. The classification used by the World Health Organization describes these appearances to stage the cyst and guide treatment. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging are used for deep, complicated, or uncertain lesions and for surgical planning, and chest radiography shows lung cysts as rounded opacities. Blood tests for antibodies support the diagnosis but are neither fully sensitive nor fully specific, eosinophilia is unreliable, and aspirating a cyst to make the diagnosis is not acceptable.

Albendazole is the main drug for cystic echinococcosis, both alone and around any intervention. A commonly used regimen is 10 to 15 milligrams per kilogram per day by mouth divided into two doses taken with food, because absorption improves with a fatty meal. Treatment may be continuous or given in cycles of 28 days on treatment followed by 14 days off, and it usually continues for 3 to 6 months around surgery or percutaneous treatment, or longer for inoperable cysts. These regimens are revised and national recommendations differ, so the guidance of the World Health Organization and the current national protocol must be checked before prescribing. Blood counts and liver tests are checked at baseline, every 2 weeks during the early weeks, and then monthly, because albendazole can cause hepatitis and bone marrow suppression as well as nausea, abdominal pain, and hair loss.

Percutaneous treatment uses puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration, and it has become the preferred approach for many liver cysts. Under ultrasound guidance a needle or catheter is placed into the cyst, some fluid is aspirated, a protoscolicidal solution such as hypertonic saline is injected and left in contact with the germinal layer long enough to kill the parasite, and the fluid is then reaspirated. The patient takes albendazole before and after the procedure to reduce the risk of secondary cysts if fluid leaks. The technique is unsuitable for superficial cysts that could leak into the peritoneum, cysts that communicate with the bile ducts, and cysts that are inaccessible or already ruptured. Careful patient selection, skilled imaging, and readiness for anaphylaxis are what make it safe.

Surgery remains necessary for very large cysts, cysts pressing on vital structures, cysts with a biliary communication, cysts containing many daughter cysts, ruptured or infected cysts, and cysts that have failed other treatment. The aim in every operation is to remove the parasite without spilling its contents, so the field is packed with pads soaked in a protoscolicidal solution, the cyst is handled gently, sharp dissection into it is avoided, and fluid is aspirated in a controlled way. Removing the intact cyst with its membrane, sometimes with a rim of liver tissue, is the most complete approach when feasible. After surgery albendazole is continued, biliary leaks are drained, and the patient is followed with imaging.

Follow up in echinococcosis is measured in years. Imaging is repeated at planned intervals to confirm that a cyst is shrinking, stable, or recurring, and serology is followed as a supportive trend rather than a verdict. Calcification suggests the parasite has died but is not proof, and a calcified cyst can still obstruct a bile duct or become infected. Recurrence is common enough that a recall system with dates, transport arrangements, and a way to reach the patient is essential, and in many programs follow up is the weakest part of the whole cascade. The nurse who maintains that system does work no other member of the team is positioned to do.

Alveolar echinococcosis is a different and worse disease caused by Echinococcus multilocularis, whose life cycle runs mainly between foxes and small rodents, with dogs and cats sometimes acting as definitive hosts, across the northern hemisphere. Instead of a smooth sac, the larva grows in small vesicles that infiltrate surrounding tissue, invade blood vessels and bile ducts, and spread to the lungs and brain, behaving like a slow-growing cancer. Early infection causes no symptoms, and by the time jaundice, right upper abdominal pain, weight loss, and fatigue appear the mass is often extensive. Untreated, it is generally fatal, and even with treatment it requires long-term, sometimes lifelong, albendazole.

Management combines surgery, prolonged drug treatment, and honest discussion of prognosis. Radical surgical resection offers the best chance of control when the disease is confined and the patient can tolerate the operation, and liver transplantation is used in selected patients with advanced disease. For most patients albendazole continues for many years or for life, because the parasite cannot reliably be eradicated and stopping treatment risks regrowth, and other measures may relieve complications such as biliary obstruction. Nursing care here is long term: supporting adherence to a drug taken indefinitely, monitoring liver tests and blood counts, managing symptoms, helping the patient plan around appointments, and talking plainly about what is known and what is not.

Across both forms of echinococcosis the nursing role has a consistent shape. You assess the exposure history, including dogs, sheep, foxes, slaughter practices, and where the patient grew up. You prepare the patient for imaging and procedures, and you make sure anaphylaxis equipment and resuscitation support are ready before any cyst is touched. You verify that albendazole cover has been prescribed around interventions, that doses and durations match current guidance, and that blood counts and liver tests are scheduled. You teach the patient how to take the drug with food, why the cycles are structured as they are, which symptoms to report, and why follow up must continue even when they feel well. You also record which guideline was used, so that the next clinician can reconstruct the reasoning.

The same discipline applies to neurocysticercosis. Confirm the diagnosis with imaging where possible before starting antiparasitic treatment, and confirm that corticosteroids are prescribed with the antiparasitic drug and that an anticonvulsant is in place or available. Look for cysts in the eye, the ventricles, and the subarachnoid space, because those change the plan. Establish a monitoring routine for headache, vomiting, drowsiness, seizures, vision, blood glucose, liver tests, and blood counts. Confirm that the patient can return for follow up and that the drugs are available. Then document the source of every regimen, because doses in this field are revised often and the guideline, not any individual memory, is the authority.

Prevention for echinococcosis follows the same one health logic, with dogs at the center. Dogs must not be fed raw offal, and home slaughter must be done where organs can be disposed of safely rather than left for dogs to eat. Periodic treatment of dogs with praziquantel reduces the adult worm burden and therefore the number of eggs reaching the environment, and this is a recognized control measure in endemic areas, while handwashing after contact with dogs, washing produce, and protecting water sources reduce human exposure. Education must be specific rather than general, because telling a family to improve hygiene changes little, while showing them that the pig must be penned away from the latrine, that pork must be cooked until it is no longer pink, that hands must be washed with soap after handling a dog, and that the child with a new seizure needs to be seen rather than hidden changes a great deal.

To summarize, Taenia solium causes two separate diseases that must never be confused: the intestinal tapeworm, acquired by eating undercooked pork, and neurocysticercosis, acquired by swallowing eggs from human feces, which produces seizures, hydrocephalus, and chronic epilepsy when larval cysts settle in the brain. Antiparasitic treatment with albendazole or praziquantel is given only when living cysts warrant it, is always paired with corticosteroids because killing the cysts inflames the brain, is supported by anticonvulsants, is coordinated with imaging, and is verified against current guidance before the first dose. Intestinal taeniasis is treated with niclosamide or praziquantel, but praziquantel must be used cautiously when hidden brain cysts may be present, and the tapeworm carrier must be treated because that person is the source of future brain disease. Echinococcosis follows a dog and sheep cycle for Echinococcus granulosus, producing hydatid cysts that grow slowly in liver and lung, threaten anaphylaxis if they rupture, and are managed with albendazole, percutaneous puncture and aspiration with injection and reaspiration, or surgery, while Echinococcus multilocularis produces a worse, infiltrating, often lifelong disease. The nurse's enduring contributions are the exposure history, the pre-treatment safety check, readiness for anaphylaxis, monitoring for drug toxicity and rising intracranial pressure, long-term follow up, and prevention education that names the specific practice in plain language.

# Chapter 18 — Intestinal Protozoa

The intestinal protozoa are single-celled parasites that live in the human gut, and together they cause a large share of the chronic and recurrent diarrheal illness seen in tropical practice. They are not bacteria, so antibacterial drugs do nothing for them, and they are not worms, so the medicines that empty the bowel of helminths leave them untouched. What unites them is a life cycle built around a tough cyst or oocyst that survives in water, on food, and on hands long enough to reach a new host, together with a growing form that multiplies in the intestine and produces the symptoms. Some are cosmopolitan and turn up in childcare centers, swimming pools, and municipal water systems in wealthy countries, while others cluster where water is unsafe and sanitation is poor. This chapter works through them in the order a clinician is most likely to meet them, amoebae first, then Giardia, then the coccidia and the microsporidia, and it closes with the laboratory work, the treatment you must verify, and the nursing care that usually decides the outcome.

Amoebiasis is caused by Entamoeba histolytica, whose name means tissue-destroying amoeba and describes exactly what it does. The parasite exists in two forms, a motile feeding trophozoite that lives in the colon and a round cyst that is passed in the stool and is the infectious stage. Infection follows the fecal-oral route, when cysts from contaminated water, food, or hands are swallowed, and as few as 10 cysts can establish an infection. In endemic areas most infections are asymptomatic, which is why the burden of infection is far larger than the burden of disease. The World Health Organization estimates that invasive amoebiasis causes tens of millions of illnesses and tens of thousands of deaths every year, nearly all of them preventable. It remains one of the most serious parasitic infections of the human intestine, and it is also one of the most treatable when it is recognized. The gap between those two facts is almost entirely a matter of access to clean water, a working laboratory, and a clinician who thinks of it.

Ingested cysts pass through the stomach, excyst in the small intestine, and release trophozoites that travel to the colon and multiply by simple division. There they live on the mucosal surface, feeding on bacteria and debris, and as they move toward the descending colon they encyst and are passed in formed stool. Trophozoites do not survive long outside the body, so they are not an important source of transmission, whereas cysts survive days to weeks in cool, moist conditions. Invasion happens when trophozoites breach the mucus layer, adhere to the epithelial cells, and release enzymes that dissolve tissue, producing the characteristic flask-shaped ulcers of amoebic colitis. Not every strain and not every host reaches that point, and the decisive variable is the species, because Entamoeba dispar looks identical under the microscope but never invades tissue and never causes disease. Distinguishing the two reliably requires antigen testing or molecular testing by PCR, since morphology alone cannot separate them. This single fact explains why a report that says only that amoebae were seen is not yet a diagnosis.

Several other amoebae and flagellates live harmlessly in the human intestine, and recognizing them matters more than treating them. Entamoeba coli, Endolimax nana, Iodamoeba buetschlii, and Entamoeba hartmanni are common commensals, especially where sanitation is poor, and their presence is a marker of fecal exposure rather than a disease. Entamoeba coli cysts contain up to 8 nuclei, while Entamoeba histolytica cysts contain up to 4, and that difference on a stained smear is often the only thing standing between a correct report and an unnecessary prescription. Blastocystis species, discussed later, belong to the same gray zone of uncertain pathogenicity. Treating every organism seen on a stool report is a familiar and costly error, because it exposes patients to drugs they do not need, wastes scarce medicines, and can delay the real diagnosis sitting behind the finding. The rule to carry into practice is that you treat a patient with symptoms, not a laboratory result on a page. When a report names an organism you do not recognize, the correct next step is to ask the laboratory what it means, not to reach for a prescription pad.

Amoebic colitis usually begins 1 to 4 weeks after the cysts were swallowed, and it starts gradually rather than explosively. The patient reports cramping abdominal pain, often in the lower abdomen, with tenesmus, urgency, and a growing number of small stools that contain blood, mucus, and little fecal material. Fever is absent or low, which distinguishes it from the bacillary dysenteries that produce a similar picture with higher fever and more systemic illness. The diarrhea can persist for weeks with remissions and relapses, and a chronic form exists in which pain, flatulence, and altered bowel habit dominate without visible blood. Severe disease occurs in a minority and includes fulminant colitis with widespread ulceration, toxic megacolon, and perforation with peritonitis, all of which carry high mortality and require surgical assessment. A mass of inflamed tissue and granulation called an ameboma can form in the colon and be mistaken for cancer on imaging. Because the presentation overlaps with inflammatory bowel disease, giving corticosteroids to a patient whose colitis is amoebic can precipitate fulminant disease, so the stool studies must be completed before immunosuppression is started. This is one of the few places in tropical medicine where a delay of a day or two in an unproven diagnosis is safer than a rapid assumption.

Amebic liver abscess develops when trophozoites enter the portal circulation and settle in the liver, and it can appear without any preceding diarrhea. It typically presents 2 to 4 weeks after infection but sometimes months later, with fever, rigors, night sweats, weight loss, and a dull pain in the right upper abdomen that worsens on deep breathing. The liver is enlarged and tender, and the patient may have a dry cough or right shoulder pain from irritation of the diaphragm. Most abscesses are single and in the right lobe, and they are filled with a thick reddish-brown material rather than pus, which is why the old description of anchovy paste is still heard. Mild jaundice is common and deep jaundice is not, so a very high bilirubin should prompt you to look for another cause. Rupture into the chest or abdomen is the feared complication, and it presents as sudden severe pain, breathlessness, or shock. Imaging with ultrasound or computed tomography shows the lesion, while serology usually confirms the cause. A patient with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and a liver lesion who has lived in or traveled to an endemic area should be treated for amebic abscess until proven otherwise.

The diagnosis of amoebiasis rests on finding the parasite, but the stool examination has to be requested correctly. Trophozoites are fragile and degenerate quickly, so a fresh specimen or a promptly preserved one is essential, and at least 3 stool samples collected on separate days are needed before a negative result means anything. A stained smear, with iron hematoxylin or trichrome, is far better than a wet mount for identifying trophozoites, and the single most useful finding is a trophozoite that has ingested red blood cells, which no harmless amoeba does. Antigen detection in stool is more sensitive than microscopy, and molecular testing by PCR is the most sensitive of all where it is available. Serology is a valuable adjunct, because antibody is present in roughly 70 per cent of patients with amoebic colitis and in more than 90 per cent of those with liver abscess, but it is often negative in asymptomatic cyst passers and it can remain positive for years after a cured infection, so a positive result does not prove active disease. For suspected liver abscess, ultrasound and computed tomography localize the lesion and guide aspiration, and antibody testing supports the diagnosis. Repeated negative stool studies in a patient with continuing bloody diarrhea should push you toward colonoscopy and biopsy rather than another blind course of treatment.

Treatment of invasive amoebiasis is a two-step sequence, and understanding why there are two steps prevents the most common therapeutic mistake. The first step is a tissue-active drug that kills trophozoites in the bowel wall and the liver, and the second is a luminal agent that clears the cysts remaining in the colon so that the patient does not remain a carrier. Current guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention gives metronidazole at 500 to 750 milligrams by mouth three times a day for 7 to 10 days for invasive disease, or tinidazole at 2 grams by mouth once daily for 3 days. Metronidazole is well absorbed and reaches the liver in high concentration, which is why it works so well for abscess, but that same absorption means little of it reaches the colonic lumen, and that is precisely why the second drug is required. The luminal agent may be paromomycin at 25 to 35 milligrams per kilogram per day by mouth divided into three doses for 7 days, or diloxanide furoate at 500 milligrams by mouth three times a day for 10 days, or iodoquinol at 650 milligrams by mouth three times a day for 20 days. Omitting the luminal step leaves the patient passing cysts and able to infect others, and it also leaves them at risk of relapse. Large liver abscesses, those at risk of rupture, or those that fail to improve within about a week may need ultrasound-guided aspiration, which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. An asymptomatic person passing Entamoeba histolytica cysts still needs a luminal agent, because carriage is the mechanism by which the disease reaches the next household.

Before you prescribe any of these regimens, verify them against current guidance, because they are revised as evidence accumulates and they differ between countries, programs, and product labels. Amoebiasis treatment is a good example, since diloxanide furoate is not marketed in the United States, tinidazole availability varies, and pediatric regimens are always weight-based and must be calculated rather than approximated. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control publish recommendations that do not always agree, and a national program may follow a different algorithm again. No dose should be given from memory, from an old chart, or from a colleague's recollection, and the current guideline, the current formulary, and the current product label must be reviewed before the first dose. Document the source you followed and the weight you used, so that the next clinician can see the reasoning. This is not bureaucratic caution; it is the difference between treatment and harm, and in a field setting it is also how you detect an error before the pharmacy or the patient does.

The adverse effects of these drugs are mostly predictable, and knowing them lets you prepare the patient instead of alarming them. Metronidazole commonly causes nausea, a metallic taste, headache, and dark urine, and it produces a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, so patients must avoid alcohol during treatment and for 3 days afterward. Prolonged use can cause peripheral neuropathy, which is one reason the course is kept short, and it interacts with warfarin and with some anticonvulsants. Tinidazole shares these effects and has a longer half-life, so a single-dose course can cause symptoms that last more than a day. Paromomycin is poorly absorbed, so systemic toxicity is uncommon, but it can cause diarrhea, abdominal pain, and rarely kidney injury or hearing loss, and it should be used cautiously in renal impairment. Iodoquinol can cause optic neuritis, peripheral neuropathy, and thyroid dysfunction when given for long periods. Monitoring after treatment means confirming that symptoms have resolved, repeating stool studies at an appropriate interval, checking liver enzymes in liver abscess, and asking directly whether the patient completed the second, luminal drug, because that is the step most often abandoned once the diarrhea stops.

Giardiasis is caused by Giardia duodenalis, a flagellated protozoan also known as Giardia lamblia and Giardia intestinalis, and it is the most commonly reported intestinal parasite in many high-income countries. The cyst is the infectious form, it is passed in stool, and the infecting dose is remarkably low, with as few as 10 cysts able to cause illness. Giardia cysts tolerate routine chlorination better than most bacteria, so municipal water that meets disinfection standards can still transmit infection, and mountain streams, untreated well water, childcare centers, and swimming pools are classic sources. The incubation period is 1 to 3 weeks. Illness begins with watery diarrhea and evolves into stools that are greasy, pale, floating, and foul smelling, the steatorrhea that reflects malabsorption of fat. Bloating, flatulence, belching with a sulfurous taste, nausea, and weight loss are common, and the malabsorption can extend to fat-soluble vitamins and to lactose, so milk worsens symptoms even after the infection has apparently cleared. Many infections resolve on their own within 2 to 6 weeks, but some become chronic, with intermittent symptoms, fatigue, and failure to thrive in children. Because the cyst is so widely distributed, a negative water history does not exclude the diagnosis.

Stool microscopy can identify cysts and trophozoites, but because excretion is intermittent, 3 samples on separate days are needed, and antigen testing or molecular testing by PCR raises the yield substantially. When stool studies remain negative and suspicion is high, duodenal aspirate or a string test can recover trophozoites, though these are rarely necessary in practice. Treatment is straightforward when the right drug is used. Tinidazole at 2 grams by mouth as a single dose is highly effective, metronidazole at 250 milligrams by mouth three times a day for 5 to 7 days is the traditional alternative, and nitazoxanide at 500 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 3 days is a further option. Children receive weight-based doses of the same drugs, and children with repeated failure may need a longer course or a change of agent. Treatment failure is common enough that it should be expected rather than treated as a mystery, and the usual causes are poor adherence, reinfection from a household member or a water source, and genuine drug resistance. Resistance to the nitroimidazole drugs can be managed by repeating with a higher dose, by combining drugs, or by using a different class, and alcohol must be avoided with tinidazole and metronidazole exactly as in the treatment of amoebiasis. Household members with symptoms should be tested and treated, and the water source should be reviewed whenever reinfection is suspected.

Cryptosporidiosis is caused mainly by Cryptosporidium parvum and Cryptosporidium hominis, and its oocyst is the reason the infection is so difficult to control. The oocyst is immediately infectious when passed, it is small enough to pass many filters, and it resists chlorine at the concentrations used in drinking water and swimming pools, so outbreaks have followed municipal water supplies, recreational pools, childcare centers, and contact with calves and lambs. The infectious dose is very low, and person-to-person spread is efficient, which is why outbreaks move quickly through households and institutions. After an incubation of 2 to 10 days, illness begins with profuse watery diarrhea, cramping, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever, and in a healthy adult it usually settles within 1 to 2 weeks, though it can relapse. Blood is not usually present and the stool is not inflammatory, so the picture is one of high-volume water loss rather than dysentery. Diagnosis depends on laboratory methods that specifically look for the organism, because routine stool examination often misses it. A modified acid-fast stain, immunofluorescence, antigen testing, and PCR are the tools that find it, and the laboratory should be told that cryptosporidiosis is suspected so that the correct stain is requested. Dehydration and electrolyte loss, not the parasite itself, are what make this illness dangerous in a small child or an older adult.

In a person with advanced HIV, cryptosporidiosis behaves differently and can become a chronic, wasting illness. The diarrhea is prolonged, high in volume, and often associated with malabsorption, and the organism can spread to the biliary tree and the pancreas, causing pain, cholestasis, and occasionally a picture resembling sclerosing cholangitis. Before effective antiretroviral therapy was available, cryptosporidiosis was one of the leading causes of chronic diarrhea and death in people with advanced HIV, and it remains a marker of severe immunodeficiency. The most important treatment is not an antiparasitic drug at all but antiretroviral therapy, which restores immune function and is usually what stops the diarrhea, so it must be started or optimized promptly. Nitazoxanide at 500 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 3 days is used in immunocompetent patients and may shorten the illness, while in advanced HIV its benefit is limited when the helper T lymphocyte count is very low, and some clinicians use a longer course. Supportive care with fluids, electrolyte replacement, and nutritional support carries the patient until immunity recovers. Antimotility drugs can reduce stool volume but should be used with care, and nitazoxanide should be taken with food to improve absorption. Relapse is common if immune recovery does not occur, which is why the helper T lymphocyte count and the viral load belong in the same conversation as the diarrhea.

Cyclospora cayetanensis is a coccidian that causes a prolonged, relapsing diarrheal illness and is increasingly recognized in travelers and in outbreaks linked to imported produce. Its oocyst is not infectious when passed, because it must spend days to weeks in the environment to mature, which means direct person-to-person transmission is unlikely and the infection usually comes from contaminated food or water. Outbreaks have been traced to raspberries, snow peas, cilantro, basil, and other fresh items that are difficult to wash thoroughly. After about a week of incubation, patients develop watery diarrhea, loss of appetite, fatigue, bloating, and weight loss, and without treatment the illness can last for weeks with a waxing and waning course. Fever is uncommon. Diagnosis uses a modified acid-fast stain, and Cyclospora oocysts autofluoresce under ultraviolet microscopy, which is a useful clue when the stain is equivocal, while molecular testing by PCR is increasingly available. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the treatment of choice, given as a tablet containing 160 milligrams of trimethoprim and 800 milligrams of sulfamethoxazole by mouth twice a day for 7 to 10 days, and patients with HIV often need a longer course followed by maintenance suppression. Sulfa allergy is the main obstacle, and it requires an alternative plan made with an expert rather than a guess.

Cystoisospora belli, formerly called Isospora belli, is a related coccidian that produces a similar but generally less explosive illness. It occurs sporadically in tropical and subtropical settings and is an important cause of chronic diarrhea in people with advanced HIV, in whom it can cause severe watery diarrhea, steatorrhea, marked weight loss, and sometimes blood eosinophilia. The oocyst is large and oval and is found with a modified acid-fast stain, and as with the other coccidia the laboratory must be asked to look for it specifically. Treatment follows the same logic as Cyclospora, with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole given as a tablet containing 160 milligrams of trimethoprim and 800 milligrams of sulfamethoxazole by mouth twice a day for 7 to 10 days. Relapse after treatment is common in immunocompromised patients, so chronic maintenance therapy is often required until immune function improves with antiretroviral therapy. When sulfa cannot be used, pyrimethamine or a fluoroquinolone has been tried with variable success, and expert advice should be sought. Supportive care, nutrition, and management of the underlying immune deficiency are as important as the antiparasitic drug itself.

The microsporidia are a large group of spore-forming organisms now classified as fungi, and two species cause most human intestinal disease: Enterocytozoon bieneusi and Encephalitozoon intestinalis. Their spores are very small, so they are easily missed on routine stool examination, and they require special stains such as chromotrope or calcofluor white, or molecular testing by PCR, to be identified. They cause chronic watery diarrhea, malabsorption, and wasting, chiefly in people with advanced HIV and in transplant recipients, and they can also infect the biliary tract and the sinuses. Management begins with restoring immunity through antiretroviral therapy, which is the intervention most likely to produce lasting resolution. Albendazole at 400 milligrams by mouth twice a day is effective against Encephalitozoon intestinalis, while Enterocytozoon bieneusi responds poorly to albendazole and has been treated with fumagillin or nitazoxanide, with limited and inconsistent results. Nutritional support and management of fluid and electrolyte losses remain central, because the diarrhea itself can be debilitating. Microsporidiosis is uncommon outside the severely immunocompromised, so a diagnosis in an apparently healthy patient should prompt a search for an underlying cause of immune suppression.

Blastocystis species, long called Blastocystis hominis, is the most common intestinal protozoan found in human stool and the most controversial. It is present in a large proportion of healthy people, it exists in many genetically distinct subtypes, and only some have been associated with symptoms, so the evidence that it causes disease remains weak and inconsistent. Patients in whom it is found may have diarrhea, abdominal pain, and flatulence, but they may equally have another cause that has not yet been found. Some clinicians offer a trial of metronidazole, tinidazole, nitazoxanide, or paromomycin when symptoms persist and no other explanation emerges, and some patients improve, but the improvement is difficult to attribute and relapses are frequent. Treating every Blastocystis finding is wrong, because it exposes patients to unnecessary drugs, reinforces the idea that the laboratory report is the diagnosis, and can delay the search for a treatable condition such as celiac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, or a bacterial infection. Dientamoeba fragilis is a related puzzle, because it has no cyst, only a fragile trophozoite, and while it has been linked to diarrhea and abdominal pain, the evidence for treating it is similarly limited. The honest position is that these organisms are common, that their pathogenicity is uncertain, and that decisions should rest on the whole clinical picture rather than on a single line of a report.

Across this whole group, the laboratory work follows a few practical rules, and the nurse often controls whether those rules are met. Collect at least 3 stool specimens on separate days, because parasite excretion fluctuates and a single sample misses a substantial share of infections. Send specimens fresh or properly preserved, since trophozoites disintegrate within hours and a delayed specimen can turn a positive case into a negative report. Ask for the right test rather than a generic stool examination: trichrome or iron hematoxylin staining for amoebae and Giardia, a modified acid-fast stain for the coccidia, and calcofluor white or chromotrope staining for the microsporidia. Antigen tests for Giardia and Cryptosporidium are rapid, sensitive, and useful in field settings, and multiplex molecular panels that detect several parasites at once by PCR are becoming standard where they are affordable. Concentration techniques such as formalin-ethyl acetate improve recovery of cysts and oocysts, and ultraviolet autofluorescence helps identify Cyclospora. A test of cure is worth arranging 2 to 4 weeks after treatment in persistent or high-risk cases, and it should use the same method as the original diagnosis so that the results can be compared. A negative result never fully excludes these infections when the clinical suspicion is strong.

The nursing work in intestinal protozoal disease begins with hydration, and it is more important than any antiparasitic prescription. Assess the patient for dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes, a rapid heart rate, low blood pressure on standing, and reduced urine output, and weigh the patient accurately, because weight change is the most reliable measure of fluid loss over time. Mild and moderate dehydration is corrected with oral rehydration salts given in small, frequent sips, and the nurse should teach the family to prepare and offer the solution rather than assume it will be done. Severe dehydration, persistent vomiting, or an inability to drink requires fluids given intravenously, and in children zinc supplementation reduces the duration and severity of diarrhea. Continue feeding during illness, because withholding food prolongs recovery and worsens malnutrition, and choose simple, well-tolerated foods. After Giardia and other malabsorptive infections, lactose intolerance may persist for weeks, so a temporary reduction in milk and a gradual reintroduction help, and fat-soluble vitamin deficiency may need specific replacement. Monitor electrolytes, especially potassium and magnesium, and watch for hypokalemia in patients with profuse diarrhea, since low potassium can cause weakness and dangerous heart rhythms. Growth monitoring in children and referral to nutrition services turn a single episode of illness into an opportunity to prevent the next one.

Infection control is where intestinal protozoa punish complacency, and the nurse is usually the person who sets the standard. Hand hygiene is the foundation, and when cryptosporidiosis is possible it must be washing with soap and running water rather than an alcohol rub, because alcohol does not reliably kill the oocyst, while alcohol rubs remain useful for most other organisms. Cohorting patients with the same infection, excluding symptomatic children and food handlers from childcare and food preparation until they are clear, and cleaning surfaces and shared equipment with an appropriate disinfectant all interrupt transmission. Water safety is a clinical intervention here: advise boiling, filtering through a filter rated to remove cysts, or using bottled water, and warn patients not to swallow water in pools, lakes, or rivers, especially during an outbreak. Food safety advice matters more than most clinicians realize, since fresh produce that cannot be peeled or cooked is a well-documented route for Cyclospora and Cryptosporidium. In an outbreak, the nurse coordinates specimen collection, keeps a line list, reports to public health authorities promptly, and communicates clearly with families who may be frightened and may not understand why a child cannot return to childcare. Education should be concrete and repeated, because advice about hand washing is followed far more often when it is tied to a specific moment in the day. Healthcare workers themselves must not work while symptomatic, and staff illness should be reported and managed rather than hidden.

Prevention and special populations deserve their own attention, because the same parasite affects different people very differently. Travelers should be advised to drink boiled, filtered, or bottled water, to avoid ice made from uncertain water, to eat food that is cooked and still hot, and to peel fruit themselves, and these measures also protect against the bacterial causes of traveler's diarrhea. In pregnancy, the treatment of amoebiasis and giardiasis requires judgment, because some clinicians prefer to defer metronidazole in the first trimester and use paromomycin, which is poorly absorbed, while others treat symptomatic disease promptly because the illness itself threatens the pregnancy, and current guidance must be checked before any decision. Children need weight-based doses calculated carefully, and adult tablets must never be split casually to approximate a pediatric dose. In people with HIV, antiretroviral therapy is the definitive management of cryptosporidiosis and microsporidiosis, so adherence support is itself an antiparasitic intervention. Returning travelers and migrants with diarrhea lasting more than 2 weeks should have parasite studies performed before they are labeled as having irritable bowel syndrome, because chronic protozoal infection is easily missed and easily treated. Antimicrobial stewardship applies here as everywhere, since an antiparasitic drug given for a commensal, a colonizer, or a misread report is still an unnecessary drug.

To summarize, the intestinal protozoa are a compact group of parasites with a shared strategy, a resistant cyst or oocyst that travels by water, food, and hands, and a growing form that damages the gut or spreads beyond it. Entamoeba histolytica is the dangerous amoeba, causing bloody colitis and liver abscess that require a tissue-active drug followed by a luminal agent, while Entamoeba dispar and the other harmless amoebae should be left alone. Giardia causes malabsorptive, fatty diarrhea and responds to tinidazole, metronidazole, or nitazoxanide, and treatment failure usually means poor adherence, reinfection, or resistance rather than a wrong diagnosis. Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora, and the microsporidia cause prolonged watery diarrhea, resist routine chlorination, and in advanced HIV are managed principally by restoring immunity with antiretroviral therapy alongside targeted antiparasitic treatment. Diagnosis depends on collecting multiple properly handled specimens and asking for the correct stain, antigen test, or molecular test rather than a generic stool examination. The nursing contribution is decisive: assess and correct dehydration, keep the patient fed, monitor electrolytes and weight, teach lactose tolerance, enforce hand washing with soap and water, and coordinate specimen collection, reporting, and family education during an outbreak. Verify every dose against current guidance from the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, because regimens change and countries differ. Treat the patient, not the laboratory report.

# Chapter 19 — Enteric Infections and Fluid Management

Enteric infections spread by the fecal-oral route and remain a leading cause of death in young children across tropical settings. The organisms differ widely, from bacteria that invade the bloodstream and seed distant organs to bacteria that never leave the gut lumen yet pour out fluid fast enough to kill within hours. They share a transmission pathway through water, food, hands, and flies, so the same measures interrupt all of them at once. Because that pathway is ordinary, these illnesses are often accepted as normal life, and that acceptance is why they stay lethal. This chapter takes typhoid and paratyphoid fever, cholera, shigellosis, and traveler's diarrhea in turn, and treats fluid management as a clinical skill in its own right. Rehydration decides whether most of these patients live, and the nurse usually delivers it.

Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella Typhi, and paratyphoid fever, similar but milder, by Salmonella Paratyphi A, B, or C. The organism infects only humans, so every case comes from another person through contact or contaminated water and food. It enters by mouth, survives stomach acid when the dose is large, and behaves differently from bacteria that stay in the lumen. The World Health Organization estimates roughly 9 million illnesses and 110,000 deaths each year, heaviest in South Asia, much of Africa, and wherever water and sewage systems are inadequate. Clean water, sanitation and hygiene would prevent most of it, so typhoid marks failing infrastructure as much as disease. The incubation period is usually 7 to 14 days but ranges from 3 days to more than a month.

After being swallowed, the organisms cross the small intestine lining, are taken up by immune cells in lymphoid tissue, and reach the bloodstream in a silent first phase. During incubation they multiply inside the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and gallbladder, and that multiplication produces the illness. A second wave entering the blood coincides with the onset of fever, when the organism can be recovered from blood reliably. The gallbladder becomes a site of continued seeding, explaining both the prolonged fever and the later risk of carriage. The intestine is injured again when the organism returns to the terminal ileum, and that injury can ulcerate through the bowel wall. This explains why stool culture is often negative early and why blood culture is the test of choice in the first week.

The fever of typhoid is called stepped because it climbs in stages over the first week, each afternoon a little higher, until it settles near 39 to 40 degrees Celsius. The pulse is often slower than the fever would predict, a finding called relative bradycardia, and it is a useful clue in prolonged fever without an obvious source. Rose spots appear in the first week in a minority of patients, as faint salmon-colored marks 2 to 4 millimeters across, in crops on the trunk, blanching when pressed and easily missed on darker skin. Constipation is common early and is followed later by diarrhea, the opposite of what most clinicians expect from an intestinal infection. The patient looks increasingly unwell, with headache, a coated tongue, loss of appetite, abdominal pain, and an enlarged tender liver or spleen. By the second week the fever persists and the patient may become confused or drowsy.

The complications of typhoid cluster in the second and third weeks and are what make it dangerous. The most feared is perforation of the terminal ileum, where lymphoid tissue has ulcerated, presenting as sudden severe abdominal pain, guarding, a rising pulse, and shock. Perforation is a surgical emergency with high mortality, and it must be suspected whenever a patient with typhoid develops abrupt abdominal pain or a rigid abdomen. Intestinal hemorrhage is the other bowel complication, and it can be massive and fatal. Beyond the gut, typhoid can cause encephalopathy, inflammation of the heart muscle, pneumonia, hepatitis, and, rarely, abscesses in the liver or spleen. Untreated, it kills roughly 10 to 20 per cent of those it infects, and relapse occurs in a small proportion after recovery.

Diagnosis rests on culture, and the specimen depends on how long the patient has been ill. Blood culture is most useful in the first week, when the organism is circulating, and it becomes less sensitive later as antibiotics clear the bloodstream. Bone marrow culture is the most sensitive test at any stage, but it requires a procedure many clinics cannot perform. Stool culture becomes positive in the second and third weeks, and urine culture can also yield the organism. The Widal test measures antibodies but is poorly specific, because previous infection, vaccination, and other infections raise the same antibodies, so a positive result never proves current typhoid. Molecular testing by PCR on blood answers within hours, though it does not replace culture, which provides the organism for susceptibility testing.

Treatment of typhoid has been reshaped by resistance. Fluoroquinolones were once the treatment of choice, but resistance spread through South Asia and much of Africa until they could no longer be relied on, and in many regions they have been removed from first-line use. Current guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention favors ceftriaxone at 2 grams intravenously once daily for 7 to 14 days, or cefixime by mouth, or azithromycin at 1 gram by mouth once daily for 5 to 7 days, with ciprofloxacin only where the organism is susceptible. Dexamethasone is sometimes given for severe typhoid with shock or encephalopathy, but it is not routine and can worsen other infections. Supportive care with fluids, fever control, and nutrition runs alongside the antibiotic. Before prescribing, verify every regimen against current guidance, because these regimens are revised and they differ between countries, programs, and product labels.

Some patients do not clear the organism and become chronic carriers, excreting Salmonella Typhi in stool for more than a year after the acute illness resolves. Carriage usually reflects colonization of the gallbladder, and it is more common in women, in older adults, and in people with gallstones. A carrier may feel entirely well and may have no memory of a significant illness, which is why carriers seed outbreaks through the food they prepare. Historical investigations traced single asymptomatic cooks to dozens of cases in households and institutions, and those findings are why food handlers are screened in many countries. Current guidance offers prolonged ciprofloxacin for several weeks, or ampicillin with probenecid, and removal of the gallbladder when medical treatment fails. Public health follow-up matters as much as the prescription, because an unmonitored carrier keeps infecting others while feeling healthy.

Prevention rests on clean water, safe food, sanitary disposal of human waste, and vaccination, in that order of importance. The typhoid conjugate vaccine is given as a single dose and can be used in children from 6 months of age, and older polysaccharide vaccines remain available in some programs. The World Health Organization recommends introducing typhoid conjugate vaccine in the countries with the highest burden, and campaigns have reduced illness where water and sanitation improvements lag behind. Vaccination does not replace safe water, because it reduces the chance of illness without stopping transmission. For the traveler, the advice is to drink boiled, filtered, or bottled water, avoid ice from uncertain water, eat food that is cooked and still hot, and peel fruit personally. When a case is confirmed, contact tracing, food handler investigation, and notification to public health authorities are part of the clinical response.

Cholera is caused by Vibrio cholerae, and epidemic strains belong mainly to serogroup O1, with serogroup O139 appearing in some regions. The organism lives in brackish water and with small aquatic animals, and it has produced pandemics that began in the Ganges delta and spread along trade and pilgrimage routes since the nineteenth century. Cholera is endemic across much of South Asia and parts of Africa, and it flares into epidemics wherever people are crowded without safe water or sanitation, which is why war, flooding, and displacement often precede outbreaks. The incubation period is short, from a few hours to 5 days, so an outbreak can grow explosively within a week. A small number of people carry the organism without symptoms and shed it for a few days. Severity ranges from mild diarrhea to a loss of fluid that kills a healthy adult within hours.

The reason cholera is so violent is a single toxin, and its mechanism explains every clinical feature of the disease. Vibrio cholerae does not invade the bowel wall; it attaches to the lining of the small intestine and releases a toxin made of two parts, one that binds to a receptor on the cell surface and one that enters the cell and does the damage. Once inside, the toxin chemically modifies a regulatory protein by attaching a small sugar and phosphate unit, and that modification locks the protein into its active state permanently. The locked protein drives an enzyme called adenylate cyclase without pause, and the level of cyclic adenosine monophosphate inside the cell rises far above normal. High cyclic adenosine monophosphate forces the chloride channels to remain open, chloride pours into the gut lumen, and sodium and water follow passively. The result is a massive secretion of isotonic fluid that overwhelms the colon's ability to reabsorb it.

The clinical picture of severe cholera is unmistakable once seen. Profuse, painless, watery diarrhea begins suddenly, and the stool is pale, cloudy, and flecked with mucus, which is why it is called rice-water stool. There is typically no fever, no tenesmus, and no blood, and the patient may vomit repeatedly, making oral replacement difficult. Fluid loss can reach 1 liter per hour in an adult, and a previously healthy person can lose more than 10 per cent of body weight within a few hours. The signs are those of profound dehydration and shock: sunken eyes, a hollowed face, dry mouth, skin that stays pinched when released, wrinkled hands, a weak rapid pulse, low blood pressure, and almost no urine. Muscle cramps are common from loss of sodium and chloride, and potassium loss causes weakness and dangerous heart rhythms. Without treatment the patient becomes unconscious and dies, and with prompt rehydration the same patient can be sitting up and drinking within hours.

Assessing the degree of dehydration determines everything that follows, and the World Health Organization classification is reliable enough to use in a tent or a hallway. A patient with no dehydration has no signs, is alert, drinks normally, and passes urine. A patient with some dehydration has two or more of restlessness, sunken eyes, thirst and eagerness to drink, a skin pinch that returns slowly, and reduced urine output. A patient with severe dehydration has two or more of lethargy or unconsciousness, very sunken eyes, inability to drink, and a skin pinch returning very slowly, along with a weak pulse and low blood pressure. The skin pinch is performed on the abdomen, and in an older person or a severely malnourished child it may retract slowly even without dehydration, so the whole picture must be read together. Weigh the patient whenever a scale is available, because weight change is the most honest measure of fluid balance, and reassess at short intervals, because dehydration can worsen within an hour.

Oral rehydration salts are the single most important medicine in this chapter, and their composition is not arbitrary. The low-osmolarity formulation recommended by the World Health Organization contains 75 millimoles of sodium, 75 millimoles of glucose, 20 millimoles of potassium, 65 millimoles of chloride, and 10 millimoles of citrate in each liter of clean water. The glucose is present at a concentration that matches the sodium, and that match is the whole trick of the solution. When glucose and sodium reach the intestinal surface together, a transporter carries them into the cell as a pair, and water follows the absorbed sodium by osmosis. This route works even while the intestine is pouring fluid outward, which is why a solution that seems too simple can rescue a patient minutes from death. One sachet is dissolved in 1 liter of clean water, because a solution that is too strong worsens dehydration and one that is too weak fails to replace sodium.

Giving oral rehydration salts well is a skill, and it is often performed badly. A child with some dehydration should receive 75 milliliters per kilogram over 4 hours, by cup and spoon in small frequent sips, and a patient who vomits should wait 10 minutes and resume more slowly. Replace ongoing losses separately, with about 10 milliliters per kilogram after each loose stool in a child under 2 years, 50 to 100 milliliters for an older child, and 200 to 250 milliliters for an adult. If a patient cannot drink because of vomiting, lethargy, or a swollen abdomen, a nasogastric tube allows the same solution to be given safely while intravenous access is arranged. Never give a soft drink, fruit juice, or sports drink instead, because the sugar is too high and the sodium too low. Teach the family to prepare and offer the solution themselves, because the person who keeps the cup filled usually decides the outcome.

For severe dehydration, fluids must go directly into the vein, and Ringer's lactate is the fluid of choice because its composition is close to the fluid being lost. Current guidance from the World Health Organization suggests 100 milliliters per kilogram over the first 3 hours, with 30 milliliters per kilogram in the first 30 minutes and the remainder over the following two and a half hours. An adult typically needs 2 to 4 liters in the first 3 hours, and the rate is adjusted continuously according to the pulse, the blood pressure, the skin pinch, and the urine output. If Ringer's lactate is unavailable, normal saline can be used, but it does not correct the acidosis and potassium loss of cholera as well. Potassium is often added to the intravenous fluid once the patient is passing urine, and low blood sugar must be anticipated in children. Reassess every 30 minutes, because both too little and too much fluid are dangerous.

Antibiotics play a supporting role in cholera, and they are not the treatment. A single dose of doxycycline at 300 milligrams by mouth for an adult shortens the diarrhea, reduces the volume of fluid lost, and shortens the time the patient sheds the organism, which limits transmission. For children the dose is 2 milligrams per kilogram by mouth as a single dose, and azithromycin at 20 milligrams per kilogram, or 1 gram for an adult, is an alternative where doxycycline resistance or pregnancy makes it preferable. Antibiotics must never delay rehydration, because no antibiotic has saved a patient whose circulation had already collapsed. Resistance to doxycycline has appeared in several outbreaks, so local susceptibility patterns and current guidance should be checked before the drug is chosen. In the nineteenth century cholera killed more than half of those it struck, and with rehydration alone the case fatality falls below 1 per cent. That change came from water, salt, and sugar, not from a new drug.

Managing a cholera outbreak is a logistical exercise as much as a clinical one, and the nurse usually holds it together. A cholera treatment center should separate triage from rehydration from the ward, so that patients can be sorted by dehydration category and treated without crowding. Oral rehydration corners stocked with sachets, clean water, cups, and spoons can treat some dehydration before a patient needs a bed, and they free the ward for those who need intravenous fluids. Supplies to count and restock daily include oral rehydration salts, Ringer's lactate, intravenous tubing and catheters, nasogastric tubes, chlorine, soap, and gloves and gowns for personal protection. Stool and vomit are highly infectious, so surfaces must be disinfected, bedding handled carefully, and hands washed with soap and running water after every contact. A patient who dies should be handled with respect and safe burial practices, and staff who become ill must be removed from duty immediately.

Shigellosis is caused by Shigella species, chiefly Shigella dysenteriae, Shigella flexneri, Shigella boydii, and Shigella sonnei, and it is the classic cause of bacillary dysentery. The organism is extraordinarily infectious, with as few as 10 organisms able to cause illness, which is why it moves so quickly through households, schools, camps, and institutions. It spreads by the fecal-oral route, and because the infecting dose is so low, contaminated fingers and food are enough even where water is safe. Shigella invades the cells lining the colon rather than remaining in the lumen, multiplying inside those cells and spreading sideways.
