Shigella dysenteriae type 1 produces Shiga toxin, a potent poison that blocks protein production inside cells by damaging the larger ribosomal subunit, and this toxin causes the most severe disease. Direct invasion combined with toxin production explains why shigellosis produces bloody, small-volume stools rather than the massive watery loss of cholera.

The illness begins 1 to 3 days after exposure with fever, cramping abdominal pain, and watery diarrhea that becomes bloody within a day or two. Stools are small, frequent, and composed largely of blood, mucus, and pus, and the patient has tenesmus, an intense painful urge to pass stool that produces almost nothing. Children may develop seizures, and severe cases can progress to toxic megacolon, intestinal perforation, or a profound inflammatory state. Dehydration is usually less extreme than in cholera, because the colon is inflamed rather than freely secreting, so the danger lies in the systemic effects of the toxin. Shigella dysenteriae type 1 is particularly associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome, the triad of anemia, a low platelet count, and acute kidney injury, which appears about a week after bloody diarrhea begins. Children are affected most often, and the illness can require dialysis, though many recover kidney function. Giving antibiotics to a patient with Shiga toxin-producing infection remains debated, because killing the organism may release more toxin, but avoiding drugs that slow the bowel and avoiding dehydration are always right.

Treatment of shigellosis shortens illness, reduces shedding, and prevents complications, but it must be accompanied by the same fluid discipline as every other enteric infection. Current guidance favors ciprofloxacin at 500 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 3 days, or azithromycin at 1 gram by mouth as a single dose, or azithromycin at 500 milligrams once daily for 3 days, with ceftriaxone reserved for severe or hospitalized patients. Resistance is a growing problem, particularly to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and to older agents, so the choice should follow local susceptibility data and current guidance rather than habit. Antibiotics are not indicated for every watery diarrhea, but they are valuable in confirmed or suspected bloody diarrhea and are most effective when started early. Antimotility drugs are dangerous in dysentery and must be withheld, because slowing the bowel traps the organism and toxin and can precipitate toxic megacolon. Continued feeding is part of recovery, and reporting matters because shigellosis spreads easily and resistance must be tracked.

Traveler's diarrhea is the enteric syndrome most often seen in clinics in wealthy countries, and it follows a predictable pattern. It is defined as three or more loose stools in 24 hours, with or without cramps, nausea, or fever, beginning during travel or within about 10 days of returning. The commonest cause is enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli, which produces toxins that drive secretion without invading tissue, and other causes include Campylobacter, Salmonella, Shigella, and several viruses and parasites. The illness is usually self-limited, lasting 3 to 5 days, and the main risk is dehydration rather than death, so the clinician's task is to identify the minority who need antibiotics or who have a more serious illness. Loperamide has a real but narrow place. It is reasonable in watery diarrhea without fever or blood, at 4 milligrams by mouth at the start and 2 milligrams after each loose stool, up to 8 milligrams in a day. It must not be used with fever or bloody diarrhea, because in dysentery it traps the organism and toxin and has been associated with toxic megacolon, and it should be avoided in children and in anyone significantly dehydrated.

The nurse's central role in enteric disease begins with assessment, and it is more consequential than any prescription. Look for dry mucous membranes, sunken eyes, absent tears in a child, reduced skin turgor, a rapid weak pulse, low blood pressure, cool extremities, delayed capillary refill, and lethargy, and record each finding rather than a general impression. Ask about thirst, vomiting, stool volume and frequency, and the ability to drink, because a patient who cannot keep fluid down needs a different plan. Weigh the patient at admission and at intervals afterward, since a falling weight is the clearest evidence of continuing loss and a rising weight may signal over-hydration. Measure urine output, and in a severe case record it hourly, because urine is the body's own report on whether circulation has been restored. Pay particular attention to the malnourished child, the older adult, and the pregnant patient, in whom the same loss produces far greater danger. Document everything you observe and everything you give, because in a busy outbreak the chart is the only memory the team has.

Monitoring during treatment is continuous and concrete. In severe cholera, urine output should be at least 30 milliliters per hour in an adult and at least 0.5 to 1 milliliter per kilogram per hour in a child, and a falling output despite fluids calls for faster infusion and a search for another problem. Follow the pulse, the blood pressure, the respiratory rate, and the level of consciousness, because they change before the laboratory does, and check the skin pinch and the eyes at each review. Measure electrolytes where possible, especially potassium, sodium, bicarbonate, and magnesium, since low potassium causes weakness and heart rhythm disturbances while low bicarbonate reflects acidosis. Check the blood sugar in children, because low blood sugar is common and dangerous. Replace ongoing losses according to measured stool and vomit volumes rather than a fixed rule. A patient who is improving passes urine, becomes alert, drinks eagerly, and has a skin pinch that returns promptly.

Getting fluid into a patient fast enough is the technical heart of this chapter, and it requires choosing the right route for the degree of illness. A patient who can drink, is alert, and has some dehydration should be rehydrated by mouth with oral rehydration salts, in small sips by cup and spoon, and watched closely for 4 hours. A patient who is vomiting repeatedly or too weak to drink should have a nasogastric tube placed, and the same solution can be given by that route in measured amounts. A patient with severe dehydration, shock, or an inability to take anything by mouth needs an intravenous line immediately, and two lines may be needed if the pulse is weak and the veins are collapsed. Do not wait for laboratory results before starting fluids, because in cholera the diagnosis is clinical and the treatment is time-critical. The commonest error in these patients is giving fluid too slowly, and the second commonest is stopping it too soon.

Special populations need modified plans, and the general rules must be adapted rather than applied mechanically. Children dehydrate faster than adults, because more of their body is water, and they are prone to low blood sugar. Older adults tolerate both dehydration and rapid rehydration poorly, and heart or kidney disease limits how fast fluids can be given, so smaller volumes are used. Pregnancy adds risk in both directions, because dehydration can precipitate preterm labor while over-hydration can cause fluid in the lungs, so treatment is planned with obstetric support. Severe acute malnutrition changes the signs of dehydration, since the skin pinch and the sunken eyes may mislead, and the World Health Organization recommends a specific low-sodium rehydration solution for these children. Continue feeding throughout, because withholding food prolongs the illness and worsens malnutrition, and keep breastfeeding a sick child. Zinc supplementation at 20 milligrams per day for 10 to 14 days reduces the duration and severity of diarrhea and lowers recurrence, and iron and vitamin A deficiencies should be treated after the acute episode.

The adverse effects of the drugs used in this chapter are mostly predictable, and knowing them lets you prepare and protect the patient. Doxycycline commonly causes nausea, vomiting, and sun sensitivity, and it should be avoided in pregnancy and in young children where alternatives exist, because it can stain developing teeth. Azithromycin is generally well tolerated but can cause nausea, abdominal discomfort, and diarrhea, and rarely it prolongs a portion of the heart rhythm in a way that can trigger dangerous arrhythmias. Ceftriaxone can cause diarrhea, rash, and allergy, and it can precipitate in the gallbladder or the kidney, so the patient should be watched for abdominal pain or reduced urine. Ciprofloxacin can cause nausea, headache, dizziness, tendon rupture, and peripheral neuropathy, and it is used cautiously in children and pregnancy because of effects on growing cartilage. Loperamide causes constipation, bloating, drowsiness, and, in excess or in the wrong patient, ileus and toxic megacolon. Ask about every drug the patient takes, because interactions are common, and report severe reactions promptly.

Infection control in enteric disease is unglamorous, cheap, and decisive, and the nurse sets the standard for the whole team. Hand hygiene is the foundation, and it must be washing with soap and running water at every opportunity, because alcohol rubs do not reliably kill all of the organisms discussed here. Separate patients with the same infection when possible, keep food preparation away from patient care, and exclude symptomatic staff and food handlers from work until they are cleared. Clean surfaces, bedding, and shared equipment with an appropriate disinfectant, and treat stool and vomit as infectious material at all times. Improving water, sanitation and hygiene in a community prevents more cases than any treatment program, and the World Health Organization and the United Nations Children's Fund treat these measures as the foundation of diarrheal disease control. Surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship are part of clinical care, so cholera is reported promptly, often within 24 hours, because a single confirmed case signals a possible outbreak. Shigellosis and typhoid should also be reported according to national rules, and a simple line list of dates, ages, locations, and outcomes reveals a common water source or a failing latrine. Use antibiotics only when indicated and complete the course, because every unnecessary prescription selects for resistance.

To summarize, enteric infections share a fecal-oral route, and the nurse's response is built on assessment, rehydration, and infection control rather than on antibiotics alone. Typhoid fever is a systemic illness of the bloodstream with stepped fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots, and the early constipation that later becomes diarrhea, and its blood culture confirms what its complications, especially intestinal perforation, make urgent. Resistance has removed fluoroquinolones from use in much of the world, and the chronic carrier must be found and treated because a well person can seed an outbreak. Cholera is a toxin-driven secretion in which cyclic adenosine monophosphate locks the intestinal cell into pouring out water, producing rice-water stool and losses that kill within hours. Oral rehydration salts with the correct sodium and glucose concentrations replace those losses, Ringer's lactate is used intravenously for severe dehydration, and a single dose of doxycycline is an adjunct that must never delay fluids. Rehydration turned cholera from a disease that killed most of its victims into one that kills fewer than 1 in 100. Shigellosis and Shiga toxin cause bloody dysentery and hemolytic uremic syndrome, while traveler's diarrhea is usually self-limited and loperamide has a narrow place with clear cautions; assess dehydration carefully, monitor urine output and electrolytes, and verify every regimen against current guidance from the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, because doses differ between countries. Treat the patient in front of you, and treat the water everyone else will drink.

# Chapter 20 — Mycobacterial Diseases: Tuberculosis, Drug Resistance, and Leprosy

The mycobacteria are rod-shaped bacteria with a cell wall so rich in long-chain fatty acids that ordinary dyes cannot penetrate it, and only heat or prolonged staining forces them in. That property gives them the name acid-fast bacilli and explains much of their behavior. The waxy wall makes them slow, so one division may take 18 to 24 hours and a culture can take weeks to turn positive, and it also lets them survive drying, dust, and the acid interior of the stomach. This chapter deals with the two mycobacteria that matter most in tropical practice, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the cause of tuberculosis, and Mycobacterium leprae, the cause of leprosy. They share a genus and a habit of striking the poor and the crowded, but they differ sharply in how they spread, how they are treated, and what the nurse must do about them.

Tuberculosis spreads almost entirely by air, and that single fact organizes everything you do to prevent it. When a person with pulmonary disease coughs, sings, or speaks forcefully, the airway secretions break into fine droplets, the water evaporates within moments, and tiny dried particles called droplet nuclei hang suspended in the air for hours. Those particles are small enough to bypass the nose and reach the alveoli, where macrophages take up the bacilli that are supposed to destroy them. Transmission therefore depends on sharing air, not on touching surfaces or sharing food or using the same toilet, and the risk rises with closeness, with time spent together, and with poor air renewal. A patient with a positive sputum smear, a cavity on the chest radiograph, and a heavy cough is far more contagious than one with minimal disease, while young children are usually not contagious because their lesions are small and their coughs generate few infectious particles.

Infection is not the same as disease, and the difference is the most important concept in tuberculosis care. When droplet nuclei reach the alveoli, most people mount an effective cell-mediated response that walls the bacilli inside granulomas, and the infection becomes latent, meaning the organism is alive but contained, the person has no symptoms, and nothing is transmitted. Only about 5 to 10 per cent of infected people ever develop active disease, most of them within the first 2 years or much later if immunity weakens, and the tuberculin skin test and the interferon gamma release assay detect this immune memory rather than illness. Anything that weakens cell-mediated immunity raises the risk of reactivation, and advanced HIV is the strongest factor, which is why tuberculosis is a leading cause of death among people living with HIV. Malnutrition, diabetes, silicosis from mining dust, kidney failure, alcohol use disorder, and treatment with corticosteroids or the biologic drugs that block tumor necrosis factor all add risk. Crowding and poor ventilation in prisons, mines, refugee camps, and slums increase the chance of being infected in the first place, acting at the level of transmission rather than reactivation, and because these factors often stack in one person, the nurse should weigh them together rather than as a checklist of single causes.

The natural history of untreated tuberculosis runs in two directions, and the patient in front of you may be at either end. Primary infection is usually silent or passes as a mild cold, but in a minority it causes pneumonia, pleural effusion, or, in infants and the immunosuppressed, widespread bloodborne spread. After that, the immune system holds the bacilli in check and the person enters the latent state with a lifelong risk of reactivation, which typically produces the chronic upper lobe illness and can appear decades after the original exposure. Without treatment, roughly half of those with active pulmonary disease die within 5 years, and the rest oscillate between illness and partial recovery while continuing to transmit. Effective treatment changes all of this within about 2 weeks for infectiousness and within 6 months for cure in most drug-susceptible cases.

Pulmonary tuberculosis is the commonest form, and its presentation is a chronic illness unfolding over weeks. The patient reports a cough lasting more than 2 weeks, at first dry and later productive of sputum that may be streaked with blood. Night sweats that soak the bedding, low-grade fever, loss of appetite, and weight loss are the constitutional features that, taken together, should raise suspicion at once in an endemic setting. Chest pain, breathlessness, and hoarseness appear as the disease destroys lung tissue, and the chest radiograph typically shows patchy consolidation or cavitation in the upper lobes with hilar or mediastinal node enlargement, though any pattern is possible. Because early disease produces few findings, the history of a cough that will not go away is often more informative than the examination.

Extrapulmonary tuberculosis accounts for roughly one fifth of cases in immunocompetent adults and a much larger share in people with advanced HIV, and it can affect almost any organ. Tuberculous lymphadenitis is the commonest form in many settings, usually painless enlargement of the cervical nodes that may later fluctuate and drain. Pleural effusion causes fever, chest pain, and breathlessness, with fluid that is an exudate low in glucose and rich in lymphocytes. Tuberculous meningitis presents with headache, fever, neck stiffness, confusion, and cranial nerve palsies, and it is one of the most lethal forms because delay costs lives. Miliary tuberculosis is bloodborne dissemination that seeds the lungs with tiny nodules and can cause a prolonged fever of unknown origin with enlargement of the liver and spleen, while skeletal disease, called Pott disease when it affects the spine, destroys vertebral bodies and can compress the spinal cord. The nurse should remember that a patient with fever and no localizing signs may have tuberculosis in a place that is not the lung.

Diagnosis begins with sputum, and how the specimen is collected determines whether the result can be trusted. Two or three samples should be obtained on separate days, at least one of them early in the morning, and the patient must produce material from deep in the chest rather than saliva. Where sputum cannot be produced, induction with inhaled hypertonic saline or collection of gastric aspirate in a child may be needed. Microscopy after Ziehl-Neelsen staining reveals acid-fast bacilli, and in a symptomatic patient in an endemic area that finding is strong evidence of disease. Its limitations matter just as much, because microscopy detects only about half of all cases, needs roughly 10,000 bacilli in each milliliter of sputum to turn positive, and cannot distinguish Mycobacterium tuberculosis from other mycobacteria or reveal drug resistance. A negative smear therefore never excludes tuberculosis.

Culture remains the reference standard because it detects far fewer organisms and because the grown organism can be tested against the drugs that will be used. A liquid culture system may turn positive within 10 to 14 days, while solid media take 4 to 8 weeks, and the laboratory then identifies the species and performs susceptibility testing. Molecular testing has changed the pace of diagnosis by detecting the organism's genetic material directly in the specimen within a few hours, and modern cartridge-based tests also detect the common mutations that confer resistance to rifampicin. Because rifampicin resistance is a reliable marker for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis in most settings, that result is both a diagnosis and a warning, and it should trigger a full resistance workup and referral to a program that manages resistant disease. Molecular tests are highly specific but do not replace culture, which still provides the full susceptibility profile and the isolate. The nurse's practical contribution is to get the specimen to the laboratory promptly, to state on the request that tuberculosis is suspected, and to discard nothing until the result returns.

The tuberculin skin test and the interferon gamma release assay both measure immune memory rather than the organism itself, and neither can separate latent infection from active disease. The skin test injects a purified protein derivative into the forearm and is read 48 to 72 hours later by the diameter of the hardened area, with the threshold for a positive result adjusted for the person's risk category. Its weaknesses are considerable, because it cross-reacts with BCG vaccination, it is falsely negative when cellular immunity is impaired by illness, malnutrition, measles, or advanced HIV, and it requires a second visit to be read. The interferon gamma release assay measures the release of interferon gamma by the patient's lymphocytes when they meet mycobacterial antigens that are not present in BCG, so it is not confused by prior vaccination, and it needs only a single blood draw. It is less available and more expensive in low-resource settings, however, and it shares the problem of being unreliable in advanced immunosuppression. In a seriously ill patient with a negative skin test, the test result should never override the clinical picture, because these tests guide preventive treatment rather than rule out active disease.

Diagnosing tuberculosis in children and in people with advanced HIV is a genuine challenge, and the nurse is often the person who assembles the evidence. Children have few bacilli in their secretions, they swallow sputum rather than expectorating it, and they cannot always cooperate with a good specimen, so pediatric diagnosis is usually clinical. It rests on a household contact with an infectious adult, symptoms lasting more than 2 weeks, a radiograph showing hilar adenopathy or miliary change, and evidence of infection on an immune test. In advanced HIV the inflammatory response is blunted, so the radiograph may look normal or show lower zone infiltrates, pleural effusion, or miliary shadowing instead of the typical cavity, while the smear and the immune tests are frequently negative. The disease is more likely to be disseminated, so blood cultures and sampling of any enlarged node or abnormal fluid may be needed, and the patient may present with fever and weight loss alone. Every person newly diagnosed with HIV should be assessed for tuberculosis, and every person with tuberculosis should be offered HIV testing, because the two epidemics feed each other. Low suspicion is the main reason these diagnoses are missed, so a patient with unexplained fever, night sweats, and weight loss deserves a sputum molecular test and a chest radiograph even when the examination is unremarkable.

The standard regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis is a 6 month course in two phases, and its design follows from the biology of the organism. The intensive phase lasts 2 months and uses four drugs, isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, because a large bacterial population must be killed quickly before resistance can emerge. The continuation phase lasts 4 months and uses two drugs, isoniazid and rifampicin, to eliminate the slow-growing persisters that survive the first phase. Doses are weight-based and given by mouth once daily, and current guidance from the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention gives isoniazid at 5 milligrams per kilogram, up to 300 milligrams, rifampicin at 10 milligrams per kilogram, up to 600 milligrams, pyrazinamide at 25 milligrams per kilogram, and ethambutol at 15 to 20 milligrams per kilogram. Fixed-dose combination tablets that contain several drugs together reduce the pill burden and the risk of a dosing error, and weight bands printed on the packaging are the safest way to prescribe for adults.

Duration is adjusted for the site and severity of disease, and this is where local guidance matters most. Standard pulmonary disease is treated for 6 months when the response is good, but when the radiograph shows cavitation and the sputum culture is still positive after 2 months, the continuation phase is extended to 7 months, making 9 months in total. Tuberculous meningitis, bone and joint disease, and disseminated disease are usually treated for 9 to 12 months, and meningitis and pericarditis also receive corticosteroids to reduce inflammation and its complications. Pregnancy is not a contraindication to treatment, streptomycin is the injectable that must be avoided because of fetal harm, and breastfeeding should continue while the infant receives preventive treatment and follow-up. Before you prescribe any regimen, verify it against current guidance, because regimens are revised as evidence accumulates, they differ between countries and programs, and the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control do not always agree. The current guideline, not memory and not an old chart, must be checked before the first dose is given.

Directly observed therapy is the practice of watching the patient swallow every dose, and its rationale is simpler than it first appears. Tuberculosis is treated over months, patients feel well long before the organism is gone, and the temptation to stop is powerful when the pills cause nausea, the clinic is far away, and the family needs income. Irregular intake is the perfect way to select resistant mutants, because the surviving bacilli are exposed to one or two drugs at a time and the resistant ones multiply. Watching every dose is one way to guarantee adherence, but the principle that matters is that a reliable, trained observer, who may be a nurse, a community health worker, a pharmacist, or a family member, supports the patient through the whole course, and video-observed therapy now serves patients who have a phone. Support must be paired with counseling, reminders, and food assistance where malnutrition is part of the problem, because adherence is a social behavior and not merely a personal virtue.

Monitoring during treatment tells you whether the plan is working and detects the two great threats, treatment failure and drug toxicity. Sputum should be examined at the end of the intensive phase, usually at 2 months, and again at the end of treatment, with culture and susceptibility testing if it is still positive. Weight should be recorded at every visit, because a falling weight may signal treatment failure, poor absorption, or a second diagnosis, while a rising weight is one of the most reassuring signs. Symptoms should be reviewed directly rather than assumed to have resolved, with specific questions about cough, fever, night sweats, and appetite. Every visit is also an opportunity to ask about the adverse effects patients do not volunteer, including numbness in the feet, changes in vision, ringing in the ears, and nausea. In a patient with HIV, the recovering immune response can cause a paradoxical worsening called immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, which is managed by treating the underlying infection and, in severe cases, with corticosteroids. Because rifampicin powerfully induces the liver enzymes that clear many other drugs, antiretroviral regimens must be adjusted with expert advice, and this interaction is a common cause of avoidable treatment failure.

The adverse effects of the antituberculosis drugs are predictable, and the nurse is usually the person who sees them first. Isoniazid causes peripheral neuropathy, prevented in patients at risk by pyridoxine at 10 to 25 milligrams by mouth daily, and it can also cause hepatitis, so it must be stopped if liver enzymes rise sharply or jaundice appears. Rifampicin harms the liver, turns urine, sweat, and tears an orange color that patients must be warned about, and reduces the effectiveness of many drugs, including hormonal contraceptives and some antiretroviral agents. Pyrazinamide is the drug most likely to injure the liver and it also raises uric acid, which can produce joint pain and, rarely, gout. Ethambutol causes optic neuritis with loss of red-green color vision and reduced acuity, so patients should be warned to report any change in vision at once and should have visual testing wherever it is available. The injectable agents, streptomycin, kanamycin, amikacin, and capreomycin, damage the eighth cranial nerve and the kidney, so hearing and kidney function must be tested before and during treatment. Bedaquiline prolongs the interval between the Q wave and the T wave on the electrocardiogram and can trigger a dangerous ventricular rhythm, while linezolid suppresses the bone marrow and can cause peripheral and optic neuropathy. Clofazimine discolors the skin and the whites of the eyes, and cycloserine and ethionamide cause psychiatric and neurological effects including confusion, depression, and seizures.

Baseline testing before treatment begins makes every later comparison possible. Liver enzymes should be measured before starting isoniazid, rifampicin, and pyrazinamide, and repeated when symptoms or risk factors suggest injury, since routine monthly testing is not always available and does not replace clinical vigilance. Kidney function and hearing should be documented before any injectable agent is used, and vision should be tested with acuity and color plates before ethambutol and at intervals afterward. A pregnancy test and a review of all other medicines, including traditional remedies and supplements, belongs in the same visit, and alcohol use should be addressed honestly because it multiplies the risk of hepatitis and undermines adherence. When a patient reports jaundice, dark urine, right upper abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, or a rash, the drugs should be held and the patient assessed the same day.

Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is defined by resistance to at least isoniazid and rifampicin, the two most powerful drugs in the standard regimen, and it arises mostly from irregular treatment, from transmission of an already resistant strain, or from both. Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis adds resistance to a fluoroquinolone and to at least one of the other second-line agents, and it leaves very few options, with mortality that remains high even where treatment is available. Resistance is not a laboratory curiosity, because a patient with resistant disease who continues to receive the standard regimen will fail treatment, remain infectious, and can pass the resistant strain to others. Any patient who remains sputum positive at the end of the intensive phase, or who deteriorates after an initial response, therefore requires susceptibility testing and expert review. Molecular tests that identify rifampicin resistance are the fastest way to raise the alarm, and the nurse's role is to recognize the failing patient, obtain the specimen, and make sure the referral actually happens.

Treating resistant tuberculosis requires a regimen built for the individual patient and supervised by an expert, and the details change as new evidence arrives. For many years the standard approach was a longer regimen of 18 to 20 months using at least five effective drugs, including a later-generation fluoroquinolone such as levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, together with agents chosen from bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, cycloserine or terizidone, ethionamide, and others, guided by susceptibility testing. A shorter regimen of 9 to 12 months was developed for selected patients with rifampicin-resistant disease who had not previously received second-line drugs, and it cured many people at lower cost. More recently, the World Health Organization has recommended a 6 month, all-oral regimen combining bedaquiline, pretomanid, linezolid, and moxifloxacin for many patients with multidrug-resistant or extensively drug-resistant disease, which shortens treatment dramatically and removes the injectable drugs. Because guidance in this area is revised frequently and differs between national programs, no regimen should be prescribed from memory, and the current national guideline must be checked for every patient. Directly observed therapy, nutritional support, and management of adverse effects matter as much here as the choice of drugs, and cure rates fall when social support is absent.

Preventing the airborne spread of tuberculosis in a clinic without a negative-pressure room is possible with attention to air, distance, time, and organization. The first measure is to identify the infectious patient at the door by asking everyone with a cough how long it has lasted, and to move anyone with a cough of more than 2 weeks to the front of the queue so that waiting time, the main determinant of exposure, is reduced. The second is to separate them from other patients while they wait, ideally outdoors or in a well-ventilated area, and to give every coughing patient a surgical mask and teach them to cover the mouth and nose with a tissue or an elbow. The third is ventilation, the most powerful engineering control available in a simple building, so open windows on opposite sides of a room to create cross-ventilation, use ceiling or standing fans to keep the air moving, and place an exhaust fan to pull air away from the waiting area. Sunlight destroys bacilli, so an outdoor waiting area or a room with open, sunlit windows is genuinely protective. Where the structure allows, upper-room ultraviolet germicidal irradiation can inactivate airborne bacilli above the heads of the people in the room without rebuilding anything.

Staff who care for infectious patients need a fit-tested particulate respirator rather than a surgical mask, and the fit test must be repeated whenever the model changes or the wearer's face changes shape. Sputum collection is the moment of greatest risk, so it should be performed outdoors or in a dedicated, well-ventilated space that other patients do not use, never in an open waiting room or a shared toilet. Hand hygiene, waste disposal, and cleaning matter for general safety but do not prevent airborne transmission, and the nurse should understand this so that effort goes to the measures that work. Health workers should be screened for tuberculosis at the start of employment and periodically afterward, and those with HIV should be offered preventive treatment. When a colleague develops a cough that lasts, the same suspicion you apply to patients must be applied to them.

BCG is a live vaccine derived from a weakened strain of Mycobacterium bovis, and what it does and does not do must be stated plainly. Given to a newborn, it protects against the most severe forms of childhood tuberculosis, disseminated disease and tuberculous meningitis, with good but not complete effectiveness. It does not reliably prevent pulmonary tuberculosis in adults, it does not prevent infection, and therefore it does not stop transmission, so a person vaccinated as a child may still develop tuberculosis and a scar on the arm is not evidence of protection. Vaccination is a reason for a positive tuberculin skin test but not for a positive interferon gamma release assay, which is why the blood test is preferred in people who have been vaccinated. In high-burden countries the vaccine is given at birth, including to infants born to mothers with HIV who are themselves well, while it is avoided in infants with symptomatic HIV because the live organism can disseminate, and in low-burden countries it is reserved for selected high-risk people.

Leprosy, also called Hansen disease, is caused by Mycobacterium leprae, an organism that has never been grown in a laboratory flask and grows only in the mouse footpad and the nine-banded armadillo. Its doubling time is about 12 to 14 days, the slowest of any known human pathogen, which explains why the incubation period is measured in years, commonly 2 to 5 years and sometimes much longer. The bacillus prefers cool areas of the body, which is why the skin, the superficial nerves, the upper airway, the eyes, and the testes are most affected. It spreads mainly through droplets from the nose and mouth during prolonged, close contact with an untreated person who has the multibacillary form, and it is not acquired by a handshake, a shared meal, or a brief encounter. Most people exposed to it never develop disease, because the cellular immune response of a healthy adult usually contains it, and this fact is central to counseling patients and their families.

The clinical spectrum of leprosy runs from tuberculoid disease at one end to lepromatous disease at the other, and where a patient falls on that spectrum determines the lesions, the bacillary load, and the risks. In tuberculoid, or paucibacillary, disease the immune response is strong, so there are few lesions, they are asymmetrical, sharply defined, and dry, sensation within them is lost, and a nearby nerve trunk is thickened and tender. The skin test is positive, slit-skin smears contain few or no bacilli, and the patient is not significantly infectious. In lepromatous, or multibacillary, disease the immune response fails, so lesions are numerous, symmetrical, and diffuse, the face thickens into the fold called leonine facies, the eyebrows and eyelashes fall out, the nasal bridge collapses, and the testes shrink. Smears are teeming with bacilli and the patient is infectious before treatment, while the borderline forms between the two poles are immunologically unstable and most likely to shift and to develop reactions. Recognizing where a patient sits on this spectrum guides the treatment duration and the intensity of surveillance for nerve damage.

The cardinal sign of leprosy is a skin lesion with loss of sensation, and the finding of a thickened nerve is its companion. The earliest lesion is often a single hypopigmented or reddish patch with a dry, hairless surface and reduced or absent sensation to light touch, pinprick, and temperature. The nerves most often thickened are the ulnar nerve above the elbow, the median nerve at the wrist, the common peroneal nerve at the knee, the posterior tibial nerve behind the ankle, the greater auricular nerve in the neck, and the facial nerve. Sensory testing with a wisp of cotton and a pin, and voluntary muscle testing of the small muscles of the hand and foot, should be performed at every visit and the results written down so that change can be detected. Slit-skin smears from several sites give the bacterial index and are used to classify disease and monitor response, while skin biopsy shows the granulomas and the bacilli, and molecular testing by PCR can identify the organism in difficult cases. Any patient with a numb patch or a thickened nerve in an endemic area should be evaluated for leprosy, because the diagnosis is still made on the skin and the nerve rather than on a blood test.

Reactions are the immunological complications of leprosy, and they are the main cause of permanent nerve damage, so they must be recognized as emergencies. A type 1 reaction, also called a reversal reaction, occurs when cellular immunity suddenly strengthens, most often in borderline disease and particularly after treatment has started, and existing lesions become red, swollen, and painful while the nerves become tender and enlarged with new weakness or sensory loss that can progress within days. A type 2 reaction, also called erythema nodosum leprosum, is an immune complex phenomenon seen in multibacillary disease, and it produces crops of painful red nodules, fever, joint pains, enlarged lymph nodes, inflammation of the eye, and inflammation of the testis. Both reactions threaten the eye, the hand, and the foot, and both can be triggered by treatment, pregnancy, infection, or stress. Type 1 reactions are treated with prednisolone, commonly starting at 40 to 60 milligrams by mouth daily and reduced slowly over 12 weeks or more. Type 2 reactions are treated with thalidomide, clofazimine, or corticosteroids, and thalidomide must never be given to a woman who could become pregnant because it causes severe birth defects, so pregnancy must be excluded first and reliable contraception used.

Antibacterial treatment of leprosy uses a fixed combination of drugs, because monotherapy rapidly selects resistance and the organism is naturally slow to die. Current World Health Organization guidance gives all patients rifampicin at 600 milligrams by mouth once a month, supervised, together with dapsone at 100 milligrams by mouth daily. Multibacillary disease adds clofazimine at 50 milligrams by mouth daily and 300 milligrams once a month, and it is treated for 12 months, while paucibacillary disease uses only rifampicin and dapsone and is treated for 6 months. Children receive weight-based doses, with rifampicin at 10 to 15 milligrams per kilogram, dapsone at 1 to 2 milligrams per kilogram, and clofazimine at 1 milligram per kilogram daily and 6 milligrams per kilogram monthly. A single-lesion, paucibacillary case can be treated with one supervised dose of rifampicin at 600 milligrams, ofloxacin at 400 milligrams, and minocycline at 100 milligrams. Some programs continue treatment longer for multibacillary disease, and rifampicin-resistant leprosy is managed with second-line drugs such as ofloxacin, minocycline, and clarithromycin under expert guidance.

These drugs have adverse effects you can anticipate and explain. Dapsone commonly causes mild anemia and can cause severe hemolytic anemia in people with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, so this deficiency should be considered before treatment wherever testing is available. Dapsone can also cause methemoglobinemia, which presents as cyanosis with breathlessness, and a rare hypersensitivity illness with fever, rash, jaundice, and enlarged lymph nodes that requires immediate withdrawal. Rifampicin can injure the liver, colors secretions orange, and reduces the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives, so alternative contraception must be advised, while clofazimine causes a harmless reddish-brown discoloration of the skin and conjunctivae that may be deeply distressing if it is not explained in advance. Corticosteroids used for reactions bring their own risks of high blood glucose, high blood pressure, weight gain, and infection, so patients on a long taper need monitoring and support.

Finding cases and following their contacts is how leprosy transmission is interrupted, and the nurse is usually at the center of it. Every patient should be asked about household members and others in close contact, and those contacts should be examined and taught the early signs of disease. The World Health Organization recommends a single dose of rifampicin at 600 milligrams for eligible household and social contacts of a person with leprosy as post-exposure prophylaxis, since this reduces the risk that a contact will develop the disease. Contacts are also advised how to recognize a numb or discolored patch and to return for evaluation, because prophylaxis does not remove the need for surveillance. Contact tracing is equally important in tuberculosis, where a systematic household investigation finds both active cases and infected people who need preventive treatment, which uses isoniazid daily for 6 to 36 months or weekly rifapentine with isoniazid for 12 weeks, offered only after active disease has been excluded.

Disability in leprosy is preventable, and much of the prevention is nursing care delivered early and carefully. Nerve damage begins insidiously and passes through a phase in which it is still reversible, so sensory testing and voluntary muscle testing at every visit, recorded on a simple chart, are what allow you to catch it in time. Once sensation is lost, the hand, the foot, and the eye are at risk from ordinary injury, burns, and pressure, so the patient must learn daily self-care, including inspection of the feet, soaking, protective footwear with a firm sole and no rough seams, eye care with lubricants, and exercises and splinting that preserve movement in clawed fingers and the dropped foot. Stigma may do more lasting harm than the bacillus, because leprosy has been feared for centuries and patients hide their lesions, delay treatment, lose work, and are sometimes rejected by their own families, and tuberculosis carries its own stigma, often bound up with HIV. Naming the disease accurately, explaining that treated leprosy is not transmitted by touch, and correcting the myths a patient has absorbed do more good than any poster. Confidentiality, respectful language, and protection of a patient's information are professional duties with concrete consequences, because a diagnosis made public can cost a person their livelihood, and mental health support should be offered rather than assumed unnecessary. The nurse who treats a patient as a person rather than a case is practicing the most effective public health intervention available for these diseases.

To summarize, tuberculosis is an airborne infection in which most people who are infected never become ill, and the task of the clinician is to tell the contained infection from the active disease, because only the active disease is contagious and only it needs the full four-drug regimen. The standard treatment is 6 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol followed by isoniazid and rifampicin, adjusted for the site of disease and supervised throughout, with pyridoxine to prevent peripheral neuropathy and careful surveillance for liver injury, visual change, and hearing loss. Resistance, whether to isoniazid and rifampicin alone or to the second-line drugs as well, changes the regimen entirely and must be detected by molecular testing and susceptibility testing rather than assumed. Airborne precautions in a simple clinic rest on finding the coughing patient at the door, separating them, moving the air, and using sunlight and ultraviolet light, rather than on a room most clinics will never have. BCG protects infants against the most severe forms of tuberculosis but does not prevent infection or transmission, so vaccination never replaces the other measures. Leprosy is a slowly progressive disease of the skin and nerves that is diagnosed by a numb patch and a thickened nerve, is treated with a fixed combination of rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine, and threatens the patient mainly through reactions and nerve damage that nursing surveillance can catch. Because all of these regimens are revised as evidence accumulates, differ between countries and programs, and change with the age, weight, pregnancy status, and other medicines of the patient, the current guideline must be checked before every prescription, and the nurse who verifies the dose, watches the patient take it, examines the skin and the nerves, and treats the person with dignity prevents more disability than any single drug.

# Chapter 21 — Zoonoses

A zoonosis is any infection that passes from an animal to a human being, and in tropical practice these are not curiosities at the edge of the syllabus but routine causes of fever, abortion, wound infection, and sudden death. The animals involved are the ones that live beside people, which means rodents in the walls and the fields, cattle and goats in the compound, dogs in the yard, bats under the roof, and the livestock and wildlife that share the water and the soil. The organisms travel by routes that seem unremarkable until someone traces them, such as urine in floodwater, milk that was never boiled, the placenta of an aborting goat, a bite on the calf, and the fine spray of a lambing pen. The principle that organizes this work is called One Health, the recognition that human health, animal health, and the health of the environment are one problem, and in a village clinic it is not an abstraction. It is the reason a case of human brucellosis is also a veterinary problem that will return next season unless the herd is addressed. This chapter takes the major zoonoses in turn, which are leptospirosis, brucellosis, rabies, anthrax, melioidosis, plague, and Q fever. The thread that holds them together is the exposure history, because a nurse who asks where the patient works, what the patient drinks, which animals the patient keeps, and what the patient was doing in the week before the fever began will recognize most of these diseases before the laboratory does.

Leptospirosis is caused by spirochetes of the genus Leptospira, and Leptospira interrogans is the species most often named in human disease. The organism is divided into hundreds of serovars that differ in their animal hosts and in the severity of illness they produce. The reservoir is the rodent, above all the rat, which carries the spirochete in the tubules of the kidney and sheds it in urine for life without ever appearing ill. Cattle, pigs, dogs, and many wild mammals do the same, and each of them adds a route of human exposure. The spirochete does not survive drying, but it survives for weeks in fresh water, damp soil, and mud, which is why the disease follows rain, flooding, and work done in wet ground. A person is infected when contaminated water or soil touches broken skin, the conjunctiva, or another mucous membrane, and the commonest settings are rice paddies, sugarcane and banana plantations, flooded streets, sewers, fish markets, slaughterhouses, veterinary practices, and freshwater swimming. The incubation period is usually 5 to 14 days, with a range of about 2 to 30 days, so a patient who fell into floodwater ten days before the fever began has handed the nurse the diagnosis.

The illness is biphasic, and the two phases are easy to miss if the nurse expects one continuous story. The first phase begins abruptly with fever, chills, severe headache, and muscle pain worst in the calves and the lower back, and it lasts about 4 to 9 days while the organism circulates in the blood. Conjunctival suffusion appears in this phase in a large proportion of patients, and it is the finding that should make the nurse think of leptospirosis rather than of a common viral conjunctivitis. The conjunctivae are red and congested, but there is no discharge, no crusting, and usually no pain, and the redness persists after the fever falls. A brief improvement may follow, and then the second phase begins with the return of fever, an aseptic meningitis, a rash, and sometimes an inflammation of the eye that can damage vision months later. Most patients, perhaps 90 per cent, have this milder form, which resolves over 5 to 7 days, though fatigue can persist for weeks. A minority develop severe leptospirosis, long called Weil's disease, with jaundice, acute kidney injury, bleeding from the nose, the gums, the gut, and the lungs, and inflammation of the heart muscle. Pulmonary hemorrhage is now a leading cause of death in severe disease and can develop within an hour in a patient who was talking normally, so a patient with jaundice, falling urine output, and a falling platelet count is a medical emergency who needs a facility with dialysis.

The laboratory confirms leptospirosis in different ways at different times, and the timing of the sample matters as much as the choice of test. During the first week the organism can be found by PCR of blood, and this is the most useful test early in the illness, while culture requires special media, grows slowly, and takes weeks to become positive. Antibodies appear after the first week and are detected by enzyme immunoassay or by the microscopic agglutination test, which remains the reference method, and a pair of samples taken two to four weeks apart that shows a rising level is the traditional proof. A single high level in a patient with the right exposure and the right illness is generally accepted as good evidence, but it must be read against the local background rate, because people in endemic areas often carry antibodies from past infection. Early antibiotic treatment can blunt the antibody response and produce a negative test in a patient who truly has the disease, so a negative serology never overrides a convincing clinical picture. The nurse's practical contribution is to draw the acute sample before the first antibiotic dose where possible, to label each sample with the date and the day of illness, and to arrange the second sample when the patient returns.

Treatment depends on severity, and the antibiotic is only one part of a supportive plan. Mild disease is treated with doxycycline at 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 7 days, or with amoxicillin or azithromycin where doxycycline is not appropriate, and these regimens shorten the illness and reduce shedding. Severe disease requires an intravenous antibiotic such as penicillin, ceftriaxone, or doxycycline in a facility where fluids, electrolytes, blood pressure, urine output, and renal function can be watched continuously. Supportive care is often what saves the patient, and it means careful fluid balance to avoid both dehydration and pulmonary edema, transfusion for hemorrhage, dialysis for kidney failure, and mechanical ventilation when the lungs fail. Antibiotic treatment can trigger a Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction within the first hours, with fever, rigors, and a fall in blood pressure, and a nurse who has been warned about it will recognize it and treat it rather than abandon the drug. Prevention rests on interrupting the path from rodent urine to human mucous membrane, which means rodent control, safe food storage, covering the skin and any wound when working in water or mud, wearing personal protective equipment in slaughterhouses and markets, and providing clean water and sanitation. Doxycycline at 200 milligrams by mouth once a week during short periods of intense exposure is used as chemoprophylaxis in some countries, though it never substitutes for keeping urine out of the water supply.

Brucellosis is caused by small bacteria of the genus Brucella, and the species that matter most to people are Brucella melitensis from goats and sheep, Brucella abortus from cattle, Brucella suis from pigs, and Brucella canis from dogs. The organism is shed in milk, urine, and above all the placenta and birth fluids of infected animals, and it survives in unpasteurized dairy products for weeks. Human infection follows one of three routes. The first is food, meaning raw milk, soft cheese made from raw milk, butter, cream, and ice cream, and this is the commonest route for the general population. The second is direct contact with an aborting animal, and the nurse should picture the shepherd who delivers a goat, the farmer who cleans the pen with bare hands, the abattoir worker who handles the uterus, and the veterinarian who assists a difficult calving. The third is inhalation, and Brucella is one of the most frequently reported laboratory-acquired infections in the world, which means that opening a culture plate and sniffing it to judge the growth is a genuinely dangerous act. The incubation period is usually 1 to 4 weeks but ranges from a few days to several months, and the disease is notoriously insidious.

Acute brucellosis is a fever with no obvious focus, and its most famous feature is its undulation. The temperature rises in the evening, falls with drenching sweats at night, and may return to normal for days before climbing again, and the sweat has a heavy musty smell that patients describe in the same words wherever they live. Weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, headache, and pain in the muscles and joints accompany it, and the patient often looks less ill than the temperature suggests. The spine and the sacroiliac joints are the sites that give brucellosis away, and sacroiliitis produces low back and buttock pain that is worse at night and on movement, with tenderness directly over the joint. Spondylitis of the lumbar spine, arthritis of the peripheral joints, inflammation of the testis and epididymis, and enlargement of the liver and the spleen all occur. Endocarditis is the complication that kills, and it should be suspected in any patient with brucellosis and a new heart murmur, a prosthetic valve, or persistent fever despite treatment. The nervous system is involved in a small proportion of patients, producing meningitis and nerve palsies that require prolonged specialist treatment.

The diagnosis is made by culture, by serology, or by PCR, and each method has a weakness the nurse should know. Blood culture is definitive when positive, but the organism grows slowly and the laboratory must be told that brucellosis is suspected so that the culture is held longer than usual. Bone marrow culture is more sensitive in acute illness and is used when the diagnosis remains uncertain. Serology is the practical mainstay, and the standard agglutination test, the Rose Bengal test, and enzyme immunoassays are all used, with results read against local thresholds. Antibodies persist for months after cure, so serology cannot decide whether treatment has succeeded, and relapse occurs in about 5 to 10 per cent of treated patients, usually within six months. A patient who becomes febrile again after finishing treatment is therefore treated again rather than dismissed as having a new illness.

Treatment is long, and the length is the point. The standard regimen is doxycycline at 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day together with rifampicin at 600 to 900 milligrams by mouth once a day for 6 weeks, because either drug alone produces an unacceptably high relapse rate. An alternative is doxycycline for 6 weeks with streptomycin given intramuscularly for the first 2 to 3 weeks, and this combination is used in some countries for severe or complicated disease. Children under 8 years of age and pregnant women cannot receive doxycycline and are usually treated with trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, sometimes with rifampicin added, under specialist advice. The patient must be told at the first visit that the fever will settle within days but the medicine must continue for the full 6 weeks, because that single piece of information prevents most relapses. Rifampicin turns the urine and the tears orange, it interacts with many other medicines including antiretroviral therapy and oral contraceptives, and it can damage the liver, so liver function and blood counts are monitored during treatment. The nurse watches adherence, asks directly about missed doses, records the laboratory results, and arranges review at the end of treatment, because brucellosis treated for two weeks feels cured and comes back.

Rabies is caused by Rabies lyssavirus, a bullet-shaped virus whose genetic material is ribonucleic acid, and it belongs to a group of viruses transmitted in the saliva of infected mammals. The virus travels from the wound along the peripheral nerves toward the spinal cord and the brain, and it does not need to enter the bloodstream to do damage. This explains the two facts that govern the incubation period, which are that a wound close to the brain and a wound in a richly innervated part of the body produce a shorter incubation time, and that a wound on the foot can take months to produce illness. The incubation period is usually 1 to 3 months, but it has ranged from a few days to more than a year, and it may be shortened in children and in people bitten on the face or the hands. Dogs are responsible for the overwhelming majority of human deaths from rabies worldwide, which is why dog vaccination is the single most effective public health measure against the disease. Bats, monkeys, cats, and cattle also transmit it, and a bat in a room where a person was sleeping is treated as an exposure even when no bite can be found.

The illness begins with a prodrome that is easy to dismiss, and the nurse who knows it may be the only person who recognizes the disease in time. Fever, headache, malaise, and loss of appetite appear first, followed by a strange sensation at the site of the healed wound, which may be pain, tingling, burning, or itching that persists after the scar has closed. This local sensation is the most specific early feature of rabies and should be taken seriously in anyone with a recent animal bite. The furious form follows, with agitation, confusion, hallucinations, and muscle spasms, and with the two signs that give the disease its terrible reputation. Hydrophobia is a spasm of the muscles of swallowing and breathing when the patient sees, hears, or tries to drink water, and it is accompanied by aerophobia, the same spasm provoked by a draught of air. The patient is fully conscious during these spasms, and the autonomic nervous system becomes unstable with fluctuating heart rate, blood pressure, and temperature. The paralytic form ascends from the bitten limb without hydrophobia and is even more easily missed. Both forms progress to coma and death, which is the outcome in nearly every patient once symptoms begin, so care at that stage is palliative and the family needs an honest explanation.

Post-exposure care is a sequence, and every step has a deadline. The first step is immediate washing of the wound with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, and this simple act, done before anything else, removes virus from the wound and saves lives. After washing, the wound is irrigated, an antiseptic such as povidone iodine or ethanol is applied, bleeding is controlled, and the wound is left open rather than sutured at once, because closing it can trap virus. Tetanus vaccination is updated, antibiotics are given for bacterial infection, and the wound is measured and recorded. Rabies vaccine is then given according to the exposure category, which depends on whether the skin was broken, whether the bite drew blood, and whether the exposure was a lick on intact skin, a scratch, or a bite. A bite that breaks the skin or contaminates a mucous membrane is treated with vaccine and with rabies immunoglobulin, and the immunoglobulin is infiltrated into and around the wound on the day the vaccine course begins. The vaccine schedules in current use include a five-dose course on days 0, 3, 7, 14, and 28, and a shortened course on days 0, 7, and 21 that gives a double dose on the first day. Immunoglobulin is given only once, on the day the course starts, and it is not repeated later.

The nurse's role in rabies is less about the medicine than about completion, and completion is where the failures happen. The patient who has been bitten is frightened, the vaccine may be expensive, the clinic may be far away, and the immunoglobulin may be out of stock, and each of these practical obstacles can end in a preventable death. The nurse should explain, in plain words, that the vaccine only works if the whole course is given, that a missed dose may mean restarting the count in some protocols, and that a patient who feels perfectly well after the first dose is not cured. A recall system is worth more than a lecture, and it means a written appointment card, a telephone reminder where that is possible, and a register that names the date of the next dose. The nurse also counsels the household about the animal and about reporting it to the veterinary service, and explains that a dog which remains alive and well ten days after the bite was not shedding virus in its saliva at the time of the bite. Pre-exposure vaccination is offered to people whose work or travel places them at continuing risk, including laboratory staff, veterinarians, animal handlers, and long-stay travelers to remote areas. Above all, the nurse never tells a patient that a small bite is nothing to worry about, because that sentence has killed people.

Anthrax is caused by Bacillus anthracis, a bacterium that forms spores able to survive in soil for decades, and the form of human disease reflects the route by which the spores enter. The natural hosts are grazing animals, especially cattle, sheep, and goats, and human cases follow contact with infected animals, their hides, their wool, their bones, or their meat. Cutaneous anthrax accounts for most human cases, and it begins as a painless itchy papule that becomes a blister and then breaks down into a depressed black eschar with striking swelling of the surrounding tissue and tender enlargement of the regional lymph nodes. The eschar itself is not painful, which is one of its most useful distinguishing features, and most patients recover with treatment although a small proportion progress to bloodstream infection. Inhalational anthrax follows the breathing of spores, which are carried to the lymph nodes in the middle of the chest and cause a hemorrhagic inflammation that widens the mediastinum, and it presents as fever, cough, chest pain, and breathlessness that can progress to respiratory failure and death within days. Gastrointestinal anthrax follows the eating of undercooked meat from an infected animal, and it causes fever, abdominal pain, vomiting, bloody diarrhea, and fluid in the abdomen, with a form that affects the throat and causes severe swelling of the neck. A fourth form has appeared among people who inject drugs, producing deep soft tissue infection and bloodstream infection that is difficult to recognize. The diagnosis is confirmed by culture and by PCR, treatment uses ciprofloxacin or doxycycline with combination therapy and an antitoxin for systemic disease, and post-exposure prophylaxis is given for 60 days after a known exposure.

Melioidosis is caused by Burkholderia pseudomallei, a bacterium that lives in soil and water in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and it is one of the most under-recognized causes of severe infection in the tropics. Rice paddies, flooded fields, and muddy water are the classic sources, and the organism enters the body by inhalation, by swallowing contaminated water, or through a break in the skin. Diabetes is the strongest risk factor by a wide margin, so the nurse should think of melioidosis in any patient with diabetes, a high fever, and a history of working in wet ground. Alcohol use disorder, chronic kidney disease, chronic lung disease, and any condition that suppresses immunity also increase the risk. The disease can present as a sudden bloodstream infection that kills within days, as a pneumonia that resembles tuberculosis, or as abscesses in the liver, the spleen, the kidney, the prostate, the joints, the bones, or the brain, and it has earned the name of the great imitator for that reason. Children often present with an abscess of the parotid gland, a clue that is rarely seen in adults. The organism can also remain silent for years after exposure and then produce disease when the patient becomes diabetic or immunosuppressed, so a patient who lived in an endemic area decades earlier may still develop melioidosis.

Treatment is long and must be explained carefully at the outset, because the relapse rate after a shortened course is high. The intensive phase uses ceftazidime or meropenem given intravenously for at least 10 to 14 days, continued until the fever has settled and the patient has improved, which may take longer when abscesses are extensive. The eradication phase then follows, using trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole by mouth for 3 to 6 months, with doxycycline and other agents used in some protocols. Every abscess that can be drained should be drained, because antibiotics penetrate pus poorly, and the nurse who notices a new swelling, a new joint, or new pain is doing the work that changes the outcome. Blood sugar must be controlled during treatment, because uncontrolled diabetes undermines the entire course. Monitoring includes renal function, blood counts, and potassium, since trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole can raise potassium and damage the kidneys. The nurse should expect the patient to feel well long before the course ends and should say so in advance, because the long eradication phase is the part that patients abandon.

Plague is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium maintained in rodents by fleas, and it has shaped human history more than any other zoonosis. When a flea feeds on an infected rodent and then bites a person, the bacteria enter the skin and travel to the nearest lymph node, which becomes inflamed, painful, and enlarged into the swelling called a bubo. Bubonic plague then presents with a sudden high fever, severe headache, and a bubo usually in the groin, the armpit, or the neck, and the patient is prostrated within hours of feeling well. If the bacteria reach the bloodstream the disease becomes septicemic plague, with bleeding, shock, and death, and if they reach the lungs, either from the blood or from inhaling droplets from another patient with pneumonia, it becomes pneumonic plague, which spreads from person to person and kills almost everyone untreated. The great pandemics of the past, including the Black Death of the fourteenth century and the pandemic that began in the nineteenth century and reached every continent, were caused by this organism, and only effective antibiotics brought the case fatality down from most patients to a small minority. The diagnosis is made by microscopy of a bubo aspirate, by culture, by PCR, and by rapid antigen testing, and treatment with streptomycin, gentamicin, doxycycline, or ciprofloxacin for 10 to 14 days cures the disease when it is started early. Because pneumonic plague spreads by droplets, patients must be isolated, contacts must be traced and offered preventive doxycycline, and the veterinary and rodent control services must be brought in at once.

Q fever is caused by Coxiella burnetii, a bacterium that is unusual in two ways that matter to the nurse. First, it forms a small variant that resists drying and heat and survives in dust for long periods, so infection can follow the breathing of contaminated dust rather than direct contact with an animal. Second, it is shed in enormous numbers in the placenta and birth fluids of infected sheep, goats, and cattle, so assisting at a birth, cleaning a lambing pen, or handling an aborted fetus is a high-risk exposure, and the organism can travel on the wind from a farm to a nearby town. The incubation period is usually 2 to 3 weeks. Acute Q fever presents as a fever with a severe headache, an atypical pneumonia, or an inflammation of the liver with raised liver enzymes, and most patients recover, although the illness can be prolonged and exhausting. Chronic Q fever is a different disease, appearing months to years later as an infection of the heart valves in patients with existing valve disease or vascular grafts and in patients whose immunity is suppressed. The danger in pregnancy is easy to understate, because infection during pregnancy can cause inflammation of the placenta, miscarriage, premature delivery, stillbirth, and low birth weight, and the infection may be entirely silent in the mother.

The diagnosis is made by serology and by PCR, with acute infection recognized by antibodies against the phase two antigen and chronic infection by high levels of antibody against the phase one antigen, and paired samples are sent when the diagnosis is suspected because a single sample taken at the wrong time can mislead. Acute Q fever is treated with doxycycline at 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 14 days. Chronic infection of the heart valves requires doxycycline together with hydroxychloroquine for at least 18 months, with a specialist involved from the beginning because the regimen is difficult and relapse is real. Pregnancy is the situation that demands the most caution, because doxycycline cannot be used, and treatment is usually given with trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole under specialist supervision, with careful monitoring of the pregnancy and the newborn. Prevention is largely a matter of animal management, and it means safe disposal of placentas and birth products, vaccination of sheep and goats, pasteurization of milk, and the use of personal protective equipment by anyone who works with pregnant animals. The nurse who teaches a farming family to treat every abortion in a goat as a contaminated event is preventing cases of Q fever in that family and in the town down the road.

The zoonoses in this chapter share a laboratory problem, and the nurse usually decides whether the laboratory can solve it. Many of these organisms are dangerous to handle on a routine bench, and Brucella, Coxiella burnetii, Burkholderia pseudomallei, Bacillus anthracis, and Yersinia pestis all require the laboratory to be warned in advance so that the sample is processed with the right containment. A blood culture for brucellosis must be held longer than the standard period, a sample for Q fever must be handled as an aerosol risk, and a sample for anthrax must not be opened in the open laboratory. The nurse therefore labels each specimen with the suspected diagnosis and the date of onset, uses the correct container and transport medium, packages the sample correctly, and telephones the laboratory when the diagnosis is urgent. Surveillance closes the circle, because plague, anthrax, rabies, and brucellosis are notifiable in most countries, and a case reported accurately and quickly sets in motion a veterinary investigation, rodent and flea control, dog vaccination, milk hygiene, and the tracing of contacts who may need preventive treatment. The same system detects the outbreak that a single clinic would miss, such as a cluster of brucellosis in one village, a group of Q fever cases downwind of a farm, or several cases of leptospirosis after a flood. Prevention at the household level is concrete and teachable, and it means boiling the milk or using only pasteurized dairy products, washing the hands after touching animals, covering open wounds before working in water or soil, controlling rodents around the house and the food store, vaccinating the dogs, and handling placentas and aborted fetuses as infectious material.

No regimen in this chapter should ever be given from memory. Doses, durations, and the choice of drug are revised as new evidence appears and as national programs change their protocols, and the same infection is managed differently in Thailand, in Kenya, in Brazil, and in the United States, so the current national guideline and the current product label must be checked before any medicine is prescribed, dispensed, or administered. The World Health Organization publishes guidance that is updated on its own schedule, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention issues advice for clinicians in the United States, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control publishes guidance for Europe, and none of these can substitute for the national protocol that governs the nurse's own practice. The dose must be calculated from the weight measured on the day, not from a weight remembered from a previous admission, and it must be adjusted for renal function, hepatic function, pregnancy, age, and the blood counts measured that week. Rifampicin, doxycycline, trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, hydroxychloroquine, and the intravenous agents used for melioidosis all carry interactions and toxicities that change as the patient changes, so the nurse reviews the latest laboratory results before the next dose and treats every new symptom as information that may alter the prescription. For medicines that require an exact dose and a second check, the protocol usually asks for a second person to verify the calculation and the preparation, and the nurse follows that requirement every time rather than only when the patient looks unwell. Monitoring is continuous rather than occasional, and it includes the temperature curve, the blood pressure, the urine output, the liver enzymes, the blood counts, the serum potassium, the blood sugar, and the patient's own account of how the medicine is being taken at home.

To summarize, the zoonoses are infections that pass from animals to people, and they are recognized at the bedside by an exposure history rather than by a laboratory result. Leptospirosis comes from rodent urine in water and soil, produces a biphasic fever with conjunctival suffusion, and in its severe form causes jaundice, kidney failure, hemorrhage, and pulmonary bleeding. Brucellosis comes from unpasteurized dairy products and from contact with aborting animals, produces an undulant fever with sacroiliitis and sweats, and requires 6 weeks of doxycycline with rifampicin because shorter courses relapse. Rabies comes from the saliva of an infected mammal, has an incubation period of 1 to 3 months, begins with pain or tingling at the healed wound, and is almost always fatal once hydrophobia appears, which is why immediate washing of the wound and completion of the vaccine course are the interventions that matter most. Anthrax, melioidosis, and plague are bacterial zoonoses with different routes and different presentations, and each is treatable when it is recognized early and treated for the full course. Q fever is a hazard of lambing and of contaminated dust, and it is especially dangerous in pregnancy. Across all of them, the nurse's work is to ask about animals, to wash and protect wounds, to secure the correct specimen and warn the laboratory, to check every dose against the current guideline and the measured weight, to monitor the adverse effects of long and toxic regimens, and to report the case so that the animal and environmental side of the problem is addressed. That combination of curiosity about the patient's world and discipline about the medicine is what prevents these infections from becoming deaths that no one saw coming.

# Chapter 22 — Viral Hemorrhagic Fevers

Viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of illnesses caused by four unrelated families of viruses that produce a similar clinical picture. The filoviruses include Ebola and Marburg, the arenaviruses include Lassa fever and the New World viruses, the nairoviruses include Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, and the phleboviruses include Rift Valley fever. All can injure small blood vessels, disturb clotting and drive fever toward shock and death within a week or two. Bleeding appears late and is absent in many fatal cases, so it cannot be the sign you wait for. This chapter follows the guidance of the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and it treats every dose as current guidance rather than settled truth.

The filoviruses are long, filamentous viruses whose genetic material is a single strand of ribonucleic acid, and they are among the most lethal pathogens known. Ebola virus disease and Marburg virus disease are the two human illnesses, and Ebola includes the Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo and Tai Forest viruses. The natural reservoir is the fruit bat, which carries the virus without illness and sheds it in bodily fluids. Outbreaks begin when a person enters the world of the bat, through mines and caves, through harvesting fruit, or through hunting and butchering infected animals, and non-human primates act as an amplifier rather than as the reservoir.

Once a person is infected, the virus spreads through direct contact with blood, vomit, stool, urine, saliva, sweat, breast milk, semen or tissue. Infectious fluid must reach a break in the skin or a mucous membrane, which is why the person washing the body without gloves is so often infected. Ordinary air does not carry Ebola across a room, but vomiting, diarrhea, suctioning and resuscitation generate sprays that demand fuller protection.
