The virus survives in body fluids after death, so funeral washing and touching have driven many outbreaks, and sexual transmission from a survivor can occur months after recovery.

The incubation period of Ebola and Marburg disease is 2 to 21 days, and most patients fall ill between 8 and 10 days after exposure. Illness begins abruptly with fever, profound fatigue, muscle pain, headache and sore throat, a picture indistinguishable from malaria, influenza or typhoid fever. Several days later come vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, dehydration and sometimes a rash. Bleeding from the gums, nose, gut or injection sites appears late, usually in the second week and only in a minority of patients. Ask about contact with a case, a funeral, a health facility or an animal, because the history raises the possibility before any test does.

The virus enters through a mucosal surface or broken skin and travels to the lymph nodes, liver, spleen and bone marrow. Its preferred targets are the monocytes, macrophages and dendritic cells, the very cells that should present the infection to the immune system. The virus multiplies inside them, releases inflammatory signals and infects the endothelium lining the blood vessels. Fluid then leaks into the tissues, circulating volume falls and blood pressure drops toward shock. The clotting system is activated and then exhausted, so bleeding reflects a broken clotting system rather than a direct attack on the vessel wall.

Case fatality varies with the virus, the outbreak and the quality of care. The Zaire species of Ebola has killed between 25 and 90 per cent of those infected, the Bundibugyo species has been closer to 25 per cent, and Marburg has ranged from 24 to 88 per cent. Death usually comes between day 6 and day 16 from shock, organ failure or hemorrhage, while a patient who survives the second week usually improves. Bleeding, confusion, low blood pressure, fast breathing and a falling urine output mark a poor prognosis and should prompt the most intensive supportive care available.

Laboratory confirmation rests on the polymerase chain reaction, which detects the genetic material of the virus, and on tests for antigen and for antibodies of the immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G classes. The polymerase chain reaction is most reliable from about the third day of illness, while antibodies appear later and may be absent in patients who die quickly. A negative test taken too early does not exclude the diagnosis, and a second sample days later is often needed. Malaria must be excluded in every febrile patient in an endemic area, because the two diseases can coexist and a positive blood film can end the search too soon.

There is no antiviral drug that cures Ebola virus disease, so treatment rests on meticulous supportive care delivered by a trained and protected team. Fluids are given by mouth when the patient can drink and intravenously when they cannot, with the volume adjusted against blood pressure, urine output and signs of overload. Electrolytes, particularly potassium and magnesium, are replaced according to measured losses, oxygen is given for low saturation, and blood products are used for significant bleeding. Two monoclonal antibody products are authorized for Ebola disease caused by the Zaire species, and both are given as a single intravenous infusion. One is ansuvimab at 50 milligrams per kilogram, and the other combines atoltivimab, maftivimab and odesivimab at 50 milligrams of each per kilogram. These products work best when given early, and the guideline must be checked and the dose verified independently by a second clinician, because the figures are revised, differ between countries and age groups, and are easy to misremember under pressure.

Vaccines have changed the shape of Ebola outbreaks. A single dose vaccine built on a weakened vesicular stomatitis virus protects against the Zaire species and is given intramuscularly, usually in ring vaccination around each case. A two dose regimen is available for health workers and responders, with the second dose about 8 weeks after the first, and the vaccine does not protect against Marburg or Lassa fever. Vaccinating the response team, the burial team and the frontline nurses is standard preparedness, and a vaccine left in a broken refrigerator is worthless, so the cold chain and a named person responsible for it are clinical concerns.

Lassa fever is an arenavirus disease carried by the multimammate rat, Mastomys natalensis, which lives in and around houses across much of West Africa. The rat sheds virus in urine and feces, and people are infected when those materials contaminate food, water, utensils or the floor where a child crawls. The disease rises in the dry months, when rats come closer to dwellings, and human to human transmission occurs through blood and body fluids, especially in hospitals where the diagnosis was never considered. Perhaps 80 per cent of infections are mild or silent, so reported cases are only a fraction of the true number.

The severe minority develops fever, sore throat, cough, chest pain, vomiting, diarrhea, facial swelling, bleeding and shock, and death can come within 14 days. Deafness is the signature complication, because the virus damages the hearing nerve and leaves permanent sensorineural hearing loss in roughly one quarter of survivors. Supportive care and infection control are the same as for the filoviruses, and the drug widely used is ribavirin, given by mouth or intravenously. A common oral regimen is a loading dose of 30 milligrams per kilogram, then 15 milligrams per kilogram every six hours for 4 days, then 7.5 milligrams per kilogram every eight hours for 6 days. The intravenous regimen is 30 milligrams per kilogram, then 16 milligrams per kilogram every six hours for 4 days, then 8 milligrams per kilogram every eight hours for 6 days.

The evidence for ribavirin comes largely from a single observational study rather than a large randomized trial, so it is offered as current guidance rather than established certainty, and the current guideline must be checked before it is given. Pregnant women with Lassa fever face a very high risk of death and of losing the fetus, and the virus can be found in the placenta, the amniotic fluid and the newborn. Every survivor needs a follow-up plan, because a hearing loss noticed only when the patient can no longer follow conversation can end a child's schooling and an adult's livelihood. That plan should name the eye and hearing assessments, the mental health review and the person who will pursue the patient if they do not return.

Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is caused by a nairovirus carried by ticks of the genus Hyalomma, and it is the most widely distributed of these diseases, found from Africa through the Balkans and the Middle East to central Asia. The tick lives on livestock, and farmers, shepherds, slaughterhouse workers and veterinarians are exposed through tick bites and through contact with infected animal blood and tissue. Health workers are infected when they care for a patient whose diagnosis was not suspected, and hospital outbreaks have followed needlestick injuries, blood splashes and inadequate protection during procedures. The incubation period is 3 to 7 days after a tick bite and 5 to 13 days after contact with infected blood.

Illness begins with sudden fever, headache, muscle pain, dizziness, neck pain, nausea and vomiting, and a hemorrhagic phase with bleeding from the gums, nose, gut and puncture sites follows. The case fatality has ranged from 10 to 40 per cent. Ribavirin has been used although the evidence for benefit remains uncertain and observational, and treatment is otherwise supportive. Prevention rests on tick avoidance, protective clothing, careful animal handling and prompt recognition of the first hospital case. A vaccine exists only in a few countries, so the nurse who suspects the diagnosis, isolates the patient and reports it without waiting for confirmation is performing the most effective preventive act available.

Rift Valley fever is a phlebovirus transmitted by mosquitoes and also by direct contact with the blood, tissues and fluids of infected animals. An outbreak among people is often announced by a storm of abortions and deaths among sheep, goats and cattle, and some Aedes eggs survive drying to carry the infection into the next rainy season. Most human infections are mild, with fever, headache and muscle pain, but a small proportion develops inflammation of the retina that can leave permanent visual loss, inflammation of the brain, a hemorrhagic form with jaundice and bleeding, or hepatitis with liver failure. There is no specific antiviral treatment for human disease, so control depends on vaccinating livestock, reducing mosquito breeding and protecting the people who handle animals and their products.

The New World arenaviruses cause a set of geographically distinct illnesses in South America, each named for the place where it was first recognized. Junin virus causes Argentine hemorrhagic fever, Machupo virus causes Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, Guanarito virus causes Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever, and Sabia and Chapare viruses have caused smaller outbreaks in Brazil and Bolivia. Each virus has a rodent reservoir, and infection follows the agricultural cycle through inhaled or eaten virus from rodent excreta, or through person to person contact during the hemorrhagic phase. Illness begins after an incubation of 7 to 14 days with fever, headache, muscle pain and dizziness, and it may progress to bleeding, neurological signs and shock, while ribavirin is used in treatment and a live attenuated vaccine against Junin virus is used in Argentina.

The differential diagnosis of a suspected viral hemorrhagic fever is long, and the clinician's task is to consider the dangerous possibilities while treating the likely ones. Malaria remains the most common cause of fever in most of the tropics, and it must be tested for and treated without waiting for any other result. Dengue, yellow fever, typhoid fever, leptospirosis, rickettsial infection, meningococcal disease, viral hepatitis and severe respiratory infections can all present with fever, bleeding or shock. The travel and exposure history is the single most useful tool, and a patient who has fever after travel to an area with active transmission should be isolated while the tests are done, not after the results return.

The case definition published by the national program and the World Health Organization guides the decision, and a suspected case is a clinical category that permits action before confirmation. Screening at the first point of contact protects everyone else in the building, so a sign and a short set of questions about fever, travel and contact should be in place before a patient reaches the waiting room. A suspected case is placed in a single room with its own toilet and hand washing station where one exists, and where single rooms are scarce, patients with the same suspected diagnosis may be cared for together in a designated area. The isolation area should have its own equipment, its own waste route and a defined boundary that visitors and staff cross only with permission. A log at the entrance records who entered, when and what protection was worn, and dedicated staff who do not rotate to the rest of the hospital reduce the chance that an infection travels out on a uniform.

Personal protective equipment is the barrier between the nurse and the virus, and it works only when it is complete, intact and correctly worn. The set includes a fluid-resistant gown or coverall, gloves, a face shield or goggles, a fluid-resistant mask, a head cover and boots or boot covers, and the exact combination depends on the task and the guidance in force. The order of donning matters, and it usually begins with the gown or coverall, then the mask, then the goggles or face shield, then the head cover, then the gloves. A buddy checks every step, looking for a gap at the neck, a torn seam, a mask that does not seal or a glove that has slipped, because the wearer cannot see their own back and neck.

Heat stress is a real hazard, so staff must drink, rest and rotate out of the protective set before exhaustion or fainting causes a breach. Doffing is the most dangerous moment of the shift, because the outside of the equipment is contaminated and the hands must not touch the skin or the clothing beneath. The sequence generally begins with removal of the outer gloves and the outer apron, then the gown or coverall, then the head cover, then the goggles or face shield, then the mask, with hand hygiene at every stage. Each item is removed by rolling or peeling it away from the body, so that the contaminated surface ends up inside. The mask is removed last, by the straps rather than the front, and the hands are washed or rubbed with alcohol based hand rub immediately afterward. Equipment is never reused, never washed for a second wear and never taken home, and every breach, however small, is reported and managed as an exposure the same day.

Waste from the care of a patient with a hemorrhagic fever is infectious, and the rules for it must be simple enough to follow when the unit is busy and the staff are tired. Sharps go into a puncture resistant container that is never filled above the marked line, never recapped by hand and never carried through a crowded corridor. The World Health Organization recommends that sharps and other infectious waste be burned in a high temperature incinerator, and where that is not available, the safe alternatives must be chosen deliberately rather than improvised at the end of a shift. Laundry is bagged at the bedside, never sorted by hand, and injections are kept to the minimum, with an intramuscular injection avoided when an oral or intravenous route will do, and a trained observer should watch the whole doffing sequence and speak only to name the next step.

Safe and dignified burial is one of the most effective interventions in an Ebola outbreak and one of the most difficult to deliver, because it touches grief, religion and community trust at once. The body remains highly infectious, and washing, touching, kissing and dressing the dead are the practices that most reliably transmit the virus to the family. A trained burial team works in full protective equipment, places the body in a leak-proof bag, disinfects the area and limits the number of people who come near. The family should not be excluded but engaged, and where tradition allows, they may watch from a distance, name the deceased, offer prayers and receive the belongings after they have been disinfected. The team should include someone who speaks the local language and can explain each step, because a burial performed without explanation is remembered as a violation and drives the next family to hide a death.

Contact tracing finds the people who have been exposed and watches them through the incubation period, which for Ebola and Marburg is 21 days. A contact is anyone who had physical contact with a suspected or confirmed patient, who touched the body or fluids of a patient, who lived in the same household or who cared for the patient without protection. Each contact is listed by name and address, assigned to a surveillance officer, and visited or telephoned twice a day for temperature and symptoms until the period ends. A contact who develops fever is isolated at once, tested and cared for, and ring vaccination around a confirmed case depends on the same lists that contact tracing produces.

The work demands vehicles, telephones, fuel and a system for recording information, and it fails when the community does not trust the people doing it. Health workers are the highest-risk group in these outbreaks, because they have repeated, close contact with patients who are vomiting and having diarrhea, they perform procedures that generate splashes, and they work long shifts in equipment that is hot and easy to breach. Understaffing multiplies the risk, since one nurse asked to care for more patients than is safe will cut corners on hand hygiene, on waste handling and on the slow, deliberate doffing sequence. An infected health worker can seed an outbreak inside a hospital, terrify the staff, close the facility and destroy the community's willingness to seek care. Every facility should therefore keep a list of isolation staff, monitor them for fever, vaccinate them where a vaccine exists and provide immediate care and compensation if they become ill.

Monitoring a patient with a suspected hemorrhagic fever is nursing work of the highest order, because the disease changes hour by hour and the interventions that save life are adjustments rather than single decisions. Record the temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, mental state and urine output at a fixed interval, and compare each set with the one before. A rising heart rate with a falling blood pressure and cool hands points to shock before the blood pressure collapses, and a falling urine output is the earliest sign that perfusion is inadequate. Fluid balance must be totaled for every shift, with all intake by mouth and by vein and all urine, vomit and stool recorded, because that arithmetic is the only way to see overload or dehydration developing. In an isolation area the nurse must often decide what can be monitored at the bedside and what can be postponed, and that judgment should be made with the team and written down.

Supportive care is the treatment, and it is delivered largely by nurses. Oral rehydration salts are offered in small, frequent sips to patients who can swallow, and intravenous fluids are used when vomiting, diarrhea or shock prevents oral intake. Potassium and magnesium are replaced when measured losses or laboratory results show the need, with attention to the urine output and the heart rhythm. Fever and pain are treated with acetaminophen, while aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are avoided because they impair clotting and irritate the stomach. Coexisting malaria must be treated and a bacterial infection must be sought, because a patient who dies of a treatable second disease while the team watches the virus is a preventable death.

Comfort, cleanliness, a cool cloth, a calm voice and honest explanation are not extras; they are the substance of what the nurse provides when there is no cure to give. Every treatment in this chapter also has a cost, and the nurse is the person who sees it first. Ribavirin causes a fall in hemoglobin through the destruction of red cells, so the blood count is monitored and a transfusion is given when the anemia becomes symptomatic or dangerous. Aggressive fluid administration can cause fluid in the lungs and heart failure, so the fluid balance is reviewed with the same care as the dose of any drug. Monoclonal antibody infusions can cause fever, chills, rash, itching, low blood pressure and difficulty in breathing, so the patient is watched closely during the first minutes and the infusion is slowed or stopped if a reaction begins. The protective equipment itself causes heat exhaustion, dehydration, headache and fainting when it is worn too long, and staff must be rotated before those signs appear.

Pregnancy makes these diseases more dangerous for both the woman and the fetus, and it also makes the clinical picture harder to read. Ebola and Marburg infection in pregnancy is associated with a very high rate of death of the mother and of pregnancy loss, and bleeding in pregnancy may be attributed to obstetric causes when the true diagnosis is an infection. Delivery, whether vaginal or by operation, must be conducted with full protection for the team, and the newborn must be cared for as a suspected case until the tests are known. Feeding at the breast is a route of transmission, and the decision about it must balance the risk of infection against the value of breast milk, with current guidance and the mother's wishes taken into account. Children often present with fever, vomiting and diarrhea but may show less obvious bleeding, and every dose for a child is calculated by weight and verified independently.

Orphans and children separated from their families during an outbreak need a named caregiver, a place to stay and someone who explains what is happening, because the measures that protect them can also terrify them. Survivors of these diseases carry consequences that outlast the fever, and many report persistent fatigue, headache, muscle and joint pain, eye pain, sleep disturbance and difficulty concentrating. Inflammation inside the eye, or uveitis, can appear weeks to months after recovery and can cause permanent visual loss if it is not recognized and treated. Hearing loss after Lassa fever and after the other hemorrhagic fevers is often permanent, and it should be managed with hearing aids, sign language or classroom support. The virus can persist in parts of the body the immune system reaches poorly, including the eye, the testes, breast milk and the central nervous system, and relapse with inflammation of the brain has been described months after recovery.

Survivors need a follow-up plan with named appointments, clear instructions about barrier protection with sexual partners and an open door to return if new symptoms appear. Stigma is one of the most damaging consequences of an outbreak, and it is directed at survivors, at their families and at the health workers who cared for them. A survivor may be refused entry to a market, dismissed from work, abandoned by a spouse or feared by neighbors who believe the virus stays in the body forever, and children who lost a parent may be shunned. The answer begins with accurate information given to the community, in the local language, by people it trusts, and it continues with visible reintegration in which leaders, employers and religious figures welcome survivors back. Survivors need practical help with food, housing, schooling and income, and they need mental health support for grief, for survivor guilt and for the fear that the illness will return. Follow-up care should combine the eye examination, the hearing assessment, the mental health review, the sexual health counseling and the management of chronic pain in one place.

Prevention works at the level of the community, the household and the health facility. Avoiding the hunting, butchering and eating of bats and non-human primates removes the most direct route from the reservoir to people, and any animal found dead should be reported rather than handled. Storing food in closed containers, keeping rodents out of the house, trapping them and cleaning surfaces reduces the risk of Lassa fever and of the South American arenaviruses. People who work with livestock should wear protective clothing, use repellents, check themselves for ticks and remove attached ticks with fine tweezers, and livestock should be vaccinated against Rift Valley fever where a program exists. Health facilities need a triage system, a stock of protective equipment, a trained team, a waste route and a plan for safe burial before the first patient arrives, because an outbreak is a bad time to write a protocol.

Community engagement and risk communication must be honest about what is known and what is not, and they must answer the fears that spread faster than the virus, including the fear that the hospital kills people. National and international systems exist to detect these outbreaks early and to stop them, and they depend on clinicians who report suspicion rather than waiting for confirmation. The International Health Regulations require countries to notify the World Health Organization of events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern, and hemorrhagic fevers are among the events that trigger that obligation. The pillars of a response are case finding, isolation and care, contact tracing, safe burial, infection control, laboratory confirmation, community engagement and logistics, and every one needs people, vehicles, fuel, food, water, communication and a supply chain. Resource allocation can become an ethical problem when beds, vaccines or protective equipment are scarce, so decisions should be made openly by a designated team, with nurses at that table because they see the consequences.

The team itself needs support, because repeated deaths, the fear of infection and the strain of the equipment produce moral distress and exhaustion. Debriefings, rest, mental health care and acknowledgment of what was done well are what allow people to keep working. When death is likely, pain, breathlessness, agitation, thirst and fear can all be relieved, and a dying patient should not be left alone. A nurse who can stay, speak gently and hold a hand provides care that no drug can replace, even through protective equipment that hides the face. Training, drills and a culture in which anyone can stop a procedure to correct a breach are the foundation of a safe unit, and duty of care never means that a nurse must work unprotected.

To summarize, viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of severe illnesses caused by filoviruses, arenaviruses, nairoviruses and phleboviruses, and they share fever, vascular injury, disordered clotting and a high case fatality. Ebola and Marburg come from the fruit bat, spread through direct contact with blood and body fluids, and cause bleeding only late, so the fever, the exposure history and the contact history are what should raise the alarm. Lassa fever comes from the multimammate rat and leaves deafness in many survivors, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever comes from ticks and infected livestock and spreads inside hospitals, Rift Valley fever follows livestock and mosquitoes, and the New World arenaviruses follow rodents in South America. Treatment begins with supportive care, careful fluids and electrolytes, and disciplined monitoring of a patient who can change within hours, and it now includes monoclonal antibodies for Ebola and ribavirin for Lassa fever and the arenaviral diseases. The nurse's responsibilities are the ones that decide whether an outbreak stays small, and they include correct wearing and removal of protective equipment, safe waste and sharps handling, safe and dignified burial, contact tracing, monitoring and comfort for the patient, and support for survivors who face stigma and long-term harm. Every regimen in this chapter is current guidance rather than settled truth, because it is revised as evidence accumulates, it differs between countries, and the current guideline must be checked, and every dose verified, before any drug, fluid or vaccine is given.

# Chapter 23 — Neglected Bacterial and Skin Diseases

The skin is the largest and most public organ. In much of the tropical world it carries disease that never reaches a record. The conditions in this chapter are bacterial or parasitic. They are neglected because they disable and disfigure rather than kill. Trachoma blinds slowly over decades. Yaws and scabies deform and isolate, and tungiasis makes every step painful. Podoconiosis swells the leg of a person infected by nothing but soil. Each is preventable and treatable, and each is wrapped in stigma.

Trachoma begins with Chlamydia trachomatis, an intracellular organism. Its variants labeled A, B, and C have adapted to the conjunctiva. Transmission is not sexual. Infection passes eye to eye on fingers, on shared cloths, and on flies. The bacterium provokes inflammation the immune system cannot fully resolve. Because immunity is incomplete, the same eye is infected repeatedly. Each episode leaves more scar. Repeated infection is the engine of trachoma.

Inflammation first produces lymphoid follicles on the tarsal conjunctiva. That tissue lies against the eye when the lid closes. Repeated episodes merge the follicles and lay down fibrous scar. The scar contracts and distorts the lid margin. It turns the upper lid inward, a condition called entropion. The lashes then rest against the cornea. This is trichiasis, and every blink drags stiff hairs across the eye. The result is pain, tearing, and light sensitivity.

Repeated abrasion leads to ulceration and bacterial superinfection. The cornea scars and becomes opaque. A person who reaches that stage is blind or nearly so, usually in both eyes by middle age. Risk factors are almost entirely environmental. Trachoma clusters where water is scarce and sanitation is poor. In such places faces are rarely washed. Households that walk far for water ration it, and the face is last. Fly density rises where animal dung and human waste lie near living space.

Test acuity in each eye if you can. Count the lashes that touch the globe. Record which eye and how many. Control rests on surgery, antibiotics, facial cleanliness, and environmental improvement. The four are not alternatives, and successful programs deliver all four together. Surgery corrects the inturned lid. Antibiotics reduce the community reservoir of infection. Facial cleanliness reduces transmission within households.

The operation is done under local anesthesia as an outpatient procedure. For a few lashes, epilation, or plucking, relieves symptoms briefly. Lashes regrow within weeks, so epilation is not a substitute for surgery. Your role is to identify who needs referral. Prepare the patient for the procedure. Provide wound and suture care afterward. Ensure the right patient reaches the operating table. Antibiotic treatment is where community and individual meet.

Current guidance from the World Health Organization gives azithromycin as a single dose. The dose is 20 milligrams per kilogram by mouth, maximum 1 gram. This equals topical tetracycline ointment applied twice a day for 6 weeks. The topical form remains useful for young infants. It is also useful when azithromycin is unavailable. Oral azithromycin has one great advantage. The course is completed in front of the person who gives it. That removes the adherence problem entirely.

For an individual case, treat the whole household at once. Reinfection from a family member is the usual cause of failure. Record the weight used, the dose given, and the date. Records are what let a program prove coverage. Mass treatment is the population-level use of the same antibiotic. The World Health Organization sets a threshold, usually around 10 per cent. Where active trachoma in children exceeds it, the community is offered azithromycin once a year. The program continues until prevalence stays below the threshold.

Coverage is the critical variable. Treating most of a community but not enough leaves transmission intact. Community drug distributors and teachers usually carry out distribution. Doses are measured by weight or height using a dosing pole. Children out of school and adults who work away are most easily missed. Registers and house-to-house sweeps are part of the method. Facial cleanliness and environmental improvement need behavior change and infrastructure. Face washing competes with carrying water for drinking and cooking.

Programs therefore improve water access as well as teach hygiene. Fly control includes safe disposal of animal and human waste. Keeping livestock away from living areas also helps. Latrine promotion reduces fly breeding and fecal contamination. These interventions are slow and political. Without them, trachoma returns when campaigns stop. Progress is measured with population-based prevalence surveys, not clinic counts. Programs track active inflammation in children and trichiasis in adults.

Those figures decide when mass treatment can stop. Surveillance then continues for several years. The World Health Organization validates elimination as a public health problem when criteria are met. Many countries have reached that point. The last cases are hardest because they occur in the poorest and most remote communities. Your monitoring role includes confirming that every person with trichiasis has been offered surgery. A program that stops at antibiotics leaves those losing sight without help.

Before leaving trachoma, a word about every regimen in this chapter. The doses here are drawn from published guidance. The sources are the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. That guidance is revised as new evidence appears. National protocols also differ, especially for pregnancy and young infants. Verify the current guideline before you prescribe or dispense. Never rely on a dose remembered from years ago. Present every regimen as what current guidance says, not as settled truth.

Write the source and the date beside the dose in your notes. Yaws is caused by Treponema pallidum pertenue, a spirochete. It is a close relative of the organism of venereal syphilis. It is transmitted by direct skin contact rather than sexually. It flourishes in warm, humid, rural settings where children run barefoot. It is a disease of childhood, with most cases before age 15. Infection requires a break in the skin and an infectious lesion. Crowding and poor hygiene facilitate spread.

Unlike syphilis, yaws is not passed from mother to fetus. It does not attack the nervous system or the heart. A diagnosis of yaws must never imply sexual transmission. The first lesion appears at the site of inoculation after roughly 3 to 5 weeks. It begins as a papule that enlarges and ulcerates. It is painless or only mildly tender, with a raised edge and moist base. It is often called the mother yaw. It usually sits on the leg or foot of a child.

It teems with treponemes and is highly infectious to other children. It heals spontaneously over weeks to months and leaves a scar. Secondary yaws follows weeks to months later. The organism spreads through the blood and lymph. The eruption is a crop of papular, macular, or nodular lesions. They are often covered with a yellow crust and favor warm surfaces. The palms and soles are frequently involved and crack painfully.

Latent infection can reactivate. Humans are the only host, with no animal reservoir and no vector. That is what makes elimination theoretically possible. Diagnosis is usually clinical in an endemic area. A child with a typical ulcerating lesion and a compatible history is treated at once. Laboratory confirmation is not required before treatment. Where laboratory support exists, dark-field microscopy can show the spirochete. It needs fresh material, a good microscope, and an experienced observer.

Serology is more practical. A non-treponemal test such as the rapid plasma reagin test shows activity. A treponemal test provides confirmation. The polymerase chain reaction, which you may know as PCR, can detect treponemal DNA from lesion swabs. Serology cannot distinguish yaws from venereal syphilis. Interpretation therefore depends on the clinical picture and the epidemiologic setting. Distinguishing the two depends on age, site, and history rather than a single test. Venereal syphilis is transmitted sexually, appears in adults, and produces genital lesions.

Venereal syphilis can affect the nervous system, the heart, and the fetus. Bejel, also called endemic syphilis, spreads among children in dry, hot, arid regions. It usually begins as oral lesions. Yaws occurs in humid tropical areas and begins on the legs and buttocks of young children. It is the only one of the three targeted for global elimination. All three respond to penicillin and azithromycin. The distinction is epidemiologic rather than a matter of different drugs. It still matters, because telling a family that a child has a sexually transmitted infection has consequences no laboratory result can undo.

Treatment of yaws has been transformed by a single drug. Current guidance gives azithromycin as a single oral dose. The dose is 30 milligrams per kilogram, maximum 2 grams. This cures the great majority of cases. Benzathine penicillin remains the older standard. It is used where azithromycin is unavailable or the patient cannot take an oral medicine. The adult dose is 1.2 million units given intramuscularly as a single injection. Younger children receive half that dose.

Because treatment is a single observed dose, adherence is not the obstacle it is in tuberculosis or HIV care. A whole village can be treated in a day. The drug is generally well tolerated, though gastrointestinal upset is common. Allergic reactions occur rarely, so check the national protocol before prescribing. The one serious threat to elimination is resistance to azithromycin. A mutation in the bacterial gene the drug targets has been detected in several countries. It can cause treatment failure and, if it spreads, undermine the campaign. Programs monitor and investigate treatment failures.

They test for the mutation when laboratory capacity allows. The operational response has been total community treatment. Everyone in a defined area receives a single dose. This reaches latent infections that would otherwise seed new cases. It requires very high coverage and careful dosing by weight. Resistance surveillance and high coverage are two halves of one strategy. After treatment, the patient should be examined again. Primary and secondary lesions usually heal within weeks.

Scabies is caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei variety hominis. It is about one third of a millimeter long and barely visible. The female burrows into the outermost skin layer, the stratum corneum. She lays eggs and deposits feces along a tunnel. The itch comes from the immune response, not from the mite itself. Symptoms take weeks after a first infestation. A previously infested person reacts within days because the immune system is primed. The mite survives away from human skin for a limited time.

Transmission requires prolonged skin-to-skin contact. That is why scabies spreads in households and institutions. A brief handshake does not usually transmit it. Ordinary scabies is dominated by intense itching that is worse at night. The lesions are small, red papules and vesicles. Burrows appear as fine, wavy, grayish lines a few millimeters long. They are most easily seen in finger webs, wrists, armpits, waist, buttocks, and genitalia. In infants the palms, soles, and scalp may be involved.

Excoriations from scratching are common and may obscure the primary lesions. The rash is often atypical and the burrow is easy to miss. Scabies is therefore mistaken for eczema, allergy, or insect bites. In an endemic area, treat an itchy rash in more than one household member as scabies. The most important complication is bacterial superinfection of scratched skin. Group A streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus enter through the excoriations. They produce impetigo, cellulitis, and abscesses. In tropical settings this pathway contributes to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

That kidney disease follows skin infection rather than sore throat. The link is well established in Pacific and Australian Indigenous communities. There, scabies control has reduced the incidence of kidney disease. Crusted, weeping skin lesions in a child may therefore signal future kidney damage. Ask about dark urine, facial swelling, and reduced urine output. Diagnosis of scabies is usually clinical. A typical itchy rash with a compatible distribution is enough to treat.

The practical rule is to treat when suspicion is reasonable. Treat the household rather than wait for laboratory proof. Crusted scabies, also called Norwegian scabies, behaves differently. It occurs when the immune response fails to control the mite. It is seen in advanced HIV infection and in people taking corticosteroids. Other immunosuppressive drugs carry the same risk. The very old and those with severe neurologic disease are also at risk. The skin may harbor thousands to millions of mites.

The lesions are thick, scaly plaques that can look like psoriasis or eczema. Itching is often minimal or absent. That is why the condition is missed until an outbreak occurs. The enormous mite burden makes it far more contagious than ordinary scabies. Even brief contact can transmit it. Any patient with a widespread scaly eruption in an institution should be considered infectious. The same applies to anyone with a suppressed immune system. Institutions are where scabies becomes an emergency.

Nursing homes, hospitals, prisons, orphanages, and boarding schools can sustain outbreaks. Dozens of residents and staff may be affected. Once crusted scabies is introduced, the environment becomes a source. Shed skin scales carry mites that survive long enough to infest others. Control requires treating every resident and every staff member at the same time. This is done whether or not they have symptoms. Treatment is repeated as the drug requires. Environmental cleaning matters, including laundering bedding and clothing.

Staff who are not treated become reinfested and reintroduce the mite. Treatment of ordinary scabies rests on two drugs. Permethrin is a topical insecticide that kills the mite on contact. The 5 per cent cream is applied from the neck down. It is left for 8 to 12 hours and then washed off. In infants the scalp, neck, and face are also treated, avoiding the eyes and mouth. Permethrin does not reliably kill the eggs. The application must therefore be repeated after 7 days.

Temporary burning, stinging, and itching can occur. These are often mistaken for treatment failure. Wash bedding and clothing used before treatment in hot water and dry hot. Sealing them in a plastic bag for several days also works. Permethrin is safe in pregnancy and in young infants when used as directed. Ivermectin is the second drug, taken by mouth as 200 micrograms per kilogram. It is repeated after 7 to 14 days because it does not kill the eggs. It is convenient and useful in mass treatment.

It helps patients who cannot apply topical therapy properly. It is effective in crusted scabies when combined with a topical agent. It should not be given to pregnant women in most guidance. Children weighing less than 15 kilograms should not receive it. Breastfeeding mothers in the first weeks are also excluded. These restrictions must be checked against current recommendations. A separate caution applies where Loa loa, the eye worm, is co-endemic. There, ivermectin can cause a severe neurologic reaction.

All household members and sexual contacts should be treated on the same day. This applies even without symptoms. Launder clothing and bedding used before treatment in hot water. Set them aside long enough for the mite to die if hot water is unavailable. Fumigants and sprays are not recommended. They do not reach the mite in the skin and may be harmful. Itching can persist for 2 to 4 weeks after successful treatment. Warn patients not to restart treatment for this reason.

Reassess persistent itching or new burrows as failure or reinfection. At the population level, scabies is increasingly managed with mass treatment. In communities with high prevalence, programs have used community-wide ivermectin. It is given alone or with permethrin. Trials show it reduces scabies and severe bacterial skin infection. The World Health Organization has added scabies to its strategy for skin-related neglected tropical diseases. Coverage must be high. The caution about Loa loa applies wherever ivermectin is distributed broadly.

Your part is to explain the medicine and to weigh and dose accurately. Record who received what. Make sure the youngest and oldest are not missed. Tungiasis is caused by Tunga penetrans, the sand flea. It lives in dry, sandy soil in parts of Latin America, the Caribbean, and sub-Saharan Africa. The adult female flea is the parasite. The male and immature stages live in the soil and feed on mammals. Dogs, cats, pigs, and rats are among the hosts.

The female attaches to human skin, usually on the foot. She burrows into the epidermis and enlarges as her eggs develop. Over about 2 weeks her abdomen swells into a nodule. It is white or yellowish with a dark opening at the center. She expels eggs through that opening and then dies in place. The flea jumps poorly and cannot fly. It therefore attacks the body parts closest to the soil. That is why the feet bear the burden.

The lesion is a firm, pea-sized nodule with a central black dot. It may be single or multiple. Clusters appear on the sole, heel, toes, and around the nails. Itching and a sensation of movement are common early symptoms. Pain develops as the nodule presses on nerve endings. Walking becomes painful and children may limp or refuse to walk. Inflammation around the lesion may be out of proportion to its size. Look carefully between the toes and under the nails.

Lesions there are easily missed and often most symptomatic. Confluent lesions on a toe can deform it and eventually cause autoamputation. The chief complications are secondary bacterial infection and tetanus. The opening in the skin gives bacteria direct access. Abscess, cellulitis, and lymph channel inflammation are common with many lesions. Tetanus is a real risk in unvaccinated people. Check and complete tetanus vaccination status in every patient. Chronic infection can destroy soft tissue and bone.

That leads to deformity and loss of the toe. Children and older adults carry the heaviest burden. Treatment is extraction of the flea with a sterile needle or forceps. Remove the intact flea without rupturing it. Rupture spills eggs and antigenic material into the wound. That increases inflammation and infection risk. Clean and dress the cavity and give tetanus prophylaxis according to history. Use antibiotics when there is cellulitis or an abscess.

Dogs and cats are reservoirs, so veterinary treatment is part of an integrated approach. Community education is essential. The condition is so familiar in some places that it is accepted as part of childhood. Podoconiosis most often masquerades as lymphatic filariasis. Understanding why it is not infectious is the key to managing it. The name means dust of the earth. The cause is prolonged barefoot contact with irritant soil. Fine volcanic clay particles are the specific culprit.

They occur in highland regions of Ethiopia, Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya, Cameroon, and Tanzania. Particles are typically less than 2 micrometers. They pass through the skin of the sole and enter the lymphatics. Chronic inflammation and years of exposure produce fibrosis and obstruction. The leg becomes firm rather than pitting. It does not respond to pressure as early edema does. There is no infectious agent, no mosquito, and no person-to-person transmission. A genetic susceptibility appears to influence who develops the disease with the same exposure.

Those features distinguish podoconiosis from filarial disease. Pain is common and walking becomes difficult. Lymphatic filariasis is caused by Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi, or Brugia timori. It is transmitted by mosquitoes and typically produces leg lymphedema and hydrocele in men. It is identified with a rapid antigen test or by finding microfilariae in blood. Podoconiosis occurs above about 1,000 meters where filarial vectors are less common. It has no hydrocele, spares the groin, and has a negative antigen test. The two conditions can coexist in the same region.

Young women are especially affected because the swelling is believed to reduce marriage prospects. Children may be withdrawn from school when a parent becomes disabled. The economic consequence extends to the next generation. Health education that names the true cause is therefore a clinical intervention. It must state that podoconiosis is not infectious and not a curse. It must show that the disease is preventable and manageable. Management is simple, inexpensive, and effective. It does not require surgery or long drug courses.

The foundation is daily foot hygiene with soap and clean water. Dry the feet carefully, especially between the toes. An emollient such as petrolatum keeps the skin supple and prevents cracking. Antifungal or antibacterial powder may be needed for macerated skin. Compression with elastic bandages or custom garments reduces swelling. Elevation of the leg when resting helps as well. Well-fitting shoes protect the feet from further soil exposure and injury. Treat acute attacks of cellulitis with antibiotics according to World Health Organization guidance and local protocols.

Attend to analgesia and rest. Surgery has no useful role in reversing established lymphedema. Protect patients from operations that promise a cure they cannot deliver. Prevention is a matter of footwear. Shoe distribution in endemic highlands, coupled with education, has been associated with reduced incidence in children. Protecting children's feet now prevents disability in middle age. A shoe that is uncomfortable or expensive will not be worn. Programs therefore work to make footwear affordable and culturally acceptable.

Integrating podoconiosis into campaigns that already distribute shoes is cost-effective. These five conditions were once addressed by separate programs. That separation was one reason each remained neglected. The current approach is integrated skin disease management. A single examination of the skin screens for several conditions at once. A community health worker can be trained to recognize several signs. These include a burrow, an embedded flea, a scaly plaque, an inturned eyelid, and a hard swollen leg. Most of these diseases can be identified in a short encounter.

Treatment can then be delivered together. Sometimes a single medicine serves, since azithromycin treats both trachoma and yaws. Integration reduces cost and reduces the number of visits. It reduces the chance that one condition is missed. Programs use simple algorithms and picture-based job aids. Community health workers and nurses can then classify common skin conditions. They decide what to treat locally and what to refer. A basic kit contains gloves, a bright light, a measuring tape, a magnifier, dressings, and a small formulary.

Ask permission before examining intimate areas and explain why it is necessary. Examine the whole skin surface in a logical order. Include the scalp, finger webs, nails, soles, spaces between the toes, and genital area. Ask about itching at night and household members with the same problem. Ask about barefoot walking, animals in the home, and previous treatments. Record what you actually see rather than what you expect. These diseases coexist, so one diagnosis does not exclude a second. Wound care is a large part of the nursing work here.

The principles are the same as anywhere else. Clean the wound with clean water or saline. Remove debris and dead tissue. Dress the wound with a material that keeps it moist and protected. Avoid macerating the surrounding skin. For embedded fleas and the lesions of yaws and tungiasis, remove the organism. Prevent bacterial infection and let the skin heal from below. Signs of spreading infection, increasing pain, fever, or foul discharge require assessment for antibiotics.

Referral may be needed. Offer pain control, because these lesions are often more painful than their size suggests. Untreated pain drives patients away from care. Verify and complete tetanus vaccination for any penetrating or contaminated lesion. Document each dressing, the wound appearance, and the pain score. Improvement or deterioration is then visible on the page. Reducing stigma is not a soft skill that follows the clinical work. In these diseases it often makes the clinical work possible.

The words you choose matter. Describe trachoma as an infection, scabies as a mite, tungiasis as a flea, and podoconiosis as a disease of soil and bare feet. Say plainly that none is a curse, a punishment, or a sign of uncleanliness. Counsel families together where possible. Treating a household as a unit improves cure and removes blame. Correct the myth of contagion for podoconiosis. Explain that yaws is not a sexually transmitted infection.

Both misunderstandings destroy lives. Support patients excluded from school or work with clear clinical letters. State the diagnosis and its management. Where culturally appropriate, involve community leaders and teachers. Community belief determines whether people come forward for treatment. Monitoring and recognition of adverse effects are core nursing responsibilities. Azithromycin for trachoma or yaws commonly causes nausea, abdominal discomfort, and loose stools. These effects are usually mild and brief.

Serious allergic reactions, including anaphylaxis, are rare but must be anticipated. Every treatment point should have a plan and the supplies to respond. Permethrin can cause local burning or stinging. Ivermectin can cause dizziness, headache, and, where Loa loa is present, a serious neurologic reaction. That requires immediate medical attention. Benzathine penicillin carries the risk of anaphylaxis. Take a penicillin allergy history and give the injection where resuscitation equipment is available. In mass treatment, a simple system for recording and reporting adverse events is essential.

The nurse usually notices the pattern first. Never dismiss a complaint as coincidence in a campaign. The logistics of these programs are unglamorous and decisive. Store azithromycin tablets and suspension dry and within expiry. The drug does not require a cold chain. It does require protection from heat and humidity. That is a real challenge in a tropical clinic. Dosing poles and scales must be available and calibrated.

Dosing by height and weight is accurate only if the tools are accurate. Community registers, treatment cards, and tally sheets must be printed, distributed, and collected. The numbers must reconcile with the medicines consumed. Schedule distribution around planting, market days, and travel. A campaign that asks people to stay home can cost income they cannot afford to lose. Agree referral pathways before the campaign begins. They must cover surgery, severe skin infection, and adverse events. Two numbers dominate success or failure.

The first is coverage, and the second is the retention of adverse event reports. Both are built by nurses who plan the practical details. They train and supervise the distributors and keep the records that prove what was done. Coverage is counted against the eligible population, and every adverse event report is reviewed rather than filed away.

To summarize, trachoma, yaws, scabies, tungiasis, and podoconiosis are neglected bacterial and skin diseases that disable and stigmatize long before they kill. Trachoma is repeated infection by Chlamydia trachomatis that scars the upper lid and drags lashes across the cornea, and it is controlled with surgery, azithromycin, facial cleanliness, and environmental improvement. Yaws is a childhood treponemal infection cured by a single dose of azithromycin, and its distinction from venereal syphilis and bejel rests on age, site, and epidemiology rather than serology alone. Scabies is a mite infestation treated with permethrin or ivermectin together with every household contact, and crusted scabies in an immunocompromised patient is a highly contagious trigger for institutional outbreaks. Tungiasis is an embedded sand flea causing pain and secondary infection, and podoconiosis is a non-infectious lymphedema of volcanic clay soil routinely mistaken for filariasis. Across all of them, your skin assessment, wound care, and accurate dosing matter, and so do your attention to adverse effects and your program logistics. The regimens in this chapter come from guidance that changes and differs between countries, so verify them against the current national protocol every time you prescribe.

# Chapter 24 — Tropical Mycoses

The fungal infections of the tropics are the least taught and the most delayed in diagnosis of all the diseases in this book. They live in soil, in guano, on plants and on decaying wood, and they enter the body by inhalation or through broken skin. Most people who meet them are never ill, because a healthy immune system contains them, and illness appears when the inoculum is large or the defenses are weakened. This chapter covers histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis, mycetoma, sporotrichosis, chromoblastomycosis and cryptococcosis. The guidance followed here is that of the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. Every dose below is current guidance rather than settled truth, because regimens are revised, guidance differs between countries, and the current guideline must be checked before prescribing.

Fungi that cause disease in humans fall into two groups. The dimorphic fungi grow as molds in cool soil and as yeasts in human tissue, and they cause histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis, paracoccidioidomycosis and sporotrichosis. Others grow in the environment and take hold only when the skin is broken or the immune system fails, which is the pattern of mycetoma, chromoblastomycosis and cryptococcosis. Because the exposure is often agricultural and repeated, the history is a diagnostic instrument that deserves the same care as the malaria travel history.

Histoplasmosis is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, a dimorphic fungus that grows best in soil enriched by the droppings of bats and birds. It is found on every continent but concentrated in the river valleys of North America, in parts of Central and South America, in Africa, in India and in Southeast Asia. The classic exposures are entering a cave, cleaning a chicken coop, clearing a starling roost, demolishing an old building, cutting trees, and turning soil that has held birds for years. A bat cave is the most concentrated exposure of all, because the guano is deep and the air is full of spores. The fungus does not pass from person to person, so the history that matters is what the patient breathed rather than whom the patient met.

After an incubation of about 3 to 17 days, most infections produce either no illness or a brief flu-like fever with cough, fatigue and muscle aching that settles without treatment. The severity depends on how many spores were inhaled, so a person who enters a cave or cleans a silo can develop a severe pneumonia with high fever, breathlessness and chest pain. The radiograph may show patchy shadowing and enlarged lymph nodes in the middle of the chest, which can later form a mass that presses on the airways. A small number of patients develop a chronic cavity in the upper lung that resembles tuberculosis and must be distinguished from it. Others develop inflammation of the joints or of the covering of the heart, because the immune response rather than the fungus causes that damage.

Disseminated histoplasmosis is the form that kills, and it appears when the immune system cannot hold the organism. Advanced HIV with a low helper T cell count, treatment with corticosteroids or with tumor necrosis factor inhibitors, organ transplantation and infancy are the settings in which it is seen most often. The patient presents with weeks of fever, weight loss, drenching sweats, enlargement of the liver and spleen, and a falling blood count, so the picture can resemble a blood cancer or miliary tuberculosis. Ulcers of the mouth, the tongue and the gut, a rash, and an enlarged adrenal gland are also described. In an infant or a severely immunosuppressed adult the course can be so rapid that treatment must begin on suspicion before any test returns.

The diagnosis of histoplasmosis rests on one test that is fast and several that are slow, and the nurse usually controls which specimen is sent. The antigen test detects a molecule shed by the organism in urine, in blood and in fluid from the lung, and it can give an answer in hours, so a urine sample should be collected before the first dose. It is not perfectly specific, because similar antigens are produced by Blastomyces, by Paracoccidioides and by Talaromyces marneffei, a fungus of Southeast Asia. Antibody tests rise later, culture takes weeks and requires a laboratory with the right safety precautions, and a biopsy can show the yeast inside the cells of the affected tissue. Send the urine, the blood, the culture and the biopsy together, and do not withhold treatment while waiting.

Current guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention describes two pathways, depending on how sick the patient is. Mild or moderate acute pulmonary histoplasmosis is treated with itraconazole, 200 milligrams by mouth three times a day for 3 days and then twice a day for 6 to 12 weeks, while some mild cases are simply observed. Severe pulmonary disease and disseminated disease are treated with liposomal amphotericin B, 3 milligrams per kilogram of body weight intravenously once a day for 1 to 2 weeks, followed by itraconazole, 200 milligrams by mouth twice a day. In disseminated disease the azole continues for at least 12 months, and in a patient with HIV it continues until the immune system recovers on antiretroviral therapy. Read those numbers as an illustration, verify them against the current guideline, and expect the durations and the alternatives to differ between countries.

Itraconazole is a difficult drug to take well, and most treatment failures in practice come from absorption rather than from resistance. The capsule needs gastric acid to dissolve, so it should be taken with food, and never with an antacid, a stomach acid blocker or a drug for reflux, because those reduce the amount that reaches the blood. The liquid formulation is better absorbed and is preferred when the patient cannot eat or is taking acid suppression. Itraconazole interferes with many medicines through the liver enzymes that handle drugs, including some statins, warfarin, rifampicin, phenytoin and several antiretroviral agents. It can also weaken the pumping of the heart, so it is used cautiously in heart failure, and it raises the liver enzymes, which should be checked before and during treatment. A drug level is often measured after 1 to 2 weeks to confirm that the dose is adequate.

Amphotericin B is the most effective drug in this chapter and the most demanding to give. The liposomal form is preferred because it carries the drug to the tissue with less damage to the kidney, and it is infused intravenously over 2 hours with fluids and careful observation. It commonly causes fever, shivering and nausea after the infusion, and those reactions are reduced by giving fluids, by slowing the infusion, and sometimes by premedication with acetaminophen and diphenhydramine. The serious effects are on the kidney, which wastes potassium and magnesium and reduces the filtering rate, so the creatinine, the potassium and the magnesium must be measured at least every 1 to 2 days, and a falling red cell count also develops. Stop and call the prescriber if the creatinine rises sharply, if the potassium cannot be maintained, or if the patient becomes short of breath.

Coccidioidomycosis is caused by Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii, dimorphic fungi that live in the dry, alkaline soil of deserts. They are found in the southwestern United States, particularly Arizona and central California, in northern Mexico, in parts of Central America, and in scattered dry regions of South America. The organism waits in the soil as a mold that fragments into infective spores, and those spores become airborne when the ground is disturbed by a dust storm, by construction, by farming or by an earthquake. The incubation period is 1 to 3 weeks, and the risk is highest for people who work outdoors in these regions and for laborers who are moved into dusty land. It does not spread from person to person, so the diagnosis depends on knowing where the patient has breathed.

The illness is often called valley fever, and most people who inhale the spores have no symptoms or a mild illness that is mistaken for influenza. When it produces illness, the patient has fever, cough, chest pain, headache, fatigue and aching joints, and a rash appears in a minority. Two skin findings are characteristic, namely tender red nodules on the shins called erythema nodosum and a blotchy rash called erythema multiforme, and both signal a vigorous immune response rather than deep spread. The joints may swell and hurt so much that the illness is nicknamed desert rheumatism. A small proportion of patients, roughly 1 per cent, develop disseminated disease, which can involve the skin, the bones and the coverings of the brain, and that risk is higher in people of Filipino or African ancestry, in pregnancy, and in anyone whose immune system is suppressed.

Diagnosis is usually made by serology, which detects immunoglobulin M early and immunoglobulin G later, supported by culture and by PCR on a respiratory sample. Culture of this organism is dangerous to laboratory staff, so the laboratory must be told what is suspected before the specimen is handled. Uncomplicated pulmonary disease is treated with fluconazole, 400 milligrams by mouth once a day, or itraconazole, 200 milligrams twice a day, for 3 to 6 months, and many mild cases settle without treatment. Severe or disseminated disease is treated with liposomal amphotericin B, 3 to 5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight intravenously once a day, followed by an azole for a prolonged period. Infection of the coverings of the brain requires an azole at a higher dose for years, often for life, and needs specialist care. The azoles are avoided in the first trimester of pregnancy because they can harm the fetus, so amphotericin is used instead.

Paracoccidioidomycosis is caused by Paracoccidioides brasiliensis and Paracoccidioides lutzii, dimorphic fungi that live in the humid soil of Latin America. It is reported most often in Brazil, Colombia, Venezuela, Argentina and Ecuador, and it is a disease of rural workers who clear land, plant crops and handle soil and vegetation. The infection is acquired by inhalation, and it can remain silent for years before producing illness, so the exposure may lie far in the past. It affects men far more often than women, a difference attributed to the protective effect of estrogen on the conversion of the mold to the yeast form. Unlike the other mycoses in this chapter, it is a chronic disease that unfolds over months and is often mistaken for tuberculosis or for a cancer of the head and neck.

The patient usually presents with weight loss, fever, cough and breathlessness, together with painful ulcers of the mouth, the nose, the gums and the larynx that make eating and speaking difficult. The lymph nodes of the neck may enlarge and drain, the skin may show crusted lesions, and the adrenal glands are involved in a minority of patients, which can produce a quiet adrenal insufficiency that appears only under stress. Diagnosis rests on microscopy that shows yeasts with multiple buds arranged like the spokes of a wheel, on culture, and on serology. Treatment is itraconazole, 200 milligrams by mouth once a day for 6 to 12 months, with trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole as an alternative when the azole is unavailable or unsuitable. Relapse is common when the course is too short, so follow the patient for at least 2 years and check adrenal function when the picture suggests it.

Mycetoma, also called Madura foot, is a chronic infection of the skin, the deeper tissues and the bone that begins when an organism is pushed through the skin by a thorn, a splinter, a stone or a sharp stem. It is a disease of people who walk and work barefoot on cultivated land, and it is reported most often in Sudan, in Mexico, in India and in Senegal. The infection grows slowly over months and years, and at first it causes a painless swelling that the patient ignores. In time it becomes a firm mass with nodules that open onto the skin and discharge through sinuses, and the discharge carries small grains whose color is a clue but never a proof. As it spreads, it destroys muscle, tendon and bone, and the foot becomes deformed and useless, though the pain may remain mild until the bone is involved. It produces disability, loss of livelihood and severe stigma, and the World Health Organization has targeted it for better recognition.

The single most important fact about mycetoma is that it has two families of causes, and the treatment is different for each. Fungal mycetoma, called eumycetoma, is caused most often by Madurella mycetomatis, responds poorly to drugs, and often requires surgery. Bacterial mycetoma, called actinomycetoma, is caused by bacteria such as Actinomadura madurae, Actinomadura pelletieri, Streptomyces somaliensis and Nocardia brasiliensis, and it responds to antibiotics, sometimes without any operation at all. Because the grains can look alike, the distinction rests on culture of the grains, on their microscopic appearance, and increasingly on molecular testing. A patient who is treated for years with an antifungal when the cause is bacterial loses time, money and tissue, and a patient treated with antibiotics when the cause is fungal may lose the foot.

Bacterial mycetoma is treated with antibiotics for months, and the combinations most often described are trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, sometimes with dapsone, or amikacin with a carbapenem in severe disease. Fungal mycetoma is treated with itraconazole, often 200 to 400 milligrams by mouth twice a day for a year or longer, and ketoconazole at 400 to 800 milligrams a day was used for many years before its liver and hormonal effects limited it. Practice in endemic countries adds surgery to remove the bulk of the diseased tissue, because a large fungal mass will not be cured by drug alone, and amputation is sometimes the only option for a destroyed foot. Imaging with ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging shows how deep the disease has reached and whether the bone is involved. Ketoconazole, once the mainstay of fungal treatment, is now limited by liver damage and by its effects on testosterone and cortisol, so liver tests and hormone effects must be watched. Verify every dose and every duration against the current guideline, and confirm the culture result before committing a patient to years of a toxic drug.

Sporotrichosis is caused by species of the genus Sporothrix, which live in soil, in hay, in straw, in sphagnum moss and on the bark of plants. The classic story is a gardener or a farmer who is scratched by a rose thorn or a barberry thorn, and the organism enters through the puncture. It is also acquired by handling hay, by working with moss, by hunting armadillos, and from the scratch of an infected cat, which has produced large urban outbreaks in Brazil. Sporotrichosis is not transmitted from person to person. Because the exposure is so specific, the nurse who asks about gardening, farming, floristry, forestry and animal contact will often make the diagnosis before the laboratory does.

After an incubation of 1 to 12 weeks, a painless nodule appears at the site of inoculation and then breaks down into a crusted ulcer. In the most common form, new nodules appear along the lymph channels that drain the area, forming a chain of lesions up the arm or the leg, and the regional lymph nodes enlarge. A fixed form stays at the site of inoculation, a disseminated form spreads through the body in immunosuppressed patients, and inhalation produces a pulmonary form that resembles tuberculosis. The diagnosis is made by culture of the discharge or a biopsy, because the organism is hard to see on microscopy. Lymphocutaneous and fixed forms are treated with itraconazole, 200 milligrams by mouth once a day for 3 to 6 months, potassium iodide solution is an older and inexpensive alternative, and severe or disseminated disease is treated with amphotericin B. Corticosteroids should not be used, because they worsen the infection.

Chromoblastomycosis is a chronic infection of the skin and the tissue beneath it, caused by dark molds that live in soil and on decaying wood and plants. The organisms include Fonsecaea pedrosoi, Cladophialophora carrionii, Phialophora verrucosa and Rhinocladiella aquaspersa, and they are found across the tropics and subtropics, with heavy reporting from Madagascar, Brazil, Mexico, Venezuela, India and parts of Africa. The infection follows a thorn, a splinter or a piece of wood pushed into the skin, usually on the lower leg or the foot, in a person who works barefoot or in sandals among vegetation. The lesion grows slowly over years into a warty, cauliflower-like plaque with black dots and crusting, and it may itch, but it rarely spreads through the body. Secondary bacterial infection, odor, disability and stigma are common, and the patient often arrives after many years of ineffective home treatment.

Diagnosis is made by scraping the lesion or taking a biopsy and looking for the dark, thick-walled cells called muriform cells, which are the form the fungus takes in tissue and which are the diagnostic finding. Culture confirms the organism. Treatment is difficult and prolonged, and current guidance describes itraconazole at 200 to 400 milligrams by mouth once a day, terbinafine at 500 milligrams a day, and flucytosine, often in combination for 6 to 12 months or longer. Small lesions are sometimes treated by surgical removal, by freezing with liquid nitrogen or by local heat, and these physical methods are valuable because the drug alone often fails. Relapse is frequent, so follow the patient for several years after the lesion has flattened, and check the liver and the blood count during a long course. Because the disease is disfiguring and slow, the psychological and economic burden is as real as the physical one.

Cryptococcosis is caused by Cryptococcus neoformans and Cryptococcus gattii, yeasts surrounded by a thick capsule that protects them from the immune system. Cryptococcus neoformans is found worldwide and is associated with soil enriched by pigeon droppings and with old, weathered wood, while Cryptococcus gattii is linked to certain trees and to soil and causes disease in people who are not immunosuppressed, particularly on Vancouver Island, in the Pacific Northwest of North America and in parts of Australia. The organism is inhaled into the lung and can stay there, and it spreads through the blood to the coverings of the brain when the immune system fails. Cryptococcosis is the second most common serious fungal infection in people with advanced HIV, and it is a major cause of death in that group in Africa and Asia. It is not spread from person to person.

The usual illness is a meningoencephalitis that develops over 1 to 4 weeks with headache, fever, neck stiffness, nausea, sensitivity to light and a change in mental state. The features that make it dangerous are the raised pressure inside the head and the swelling of the brain, which can cause blindness, hearing loss and death within days. Some patients have no fever and no neck stiffness, and a patient with HIV may look deceptively well, so the diagnosis is easily missed. The antigen test on serum and on cerebrospinal fluid is the key investigation, because it is fast, it is sensitive, and a rapid version can be done at the bedside in many programs. A positive serum antigen test in a person with advanced HIV and a low helper T cell count identifies disease before symptoms appear, which is why screening is recommended. Culture and microscopy with India ink staining are used where the antigen test is unavailable.

The World Health Organization recommends a short induction course of liposomal amphotericin B, 3 to 4 milligrams per kilogram of body weight intravenously once a day, with flucytosine, 25 milligrams per kilogram by mouth four times a day, for 1 week, followed by a second week of fluconazole, 1200 milligrams by mouth once a day. Consolidation then uses fluconazole, 400 to 800 milligrams by mouth once a day for 8 weeks, and maintenance uses fluconazole, 200 milligrams once a day, continued until the immune system recovers on antiretroviral therapy. Where flucytosine is unavailable, amphotericin B with fluconazole is used, and where amphotericin is unavailable, high-dose fluconazole alone is the fallback. Raised pressure inside the head is managed by draining cerebrospinal fluid through repeated lumbar puncture, and it must be treated even when the antifungal is working. Antiretroviral therapy is usually started 4 to 6 weeks after antifungal treatment begins, because starting it earlier increases the risk of immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, the paradoxical worsening that follows immune recovery.

The defining practical problem of this chapter is that these diseases are diagnosed late, and the reason is not clinical ignorance alone. The antigen tests are not licensed or stocked in many countries, culture takes weeks and needs a laboratory with a mycology capacity that most district hospitals do not have, and biopsy and histopathology may be days of travel away. The drugs are worse, because liposomal amphotericin B, flucytosine and itraconazole are expensive, available only in referral centers, and subject to stockouts that can interrupt a course. This is why fungal disease earns the name of a neglected disease, even though the organisms are everywhere. The nurse who documents a failure of access, who escalates it, and who starts whatever treatment is available is doing as much for the patient as the clinician who names the organism.

Logistics decide outcomes here as much as pharmacology, and the nursing role in logistics is central. Keep a written stock record of every antifungal your clinic holds, know the expiry dates, rotate the older supply first, and know the referral pharmacy that can supply what you lack. Amphotericin B needs a controlled temperature and protection from light, the reconstituted drug must be used within the time stated on the label, and the liposomal form must not be frozen. Flucytosine and itraconazole come in limited pack sizes, so a patient beginning a year of treatment may need a plan for refills, transport and money before the first dose is given. Specimens for antigen testing need the correct container, prompt transport and a laboratory that will accept them, and the nurse usually controls that chain. Write the plan in the notes so that the next nurse can continue it.

Monitoring during antifungal treatment is a set of ordinary observations repeated with discipline. Record temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate and weight at every visit, because weight change reflects both the disease and the dose calculation in a child. Check the liver enzymes, the kidney function, the potassium, the magnesium and the blood counts on the schedule the guideline sets, and respond to a rising creatinine or a falling potassium before the patient becomes ill. Ask about vision, hearing and headache at every visit when the brain has been involved, because raised pressure and nerve damage can progress quietly. Ask directly about missed doses, nausea, stomach pain, rash and sensitivity to sunlight, since patients often stop a toxic medicine without saying so. In a long course, also screen for depression and for loss of income, because the illness and the treatment both consume the patient's life.

Adherence over years is a different problem from adherence over days, and it needs a different approach. The patient must understand why the medicine continues after the fever has gone, what happens if it stops, and which symptoms must bring them back, and that conversation must be repeated at several visits rather than delivered once.
