Weight loss, night sweats, and a cough that will not settle should trigger a full workup rather than a course of antibiotics and a wait.

Malaria in a person living with HIV is more severe at every step. Parasite densities are higher, fever lasts longer, severe anemia is more common, and the risk of cerebral malaria and death rises, particularly when the immune decline is advanced and when the person is not taking cotrimoxazole prophylaxis. The effect is not symmetrical, because malaria transiently raises the viral load and may accelerate the loss of helper T lymphocytes, so an episode of malaria can move the HIV disease forward. In pregnancy the combination is especially dangerous, because both infections contribute to maternal anemia, miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight, and infant death, and each one makes the other harder to treat. The practical consequence is that a positive malaria test in a person with HIV never means only malaria. You must ask whether tuberculosis has been excluded, whether prophylaxis is being taken, whether the antiretroviral regimen is working, and whether the anemia is severe enough to need transfusion or a change of plan.

A single fever may have more than one cause at the same time, and this is the rule rather than the exception in co-infection. A patient with HIV who presents with fever, cough, and a positive malaria test may also have tuberculosis, and treating only the malaria produces a brief improvement followed by deterioration. The nurse should treat the confirmed malaria while continuing to investigate, because the disappearance of parasites does not explain a cough that has lasted 3 weeks or a weight loss that has lasted 3 months. Conversely, a patient started on tuberculosis treatment whose fever persists may have malaria, a bacterial infection, or the immune reconstitution reaction described later in this chapter. Holding several possibilities open at once, and documenting the reasoning, is what prevents the missed second diagnosis.

Every person diagnosed with tuberculosis should be offered an HIV test, and this should happen at the first encounter rather than after treatment has begun. The World Health Organization recommends provider-initiated testing with an opt-out approach, meaning that the test is presented as a routine part of tuberculosis care, the patient is told why it matters, and the test proceeds unless the patient declines. The reason is practical, because the result changes the treatment regimen, the timing of antiretroviral therapy, the choice of prophylaxis, and the intensity of follow-up, so a delayed result delays all four. The same offer belongs in the reverse direction, because every person entering HIV care should be screened for tuberculosis symptoms, and every person with a new HIV diagnosis in a high-burden setting needs a systematic assessment for active tuberculosis and consideration of preventive treatment. The nurse who normalizes the offer, explains that the result is confidential, and answers the question the patient is afraid to ask does more to find cases than any poster on the wall.

The offer of an HIV test belongs throughout tropical medicine, not only in dedicated tuberculosis and HIV clinics. Any adult with a fever of unknown origin, severe or recurrent malaria, a sexually transmitted infection, chronic diarrhea, tuberculosis at any site, shingles, unexplained weight loss, or a persistent skin problem should be offered a test. Pregnant women should be tested at the first antenatal visit and retested in the third trimester where the incidence is high, because treatment protects both mother and child. Children who are malnourished, repeatedly ill, or failing to thrive should be tested where the mother's status is unknown. The test itself is rapid and simple, usually a finger-prick blood sample read within minutes, but the result must be confirmed by a second, different test before it is communicated as a diagnosis. A positive screening test is a preliminary result, and the patient deserves an explanation of that distinction in plain language.

Confidentiality is not a courtesy in HIV care, it is a clinical instrument. If a patient believes that a result will be shared with family, employers, or neighbors, that patient will avoid testing, postpone treatment, and conceal missed doses, and the whole cascade weakens. Disclosure should be supported rather than demanded, because the patient carries the risk, and the nurse's task is to help the patient weigh who needs to know, who will be supportive, and how to be safe. Partner notification can be offered as a service the patient controls, and in many programs the patient is encouraged to bring partners in for testing voluntarily. Where a partner is at risk and the patient refuses disclosure, the local legal framework and the guidance of the World Health Organization and the national program set the limits of what the clinician may do, and those limits must be known before the situation arises. The same conversation should include the fact that treatment which suppresses the virus protects the partner, which is one of the strongest reasons to start therapy and stay on it.

Antiretroviral therapy is now recommended for every person living with HIV, regardless of the helper T lymphocyte count and regardless of symptoms, and it should begin as soon as the patient is ready and the diagnosis is confirmed. The World Health Organization has moved to rapid initiation, ideally on the same day as the diagnosis, because every week of delay carries a measurable risk of illness and death and because a patient who leaves the clinic untreated may not return. The exceptions are narrow and clinical. In cryptococcal meningitis, therapy is usually delayed by 4 to 6 weeks, because starting too early in that infection increases mortality. In tuberculous meningitis, therapy is generally delayed for 4 to 8 weeks for the same reason. For everyone else, the default is to start promptly, and the nurse should treat the start date as a clinical target with the same weight as a prescription.

When tuberculosis and HIV are diagnosed together, the order and timing of treatment matter as much as the drugs. Current guidance from the World Health Organization is to begin tuberculosis treatment first and to add antiretroviral therapy within the first 8 weeks, with the interval chosen according to the helper T lymphocyte count. When that count is very low, therapy begins within 2 weeks, because the risk of death from HIV outruns the risk of the immune reaction. When the count is higher and the tuberculosis is not meningitis, therapy can begin after 2 to 4 weeks, which allows the patient to settle on the larger regimen before the second one is added. In tuberculous meningitis, therapy is deferred for 4 to 8 weeks. These intervals are revised as trials accumulate and differ between national programs, so the current guideline must be checked before the start date is set.

First-line antiretroviral therapy in most programs today is a single tablet taken once daily that combines tenofovir, lamivudine, and dolutegravir. This combination is potent, well tolerated, and forgiving of a missed dose, and it suppresses the virus quickly in most patients. Dolutegravir is given at 50 milligrams by mouth once daily in the ordinary case. Tenofovir is given at 300 milligrams and lamivudine at 300 milligrams in the fixed-dose combination, though weight bands for children and lower doses for kidney impairment change the arithmetic. Where dolutegravir is not available, efavirenz at 600 milligrams by mouth once daily with tenofovir and lamivudine remains a common alternative, and nevirapine is still used in some settings. The nurse should verify the dose against the national guideline, the patient's weight, kidney function, pregnancy status, and the other medicines in the regimen, because the tablet that suits one patient may be wrong for the next.

Rifampicin is the backbone of tuberculosis treatment and the most disruptive drug in the room, because it strongly induces the liver enzymes that clear other medicines. When it meets the protease inhibitors, the blood levels of those drugs fall so far that the virus is no longer suppressed, and the standard guidance is therefore not to use protease inhibitors with rifampicin at all. Where a protease inhibitor is essential, the tuberculosis regimen may be changed to rifabutin, which induces the same enzymes far less, but even then the protease inhibitor dose usually needs adjustment with a boosting agent, and that decision belongs to an experienced clinician. The same enzyme induction lowers the levels of many other drugs, including hormonal contraceptives, some anticonvulsants, azole antifungals, and methadone, so a medication review is part of every tuberculosis start. The nurse should ask about every medicine the patient takes, including those bought without a prescription and those given by traditional healers, because the interaction that causes failure is often the one nobody mentioned.

With dolutegravir, the interaction with rifampicin is manageable but requires an explicit dose change. When the two are given together, dolutegravir is increased from 50 milligrams by mouth once daily to 50 milligrams by mouth twice daily, taken 12 hours apart, so that the enzyme induction does not leave the patient with too little drug. When rifampicin is stopped at the end of tuberculosis treatment, the dolutegravir dose returns to once daily, and that step must be recorded and communicated, because a patient left on the higher dose or dropped to the lower dose at the wrong moment loses either safety or potency. Some guidance, including recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, has supported 50 milligrams twice daily with rifampicin, while newer formulations of dolutegravir at higher strength allow once-daily dosing with rifampicin in certain regimens. Because these recommendations have changed more than once in recent years and differ between countries, the current national guideline and the current product information must be checked before every change. The nurse's role is to verify, to write the change plainly on the patient's card, and to confirm at each visit which dose the patient is actually swallowing.

Malaria treatment brings its own interactions. Artemether with lumefantrine is the most widely used artemisinin-based combination therapy, and lumefantrine is metabolized by the same liver enzymes that rifampicin induces, so cure rates can fall when the two are used together, and some programs prefer a different combination in that situation. Artesunate with amodiaquine is another common option, and amodiaquine can add to liver and bone marrow toxicity when combined with other drugs. Efavirenz lowers the level of some artemisinin compounds, while dolutegravir and artemether with lumefantrine can be given together with attention to timing, and the practical rule is to check the interaction table in the current guideline rather than to reason from memory. Cotrimoxazole interacts with several drugs as well, adding to the risk of high potassium and kidney injury with some blood pressure medicines and increasing the blood-thinning effect of warfarin. A single pharmacist review, or a nurse working from the program's interaction chart, catches most of these problems before they reach the patient.

Tuberculosis treatment itself follows the same principles in a person with HIV as in anyone else, with two additions. The standard regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary disease is 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin, given daily and supervised where the program can provide it. Isoniazid is given at 5 milligrams per kilogram by mouth daily, usually 300 milligrams for an adult, rifampicin at 10 milligrams per kilogram, pyrazinamide at 25 milligrams per kilogram, and ethambutol at 15 milligrams per kilogram, all as fixed-dose combinations where possible. Pyridoxine at 25 to 50 milligrams by mouth daily is added to prevent the peripheral neuropathy that isoniazid causes, and that prevention matters more in people with HIV, in pregnancy, in diabetes, and in malnutrition. Treatment is prolonged in some situations, including tuberculosis of the bone and of the central nervous system, and the duration is decided by the national program rather than by habit. The first addition is antiretroviral therapy, timed as described above, and the second is vigilance for the immune reconstitution reaction, which is the next subject.

When antiretroviral therapy restores the immune system, that recovery can itself cause illness, and the phenomenon is called immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. The mechanism is an exaggerated inflammatory response to an infection that was already present, or to dead organisms still in the tissues, as the newly competent immune cells arrive and react vigorously where previously they could not. It typically appears in the first 4 to 8 weeks after therapy begins, though it can occur up to several months later, and it is more likely when therapy starts while the helper T lymphocyte count is very low and the infection burden is high. The two forms are distinguished by whether the infection was known before. In paradoxical immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, a patient already being treated for a known infection suddenly worsens. In unmasking immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, a previously unnoticed infection reveals itself as the immune system begins to fight it. Neither form means that the antiretroviral therapy has failed, and neither means that the antimicrobial treatment should be stopped.

The appearances are varied and can be alarming. In tuberculosis, the classic pattern is a patient who was improving on treatment and then develops new fever, enlarging and painful lymph nodes, worsening breathlessness, or new infiltrates on the chest radiograph, while the tuberculosis itself is under control. In cryptococcal meningitis, the reaction can produce worsening headache, raised pressure in the head, and new neurological signs. In other patients, the syndrome presents as painful skin lesions, an enlarging liver, inflammation of the eye, or a collection of fluid around the heart or the lung. The timing, the clinical picture, and the exclusion of drug resistance, treatment failure, and a new infection are what support the diagnosis, because there is no laboratory test that confirms it. The nurse who knows the pattern will notice the change on the day it appears rather than at the next scheduled visit.

Management rests on treating the underlying infection properly, because the reaction is a sign that the organism is being attacked, not a reason to abandon treatment. Antiretroviral therapy is continued in almost every case, because stopping it reverses the immune recovery and does not reliably end the reaction, and the important exception is severe cryptococcal disease with raised pressure in the head, where specialist advice and sometimes a brief delay are needed. Symptoms are relieved with anti-inflammatory treatment, and corticosteroids are used when the reaction is severe or threatens an organ, as in tuberculosis involving the central nervous system or the pericardium, where prednisolone or dexamethasone is added under specialist guidance. The complications that make the reaction dangerous must be watched for, including airway obstruction from enlarged lymph nodes, compression of the spinal cord, and raised pressure in the head, and these require urgent referral. In many patients the reaction is mild and settles over weeks with explanation and simple pain relief, and reassurance is a real treatment.

Tuberculosis in pregnancy threatens two patients, and it is treated rather than deferred. Untreated disease causes miscarriage, premature birth, low birth weight, and death of the mother, and the first-line drugs are considered safe enough in pregnancy that the risk of not treating is far greater than the risk of treating. Isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide are used in the standard regimen, with pyridoxine added to prevent neuropathy and seizures in the newborn. Streptomycin is avoided because it damages the hearing of the fetus. Active tuberculosis is not a reason to avoid breastfeeding, and the mother should be supported to continue, though she should wear a mask while she is infectious and the infant should be assessed. Pregnant women with HIV should also be offered preventive treatment for latent tuberculosis where the program provides it, and the choice of preventive regimen depends on current national guidance. The nurse should arrange the birth plan, the infant's assessment, and the screening of the household together, because a mother with tuberculosis usually lives with people who are also at risk.

Tuberculosis in children is harder to diagnose and easier to prevent, and both facts shape nursing practice. Children often cannot produce sputum, their chest radiographs are difficult to interpret, and the tuberculin skin test is unreliable in the very young and in those with HIV, so the diagnosis usually rests on a history of contact with an infectious adult, on symptoms, on examination, and on a decision by an experienced clinician. Every child in a household with an adult who has pulmonary tuberculosis should be screened, and those who are well but infected should receive preventive treatment according to the national guideline. Dosing is by weight, and children are given child-friendly dispersible fixed-dose combinations, with isoniazid at 10 milligrams per kilogram, rifampicin at 15 milligrams per kilogram, pyrazinamide at 35 milligrams per kilogram, and ethambutol at 20 milligrams per kilogram by mouth daily, adjusted as the child grows. BCG vaccination at birth protects against the most severe forms of tuberculosis in infancy but does not prevent infection or transmission, so it never replaces the other measures. Growth monitoring and nutritional support belong in the same visit, because a child who does not gain weight is a child who is not responding.

Malaria in a person with HIV is treated with the same artemisinin-based combination therapies used in anyone else, and the choice depends on the local resistance pattern and on the medicines the patient already takes. Artemether with lumefantrine is the most common, given as a weight-based course of 6 doses over 3 days, with the first dose repeated if the patient vomits within 30 minutes. Artemisinin-based combination therapy is given by mouth for uncomplicated disease, while severe malaria is treated with artesunate intravenously at a weight-based dose and then followed by a full oral course once the patient can swallow. The nurse must verify the dose against the patient's weight, confirm that the patient has eaten enough fat to absorb lumefantrine properly, and check for interactions with the antiretroviral regimen as described earlier. Follow-up should include a repeat test to confirm clearance in areas where resistance is a concern, and a reassessment of the anemia, because the fall in hemoglobin can be delayed. The World Health Organization warns that resistance to artemisinin is spreading in parts of Southeast Asia and has emerged in East Africa, so a patient who does not clear parasites on time needs prompt review rather than a second identical course.

Cotrimoxazole prophylaxis is one of the most valuable and least glamorous interventions in co-infection care. It is a combination of trimethoprim at 160 milligrams and sulfamethoxazole at 800 milligrams, given as one tablet by mouth daily, and in children the dose is weight-based. It protects against Pneumocystis pneumonia, toxoplasmosis, and a range of bacterial infections, and it also reduces episodes of malaria, which makes it doubly useful in a person living with HIV in a malarious region. It is started for adults with advanced immune suppression, defined by the helper T lymphocyte count, or with a World Health Organization clinical stage that warrants it, and it is continued until the immune recovery is secure and sustained on antiretroviral therapy. It is stopped when the patient has been stable on therapy with a good count for a defined period, and the current guideline defines that period. The nurse should watch for rash, nausea, low white cell counts, high potassium, and kidney injury, and should never restart the drug after a severe reaction, because sulfonamide hypersensitivity can be fatal on re-exposure.

Prevention of malaria in a person living with HIV combines the usual vector measures with the specific protection that cotrimoxazole already provides. Insecticide-treated bed nets should be provided and their use explained and checked, because a net that is stored in a cupboard protects nobody. Indoor residual spraying reduces the mosquito population and the human biting rate, and it works best when a high proportion of households in the community participate. Where cotrimoxazole is being taken, it replaces the intermittent preventive treatment with sulfadoxine and pyrimethamine that is otherwise given to pregnant women, because the two sulfonamide drugs should not be combined. Pregnant women who are not taking cotrimoxazole should receive that preventive treatment according to the national schedule, usually at each antenatal visit after the first trimester. Seasonal preventive treatment for young children in areas of high transmission is a separate program and should be integrated with these efforts rather than run in parallel.

Adherence decides the outcome of all three infections, and it is a behavior shaped by circumstance rather than a character trait. A patient who misses doses is usually responding to side effects, a pill burden that is too large, food requirements that cannot be met, a long walk to the clinic, a stockout at the pharmacy, depression, alcohol use, or a fear of being seen with the medicines. Adherence counseling therefore begins with a simple question about how the medicines are actually being taken, asked without blame, and continues with practical problem solving. Once-daily fixed-dose combinations, taking medicines at the same time as a daily habit such as a meal or a radio program, and involving a treatment supporter chosen by the patient all improve the odds. The nurse should explain what each medicine does and what happens if it is stopped, because understanding is the foundation of persistence. When a patient reports stopping treatment, the right response is to find out why and to restart, not to lecture.

Retention in care is measured, and the measurements should be acted on. Every clinic needs a simple system that records the next appointment, identifies who missed it, and produces a list of people to contact within a few days, because a patient who is lost to follow-up is at high risk of death and of developing resistant disease. Contact should begin with a telephone call or a text message, using the number and the method the patient consented to, and should escalate to a home visit by a community health worker where that is acceptable to the patient. The person who makes the call needs training in confidentiality, because a message that reveals a diagnosis to a relative can destroy the relationship that the tracing was meant to save. Tracing should aim to solve the problem that caused the absence, whether it was transport, cost, side effects, work, or fear, and to offer a route back that does not shame the patient. A clinic that counts its losses and goes looking for them will keep far more people in care than one that waits.

Stigma is a clinical variable, not a background sentiment, and it changes what patients do. Enacted stigma is the discrimination a person actually experiences, in the family, in the workplace, or in the health service. Anticipated stigma is the discrimination a person expects, and it is often the more powerful of the two, because it prevents people from being tested, from collecting medicines, and from disclosing to a partner. Internalized stigma is the shame a person turns against themselves, and it is strongly associated with depression and with stopping treatment. The nurse shapes all three every day, through the words used at the desk, the placement of the queue, the privacy of the counseling room, and the tone of the question about how the medicines are going. A diagnosis spoken aloud in a waiting area can cost a patient a marriage or a job, and the harm is entirely preventable. Where the law criminalizes a person's behavior or identity, the nurse should know the local rules and should never become an instrument of them.

Depression, anxiety, and alcohol use disorder are common in this population, and they undermine every other intervention. Depression reduces adherence, delays clinic attendance, and increases mortality, and it is treatable. Screening should be routine, brief, and repeated, using the tools the program provides, and a positive screen should lead to assessment and management rather than to a note in the file. Alcohol use increases the risk of missing doses, of liver injury from tuberculosis drugs, and of unsafe sex, and it should be discussed without moralizing. Pain, poor sleep, and the fear of dying are frequent and should be named and treated, because untreated distress is read by patients as evidence that nothing can be done. The nurse is often the first person to hear about these problems, and the response should be practical, offering a referral, a follow-up appointment, and an explicit statement that the patient is not being abandoned.

Monitoring is how you find out whether the plan is working, and it has to be feasible in the setting where you work. Viral load measurement is the preferred way to follow HIV treatment, taken at 6 months after starting and then at least once a year, with a rising result meaning adherence problems or resistance and needing investigation rather than an immediate switch. The helper T lymphocyte count remains useful for decisions about prophylaxis and for tracking immune recovery where viral load is unavailable. Tuberculosis treatment is monitored by symptoms, by weight, and by sputum testing at defined points, and in a person with HIV the smear may remain negative throughout, so clinical response and culture where available carry more weight. Malaria is monitored by repeat testing, by the resolution of fever, and by the recovery of the blood count. Kidney function, liver enzymes, blood counts, and blood glucose should be checked at the intervals the national guideline specifies, and the results should be explained to the patient rather than filed.

Adverse effects are predictable, and anticipating them prevents most of the harm they cause. Dolutegravir is generally well tolerated but can cause weight gain and, rarely, allergic reactions and liver injury. Tenofovir can reduce kidney function and lower bone mineral density, and the older form of tenofovir is more likely to do so than the newer form, so kidney function should be checked before and during treatment. Efavirenz can cause vivid dreams, dizziness, and mood change, which is why it is taken at night and why depression must be screened for. Isoniazid injures the liver and causes peripheral neuropathy, which pyridoxine prevents, and rifampicin injures the liver, turns urine and secretions orange, and interacts with many other drugs. Cotrimoxazole can cause rash, suppression of the blood count, and high potassium. Artemisinin-based combination therapies are well tolerated, though lumefantrine can disturb sleep and appetite, and any drug that prolongs the electrical recovery of the heart must be used with care when other such drugs are given.

Drug-resistant tuberculosis changes the whole plan and must be identified rather than assumed. Molecular testing at the time of diagnosis detects resistance to rifampicin, which usually signals resistance to isoniazid as well, and that result should trigger a full susceptibility test and referral to a program that manages resistant disease. Treating a resistant infection with the standard first-line regimen produces failure, continued transmission, and further resistance, so the correct response to a rifampicin-resistant result is to stop and rebuild the regimen under expert guidance rather than to add a single drug. In a person with HIV, the second-line tuberculosis drugs bring additional interactions, especially with certain antiretroviral agents and with drugs that affect the rhythm of the heart, and the timing of antiretroviral therapy may need to change. These patients are best managed by a team that includes an infectious disease or tuberculosis specialist, and the nurse's job is to ensure that the referral happens, that the specimens reach the laboratory, and that the patient is supported through a longer and harder treatment. Injection-free regimens have widened access to treatment in recent years, but availability and eligibility vary, and the national program is the authority on what is offered.

The nurse's role in co-infection is broad, because in many settings the nurse practitioner is the person who holds the whole picture together. That means offering the HIV test, screening for tuberculosis symptoms at every visit, recognizing severe malaria, checking each prescription against the current guideline and the patient's other medicines, and following up the patient who does not return. It includes teaching the patient what each medicine is for, how to take it, what side effects to report, and when to come back urgently, and it includes protecting confidentiality at every step. Task sharing allows nurses to initiate and manage antiretroviral therapy and tuberculosis treatment where national policy permits, and that authority carries an obligation to work within the protocol and to refer when the situation exceeds it. Supply is part of clinical care, and the nurse should report stockouts and expiry dates as patient safety events, because a regimen interrupted by an empty shelf produces resistance as surely as a regimen taken badly. The integration of services matters too, because a patient who must attend three clinics on three different days will attend none of them reliably.

Nothing in this chapter should be read as settled. Antiretroviral regimens, tuberculosis regimens, malaria treatments, and preventive schedules are revised as evidence accumulates, and the guidance of the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control differs in emphasis and sometimes in substance from one another and from national programs. Doses depend on weight, on age, on pregnancy, on kidney and liver function, and on the other medicines being taken, so the same drug can require three different doses in three patients sitting in the same room. Before prescribing or administering, the nurse must verify the dose against the current national guideline and the product information, confirm the patient's weight and allergies, check the interaction list, and confirm what the patient is already taking at home. This verification is not a formality, it is the intervention that prevents most avoidable harm in this field, and it should be done out loud with the patient whenever possible.

To summarize, HIV, tuberculosis, and malaria cluster in the same populations because they are driven by the same poverty, crowding, displacement, and weak services, and they worsen one another through the immune system and through the daily realities of treatment. Every person with tuberculosis should be offered an HIV test, every person with HIV should be screened for tuberculosis, and malaria in a person with HIV should be treated as a potentially severe illness rather than a simple fever. Antiretroviral therapy is now recommended for everyone and should begin promptly, with tuberculosis treatment started first and therapy added within 8 weeks, sooner when the helper T lymphocyte count is very low and later in tuberculous meningitis. Rifampicin dominates the interaction list, forcing the choice of a different regimen or a doubled dolutegravir dose, and the immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome must be recognized as a treatable consequence of recovery rather than as failure. Cotrimoxazole prevents pneumonia, bacterial infection, and malaria, and isoniazid prevents tuberculosis in those who are infected but not ill. Adherence, retention, and tracing are clinical interventions with the same standing as any prescription, and stigma is a variable that determines whether any of them happens. Above all, every regimen described here is subject to revision and to national variation, so the current guideline must be checked before every dose, and the nurse who verifies, explains, follows up, and treats the patient with dignity is the strongest link in the chain.

# Chapter 28 — Nutrition and Tropical Medicine

Malnutrition is not a separate subject from tropical medicine. It is the ground on which many tropical infections grow and the residue that many of them leave behind. A child who is undernourished has thinner skin and mucosa, a weaker cell-mediated immune response, and smaller reserves of every nutrient the body needs to survive an acute illness. An adult with a chronic parasitic infection loses nutrients continuously through blood loss, poor absorption, and the metabolic cost of inflammation. Nutrition and infection therefore form a loop, and the loop turns in both directions at once, which is why feeding is a clinical intervention and not a background condition. This chapter follows that loop from the most severe forms of undernutrition to the deficiencies that still cause blindness, heart failure, and bleeding gums, and it ends with the work the nurse actually does, which is measuring, feeding, teaching, and following up.

Malnutrition in the tropics takes two broad shapes that are not opposites. Undernutrition is the shortage of energy, protein, and micronutrients that leaves a person small, thin, and vulnerable to infection. Overnutrition is the excess of energy that produces obesity, diabetes, and their complications. Both can exist in the same village, the same street, and sometimes the same household, so a clinic that screens only for thinness will miss half of the problem. Growth failure is described with three measurements that a voice can carry: stunting, which is low height for age and reflects long-standing deprivation; wasting, which is low weight for height and reflects recent, severe deprivation; and underweight, which is low weight for age and blends the two. The World Health Organization attributes roughly 45 per cent of deaths among children under 5 years of age to undernutrition, acting through diarrhea, pneumonia, measles, and malaria. The nurse should therefore read every growth chart as a record of both nutrition and infection.

The two classic severe forms of protein-energy malnutrition are marasmus and kwashiorkor, and the fastest way to tell them apart at the bedside is to press a thumb against the child's lower leg. Marasmus is severe wasting: the child has lost fat and muscle, the ribs and the bones of the face are visible, the skin is loose over the buttocks, and the child is often alert, hungry, and irritable. Kwashiorkor is the edematous form: the child retains fluid, the legs and feet swell, the belly may be distended, the hair becomes sparse and pale, and the skin may peel in patches. A child with kwashiorkor may look well fed on a scale, because the edema adds kilograms that the body does not have. Many children have both problems at once, and this mixed picture is called marasmic kwashiorkor, with edema layered on top of severe wasting.

The edema of kwashiorkor is bilateral, pitting, and dependent, beginning in the feet and lower legs and moving upward as it worsens. It does not respond to diuretics, and giving a diuretic to a child with nutritional edema is a serious error that can cause circulatory collapse. Nutritional edema is driven by low plasma protein, altered sodium handling, and inflammation, not by a failing heart. The nurse must distinguish it from nephrotic syndrome, in which protein appears in the urine, and from cardiac failure, in which the neck veins are raised and the liver is enlarged. Edema also inflates the weight-for-height measurement, so a child with kwashiorkor can be scored as only moderately wasted while actually being severely depleted of tissue. This is why edema is recorded as a separate finding on every assessment form and not folded into the weight.

Marasmus and kwashiorkor share a common background of poverty, food insecurity, repeated infection, and interrupted feeding. What separates them is partly the pattern of the diet and partly the body's inflammatory response, and the exact mechanism remains debated. Children with either form are at high risk of low blood sugar, low body temperature, infection, and electrolyte disturbance, and they can die within the first days of treatment if feeding is handled carelessly. Both forms impair the immune system, delay wound healing, and reduce the response to vaccines and to treatment of tuberculosis. The child who survives may carry stunting, cognitive delay, and a lifelong tendency toward metabolic disease, so recovery is measured in years and not in weeks.

Severe acute malnutrition is diagnosed in a child 6 to 59 months of age when any one of three findings is present. The first is a weight-for-height that falls far below the median, conventionally more than three standard deviations below it. The second is a mid-upper arm circumference of less than 115 millimeters, measured on the left arm at the midpoint between the shoulder tip and the elbow. The third is bilateral pitting edema of any grade, which by itself defines severe acute malnutrition regardless of the weight. A mid-upper arm circumference between 115 and 125 millimeters identifies moderate acute malnutrition, which carries less immediate risk but still needs a feeding program. In older children and adults the same logic applies with different thresholds, and a body mass index below 16 in an adult signals severe depletion.

Assessment begins with the measurement and never with the impression. The nurse needs a scale that is calibrated and zeroed, a length board for children under 2 years of age and a height stand for older children, and a tape that does not stretch. The child is weighed without shoes and in light clothing, the length is taken lying down for infants and standing for children old enough to stand, and the mid-upper arm circumference is taken three times and recorded. The appetite test, in which the child is offered ready-to-use therapeutic food and observed, separates those who can be treated at home from those who need admission. The history should record breastfeeding, the timing and content of complementary feeds, recent diarrhea or fever, immunizations, and whether food is actually available in the household. The examination should look for pneumonia, tuberculosis, malaria, skin infection, anemia, and dehydration, because each of these changes the plan.

Management of severe acute malnutrition proceeds in phases, and the World Health Organization organizes it into ten steps that can be remembered as the order of danger. The first steps address the immediate threats to life: low blood sugar, low body temperature, dehydration, and electrolyte imbalance. The next steps address infection and micronutrient deficiencies, and only then does the plan turn to the food that will rebuild the child. The phases that carry this sequence are stabilization, transition, and rehabilitation, and each has its own feeding formula, its own monitoring, and its own risks. Trying to rush from admission to catch-up growth is the single most common way to kill a child who was expected to survive.

During stabilization, which covers roughly the first week, the child is kept warm, given glucose if the blood sugar is low, and rehydrated cautiously with oral rehydration salts or, when oral intake fails, with fluids given intravenously. Potassium and magnesium are replaced even when the blood levels look near normal, because total body stores are depleted, and sodium is restricted because the edematous child cannot excrete a load. Broad-spectrum antibiotics are given routinely, because the signs of infection are blunted and the risk of death from unrecognized sepsis is high. Vitamin A is given, along with a multivitamin and folate, but iron is withheld at this stage because free iron can feed bacteria and malaria parasites. Feeding is frequent and small, using a low-energy, low-protein therapeutic milk often labeled F-75, and the child is watched for signs of fluid overload.

Refeeding too fast produces a recognizable syndrome, and the nurse who knows it will prevent most of it. As cells suddenly receive glucose and phosphate, they pull phosphate, potassium, and magnesium out of the blood, and the resulting low phosphate can cause muscle weakness, respiratory failure, heart failure, and seizures. Thiamine is consumed rapidly during this shift, so thiamine deficiency can appear or worsen when feeding begins. The warning signs are a rising pulse, a falling blood pressure, new edema, breathlessness, and lethargy in a child who had been improving. Prevention consists of starting with small volumes, advancing slowly, giving potassium, magnesium, and thiamine, and checking electrolytes when they can be checked. Feeding is advanced only when the child is truly stable, and the appetite is allowed to set the pace.

The transition phase begins when the child's appetite returns and the edema is resolving, usually somewhere between the seventh and fourteenth day. Feeding switches to a higher-energy therapeutic milk often labeled F-100, given in larger volumes at longer intervals, and the child is watched closely for the reappearance of edema or heart failure. Once the child is taking the higher-energy milk without difficulty, the diet widens to include ready-to-use therapeutic food and then ordinary family foods. The rehabilitation phase is the long stretch of catch-up growth, during which the child gains weight quickly and needs more energy and protein than a healthy child of the same age. This phase also includes stimulation, play, and emotional care, because recovery from severe malnutrition is neurological and developmental as much as it is physical.

Ready-to-use therapeutic food has changed the logistics of treating malnutrition more than any other product of the past generation. It is an energy-dense paste, usually based on peanut, fortified with vitamins and minerals, that needs no water, no cooking, and no refrigeration. It comes in sealed sachets with a long shelf life, so it can be stored in a health post or carried home in a bag, and it can be eaten directly by the child from the packet. Because it tolerates heat and poor roads, it allows children without medical complications to be treated at home through community-based programs rather than occupying a hospital bed for weeks. The nurse's role in this system is to decide who qualifies, to teach the caregiver exactly how much to give and when, and to schedule the return visit that catches failure early.

The child who cannot be treated at home must be admitted, and the reasons are specific. Admitted care is needed when the child fails the appetite test, when there is severe edema, when there is an obvious infection or danger sign, when the child is under 6 months of age, or when the caregiver cannot manage the feeding or cannot return for follow-up. Discharge criteria usually combine a good appetite, resolving edema, a rising weight, and a caregiver who has been taught what to do. After discharge the child returns regularly for weighing, and any loss of weight triggers reassessment and possible readmission. Relapse is common in the months after discharge, especially where food insecurity, tuberculosis, or HIV is present in the household.

Vitamin A deficiency remains one of the great preventable causes of blindness in the world. Vitamin A is needed to make rhodopsin in the retina and to maintain epithelial surfaces, and its absence first causes night blindness, then dry conjunctiva, then the foamy patches known as Bitot spots, and finally corneal ulceration and softening that can dissolve the eye within days. The same deficiency weakens the immune response, so children with vitamin A deficiency are more likely to die of measles, diarrhea, and respiratory infection. Measles itself depletes vitamin A stores, which is why the two problems travel together and why supplementation after measles is not optional. The World Health Organization recommends a dose of 200,000 international units by mouth for children 12 months of age and older, 100,000 international units for infants 6 to 11 months of age, and 50,000 international units for infants under 6 months, repeated the next day and again at two to four weeks in the treatment of clinical deficiency.

Preventive supplementation is delivered in campaigns, often alongside immunization and deworming, and it must be repeated every four to six months to maintain protection in places where dietary sources are scarce. Toxicity is real but uncommon: a single large dose can cause vomiting, headache, and a bulging fontanelle in an infant, and repeated very high doses over months can cause liver injury and bone changes. The nurse should therefore never repeat a campaign dose early because a caregiver asks for it, and should record each dose in the child's card. Pregnant women need a much lower dose, because high doses of vitamin A early in pregnancy can harm the fetus, and this is one of the places where national guidance differs sharply from country to country. Food-based approaches, including eggs, liver, orange-fleshed sweet potato, dark green leaves, and fortified oils, are the sustainable complement to campaigns.

Iron deficiency anemia is the commonest nutritional deficiency in the tropics, and hookworm infection is one of its commonest causes. Hookworms attach to the small intestine and feed on blood, and each worm removes a small but continuous volume every day, so a heavy burden over months can empty the body's iron stores. The anemia is compounded by malaria, by schistosomiasis, by other intestinal worms, and by diets that are rich in fiber and phytate and poor in absorbable iron. The World Health Organization recommends treating anemia with 2 to 3 milligrams of elemental iron per kilogram per day for children, given in divided doses by mouth, and with 60 milligrams of elemental iron plus 400 micrograms of folic acid daily for pregnant women, usually with deworming after the first trimester in areas where hookworm is common. Iron therapy should be continued for several months after the hemoglobin returns to normal, because stores refill slowly.

The timing of iron where malaria exists is a genuine clinical problem and not a superstition. Iron is needed by the malaria parasite as much as by the child, and the body responds to infection by raising hepcidin, which locks iron inside cells and lowers its level in the blood. Giving iron to a child during an acute malaria episode, or to a child with untreated infection, has been associated with worse outcomes in some trials, and a large trial in a malaria-endemic area found increased serious adverse events among children who received iron without adequate malaria treatment and prevention. The practical rule that follows is to screen and treat malaria and other infections first, to avoid iron during the acute illness, and to ensure that malaria prevention is in place before supplements are given to children in endemic areas. National policies differ on this point, and the current national guideline must be checked before iron is started in any child in a malaria zone.

Iodine deficiency is quieter than the other deficiencies and its consequences last a lifetime. Iodine is required to make thyroid hormone, and when it is scarce the thyroid enlarges into a goiter, the person becomes hypothyroid, and in pregnancy the developing brain is damaged. The severe end of the spectrum includes miscarriage, stillbirth, cretinism with deafness and intellectual disability, and a measurable loss of cognitive capacity across whole populations. The World Health Organization and the United Nations Children's Fund promote universal salt iodization, which is the cheapest and most durable public health measure in this chapter and requires no individual behavior change. Monitoring uses urinary iodine concentration in school-age children and thyroid stimulating hormone screening in newborns, and the nurse may be the person who collects those samples and explains the result. Iodine excess is also possible, particularly where salt is over-iodized or where iodized salt and supplements are combined, so the program must be monitored rather than simply expanded.

Zinc is not a cure for diarrhea, but it shortens it, and that is enough to matter. Zinc is involved in the repair of the intestinal lining and in immune function, and deficiency is common in the same children who have repeated diarrheal illness. The World Health Organization and the United Nations Children's Fund recommend 20 milligrams of zinc per day by mouth for 10 to 14 days in children 6 months of age and older, and 10 milligrams per day for 10 to 14 days in infants under 6 months, given alongside oral rehydration salts and continued feeding. The effect is a shorter episode, less stool volume, and fewer episodes in the following months. Zinc can cause nausea and vomiting if given on an empty stomach, so it is given with food where possible, and it should not be used as a substitute for assessment of the child's hydration and for the treatment of dysentery or cholera.

Thiamine deficiency still causes beriberi in the twenty-first century, and it appears wherever polished rice or white flour dominates the diet and fresh foods are scarce. Wet beriberi is high-output heart failure with edema, a fast pulse, and breathlessness, and it can kill quickly if it is mistaken for cardiac disease and treated only with diuretics. Dry beriberi is a peripheral neuropathy with numbness, weakness, and loss of reflexes that begins in the feet and rises. Wernicke encephalopathy adds confusion, eye movement abnormalities, and unsteadiness, and it becomes Korsakoff syndrome with permanent memory loss if thiamine is not given promptly. Severe cases are treated with thiamine given intravenously or intramuscularly, and mild cases with thiamine by mouth, with the exact dose and schedule taken from current national guidance. Thiamine is given before glucose in any malnourished or confused patient, because a glucose load in a thiamine-depleted person can precipitate the neurological syndrome.

Pellagra is the deficiency of niacin and it still appears among people who eat maize as their staple and little else. Its features are remembered as the four Ds, which are dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia, and death, and the dermatitis is the one that points to the diagnosis. The rash is photosensitive, appearing on skin exposed to sun such as the face, the neck in a band known as Casal's necklace, the forearms, and the feet, and it looks like a burn that later thickens and darkens. Niacin can also be lost in the urine in carcinoid syndrome and can fail to be absorbed in Hartnup disease, so the same picture can appear without a diet of maize. Treatment uses nicotinamide, which avoids the flushing that niacin causes, usually in divided doses by mouth for several weeks together with a balanced diet and other vitamins.

Scurvy appears wherever fresh fruit and vegetables disappear, and that happens in refugee camps, conflict zones, famine, long sea voyages, prisons, and in children whose diets are restricted by illness or by poverty. Vitamin C is required to build collagen, so its absence causes blood vessels to leak, gums to bleed, hair follicles to bleed under the skin, and wounds to heal badly. The classic signs are corkscrew hairs, perifollicular hemorrhage on the legs, swollen and bleeding gums, and easy bruising, and in infants the condition causes painful swelling of the limbs with pseudoparalysis. Treatment is ascorbic acid by mouth for at least one month, with the dose set by current guidance, and the response is usually dramatic within days. Scurvy is a reminder that a deficiency can appear wherever the diet loses its variety, and that the diagnosis is often made by a nurse who asks what the person has actually eaten.

Alongside this burden of deficiency, the same communities are now carrying a double burden of obesity and diabetes. The nutrition transition brings cheap energy-dense food, sugary drinks, refined grains, and less physical work, and it arrives in places that still have stunted children and infectious disease. It is common to find a stunted child, an anemic adolescent, and an obese grandmother in one household, each needing a different conversation. Diabetes in a tropical setting is dangerous in a particular way, because high blood sugar worsens tuberculosis, predisposes to skin and soft tissue infection, and makes any infection harder to control. Gestational diabetes produces large babies, birth injury, and a next generation at higher risk of obesity and diabetes themselves. The nurse should therefore screen for both ends of the spectrum in the same visit and avoid the assumption that a thin patient is the only patient with a nutrition problem.

The interaction between infection and nutrition deserves its own place in the nurse's thinking. Tuberculosis causes wasting through reduced appetite, fever, and the catabolic effect of inflammation, and weight loss before treatment predicts a worse outcome. HIV does the same through opportunistic infection, poor intake, diarrhea, and malabsorption, and antiretroviral therapy reverses much of the loss by restoring appetite and health. Intestinal worms take blood directly and nutrients indirectly, and they reduce growth and cognitive development in children who carry them for years. Measles, cholera, and other acute infections drain reserves within days, and each illness makes the next one more likely. The practical consequence is that every nutrition assessment in the tropics is also an assessment for infection, and every serious infection should prompt a plan for feeding during recovery.

Nutritional support in tuberculosis is mostly ordinary food, given in adequate amounts, and the evidence for high-dose single micronutrients is disappointing. Trials of high-dose vitamin A, zinc, and other supplements have generally failed to improve treatment outcomes, and some have suggested harm, so the safe plan is a balanced diet with sufficient energy and protein plus correction of specific deficiencies that are actually documented. Weight gain during treatment is a useful marker of response, and a patient who is losing weight after several weeks of therapy may have drug resistance, poor adherence, another infection, or simply not enough food. Food assistance improves adherence and completion in programs where patients are hungry, and it is a clinical intervention when the alternative is defaulting from treatment. The nurse should ask about food at every visit, because a full blister pack does nothing for a patient with nothing in the pot.

HIV care and nutrition are inseparable, and the nurse is usually the person who holds them together. Food insecurity drives risky behavior, reduces adherence to antiretroviral therapy, and worsens outcomes at every stage, while treatment itself restores appetite and can lead to weight gain that is initially welcome and later becomes obesity. The metabolic complications of long-term treatment, including fat redistribution and disordered blood sugar and lipids, need dietary counseling rather than a change in the regimen. Infants born to mothers with HIV require a clear feeding plan built around the mother's treatment and viral suppression, and staff must give consistent advice rather than mixing messages about breastfeeding. Every clinic that provides treatment should also screen for food insecurity, because a patient who cannot eat cannot take medicine reliably.

Deworming is the simplest nutritional intervention in tropical practice and one of the most cost-effective. Hookworm causes iron deficiency anemia, Ascaris and Trichuris compete for nutrients and worsen growth, and schistosomiasis causes anemia and chronic inflammation. Periodic treatment of school-age children and at-risk adults reduces worm burden, improves hemoglobin, and modestly improves growth and school performance, and it is usually delivered through schools, child health days, and community programs. Because reinfection follows, treatment is repeated at intervals set by national programs, and the nurse's role is often to explain why the same child is treated again and again. Sanitation, safe water, footwear, and hand washing prevent reinfection, and without them the medicine is a temporary fix that must be repeated forever.

Growth monitoring is the nurse's signature contribution to nutrition, and it only works when the technique is trustworthy. Every child should be weighed at every opportunity, the weight plotted on a chart that shows the trend, and any flattening of the curve treated as a signal to act before the child becomes wasted. The same tape, the same scale, and the same technique must be used each time, and staff should be standardized against each other so that two nurses reading one child agree. Growth faltering in the first two years of life is the point at which stunting becomes irreversible, so the early months carry the greatest weight in the whole program. The nurse also counsels, supporting early and exclusive breastfeeding, timely and diverse complementary feeding, continued feeding during illness, and careful hand hygiene before food preparation.

Counseling must be concrete and affordable, because advice that costs more than the family earns will not be followed. The nurse should learn what food is actually available in the local market and season, and build advice around it rather than around imported products. A discussion about dietary diversity can be as simple as adding a green leaf, an egg, or a spoonful of oil to the usual staple, and a message about frequency can be as simple as feeding a young child five times a day. Kitchen gardens, small animal rearing, and food preservation are legitimate partners of clinical care, and clinics that link to them see nutrition improve. Where food insecurity is the real diagnosis, the honest response is to connect the family to food assistance and cash support and to document that the problem is poverty, not ignorance.

Monitoring and logistics decide whether any of this reaches the patient. Supplies such as therapeutic milk, ready-to-use therapeutic food, vitamin A, zinc, iron and folic acid tablets, and deworming medicine must be forecast, stored, and protected from heat and moisture, and a stockout in the middle of a treatment course is a clinical failure rather than an administrative one. Registers should record admission, weight, mid-upper arm circumference, edema, treatment given, and outcome, and monthly reports should track cure, default, death, and relapse. The nurse should expect supervision and quality checks on measurement, because a program with a perfect cure rate and impossible measurements is a program with a broken scale. Referral links to hospital care must be tested before they are needed, with a plan for transport that a poor family can actually use.

Safety surrounds every one of these interventions, and the nurse should know the adverse effects as well as the benefits. Vitamin A in repeated high doses can cause headache, vomiting, and liver injury, and high doses in early pregnancy can harm the fetus. Zinc commonly causes nausea and may cause vomiting if given without food. Iron given during acute infection or untreated malaria has been associated with harm, and iron overload occurs in people who receive repeated transfusions or unnecessary supplements. Iodine excess can cause thyroid dysfunction, and selenium deficiency can worsen the effects of iodine in some settings. Refeeding syndrome is the most dangerous of all, and the diuretic treatment of nutritional edema is perhaps the most avoidable error in this chapter.

Regimens in nutrition change as often as regimens in infection, and guidance differs between countries. The World Health Organization sets global norms for the management of severe acute malnutrition, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention publishes guidance for micronutrient programs and for nutrition in refugee settings, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control addresses nutrition in displaced populations arriving in Europe. The doses and schedules quoted in this chapter are drawn from that guidance as it stood when this course was written, and they are quoted so that the listener understands the scale and the logic, not so that they can be copied from memory. Before prescribing or dispensing any product, the nurse must check the current national guideline, the product label, and the supply actually in the clinic, and must confirm the dose with a second qualified colleague when the patient is a child or a pregnant woman. When the local guideline and this recording disagree, the local guideline and the current product label win.

Nutrition work is also where the ethics of tropical medicine are most visible, because the nurse often has food and the patient does not. Screening for food insecurity should be as routine as checking a temperature, and the result should change the plan rather than merely being recorded. Stigma attaches to both thinness and obesity, and a judgmental tone closes the conversation before it begins. Food assistance programs raise difficult questions about targeting, dependency, and sustainability, and no nurse resolves them alone, but silence about hunger is never neutral. The most useful thing a nurse can do is measure honestly, feed safely, teach clearly, and make sure the family is connected to whatever the system actually provides.

To summarize, nutrition and tropical medicine are one subject, joined by the loop in which infection causes malnutrition and malnutrition worsens infection. Severe acute malnutrition appears as marasmus with wasting or kwashiorkor with edema, it is diagnosed with weight-for-height, mid-upper arm circumference, and the presence of edema, and it is treated in phases that stabilize the child before feeding is advanced, because feeding too fast can kill. Specific deficiencies still matter, and vitamin A, iron, iodine, zinc, thiamine, niacin, and vitamin C each produce a recognizable illness with a recognizable treatment that must be checked against current guidance. The same communities now carry obesity and diabetes alongside undernutrition, so screening must look in both directions. The nurse's contribution is measurement that can be trusted, feeding that is safe, counseling that is affordable, and follow-up that does not lose the patient.

# Chapter 29 — Immunocompromised and Chronically Ill Patients

Immunosuppression changes the rules of infection, and it changes them everywhere in tropical medicine. It changes which organisms are likely, how quickly they move, how loudly they announce themselves, and how much of the ordinary clinical picture you can trust. A patient whose immune defenses are intact usually turns an exposure into either no illness or an illness with recognizable features. A patient whose defenses are damaged can turn the same exposure into disseminated disease with a modest fever and a chest that sounds clear. The advanced practice nurse therefore works from a different set of expectations in this population, and the most dangerous habit is to be reassured by the absence of signs. This chapter describes what immunodeficiency does to the encounter with tropical infection, the specific infections that follow advanced HIV, the chronic illnesses that behave in similar ways, and the practical nursing work of screening, vaccinating, monitoring, and recognizing deterioration early enough to act.

The immune system fails in patterns, and each pattern points to a predictable family of organisms. When the helper T lymphocyte population falls, the body loses its coordinator for organisms that live inside cells, which opens the door to fungi, protozoa, and mycobacteria. When the neutrophil count falls, the body loses its first responder against bacteria and molds, which opens the door to bloodstream infection and invasive fungal disease. When the spleen is absent or no longer functions, the body loses its filter for organisms carrying a polysaccharide capsule, and those organisms can multiply in the blood with startling speed. When the skin and the gut lining are breached by catheters, surgery, or the inflammation of chemotherapy, the barrier that kept the internal environment sterile is gone. Learning this map is not an academic exercise, because it tells you what to look for before any test result returns, and it tells you which prevention belongs in the plan.

The most useful thing to understand is why severe disease can look mild. Inflammation is not the injury itself, it is the response to the injury, and that response requires a working immune system. A person who cannot mount a vigorous inflammatory response may have a normal temperature, a normal white cell count, and unremarkable examination findings while bacteria or fungi are multiplying in the bloodstream. A patient with advanced HIV and cryptococcal infection may complain only of a headache that has been building for two weeks. A patient whose neutrophil count has collapsed after chemotherapy may have nothing more than a feeling of unease and a slight rise in heart rate. The nurse who waits for a high fever, a productive cough, or a purulent wound before escalating care will wait past the point at which treatment changes the outcome.

Because the usual warning signs are unreliable, the reliable ones are trends and function. You watch how the patient looks compared with yesterday, whether they are eating, whether they are walking as far, whether the family says something has changed, and whether the simple measures of circulation and breathing are drifting. A rising respiratory rate, a falling blood pressure, a new confusion, a decreasing urine output, and a temperature that is unexpectedly low all deserve the same attention that a high fever would receive in a healthy adult. Charting those observations at fixed intervals, and acting on a change rather than waiting for the next scheduled round, is the single most valuable nursing contribution in this population. When the numbers are ambiguous, trust the trajectory and trust the person who knows the patient best.

Prevention before suppression is the organizing principle of care for anyone who is about to lose immune function. Chemotherapy, transplantation, high-dose corticosteroids, and the biologic agents that block tumor necrosis factor all create a window of vulnerability, and that window is easiest to influence before it opens. Screening for latent infection, updating vaccination, and treating whatever is found are tasks that must be finished before the suppressive treatment starts, not after. A program that treats this sequence as optional will discover reactivated tuberculosis, disseminated strongyloidiasis, or a hepatitis B flare at the worst possible moment. The nurse who owns this checklist owns the difference between a planned course of treatment and an unplanned catastrophe.

The threadworm Strongyloides stercoralis is the organism that makes this principle concrete, because it is the classic infection that lies quiet for decades and then explodes when immunity falls. The larvae persist in the gut and can complete their life cycle within the host, so infection can continue silently for a lifetime, and it is common across tropical and subtropical regions. When corticosteroids or other suppressive treatment remove immune control, the parasite can accelerate its cycle, producing hyperinfection with massive larval migration through the lungs and the gut, and dissemination to the brain, the liver, and other organs, with Gram-negative bloodstream infection carried on the migrating larvae. The mortality of the disseminated form is high even with treatment, which is why screening is mandatory rather than optional in anyone from an endemic area who is about to be immunosuppressed.

Screening for Strongyloides stercoralis combines a blood test for antibodies with repeated stool examination, and neither test is perfect. Antibody testing is sensitive but can be positive from past exposure and can be falsely negative in people whose immune response is already blunted, while stool microscopy is specific but misses infection when the larval output is low. Where the organism is suspected and the patient is about to be immunosuppressed, many programs treat presumptively rather than wait for a perfect result, because the treatment is safer than the disease. The usual regimen is ivermectin at 200 micrograms per kilogram by mouth once daily for 2 days, with albendazole at 400 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 7 days as an alternative where ivermectin is unavailable, and a follow-up test several weeks later confirms the response. In hyperinfection the treatment is prolonged and repeated, and expert advice should be sought. Because these regimens are revised as evidence accumulates and national guidance differs between countries, the current guideline must be checked before prescribing.

Hepatitis B belongs in the same pre-suppression conversation, because the virus can flare violently when immune control is withdrawn. Anyone facing chemotherapy, transplantation, or a biologic agent should be tested before treatment begins, and those who carry the virus should receive antiviral suppression that continues through the period of risk and for a defined interval afterward. Tuberculosis screening is the other routine step, using symptoms, a chest radiograph, and an interferon gamma release assay or a tuberculin skin test, with preventive treatment given before suppression where infection is documented and active disease has been excluded. Vaccination should also be updated before the window closes, because the response to a vaccine is far better while the immune system is still intact. The practical order is screen, treat, and vaccinate, and only then proceed with the treatment that suppresses.

Advanced HIV remains the most common and most instructive form of acquired immunodeficiency in tropical practice, and the specific infections that appear as the helper T lymphocyte count falls are the core curriculum of this chapter. The count is not a number to file away, it is a map of risk. As the count falls below about 200 cells per microliter, Pneumocystis pneumonia and toxoplasmosis become the concerns. Below about 100 cells per microliter, cryptococcal meningitis and disseminated histoplasmosis move to the front. Below about 50 cells per microliter, the risk of these infections and of chronic cryptosporidiosis is highest. Antiretroviral therapy changes all of this, because restoring immunity prevents most of these infections, and the nurse who pushes for early treatment and sustained adherence is doing opportunistic infection prevention with every visit.

Cryptococcal meningitis is the infection that kills more people with advanced HIV than any other in many tropical settings, and it is deceptive in its ordinariness. The fungus Cryptococcus neoformans is inhaled from the environment, often from soil contaminated by bird droppings, and in a person with advanced immunodeficiency it spreads from the lung to the membranes around the brain. The usual presentation is a headache that has developed over 1 to 2 weeks, sometimes with fever, neck stiffness, confusion, nausea, or visual disturbance, and sometimes with almost nothing else. Diagnosis rests on a lumbar puncture with measurement of the opening pressure and on testing the cerebrospinal fluid with a cryptococcal antigen test, which is rapid and highly sensitive, supported by culture and staining where available. Because the pressure inside the head can rise dangerously, and because that pressure causes much of the blindness and death, repeated lumbar punctures to drain fluid are a treatment in their own right and not merely a diagnostic step.

Treatment of cryptococcal meningitis follows an induction phase, a consolidation phase, and a maintenance phase, and the World Health Organization has revised the preferred regimen in recent years. The current recommendation favors a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B at 10 milligrams per kilogram intravenously together with flucytosine at 25 milligrams per kilogram by mouth four times a day for one week, followed by fluconazole at 400 to 800 milligrams by mouth daily, although older guidance used liposomal amphotericin B at 3 to 4 milligrams per kilogram intravenously daily for two weeks and many programs still follow it. Where flucytosine is unavailable, amphotericin B is combined with fluconazole. After induction, fluconazole continues at 400 milligrams daily for consolidation and then at 200 milligrams daily as long-term maintenance until immunity recovers. Liposomal amphotericin B damages the kidneys and lowers potassium and magnesium, and flucytosine suppresses the bone marrow, so kidney function, electrolytes, and blood counts must be monitored closely. Antiretroviral therapy is usually delayed by several weeks in this infection, because starting it too early increases death, and the exact interval is set by the current guideline.

Pneumocystis pneumonia is the other classic AIDS-defining infection, caused by the fungus Pneumocystis jirovecii, and it presents with a dry cough, breathlessness on exertion, and a slow decline over days to weeks. The chest radiograph may look normal early, and the oxygen level can fall sharply with exercise before it falls at rest, which is why a walking oxygen measurement is more informative than a resting one. Diagnosis is often clinical in a patient with advanced immunodeficiency and a compatible picture, and where a laboratory is available the organism can be found by PCR or by special staining of induced sputum or of fluid obtained by washing the lung. Treatment is trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole at 15 to 20 milligrams per kilogram per day of the trimethoprim component, divided and given by mouth or intravenously every six to eight hours for three weeks, and moderate to severe disease also receives a corticosteroid such as prednisone at 40 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 5 days and then tapered, because the inflammatory response to dying organisms can worsen breathing. Adverse effects include rash, fever, low white cell counts, high potassium, and kidney injury, and alternative drugs are used when the reaction is severe. Prophylaxis with the same combination at a lower dose prevents the disease and is continued until immune recovery is secure.

Toxoplasmosis, caused by the protozoan parasite Toxoplasma gondii, is usually a reactivation of a latent infection acquired years earlier from undercooked meat, from soil, or from cat feces. In advanced HIV it presents as encephalitis with headache, fever, confusion, seizures, or weakness on one side of the body, and imaging shows multiple rounded lesions with swelling around them in the deep parts of the brain. Treatment is pyrimethamine given as a loading dose of 200 milligrams by mouth and then 50 to 75 milligrams daily, combined with sulfadiazine at 1000 to 1500 milligrams by mouth every six hours, and leucovorin at 10 to 25 milligrams by mouth daily is added to protect the bone marrow. Where sulfadiazine cannot be used, trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole is a common alternative. The response is judged clinically and by repeated imaging after 2 to 3 weeks, and treatment is then continued at a lower maintenance dose until immunity recovers. Prophylaxis is indicated for patients with advanced immunodeficiency who carry antibodies to the parasite.

Tuberculosis is the leading cause of death among people living with HIV, and it behaves differently as immunity falls, as the preceding chapter describes in detail. In this chapter the emphasis falls on the nursing tasks around it. Every person with advanced HIV should be screened for tuberculosis symptoms at every visit, and the absence of a cough does not exclude disease. Preventive treatment for latent infection is offered where active disease has been excluded, and the choice of regimen depends on the national guideline and on interactions with antiretroviral therapy. The immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome, the paradoxical worsening that can follow the restoration of immunity, must be anticipated, because it can look like treatment failure when it is in fact a sign that the immune system has returned. Monitoring must include weight, symptoms, and adherence, and the nurse should confirm which medicines the patient is actually taking, because rifampicin and the antiretroviral drugs interact strongly.

Disseminated histoplasmosis is the fungal infection most often mistaken for tuberculosis in tropical practice, and it is caused by Histoplasma capsulatum, acquired by inhaling spores from soil enriched by bird or bat droppings. In advanced HIV it produces prolonged fever, weight loss, an enlarged liver and spleen, low blood counts, and sometimes skin or mouth lesions, while the chest radiograph may be unremarkable. Diagnosis is by antigen testing of blood or urine where available, by culture, or by examination of a bone marrow or tissue sample, and it is frequently missed because it is not considered. Treatment begins with liposomal amphotericin B intravenously for severe disease, followed by itraconazole at 200 milligrams by mouth three times a day for 3 days and then 200 milligrams twice a day for at least a year in the setting of advanced immunodeficiency. Itraconazole absorption depends on stomach acid, so it is taken with food, and its blood level should be measured where possible, because low levels lead to relapse and high levels to toxicity. It also interacts with many other medicines, so the whole medication list must be reviewed before it is started.

Chronic cryptosporidiosis is a protozoal infection of the gut that causes watery diarrhea, cramps, and malabsorption, and in a person with advanced HIV it can persist for weeks or months and waste the patient. It is acquired from contaminated water and food, and it occurs wherever sanitation is fragile. There is no reliably effective antimicrobial cure, though nitazoxanide at 500 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 3 days is often given and may shorten the illness in patients with better preserved immunity, and paromomycin is sometimes used. The decisive treatment is the restoration of immunity with antiretroviral therapy, because the diarrhea often resolves when the helper T lymphocyte count recovers. In the meantime the nursing work is fluid and electrolyte replacement, nutritional support, skin care to protect against excoriation, and the practical hygiene teaching that prevents reinfection within a household.
