Handwashing with soap, safe drinking water, and careful food handling are the measures that matter most.

The transplant recipient who travels is a distinct patient with a distinct set of questions, and the pre-travel consultation is where most of the risk is managed. Immunosuppressive drugs such as tacrolimus and mycophenolate weaken the response to infection and also to vaccination, so the timing of every vaccine must be planned around the regimen. Live vaccines are generally avoided after transplantation, while inactivated vaccines are safe but may produce a weaker response, and household members should be fully vaccinated to reduce the risk they bring home. Food and water precautions matter more than they do for other travelers, because organisms such as Salmonella, Cryptosporidium, and Listeria cause far more severe disease in this group. Malaria prevention must be chosen with attention to drug interactions, since some antimalarial drugs alter the levels of the immunosuppressive medicines and can threaten the graft, and the choice must be made with the transplant team rather than from a standard travel list. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control both publish guidance for the immunocompromised traveler, and that guidance is revised regularly, so the current version must be consulted before advice is given.

Screening before transplantation reaches beyond the recipient to the donor and to the geography of the infection. Donors and recipients are tested for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, syphilis, and other transmissible infections, and in tropical settings the assessment also considers Chagas disease, strongyloidiasis, and tuberculosis, because these can be transmitted with the organ or reactivated by the drugs that follow. A recipient who has lived in a region where Chagas disease is endemic should be tested for antibodies to Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite that causes it, because immunosuppression can reactivate a silent infection into fever, heart involvement, and skin lesions. Strongyloidiasis must be excluded in anyone with past residence in an endemic area, as described earlier, and tuberculosis must be screened for in every candidate. The nurse's part in this work is to take a careful geographic and exposure history, to ensure the tests are actually done and the results acted upon, and to record the plan so that it survives the transfer between teams.

Chemotherapy and corticosteroids suppress immunity in ways that are predictable and therefore partly preventable. A course of prednisone at 20 milligrams or more daily for more than two weeks, or repeated pulses of high-dose corticosteroid, is enough to raise the risk of opportunistic infection, and the risk rises further with age, malnutrition, and diabetes. Chemotherapy that lowers the neutrophil count opens a short but dangerous window in which fever is an emergency, and bacterial infection can progress to shock within hours. Prophylaxis against Pneumocystis pneumonia is standard for many regimens, and antifungal and antiviral prophylaxis is added according to the protocol and the patient's serology. Fever during neutropenia requires blood cultures and broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour, without waiting for the results, because delay costs lives. The nurse who monitors the white cell count, teaches the patient to take a temperature at home, and makes sure the emergency plan is written down does more than any single drug.

The biologic agents that block tumor necrosis factor deserve their own warning, because they are among the strongest reactivators of tuberculosis known. These medicines are used for inflammatory bowel disease, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and other conditions that are increasingly common in tropical countries, and they can convert a lifetime of quiet infection into active disease within weeks. Screening for tuberculosis must therefore be completed before the first dose, and preventive treatment must be started and often finished before the biologic agent is given where the infection is documented. The same caution applies to hepatitis B, to histoplasmosis in endemic areas, and to strongyloidiasis, and vaccination should be completed before the regimen begins where possible. The nurse should treat the biologic prescription as a trigger for the entire pre-suppression checklist, not as an isolated decision made by another specialist. Communication between the prescribing team and the primary care team is the mechanism that prevents the gap.

Diabetes is the chronic illness that most changes the course of tropical infection, and its effect is both immunological and mechanical. High blood glucose impairs the function of neutrophils and the migration of immune cells, reduces blood flow through small vessels, and provides a ready fuel supply for organisms, and nerve damage hides the early warning signs in the feet. Tuberculosis is several times more common in people with diabetes, and it is more likely to be severe, to relapse, and to be accompanied by drug resistance. Melioidosis, the infection caused by the bacterium Burkholderia pseudomallei, is strongly associated with diabetes and with exposure to soil and water in Southeast Asia and northern Australia, and it can present as pneumonia, bloodstream infection, or abscesses in many organs, especially during the rainy season. Necrotizing skin and soft tissue infection is another danger, often polymicrobial, spreading faster than the skin changes suggest, and it requires surgical debridement as an emergency. The nurse's contribution is glucose control, careful foot examination at every visit, education about footwear and skin care, and a low threshold for urgent referral when an ulcer looks worse than it should.

Melioidosis is worth describing in detail because its treatment is long and its relapse rate is high when it is cut short. The presentation can imitate tuberculosis, typhoid, or severe pneumonia, and the organism is resistant to many common antibiotics, so the diagnosis depends on the laboratory growing it from blood, sputum, urine, or pus, and on the clinician having considered it. The intensive phase usually uses ceftazidime at 50 milligrams per kilogram intravenously every six hours, or meropenem at 25 milligrams per kilogram intravenously every eight hours for severe disease, for at least 2 weeks and until the patient has clearly improved. The eradication phase then uses trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole by mouth for 3 to 6 months, because the organism can hide inside cells and return if treatment is stopped too early. The World Health Organization and national programs in endemic countries publish the current regimens for melioidosis, and because these differ between settings and are revised as resistance patterns change, the current guideline must be checked before prescribing. The nurse should prepare the patient for months of treatment, monitor kidney function and blood counts, and explain that feeling well is not the same as being cured.

Chronic kidney disease changes drug handling long before it is severe, and it also changes the risk of infection itself. As kidney function falls, the clearance of many drugs falls with it, so a dose that is safe for one patient becomes toxic for another, and the correct dose depends on the measured kidney function rather than on habit or on weight alone. Some medicines should be avoided altogether, including nitrofurantoin, high-dose trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, aminoglycosides, and amphotericin B where an alternative exists, and others such as metformin, tenofovir, and many antibiotics require dose reduction or a longer interval between doses. Dialysis adds another layer, because the timing of a dose relative to the dialysis session changes the blood level that the patient actually experiences, and the medication chart must record that timing explicitly. Kidney disease also blunts the response to vaccination and increases the severity of many infections, so prevention carries extra weight. The practical rule is to check every prescription against the current formulary and the measured kidney function, and to involve a pharmacist wherever one is available.

Sickle cell disease creates a specific and lifelong vulnerability to infection that is easy to forget between crises. The spleen in sickle cell disease is damaged by repeated sickling and often stops working early in childhood, so the patient loses the filtering function that removes encapsulated bacteria from the blood, and severe infection becomes a leading cause of death. The organisms that matter most are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and Salmonella, and infection with Salmonella is a recognized cause of the bone infection that these patients develop. Infection with parvovirus B19 can produce a sudden aplastic crisis with a rapid fall in hemoglobin that requires transfusion, and malaria is more severe and more likely to cause death, although the sickle cell trait offers partial protection while the disease itself does not. Acute chest syndrome, a dangerous combination of infection, infarction, and breathing failure, must be considered whenever a patient with sickle cell disease has fever, chest pain, or breathlessness. For the nurse, fever in a patient with sickle cell disease is an emergency that requires immediate assessment and antibiotics rather than an appointment later in the week.

Asplenia, whether from surgery, trauma, or a congenital absence, concentrates the risk in a small and predictable group of organisms. The spleen filters the blood, removes organisms that carry a polysaccharide capsule, and produces antibodies against them, so a person without a functioning spleen is vulnerable to overwhelming infection with Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Haemophilus influenzae type b, which can become fatal within a day. Prevention begins with vaccination against those organisms, ideally at least 2 weeks before a planned splenectomy and with boosters afterward, and with daily prophylactic penicillin at 250 milligrams by mouth twice a day in children and in some adults, according to the current guideline. Patients should carry a card or a medical alert record stating that they have no spleen, so that any clinician meeting them in an emergency understands the risk immediately. Fever in an asplenic patient is never routine, and it requires urgent assessment and empirical antibiotics, because the illness can be overwhelming before a diagnosis is made. Travel advice should also include the higher risk of severe malaria, the danger of animal bites, which can transmit a bacterium that causes fulminant sepsis in this group, and the need to seek care early wherever they are.

Vaccination before suppression is a time-limited opportunity, and it has its own logic. The best response to a vaccine comes when the immune system is intact, so the target is to complete the routine and travel schedule at least 2 weeks before chemotherapy, transplant, or biologic treatment begins, whenever the clinical situation allows. Live vaccines, including yellow fever, measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, and oral typhoid, are generally avoided once immunosuppression is established, because a weakened vaccine organism can cause disease in a patient who cannot control it, and they are also avoided in people with advanced HIV. Inactivated and subunit vaccines are safe, but the response may be poor, so the schedule may need additional doses, higher doses in some cases, or revaccination after immune recovery. Household members should be fully vaccinated, both to protect themselves and to reduce the risk of bringing an infection home, and this is especially important for influenza. BCG vaccination is given at birth in many countries but is avoided in children with symptomatic HIV, because of the risk of disseminated infection, and the decision belongs to the national program. The nurse should hold the vaccination plan alongside the treatment plan, because a vaccine given too late is a missed opportunity that cannot be recovered.

Monitoring in this population has to be deliberate, because the usual symptoms will not call for help. A practical plan names what is measured, how often, and what result triggers action, and it is written where the whole team can see it. Blood counts, kidney function, liver enzymes, blood glucose, and the relevant drug levels are checked at the intervals the national guideline specifies, and therapeutic drug monitoring is used for medicines such as itraconazole and some antiretroviral and antituberculous drugs where it is available. Weight, appetite, and functional status are recorded at every visit, because a decline in any of them is often the first sign of an infection that the patient cannot describe. Adherence is assessed by asking how the medicines are actually being taken rather than by asking whether they are being taken, and a missed dose should lead to a search for the reason. The nurse should also watch for the adverse effects of the treatment itself, because kidney injury, bone marrow suppression, rash, and drug interactions are common and are frequently mistaken for the underlying disease.

Logistics decide whether any of this reaches the patient, and the nurse is usually the person who makes the supply chain work at the point of care. Many of these drugs are expensive, some require refrigeration, and some are subject to stockouts, so the patient's plan must be built with a realistic view of what is available this month and next. Liposomal amphotericin B must be stored and transported correctly, flucytosine and itraconazole may be scarce, and a course that is interrupted by an empty shelf can lead to relapse and resistance. Transport is another constraint, because a patient who must travel a day to reach the clinic cannot return for weekly monitoring, so follow-up must be arranged closer to home, with a community health worker, a local clinic, and a written plan that travels with the patient. Referral letters should state the diagnosis, the current medicines and doses, the monitoring results, and the specific question being asked, because a referral without that information usually produces a delay. Documentation is also a clinical instrument in this population, since the patient may be seen by several teams, and a clear record is what prevents the same test being repeated and the same interaction being missed.

The nursing role in all of this can be stated in three parts, and each part is ordinary work rather than heroism. The first is screening before suppression, which means taking the geographic and exposure history seriously, ordering the tests that the checklist requires, and following up until the results are acted upon. The second is vaccinating before suppression, which means protecting the window of intact immunity and coordinating the schedule with the treatment rather than after it. The third is recognizing that a patient with damaged immunity may have severe disease with few signs, which means trusting trends, function, and family observation over the reassuring absence of fever. Around those three parts sits the work of explanation, adherence support, monitoring, and coordination that determines whether the plan is actually followed. None of it requires a laboratory that a tropical clinic does not have, and most of it requires only attention and consistency.

Caring for the chronically ill and the immunosuppressed also means caring for the person who carries the burden. A patient on lifelong suppressive treatment, repeated clinic visits, and a long list of medicines can lose hope, and hopelessness shows up as missed appointments and stopped treatment. Stigma adds to this, whether it concerns HIV, a transplant, or a diagnosis that the neighbors can recognize, and the nurse shapes whether the clinic feels safe by the words used at the desk and the privacy of the consultation. Depression and anxiety are common in this population and they reduce adherence, so they should be asked about and treated rather than noted and left. Practical support, such as a treatment supporter chosen by the patient, a pill organiser, and a plan for what to do when a dose is missed, is often more effective than encouragement alone. A patient who understands why each medicine matters and what happens if it stops is far more likely to persist, and that understanding is built in conversation, not in a leaflet.

To summarize, immunosuppression changes which infections occur, how severe they become, and how little they may show on examination, so the nurse must work from an expectation of severe disease with few signs. The pattern of immune failure predicts the organisms, with helper T lymphocyte loss opening the door to fungi, protozoa, and mycobacteria, neutrophil loss to bacteria and molds, and loss of splenic function to encapsulated bacteria. The pre-suppression checklist of screening, treating, and vaccinating must be completed before chemotherapy, transplantation, corticosteroids, or biologic agents begin, and Strongyloides stercoralis is the organism that makes that rule unforgettable. Advanced HIV brings cryptococcal meningitis, Pneumocystis pneumonia, toxoplasmosis, histoplasmosis, tuberculosis, and chronic cryptosporidiosis, each with its own treatment, monitoring, and adverse effects. Diabetes, chronic kidney disease, sickle cell disease, and asplenia each add their own vulnerability and their own nursing work, and the transplant recipient who travels needs a plan built around drug interactions and vaccine timing. Because regimens are revised and guidance differs between countries, every dose in this chapter must be verified against the current national guideline and the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control before it is prescribed. The nurse who screens before suppression, vaccinates before suppression, and watches the trend rather than the fever is the person who keeps this patient alive.

# Chapter 30 — Migrant and Refugee Health

Migrant and refugee health is not a specialty at the edge of tropical medicine. It sits at its center, because the movement of people is one of the most powerful forces that distributes infection across the world. The nurse who works in a refugee camp, a border clinic, an urban community health center, or a hospital emergency department meets the same diseases in the same bodies, and only the point on the journey differs. The person in front of you may have walked for weeks, spent years in a settlement, crossed a sea, or arrived by air with a visa and a folder of records. Place that person on a timeline, because the timeline tells you what is possible, what is urgent, and what can wait.

One discipline governs this whole chapter, and it is stated plainly because it is easily lost. Never treat a migrant as a diagnosis rather than a person. The labels migrant, refugee, asylum seeker, and undocumented patient carry legal and social meaning, but none of them describes a body, and each can quietly replace clinical reasoning with assumption. A cough is not automatically tuberculosis, and a headache is not automatically trauma, just as a healthy looking young arrival is not automatically free of chronic infection. Ask, examine, and test when testing changes management, and let the person tell you who they are before the chart does.

Think of migration as four stages, because each produces its own pattern of disease. There is the origin phase, the time before departure in the home country or region. There is the transit phase, the weeks, months, or years spent moving and waiting in camps, border towns, detention centers, or rented rooms. There is the destination phase, the first months and years after arrival, when acute problems surface and chronic ones remain silent. Then there is the ongoing phase, which includes resettlement, family reunion, return visits to the country of origin, and onward movement to another country. Many patients pass through all four, and their health record passes through none of them, because records rarely travel as far as people do.

In the origin phase the exposures are the ordinary exposures of the place. Malaria transmission may be intense and repeated, so the patient arrives with partial acquired immunity that fades once transmission stops. Tuberculosis infection may have been acquired in childhood and now sit latent, waiting for a trigger. Soil-transmitted helminths, schistosomiasis, and other parasitic infections are common where water, sanitation, and hygiene are limited. Hepatitis B is highly prevalent in much of Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, and the western Pacific, and it is usually acquired at birth or in early childhood. HIV, leishmaniasis, Chagas disease, and human African trypanosomiasis each have their own geographic map. The origin history is a geographic exposure history and deserves the care given to any travel history.

The transit phase is where crowding writes the clinical story. Camps and informal settlements group large numbers of people into small areas with shared water points and latrines, and that arrangement transmits whatever is already present. Measles spreads rapidly among unvaccinated children, while cholera, typhoid, and shigellosis travel through contaminated water. Tuberculosis transmission is favored by crowding, poor ventilation, and long contact, so a transit camp can turn a few infectious cases into many new infections. Scabies, lice, and other infestations flourish where washing is difficult, and diphtheria and meningococcal disease can appear in crowded shelters. Density, shelter design, water quantity, and the number of people sharing a latrine are therefore clinical variables rather than a backdrop. Protracted displacement, in which a family lives in a camp for a decade or more, converts acute risks into chronic ones, including malnutrition, anemia, delayed development, and untreated mental illness.

The destination phase is where the tropical medicine curriculum is most often tested. Acute illness in the first weeks may be malaria, dengue, typhoid, or another infection acquired in transit and now incubating. Chronic infection reveals itself more slowly. Latent tuberculosis infection can reactivate months or years after arrival, sometimes when the immune system is stressed by pregnancy, diabetes, HIV, or the hardship of resettlement. Schistosomiasis and strongyloidiasis may have been carried silently for decades, chronic hepatitis B may be found only when the liver is already scarred, and Chagas disease may appear first as a cardiac arrhythmia in middle age. A normal examination at arrival does not close the file.

The healthy migrant effect is the observation that people who migrate are on average healthier than the populations they leave and often healthier than the population they join, at least in the first years. Migration selects for people with the resources, stamina, and determination to move, while the frail and the very ill are less likely to attempt or survive the journey. Early statistics therefore make new arrivals look better than they are, and a clinic that sees only those who come through its door sees a selected sample. The effect fades as that selection is worn down by poor housing, low income, discrimination, and limited access to care. There is a further trap, because some of the sickest people return home, so their deaths are recorded elsewhere and the remaining population looks healthier still. Use population data to set your prior probability, then let the person in the room change it.

Vaccination gaps are almost universal in people who have been displaced, and closing them is among the most valuable things a nurse can do. Routine immunization is one of the first services to break down in conflict, so a child born in a camp may have received nothing, or may have received doses that were never recorded. Records that exist may be written in a script you cannot read or in a numbering system that does not match your national schedule. Do not restart every series blindly; treat the person as susceptible to whatever is not documented and provide catch-up vaccination according to the national schedule. Several vaccines may be given at one visit at separate sites, and inactivated vaccines impose no interval between them, while live vaccines are generally given together or separated by 4 weeks. Where measles is circulating, protect against measles and rubella first.

Some vaccines require a specific judgment. BCG is given at birth in many countries and leaves a scar, but the scar is an unreliable guide to prior protection and revaccination is not generally recommended. Hepatitis B vaccine should be given to anyone who is neither immune nor infected, because the series is safe and effective. Tetanus and diphtheria toxoid should be brought up to date in everyone, and a tetanus-containing vaccine in pregnancy protects both the woman and the newborn. Polio and measles deserve particular attention because they spread widely in under-vaccinated communities, and human papillomavirus vaccine should be offered to eligible adolescents and young adults according to national guidance. Every vaccination encounter is also an opportunity to bring a patient into care, so make it a visit about more than a needle.

Screening programs for migrants are common, well intentioned, and limited, and every nurse should be able to state the limits. Screening applies a test to people without symptoms in order to find disease early enough to change its course. Its value depends on how common the condition is in the group tested, on the accuracy of the test, and on the existence of an effective and acceptable treatment. When the condition is uncommon, even a good test produces many false positive results, and each false positive creates anxiety, further tests, and sometimes harm. Screening must be linked to treatment, because identifying an infection that no one will treat is an ethical failure rather than a public health success. A program that tests a thousand people and follows up fifty has produced paperwork, not health.

The most useful distinction in this field is the difference between testing for infection and testing for disease. Testing for infection asks whether the organism has ever met the person's immune system, and a positive result says only that the meeting happened. Testing for disease asks whether the organism is present now and causing harm. A positive tuberculin skin test or interferon gamma release assay indicates infection with the tuberculosis bacterium, not tuberculosis disease, and most people with that result are neither ill nor infectious. A positive hepatitis B surface antigen test is different again, because it indicates current infection, which may be chronic and may damage the liver even when the person feels well. A positive HIV antibody test indicates infection and requires confirmation and treatment, not a diagnosis of AIDS. Confusing these categories produces two errors: telling a well person that they are ill, and telling a person with treatable disease that they are only a carrier.

Tuberculosis screening in migrant populations shows the distinction at work. A symptom screen asks about cough, fever, night sweats, weight loss, and blood in the sputum, and it is inexpensive and reasonably sensitive when done properly. A chest radiograph adds information but is not diagnostic, and sputum smear, culture, and PCR are what confirm disease. Active tuberculosis must be excluded before latent infection is treated, because giving a single drug while active disease is present can select for resistance. Latent infection may then be treated according to current guidance, and these regimens are revised periodically, differ between countries, and must be checked against the current national guideline before prescribing. What the World Health Organization currently describes includes 6 to 9 months of isoniazid, 4 months of rifampicin, or 12 weeks of weekly isoniazid with rifapentine, with the choice depending on age, pregnancy, drug interactions, and resistance patterns. Isoniazid is commonly given at 300 milligrams by mouth once a day with pyridoxine 25 to 50 milligrams a day to prevent peripheral neuropathy, and these figures illustrate the regimens rather than prescribe them. Doses are verified against the current guideline and against the patient's weight, kidney function, and other medicines before they are given.

Children in migrant families deserve particular attention in tuberculosis screening. A child who is a household contact of an infectious case is at high risk of progression, and young children progress quickly to severe forms including miliary tuberculosis and tuberculosis of the meninges. Active disease should be excluded and preventive treatment offered when disease is absent, according to national guidance. A child may be infected and still have a normal chest radiograph, and a negative tuberculin test does not exclude infection in a child who is malnourished, very young, or living with HIV. Weigh the child, dose by weight, and record the weight you used.

Hepatitis B and hepatitis C are chronic viral infections that migration carries across borders and that produce disease decades later. Hepatitis B passes from mother to child at birth and also through sexual contact and blood, and the birth dose of vaccine is the single most effective way to prevent lifelong infection. Screening usually begins with hepatitis B surface antigen, followed by other markers when the result is positive. Chronic infection requires assessment of liver function and viral activity, and treatment with an antiviral such as tenofovir, commonly 300 milligrams by mouth once a day, is offered according to current guidance. Hepatitis C passes mainly through blood and is now curable in most people with direct-acting antiviral medicines taken by mouth for 8 to 12 weeks. The obstacle is rarely biology; it is cost, availability, and the pathway into care, and the nurse often makes that pathway real.

HIV testing must be voluntary, confidential, and linked to treatment, and stigma is a clinical problem rather than a social footnote. A person who fears that a positive result will reach family, employer, or immigration authorities may refuse testing, delay treatment, and disappear from care. Use opt-out testing where it is permitted, explain what is being tested and why, and state plainly who will see the result. Same-day initiation of antiretroviral therapy is now standard in many programs, typically with a regimen containing dolutegravir 50 milligrams, tenofovir, and lamivudine, all by mouth once a day, and that regimen must be checked against current national guidance and against the patient's kidney function, pregnancy status, and other medicines. Partner notification, where it exists, requires consent and attention to the real risk of violence. Your manner in that room may determine whether the patient returns at all.

Beyond the first test, the work is retention. A migrant living with HIV may lose access to medicines when status, address, or country changes, and an interruption risks viral rebound, resistance, and onward transmission. Ask at every visit whether the patient has enough medicine to reach the next visit, and count the days together if necessary. Children and adolescents who acquired HIV at birth may arrive with no records and no understanding of their own diagnosis, and disclosure must be planned with the family rather than improvised. Prevention, including condoms, pre-exposure prophylaxis where available, and treatment as prevention, belongs in the same conversation. Confidentiality practices should be designed so that one misplaced paper cannot expose a patient to harm.

Mental health is part of tropical medicine for a simple reason: the body keeps the record of what the mind has survived. People who flee war, persecution, or torture carry post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety, prolonged grief, and somatic symptoms that present first as headache, chest pain, fatigue, dizziness, or unexplained pain. Survivors of torture may have specific sequelae, including chronic pain, hearing loss, sexual dysfunction, and scars whose pattern tells a story. Ask about trauma only after basic trust exists, using an interpreter who is trained and not drawn from the patient's own small community, and never press for details that are not needed for care. Treat what you find with psychological therapy, sleep support, and antidepressant medication when indicated, checking every choice and dose against current guidance and against interactions with tuberculosis and HIV medicines. Somatic complaints are real and should be investigated rather than dismissed as stress, and a normal workup is no reason to stop attending to distress.

Children carry their own version of this burden. A child who has witnessed violence, lost a parent, or spent years in a camp may present with bedwetting, school failure, aggression, withdrawal, or physical complaints, and the family may describe the child as difficult rather than distressed. Adolescents may be navigating the ordinary turbulence of that age and the extraordinary weight of migration at the same time, and they may also be the family interpreter. Screening for mental health problems belongs in routine care for this population rather than in a specialty referral that never happens. Assess safety, including suicidal thoughts and any risk of violence at home, and involve the family where that is safe and exclude them where it is not.

Female genital mutilation causes lifelong physical and psychological harm and belongs to tropical medicine because it is encountered in women and girls who migrate from regions where it is practiced. It includes several forms, from cutting of the clitoral hood to removal of tissue and narrowing of the vaginal opening. Immediate complications include severe pain, hemorrhage, infection, urinary retention, and injury to nearby structures, and these may present in an emergency department years after the event. Long-term consequences include chronic pain, painful intercourse, difficulty passing urine, recurrent urinary infection, menstrual obstruction, and psychological distress. Childbirth is where the harm becomes most visible, because scar tissue can obstruct labor and lead to prolonged labor, tearing, hemorrhage, and obstetric fistula. Care must be nonjudgmental, private, and led by what the woman wants, and deinfibulation and reconstructive surgery are options to discuss without pressure. In many destination countries the practice is illegal, including when performed abroad, and safeguarding duties must be explained honestly rather than kept from the patient.

Maternal health in migrant populations is shaped by late presentation and missing information. A woman may arrive in the third trimester with no antenatal records, uncertain dates, and a history of female genital mutilation, anemia, or untreated infection. She may fear that maternity care will cost money she does not have or will expose her to immigration authorities. The first visit should establish gestational age, screen for anemia, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, and malaria where transmission is possible, and check vaccination status, especially for tetanus and influenza. Blood pressure, urine protein, and blood glucose deserve the same attention as in any pregnancy, and danger signs must be explained in words the woman can repeat back. Postpartum care should include contraception, mental health, and the newborn's screening and vaccination, because the baby of a migrant mother can fall out of the system at exactly the moment when follow-up matters most.

Where malaria is transmitted, pregnancy changes the risk in both directions. Infection in pregnancy causes maternal anemia, miscarriage, stillbirth, prematurity, and low birth weight, and it is often asymptomatic. Prevention and treatment follow national policy, and in many settings intermittent preventive treatment is given with sulfadoxine and pyrimethamine, while treatment of confirmed disease uses an artemisinin-based combination therapy chosen for the trimester. These regimens are revised, differ between countries, and must be verified against the current national guideline before they are prescribed. Weigh the woman at each visit, because doses depend on weight, and record the weight you used. Congenital syphilis and hepatitis B are both preventable with timely screening and treatment, which is why the first antenatal visit is worth protecting in a busy clinic.

Language is a clinical instrument, and when it fails the diagnosis fails with it. Never use a child as an interpreter for a parent's symptoms, for a mental health assessment, or for a discussion of sexual health, because it reverses the family hierarchy and places the child in a position that can harm everyone. Never use a bystander from the same community for sensitive information, because confidentiality may be lost and gossip can follow a patient for years. Use a professional interpreter, in person or by telephone, and brief that interpreter on the purpose of the encounter. Speak directly to the patient rather than to the interpreter, in short sentences, without jargon, and use teach-back to confirm understanding. Translate written material only when the translation is competent, because a machine translation of a medicine instruction can mislead a patient into harm.

Cultural and religious considerations are best approached as questions rather than as lists. Ask how the patient understands the illness, who makes decisions in the family, what foods are eaten or avoided, whether fasting is observed, and whether prayer or traditional medicine is part of the plan. Modesty may determine who can be examined and by whom, and gender concordance may be essential before a woman accepts a pelvic examination. Some patients take herbal preparations or see a traditional healer, and the useful response is curiosity rather than prohibition, because a patient who feels judged will stop telling you. Dietary advice during Ramadan or another fast must be adapted, particularly for diabetes and for medicines taken with food. Where a treatment plan conflicts with a belief, negotiate the parts that are flexible and be honest about the parts that are not.

The right to care and the legal barriers set in front of it are in direct tension, and the nurse stands in the middle of that tension. In many countries undocumented people are entitled to emergency care, to care for certain infectious diseases, and to maternity care, while other services are restricted or chargeable. Fear of being reported to immigration authorities keeps people away even when care is legally available, so state clearly what the service does and does not share, and keep health and immigration functions separate. Cost is a barrier even when care is permitted, and a bill of uncertain size can frighten a patient more than a diagnosis. Advocacy is therefore part of the nursing role here, whether it means finding a clinic that will see an undocumented patient, arranging a payment plan, or writing a letter that describes medical need without describing legal status. Know the local rules, ask about the patient's concerns directly, and never promise what the system will not deliver.

Continuity of care across borders is one of the hardest logistics problems in medicine, because neither infection nor chronic disease respects a frontier. Tuberculosis treatment is the clearest example, since an interrupted course can lead to relapse and to drug resistance that is far harder and more expensive to treat. The World Health Organization has long supported mechanisms for transferring tuberculosis care between countries, and the nurse should use them rather than start blind. Antiretroviral therapy for HIV must not lapse during resettlement or deportation, and a supply covering the journey plus a written summary of the regimen is the minimum. Give the patient a copy of the record in a language they can at least partly read, and tell them to carry it with the medicines.

The logistics of the clinic determine whether any of this happens. Appointment systems assume a fixed address and a working telephone number, and many migrant patients have neither, so walk-in hours, text reminders, and one stable point of contact matter more than an elegant booking system. Transport cost and childcare can decide whether a woman returns for follow-up, so fit several needs into one visit where you can. Vaccines and some medicines require a functioning cold chain, which fails when electricity is intermittent, so temperature monitoring and a plan for power failure are clinical duties. Laboratory specimens must be tracked, because a result that never reaches the patient is a test that was never done. Keep the record short, legible, and complete enough that the next clinician, in the next country, can act on it.

Monitoring is where good intentions are usually lost. A screening program counts how many people were tested, but it should count how many were treated and how many completed treatment. If a patient begins treatment for latent tuberculosis infection, the plan should include a defined follow-up schedule, a review for hepatitis and neuropathy, and clear instructions about what to do if jaundice or numbness appears. If a patient begins antiretroviral therapy, viral load and kidney function should be monitored according to guidance, and adherence should be discussed without accusation. Recall systems should use contact information that actually works, including a trusted friend or community organization, but only with the patient's permission. Outcomes should be recorded, counted, and reviewed, because programs improve when they look honestly at who was lost.

Adverse effects deserve explicit attention, because a patient may be taking several medicines with overlapping toxicity. Isoniazid can cause hepatitis and peripheral neuropathy, and pyridoxine reduces the neuropathy, while rifampicin induces liver enzymes and can reduce the effectiveness of other drugs, including some antiretrovirals and hormonal contraceptives. Tenofovir can affect kidney function and bone density, and dolutegravir interacts with some antituberculosis medicines, so combinations must be checked for interactions before they are prescribed. Antidepressants and antipsychotics require attention to dose, to interactions, and to the possibility of increased suicidal thinking early in treatment. Vaccines cause local reactions and occasionally systemic ones, which should be recorded and reported through the national system for adverse events following immunization. Every one of these medicines is dosed against the current guideline, the current weight, and current kidney and liver function, because a dose copied from an old chart is not a dose.

The nursing role in migrant and refugee health can be described as five continuous tasks. The first is engagement, which means making the first contact safe enough that the person returns. The second is assessment, which means taking the migration history as carefully as the medical history and letting it direct the examination. The third is action, which means vaccinating, screening, treating, and referring according to the guidance in force. The fourth is navigation, which means helping the patient through a system that was not designed with them in mind. The fifth is advocacy, which means changing the parts of the system that keep people out. None of the five is optional, and the last is what makes the first four sustainable.

One exposure is easily missed: the return visit. A migrant who has resettled may travel back to the country of origin to see family, and may stay for weeks in a rural area with intense transmission and no pretravel advice. Children born abroad may accompany them and meet malaria, typhoid, hepatitis A, and other infections for the first time with no acquired immunity at all. These travelers carry higher risk than ordinary tourists because they stay longer, live in family homes rather than hotels, and often seek no pretravel care. Ask every migrant patient about planned travel, and treat that travel as a clinical event with its own assessment, vaccination, and prevention plan.

Tuberculosis in mobile populations also raises the problem of drug resistance. A patient may have started treatment in one country and arrive in another having received partial or interrupted therapy, which is one of the settings in which resistance is selected. Take a precise treatment history, including each drug, the dose if known, the start date, and the reason for any interruption, and obtain whatever records exist. Never add a single new drug to a failing regimen. If resistance is suspected, refer for proper testing and expert management rather than improvising.

Malnutrition travels with displacement and interacts with infection in both directions. A child who is undernourished is more vulnerable to infection and more likely to have a severe course, and repeated infection worsens nutritional status in a cycle that is hard to break. Anemia may be caused by iron deficiency, by hookworm or schistosomiasis, by malaria, by chronic disease, or by several of these at once, so treating anemia without finding the cause is often ineffective. Growth should be plotted on the correct chart and the child weighed at every opportunity. Skin problems matter too, because scabies, fungal infection, impetigo, and infected insect bites are frequent in crowded housing and their treatment is simple when it is offered. Noninfectious problems such as dental disease, poor vision, hearing loss, high blood pressure, and diabetes are often untreated and should not be crowded out by the search for exotic infection.

Consent deserves attention in a population that may have learned that officials cannot be trusted. Consent must be informed, voluntary, and specific to what is proposed, and it must be genuine rather than a signature on a form in a language the patient cannot read. Explain what will be tested, what the result means, who will see it, and what happens next, then confirm understanding. Capacity should be assumed unless there is a reason to question it, and a language barrier is not such a reason. When a patient refuses a test, record the refusal and offer again at a later visit rather than imposing it. Coercion in the name of public health damages the trust on which all future care depends.

It is worth naming the wider context. Displacement worldwide is at a level not seen in recent decades, driven by conflict, persecution, economic collapse, and increasingly by climate-related disaster, and most displaced people are hosted by countries that are themselves low- and middle-income. The burden therefore falls hardest on the systems with the least capacity, while a nurse practicing in a high-income country may meet the same problems with far more resources. The ethical standard does not change with the setting: care should be offered on the basis of need, delivered with consent, and documented with the patient's interests first.

This work is also heavy for the nurse. The stories are difficult, the systems are frustrating, and the moral distress of being unable to provide what a patient needs is real. Supervision, peer support, clear boundaries, and attention to one's own health are conditions of sustainable practice rather than luxuries. Recognizing exhaustion in yourself and in colleagues is part of professional responsibility, and it protects patients as well as staff. A nurse who is depleted cannot extend the patience that this population requires.

Before leaving this chapter, take the framing that governs every dose in this book. Regimens described here reflect current guidance at the time of writing, guidance is revised periodically, and guidance differs between countries, so the current national guideline and a reliable drug reference must be checked before prescribing. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control all publish migrant health guidance that is updated as evidence changes. Doses are calculated from the patient's current weight, adjusted for kidney and liver function, and verified by a second qualified person where policy requires it. When a dose is uncertain, the correct action is to delay it and check, not to guess and proceed.

Finally, return to the patient in front of you. The most sophisticated screening program in the world fails if the person does not come back, and the reason a person comes back is usually a relationship rather than a protocol. That relationship is built in ordinary ways: by listening, by being on time, by remembering the name, by explaining the plan, and by being honest when you do not know. It is built when the nurse says what will happen to the information and then does exactly that. Continuity of care across borders begins with continuity of care within a single room.

To summarize, migrant and refugee health requires the nurse to place every patient on a migration timeline of origin, transit, destination, and ongoing movement, and to know what each phase makes likely. The healthy migrant effect makes early arrivals look healthier than they are, and screening programs reveal only what they are designed and resourced to treat. The distinction between testing for infection and testing for disease prevents both false reassurance and unnecessary alarm. Tuberculosis, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV each require a defined pathway from test to treatment, with attention to latent infection, to stigma, and to continuity across borders. Mental health, the consequences of female genital mutilation, maternal care, language, culture, and the legal barriers to care are clinical subjects rather than background. The logistics of follow-up, the monitoring of adherence, and the recognition of adverse effects decide whether the rest succeeds. The discipline that holds it all together is simple: treat the person, not the label.

# Chapter 31 — Vaccination for Tropical Settings

Vaccination is the intervention that prevents tropical disease before the encounter with the health system ever happens, and in settings where diagnostic capacity is thin and referral is difficult, that prevention carries more weight than it does anywhere else. A child who never develops measles never needs a hospital bed, and a traveler who never develops yellow fever never needs a bed in an intensive care unit. The advanced practice nurse working in tropical medicine therefore handles vaccines on three levels at once: the individual traveler who needs protection for a specific itinerary, the resident population that depends on routine immunization for its baseline safety, and the community whose unvaccinated members determine whether an outbreak can spread. This chapter explains how vaccines produce protection, walks through the vaccines that matter most in tropical and travel practice, and then turns to the unglamorous parts of the work that decide whether any of it succeeds, which are the cold chain, the monitoring, the contraindications, the adverse effects, and the daily nursing tasks of counseling, administration, and documentation.

How a vaccine works is worth understanding before the products themselves, because the mechanism explains nearly every practical rule that follows. The immune system learns by encounter, and a vaccine arranges a safe encounter with an antigen, the part of an organism that the immune system recognizes. When that antigen arrives with the right signals, the B lymphocytes produce antibodies that bind the organism and block it, while the T lymphocytes coordinate the killing of infected cells and support the antibody response. A small number of those cells remain afterward as memory cells, and they are the point of the whole exercise, because they turn a first infection that might take a week into a second encounter that is stopped within a day. Some vaccines need repeated doses because the first dose only primes the response and later doses deepen and lengthen it. Some need periodic boosters because antibody levels fall over years, and some, particularly the live attenuated products, produce such durable protection that a single course lasts a lifetime.

Vaccines come in families, and the family determines whether the product may be given to a pregnant woman or to an immunosuppressed patient. Live attenuated vaccines contain organisms that have been weakened so that they multiply enough to provoke immunity without causing disease, and they include the vaccines against yellow fever, measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox, oral typhoid, and BCG. Because they multiply, they are the products that can cause serious infection when immunity is impaired, and they are the ones generally avoided in pregnancy. Inactivated vaccines contain killed organisms or purified pieces of them, and they include the vaccines against hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rabies, the inactivated Japanese encephalitis vaccine, influenza, and the injectable typhoid vaccine, none of which can replicate, so they are safe in principle for immunocompromised patients even though the response may be weaker. Toxoid vaccines such as those against tetanus and diphtheria use a chemically modified toxin that the immune system can recognize without suffering its effects. Conjugate and subunit vaccines attach a weak antigen to a carrier protein or use a single purified protein, which is how the pneumococcal, meningococcal, Haemophilus influenzae type b, and human papillomavirus vaccines work. The newer platforms, including messenger RNA, deliver genetic instructions for a single antigen rather than the antigen itself.

What makes tropical practice different is not the vaccines but the arithmetic of risk that surrounds them. The same product given to a child in a temperate city and to a child in a village where hepatitis A is universal has a different value, because the chance of encounter is different, and the same logic governs every recommendation in this chapter. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control all publish immunization guidance that reflects this arithmetic, and they do not always agree with one another, because each weighs local epidemiology, cost, and program capacity differently. Guidance also changes as evidence accumulates, and a schedule that was standard a decade ago may no longer be current. Every dose, interval, and age limit described here is therefore a summary of what current guidance says rather than a settled fact, and the current national guideline and the product insert must always be checked before a vaccine is prescribed or administered.

Hepatitis A is the vaccine most travelers genuinely need, because the virus spreads by the fecal-oral route, it is common wherever sanitation is unreliable, and an infected adult can become seriously ill. The illness produces fever, nausea, abdominal discomfort, and jaundice, and while young children often have a mild or silent infection, adults can be unwell for weeks and occasionally develop acute liver failure. The vaccine is an inactivated product given by injection into the muscle, and the standard schedule is 2 doses separated by 6 to 12 months, with the second dose never given sooner than 6 months after the first. Protection begins within about 2 to 4 weeks of the first dose and is expected to last for decades once the series is complete. A combined vaccine against hepatitis A and hepatitis B exists and follows a similar principle using 3 doses. Where a traveler must depart within days, a single dose still provides substantial short-term protection, and the second dose can be completed after return.

Hepatitis B deserves more attention than it usually receives in travel clinics, because it is transmitted through blood, sexual contact, and contaminated needles rather than through food and water, so its risk follows behavior and occupation more than itinerary. The virus causes acute hepatitis that may be silent, and it can persist as a chronic infection that leads to cirrhosis and liver cancer decades later. The vaccine is given as 3 doses, commonly at the first visit, 1 month later, and 6 months later, and an accelerated schedule at the first visit, 1 month, and 2 months followed by a final dose at 12 months is used when protection is needed quickly. In countries where the virus is common, the birth dose given within 24 hours of delivery is the single most valuable dose in the entire program, because it prevents transmission from mother to newborn. Health care workers, people living with HIV, household contacts of infected people, and anyone likely to need transfusions or injections abroad should be vaccinated. After a needlestick or sexual exposure, immunoglobulin and vaccine are both given, and the interval and dose must be confirmed against the current guideline.

Typhoid fever is caused by the bacterium Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, it spreads through food and water contaminated by human waste, and it produces a prolonged fever with abdominal pain, constipation or diarrhea, and sometimes intestinal hemorrhage. Three vaccine options exist and they differ in age limits, duration, and whether they are live. The injectable polysaccharide vaccine is a single dose given into the muscle, licensed from about 2 years of age, with a booster every 2 to 3 years for continued protection. The oral live attenuated vaccine is given as 4 capsules on alternate days across one week, with a booster every 5 years, and because it is live it is avoided in pregnancy and in immunosuppression. The newer conjugate vaccine is a single dose that can be given from 6 months of age, and it is being introduced into routine childhood programs in countries where the disease is common. None of the three is fully protective, so vaccination never replaces safe food and water, and hand hygiene remains the core of prevention.

Cholera vaccine has a narrower role than many travelers assume, because the disease is rare in ordinary tourist itineraries and the vaccine is most valuable as a public health tool. The oral killed whole-cell vaccine is given as 2 doses between 1 and 6 weeks apart, and protection lasts roughly 2 years, after which a booster is needed. A live attenuated single-dose vaccine is available in some countries. In outbreak settings and in humanitarian emergencies, the killed vaccine is deployed in reactive campaigns that target entire affected communities rather than individual patients, and the World Health Organization maintains a global stockpile for that purpose. Aid workers, health staff, and people living in camps or areas with poor sanitation may reasonably be vaccinated before deployment. As with typhoid, the vaccine supplements clean water, safe sanitation, and prompt rehydration, and it does not replace them.

Rabies is the vaccine that is most clearly a matter of life and death, because once symptoms begin the disease is almost always fatal, and prevention is therefore everything. The virus travels from a bite or scratch along the nerves toward the brain, and the interval between exposure and illness is usually weeks to months, which is the window that treatment uses. Pre-exposure vaccination uses 3 doses given on days 0, 7, and 21 or 28 by injection into the muscle, and it does not remove the need for treatment after a bite, but it simplifies that treatment and buys time in places where vaccine is scarce. After an exposure, the wound must be washed immediately with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes, and then a vaccine course is given on days 0, 3, 7, and 14, with a fifth dose on day 28 for people who are immunosuppressed. Category 3 exposures, which include bites that break the skin and contamination of mucous membranes or broken skin, also require rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into and around the wound. Intradermal regimens that place a small volume of vaccine at several sites are used in many countries to stretch limited supplies, and the exact regimen and immunoglobulin dose must be verified against the current guideline.

Japanese encephalitis is a mosquito-borne viral infection of rural Asia, where the virus circulates between pigs, wading birds, and the mosquitoes that breed in flooded rice fields. Most infections are silent, but roughly 1 in 250 produces illness, and among those who develop encephalitis the death rate is high and a large share of survivors are left with weakness, seizures, or cognitive change. Two vaccine types are in common use: an inactivated vaccine given as 2 doses 28 days apart with a booster after 1 to 2 years, and a live attenuated vaccine given as a single dose in some countries. Vaccination is recommended for travelers who will spend a month or more in rural endemic areas, particularly during the transmission season, and for anyone whose work takes them into rice-growing districts, pig farms, or long stays in endemic countries. A short visit confined to a major city rarely justifies it. The older mouse brain derived vaccine is still used in a few settings but has been replaced almost everywhere by safer products.

Tick-borne encephalitis is the other viral encephalitis that tropical and travel nurses should recognize, and its geography is European and central Asian rather than tropical, which is exactly why it is easy to overlook. The virus is spread by the bite of an infected tick and, less commonly, by drinking unpasteurized milk or eating unpasteurized dairy products from infected goats, sheep, or cows. Illness begins like a flu, and after a quiet interval a proportion of patients develop meningitis or encephalitis with headache, neck stiffness, confusion, and sometimes paralysis, and the neurological consequences can be permanent. Vaccination follows either a rapid schedule with doses on days 0, 7, and 21 or a conventional schedule with the second dose 1 to 3 months later and the third dose 5 to 12 months after the first, with boosters every 3 to 5 years. Travelers to forested areas of central and eastern Europe and to parts of Asia during the warmer months should consider it. Avoiding unpasteurized dairy during those trips is a simple protective measure that costs nothing.

Yellow fever is the vaccine with the most complicated rules, and the nurse must know both the medical and the regulatory dimensions. The disease is a viral hemorrhagic illness transmitted by mosquitoes in parts of Africa and South America, and it can cause fever, jaundice, bleeding, kidney failure, and death. The vaccine is a live attenuated product, a single dose confers lifelong protection, and since 2016 the World Health Organization considers one documented dose sufficient for the international certificate for the whole of a person's life. Under the International Health Regulations, certain countries require a certificate of vaccination against yellow fever for entry, and the certificate becomes valid 10 days after vaccination, which is why it can never be given at the airport gate. The vaccine is contraindicated in severe immunodeficiency, in symptomatic HIV infection, in thymus disease, and in infants under 9 months of age, and it is used in pregnancy only when the risk of disease clearly outweighs the risk of the vaccine. Rare but serious reactions include yellow fever vaccine associated viscerotropic disease and neurotropic disease, both of which require prompt recognition and reporting.

Meningococcal disease is a bacterial infection that produces meningitis and a rapidly progressive bloodstream infection with rash and shock, and the organism Neisseria meningitidis has several serogroups with different geographic patterns. The quadrivalent conjugate vaccine covers serogroups A, C, W, and Y and is the product used for most travel indications. Saudi Arabia requires pilgrims traveling for the Hajj and Umrah to show a certificate of vaccination with a quadrivalent vaccine given at least 10 days before arrival and within the previous 5 years, and this requirement is enforced at the points of entry. Across the African meningitis belt, mass campaigns with a conjugate vaccine against serogroup A have substantially reduced epidemic disease, and routine childhood vaccination is expanding there. Close contacts of a patient with meningococcal disease require preventive antibiotics, and the choice of drug follows the national guideline.

Influenza is included here because it is the vaccine that tropical programs most often neglect and most often need. Influenza circulates throughout the year in tropical countries rather than following the sharp winter season of temperate regions, so a single annual dose in the autumn does not map onto local epidemiology. The vaccine is inactivated and given by injection into the muscle, and it is recommended from 6 months of age for everyone, with the strongest recommendation for pregnant women, young children, older adults, people with chronic heart, lung, kidney, or metabolic disease, and people living with HIV. In tropical settings the World Health Organization advises vaccinating before the main local peak rather than assuming the temperate calendar applies. Health care workers should be vaccinated partly to protect themselves and largely to avoid carrying the virus into wards where vulnerable patients are clustered. The strain composition changes each year, which is why the dose is repeated annually.

The vaccines against coronavirus disease 2019 belong in this chapter for the same reason, because the pandemic reshaped travel medicine and because several products were designed with resource-limited settings in mind. The available platforms have included inactivated whole virus vaccines, protein subunit vaccines, viral vector vaccines, and messenger RNA vaccines, and they differ in storage requirements, in the number of doses, and in how quickly their protection wanes. The inactivated and protein subunit products generally tolerate ordinary cold chain conditions between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, which made them usable in places where ultra-cold storage was impossible. Older adults, pregnant women, and immunocompromised patients remain the groups for whom booster doses matter most, and the virus continues to evolve, so the recommended composition is revised periodically. The same rule that governs every vaccine in this chapter applies here, which is that the current national guidance and the product insert must be consulted rather than a schedule remembered from an earlier year.

BCG is the oldest vaccine in this chapter, a live attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis given by injection into the skin, and its reputation exceeds what it actually does. It protects infants and young children against disseminated tuberculosis and tuberculous meningitis, which are the forms that kill quickly, and it does not reliably protect adults against pulmonary tuberculosis and does not prevent infection in the first place. The World Health Organization recommends a birth dose in countries with a high burden of disease, and in low-incidence countries the vaccine is reserved for infants at specific high risk. The scar that often follows is not proof of protection, and its absence is not proof of failure, because the immune response does not depend on the scar. BCG is contraindicated in infants with symptomatic HIV infection or other severe immunodeficiency, and the decision in a child with HIV exposure requires the current guideline. Because the chapter has emphasized mechanism, this is the clearest example of a vaccine whose benefit is real but strictly bounded.

The dengue vaccine is the one product whose use depends entirely on a laboratory result, and this makes it a test of how well a program can establish prior infection status. The first licensed dengue vaccine is a live attenuated product given as 3 doses across 12 months, and it is approved only for people with documented prior dengue virus infection. In a person who has never been infected, the vaccine acts like a silent first infection and increases the risk of severe dengue during a later natural infection, which is why serological testing before vaccination is mandatory rather than optional. The difficulty is that the available tests cannot always distinguish a past dengue infection from a past infection with a related virus, and test performance varies between laboratories, so the result must be interpreted with care. A second dengue vaccine has since been licensed in some countries with a different approach to pre-vaccination testing, and its indications continue to evolve. Because the product is live, it is avoided in pregnancy and in immunosuppression, and vector control remains the primary defense against the disease.

The malaria vaccines are the newest products in this chapter and the ones most easily misunderstood, so they must be described honestly rather than as a solution. The first, known as RTS,S and marketed as Mosquirix, targets a protein on the surface of the parasite Plasmodium falciparum, and the second, known as R21, uses the same target with a different immune-stimulating adjuvant. The RTS,S schedule gives 4 doses to young children beginning at about 5 months of age, with the first 3 doses given monthly and the fourth at about 18 months, and some programs add a fifth dose about a year later, while the R21 schedule uses 3 doses with a booster. Both reduce clinical malaria by roughly 30 to 40 per cent in the first year, that protection wanes over time, and the reduction in severe malaria and death becomes substantial when the vaccine is combined with other measures. The evidence base came from pilot implementation in Ghana, Kenya, and Malawi beginning in 2019, which followed children through routine health systems rather than through trial conditions. The World Health Organization now recommends these vaccines for children in areas of moderate to high transmission, and seasonal schedules are used where transmission is concentrated in a few months, but they do not replace insecticide-treated bed nets, indoor residual spraying, prompt diagnosis, and effective treatment.

The routine childhood schedule is the backbone of prevention in every tropical country, and the travel or tropical medicine nurse should be able to read it and explain it to a parent. A typical schedule includes BCG at birth, a birth dose of hepatitis B vaccine, oral and injectable polio vaccines, a combined vaccine against diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis, Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine, pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, rotavirus vaccine, and later measles and rubella vaccine followed in adolescence by human papillomavirus vaccine. What limits these programs is rarely the existence of the vaccines and almost always the coverage, because a child who receives the first dose and misses the third is not protected in the way the schedule intends. The nurse who checks a child's card during an unrelated visit, notices a missed dose, and offers it before the family leaves is doing more for that child than a specialist consultation would. The same principle applies to adults, whose immunity against tetanus, diphtheria, measles, and hepatitis B is often simply unknown.

The cold chain is the part of vaccination that fails quietly, and its failure is invisible at the moment of injection. Most vaccines must be kept between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius from the factory to the patient, and the chain is only as strong as its weakest link, which is usually the last one, the health post with an unreliable refrigerator and no one assigned to watch it. Several vaccines are damaged by freezing, including hepatitis B vaccine, the diphtheria and tetanus containing vaccines, and pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, and a vial that has been frozen may look perfectly normal while providing no protection at all. The messenger RNA vaccines against coronavirus disease 2019 require much colder storage, which is why their introduction depended on equipment that many tropical programs did not have. Temperature must be monitored at every level with a logger or a thermometer read twice each day, and a break in the chain requires immediate assessment rather than guesswork. The nurse who records those readings and reports excursions is protecting the entire program, not completing a formality.

The vaccine vial monitor is a small square printed on the label that darkens with cumulative heat exposure, and it is the simplest tool available for deciding whether a vial may still be used. It answers a question that no thermometer can answer after the fact, which is how much heat the vial has already absorbed across its journey. The rule is to compare the inner square with the outer circle: if the inner square is lighter than the outer circle, the vaccine may be used, and if the inner square is the same shade or darker, the vial must be discarded. The monitor does not detect freezing, so freeze-sensitive vaccines require the separate shake test, in which a suspect vial and a known unfrozen control vial are shaken side by side and compared for the granular sediment that indicates damage. Any vial that fails either check is discarded and the loss is documented, because unexplained wastage is itself a signal that the chain has a problem.

Multi-dose vials create a decision that has to be made correctly every single day. The World Health Organization multi-dose vial policy allows a vial that has been opened to be kept and reused for up to 28 days when four conditions are met: the vaccine is one of the products covered by the policy, it has been stored correctly between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, it has not been contaminated, and the vaccine vial monitor has not reached its discard point. Vials that contain no preservative, such as reconstituted BCG vaccine and reconstituted measles vaccine, must be discarded 6 hours after reconstitution or at the end of the session, whichever comes first, because bacterial contamination can multiply in them. Discarding a partly used vial feels wasteful, and reusing one past its limit feels thrifty, but the second choice can cause a fatal infection, so the rule is not negotiable. The nurse should also track how much vaccine is wasted and why, because a sudden rise in wastage usually points to a fixable problem in session size, refrigeration, or technique.

Pregnancy changes the vaccination decision, and the reason is the same mechanism described at the opening of this chapter. Live vaccines are avoided as a rule, which includes yellow fever vaccine, oral typhoid vaccine, live Japanese encephalitis vaccine in most circumstances, live dengue vaccine, and the vaccines against measles, mumps, rubella, and chickenpox. Yellow fever is the difficult exception, because in a pregnant traveler going to an area of active transmission the risk of the disease may be greater than the risk of the vaccine, and that judgment belongs to the current guideline and to a clinician experienced in travel medicine. Inactivated vaccines may be given when the risk justifies them, and hepatitis A vaccine, hepatitis B vaccine, and rabies vaccine fall into that group. Influenza vaccine and the combined tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis vaccine are actively recommended during pregnancy, because they protect both the woman and the newborn during the first months of life. Every one of these decisions should be documented with the reasoning behind it.

Immunosuppression is the other great divider, and it appears in tropical practice more often than anywhere else because of HIV, malnutrition, cancer treatment, transplantation, and the biologic agents used for inflammatory disease. Live vaccines are contraindicated in anyone with severely impaired immunity, because a weakened organism can still cause disseminated disease when the defenses that contain it are absent. BCG is contraindicated in symptomatic HIV infection, yellow fever vaccine is contraindicated in advanced HIV, and the live oral typhoid, live Japanese encephalitis, and live dengue vaccines are all avoided. Inactivated vaccines are safe in principle, but the response may be blunted, which means the patient may not achieve the protection the record suggests they have. The timing matters enormously, because vaccination given before chemotherapy, transplantation, or the start of a biologic agent produces a far better response than the same vaccine given afterward, and this is why the pre-treatment visit is the right moment to complete the schedule. Household members of an immunosuppressed patient should be fully vaccinated where possible, and the question of live vaccine virus shedding in the home follows the current guidance rather than habit.

Adverse effects after vaccination range from the trivial to the catastrophic, and the nurse must be able to sort them quickly. Local reactions such as pain, redness, and swelling at the injection site are common and expected, and systemic reactions such as fever, muscle aches, headache, and irritability usually appear within a day and resolve within 2 to 3 days. Serious allergic reactions are rare, occurring at roughly 1 per million doses, and they begin within minutes, which is why every vaccination session needs a period of observation and a plan. Anaphylaxis is treated with epinephrine at 0.5 milligrams given intramuscularly into the outer thigh for an adult, and at 0.01 milligrams per kilogram for a child, repeated every 5 to 15 minutes as needed while help is summoned. Fainting is far more common than anaphylaxis and is managed by laying the patient flat with the legs raised, but it must never be assumed when the airway or the blood pressure is in question. Every serious event must be reported to the national authority and into the international monitoring system that the World Health Organization maintains, because rare effects are only detected when reports accumulate across many countries.

Counseling is where most of the nursing value in vaccination lies, and it is also the part that gets squeezed when a clinic is busy. Before recommending anything, ask what the patient already believes and what they have heard, because a concern that is never spoken cannot be answered. Address the specific worry rather than reciting a list of facts, and use the conversation to find out whether the barrier is fear, cost, distance, religious belief, or a previous bad experience with a vaccine or with the health system itself. Explain what to expect after the injection, including the timing of fever and the fact that a sore arm is a sign of an immune response rather than a complication. Explain the intervals honestly, because a traveler who learns at the airport that a course needs weeks will not return for the next dose. Where a patient declines, document the conversation and leave the door open, since a respectful refusal today often becomes acceptance at the next visit.

Administration technique determines whether the dose that was given actually works, and the details are not optional. The deltoid muscle is the site for adults and older children, and the vastus lateralis of the thigh is the site for infants, while the needle length must match the muscle mass of the patient, because a short needle that deposits vaccine into fat produces a weaker response.
