The skin is cleaned and allowed to dry, the needle is inserted at the angle the product requires, and the vaccine is injected without aspiration, since aspiration is no longer recommended for any of these products. The site is not massaged afterward. A sterile needle and syringe must be used for every injection and discarded immediately into a sharps container, because reuse is one of the ways blood-borne infection spreads in exactly the settings this book describes. The patient should be positioned safely before the injection, particularly a child or a nervous adult, so that a faint does not become a fall.

Documentation is the thread that holds the whole program together, and it is the part most easily rushed. The record should carry the date, the vaccine and its presentation, the dose volume, the route, the site, the lot number, and the expiry date, together with the name of the person who administered it. The patient should leave with a personal record in hand, because in many countries that card is the only evidence of protection that will ever exist, and it must survive moves, floods, and changes of clinic. For yellow fever and for meningococcal vaccination before the pilgrimage, the official international certificate must be completed correctly, with the product details and the signature of the authorized provider, since an incomplete certificate can stop a traveler at a border. Documentation is also how the program learns, because coverage figures, dropout between doses, and adverse events are all built from the same entries the nurse makes at the end of a session.

Finally, the nurse's role extends beyond the individual encounter into the life of the program, and this is where vaccination succeeds or fails. Tracing children who have missed a dose, running outreach sessions in the communities farthest from the clinic, monitoring stock and cold chain, reporting adverse events, and keeping coverage records accurate are all nursing tasks, and they determine whether a vaccine that exists in the refrigerator becomes protection in a body. Integrating vaccination with other services, such as growth monitoring, antenatal care, and HIV care, brings people in and reduces the number of visits a family must make. The communities that return for the second and third doses are usually the ones where a trusted health worker explained the schedule in a language the family speaks.

To summarize, vaccines are the most powerful preventive tools in tropical medicine, they work by teaching the immune system through a safe encounter with a weakened organism or a purified antigen, and they span a wide range from the lifetime protection of a single live yellow fever dose to the modest and waning protection of the newest malaria products. The choice of product depends on the patient's age, pregnancy status, immune status, and itinerary, and the cold chain, the vaccine vial monitor, and the multi-dose vial policy decide whether the product that was chosen still works when it reaches the arm. The monitoring that follows administration, from the observation period to the report of a serious adverse event, protects both the individual and the program. None of these vaccines is a substitute for clean water, vector control, sanitation, prompt diagnosis, or effective treatment, and each of them is only as good as the schedule that is completed. The nurse who understands the mechanism, the schedule, the cold chain, the contraindications, the monitoring, and the conversation is the person who turns a fragile supply chain into actual immunity for a traveler, a child, or a whole village.

# Chapter 32 — The Pre-Travel Consultation

The pre-travel consultation is the moment when tropical medicine stops being a subject and becomes a plan for one person, and for a healthy traveler it is often the only contact with the health system before departure. Its purpose is narrow and practical, which is to estimate what this particular journey will expose this particular body to, and then to reduce that exposure with vaccines, medicines, behavior, and equipment. The visit is not a lecture about exotic diseases and not a catalogue of everything that could go wrong. It is a matched intervention, and the match comes from the questions the nurse asks and from a careful reading of the itinerary rather than from the reputation of the country on the ticket. Nurses carry most of this work, and in many clinics the advanced practice nurse assesses, prescribes under protocol, counsels, and documents within one appointment. The quality of the consultation depends less on memorized facts than on a reliable sequence that never omits the unglamorous parts.

Structure the visit in three movements and keep the order steady, because a fixed sequence is what protects the consultation when the appointment runs short. The first movement is the risk assessment, a structured conversation about the trip and the traveler. The second is the plan, which converts that assessment into vaccines, medicines, behavior, and equipment. The third is the record and the follow-up, which allows the plan to survive contact with the journey. Begin with a pre-visit questionnaire sent by message or handed over at check-in, because it buys the one resource that travel medicine never has enough of, which is time. The form asks for destinations in the order of travel, dates, purpose, accommodation, rural travel, fresh water contact, animal contact, sexual activity, and previous travel, together with the medical questions that change everything, which are pregnancy, immune status, chronic disease, current medicines, and allergies. A traveler who completes it in the waiting room has already done half the assessment, and the nurse then spends the appointment confirming, correcting, and explaining.

Begin the risk assessment with geography and time, because those two variables decide most of what follows. Ask for the itinerary city by city and region by region rather than for the country alone, since malaria may be absent from one province and intense in the next. Ask when the traveler arrives and when they leave, and ask about the season at the destination rather than the season at home, because the rains change mosquito abundance, road access, and the availability of care. Ask how long the trip lasts, since a two week business visit and a six month stay with family are entirely different problems. Ask where the traveler will sleep, because a screened hotel room with air conditioning removes much of the night-biting risk that a rural guesthouse or a tent preserves. Ask the purpose of travel, because a conference in a capital city, a pilgrimage, a safari, and a family visit expose the same body in different ways.

Medical history is the second half of the assessment, and it is where the nurse works as a clinician rather than as an adviser. Ask about every prescription medicine, every nonprescription medicine, and every herbal or traditional product, because interactions with antimalarial drugs are common and occasionally serious. Ask directly about heart rhythm problems and psychiatric history, because those two answers remove some antimalarial options immediately. Ask about epilepsy, kidney disease, liver disease, and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, because each changes drug selection and because many travelers do not know their status. Ask about pregnancy, the possibility of pregnancy, and breastfeeding, and ask about immune status, including HIV infection, cancer treatment, transplant, biologic therapy, and long term corticosteroid use. Ask about allergies, including to the sulfa drugs present in some antimalarials and antibiotics, and ask about previous vaccinations and previous travel illness.

Destination risk must then be delivered as prose, because the listener has no map and no table to consult. Describe risk as a pattern of exposure rather than a label attached to a country, and name the hazards the itinerary actually creates. A dry season trip to a West African city with hotel accommodation is not the same risk as a rainy season trip to the same country with two weeks in a village. Explain the vector and its habits first when vector-borne disease dominates, because the habit is what the traveler can act on. The Anopheles mosquito, which transmits malaria, bites between dusk and dawn and therefore yields to nets, screens, and repellent used at night. The Aedes mosquito, which transmits dengue, chikungunya, and Zika virus, bites in daylight, breeds in domestic containers of clean water, and is untouched by a bed net. Fresh water contact leads to schistosomiasis, and altitude is a hazard that has nothing to do with latitude.

Draw on published country guidance, and say plainly that the sources do not always agree, because they weigh local data differently. The World Health Organization publishes international travel and health guidance, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention publishes destination pages organized by country, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control publishes its own assessments, and a nurse who reads all three will sometimes find different recommendations for the same itinerary. That disagreement reflects genuine uncertainty, since transmission is focal, seasonal, and incompletely measured. Never promise that a destination is safe and never imply that a vaccine or a tablet abolishes risk. The correct sentence is that this is what current guidance says for this itinerary, and that these measures reduce risk substantially without removing it.

Malaria chemoprophylaxis is the decision most travelers come for, and the mechanism explains why it is a choice rather than a single answer. The parasite enters the blood through the bite of an infected mosquito, travels to the liver, multiplies there, and returns to the blood to cause illness, and the available drugs interrupt that process at different points. A drug acting on the liver stage can stop the infection before it reaches the blood, while a drug acting on the blood stage suppresses illness for as long as it is taken. That is why the timing of the first and last doses differs between products, and why the final dose matters as much as the first. The choice depends on the destination and its resistance pattern, the length of the trip, the traveler's medical history, cost, and what the traveler can actually take reliably. Treat adherence as a clinical variable rather than a moral one, because the best regimen is the one the traveler will finish.

Describe the options one at a time, with the dose spoken plainly and then verified. Atovaquone with proguanil is a fixed combination tablet containing 250 milligrams of atovaquone and 100 milligrams of proguanil, taken by mouth once daily with food, beginning 1 to 2 days before arrival and continuing for 7 days after leaving the risk area. It is generally well tolerated, but it is expensive and not recommended in severe kidney impairment. Doxycycline is 100 milligrams by mouth once daily, beginning 1 to 2 days before arrival and continuing for 4 weeks after departure. It is inexpensive and effective, but it causes photosensitivity, it can irritate the esophagus when a capsule is swallowed lying down, and it can provoke vaginal candidiasis. It is avoided in pregnancy and in children under 8 years of age.

Mefloquine is 250 milligrams by mouth once weekly, beginning 2 to 3 weeks before travel so that tolerance can be judged, continuing weekly during the trip and for 4 weeks afterward. It is contraindicated in people with a history of seizures, a history of psychiatric illness, or certain disorders of heart rhythm, and the nurse must ask those questions directly. Chloroquine remains useful only where the parasite is still fully susceptible, given as 300 milligrams of base once weekly, which equals 500 milligrams of the chloroquine salt. Tafenoquine is a longer-acting option available in some countries, given as 200 milligrams by mouth once daily for 3 days before travel, then 200 milligrams once weekly during travel, then a single 200 milligram dose after return, and it must not be used in pregnancy or in glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Primaquine may be added after leaving an area where Plasmodium vivax is common, at 30 milligrams of base by mouth once daily for 14 days, but only after glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase status is checked, because it can cause severe hemolysis in deficiency.

Resistance patterns narrow the choice, and they change over time, which is why no remembered regimen should be trusted indefinitely. Chloroquine resistance in Plasmodium falciparum is widespread across most of the tropics, so chloroquine is reserved for the few remaining susceptible areas, mostly in parts of Central America and the Caribbean. Mefloquine resistance is concentrated in parts of Southeast Asia, particularly along the borders of Thailand, Myanmar, and Cambodia, so mefloquine is a poor choice there. Atovaquone with proguanil and doxycycline have the broadest activity and are the usual first choices where resistant Plasmodium falciparum circulates. Consider what the traveler can buy and take locally, because a regimen interrupted by an unavailable refill is worse than a slightly less elegant regimen that lasts. Every recommendation here is a summary of what current guidance says, the regimens are revised as resistance and evidence change, guidance differs between countries, and the current national guideline must be checked before a prescription is written.

Adherence deserves its own conversation, and an honest discussion is more useful than a warning. Travelers stop their tablets for predictable reasons, which include side effects, forgetfulness, the belief that the risk has passed, and the belief that a few missed doses do not matter. Some save the drug for the days they are bitten, which misunderstands the mechanism, because the drug must already be in the blood before the parasite arrives. Others stop doxycycline the day they leave the risk area and abandon the 4 week tail that covers the incubation period after return. Ask the traveler to describe how the regimen will fit the daily routine, and solve the specific obstacles, such as a work schedule that makes a weekly dose easy to forget. Suggest pairing the dose with a fixed habit such as breakfast, explain the post-travel continuation plainly, and give a written and spoken plan for a missed dose.

The travel health kit is a portable pharmacy matched to the itinerary, and the nurse builds it rather than merely recommending it. The kit exists because the first hours of an illness often happen far from a pharmacy, where the available medicines are unfamiliar, substandard, or falsified. A basic kit includes oral rehydration salts, an antidiarrheal medicine, an antibiotic for traveler's diarrhea, a fever reducer, an antihistamine, an antiseptic, bandages and blister care, sunscreen, an insect repellent, and enough of every personal prescription for the whole trip plus a few extra days. For remote travel, add a water treatment method, a mosquito net, a thermometer, and sterile needles and syringes where injections may be needed. Any controlled substance needs a signed letter from the prescriber stating the diagnosis, medicine, dose, and travel dates, and it should travel in its original labeled container. Write the medicine list using generic names, pack it in hand luggage, and check the destination's rules about restricted medicines before departure.

Food and water advice follows from a simple mechanism, which is that most traveler's diarrhea is acquired by swallowing organisms that came from human or animal feces. The safest water is water that has been boiled, and bringing it to a rolling boil for 1 minute is sufficient at ordinary altitudes, with 3 minutes advised above 2,000 meters. When boiling is impossible, filtration through a device with a pore size of 0.2 micrometers removes bacteria and protozoa, and treatment with chlorine or iodine tablets adds a second layer, though it works less reliably against the parasite Cryptosporidium. Bottled water with an intact seal is generally safe, and the seal is the point, because refilled bottles are common. Avoid ice unless it was made from safe water, avoid raw vegetables and unpeeled fruit, and avoid unpasteurized dairy where tuberculosis and brucellosis circulate in cattle.

Traveler's diarrhea is the most common illness of the journey, and most of it is self-limited, which is why the plan is rehydration first and antibiotics second. The illness usually begins within the first week, produces loose stools, cramps, and sometimes fever, and settles within 3 to 5 days without treatment in most cases. Oral rehydration salts are the mainstay, started at the first loose stool rather than after dehydration appears. Loperamide reduces cramps and frequency, given as 4 milligrams by mouth at the start and then 2 milligrams after each loose stool, with no more than 16 milligrams in a day, but it should not be used with fever or blood in the stool, because slowing the bowel in invasive infection can worsen it. When treatment is needed, azithromycin is given as 1,000 milligrams by mouth as a single dose or 500 milligrams once daily for 3 days, and it is preferred in Southeast Asia and South Asia, where resistance to the fluoroquinolones is common. Ciprofloxacin remains an option where susceptibility is likely, and rifaximin is used for noninvasive disease. These regimens are revised periodically, guidance differs between countries, and the current guideline must be checked before a drug is prescribed or a self-treatment kit is assembled.

Insect avoidance is the intervention that works when no vaccine and no tablet exists, and it depends on knowing when and where the local vectors bite. The Anopheles mosquito transmits malaria and bites mainly between dusk and dawn, so the goal is to keep it away from sleeping people, which means an insecticide-treated bed net, screens on windows, air conditioning where available, and repellent applied before sleep. The Aedes mosquito transmits dengue, chikungunya, and Zika virus, bites during the day, and breeds in small containers of clean water around houses, so nets offer nothing against it and the defenses are repellent on exposed skin, long sleeves and trousers, and the elimination of standing water. Sandflies transmit leishmaniasis, are tiny, quiet, and active from dusk into the night, and pass through ordinary mesh, so a finer net and repellent on ankles and wrists are needed. Ticks transmit rickettsial disease and tick-borne encephalitis, wait in vegetation, and are avoided with long trousers tucked into socks and a body check at the end of the day.

Repellent must be used correctly or it accomplishes nothing. The repellent diethyltoluamide is effective at concentrations of 20 to 50 per cent, and higher concentrations do not work better, they simply last longer. Apply it to exposed skin and to clothing rather than under clothing, and reapply it after swimming, after heavy sweating, and every few hours while the vector is active. Do not apply it to the hands of young children, to broken skin, or around the eyes and mouth, and wash it off when the exposure ends. Permethrin is applied to clothing and to bed nets rather than to skin, and it kills or disables insects that land on the fabric, which is why treated clothing and treated nets add protection that repellent alone cannot provide. The honest limit is that no repellent prevents every bite, so insect avoidance is a set of layers rather than a single product.

Altitude illness is a hazard of the itinerary rather than of the country, and it belongs in every consultation that includes mountains. As a traveler ascends, the barometric pressure falls, so each breath delivers fewer oxygen molecules even though the proportion of oxygen in the air is unchanged. The body compensates by breathing faster and producing more red blood cells, and symptoms appear when that compensation is outpaced by the rate of ascent. Acute mountain sickness usually begins within 6 to 12 hours of arrival at altitude and produces headache plus at least one of nausea, dizziness, fatigue, or difficulty sleeping. The most effective prevention is a graded ascent, which above 3,000 meters means sleeping no more than 500 meters higher than the previous night and taking a rest day every 1,000 meters of gain. Acetazolamide at 125 milligrams by mouth twice a day, begun the day before the ascent, reduces symptoms for many travelers, and dexamethasone at 4 milligrams by mouth every six hours is reserved for treatment or forced rapid ascent. The definitive treatment for severe altitude illness is descent, and no medicine substitutes for it.

The timeline problem is the structural difficulty of pre-travel care, and every experienced nurse has met it. Some vaccines need weeks to produce protection, with hepatitis A requiring about 2 to 4 weeks after the first dose, the inactivated Japanese encephalitis vaccine requiring 2 doses 28 days apart, rabies pre-exposure requiring 3 doses across 21 to 28 days, and the oral typhoid series requiring 4 capsules on alternate days across a week. At the same time, many travelers book within 2 weeks of departure, and some arrive 3 days before the flight with a guidebook and no immunity. The rule is not to turn them away, because late advice still prevents illness, and a single dose of hepatitis A vaccine given days before departure provides substantial short term protection that can be completed after return. Prioritize what cannot be compressed, which includes yellow fever vaccine when a certificate is required, since the certificate only becomes valid 10 days after vaccination and cannot be issued at the airport. Then decide what can be accelerated, what can be replaced by behavior, and what can wait until after return.

Special travelers require the assessment to be repeated with different weights, and the first group is the traveler visiting friends and relatives. These travelers often return to the family's region of origin, stay in a private home rather than a hotel, remain for weeks or months, spend time in rural areas, and have close contact with children and animals. Their risk of malaria, typhoid fever, hepatitis A, tuberculosis, and dengue is frequently higher than that of the leisure traveler, yet they are the least likely to attend a travel clinic and the most likely to believe that childhood residence left them immune. That belief is partly true for some infections and dangerously false for malaria, because immunity to malaria fades within months of leaving an endemic area. Discuss cost, because cost is why many present late or not at all, and point out that prophylaxis is inexpensive compared with treating severe malaria abroad. Address family pressure, needle fear, and the notion that vaccines are for children, and consider serological testing before vaccinating adults who may have been infected in childhood.

Pregnant travelers need a plan that protects two patients at once, and pregnancy changes both the susceptibility to severe disease and the safety of the tools. Malaria in pregnancy is more likely to be severe, more likely to cause anemia, and more likely to end in miscarriage, premature delivery, or low birth weight, so prevention becomes more important rather than less. At the same time, the live attenuated vaccines, including yellow fever, measles, mumps, rubella, and chickenpox, are generally avoided in pregnancy, and doxycycline is avoided because it affects the teeth and bones of the fetus. Mefloquine may be used in some trimesters under current guidance, while atovaquone with proguanil and tafenoquine are generally avoided, so the choice of prophylaxis is narrow. The safest conversation is often whether the trip can be postponed or moved to a lower risk itinerary. Where travel is unavoidable, confirm that the destination has obstetric care and that the traveler knows the warning signs of malaria and of preterm labor.

Children bring a different arithmetic, because doses are given by weight and some products have minimum ages. Ask for the child's weight rather than the age alone, since weight determines the dose of every medicine and the number of doses in some schedules. Children tolerate dehydration from diarrhea poorly, so oral rehydration salts belong in the kit and the caregiver must be taught to give them by small, frequent sips. Malaria in a young child can deteriorate within hours, so fever in a child in an endemic area is an emergency rather than a wait and see problem, and the family should identify the nearest reliable facility before arrival. An adult should apply repellent to the child's exposed skin, sparing the hands and face, and the child should sleep under an insecticide-treated bed net every night.

Older adults bring chronic disease and polypharmacy into the consultation, and both change the plan. Ask about heart disease, kidney disease, diabetes, and lung disease, and review every medicine for interactions with antimalarials and antibiotics, since the list is often long and the traveler may not know why each drug was prescribed. Discuss venous thrombosis on long flights in plain language, with hydration, movement, and compression stockings where appropriate. Discuss travel insurance and medical evacuation explicitly, because older travelers with chronic disease are the group for whom evacuation cover is not a luxury, and ask to see that the policy covers the intended activities and the pre-existing conditions. Warn against attributing fever, breathlessness, or confusion to age or to the flight, because that assumption delays the diagnosis of malaria, pneumonia, and pulmonary embolism.

Immunocompromised travelers require the most careful consultation and often the shortest list of options. Live attenuated vaccines are generally contraindicated when immunity is impaired, which removes yellow fever, measles, mumps, rubella, chickenpox, oral typhoid, and BCG from the plan, and inactivated alternatives are used where they exist. The response to any vaccine may be weaker, so protection is partial and behavioral measures carry more of the burden. Malaria is more likely to be severe in the immunocompromised and in people living with HIV who are not taking effective treatment, so chemoprophylaxis is usually more important rather than less, and the choice must account for interactions with antiretroviral therapy. Every immunosuppressed traveler should carry a written summary of the diagnosis, the medicines, and the treating clinician's contact details, and should know which hospital at the destination can manage the condition. Coordinate with the treating specialist before departure rather than deciding alone.

Documentation is the part of the consultation that outlives the conversation, and it protects the patient, the next clinician, and the nurse. Record the itinerary and the dates of travel, the risk assessment in the traveler's own terms, the vaccines given with their dates and sites, the medicines prescribed with dose and duration, the advice given, and the advice declined. A note that says only that counseling occurred is worthless later, while a note that names the specific hazards discussed and the specific plan agreed is a clinical document. Complete the international certificate of vaccination where one is required, and make sure the traveler knows when it becomes valid and that it must be carried with the passport rather than packed in a suitcase. Give the traveler a written copy of the medication list in generic names, together with allergies, chronic conditions, and emergency contacts. Where a controlled substance or an injectable medicine is involved, hand over the signed letter at the visit, because it cannot be produced from another continent.

The nurse's role when advice must be compressed into a short appointment is a matter of triage rather than of speed. Identify the few items that carry the largest reduction in risk for this particular itinerary, deliver those completely, and summarize the rest in writing for later reading. The highest yield items are usually the antimalarial plan and its adherence, the food, water, and diarrhea plan, the insect avoidance plan, and the vaccines that cannot be given late. Use the pre-visit questionnaire to move the assessment out of the appointment, use standing orders and protocols to move prescribing out of the queue, and use a printed or digital itinerary summary so that the traveler leaves with something to reread. Teach back is the technique that makes a compressed visit honest, because asking the traveler to explain the plan in their own words uncovers the misunderstanding that a nod conceals. A short appointment that ends with a correct and repeatable plan is a success, and a long appointment that ends with a satisfied but confused traveler is not.

Know the limits of the compressed visit and refer when the case exceeds it. Refer when the traveler is pregnant and the prophylaxis choice is genuinely uncertain, when immune status is complex or changing, when a psychiatric or cardiac contraindication rules out the available antimalarials, and when the itinerary includes extreme altitude, remote wilderness, or an activity such as diving that has its own medical standards. Monitoring and adverse effects are part of the plan, because a medicine stopped on the second day protects no one. Tell the traveler which effects are expected and harmless, such as mild nausea with atovaquone with proguanil or vivid dreams with mefloquine, and which should stop the drug and prompt contact, such as palpitations, confusion, severe anxiety, or a spreading rash. Explain that doxycycline can cause a burn-like reaction on exposed skin and that mefloquine's neuropsychiatric effects can appear at any point in the course, and give a telephone or message route for questions, because a traveler who can reach the clinic is more likely to report a problem than to abandon the tablets.

The post-travel period is the second half of prevention, and it is where the tropical medicine nurse most often saves a life. Fever in a returning traveler is a medical emergency until malaria has been excluded, and the interval between return and illness can be as short as a few days or as long as several months, depending on the infection. Tell the traveler to seek care for fever rather than to self-treat with leftover antibiotics, and to name the destinations and the dates without being asked, because that sentence changes the tests that are ordered. Fever with diarrhea, jaundice, rash, or bleeding requires urgent assessment, and fever in a pregnant traveler requires immediate attention. Where a returning traveler has a nationally notifiable illness, the nurse should know the reporting route and the timelines, because notification is a clinical duty. Keep the pre-travel record accessible, because it turns a vague history into a precise one when the next visit happens at a different clinic.

Prevention delivered in a consultation is the most cost-effective work in tropical medicine, because it trades a conversation for a hospital bed. The traveler who never develops malaria frees a bed, a blood film, and a clinician's attention for the patient who does, and where those resources are scarce the trade is not theoretical. The consultation also protects the destination, because a traveler who carries an infection home can seed an outbreak in a place that has the vector but not the immunity. Equity matters here, since the traveler with the least money and the least access to advice often carries the greatest risk. A pre-travel consultation is therefore never only about the individual in the chair. Every regimen, dose, and interval described above is a summary of current guidance rather than a settled fact, guidance is revised and differs between countries, and the current national guideline must be checked before anything is prescribed.

To summarize, the pre-travel consultation is a structured exercise in matching a specific journey to a specific body, and it succeeds when the nurse moves through a fixed sequence without skipping the tedious parts. Assess the itinerary, the season, the accommodation, the purpose of travel, the medical history, the medicines, the pregnancy status, and the immune status before offering anything. Describe destination risk as a pattern of exposure, name the vector and its habits, admit what the guidance does not know, and choose malaria chemoprophylaxis according to resistance, tolerance, cost, and the traveler's ability to finish the course. Build the kit, teach the food and water rules, teach insect avoidance and altitude prevention, and deal honestly with the timeline by prioritizing what cannot be compressed. Give special attention to travelers visiting friends and relatives, to pregnant travelers, to children, to older adults, and to the immunocompromised, whose risks and options differ from the average. Document the plan and the advice declined, monitor tolerance and adverse effects, and arrange the post-travel follow-up that catches the illness prevention could not stop. Guidance is revised, countries differ, and the current national guideline must be checked before prescribing, but the sequence itself remains the most reliable protection a traveler can carry.

# Chapter 33 — Vector Control, Water, Sanitation and Hygiene

Most infections in this book reach a person through the environment rather than the clinic, and the measures in this chapter close the door before the pathogen arrives. A mosquito that never bites, a latrine that is used, and a water jar that stays covered decide how much disease a community carries. The World Health Organization attributes much of the global burden of communicable disease to unsafe water, poor sanitation, poor hygiene, and vector exposure, and that burden falls hardest on children under 5 years of age. Vector control and water, sanitation and hygiene are therefore the foundation of tropical medicine rather than its background, and the advanced practice nurse usually designs, delivers, and repairs them.

Integrated vector management is a concept rather than a product. It means choosing a combination of methods that fits the local vector, house, disease, and budget, and then measuring whether the combination works. No single tool controls every mosquito, and a program that relies on one tool fails when resistance, behavior, or a change in housing defeats it. The World Health Organization frames integrated vector management around evidence, collaboration across sectors, community engagement, and the rational use of insecticides so that their effectiveness is preserved. The practical question for the nurse is which intervention will reach this vector in this village, and who will keep it working next year.

Vectors differ in ways that make tools interchangeable only on paper. The Anopheles mosquitoes that carry malaria bite mostly at night and rest on walls afterward, so nets and indoor spraying reach them. The Aedes mosquitoes that carry dengue, chikungunya, Zika, and yellow fever bite by day and breed in household containers, so nets and wall spraying largely miss them. Culex mosquitoes breed in polluted water, sandflies in moist organic debris, blackflies in fast rivers, and tsetse flies and triatomine bugs in niches of their own. A plan that ignores these differences wastes money and misses the vector it was meant to stop.

Insecticide-treated bed nets work through two barriers at once. The mesh keeps a mosquito away from a sleeping body, and the insecticide bound into the fibers irritates, knocks down, or kills a mosquito that lands on it, because the pyrethroid acts on the mosquito nervous system through contact. When coverage is high, nets also reduce the number of older infectious mosquitoes, so even people who are not under a net gain some protection, and mass campaigns that give nets free of charge reach a coverage that retail sales never achieve. The limitations are practical and predictable. A net is hot, so a household may not hang it in the cool season and then forget it when the rains return, and a net tears, is used for fishing, or is left behind when a family moves. The insecticide washes out with repeated laundering unless the net is a long-lasting product, and even those remain effective for only about 3 years of use and 20 washes. Nets do not protect people who are awake before bedtime, they do not protect anyone outdoors, and they do not touch a day-biting Aedes mosquito, so a net on the shelf protects no one and use matters as much as ownership.

Because ownership and use are not the same thing, monitoring must look at both. A coverage survey asks whether a household has a net and how many people slept under one the previous night, and the ratio of use to ownership tells a program whether its nets are working. During a home visit the nurse can check whether the net is hung, tucked in, or torn beyond a finger width, and whether the family knows it must be used every night. Teaching a household to hang and repair a net, and explaining why a treated net should not be laundered in the river, are small acts with large consequences. Reporting the reasons people give for not using nets is as valuable as reporting the number distributed.

Indoor residual spraying works on a different principle. A trained sprayer applies a residual insecticide to the interior walls, eaves, and ceilings of a dwelling, and the deposit remains active for months. A mosquito that rests on the treated surface after feeding picks up a lethal dose through its legs and body, so the spray kills the vector after it has fed but before it can transmit the next infection. For this to work, the insecticide must suit the local vector and be applied at the correct concentration. The walls must be sprayable, coverage of dwellings must be high, and the timing must place the residual effect across the transmission season. Those conditions fail in ways that are usually logistical or social. Walls of mud, dung, or unfinished plaster absorb the insecticide and may be replastered soon after spraying, removing the deposit. Householders must cover food and water and accept strangers walking through their rooms, which depends on trust built long before the first sprayer arrives. Programs must train and supervise sprayers, supply compressors and nozzles, and keep insecticide within its expiry date, because stopping abruptly after several seasons can let transmission rebound. Sprayers need gloves, coveralls, eye protection, and washing facilities, and programs using organophosphate or carbamate compounds should monitor exposure, since those classes can cause headache, sweating, blurred vision, and weakness. Insecticide containers must never be reused for drinking water, and every serious exposure should be documented and reported, because the pattern of reports protects the next community.

Larval source management attacks the mosquito before it can fly. Environmental management changes the land or the container so water no longer stands where larvae develop, by draining ditches, filling borrow pits, clearing irrigation channels, and covering domestic containers. Larviciding adds a product that kills the aquatic stages, such as the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis israelensis, the growth regulator diflubenzuron, or the organophosphate temephos, and it may also mean introducing larvivorous fish into wells. These methods work best where breeding sites are few, fixed, and findable, because every site must be identified, treated, and revisited on a schedule that matches the local mosquito. In a landscape of countless transient puddles, larviciding is expensive and rarely keeps pace. Space spraying is the emergency tool, and its name describes its limit. Thermal fogging or ultra-low-volume spraying puts a fine cloud of insecticide into the air, and the droplets kill adult mosquitoes flying at the moment of application. The effect lasts hours to a few days, not weeks, because the cloud disperses and leaves almost no deposit. Programs use it during a dengue outbreak to cut the adult population quickly, and it requires access to houses and yards, favorable wind, working equipment, and timing for the hours when the vector is active. Repeated application is costly and increases insecticide pressure, so space spraying supplements source reduction rather than replacing it.

Insecticide resistance is the slow emergency that decides whether these chemical tools will still exist in 20 years. Resistance appears when a population survives exposure often enough that the survivors reproduce, and it accelerates when the same insecticide classes are used in agriculture and public health at once. A mosquito may resist by changing the target site in its nervous system so the insecticide no longer binds, or by producing enzymes that break the molecule down before it acts. Programs monitor resistance with bioassays and molecular tests, then respond by rotating insecticide classes, by using mosaics or mixtures, and by leaning harder on nets, screening, environmental management, and behavior. For the nurse, resistance appears as an intervention that used to work and no longer does, and reporting that observation is the first step in the response.

The Aedes problem breaks the assumptions of malaria control. Aedes aegypti is a small, dark mosquito with white markings that bites during the day and breeds in the clean water people keep around their homes. Tires, buckets, flower pots, discarded bottles, roof gutters, and storage jars all hold enough water for a brood. A bed net offers nothing to a person sitting in the yard at noon, and indoor spraying does little to a mosquito that rests in a shaded corner of the compound. Because these mosquitoes live close to people and fly short distances, the containers themselves are the target. Source reduction, which means emptying, scrubbing, covering, or discarding every container that can hold water, matters most, and it must be repeated weekly because the aquatic stages develop in about 1 week in warm weather.

Source reduction exposes a paradox that field workers learn early. Households without a reliable piped supply must store water, and every storage container is a potential breeding site, so improving the water supply is itself a dengue intervention. When supply is intermittent, families store more water for longer and the risk rises. Covering storage jars with tight lids, screening the openings, and treating stored water with a larvicide reduce the risk without depriving a family of water. Community clean-up campaigns, in which neighbors and students walk the same route every week, remove the containers individual families overlook, and the nurse who organizes them is practicing vector control in its most durable form.

The sandflies that transmit leishmaniasis require a different approach because their bites are easy to miss. The sandflies of the genus Phlebotomus in the Old World and Lutzomyia in the New World are tiny, silent, hairy insects that bite at night, often indoors, and breed in moist soil, cracks in walls and floors, rubbish, and animal sheds. They do not breed in open standing water, so larviciding ponds is irrelevant to them. Fine-mesh nets work, because the mesh must be small enough to exclude an insect that can pass through a standard mosquito net, and treating those nets with insecticide adds a chemical barrier. Indoor residual spraying of houses and animal shelters reduces the resting population, and clearing organic debris and moving animal shelters away from sleeping quarters lowers the sites around the home. House screening is the quiet intervention that keeps giving, because screens on windows and doors, closed eaves, ceilings, and insecticide-treated curtains reduce the number of mosquitoes that enter a dwelling and work against both night-biting Anopheles and day-biting Aedes. Unlike a spray, screening does not need renewal every season, and unlike a net, it protects everyone in the house at every hour. The obstacles are cost, maintenance, and design, because a torn screen or a gap under the door restores the entrance, and screens can be difficult to fit on traditional housing. The nurse can identify the entry points during a home visit, suggest the cheapest effective changes, and check later that they were made.

Repellents protect an individual rather than a community, and they are most useful for the traveler, the outdoor worker, and anyone who must be outside during biting hours. Diethyltoluamide is effective at concentrations of about 20 to 50 per cent, and higher concentrations do not repel better but do last longer. Picaridin and oil of lemon eucalyptus are common alternatives. A repellent is applied to exposed skin and clothing, reapplied according to the product and the sweating and washing of the user, washed off when protection is no longer needed, and applied after sunscreen rather than before it. It should not be applied to the hands of a small child, to broken skin, or to an infant younger than 2 months. Clothing and bed nets can be treated with permethrin, which kills rather than repels, while coils and vaporizing mats reduce biting in a room but do not replace nets or screening.

For the clinician, personal protection is part of professional practice. Long sleeves and trousers, permethrin-treated clothing, avoidance of outdoor activity during peak biting hours, and chemoprophylaxis where the itinerary and the parasite justify it reduce the chance that a nurse becomes a patient. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control publish guidance on these measures, and their recommendations differ because they weigh local epidemiology, cost, and program capacity differently. Guidance is revised as evidence accumulates, so every dose, concentration, and interval in this chapter is a summary of what current guidance says rather than a settled fact. The current national guideline and the product label must always be checked before a substance is prescribed, mixed, or applied.

Water, sanitation and hygiene is the second half of this chapter, and its target is the fecal-oral route. Waterborne and water-washed infections include cholera, typhoid fever, other bacterial diarrheas, hepatitis A, hepatitis E, giardiasis, cryptosporidiosis, and the soil-transmitted helminths, and inadequate sanitation also sustains schistosomiasis and trachoma. The route runs from feces, through fingers, fluids, flies, and fields, to a new mouth, and every link can be broken. The interventions concern not only the water a person drinks but the hands that prepare food, the flies that visit both the latrine and the plate, and the soil that receives the excreta. A program that treats drinking water and leaves the hands unwashed has broken one link and left four intact.

Thinking of a safe water chain helps the nurse find where contamination happens. Water is drawn from a source, carried home, stored, treated or not, and finally poured or dipped out for use, and each step can undo the one before it. A source may be protected and clean, and the water may still be contaminated by a dirty container, by a cup that was dipped back into the jar, or by hands that touched the water while drawing it. Storage in a covered container with a narrow opening and a long-handled ladle preserves quality far better than an open bucket with a shared cup. The nurse who checks the chain from source to cup, rather than only the source, will find the point of failure. No single household method is perfect, so the practical rule is to stack barriers in a way that fits the household. Settling or filtering removes the particles that would consume chlorine, chlorination or boiling inactivates the organisms that remain, and safe storage protects whatever quality was achieved. A family that understands this sequence can choose the cheapest combination that works in its circumstances instead of relying on one method that fails, and the nurse who asks the household to explain the sequence back learns whether the message landed.

Boiling is the most reliable household method, because heat kills bacteria, viruses, protozoan cysts, and helminth eggs alike. Bringing water to a rolling boil for 1 minute is enough at ordinary altitudes, and about 3 minutes is recommended at high altitude, where water boils at a lower temperature. The costs are real, because fuel must be bought or gathered, boiling consumes time and contributes to indoor air pollution, and the water must then be stored in a clean, covered container. Boiled water can be recontaminated within minutes by a dirty cup, so a household that pours it back into the same open jar has gained less than it thinks. Teaching a family to boil, to cool the water covered, and to keep a separate ladle is a short conversation with a durable effect. Chlorination is cheaper and easier to scale than boiling, but it has boundaries. Chlorine reliably kills bacteria and viruses and is less effective against the protozoan Cryptosporidium, so it should not be the only barrier where that organism circulates. The World Health Organization recommends that drinking water retain a free chlorine residual of at least 0.2 to 0.5 milligrams per liter at the point of delivery, and in emergencies a residual of 0.5 milligrams per liter or more is often targeted, with a contact time of about 30 minutes. Turbidity consumes chlorine, so cloudy water should be settled or filtered first, and the dose must be adjusted to the volume and quality of the water treated. Household products include sodium hypochlorite solution and chlorine tablets, and each has its own concentration, so the label must be read rather than assumed. Where the residual can be measured, a simple test kit lets the nurse verify that the dose was adequate, and where the taste of chlorine discourages use, that objection must be addressed honestly.

Filtration removes the larger pathogens physically, and its performance depends on the pore size of the barrier. Ceramic candle filters, biosand filters, and membrane filters remove protozoan cysts, helminth eggs, and much of the bacteria, and simple cloth filtration removes the copepods that carry Guinea worm larvae. Most household filters do not reliably remove viruses, which are small enough to pass through pores that catch a cyst, so a filter is best combined with chlorination or boiling, and it demands maintenance, because the element must be scrubbed, inspected for cracks, and eventually replaced. Solar disinfection uses sunlight instead of fuel, and it works when clear plastic bottles filled with water lie in full sun for about 6 hours, or for a full day when the sky is overcast, so that heat and ultraviolet light inactivate most organisms. It requires clear water and bottles that transmit light, and the treated water must still be stored covered and drawn with a clean utensil, so the method is easily abandoned when the household does not understand why the bottle must lie in the sun.

Sanitation is the link that most programs underestimate, and it is described as a ladder. At the bottom is open defecation, above it an unimproved latrine without a slab or with an open pit, above that a shared facility used by several households, then a basic household latrine that is not shared, and at the top safely managed sanitation in which excreta is contained, emptied, treated, and disposed of without contact with people. A simple pit latrine with a slab and a lid interrupts the route from feces to mouth, and a ventilated improved pit latrine adds a pipe that reduces flies and odor and therefore increases use. Siting matters, because a shallow pit in sandy soil over a high water table can contaminate the groundwater that neighbors drink, and the best latrine on paper is worthless if the household will not use it, so design and location must be decided with the family. Maintenance is what turns a latrine from a construction project into sanitation. A full pit must be emptied, covered, and replaced, and the process requires equipment, trained workers, protective clothing, and a plan for the sludge, because dumping it in a stream reintroduces the pathogen to the community. Shared latrines fail when no one is responsible for cleaning them, when the door does not lock, when there is no light at night, or when the distance discourages children and older people. Handwashing water and soap or ash must be present at the latrine, or the handwashing step is simply skipped, and menstrual hygiene needs, anal cleansing materials, and the needs of people with disabilities belong in the design rather than being added later. Where a committee is responsible for repairs and a small fund exists for spare parts, facilities last, and where responsibility is vague, they do not.

Community-led total sanitation addresses the demand side by putting the decision in the community's hands. Facilitators help a village map where people defecate, estimate how much feces reaches the environment, and trace the routes by which it reaches food and water, and the community then decides for itself to end open defecation. The method relies on collective action and social pressure rather than on a subsidy for each household latrine, and villages that reach the goal are recognized as open defecation free. Recognition is only the beginning, because facilities fall into disrepair and families slip back into old habits, so the status must be verified and revisited rather than declared once. The nurse who supports the process and returns a year later to see whether latrines are still used and still clean is doing the part of the work that determines whether the achievement survives.

The health gains from sanitation are easiest to see in the soil-transmitted helminths and in schistosomiasis. Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura, and the hookworms spread through eggs or larvae that reach soil contaminated with human feces, and a latrine that keeps feces out of the yard removes the source. Where transmission is intense, treatment reduces the worm burden while sanitation reduces the force of reinfection, so the two are complementary rather than alternative. The World Health Organization recommends periodic preventive treatment, for example albendazole 400 milligrams as a single dose, or mebendazole 500 milligrams as a single dose, or mebendazole 100 milligrams twice a day for 3 days, with the choice and schedule set by the national program and the age of the child. The exact product, dose, and interval must be confirmed against the current national guideline before it is prescribed, because recommendations are revised and they differ between countries.

Even a well-built latrine changes nothing if the last few steps of behavior do not follow. The feces of infants and young children are often considered harmless, yet they carry the same pathogens as adult feces and must go into the latrine, and anal cleansing materials must be put into the pit rather than left on the ground. Hands must be washed after defecation and after cleaning a child, not only before eating. Where a latrine is dark, distant, or frightening to a child, the household returns to the bush, so lighting, a safe path, and a child-sized opening are practical health measures. The nurse who observes how a household actually behaves, rather than how the survey says it behaves, learns where the intervention is failing. Handwashing with soap is the single most cost-effective hygiene intervention in this chapter, and it depends on critical moments rather than on frequency alone. Hands should be washed after defecation, after cleaning a child who has defecated, after handling animal waste, before preparing or handling food, before eating, and before feeding a child or administering medicine. Soap and running water are ideal, and where soap is scarce, ash can serve as an abrasive that lifts contamination, though it must be kept dry and used with water. A tippy tap, a jerrycan with a small hole and a string, makes handwashing possible with a very small volume of water and is cheap to build. Alcohol-based hand rub is useful in a clinic but does not remove all pathogens, including Cryptosporidium, and the nurse who places water and soap beside the latrine and the kitchen has done more than the nurse who gives a lecture about germs.

The evidence behind handwashing reaches well beyond diarrheal disease. Consistent handwashing at the critical moments reduces diarrheal illness, respiratory infection, and the transmission of trachoma, and it improves outcomes in maternal and newborn care, where clean hands at delivery protect both mother and infant. In a clinic, hand hygiene before and after every patient contact protects the next patient as much as the current one, and it is the cheapest infection control measure available. The constraint in most communities is not knowledge but access, because a household may know that washing matters and still have no water at the latrine and no soap that is not reserved for laundry. Measuring whether handwashing stations exist, whether they hold water, and whether soap or ash is present tells a program far more than asking people whether they wash their hands.

Footwear is an unglamorous intervention that prevents one of the most common infections in tropical practice. Hookworm larvae, including those of Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale, develop in moist soil and penetrate the skin of a bare foot that steps on contaminated ground. The same route is used by Strongyloides stercoralis, and the result can be chronic anemia in a person who never notices an acute illness, because the worms feed on blood in the small intestine over years. Wearing shoes or sandals interrupts this step, and it is especially important for children who walk to school, for farmers, and for workers in plantations, mines, and construction sites. Shoes alone are not enough where the environment is heavily contaminated, so footwear belongs in the same package as latrines, handwashing, and periodic deworming treatment. The nurse who can explain the route from soil to skin can persuade a family to buy the cheapest pair of shoes it will ever own.

Guinea worm disease ties water treatment, environmental change, and community behavior together in a single story, and it is close to becoming the second human disease ever eradicated. The parasite Dracunculus medinensis develops in people and releases larvae into water when an infected person enters a pond to relieve the burning pain of the emerging worm. The larvae are swallowed by tiny water fleas of the genus Cyclops, and a person who drinks unfiltered water containing those fleas becomes the next host. The intervention is astonishingly simple, because drinking water can be filtered through a fine cloth or treated so that the fleas are killed. Because the same ponds are shared, the cloth filter works only if everyone uses it, which is why the campaign joined the filter to case containment, surveillance, and community commitment. The nurse who teaches the filter, distributes it, and checks that it is used is practicing the blend of technology and trust that has brought the disease to the edge of elimination.

When a person does develop Guinea worm disease, the nursing care is slow, gentle, and decisive for the community. The worm emerges through a blister, usually on a leg or foot, and it is extracted by winding a few centimeters each day around a small stick, over days to weeks, without pulling hard enough to break it, because a ruptured worm causes intense inflammation and secondary infection. The wound is kept clean and covered, tetanus vaccination status is checked, and antibiotics are used only when a bacterial infection is present. The essential public health action is to keep the patient out of every source of drinking water until the worm has finished emerging, because a single immersion can release thousands of larvae and restart transmission in a village. That rule is hard for a patient in pain, so the program provides water at the bedside, a shaded place to rest, and food while the nurse explains why the restriction protects the neighbors. Cases are reported and investigated quickly, because the final stage of eradication depends on finding every case and every contamination event.

The nurse in this chapter is a health educator, and education that changes behavior is a craft rather than a lecture. Adults learn best when the subject answers a problem they already have, so the conversation about nets begins with the child who had fever last month rather than with the life cycle of the parasite. Demonstration and teach-back work better than explanation, because the nurse can show how to hang a net or cover a jar, ask the household to do it while watching, and then ask the household to explain it back in its own words. Messages should be delivered in the language the family uses, at the literacy level it has, and with pictures where reading is limited. One message at a time, repeated on later visits, is remembered, while a list of ten instructions at the end of a clinic visit is not.

The nurse is also a community organizer, and this is where the work becomes political in the ordinary sense of the word. Durable programs are built with the people who will maintain them, including village committees that set a small fee for repairs, community health workers who visit households and report failures, schools that run container clean-ups, women's groups that manage water points, and religious leaders whose support legitimizes a new practice. Participatory planning, in which the community identifies its own priorities and its own solutions, produces an ownership that a vertical campaign cannot buy. The nurse brings technical knowledge into that process without taking it over, connects the community to the district supply system, and makes sure the voices of women, older people, and people with disabilities are heard when a site or a schedule is chosen. A program the community helped design is a program the community will repair.

Logistics decide whether a good intervention exists on the day it is needed, and they are as much a nursing responsibility as any dressing change. Nets must be forecast, procured, stored dry, and delivered before the transmission season, insecticide must arrive in the correct formulation with a valid expiry date, and chlorine loses strength over time and in heat and light, so it must be stored cool and dark and used before it degrades. Latrine slabs, pipes, taps, filter elements, sprayer nozzles, and spare parts must be available locally, because a broken hand pump that waits 6 months for a part is a household that returns to the river. Distribution over the last kilometer is the hardest part, particularly where roads are seasonal and settlements are scattered, and the nurse who helps plan a route or a community pickup point prevents the stock-out that undoes a year of preparation. Recording what arrived, what was used, and what remains is what allows the next order to be correct.

Monitoring closes the loop between intention and effect, and it uses a small number of measures well rather than a large number badly. For vector control, programs track net ownership and use, the proportion of houses sprayed, and entomological indicators such as the number of adult mosquitoes resting in houses or the proportion of containers holding larvae. For water, they test the free chlorine residual and the presence of indicator bacteria at the point of use rather than only at the source, because contamination often happens in the home. For sanitation, they measure the proportion of households with a latrine and the proportion of those latrines that are actually used and clean, and for hygiene they record whether a handwashing station with water and soap or ash is present. Data quality, timeliness, and completeness matter more than the sophistication of the analysis, because a figure collected late or entered twice cannot guide a decision. Feeding the results back to the community in a form people can understand is what turns monitoring into accountability.

Adverse effects and safety reporting belong to the same monitoring system, and the nurse is usually the first to see them. Insecticides can cause skin irritation, eye injury, headache, and nausea, and in severe cases the cholinergic syndrome of organophosphate poisoning, so anyone with symptoms after mixing or applying a product needs to stop, wash, and be assessed. Chlorine solutions irritate the skin, eyes, and airways, and they must never be mixed with ammonia or with acid, because the resulting gas can be lethal. Alcohol-based hand rub has been contaminated with methanol in some supply chains, causing outbreaks of poisoning, so the source and the label must be verified rather than trusted. Burns from cooking fires and from carrying boiling water, and injuries from broken filters, are common household harms that a program should anticipate. Every serious event should be documented and reported through the national system, because a safety system for medicines and pesticides is built from reports that clinicians take the time to make.

The most important lesson in this chapter is that programs rarely fail on biology and usually fail on acceptance and maintenance. The mosquito is well understood, the chlorine kills the organism, and the latrine design works, so what fails is the last meter between the technology and the household. A net becomes a fishing net because the family was never asked whether it wanted one, a latrine becomes a store room because it was built in the wrong place, a hand pump stands idle because no one collected money for the spare part, and a spray campaign is refused because the sprayers arrived without warning the year before. Trust, convenience, cost, gender, and habit decide more outcomes than efficacy data ever will. This is why the nurse, present in the household across time and able to hear the objection behind a refusal, is the person best placed to keep a program alive. The hardware is purchased once, while the software, which is the conversation, the follow-up, and the repair, must be renewed every season.

Because so much of this chapter involves substances that are measured and applied, one rule deserves to be stated plainly before the chapter closes. The concentrations, doses, and intervals described here, from the chlorine residual that protects stored drinking water to the albendazole or mebendazole dose used in deworming and the insecticide load applied to a wall, are summaries of current guidance rather than fixed truths. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and national programs revise their recommendations as resistance patterns, product formulations, and evidence change, and they do not always agree with one another. The current national guideline, the product label, and the local protocol must therefore be checked every time a substance is mixed, applied, or prescribed, and any discrepancy between a remembered figure and the current document is a reason to stop and verify.

To summarize, vector control and water, sanitation and hygiene are the preventive foundation of tropical medicine, and they work by interrupting the environmental steps that carry a pathogen from one person to the next. Integrated vector management combines nets, indoor residual spraying, larval source management, screening, and personal protection in a mix that fits the local vector, and it treats insecticides as a resource whose effectiveness must be preserved through resistance monitoring and rotation. The Aedes mosquito, which bites by day and breeds in household containers, requires source reduction rather than nets, while the sandfly, the blackfly, the tsetse fly, and the triatomine bug each demand their own approach. Safe water is achieved through boiling, chlorination, filtration, solar disinfection, and safe storage stacked together, while sanitation depends on latrines that are used, emptied, and maintained, and hygiene depends on handwashing at the critical moments and on footwear that keeps hookworm larvae out of bare skin. Guinea worm shows how a simple cloth filter, joined to case containment and community trust, can bring a disease to the edge of eradication. Programs succeed or fail on acceptance and maintenance rather than on biology, and the nurse who educates, organizes, monitors, and repairs is the person who turns these tools into protection.

# Chapter 34 — Mass Drug Administration and Elimination Programs

Mass drug administration is the practice of offering a medicine to every eligible person in a defined community, whether or not that person has been diagnosed with the infection the medicine is meant to treat. The World Health Organization more often uses the term preventive chemotherapy when it speaks of the neglected tropical diseases, and the two phrases describe the same act of repeated population-level treatment delivered on a fixed schedule. The idea is uncomfortable at first hearing, because it reverses the ordinary order of clinical medicine, in which a diagnosis precedes a prescription. In these programs the unit of care is not the patient in front of you but the entire community, and the aim is to reduce the amount of infection circulating in that community until transmission can no longer sustain itself. A nurse who understands why that reversal is necessary will run a campaign far better than one who only follows the calendar.

The population principle rests on the biology of these parasites and on plain arithmetic. For lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis, the soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma and yaws, a large proportion of infected people carry the organism silently and pass it on while feeling entirely well. Many of these infections can be found only by tests that are unavailable, slow or too costly for a district clinic, and no campaign can examine a million people one at a time. The medicines used are inexpensive or donated, safe enough for wide use, and effective against the stages of the parasite that keep transmission going. Treating everyone therefore drains the reservoir of infection far more completely and far more quickly than treating only the people who happen to be diagnosed.

The strategy was assembled over the twentieth century and refined in its final decades. Campaigns against yaws after the Second World War treated millions of people with penicillin and drove the disease down, only to see it return when the programs were stopped, a lesson that shaped everything that followed. The eradication of smallpox proved that a population-wide effort joined to strong surveillance could end a disease permanently. The campaign against Guinea worm showed what village-level work, a cloth filter and careful case finding could accomplish when the goal was absolute. In West Africa, programs against river blindness combined spraying of the rivers that bred the blackfly with community distribution of ivermectin, and the discovery that trained community members could give the medicine safely changed the scale of what was possible. Donated medicine programs, in which manufacturers provide the tablets free of charge for as long as they are needed, made repeated mass treatment affordable in countries that could never have paid for it.

The diseases that dominate this work are lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis, the soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma and yaws. Each is a candidate for population treatment because it is common, because it causes avoidable suffering, because a safe single-dose or short-course medicine exists, and because the parasite cannot easily hide in an animal reservoir or multiply freely in the environment. The World Health Organization gathers most of them under the heading of preventive chemotherapy, while yaws is approached through a different design that treats whole communities at the start and then narrows to cases and their contacts. Other conditions enter this field as well, including scabies and leprosy, and the organization now counts 20 neglected tropical diseases, having most recently added noma, the destructive infection of the mouth and face. What unites them is not a single parasite but a single logic, which is that the medicine is safe enough and the burden large enough that treating the many protects the many.

Lymphatic filariasis is the infection for which the modern mass campaign was designed, and it remains the largest of these programs. The World Health Organization estimates that about 120 million people are infected and that hundreds of millions more live in areas where transmission continues. The parasites Wuchereria bancrofti, Brugia malayi and Brugia timori, the worms that cause lymphatic filariasis, live for years in the lymphatic vessels, and the microscopic offspring they release circulate in the blood, where mosquitoes pick them up and pass them to other people. The strategy has two pillars, and both matter to nursing. The first is repeated treatment of the whole community to wipe out the microfilariae that feed transmission, and the second is care of the people already damaged, through hygiene of the limb, treatment of skin infection and surgery for hydrocele. A program that treats but does not care for the swollen leg has done only half of its work.

Onchocerciasis, also called river blindness, is caused by the worm Onchocerca volvulus and transmitted by blackflies that breed in fast-flowing rivers. Adult worms gather in nodules beneath the skin and release microfilariae that migrate through the skin and the eye, producing intense itching, disfiguring skin disease and irreversible blindness. Because the adult worms live for more than a decade and the microfilariae cause the damage, the treatment is not curative in one course but suppressive, and it must be repeated for many years. Community-directed treatment with ivermectin, in which the village itself chooses the distributors and manages the distribution, has been the engine of control in Africa, and it proved durable where externally run campaigns faltered. In the Americas, a combination of repeated treatment and vector control interrupted transmission across the whole affected region, and the goal in Africa has now shifted from control toward the elimination of transmission in selected countries.

Schistosomiasis, caused by blood flukes including Schistosoma haematobium and Schistosoma mansoni, follows a different route, because the parasite passes through fresh-water snails and infects people who wade, swim, wash or work in contaminated water. The worms live in the blood vessels around the bladder or the intestine, release eggs that damage those organs, and cause blood in the urine or stool, anemia, poor growth in children and, over years, bladder and liver disease. The medicine praziquantel kills the adult worms effectively but does not prevent reinfection, so a single round buys relief rather than freedom, and repeated annual treatment is needed while exposure continues. School-age children carry the heaviest burden in most settings, which is why schools are the natural platform, but fishermen, farmers, irrigation workers and women who wash clothes at the water's edge are also heavily exposed and are often missed by a campaign that counts only children. Treatment must therefore be paired with safe water, latrines and explicit advice about which contact with water carries the greatest risk.

The soil-transmitted helminths are the most numerous of these infections and the easiest to treat. Ascaris lumbricoides, the large roundworm, Trichuris trichiura, the whipworm, and the hookworms Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale infect more than a billion people, and they are transmitted by eggs or larvae in soil contaminated with human waste. Hookworm causes chronic intestinal blood loss and iron deficiency anemia, Ascaris can obstruct the bowel or the bile ducts, and whipworm can cause dysentery and rectal prolapse in heavy infection. The World Health Organization recommends periodic treatment of preschool children, school-age children and women of reproductive age without individual diagnosis, with albendazole or mebendazole, and the purpose is not to cure every worm but to keep the burden low enough that growth, learning and hemoglobin are protected. Because reinfection follows quickly where sanitation is poor, deworming is deliberately coupled with water supply, latrines, hygiene education and footwear rather than presented as a cure on its own.

Trachoma is caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis, and its path to blindness is a story of repetition. Repeated episodes of conjunctivitis in childhood scar the inner surface of the eyelid, the scarred lid turns inward, and the lashes scrape the cornea until it clouds and sight is lost. The World Health Organization strategy combines surgery for the inturned lashes, antibiotics for the community, facial cleanliness and environmental improvement, and the four parts are meant to work together rather than as alternatives. Mass treatment with azithromycin reduces the bacterial load across the district, facial cleanliness reduces the transmission that happens from face to face and from eye-seeking flies, and better water supply makes washing possible. The elimination threshold is demanding: the prevalence of active trachoma in young children must fall below 5 per cent, and the prevalence of the blinding complication in adults must become very low, and both must then stay there under surveillance.

Yaws is caused by the bacterium Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, a relative of the organism that causes syphilis, and it spreads by direct skin contact among children in warm, humid and crowded conditions. It begins as a painless ulcer on the leg or elsewhere, then produces widespread skin lesions and, after years, destruction of the bones of the nose, the palate and the legs. The disease is exquisitely sensitive to azithromycin, and the eradication strategy begins with total community treatment of every person in an affected district, followed by a second round months later, and then by total targeted treatment of cases and their contacts as the disease recedes. Where azithromycin is unavailable, benzathine penicillin by intramuscular injection remains effective. Yaws is one of the two diseases the world currently aims to eradicate, and its history warns that the last cases are the hardest, because the disease becomes rare and invisible just when surveillance needs to be most active.

The medicines themselves are few, and the combination chosen depends on which diseases circulate in the district. For lymphatic filariasis where onchocerciasis is absent, the usual regimen is diethylcarbamazine at 6 milligrams per kilogram of body weight together with albendazole at 400 milligrams, both by mouth as a single dose, repeated once a year. Where onchocerciasis is present, ivermectin at 150 to 200 micrograms per kilogram of body weight replaces diethylcarbamazine, because diethylcarbamazine can provoke dangerous reactions in people who carry the eye worm. A three-drug combination of ivermectin, diethylcarbamazine and albendazole has been introduced in settings where it is safe, and it can interrupt transmission in fewer annual rounds than the older two-drug regimens.
