The number of rounds is therefore no longer fixed at 4 to 6 everywhere, and the duration must be read from the current national protocol rather than assumed.

Onchocerciasis is treated with ivermectin at 150 micrograms per kilogram of body weight by mouth, repeated once or twice a year for many years, because the drug kills microfilariae but does not reliably kill the adult worms. Schistosomiasis is treated with praziquantel at 40 milligrams per kilogram of body weight as a single dose by mouth for the urinary and intestinal forms, while the species found in parts of East Asia are treated with 60 milligrams per kilogram divided into 2 or 3 doses given within one day. In young children the tablet is crushed or a pediatric formulation is used, and the bitter taste is a practical problem that the nurse should anticipate rather than discover at the doorway. A preschool child with schistosomiasis now can and should be treated, and the older habit of excluding all young children from praziquantel is no longer correct.

The soil-transmitted helminths are treated with albendazole at 400 milligrams or mebendazole at 500 milligrams as a single dose by mouth, repeated once or twice a year according to the intensity of transmission, with heavy whipworm infection often treated with albendazole at 400 milligrams a day for 3 days because a single dose is less effective against that worm. Trachoma is treated with azithromycin at 20 milligrams per kilogram of body weight by mouth, to a maximum of 1 gram, given once a year to the whole district for 3 to 5 years, while an individual with active infection may also receive tetracycline eye ointment at 1 per cent applied twice a day for 6 weeks. Yaws is treated with azithromycin at 30 milligrams per kilogram of body weight by mouth, to a maximum of 2 grams, and benzathine penicillin at 1.2 million units intramuscularly for an adult or 600,000 units for a young child is the alternative. Ivermectin is also used at 200 micrograms per kilogram for scabies in population treatment, and each of these schedules belongs to a specific disease and setting rather than to a general rule.

None of these doses should be given from memory, and the nurse is the person who keeps that rule alive in a campaign. Antiparasitic regimens are revised as new evidence appears, guidance differs between countries, and the same infection may be treated with one schedule in a national program and another in the clinic next door. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control each publish their own documents, updated on their own schedules and written for different populations, so no single number can be treated as settled truth. The current national protocol, the current product label and the local program instructions must all be checked before a medicine is given, and the check is repeated at every round because the protocol may have changed since the last one. The weight is measured on the day of treatment rather than recalled from a previous visit, the child stands straight against the dose pole, and the tablet handed out is compared with the strength written on its label. A dose that was correct at the last campaign may be wrong at this one, and the guideline is the authority rather than the habit of the team.

The delivery platform decides whether a campaign reaches the people who need it, and the model that transformed this field is community-directed treatment. In that model the community itself selects its distributors, decides how and when the medicine will be given, and keeps its own records, while the health system supplies the medicine, the training and the supervision. The distributors are usually farmers, teachers or local leaders who receive a few days of instruction and a small allowance, and they reach households that a clinic could never reach on foot. Schools are the natural platform for deworming school-age children, because the children are already gathered, the teachers can be trained to use the dose pole and the register, and treatment becomes part of the school day. Community health workers and midwives carry the campaign for preschool children and women of reproductive age, often on child health days that also deliver vaccination and vitamin supplements, and fixed posts at a market or a health center serve the towns. House-to-house visiting remains essential for the people who never come to either.

Where several diseases overlap, the programs are integrated so that one visit can address lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, soil-transmitted helminths and schistosomiasis at once, with trachoma included where azithromycin is also being distributed. Integration reduces the number of visits to the same village, the number of registers, the number of community meetings and the fatigue of the volunteers, and it makes better use of the community's patience. It also creates a new risk, because a single round now carries several medicines and every eligibility rule for each medicine must be applied at the same doorway. The nurse who supervises an integrated round has to know which drug is withheld from whom and why, and has to be able to explain that clearly to a distributor standing in front of a family. Integration that is only a matter of convenience, without that knowledge, produces errors that damage the whole program.

The unglamorous work of logistics begins months before the first tablet is swallowed. Districts must be mapped so that every eligible community is named, and a census or an agreed population estimate must be settled so that the denominator for coverage is honest rather than convenient. The quantity of each medicine is forecast from that population, ordered through the national program, moved to the district store and then broken down into smaller packets for each distribution team. Storage is simpler than for vaccines because these tablets tolerate heat, but they still need a dry place, protection from direct sun and stock records that match what is on the shelf. Registers, tally sheets, pens, weighing scales, height poles, megaphones and bicycles all belong on the supply list, and a campaign that runs out of tally sheets in the third village will never know what it achieved.

A day of distribution begins with a short team meeting, and the routine of that meeting protects the whole round. The team checks the stock against the register, agrees the route, reviews the exclusions and confirms who will carry the medicines and the records. Each distributor carries only the quantity needed for the day, because a large supply in a single bag invites loss and diversion. At the end of the day the unused tablets are counted back, and any discrepancy is investigated the same day, since a missing box is either a recording error or a theft and both matter. The nurse supervisor visits a sample of distribution points rather than trusting the reports, watches a distributor measure a dose, asks a treated person what he was told about possible reactions and checks that refusals and exclusions were written down with a reason. Supervision that only counts tablets will miss the household that was skipped because the mother was away, and it is exactly that household that will keep transmission alive.

Interrupting transmission requires a high proportion of the community to be treated, and the threshold differs by disease. For lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis the World Health Organization advises that at least 65 per cent of the total population in an implementation unit must take the medicine in each round. For the soil-transmitted helminths and schistosomiasis the target is at least 75 per cent of the at-risk group, usually school-age children, and for trachoma the azithromycin campaign aims at 80 per cent of the total population, because the antibiotic must reach enough of the children who carry the infection. These figures are not aspirations but biological requirements, because the parasite reproduces rapidly enough that a smaller share of untreated people can sustain transmission between rounds. Coverage is measured in every implementation unit separately, and a low-coverage unit is treated as a failing unit rather than hidden inside a flattering national average.

A campaign that reaches 60 per cent of a community may feel like a triumph and may still fail to interrupt transmission. Each round kills a large share of the parasites in the people who are treated, but the untreated continue to produce the stages that infect mosquitoes or contaminate water, and by the time the next round arrives the parasite population has partly recovered. Coverage that is high in the towns and low in the remote hamlets leaves a refuge from which infection spreads back into the treated areas. This is why repeated rounds are needed rather than one heroic effort: the first round reduces the burden, and the later rounds drive it below the level at which transmission can continue. The nurse should explain this to the community plainly, because the idea that a single dose would last forever is one of the most common reasons for poor participation in the second round.

The distribution of non-participation matters as much as its amount. If the same people refuse every year while others always accept, the effective coverage is far lower than the reported figure suggests, because a stable untreated group becomes a stable reservoir. This pattern is called systematic non-participation, and it is often concentrated among people who are absent for work, who fear the medicine, who belong to a group that has been poorly engaged, or who were badly treated at an earlier campaign. A district that counts only the tablets given cannot see this pattern, and it needs registers that follow households across rounds and a nurse who asks why the same names are missing each year. Reaching those households is slower and more expensive than reaching the willing ones, which is precisely why programs tend to fail near the end rather than at the beginning.

Coverage figures themselves must be checked against reality rather than accepted as record. Reported coverage can be inflated when a tablet is recorded as swallowed although it was dropped, when the same person is counted twice, or when the denominator is taken from an old and generous population estimate. Small cluster surveys, in which a set number of villages and households are sampled and people are asked whether they took the medicine, are the honest check on the register, and they can be reinforced by looking for the bitter taste of the drug or by counting remaining tablets. A program that reports 90 per cent coverage and cannot demonstrate it under survey has a measurement problem that will eventually become a transmission problem. The nurse who keeps records carefully and welcomes the survey is protecting both the community and the program's reputation.

The most important safety problem in this field arises where onchocerciasis and loiasis overlap, and every campaign team must know whether its district lies in that zone. Ivermectin kills the microfilariae of Loa loa rapidly, and in a person who carries a very heavy load the dying parasites provoke an inflammatory reaction in the brain that can cause confusion, coma and death. The danger rises sharply when the count of microfilariae in the blood exceeds roughly 30,000 per milliliter, and it is greatest in people who have lived for years in the forest where the deerfly transmits the worm. A program that simply adds ivermectin to a campaign in such a district may cause encephalopathy in people who were entirely well before the campaign. Diethylcarbamazine is also hazardous in heavy loiasis, so the whole treatment combination, and not only one drug, has to be designed around the local geography of this infection. Several strategies exist, including counting microfilariae in a drop of blood at the point of treatment and withholding the drug from anyone above the threshold, and mapping that excludes whole villages where the risk is too high. The nurse's responsibility is to know the risk zone and to refuse to improvise.

Reactions to treatment are common and should be expected rather than treated as failure. When a person who carries microfilariae receives ivermectin or diethylcarbamazine, the rapid death of the parasites releases antigens and bacterial products and produces the Mazzotti reaction, with fever, headache, itching, rash, muscle and joint pain, dizziness and tender lymph nodes beginning within a day of treatment. Praziquantel commonly causes abdominal discomfort, nausea, headache and drowsiness that settle within a day or two, and azithromycin may cause nausea, abdominal cramping and, rarely, an irregular heartbeat. Management is supportive, with rest, fluids by mouth, acetaminophen for fever and pain, and an antihistamine when itching is severe. The single most valuable nursing act is to warn the community beforehand that some people feel unwell for a day or two, because an unexpected reaction frightens far more people than the reaction itself.

The team must also recognize the rare event that is not ordinary and must act on it immediately. Danger signs include difficulty breathing, swelling of the face or throat, loss of consciousness, a seizure, severe eye pain and a rapidly spreading skin infection. A person who becomes confused or cannot be woken after treatment in an area where loiasis is present may have encephalopathy and needs urgent transfer, with the drug, the dose and the time recorded and sent with the patient. Any death, hospitalization or persistent disability after treatment must be reported to the national program within the required time, whatever the suspected cause. The nurse should not wait for certainty before reporting, because a report can always be revised while a case that is never reported cannot be investigated at all.

Every campaign needs a working pharmacovigilance system, not merely a reaction register kept in a drawer. An adverse event report should name the medicine, the dose, the route, the time, the symptoms and the interval before they began, the treatment given and the outcome. The national program forwards these reports to the drug regulatory authority and to the World Health Organization system for international drug monitoring, where signals from many countries are compared and rare harms become visible. Active surveillance, in which a sample of treated people is followed deliberately rather than waiting for complaints, detects reactions that passive reporting misses. The nurse is usually the first and often the only person able to complete such a report properly, and a program that hides its adverse events eventually loses both its credibility and its community.

Training is a nursing function even where the nurse never gives a tablet, and the quality of that training sets the ceiling on the campaign. Before a round, the nurse teaches the distributors how to greet a household, how to explain the purpose of treatment, how to apply the exclusion rules, how to read the dose pole and measure weight, how to record every person treated, refused or excluded, how to manage a mild reaction and when to send someone to the health center. The teaching uses the materials of the national program and the local language, and it is repeated rather than delivered once, because volunteers change and memory fades between rounds. Supervision continues throughout the campaign, as the nurse observes, corrects gently, answers questions and confirms that each team has enough tablets and enough light to write by. The nurse also protects the volunteers themselves, because a distributor blamed for a reaction that was unavoidable will not return for the next round.

A campaign is a social event before it is a clinical one, and trust is its currency. Rumors about infertility, about poison and about a hidden agenda spread quickly, and they are answered best by a known local person who listens first and then speaks plainly. Permission must be sought from community leaders and the purpose explained in open meetings, but permission is not the same as consent, and every person retains the right to refuse. Ethical programs explain the purpose, the possible reactions and the alternatives, do not pressure people, do not tie treatment to the receipt of food or other services, and record refusals without punishment. Where a serious risk is known, as with ivermectin in an area of heavy loiasis, the duty to avoid harm outweighs the ambition of coverage, and the nurse should say so openly rather than treat hesitation as resistance.

Eligibility rules protect the people in whom the medicine might do harm, and they must be applied without shortcuts. Pregnant women are usually excluded and offered treatment after delivery, and women who might be pregnant are handled according to the national protocol, which varies between countries. Very young children are excluded from some medicines, with the age or weight threshold set by the program and confirmed rather than remembered. People who are acutely ill, and those whose chronic illness is not controlled, are usually deferred until they are stable, and anyone with a history of a severe reaction to the medicine is excluded permanently. In areas where a medicine is given for one disease but is risky for another, the local protocol determines the choice, and people living with HIV who are taking antiretroviral therapy are generally eligible but the current interaction guidance should be checked. Every exclusion is written with a reason so that the next round can find the person, and the excluded person is told when to return.

Monitoring during a campaign has two faces, one measuring the work and the other measuring the effect. The process indicators are coverage, the number treated, the number who refused, the number excluded, the stock consumed and the completeness of the registers, and they tell the supervisor whether the round was delivered as planned. The impact indicators are prevalence and intensity of infection, antigen prevalence in children, egg counts in stool or urine and the detection of new cases, and they tell the program whether the parasite is actually retreating. Programs also monitor the quality and potency of the donated medicines by sampling them in the field, because a substandard tablet wastes a round and destroys confidence. Therapeutic efficacy is watched as well, since a falling egg reduction rate after albendazole or a poor response in a treated person may be an early sign of reduced drug effectiveness. The nurse who records accurately at the point of care is supplying the raw material for every one of these judgments.

The decision to stop treatment is not the end of the program but the beginning of a different kind of work. After several annual rounds, the program conducts a transmission assessment survey in which children born after the campaigns began are tested for the parasite antigen, and if very few or none are positive, transmission is judged to have been interrupted and mass treatment may stop. Mosquitoes are collected and tested for parasite DNA, an approach called xenomonitoring, to look for the parasite in the vector when the human survey is reassuring but not conclusive. For onchocerciasis the evidence comes from the blackfly and from children, since antibody in a young child shows that transmission is still occurring. For schistosomiasis the snails themselves are examined, and for trachoma and yaws repeated surveys of prevalence and of new cases take the place of the antigen test. Each of these methods is a way of asking the same question, which is whether the parasite is still finding new hosts.

Surveillance after treatment stops must continue for years, and sometimes for decades, because the last infections are the ones nobody sees. In lymphatic filariasis a second assessment several years after the first confirms that the parasite has not returned, and in onchocerciasis the watch is longer still, because adult worms live for more than 10 years and can resume producing microfilariae long after the final round. A single imported case or a small hidden focus can restart transmission, and the surveillance system must be able to find it while it is still small and containable. Programs therefore keep their registers, their trained distributors and their laboratory links alive during the quiet years, even when the visible disease has disappeared from the clinic. The endgame is not a campaign at all but a standing watching brief, and it is the least dramatic and most easily abandoned part of elimination.

The words control, elimination and eradication describe different promises, and a program is judged by which promise it made. Control means reducing the burden of a disease to a level the health system can manage and keeping it there, with treatment or another intervention continuing indefinitely. Elimination means reducing new locally acquired cases to zero in a defined area, with continued measures to stop the disease from being reintroduced. Eradication means reducing new cases to zero everywhere in the world, permanently, so that intervention can stop altogether. Only smallpox and rinderpest, a disease of cattle, have been eradicated, and Guinea worm is close but unfinished, partly because the worm has found a reservoir in dogs. A program that uses the strongest of these words to describe the weakest of these achievements misleads both its funders and its community.

Even the word elimination needs a qualifier, because there are two different goals hidden inside it. Trachoma and lymphatic filariasis are eliminated as a public health problem when the prevalence of the disease and of its complications falls below defined thresholds, even though the organism may still be present at very low levels. The World Health Organization uses the word validation for this kind of achievement, and the proof rests on surveys repeated over years. Onchocerciasis and, in some countries, schistosomiasis aim at the stronger goal of elimination of transmission, in which no new infections occur and the evidence must come from vector and child surveillance as well as from patients. Verification and certification are reserved for the formal, independent confirmation of elimination of transmission and of eradication respectively. The distinction is not pedantry, because the two goals require different budgets, different surveillance and different timelines.

Certification is a formal and independent judgment, and it is deliberately difficult to obtain. For Guinea worm, an international commission reviews the evidence country by country and certifies a country as free of transmission only after years without an indigenous case and after surveillance has been shown to work. For onchocerciasis, the World Health Organization verifies the elimination of transmission through a documented dossier and expert review, and for lymphatic filariasis it validates the elimination of the disease as a public health problem through its own process. For yaws, eradication requires that the world be free of the disease and that surveillance be able to prove it, which is one reason the target is so demanding. The nurse may never sit on such a committee, but the data the nurse records are the raw material of the decision, and inaccurate registers can delay a country's case by years.

The current frame for all of this work is the World Health Organization road map for neglected tropical diseases for the years 2021 to 2030. Its headline goals are a 90 per cent reduction in the number of people needing treatment for these diseases, a 75 per cent reduction in the disability-adjusted life years they cause, the elimination of at least one neglected tropical disease in 100 countries, and 2 eradications, Guinea worm and yaws. Lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis and trachoma are each targeted for elimination as a public health problem, or in some settings for elimination of transmission, by 2030. Guinea worm is the closest to eradication, with fewer than 20 human cases reported worldwide in recent years, down from millions in the 1980s. The road map follows the London Declaration of 2012 and the Kigali Declaration of 2022, in which governments, donors, manufacturers and international organizations pledged to sustain the effort for a decade at a time.

Progress is real and it is fragile, and the threats to it are mostly not biological. Armed conflict and displacement scatter the populations that campaigns are built to reach, and they destroy the registers and the supply chains on which coverage depends. Funding gaps and the diversion of health workers to other emergencies interrupt rounds, and the pause that occurred during the pandemic of the coronavirus disease of 2019 showed how quickly a parasite recovers when treatment stops. Climate change is shifting the range of the mosquitoes, blackflies and snails that carry these infections, and rapid urbanization is creating new habitats and new concentrations of susceptible people. Complacency is a quieter threat, because a disease that is no longer visible stops attracting money, and the last cases are always the most expensive to find. Reduced drug effectiveness is watched closely, particularly in the worms treated repeatedly with albendazole and in the bacteria exposed to repeated azithromycin, and it is one reason that coverage and dose accuracy are treated as resistance issues as well as delivery issues.

Mass treatment also carries a stewardship obligation that belongs in every training session. Giving an antibiotic to a whole population selects for resistance in the bacteria that are not the target, and repeated azithromycin campaigns for trachoma and yaws are monitored for exactly that reason. This is a serious concern but it is not a reason to withhold treatment where blindness and disfiguring disease are common, and the honest position is that the benefit and the risk must both be measured and reported. The nurse should record and report treatment failures and unexpected lack of response, because those are the earliest signals of reduced efficacy. Medicines must also be stored and dispensed legitimately, and leftover tablets must never be diverted into informal markets, where casual use breeds resistance and harms patients.

Mass treatment is also only one component of a program, and it must be paired with the work that prevents reinfection. The control of the soil-transmitted helminths and schistosomiasis cannot be sustained by tablets alone, because people are reinfected when they drink contaminated water, wade in infected lakes or walk barefoot, so treatment is paired with latrines, safe water, hygiene education and shoes. Lymphatic filariasis programs pair repeated treatment with limb hygiene, skin care and hydrocele surgery, and trachoma programs pair azithromycin with facial cleanliness and environmental improvement. The nurse who understands the full package can explain to a community why the tablets alone will not be enough and why a latrine, a clean face and a pair of shoes are part of the cure rather than a distraction from it. A program that delivers only the medicine may lower the burden for a season and will watch it return.

As prevalence falls, the cost of finding each remaining case rises, and the last mile is the hardest part of any elimination effort. A campaign that once treated a million people for a few cents each must later map, train, distribute and report in a handful of remote villages with the same apparatus and a smaller budget. Programs must decide when to stop mass treatment and move to targeted treatment and surveillance, and that decision has to rest on survey evidence rather than on the calendar or on convenience. Donor fatigue and competing health priorities threaten the endgame precisely when the investment is closest to paying off. The nurse who has kept good records, who knows the missing households and who has earned the community's trust is often the person who makes the final phase possible at all.

The tools themselves continue to change, and a chapter like this one is a snapshot rather than a settlement. A longer-acting drug against the worms of onchocerciasis is being introduced, a child-friendly formulation of praziquantel has made treatment of preschool children practical, and better point-of-care tests for loiasis are reducing the guesswork in co-endemic areas. Research continues into new medicines that kill the adult worms rather than only their offspring, and into vaccines against schistosomiasis and leishmaniasis, though none is yet part of a routine campaign. Diagnostics for trachoma and yaws are being simplified so that surveillance can be done closer to the village. The nurse should expect the protocols to change and should treat each new recommendation as something to verify rather than something to assume.

The nurse stands at the center of this entire field, and the role is broader than any single task. Training and supervising community distributors, measuring and verifying every dose, monitoring adverse events and completing pharmacovigilance reports, engaging the community and answering its fears, managing stock and records, applying the exclusion rules and protecting the people they exclude, and explaining why the second round matters as much as the first are all nursing work. The nurse is the bridge between the national protocol and the household doorway, and the strength of that bridge decides whether a round of treatment actually protects a community. That work is unglamorous, it is repetitive, and it is the work that ends diseases.

To summarize, mass drug administration, which the World Health Organization also calls preventive chemotherapy, treats whole eligible populations rather than diagnosed individuals in order to reduce the reservoir of infection below the level that sustains transmission. Its principal targets are lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, schistosomiasis, the soil-transmitted helminths, trachoma and yaws, and the medicines are few and well established, including diethylcarbamazine, ivermectin, albendazole, mebendazole, praziquantel and azithromycin, each given at a defined dose by mouth or by injection and repeated on a schedule set by the current national protocol. Success depends on coverage above a biological threshold, on community-directed distributors, schools and community health workers, on reliable logistics and honest records, and on reaching the households that refuse or are absent year after year. The gravest safety problem is ivermectin in areas where loiasis is also transmitted, where a heavy microfilarial load can lead to encephalopathy, and the ordinary reactions of treatment must be anticipated, explained, managed supportively and reported. Control, elimination and eradication are different promises, and validation, verification and certification are the formal processes that confirm them, with surveillance continuing long after treatment stops. The nurse carries the training, the supervision, the dose verification, the adverse event monitoring and the community trust on which every one of these programs ultimately rests. Because regimens are revised, because guidance differs between countries and because the current guideline must always be checked before prescribing or dispensing, the practitioner who verifies the protocol at every round is the one who practices safely.

# Chapter 35 — Surveillance, Outbreak Response, and Notification

Surveillance is the nervous system of public health, and its purpose is not to produce reports but to produce action. It is the continuous and systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data, tied from the start to the dissemination of what those data mean to the people who can act on them. A system that measures disease and never triggers a response is an expensive diary, and a response that begins without measurement is guesswork. The World Health Organization describes surveillance as covering both the early detection of outbreaks and the monitoring of trends over time, so that a program can know whether it is winning or losing. For the advanced practice nurse, surveillance is not an administrative duty that sits outside clinical work, because it is what happens when the observation made at the bedside is carried onward fast enough to protect someone you will never meet.

Surveillance answers several different questions with the same machinery. It detects outbreaks early, when the number of cases is still small enough that containment is possible. It tracks the burden of endemic disease so that ministries, donors, and clinics can place scarce staff and medicines where they are needed. It measures whether an intervention is working, which is why a vaccination campaign or an insecticide-treated bed net distribution must be followed by surveillance rather than by a closing ceremony. Programs for HIV, for tuberculosis, and for malaria each keep their own reporting streams, and those streams are strongest when they feed one district analysis instead of competing for the same nurse's time. When surveillance is weak, every one of these functions fails at once, and the failure is usually invisible until an outbreak has already escaped the district.

There are two broad ways of gathering this information, and mature systems run both at the same time. Indicator-based surveillance collects structured data on a defined list of diseases, reported at fixed intervals from fixed sites against agreed case definitions, so that counts can be compared from week to week and from place to place. Event-based surveillance is looser and faster, gathering unstructured signals from clinicians, laboratory staff, community members, journalists, teachers, and informal networks, and then verifying each signal before deciding whether it deserves investigation. An unusual cluster of deaths in a village, a rumor raised on a radio phone-in program, a pharmacist who notices that one antibiotic has suddenly sold out, and a spike in school absenteeism are all events in this sense. The two systems are complementary, because indicator-based reporting is reliable but slow and rigid, while event-based monitoring is fast and sensitive but noisy. A signal from either path is not yet an outbreak, and it becomes one only after someone verifies it.

Before any case can be counted, it has to be defined, and the case definition is the foundation on which everything else rests. A case definition is a standard set of clinical, epidemiological, and laboratory criteria that decides who counts and who does not, and it usually has tiers such as suspected, probable, and confirmed. Without a shared definition, two clinics reporting the same disease to the same district will count different patients, and the resulting line on the graph will be meaningless. A definition is a working tool rather than a statement of biological truth, and during an outbreak it is deliberately made sensitive so that few cases are missed, even at the cost of including some patients who turn out to have something else. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control all publish standard case definitions, and they do not always agree, which is why the national definition is the one to use. Because the definition changes as the outbreak evolves, every revision must be communicated immediately to the people doing the counting.

Surveillance systems are usually described by how the data arrive, and the four common types have very different strengths. Passive surveillance waits for health workers to report what they see, which is inexpensive and covers the whole country but depends on the diligence and available time of people who are already overloaded. Active surveillance sends someone out to look, visiting clinics and communities for cases that would otherwise go unreported, which is far more complete but costly and therefore reserved for outbreaks, elimination programs, and high-consequence diseases. Sentinel surveillance follows a chosen set of sites that report in greater detail than the rest of the system, which is how influenza and antimicrobial resistance are monitored without burdening every clinic. Syndromic surveillance counts patients by their presenting syndrome rather than by a confirmed diagnosis, so it can detect a rise in fever with rash or in acute watery diarrhea before any laboratory result exists, making it the fastest approach and the least specific. Most national systems combine all four, accepting that each has a characteristic failure mode that the others partly cover.

Much of Africa works within a framework called integrated disease surveillance and response, developed by the World Health Organization together with its regional office for Africa and used as the organizing logic of district health reporting in dozens of countries. The idea is integration, so that a single district team collects and analyzes data on a prioritized list of diseases rather than each vertical program demanding its own forms. The framework places responsibility at the district level, where data are analyzed and acted on locally, and it reaches into the community through trained community health workers who can recognize and report a small number of high-priority events. It also builds response into the same system, so that an alert is linked to a defined action rather than to another report. When it works, the district officer knows within a week what is happening at the periphery, and the periphery knows that someone is reading what it sends. When it fails, the forms still arrive at the capital and nobody at the district level has ever seen them.

The constraints that decide whether surveillance succeeds are almost never analytic, and they are completeness and timeliness. Completeness means the proportion of expected reports that actually arrive, and a district that receives 60 per cent of its weekly reports cannot distinguish a real decline in cases from a collapse in reporting. Timeliness means the interval between a case occurring and the information reaching a person who can act, and a confirmed case reported three weeks late has already had time to generate a hundred more. A useful discipline is the reporting of zeros, because a clinic that sends a report saying it saw no cases is giving information, while a clinic that sends nothing is giving none. Denominators are equally essential and equally unglamorous, since a count of cases without the population it came from cannot produce a rate. Feedback is the fuel of the whole arrangement, because health workers who never hear what became of their reports stop sending them. Supervision visits check that registers are complete and that case definitions are applied, and data audits compare what was written in the register with what reached the district office. Training must be repeated rather than delivered once, because staff rotate, and a new nurse who has never been taught the local case definitions will report either nothing or everything.

Numbers become decisions through thresholds. A threshold is a level of disease at which the system commits to an investigation, and it is built by comparing the current count with what would be expected at that place and in that season. The expected level is usually derived from several years of historical data and expressed as a baseline or a rolling average, and the alert threshold is set low enough to catch a rise early while the epidemic threshold is set at a level that clearly signals an outbreak. A single case of a disease that has been eliminated, such as polio or Guinea worm disease, is itself an outbreak and needs no threshold at all. A cluster of deaths, an unusual age group, an unusual place, or an unusual season can breach a threshold even when the total number is small. The trap is to treat the threshold as a mechanical line, when in practice it is a judgment that depends on the quality of the baseline and on how alarming the disease is.

When a threshold is crossed, the investigation proceeds through a sequence refined over decades, and the first step is to verify that the diagnosis is real. Verification means confirming that the cases exist, that the laboratory result is credible, that the same patient has not been counted twice, and that a change in testing practice, a new clinician, or a clerical error has not manufactured a cluster. It also means asking whether the event is genuinely unusual for that place and season, or whether it is the expected background that is finally being counted properly. Once the signal survives, the team defines the case for this particular event, writes the definition down, and makes sure everyone uses the same one. A definition that is too narrow will miss cases and hide the true extent of the outbreak, while one that is too broad will dilute the investigation with unrelated illness. Early in an outbreak the working definition is often clinical, because laboratory confirmation is slow and may be available in only one place. The definition will be revised, and each revision changes the shape of the epidemic curve, which is why the date of every revision is recorded.

Next comes the search for cases, which in practice means active case finding rather than waiting for patients to arrive. The team visits health facilities and reviews registers, goes into the community with community health workers, screens the contacts of every known patient, and follows up rumors that have not yet reached a clinic. Each person identified is entered on a line list, a single table in which every row is one patient with a name, an age, a sex, a place, a date of symptom onset, a date of report, a laboratory result, and an outcome. The line list is the most valuable object in an outbreak investigation, because nearly every later analysis is a rearrangement of its columns. It also protects patients, because it makes duplicate entries visible and makes it possible to find someone lost between facilities. Keeping it complete, legible, and current is unglamorous work, and the nurse who does it is doing some of the most consequential work in the response.

From the line list the team describes the outbreak by time, by place, and by person, and these are three views of one event rather than three separate descriptions. Description by place asks where cases occurred, mapped by village, neighborhood, school, workplace, or water source, and clustering in space often points directly at a shared exposure. Description by person asks who was affected, in terms of age, sex, occupation, pregnancy, vaccination status, and travel. It should also ask who was not affected, because the people who escaped a cluster often hold the clue to what protected them. A cluster confined to one age group suggests a shared exposure, a cluster confined to one water source suggests a common vehicle, and cases scattered along a road suggest a moving source or a mobile population. The pattern that emerges from these descriptions usually tells the team where to look next.

The description by time is drawn as an epidemic curve, a histogram of cases plotted against their date of onset, and learning to read it is one of the most useful skills in field epidemiology. The width of each column represents one interval, usually chosen as a fraction of the incubation period so that the curve has enough resolution to show its shape. The classic shapes have clear meanings: a single sharp peak suggests a point source exposure such as one contaminated meal, a plateau suggests a continuous common source such as a water supply that stays contaminated, and a series of progressively taller peaks suggests person-to-person transmission with each generation of cases larger than the one before it. The first case shown may be the true index case or simply the first one detected, and the gap between successive peaks can be used to estimate the incubation period and the serial interval. The curve also shows whether the outbreak is growing, stable, or shrinking, which tells the team whether control measures have begun to work, although that effect is always delayed by the incubation period. A curve can mislead badly if cases are plotted by the date they were reported rather than by the date their symptoms began, because a sudden improvement in laboratory capacity then looks exactly like a sudden increase in disease.

With the outbreak described, the team generates hypotheses about its source and its mode of transmission, and then tests them rather than assuming them. Hypotheses come from interviews, from visits to homes and markets, from food and water histories, and from the local knowledge that only people who live there can supply. A useful hypothesis is stated in a form that can be wrong, so that data can support it or discard it. The team asks what the cases have in common, what the people who remained well did differently, and whether the timing fits a single exposure or continuing transmission. It also asks whether the pattern fits a known disease, because the incubation period and the usual route of spread constrain the possibilities long before any laboratory result arrives. A hypothesis that is never tested can harden into an official story, and an official story that is wrong damages the response far more than an admitted uncertainty.

Testing a hypothesis usually means an analytic study, and the choice of design follows the situation. A cohort study follows a defined group, such as everyone who attended a funeral or ate at a wedding, and compares the attack rate among those exposed with the attack rate among those not exposed. A case-control study is used when the population is too large or too diffuse to enumerate, and it compares people with the disease against unaffected people from the same community, looking backward for differences in exposure. Either design produces a measure of association that tells the team how much more likely illness was among the exposed, with an indication of how much confidence to place in the result. The team must also consider bias, because people who are ill remember exposures differently from people who are well, and because the way cases were found may itself distort the comparison. A hypothesis that survives guides control, and a hypothesis that fails is discarded, which narrows the search rather than wasting it.

Control does not wait for the investigation to finish, because people are becoming ill while the analysis is underway. Measures follow from the mode of transmission, and they are often started on a reasonable hypothesis and refined later. For a waterborne outbreak the measures are disinfection of the supply, provision of safe water, and separation of sewage from drinking sources. For a foodborne outbreak they are removal of the implicated food, inspection of the premises, and education of the people who handle it. For a vector-borne outbreak they are vector control, including insecticide spraying and the elimination of breeding sites. For an outbreak spread by respiratory droplets or direct contact they are isolation, hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, and where relevant vaccination. Broader measures such as reactive vaccination campaigns, mass drug administration, or the closing of schools and markets carry their own costs and must be weighed against the harm of the disease and the harm of disruption. Every measure needs a defined owner, a start rule, a stop rule, and a way of measuring whether it worked.

Outbreaks are managed through an incident management system, a command structure that assigns clear responsibilities so that decisions are made once and communicated to everyone. The incident manager leads, and beneath that person sit a technical lead or epidemiologist, a laboratory coordinator, a case management lead, a logistics officer, an infection prevention and control lead, a risk communication lead, and a data manager. Case management is where the advanced practice nurse is most obviously essential, because the clinical care of patients during an outbreak is nursing work as much as medical work. Nurses also staff triage and screening points, collect specimens correctly, maintain the line list and the case notes, administer treatments and vaccines, monitor patients for deterioration, and supervise the infection prevention practices that keep a health facility from amplifying the outbreak. Community liaison is another nursing strength, because the nurse is often the person the community already knows and trusts. In a large response these roles are formal and full time, while in a small district the same nurse may hold three of them at once. That is why the nurse who has written the notification, kept the line list, and knows the stock levels is not peripheral to the response but central to it.

Case management during an outbreak rests on a small number of high-yield interventions, and the nurse should know them before the outbreak arrives. In cholera, the intervention that saves lives is rapid rehydration, given by mouth as oral rehydration salts wherever the patient can drink and intravenously as Ringer lactate solution when they cannot, with the volume judged by the degree of dehydration and repeated as needed. In measles, vitamin A is given by mouth on two consecutive days because it reduces mortality in children, at a dose of 200,000 international units for a child aged 12 months or older, 100,000 international units for an infant aged 6 to 11 months, and 50,000 international units for a child younger than 6 months. In meningococcal meningitis, a single dose of ceftriaxone given intramuscularly or intravenously is standard treatment and is often sufficient in a mass campaign setting. In an outbreak of viral hemorrhagic fever, care is largely supportive, with careful fluid and electrolyte management and strict attention to infection prevention. All of these regimens are revised from time to time, guidance differs between countries, and the current national guideline and product insert must always be checked before a drug is prescribed or administered. A nurse who has memorized an old dose and cannot find the current reference is more dangerous in an outbreak than a nurse who knows where to look.

Logistics is the part of outbreak response that decides whether any of the clinical intentions can be carried out, and it is the part most often underestimated. The team needs vehicles that run, fuel, drivers, communication equipment, and a way of moving specimens and supplies to places that may be far from any paved road. It needs a cold chain that keeps vaccines and certain medicines within their required temperature range from the national store to the last village, with temperature monitoring and a contingency plan for power failure. It needs a stock management system that knows what is on hand, what has been consumed, and what must be ordered, because a stockout of rehydration salts or antibiotics during an outbreak is a clinical disaster with an administrative cause. It needs enough trained staff and a plan for resting and rotating them, since exhausted responders make errors and can carry infection home. It needs money that can be released quickly, because slow financing is a reliable way to lose an outbreak. A nurse who understands the supply chain, and who reports consumption honestly and early, is doing outbreak response even when no patient is in front of her.

Whenever an outbreak response delivers medicines or vaccines to large numbers of people, it must also watch for harm, because the same intervention that saves lives can injure them. Adverse events following immunization, drug reactions, and errors in administration must be recognized, managed, and reported through the national pharmacovigilance system. The nurse is usually the first to see an adverse event, because she gives the injection or the tablet and because a family returns to her when something goes wrong. Reporting must be prompt and detailed, and it must avoid the assumption that the event was caused by the product, because the purpose of the report is to determine causation rather than to presume it. A program that conceals its adverse events loses the community's confidence the moment the truth emerges, and the damage spreads to every future campaign in that place. Honest surveillance of harm is not an obstacle to outbreak control, and it is what makes outbreak control sustainable.

The response itself must be monitored while it runs, so that it can be corrected before the outbreak ends. A daily situation report gives the team a common picture: new cases, new deaths, cases by location, patients under treatment, specimens pending, beds available, and supplies remaining. Indicators are chosen in advance so that the team is not inventing its measures in the middle of the emergency, and they usually cover speed, coverage, quality, and equity. Monitoring asks whether the interventions are reaching the people who need them, whether the most affected groups are being missed, and whether the response is creating new risks such as crowding in a treatment center or unsafe injections. Regular review meetings turn those numbers into decisions about redeploying staff, reallocating supplies, and revising the plan. The nurse's daily documentation is the raw material of this monitoring, which is why accurate records at the bedside are an instrument of policy and not merely a chore.

Because an outbreak in one country is a risk to every other, the world has a binding legal framework for notification. The International Health Regulations, revised in 2005 and binding on all member states of the World Health Organization, require countries to detect, assess, report, and respond to events that may constitute a public health emergency of international concern. Four questions decide whether an event must be notified: is the public health impact serious, is the event unusual or unexpected, is there a significant risk of international spread, and is there a significant risk of restrictions on travel or trade. Each country designates a national focal point that must report a qualifying event to the World Health Organization within 24 hours of assessment, after which the organization may convene an emergency committee and issue temporary recommendations. The regulations also require every country to maintain core capacities for surveillance and response, which is the part most often underfunded and the part that matters most in the long run. Reporting is not a courtesy to be offered when convenient, and it is a legal obligation that exists because the alternative is a fire nobody knows about until it has crossed a border.

Most countries also maintain their own notifiable disease lists, which are usually broader than the international obligation and are set by national law or regulation. The list varies from country to country, which is one reason a nurse moving between systems must learn the local list rather than assuming a previous one applies. The duty to notify usually falls on the clinician who first suspects the disease, and in practice that clinician is very often the nurse, which places notification squarely within nursing practice. Notification must be timely, which means knowing the required interval, often 24 hours for the most urgent conditions and one week for others, and knowing the route, which may be a paper form, a telephone call, a text message, or an entry in an electronic system. The report should contain the minimum needed to act: who is ill, where, when the symptoms began, what is suspected, and how the diagnosis was made or is being pursued. When in doubt, the nurse reports rather than waits, because the cost of a false alarm is a conversation and the cost of silence can be an epidemic.

Behind every confirmed case is a laboratory, and laboratory networks are the tiered backbone of surveillance. A typical network has a peripheral level that collects specimens and performs simple tests, a district or regional level with greater capacity, and a national reference laboratory that performs confirmatory and specialized testing such as culture, PCR, typing, and genomic sequencing. Specimens move between these levels along a defined transport chain, with triple packaging, cold chain maintenance, and documentation at every step, because a specimen that arrives degraded or leaking is worse than no specimen at all. Quality assurance matters as much as capacity, and laboratories that take part in external quality assessment produce results that can be compared across sites and over time. During an outbreak the network must absorb a sudden surge in demand, which is why the ability to prioritize specimens and to add capacity quickly is planned in advance. The laboratory is often the rate-limiting step in an investigation, and a nurse who collects the right specimen, at the right time, from the right patient, and sends it with the right form, does more for the response than a nurse who collects many specimens badly.

Risk communication is not public relations and it is not the last item on the response agenda, because an outbreak is as much a social event as a biological one. Good risk communication is fast, honest, consistent, and addressed to the specific fears people actually hold, in the language they speak, through messengers they already trust. It acknowledges what is not yet known, since a message that pretends to certainty and then changes is remembered as a lie, while a message that says the evidence is still developing keeps its credibility. Trust is destroyed in predictable ways: by denying an outbreak that everyone can see, by disclosing information late or only after it leaks, by giving different answers to different audiences, by promising supplies that never arrive, and by treating a community as a problem rather than a partner. Stigmatization is especially corrosive, because it drives the sick into hiding and makes every case harder to find. Community engagement is the practical form that trust takes, and it begins before the outbreak does, when a health committee, trained community health workers, and a working relationship with the local clinic can move an alert from a village to a district office in hours. During an outbreak, engagement means listening as much as broadcasting, holding meetings with leaders, and designing interventions around how people actually live rather than banning the practices they rely on.

Outbreaks end in a small number of ways, and understanding those ways helps a team know whether it is finished. An outbreak fueled by susceptible people ends when the pool of susceptibles is exhausted, either because people have been infected and are now immune or because they have been vaccinated. An outbreak driven by a common source ends when the source is removed, which is why finding the contaminated water point or the implicated food matters so much. An outbreak sustained by transmission from person to person or by a vector ends when the effective contact rate falls below the level needed to keep it going, through isolation, behavior change, vector control, or immunity. Seasonality can also end an outbreak, because the mosquito population or the environmental conditions that drive transmission change, and this ending is real but temporary. Some outbreaks simply burn out for reasons that are never fully explained, which is unsatisfying but common. Surveillance must continue after the last case, usually for a period equal to twice the maximum incubation period, before the outbreak can be declared over, because the last case detected is rarely the last case that will occur.

The period after an outbreak is where the next one is prevented or guaranteed. An after-action review brings the response team together to examine what worked, what failed, and why, and to write the lessons down while memory is still fresh. The surveillance system is strengthened by the experience if the new capacity is institutionalized rather than allowed to decay when emergency funding ends. Stockpiles are replenished, laboratory capacity is maintained, training is repeated, and the relationships built with the community during the response are kept alive rather than abandoned. The people who responded also need attention, because fatigue, fear, grief, and moral distress accumulate during an outbreak and are rarely acknowledged afterward. A health system that treats the end of an outbreak as a return to normal has learned nothing from it, and it will meet the next outbreak with exactly the same gaps.

To summarize, surveillance exists to turn observation into action, and it fails when reporting is slow, incomplete, or disconnected from a response. Indicator-based and event-based systems serve a common purpose, case definitions make counting possible, and passive, active, sentinel, and syndromic approaches each compensate for the weaknesses of the others. The integrated disease surveillance and response framework shows how a district can analyze its own data and act on them, but completeness, timeliness, and feedback remain the constraints that decide whether the system is real. Thresholds convert numbers into decisions, and when one is crossed the investigation moves through verification, case definition, case finding, description by time, place, and person, hypothesis, testing, and control, with the epidemic curve as the clearest picture of what is happening. The duty to notify is legal as well as ethical, laboratory networks make confirmation possible, and risk communication and community trust decide whether any of the technical work will be accepted. Outbreaks end through immunity, removal of the source, interruption of transmission, or the change of season, and they end safely only when surveillance continues well past the last case. Your part in all of this is concrete: recognize the signal, define it, report it promptly, document it accurately, care for the patient in front of you, and keep the community with you rather than against you.

# Chapter 36 — Antimicrobial Stewardship and Resistance

Antimicrobial resistance is not a failure of a drug; it is evolution happening in front of you, because every dose of an antibiotic is also a selection experiment. When a bacterial population meets an antibiotic, most cells die, but a very small number may already carry a gene or a mutation that lets them survive, and those survivors then multiply without competition. The result is a population no longer susceptible to the drug that once killed it, and the change is heritable, so the daughter cells inherit the advantage. Resistance arises by spontaneous mutation in the chromosome, and it also arrives from outside when a bacterium takes up a small circular piece of DNA called a plasmid that carries a resistance gene. Because bacteria share these elements across species, resistance is a common pool that any organism can draw from. The nurse who prescribes, dispenses, or administers an antibiotic is therefore influencing the genetics of a whole microbial community.

Several mechanisms of transfer explain why resistance travels so fast. Conjugation passes a plasmid directly from one bacterium to another through a bridge, and it can move a resistance gene between organisms that are not closely related. Transduction carries genes inside a bacterial virus, and transformation takes up free DNA from the environment, so even a dying bacterium can donate its resistance to a living neighbor. Integrons, which are genetic cassettes that capture resistance genes one after another, allow one organism to accumulate resistance to several drug classes at once. Resistance then spreads through carriage as much as through illness, because a patient may carry a resistant organism in the gut or on the skin, feel entirely well, and still pass it on through the hands of a caregiver. In crowded hospitals and households, in food and untreated water, and along the routes of migration and trade, resistant organisms move steadily between people and continents.

Resistance usually carries a fitness cost, because the protective gene often makes the organism less efficient when the drug is absent, but a second mutation can compensate, and the resistant strain then persists even when the antibiotic is withdrawn. That is why resistance rarely reverses quickly on its own and why prevention is so much easier than reversal. The burden falls hardest where the infections are already most lethal, where the laboratory cannot tell you what you are treating, and where the next effective drug may be unavailable or unaffordable. In those settings the nurse often stands at the point where the decision is actually made, which is why stewardship is a nursing subject as much as a medical one.

The drivers of resistance are not mysterious, and most are visible in any busy clinic or market in a tropical country. The first and largest is access without a prescription, because antibiotics are sold openly by shopkeepers, market vendors, and unlicensed dispensers, and a patient with a fever can buy a capsule without ever seeing a clinician. In many places the purchase follows a neighbor's advice or the memory of what worked last time, and the drug chosen may be the wrong class, the wrong dose, or an old preparation kept in a hot room. This is not simply ignorance, because the alternative may be a long walk, a lost day of work, and a fee the family cannot pay, so buying a cheap antibiotic is a rational act within a constrained life. The danger is that a low, irregular exposure selects resistant organisms while failing to cure the patient.

Substandard and falsified medicines are a second driver, and they are a supply chain problem rather than a patient behavior. A substandard medicine was made by a legitimate manufacturer but contains less active ingredient than the label claims, or it degrades before its expiry because it was stored in heat and humidity, while a falsified medicine deliberately misrepresents its identity or its source. Either way the patient receives a dose too low to kill the organism, so a substandard course is functionally the same as a course stopped early, exposing the bacteria to a drug without finishing them off. The problem is worst where regulation is weak and where a genuine product and a counterfeit look and smell the same. Nurses can act on this by checking packaging, batch numbers, and expiry dates, by storing medicines correctly, and by reporting products that fail to work. When a patient does not respond to a correctly prescribed antibiotic, a counterfeit medicine belongs on the list of explanations alongside resistance and a wrong diagnosis.

Stopping a course early is the third driver, and it is the one most amenable to nursing action. Patients stop for reasons that make sense to them: the fever settles after 2 days, the pills cost money that is needed for food, the side effects are unpleasant, or the clinic is a full day's journey and the family cannot spare another trip. From the organism's point of view the reason does not matter, because the bacteria that survive an incomplete course are precisely the ones that were least susceptible, and they now multiply in a body that has been given a partial selection advantage. The classic teaching about finishing every course has been refined, because some infections are now treated for a shorter, precisely defined duration, but the principle is unchanged: the duration should be the one current guidance recommends for that diagnosis, and it should be completed. Ask directly about the pills left in the packet, because unfinished packets at home are both a sign of failure and a future source of unsupervised self-treatment.

Agriculture is the fourth driver, and it operates on a scale that dwarfs human medicine in several countries. Antibiotics are given to poultry, pigs, and cattle not only to treat illness but to promote growth and to offset crowded, stressful conditions, and they are also used in fish farming and sprayed on crops in some regions. A large share is excreted unchanged into soil and water, where it continues to select resistant organisms in the environment and in the gut flora of farm workers and their families. Resistant bacteria and resistance genes then move from farms into food, into rivers, and into the human population. This is why stewardship is described as a single health problem linking human medicine, veterinary medicine, and the environment, and why nurses should support policies that end the routine use of medically important antibiotics for growth promotion.

The fifth driver is the absence of diagnostics, and it most often forces a nurse to treat blindly. In a clinic without a microscope, a culture incubator, or a reliable rapid test, a child with a fever can be treated only by pattern recognition, and the temptation is to cover every possibility with an antibiotic. Malaria and bacterial illness look alike in the early hours, a viral respiratory infection and pneumonia may both begin with a cough and a fever, and a diarrheal illness is usually viral even when an antibiotic is handed over. When the only available test is a rapid diagnostic test for malaria, a negative result removes one diagnosis but does not say which of the remaining diagnoses is responsible. The result is empirical treatment on a large scale, and much of it selects resistance without benefiting the patient, so better diagnostics are a stewardship intervention in their own right.

The consequences are already visible in the organisms that cause the most common serious infections. The beta-lactam antibiotics, which include the penicillins and the cephalosporins, share a chemical ring that many bacteria destroy with enzymes called beta-lactamases. Some of these enzymes, the extended-spectrum beta-lactamases, break down not only the older penicillins but also the modern cephalosporins designed to resist them. They are usually carried on plasmids, so they spread easily, and they are found most often in Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae, two of the commonest causes of urinary tract and bloodstream infection. An infection with one of these organisms may resist almost every oral antibiotic a clinic stocks, turning a simple bladder infection into a problem needing an intravenous drug and a hospital bed. A patient with a previous resistant urinary infection or a recent hospital stay is at higher risk, and a culture before treatment is especially valuable in that patient.

Carbapenems are the broadest and often the last reliable class of beta-lactam antibiotics, and resistance to them is the most serious development in this field. Some organisms produce carbapenemase enzymes that destroy these drugs as well, and the genes for these enzymes are also mobile, which has let them spread among Klebsiella pneumoniae, Escherichia coli, Acinetobacter species, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. An organism resistant to carbapenems is frequently resistant to nearly everything else, so treatment may depend on older, more toxic drugs such as colistin or on newer agents unavailable or unaffordable in many tropical settings. These infections cluster in intensive care units, in neonatal wards, and among patients with long hospital stays or invasive devices, and they carry a very high death rate. The nurse's contribution to control is unglamorous and decisive: hand hygiene, care of intravenous lines, removal of unnecessary catheters, and separation of affected patients. Because treatment options are so few, prevention is the main strategy rather than one strategy among several.

Typhoid fever, caused by the bacterium Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, shows how resistance reshapes a familiar disease. The organism was once controlled easily with chloramphenicol, then with ampicillin and co-trimoxazole, and resistance to each followed widespread use in turn. Fluoroquinolones became the treatment of choice, and resistance to them is now common across South Asia and beyond, so a traveler with typhoid may need a third-generation cephalosporin such as ceftriaxone or an oral macrolide such as azithromycin instead of the older tablets. More recently, strains have appeared in Pakistan that produce extended-spectrum beta-lactamases and resist even ceftriaxone, which leaves few oral options and raises the prospect of a disease that once needed a single week of tablets requiring intravenous treatment. Because the diagnosis is often made clinically, and because blood culture is unavailable in many settings where the disease is common, much of this resistance is generated and transmitted without ever being documented.

Malaria provides the clearest example of how resistance can undo decades of progress, and it deserves close attention because it is measured in child deaths. Artemisinin-based combination therapy works because the artemisinin component kills the bulk of the parasites quickly while the partner drug clears the remainder, and resistance begins when parasites clear more slowly than expected. The first signs appeared in the Greater Mekong subregion, where mutations in the parasite, particularly in a gene called kelch13, allow a fraction of the parasites to survive the artemisinin exposure, and these parasites have since been detected in eastern Africa. Partial resistance to artemisinin alone is dangerous because it leaves more parasites for the partner drug to handle, and if the partner drug also fails, the combination fails as a whole. The nurse who performs a follow-up test on day three, records the result, and reports delayed clearance is protecting the drug for everyone else.

Mass treatment programs against trachoma and yaws have produced a different kind of resistance, and they show that even a well-run public health campaign must be watched. Trachoma, an infection of the eye caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, and yaws, a skin disease caused by Treponema pallidum subspecies pertenue, have both been targets of repeated mass administration of azithromycin to whole communities. This approach is effective and has brought both diseases close to elimination in several countries, but azithromycin is also a macrolide, and macrolides are used for pneumonia and other respiratory infections. Where the drug has been distributed repeatedly and widely, resistance has emerged in Streptococcus pneumoniae and in other organisms, and the same concern applies to the treponeme itself. The answer is not to abandon mass treatment, which saves sight and prevents disfigurement, but to monitor resistance and to use the campaigns alongside water, sanitation and hygiene measures that reduce the need to repeat them.

Stewardship is the set of practices that keep antimicrobials effective for the patients who need them, and it is a discipline of balance rather than of restriction. It asks four questions at once: does this patient have an infection that an antimicrobial will treat, is this the right drug for the likely organism, is the dose and duration right for this person, and can the treatment be narrowed or stopped sooner than planned. It is not the same as withholding treatment, and it is not the same as always prescribing the cheapest or narrowest option, because an ineffective antibiotic is not stewardship but harm. In a working system stewardship is shared among prescribers, pharmacists, laboratory staff, infection prevention teams, and nurses, and the nurse often notices that a drug has been running for days without a plan. Good stewardship improves outcomes, reduces adverse effects and cost, and slows resistance at the same time.

Local guidelines and formularies are the foundation, because a general recommendation from a distant authority cannot tell you which organisms are circulating in your own hospital. A formulary is a short, agreed list of the medicines a facility will stock and use, with the indication, dose, and duration for each, and it narrows choice in a way that improves consistency and simplifies procurement. An antibiogram is a yearly summary of which organisms were isolated in your laboratory and which drugs they were susceptible to, and it converts your own culture results into a guide for empirical treatment. Standard treatment guidelines built on that local data tell the clinician what to start before the culture returns. The World Health Organization publishes an essential medicines list and model treatment guidance that many countries adapt, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control both publish stewardship frameworks, but adaptation to local resistance and local supply is what makes a guideline usable.

Better diagnostics are the intervention with the largest effect on antibiotic use, because they replace a guess with a result. Blood culture is the reference standard for invasive bacterial infection, and it is often the only way to know which drug will work, but it requires a specimen taken before the first dose, careful technique to avoid contamination, and a laboratory that can incubate and identify organisms reliably. Rapid diagnostic tests for malaria have already changed fever management by allowing a negative result to redirect the clinician away from antimalarials, and similar point-of-care tests are beginning to do the same for other infections. Markers of inflammation such as C-reactive protein can help distinguish a bacterial infection from a viral one in some settings, and their greatest value may be in giving the clinician confidence to stop an antibiotic rather than to start one. Molecular tests identify organisms and resistance genes directly from a specimen within hours, but they are costly and must be linked to a clinical decision or their information is wasted.

Right drug, right dose, and right duration is a single idea with three parts, and dose is where nursing practice has the most direct leverage. Underdosing is not a cautious choice but a resistance risk, because a concentration below the level needed to kill the organism suppresses the susceptible bacteria and leaves the less susceptible ones to grow. Many antibiotics are dosed by weight, and low body weight, malnutrition, and edema all change the volume into which a drug distributes, so a dose copied from an adult who weighs 80 kilograms may be wrong for the patient in front of you. A dose correct for a healthy kidney can become toxic when clearance falls, so a baseline creatinine measurement belongs before the first dose. Current guidance from the World Health Organization gives amoxicillin at 500 milligrams by mouth every eight hours for many respiratory infections, ceftriaxone at 1 to 2 grams intravenously once daily for severe infection, and gentamicin at 5 to 7 milligrams per kilogram once daily with monitoring of kidney function and hearing, but these are examples of what guidance looks like and not a substitute for it. Regimens are revised as evidence accumulates, they differ between countries and between programs, and the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control do not always agree, so the current guideline must be checked before the first dose is given. Reading the dose aloud, confirming the weight, and having a second person verify a high-risk medicine prevent the opposite errors of overdose and underdose.
