De-escalation is the practice of narrowing treatment once the organism and its susceptibilities are known, and it is the step most often forgotten because starting feels more urgent than refining. When the culture identifies an organism susceptible to a narrow drug, the broad agent should be replaced, both to reduce collateral damage to the patient's own flora and to preserve the broad agent for someone who will need it. The switch from intravenous to oral therapy is a related decision, and it can be made when the patient has been free of fever for a defined period, is eating and absorbing well, and has no infection that requires intravenous treatment such as infection of the heart valves, meningitis, or a deep abscess. This switch shortens hospital stay, lowers the risk of line infection, and frees a bed, and in many infections the oral drug achieves the same tissue concentrations if it is well absorbed. The nurse is usually the first to notice that the patient has met those criteria, because the nurse takes the temperature, watches the meals, and counts the days of the intravenous line.

Cultures before antibiotics is an easy rule to state and a difficult one to keep, because the sickest patient needs the drug immediately and the specimen takes time. The rule exists because a culture taken after the first dose may be sterile, and then the clinician is left with a resistant organism that has never been identified and a treatment that cannot be narrowed. The practical compromise is to draw the cultures and take the other specimens first, then give the antibiotic without delay, so the order is specimen, then drug, within the same few minutes. The nurse should know the correct volume of blood for each bottle, because too little blood is the commonest reason a culture is falsely negative, and should label the specimen at the bedside with the time, the site, and whether antibiotics have already been given. The antibiotic time-out then reviews every antibiotic at 48 to 72 hours, when the cultures are often available and the patient's response can be judged. It asks whether the patient still needs an antibiotic, whether the diagnosis is still right, whether the drug can be narrowed or given by mouth, and how many more days it should run, and a time-out that ends in stopping an antibiotic is a success rather than a failure. Nurses can initiate it, because they hold the information about the fever curve and the patient's tolerance.

Adherence counseling is where stewardship becomes a conversation, and it decides whether the plan you write is the plan the patient follows. The patient needs to know what the medicine is for, how many days it should be taken, and what to do if a dose is missed, in plain language and without a lecture. Teaching should include the expected side effects and those that should bring the patient back, because a patient who is not warned about nausea or a rash may simply stop the drug and say nothing. The teach-back method, in which the patient explains the plan in their own words, reveals misunderstanding far better than asking whether they have understood. Practical barriers should be named and solved: the cost of a full course, the distance to the clinic, the need to take a dose at work, the storage of a medicine that must stay cool, and any belief that the illness was caused by something else. Counseling before the first dose and repeated at every contact prevents the incomplete courses that breed resistance.

Monitoring is the other half of safe prescribing, because an antibiotic that is working can still injure the patient, and the injury is often detectable before it becomes serious. Kidney function should be watched in anyone receiving an aminoglycoside or a glycopeptide such as vancomycin, and hearing should be assessed in anyone receiving an aminoglycoside, because the damage from these drugs can be permanent. Liver enzymes matter for the antituberculosis drugs, and a patient on a prolonged course should be asked about nausea, dark urine, and yellowing of the eyes. Allergic reactions range from a mild rash to anaphylaxis, and the nurse should record the exact drug and the exact reaction rather than the vague label of an allergy, because an unverified allergy label pushes prescribers toward broader and more expensive drugs. Diarrhea during or after a course may signal infection with Clostridioides difficile, which requires specific treatment and isolation precautions. Prolonged courses also promote fungal overgrowth, so the mouth, the skin folds, and the genital area should be inspected in any patient who has received repeated antibiotics.

The logistical side of stewardship is unglamorous and decisive, because a guideline can only work if the right drug is on the shelf when it is needed. A facility needs a reliable system for forecasting how much of each antibiotic it will use, for ordering in time, and for keeping a buffer against delays, since a stockout forces substitution with whatever is available and substitution is a common route to inappropriate treatment. Antibiotics must be kept dry, out of direct sun, and within the temperature range on the label, with the cold chain protected where a product requires it. Expiry dates should be checked on receipt and on the shelf, and stock should be rotated so older supplies are used first, because an expired medicine that is given anyway is a substandard dose. When a shortage is unavoidable, the clinician should know in advance which alternative is acceptable and which is not. The nurse who manages the cupboard, records the consumption, and reports a shortage early is performing stewardship as surely as the prescriber who narrows a drug.

Infection prevention and control is stewardship by another name, because an infection that never occurs never needs an antibiotic. Hand hygiene at the five moments of patient contact remains the single most effective measure, and it requires not only knowledge but also working sinks, clean water, soap, and alcohol-based rub placed where the work happens. Clean equipment, sterile technique for intravenous lines and urinary catheters, prompt removal of those devices, and safe handling of waste and sharps all reduce the bacterial burden that antibiotics are asked to control. In outbreaks of resistant organisms, grouping affected patients together, dedicating equipment, and screening high-risk admissions can interrupt transmission when the environment itself is colonized. Vaccination reduces the infections that would otherwise be treated empirically, and environmental cleaning deserves particular attention, because resistant organisms survive on surfaces and a ward that looks clean is not necessarily disinfected. None of these measures is dramatic, and together they do more than any new drug likely will.

The hardest question in stewardship is the ethical one, and it must be answered honestly rather than avoided. In a setting where the next clinic is a day's journey away, where a laboratory result will never return, and where the patient may not be able to come back, withholding an antibiotic from a febrile child in order to protect a global resource is not obviously right. The principles collide: the duty to help this patient, the duty to avoid harm, the duty to use scarce resources fairly, and the duty to respect the patient's own judgment about their care. A stewardship program that ignores this reality becomes rationing dressed as science, and it loses the trust of the staff and the community on which it depends. The defensible answer is usually to treat the patient in front of you with the best available assessment, to document the reasoning, to use a narrow drug when the diagnosis supports it, and to arrange a follow-up that is actually possible, whether by a return visit, a community health worker, or a telephone contact. Where resources are genuinely limited, the fair question is not whether to treat but how to distribute the treatment that exists, and that question should be answered openly by the team rather than silently at the bedside.

The global response is organized around a plan adopted by the World Health Assembly in 2015, the Global Action Plan on Antimicrobial Resistance, which set five strategic objectives for every country. Those objectives are to improve awareness and understanding of resistance, to strengthen surveillance and research, to reduce the incidence of infection through sanitation and infection control, to optimize the use of antimicrobial medicines in human and animal health, and to ensure sustainable investment in new medicines, diagnostics, and vaccines. Countries were asked to write national action plans, and many have done so, though implementation depends on funding, laboratory capacity, and political attention that are unevenly distributed. The plan rests on the recognition that human health, animal health, and the environment form one system, so action in a hospital alone cannot succeed while agricultural use continues unchecked. New antibiotics will help but will not solve the problem alone, because developing one is expensive and slow and the commercial incentive is weak when the drug must be used sparingly. Vaccines against the organisms that drive resistance, including pneumococcus, typhoid, and Haemophilus influenzae type b, prevent the infections that lead to antibiotic use, and faster bedside tests would change decisions more than any single drug. Behavior change among prescribers and patients, supported by training, feedback, and public communication, remains the least expensive and most underused intervention, and the nurse is well placed to deliver it.

To summarize, resistance is evolution driven by use, and every antibiotic decision is a selection pressure that reaches beyond the patient in front of you. It emerges through mutation and through the exchange of mobile genetic elements, and it spreads through hands, food, water, devices, and the movement of people, so it belongs to the whole community and not only to the hospital. In tropical settings the drivers are access without a prescription, substandard and falsified medicines, courses stopped early, routine use in agriculture, and the absence of diagnostics that can tell a bacterial infection from a viral one. The consequences already include extended-spectrum beta-lactamase producing organisms, carbapenem resistance, resistant typhoid, partial resistance of malaria parasites to artemisinin, and macrolide resistance after mass treatment of trachoma and yaws. The interventions that work are local guidelines and formularies, better diagnostics, the right drug at the right dose for the right duration, de-escalation, and the early switch from intravenous to oral treatment. Your part is concrete: take the cultures before the first dose, run the antibiotic time-out, counsel for adherence, monitor for adverse effects, keep the supply chain honest, prevent infection, and speak plainly when scarcity forces a choice. Check current guidance from the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control before you prescribe, because regimens change and they differ between countries, and hold the balance between protecting this patient and preserving the drugs for the next one.

# Chapter 37 — Critical Care in Resource-Limited Settings

Critical illness where resources are few follows a different logic from critical illness in a wealthy hospital. Without a ventilator, an arterial line or a laboratory that runs at night, the clinician substitutes frequent observation and disciplined reasoning for the missing machines. Critical here means the patient can die within hours unless someone recognizes the direction of travel and acts. This chapter follows the guidance of the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and it treats every dose as current guidance rather than settled truth.

The physiology that kills is consistent across malaria, pneumonia, diarrhea, sepsis and hemorrhage. Circulation fails, so oxygen stops reaching the tissues; breathing fails, so oxygen never enters the blood; the airway closes; the blood sugar falls. Each has a bedside sign that costs nothing and an intervention a nurse can begin before a physician arrives. Recognizing the pattern matters more than naming the organism, because the cause decides the definitive drug while the physiology decides whether the patient survives to receive it.

Triage is the first clinical act and the one that decides who lives, so it begins at the gate rather than at the registration desk. The simplest system asks four questions: can the patient walk, is the patient breathing fast, is the patient conscious, and is there severe bleeding. Anyone who cannot walk, who breathes rapidly, who is confused or who is bleeding heavily goes to the resuscitation area at once, while a patient with fever and a rash or a travel history waits briefly. Triage is a repeated judgment rather than a single stamp, and the nurse who performs it must be able to move a patient and start oxygen without waiting for permission.

Deterioration announces itself before it becomes arrest, and the signs need no equipment at all. In the hours before death, patients almost always show one of a small set of changes: a rising respiratory rate, a falling level of consciousness, a falling urine output, cold clammy skin, or a new inability to drink or sit upright. The respiratory rate is the earliest and most neglected sign, and it is measured by watching the chest for one full minute with a watch. A rate above 20 breaths per minute in an adult, above 30 in an older child or above 40 in a calm young child should stop the clinician and demand reassessment.

The vital signs that matter most are mental status, respiratory rate, systolic blood pressure, heart rate, temperature, oxygen saturation and urine output. Mental status is checked with a repeatable scale such as the Glasgow Coma Scale, or more practically by asking the patient's name, the place, the date and a simple command. Urine output is the most honest measure of perfusion in a patient who cannot speak, and a fall below 0.5 milliliters per kilogram per hour in an adult warns that the circulation is failing. An early warning system assigns points for values that deviate from normal, sums them and triggers a defined response at a defined threshold. It works only when the response is decided in advance and everyone knows it, because an alarm with no agreed action merely creates anxiety.

Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection, and septic shock is the point at which the circulation can no longer deliver enough oxygen even after fluids. The infection triggers inflammatory signals that dilate blood vessels, make the capillary walls leaky and disturb the heart and the clotting system, so blood pressure falls, tissues are underperfused and the patient becomes confused, oliguric and acidotic. The signs are fever or an abnormally low temperature, a fast heart rate, fast breathing, low blood pressure, delayed capillary refill, mottled skin, confusion and reduced urine output. In an older patient or a patient with HIV, fever may be absent, and the only sign may be sudden confusion or a fall.

Fluid resuscitation begins with a balanced crystalloid such as Ringer's lactate or normal saline, given as a bolus of 10 to 20 milliliters per kilogram over 30 minutes and repeated while the patient stays hypotensive and shows no sign of fluid overload. The World Health Organization suggests an initial 30 milliliters per kilogram for children in shock, given in divided boluses with reassessment after each, but guidance differs between countries and the national guideline must be checked before the first milliliter is given. The narrow line between too little and too much is the central difficulty, because too little leaves the patient in shock and too much produces pulmonary edema, a patient who drowns in the resuscitation meant to save them. Reassess after every bolus by listening to the lung bases and watching the respiratory rate, the jugular venous pressure where visible, the liver size in a child and the oxygen saturation. Stop the bolus if new crackles, a rising respiratory rate or a falling saturation appear, and in children with severe anemia, severe acute malnutrition or heart disease, give fluid more slowly and in smaller amounts.

When fluids alone do not restore the blood pressure, a vasopressor is started and the flow of fluid is slowed. Norepinephrine is the first choice, infused intravenously at 0.05 to 0.5 micrograms per kilogram per minute and adjusted to a mean arterial pressure of at least 65 millimeters of mercury in an adult. It must run through a secure intravenous line, and where a central line is impossible, a well-sited peripheral cannula in a large vein is used and checked often for leakage, because the drug damages tissue when it escapes the vein. Injection of a vasopressor into muscle or under the skin is never acceptable. If norepinephrine is unavailable, epinephrine or dopamine is used according to the national guideline, and the dose must be verified by a second clinician and written down, because vasopressor arithmetic is a common and lethal source of error.

Antibiotics are the definitive treatment for septic shock and should be given within the first hour of recognition, after blood cultures are drawn where a laboratory can process them. Drawing cultures first is ideal but must not delay the antibiotic by more than a few minutes, because in sepsis the delay costs lives. A common empirical choice for a severely ill adult is ceftriaxone 2 grams intravenously every 24 hours, with local resistance and the national guideline deciding whether a second agent is needed. In children the dose is usually 50 to 80 milligrams per kilogram intravenously once daily, and in meningitis the dose is higher and must be confirmed against current guidance. Where the source is probably the abdomen or the gut, metronidazole is commonly added at 500 milligrams intravenously every eight hours in an adult. Every one of these figures is current guidance rather than settled truth, because regimens are revised and differ between countries and age groups, so check the current guideline and verify the dose independently before the drug is given.

Severe malaria is a different fluid problem from sepsis, and treating it like sepsis can kill the patient. The parasite Plasmodium falciparum causes infected red cells to stick to the lining of small vessels, obstructing the capillaries of the brain, the gut, the kidney and the lung, so the patient is underperfused even when the circulating volume is adequate. These patients are often not depleted of volume, and a rapid bolus can precipitate pulmonary edema and brain swelling, which is why the recommendation is cautious, measured replacement rather than aggressive resuscitation. Give maintenance fluid, replace measured losses, correct hypoglycemia and severe anemia, and avoid the large boluses that sepsis guidance endorses. The specific treatment is artesunate, given intravenously at 2.4 milligrams per kilogram at the start, again at 12 hours and again at 24 hours, then once every 24 hours until the patient can take oral therapy. Where artesunate is unavailable, quinine is given as a loading dose of 20 milligrams per kilogram intravenously over four hours, then 10 milligrams per kilogram every eight hours, and the infusion must be rate-controlled because rapid quinine causes dangerous hypotension.

Severe malaria also brings complications that must be anticipated rather than discovered. Hypoglycemia is common, particularly in children and pregnant women, and it recurs, so glucose is checked at least every four hours and after any change in consciousness. Severe anemia from destroyed red cells needs a transfusion where blood is safe and available, and the decision is made on the hemoglobin and the clinical state together. Convulsions are treated with a benzodiazepine, the airway is protected and the patient is nursed on their side, because aspiration is a common and preventable death. Acute kidney injury is monitored through urine output and, where possible, creatinine, and the patient who stops passing urine needs dialysis or a clear referral plan. Every one of these patients should also be reviewed for a bacterial infection, because malaria and sepsis frequently coexist and a positive malaria test does not end the search.

Severe dengue presents the opposite problem, and understanding why changes the fluid plan. The dengue virus infects and activates the cells lining the capillaries and triggers an increase in vascular permeability, so plasma leaks out of the vessels into the chest, the abdomen and the tissues. The fluid has not been lost from the body but has left the vessels, so the patient may be swollen and heavy while the circulation collapses from a falling intravascular volume. The critical phase begins around the time the fever falls, usually between the third and the seventh day, and it lasts about 24 to 48 hours, which is the window in which shock occurs. Warning signs include persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, a tender liver, bleeding gums, restlessness, cold extremities, a rising or falling hematocrit and a narrowing pulse pressure. The fluid of choice is a balanced crystalloid at 5 to 10 milliliters per kilogram per hour during the critical phase, adjusted hour by hour against the hematocrit, the urine output and the vital signs. Reassess constantly, because the leaky vessels will return the fluid to the circulation as the critical phase ends, when the infusion must be reduced to avoid overload.

Hypoglycemia is a constant threat in every critically ill tropical patient and it kills quietly. It arises from malaria, severe malnutrition, sepsis, liver failure, alcohol, quinine therapy, and the fasting that follows admission to a busy hospital where nobody has prescribed food. The classic signs of sweating, tremor and hunger may be absent, and the patient may simply become drowsy, agitated, convulsing or comatose, so every change in consciousness demands a glucose measurement before any other explanation. Where no glucometer exists, the safest practice is to treat on suspicion, because dextrose given unnecessarily is far less harmful than hypoglycemia missed. An adult is given 50 milliliters of 50 per cent dextrose intravenously, followed by an infusion of 10 per cent dextrose at a rate that keeps the glucose above 60 milligrams per deciliter, and a child is given 2 to 5 milliliters per kilogram of 10 per cent dextrose intravenously slowly. Where intravenous access is impossible, glucagon may be given intramuscularly according to the guideline, but this is temporary and access should continue to be sought.

Severe acute malnutrition deserves its own paragraph, because the usual resuscitation rules are wrong in these children. Their hearts are small and underpowered, their cells are short of potassium and magnesium, and a standard fluid bolus can overwhelm the circulation and cause heart failure. Fluid is therefore given conservatively, blood glucose is watched obsessively, and the temperature is kept up, because a low temperature in a malnourished child signals sepsis and a step toward death. This is also where the dose of every drug must be checked against the child's weight and the malnutrition guideline, since the standard pediatric dose may be too high. The nurse who weighs the child accurately, records the weight in the chart and refuses to let a dose be calculated from a guessed weight is doing important clinical work.

The airway is the first priority, and most of the work can be done with hands, a position and a piece of tubing. A drowsy patient should be placed in the recovery position and suctioned when secretions or vomit are audible, because the tongue and the fluid are the two commonest causes of obstruction. The head tilt and chin lift opens the airway, the jaw thrust is used where a neck injury is suspected, and an oropharyngeal airway may be inserted in the unconscious patient who has no gag reflex. Where breathing is inadequate but the patient has a pulse, bag-valve-mask ventilation with a good seal and a slow steady squeeze can support the patient for a long time if a second person helps and the mask is held correctly. A supraglottic airway may be placed where trained staff and equipment exist, but it does not replace the ability to correct the simple mechanical causes of obstruction.

Oxygen is a drug with a dose, and it should be given for a reason rather than as a reflex. The patient with an oxygen saturation below 90 per cent, the patient with severe respiratory distress and the patient in shock should receive oxygen, started at 1 to 2 liters per minute by nasal prongs and increased according to the response, with a target saturation usually between 94 and 98 per cent. In a patient with chronic lung disease the target is lower, around 88 to 92 per cent, because too much oxygen can suppress the drive to breathe. Position matters as much as the gas, because sitting the breathless patient upright reduces the work of breathing, and the patient with a one-sided lung problem may lie with the healthy lung down according to tolerance. Non-invasive support includes continuous positive airway pressure, delivered with a tight-fitting mask and a simple flow generator, which helps the patient with fluid in the lungs or a collapsing airway, and where a ventilator does not exist the nurse creates the best conditions for the patient's own breathing.

The logistics of oxygen are unglamorous and decisive. Cylinders run out at night, concentrators fail when the power fails, tubing is reused until it cracks, and the patient who needs the most oxygen is often attached to the emptiest cylinder. Count the cylinders at the start of every shift, write the remaining pressure on the chart, and know how long the current flow rate will last before it becomes a crisis. Where concentrators are the main source, ensure a backup cylinder and a working plan for the generator, because a concentrator without electricity is a piece of furniture. Split the flow between two patients only where the tubing and the guideline allow it, and never divide a single source so far that neither patient receives an adequate dose. Train whoever is on duty at night to change a cylinder, because these tasks do not appear in clinical guidelines and they decide outcomes more often than many therapies do.

Monitoring in this setting is a rhythm rather than a machine, and the rhythm is set by how sick the patient is. A patient in shock is observed every 15 minutes until stable and then every hour, and the observation includes consciousness, respiratory rate, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, urine output, capillary refill and the intravenous site. Every drug that is given needs a corresponding watch, because each has a characteristic harm. Artesunate can cause a delayed destruction of red cells days after the patient improves, so a falling hemoglobin after apparent recovery is a known and reportable event. Quinine causes hypoglycemia and can prolong the heart's electrical recovery, so glucose and the heart rhythm are watched, and norepinephrine given through a peripheral vein can damage tissue if it leaks, so the limb is inspected every hour. The point of observation is not the record but the decision it triggers, and a nurse who writes a number without acting on it has produced paperwork rather than care.

Every intervention in this chapter has a harm attached to it, and the nurse is the person most likely to see the harm first. Fluid overload produces a rising respiratory rate, new crackles at the lung bases, a swollen abdomen and a falling oxygen saturation, and the correct response is to stop the fluid rather than merely to note the findings. Quinine must never be pushed in as a rapid injection, because rapid administration causes hypotension and arrhythmia. Norepinephrine causes tissue injury when it escapes from a vein, so the site is inspected hourly and changed at the first sign of blanching or pain. Blood transfusion carries the risk of a reaction, and the patient's temperature, urine color and breathing are watched during and after every unit. Opioids can suppress breathing, so the observation attached to them is the respiratory rate rather than the pain score alone.

Some patients cannot be treated where they are, and recognizing that early is a clinical skill rather than a failure. The patient who needs a ventilator, dialysis, surgery, blood transfusion, safe anesthesia or a diagnostic test that this facility does not have must be moved, and the decision should be made while the patient is still stable enough to travel. The patient who is deteriorating despite adequate fluid, antibiotics and oxygen is also a referral, and so is the patient whose cause remains unclear after the basic assessment. The decision belongs to the team, but the nurse is often the first to notice the pattern and should say so plainly and early. Delay is the commonest error, because a patient who could have traveled at dawn is too unstable to travel by evening.

Stabilization before transport means attending to the things that will kill the patient on the road. Secure the airway, give oxygen, secure at least one reliable intravenous line and tape it well, start antibiotics and antimalarials that are due, correct hypoglycemia, control convulsions, splint fractures, cover wounds and keep the patient warm. Insert a urinary catheter where the transfer is long, so that the urine output can be observed on arrival, and record the last measurement before departure. Send the drugs the patient will need during the journey, including the next dose of antibiotic or antimalarial, because the receiving hospital may not have the same medicines. Confirm that the vehicle, the driver, the fuel, the escort and the receiving facility are all arranged before the patient leaves, and confirm that the receiving facility has accepted the patient by name, because a transfer without acceptance is a journey to a closed door.

Communication before transfer is as important as the oxygen cylinder. Speak directly to a named clinician at the receiving facility, describe the patient in a few structured sentences, state what is needed and obtain agreement to accept. Where the telephone network is unreliable, use the radio or the messenger system the district has agreed, and confirm the arrival. Document who was spoken to, when, and what was agreed, because the record protects the patient and the team. The escort should be a person who can give oxygen, ventilate the patient if breathing stops and recognize deterioration, so a skilled nurse or clinical officer travels with the patient rather than a driver alone. Give the family the destination, the reason and the expected cost, and where transfer is impossible, say so honestly and turn the plan toward the best available care in place, including palliation.

The documentation that travels with the patient is often the only continuity the receiving team will have. Send a concise structured summary: the presenting complaint, the history that matters, the examination findings with the trends, the working diagnosis, the treatments given with times and doses, the results of every test performed, the current observations, the weight, any allergies and the contact details of the referring clinician. Include the trends rather than only the latest value, because a blood pressure of 90 that fell from 120 tells a different story from one that rose from 70. Include what has not been done and why, and include the family name and the language they speak, so that the receiving team can communicate. Sign it, date it, time it and keep a copy, because the record is a legal document and a clinical instrument at the same time.

In many of these facilities the nurse is the most skilled person present, and this chapter should say so without embarrassment. The physician may be miles away, the clinical officer may be covering three wards, and the laboratory may be closed, so the nurse assesses, decides, starts treatment and calls for help in the same breath. That reality requires clear standing orders, agreed protocols and a defined scope of practice, so that acting quickly is authorized rather than improvised. It also requires training in the skills that matter most: airway opening, bag-valve-mask ventilation, intravenous cannulation, fluid calculation, glucose measurement, and the recognition of shock. Task-sharing is not a lowering of standards but a redistribution of them, and it works when the training is real, the supervision is available and the protocols are written down.

Scarcity forces choices that wealthy hospitals avoid, and the choices must be made openly rather than by default. When there is one functioning ventilator, one unit of blood or one oxygen cylinder, the decision about who receives it should follow a stated rule such as the greatest chance of survival within the resources available, applied to all patients alike, rather than the influence of the family or the seniority of the person asking. The ethical discomfort of rationing is real, because the nurse who must choose between two patients carries a moral weight that no protocol removes, and the team should debrief afterward not to relitigate the decision but to name that distress. Stewardship and the denial of treatment are not the same thing, because withholding an antibiotic that will not help is good practice, while withholding one that will help because of cost alone deserves to be named as what it is. Where the resource is absent, the ethical obligation shifts to advocacy, because the shortage itself is a political fact that can be changed.

Documentation is the thread that holds care together when shifts change, staff rotate and the patient moves. Write in a way that a stranger can understand, using the date and time for every entry, writing legibly, avoiding shortened words that another nurse may misread, and recording the clinical reason for each action rather than only the action itself. Record the observations as numbers with units, the drugs with dose, route and time, the fluids with volume and rate, and the response to each intervention. Record the conversations with the family and the decisions they made, because consent and refusal are clinical facts. Record what you were told at handover and by whom, and record what you told the next person, because a gap in the chain of information is where patients are lost. The record is also a legal document and, in an outbreak, a surveillance instrument, so a diagnosis written plainly and a case reported promptly can protect a whole community.

Infection control is critical care, because the patient who survives the shock can die of the infection acquired in the resuscitation room. Hand hygiene before and after every contact, clean gloves for body fluids, sterile technique for every intravenous line, and disinfection of shared equipment between patients are the same acts that prevent transmission of everything from malaria to viral hemorrhagic fever. Where protective equipment is scarce, use it for the tasks that generate the most contamination, and never reuse a needle or a glove as a substitute for washing hands. Sharps are disposed of in a rigid container at the point of use, and the container is replaced before it is full, because the needlestick injury happens when a nurse tries to force one more needle inside. Waste from a critically ill patient is infectious until proven otherwise, so it follows the facility waste route to the incinerator and not to the open pit.

The equipment that exists must be kept working, and this is a nursing responsibility rather than a technical footnote. Check the oxygen cylinders, the pulse oximeter and its batteries, the suction machine, the blood pressure cuff and the thermometer at the start of every shift, and report a broken item the same day rather than the same week. Keep a small resuscitation trolley stocked with the drugs, the airway equipment, the intravenous fluids, the dextrose and the gloves, with a written list and a named person responsible for restocking. Where a solar panel, a generator or a battery bank provides power, know how many hours it will last and what it can run. Surges from an outbreak, a flood or a road crash are predictable in shape even when they are unpredictable in timing, so decide in advance which space becomes the resuscitation area, where the extra beds go and who is called in first.

Critical care in a resource-limited setting still has room for comfort, and comfort is not the opposite of treatment. Keep the patient warm, relieve pain, moisten the mouth, position for breathing, treat fever, and speak to the patient even when they seem unresponsive, because hearing is often preserved. Explain to the family what is happening in plain language, in their own language, and allow them to stay and to help with feeding and washing where it is safe. Where death is inevitable, say so clearly and gently, and make the last hours free of avoidable distress, because a death without pain and without abandonment is an outcome that can be delivered everywhere. Prepare the family for what they will see, including the tubing and the monitors that make a dying patient look frightening, and give them permission to touch the patient. The referral does not end when the vehicle leaves, so telephone the receiving facility to confirm arrival, record the answer, and follow up the survivors, because continuity is a clinical intervention that costs almost nothing.

To summarize, critical care where resources are limited is the practice of substituting observation, repetition and judgment for the machines that are absent. Triage is the first act and the most consequential, and the signs that matter most are mental status, respiratory rate, blood pressure, temperature, urine output and oxygen saturation. Sepsis demands early antibiotics, careful fluid and a vasopressor when fluids fail, while severe malaria calls for cautious fluid and artesunate, and severe dengue calls for small, frequently adjusted volumes because the fluid has left the vessels. Hypoglycemia is a constant threat and should be treated on suspicion, the airway can be supported without a ventilator through positioning, oxygen, suction and bag-valve-mask ventilation, and the patient who cannot be treated here must be stabilized, communicated about and documented before transport. The nurse is frequently the most skilled person present, so standing orders, real training and a clear scope of practice matter, and every regimen here is current guidance rather than settled truth. Check the current guideline and verify every dose before any drug, fluid or oxygen is given.

# Chapter 38 — Palliative Care and Chronic Sequelae

Palliative care is the active, total care of a person whose illness can no longer be cured, and it is defined less by a place than by an intention. It begins with the relief of pain and other distressing symptoms, and it reaches into the psychological, social and spiritual suffering that serious illness creates in a patient and in the family around that patient. The World Health Organization describes it as an approach that improves the quality of life of patients and families facing life-threatening illness, and it insists that palliative care can be provided early, alongside treatments that still aim to modify the disease. That early framing matters, because the phrase is often heard as a synonym for the final days, for the withdrawal of care, for giving up. In tropical medicine that misunderstanding carries a heavy cost, since the conditions described throughout this book generate years of chronic suffering long before death arrives, and much of that suffering responds to simple medicines and attentive nursing. Palliative care is therefore not the opposite of cure. It is what continues when cure becomes uncertain, and it is often what makes an aggressive cure tolerable in the first place.

The need for this care in low-resource tropical settings is vast, and the supply of it is thin. The World Health Organization and other bodies have estimated that most of the people in the world who need palliative care live in low-income and middle-income countries, while the great majority of them never receive it in any formal sense. The diseases that create the need are the ones this book has followed from the beginning. Advanced cervical cancer and breast cancer present late where screening does not reach, Kaposi sarcoma accompanies advanced HIV infection, and tuberculosis leaves survivors with destroyed lungs and chronic breathlessness. Beyond those, the long aftermath of the neglected tropical diseases produces disability that lasts for decades, in limbs, in eyes, in nerves and in hearts. As antiretroviral therapy and tuberculosis treatment reach more people, the number of survivors living with chronic complications grows rather than falls, and the same clinics now carry diabetes, hypertension and cancer alongside infection. Palliative care, in other words, is not a specialty reserved for the wealthy or the dying. It is a general competence that tropical nursing already requires.

Where does this care actually happen? Mostly at home, in a health center, on a district hospital ward, and only rarely in a dedicated hospice or a room with a door that closes. The setting determines the method. There is often no oxygen, no infusion pump, no refrigerator for medicines, no night nurse and no ambulance. The family becomes the nursing team, and the advanced practice nurse becomes the teacher, the prescriber working under protocol, and the person who returns.

Care of this kind depends on a small list of medicines that must exist in oral form, and the most important of them is morphine. The World Health Organization includes morphine on its list of essential medicines and treats the relief of severe pain as a matter of human rights, yet in many countries the drug is legally permitted and practically absent. Global consumption of morphine remains concentrated in a small number of wealthy nations, while the countries with the greatest burden of cancer pain and AIDS-related pain consume almost none of it. That gap is not a matter of pharmacology. It is logistics, regulation, fear and neglect, and it is a gap that a nurse can learn to name and, in some places, to close.

Pain is the symptom patients fear most, and it is the one most reliably relieved when the right medicine is available. The analgesic ladder published by the World Health Organization remains the simplest guide, and a nurse should be able to recite its three steps aloud. For mild pain, begin with a non-opioid such as paracetamol, given in a dose of 500 to 1000 milligrams every four to six hours in an adult, to a maximum of 4 grams in 24 hours, together with attention to the cause of the pain. For moderate pain, or for pain that persists at the first step, add a weak opioid such as codeine, commonly 30 to 60 milligrams every four hours by mouth, or tramadol at 50 to 100 milligrams every six hours, while the non-opioid is continued. For severe pain, move to a strong opioid, which in almost every setting means morphine. Adjuvant medicines are added at any step when the pain has a particular character: an antidepressant such as amitriptyline for burning neuropathic pain, an anticonvulsant such as gabapentin or carbamazepine for shooting pain, a corticosteroid for pain from bone deposits, nerve compression or raised pressure inside the head, and radiotherapy where it exists for a painful bone metastasis. The ladder is not a staircase to be climbed timidly. When the pain is severe at the outset, the third step is where treatment starts, and there is no obligation to begin at the bottom.

Morphine is titrated to the patient rather than fixed by a printed table, and this is the single skill that most changes what a dying person experiences. In an adult who has not taken an opioid, a reasonable start is 5 to 10 milligrams of immediate-release oral morphine every four hours, with an additional dose of the same size offered for breakthrough pain. When two or more breakthrough doses are needed in a day, the regular four-hourly dose is increased by the total of the breakthrough doses, and the process repeats until the pain is controlled. A sustained-release preparation may then be substituted for convenience, but never for a patient whose pain has not yet been stabilized on the immediate-release form. The predictable adverse effects are constipation, nausea, drowsiness and, at higher doses, respiratory depression, and constipation in particular must be anticipated with a stimulant laxative and an osmotic agent rather than treated after it becomes an obstruction. Drowsiness usually settles within a few days and should not be mistaken for impending death. Respiratory depression is uncommon when the dose is titrated against pain, because pain itself opposes the depressant effect, and the genuine clinical danger is that a nurse frightened of the drug will under-dose a patient who is dying in pain. The same principles apply at the end of life, where the dose may need to rise sharply as the patient weakens, and where the appropriate ceiling is the relief of suffering rather than a number in a formulary.

The barriers that keep morphine from patients are mostly not clinical. A country may have signed the international conventions that govern narcotic drugs and still fail to make morphine available, because a national law requires a special licence that no district hospital holds, because the annual import quota is set far below the amount that patients need, because only physicians may prescribe and there is no physician within a day of travel, or because a pharmacist fears inspection more than a patient fears pain. Some ministries worry, with reason, about diversion and misuse, and that caution is not irrational; the answer is not unrestricted supply but a regulated system that counts what it dispenses and still allows a nurse working under standing orders to give the medicine to the person in front of them. Where oral morphine does not exist, an injectable form may be the only one available, and the nurse must then know the conversion, roughly one milligram of morphine by injection for every two to three milligrams by mouth, and must know that a subcutaneous injection lasts about four hours in the same way that the oral dose does. Barriers of distance, cost, cultural fear and family shame add to the legal ones, and a nurse who understands all of them is better placed to work around the ones that can be worked around. Regimens and controlled-medicine rules are revised periodically and differ between countries, so the current national guideline must be checked before prescribing. That verification step is not a formality; it is the difference between relieving pain and causing harm.

Breathlessness in advanced disease comes from many causes, and the nurse should separate those that can be reversed from those that cannot. A pleural effusion can be drained, a large airway obstruction may respond to a corticosteroid, anemia may be correctable, and in a tropical setting a new fever with breathlessness may be pneumonia, tuberculosis or heart failure rather than the underlying cancer alone. When the cause cannot be removed, the measures that help are simple: sitting the patient upright, opening a window, using a hand-held fan across the cheek, teaching breathing that slows the exhale, and small doses of morphine, often 2.5 to 5 milligrams by mouth every four hours, which reduce the sensation of breathlessness rather than the respiratory rate. Oxygen helps the patient who is short of oxygen and does little for the patient who is not, and it is frequently unavailable in any case. Nausea and vomiting in advanced illness arise from the gut, the brain, the medicines and the metabolic state, and the choice of antiemetic follows the cause: metoclopramide when the stomach empties slowly, haloperidol or a phenothiazine when a chemical trigger is suspected, dexamethasone when raised pressure inside the head or stretching of the liver capsule is responsible, and a serotonin-blocking drug such as ondansetron when the cause is chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Whichever is chosen, the nurse should give it by a route the patient can tolerate, which in the last days is often under the skin rather than by mouth, and should review its effect after 24 hours rather than leaving it unchallenged.

Other symptoms fill the days of a patient with advanced disease, and each has a practical nursing answer. Fever may be the disease itself, but in the tropics it is more often an untreated infection, and a fever in a person with advanced illness deserves the same malaria film, the same search for tuberculosis and the same attention to a urinary or wound source that any other patient receives, because treatment of the cause can restore weeks of comfort. When fever is not reversible, paracetamol and tepid sponging relieve it, and the nurse should not forget that the dying patient may be warm from the process of dying itself. A fungating wound that smells is one of the most isolating experiences in medicine, and it is controllable: gentle cleansing, a dressing that does not adhere, metronidazole by mouth or applied to the wound for the odor of anaerobic bacteria, and charcoal dressings where they exist. Agitation and confusion in the final weeks usually have a reversible cause, and the nurse should look for unrelieved pain, a full bladder, constipation, dehydration, a lack of oxygen, an unfamiliar room and a medicine that has been added, rather than assuming that delirium is simply part of dying. When agitation persists and distresses the patient, haloperidol or a benzodiazepine may be needed, and in the last hours a small dose can allow a family to sit with a calm relative instead of a terrified one. Mouth care, pressure area care and the treatment of constipation are never optional, because a dry mouth, a sacral ulcer and an unrelieved bowel obstruction are the failures that families remember.

Telling a family bad news is a skill that can be learned, and in tropical settings it is inseparable from culture. In many communities the family, not the patient, is the unit that receives the diagnosis, and relatives may ask the clinician to withhold the news from the person who is ill. That request deserves respect and negotiation rather than a lecture on autonomy. The nurse can begin by asking the family what they already understand and what they fear, then asking what the patient wishes to know, and then offering the truth in words that are simple and unhurried. Choose a private place, sit at the same level, turn off distractions, use the name of the illness rather than a euphemism, and then stop talking. Silence gives the family room to absorb what has been said, and the first question they ask is the one that matters most to them. An interpreter, if one is needed, should be briefed beforehand and should translate the meaning rather than the words, and a child in the family should not be pressed into that role. After the conversation, write down what was said and what was decided, because the family will remember it differently and the next clinician will need it.

Good communication leads naturally to a plan, and the plan should be made while the patient can still take part in it. Where does this person want to die, at home or in the hospital, and who will be there, and what will the family do when the breathing changes or the pain breaks through? In settings where there is no telephone number to call at night, the family needs written instructions, a supply of medicines and a named person to contact. The nurse should also discuss the limits of treatment honestly, which in a district hospital often means deciding that a patient will not be sent on a futile journey, and recording that decision so that the next shift does not undo it. In the last days of life, the signs of dying should be recognized rather than fought: the patient becomes drowsy, the swallow weakens, the urine output falls, the hands and feet cool, and breathing becomes irregular. At that point the appropriate nursing action is to stop unnecessary monitoring and medicines, continue pain relief and mouth care, position the patient for comfort, keep the family present if they wish, and explain each change as it comes. Anticipatory prescribing of morphine and of a medicine for agitation prevents the crisis call at two in the morning, and it is one of the most valuable things an advanced practice nurse can arrange.

Now the chronic sequelae, which this book has been describing all along, and which are the reason that palliative and rehabilitative care overlap so heavily in tropical medicine. Lymphedema of the leg from lymphatic filariasis, and the identical swelling of podoconiosis that follows years of walking barefoot on irritant clay soil, both progress if they are left alone and both can be halted and partly reversed by a regimen the patient can learn. The limb is washed every day with soap and clean water, kept short and clean at the toenails, and examined between the toes for the cracks and fungal infection that allow bacteria to enter. The leg is elevated whenever the patient sits or lies, exercised through a range of movements to pump the lymph, and then wrapped in layers of short-stretch bandages that create a graded pressure discouraging further fluid accumulation. Compression garments replace the bandages once the limb has shrunk, and shoes that fit the swollen foot must be found or made. The acute attacks of pain, redness and fever that punctuate the disease are treated promptly with an antibiotic and with rest, because each attack leaves the limb harder and larger, and antiseptic care of entry wounds prevents the next one. Where the health system supports them, self-care groups let patients teach one another and reduce the isolation that the disease imposes.

Hydrocele is the complication of lymphatic filariasis that men hide most carefully and that surgery cures most completely. The swelling of the scrotum can reach the size of a football, makes walking and work painful, and carries a shame that keeps men from seeking care even when a hospital is near. The nurse's first task is to name the condition without disgust, and to explain that the fluid is lymph, that it is not a sexually transmitted disease and that it does not by itself make a man infertile. Surgical repair by hydrocelectomy is a short operation with a good result, and campaigns in endemic districts have shown that demand appears as soon as the operation is offered locally and respectfully. Where lymphedema of the leg and hydrocele coexist in the same household, the whole family benefits from care delivered together. After surgery the nurse watches the wound, supports the scrotum, and teaches the patient what to expect in the first weeks, including the swelling that is normal and the redness that is not.

Blindness in the tropics is often preventable and almost never reversible once it has arrived. Onchocerciasis, caused by the worm Onchocerca volvulus and spread by the blackfly, produces the itching, skin damage and disease of the cornea and retina that earned it the name river blindness. Ivermectin, given as a single oral dose of about 150 micrograms per kilogram and repeated once a year in community-directed treatment, prevents new eye disease and relieves the itching, but it does not restore sight that has already been lost. Trachoma, caused by repeated infection with Chlamydia trachomatis, scars the inner eyelid until the lashes turn inward and scrape the cornea, and the surgery that corrects that trichiasis can save the remaining sight if it is done before the cornea is destroyed. Azithromycin at 20 milligrams per kilogram as a single dose reduces infection in a community, while facial cleanliness and access to clean water and latrines reduce transmission. For the person who is already blind, the nurse's work shifts to rehabilitation: teaching orientation and mobility, connecting the patient to a white cane or a community guide, screening the household for other affected members, and treating the depression and dependency that follow the loss of sight. A blind adult in a rural household is often also a person who cannot farm, and the social consequences of that are as clinical as the eye itself.

The brain that survives a severe infection does not always survive intact. Children who recover from cerebral malaria may be left with cognitive impairment, behavioral change, epilepsy, unsteadiness of gait, or a subtle loss of language and memory that is only noticed when school begins. Bacterial meningitis leaves hearing loss in a substantial proportion of survivors, and that hearing loss is frequently missed because no one tests for it before the child fails to learn to speak. The deficit may appear months after discharge, which is exactly when follow-up has usually ended, and the nurse should therefore schedule a developmental and hearing review rather than assuming that a child who walks out of the ward is cured. Where audiology exists, referral is straightforward; where it does not, simple behavioral testing, observation of responses to sound and attention to parental concern can identify the children who need help. Anticonvulsants, hearing aids, school support and family education are cheap compared with the lifetime cost of untreated disability, and a nurse who writes the follow-up appointment into the discharge plan is doing prevention as much as care.

Epilepsy is the most common neurological consequence of a tropical parasitic infection, and neurocysticercosis is its leading cause in many parts of Latin America, Asia and Africa. The larval cysts of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium lodge in the brain and cause seizures when they degenerate and provoke inflammation, and the seizures may continue for years after the cysts have calcified. Treatment has two arms that must move together: an anticonvulsant to stop the seizures, and, for viable cysts, a course of albendazole or praziquantel with a corticosteroid to control the inflammatory reaction that treatment itself provokes. The choice of anticonvulsant depends on what is available, and carbamazepine, phenobarbital and levetiracetam all have a place, each with its own burden of monitoring, sedation and interaction with antiretroviral medicines. Adherence is the real determinant of outcome, and the nurse should treat a missed prescription as a clinical event rather than a moral failing. Stigma around epilepsy is severe in many communities, and counseling the family and the school is as important as the tablets in the bottle.

Chagas disease produces a chronic disease of the heart muscle that can remain silent for decades and then present as heart failure, abnormal rhythm or sudden death. The parasite Trypanosoma cruzi damages the conduction system, the muscle of the heart and the apex of the left ventricle, so a patient may arrive with complete heart block, with a rapid ventricular rhythm, with a stroke from a clot inside the heart, or with the swollen legs and breathlessness of advanced heart failure. Antiparasitic treatment with benznidazole or nifurtimox is considered mainly in younger patients and in the earlier phases, and its role in established cardiac disease is limited and must be weighed against its toxicities. The heart failure itself is managed with the standard medicines: a diuretic for congestion, an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker when the blood pressure allows, spironolactone for advanced disease, amiodarone for abnormal rhythm, and anticoagulation when there is atrial fibrillation or a visible clot, though the bleeding risk in a rural setting must be part of that decision. A pacemaker transforms the life of a patient with a slow pulse and fainting, and a nurse who recognizes those signs should refer before the next collapse. At the end of the illness the same palliative principles apply, and the relief of breathlessness and pain becomes the priority.

Loss of a limb is a common end point in tropical practice, whether from a diabetic foot that necrosed, a snakebite that destroyed tissue, a mycetoma that invaded bone, an untreated infection in a person with leprosy, or a road injury on a highway with no ambulance. The chronic wounds of mycetoma deserve particular mention because they are so often tolerated for years. The painless swelling of the foot with sinuses that discharge grains is caused by a fungus or by a bacterium, the distinction determines the drug, and treatment may require itraconazole or ketoconazole for many months or years together with surgery. The nurse keeps the wound clean, controls odor, supports the limb, monitors liver function when the antifungal is prolonged, and helps the patient decide when amputation is the kinder option rather than a defeat. Amputation carries a grief of its own, and the pain does not always stop at the incision. Phantom limb pain and a stump neuroma are neuropathic, and they respond to the analgesic ladder with an adjuvant such as amitriptyline or gabapentin rather than to more opioid alone. Stump care, shaping and preparation for a prosthesis belong in the same nursing plan.

Rehabilitation is what turns survival into a life, and it is chronically under-provided in exactly the places where it is most needed. Physiotherapy restores strength and movement after a stroke, a meningitis, a burn or an amputation; occupational therapy adapts the tasks of daily living to a changed body; and speech therapy addresses the swallowing and communication problems that follow neurological injury. Assistive devices are the tools that make those gains usable: a wheelchair, crutches, a walking frame, a hearing aid, a white cane, a prosthesis, a pressure-relieving cushion, a raised toilet seat. The World Health Organization maintains a list of priority assistive products precisely because most people who need them cannot get them, and the shortage is as much about repair and maintenance as about the first fitting. A wheelchair that cannot be repaired on a dirt road becomes furniture within a year. The nurse's part is to identify the need during the admission rather than after discharge, to make the referral while the patient is still on the ward, to teach the family how to use and care for the device, and to improvise the cheap adaptations that make a home navigable: a ramp of packed earth, a rope beside the latrine, a chair with arms.

Disability in tropical medicine is best understood through the social model, which locates the problem not in the impaired body but in the barriers the world places around it. A person who cannot walk may still farm, trade or teach if the path is passable, the clinic is on the ground floor and the employer does not equate disability with incapacity. The Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities sets out the obligations that follow, and most countries have signed it, yet the gap between signature and practice is wide. Inclusion means accessible clinics with level entrances and a latrine a wheelchair can enter, information in formats a person with sensory loss can use, inclusive schooling for children with epilepsy or learning difficulty, and the deliberate presence of disabled people in the planning of programs that concern them. It also means noticing that the burden of disability from neglected tropical diseases is largely preventable, because lymphedema, blindness, amputation and epilepsy all begin with an infection that treatment can stop or slow. Prevention and inclusion are therefore two ends of one nursing responsibility, and neither can be left to a specialist service that a rural patient will never reach.

Stigma is a clinical variable, and it changes outcomes in every disease this book has covered. Leprosy is the classic example, a disease that became curable in the middle of the twentieth century and still causes people to be driven from their villages by a fear that outlived the bacillus. Lymphatic filariasis, HIV infection, tuberculosis, epilepsy and mental illness carry their own versions, and the mechanisms are recognizable: fear of contagion, horror at disfigurement, the belief that illness is a punishment or a curse, and the calculation that a sick family member damages the marriage prospects of everyone related to them. The consequences are delayed diagnosis, concealment, loss of work, isolation and depression, and that depression is treatable and frequently untreated. The nurse has specific tools: keep confidences absolutely, use language that names a person before a disease, explain transmission accurately and repeatedly, invite cured patients to speak to the community, involve traditional and religious leaders rather than opposing them, and screen for the despair that stigma produces. Stigma is not defeated by a poster. It is reduced by ordinary contact with a treated person, which is something a nurse can arrange in a single afternoon.

The nurse holds this whole field together, and the reason is continuity. In settings where the physician changes with each visit, the nurse is often the only person who has watched the same patient across months, who knows that the dose was increased last week, who remembers the name of the daughter who does the lifting, and who will still be working in the district next year. That continuity makes the nurse the natural author of the care plan, the person who writes the standing order that lets a colleague act at night, and the one who teaches the family what to do. It also makes the nurse a witness to indignity, and the response to indignity is practical: wash the patient, cover the wound, close the curtain, ask permission before touching, address the adult by name, and never discuss the diagnosis over the patient's head. Bereavement care does not end at the funeral. A follow-up visit or a telephone call to the family six weeks later identifies the relative who has slid into depression, the child who has stopped attending school and the household that has lost its income with the patient. Nothing about this work is optional in a well-run service, and nothing about it is easy in an understaffed one. Scarcity forces choices, and the nurse who makes them should record them plainly rather than carry them silently, because unshared moral distress is the shortest road to burnout.

To summarize, palliative care in tropical medicine is active total care for patients and families facing life-threatening illness, provided early and alongside curative treatment, and it belongs in homes and district wards rather than only in specialist units. Pain is controlled through the analgesic ladder of the World Health Organization, with oral morphine titrated to the individual and with the fear of the medicine recognized as a barrier in its own right, and the regulatory and supply obstacles that keep opioids from patients must be named and worked at locally. Symptoms, including breathlessness, nausea, fever, wounds, agitation, constipation and the dry mouth of the final days, each have a practical nursing answer, and honest negotiated communication allows a family to receive hard news without being abandoned by it. The chronic sequelae described throughout this book, lymphedema, hydrocele, blindness, neurological deficit, epilepsy, chagasic heart failure, amputation and the wounds of mycetoma, are managed with self-care teaching, rehabilitation, assistive devices and disability inclusion rather than with resignation. Stigma is a clinical variable that shrinks under accurate explanation and ordinary contact, and the nurse is the professional best placed to sustain continuity, dignity and bereavement care. Above all, every regimen and dose in this chapter reflects guidance that is revised periodically and that differs between countries, so the current national guideline must be checked before prescribing, and the nurse who verifies a dose before giving it is practicing the same careful attention that this chapter describes.

# Chapter 39 — Research and Evidence Appraisal

A nurse practitioner in a district hospital holds a plastic cassette that has just turned positive in front of a child with fever. By the end of the consultation she will have made three decisions that no protocol can make entirely on her behalf. How much does she believe the cassette, given how it was stored and what she knows about malaria in her district this month? Does the study she read last year apply to this child, who is malnourished and possibly infected with something the study excluded? Is the guideline in front of her answering the question she is asking, or a different question that resembles it? Every one of those decisions is evidence appraisal, and evidence is not something that arrives finished. It is something a clinician finishes, in a particular place, for a particular patient.

Two instincts pull in opposite directions, and both have to be resisted. One says that guidelines exist for a reason and that a nurse who improvises causes harm, and that instinct is largely correct. The other says that the medicine practiced in high-income teaching hospitals has little to do with a clinic that has no reliable refrigerator and no night staff, and that instinct is also largely correct. A guideline is not the opposite of evidence; it is evidence that has already been interpreted, weighed against cost and feasibility, and written down by people who had a particular health system in mind. To follow it well, you have to understand what went into it, and to depart from it well, you have to be able to say why.

There is a small set of questions that can be asked of any piece of evidence, whether it concerns a drug, a diagnostic test, a staffing model or a bed net distribution. Was the comparison fair, was the measurement trustworthy, and does the result apply to the patient in front of me? Those three questions, asked without jargon, will get you most of the way through most of what you will read. The vocabulary changes with the design and the arithmetic changes with the outcome, but the underlying demand does not change. You are asking whether the answer you are being offered was produced in a way that earns your confidence for this person, in this place, today.

Begin with the designs, because the design tells you what question a study was even capable of answering. A case report or a case series describes one patient or a handful of patients whom a clinician found unusual or alarming, and it is often the first report of a new disease, a new complication or a new adverse effect. But it cannot tell you how common a problem is, cannot tell you whether an exposure caused an outcome, and cannot compare one treatment with another, because nobody was chosen to be a comparison. The cross-sectional survey measures exposure and outcome at the same moment across a defined population, so it can tell you how many people in a village have trachoma, how many households own an insecticide-treated bed net, or how many health workers can state the first-line drug correctly. What it cannot tell you is which came first, so it is a picture rather than a story.

The case-control study works backward, and its efficiency is its genius. You identify people who already have the outcome, find comparable people who do not, and compare what each group was exposed to in the past, which is how you study a rare disease without following a hundred thousand people for a decade. Its great weakness is that both exposure and outcome have already happened when the study begins, so the investigator is asking people to remember, and memory is unreliable and unequal between those who are ill and those who are not. The cohort study moves forward instead, following groups that differ in their exposure and counting what happens in each, so it can establish that the exposure came before the outcome and can measure how often the outcome occurs. Cohorts are honest about time but expensive, and they leak participants along the way, usually the ones who moved, died or became too ill to return.

The randomized trial is the strongest individual design for the narrow question of whether one treatment works better than another. Random assignment does not guarantee that the groups are balanced in every respect, but it leaves the way they differ to chance rather than to the judgment of the person doing the assigning. Blinding is the companion protection, because a patient who knows which treatment they received will report differently, and a nurse who knows will assess differently, even with the best intentions in the world. Even randomization cannot rescue a trial in which many participants were lost, in which the groups were compared on the wrong outcome, or in which the analysis quietly excluded the people who did badly, because the design is a ceiling on quality rather than a substitute for it.

Two designs sit above the individual study rather than inside it. A systematic review asks a single answerable question, searches for every study that has addressed it according to criteria written down in advance, assesses each study for bias, and describes what the whole body of work says. A meta-analysis goes one step further and pools the results numerically, which increases precision and can reveal a consistent small effect that no single trial was large enough to demonstrate. The power of these methods is real, and guidelines rest heavily on them, but their authority is borrowed, because a review of ten biased studies produces a confident and precise summary of ten biased studies. Publication bias is a particular hazard in tropical medicine, where negative results from low-resource settings travel poorly, so a review conducted to a published protocol with a search strategy you can inspect is worth more than one that does not say how it was done.

Now the concepts that explain most of the errors, beginning with bias. Bias is not the same as error, because random error is the wobble you get from chance and it shrinks as a study grows, while bias is a systematic distortion that gets worse rather than better as you add participants. Selection bias is who gets into the study in the first place, so a tuberculosis survey that recruits only people who reach a clinic has described the health-seeking behavior of the patients who could travel. Bias cannot usually be repaired by statistics after the fact, so it has to be prevented in the design and in the field.

Confounding is the idea that most often fools careful people. A confounder is a factor that is associated with the exposure and independently associated with the outcome, so it creates a link that looks causal and is not, as when poverty raises the risk of malnutrition and independently raises the risk of infection, so that a study finds the two associated and calls the association causal. A confounder can be controlled for if it has been measured and recorded, but every adjustment is only as good as the variable you adjusted with, and unmeasured confounders survive every technique. Effect modification is different, and the difference is worth holding on to, because it is the concept most often confused with confounding. A confounder distorts the truth, while an effect modifier is part of the truth, because it means the intervention genuinely works differently in different groups. A vaccine that protects children well and adults poorly is asking you to change who you vaccinate, not asking you to adjust the numbers.

Sensitivity and specificity are the properties of a test, and predictive value is what the patient in front of you actually needs to know. Sensitivity is the proportion of people who truly have the disease and are correctly identified by the test, so a highly sensitive test rarely misses disease when it is there, and specificity is the proportion of people who truly do not have the disease and are correctly identified as negative. Predictive value reverses the direction of the question, because it asks what the probability of disease is when the test is positive, and that probability depends on how common the disease is in the population being tested. Nowhere is that dependence more consequential than in tropical medicine, where a test that looks excellent in one district can mislead in the next.

Consider what happens when prevalence falls, because this is the arithmetic that most often goes wrong at the bedside. Suppose 100 people are tested and 10 of them truly have the disease, suppose the test detects 9 of those 10, and suppose that among the 90 people without disease the test is falsely positive in 14 of them. There are then 23 positive results, but only 9 belong to someone with the disease, so barely more than a third of the positives are true positives, even though the test looks excellent on paper. That is why a positive test in a person with no symptoms can lead to treatment for a disease they do not have and to the neglect of the disease they do have. As transmission declines and prevalence falls, the same test performs worse in exactly the same populations, so a positive result is a statement about probability rather than a verdict.

Treatment effects are usually reported in two ways, and the difference between them changes how you counsel a patient. A relative reduction describes how much the risk fell compared with the untreated group, while an absolute reduction describes how many actual people were spared the outcome. A drug that reduces the risk of a complication by one half sounds dramatic until you learn that the risk was 2 per cent without treatment and 1 per cent with it, so the absolute reduction is 1 per cent and 100 patients must be treated for one to benefit. That number, the reciprocal of the absolute reduction, is the number needed to treat, and it is a far better guide to a decision than the relative figure, because it can be set against the number needed to harm, the cost and the adverse effects of the same intervention.

Where clinical management appears in this chapter, the same rule that governs every other chapter governs here. Current guidance from the World Health Organization recommends intravenous artesunate at 2.4 milligrams per kilogram at the start of treatment, again at 12 hours and again at 24 hours, and then once a day until the patient can swallow, followed by a full course of artemisinin-based combination therapy by mouth. Those figures are the ones in the guideline at the time of writing, and they are not the point, because every number in a guideline carries the assumptions of the trials behind it, and those assumptions were made about particular patients in particular places with particular capacity. Regimens are revised, guidance differs between countries, and the current national guideline must be checked before prescribing. A nurse who can say where a dose came from, and what it was demonstrated to do, and what was not studied, is far safer than one who can recite it without that context, and monitoring is part of appraisal, because after artesunate delayed anemia from the destruction of red blood cells can appear a week or two after recovery.
