The largest single problem in tropical evidence appraisal is not statistical but geographical. Most of the world's clinical research is conducted in high-income countries, on patients who differ from yours in nutrition, in co-infection, in genetics, in age structure and in what happens to them after they leave the clinic. A treatment tested in a well-nourished, well-monitored population with reliable laboratory support may behave differently where anemia is nearly universal and where a follow-up appointment competes with a harvest. The health system around the intervention matters as much as the intervention, because an effective drug that requires refrigeration, electricity, a functioning supply chain, a nurse who can give it and a patient who can return will not deliver its trial result where any of those links is missing. And the outcome that was measured may not be the outcome that matters, because a nurse who translates a laboratory value into a promise of survival, function or comfort has gone further than the data.

None of this means that evidence from elsewhere should be discarded, and the honest position is more interesting than either extreme. Mechanisms travel, because the way a drug kills a parasite, the way a mosquito finds a host and the way dehydration kills a child are biology, and they do not change at a border. Pathophysiological reasoning travels in the same way, which is why the same rehydration principles hold from a hospital in Europe to a village in the Sahel. Safety signals also travel more reliably than benefits, because harm that is real tends to appear wherever the drug is used, while benefit is vulnerable to the patients, the adherence, the dose and the system. The skill is to say which parts of a finding are universal and which are local, and then to be explicit about the assumptions you are making when you borrow.

Reading a guideline critically begins with the recognition that a guideline is not a summary of evidence alone but a set of judgments built on top of evidence. Ask who wrote it, when it was last revised, and what conflicts of interest were declared, because a guideline that has not changed in 15 years while its subject has changed repeatedly is a warning sign. The grading systems that most guidelines now use separate the certainty of the evidence from the strength of the recommendation, so it becomes possible to say that the evidence is weak and the recommendation is strong, or that the evidence is moderate and the recommendation is conditional. A strong recommendation resting on weak evidence is not automatically a failure, because it usually means that those who wrote it judged the values at stake, or the practical constraints, to be more important than the statistical uncertainty, and a recommendation is a promise about the balance of benefits and harms under stated conditions rather than a promise that a patient will do well.

National adaptation adds another layer, and the differences between international and local guidance are usually deliberate rather than careless. A country adjusts a recommendation for the drugs it can actually procure, for the resistance patterns in its own parasites and bacteria, for what its nurses are permitted by law to prescribe, and for what its budget can sustain. So the first-line drug in one country may differ from the first-line drug in its neighbor, and both may differ from the international recommendation, and all three may be defensible. The practical question is always whether the patient in front of you matches the population the recommendation was built for, because if she does not, the thoughtful response is not to abandon the guideline but to say why it may not fit and to write that reasoning in the record. Guidelines are also written for a system that may not be the system you work in, which means a recommendation to investigate before treating can be impossible to follow in a place with no laboratory, and the safe adaptation has to be reasoned aloud rather than improvised in silence.

Implementation science exists because the distance between what works in a trial and what works in a clinic is a research problem in its own right. An intervention with excellent trial results can fail completely at scale, and the failure is rarely a mystery once it is examined. A vaccine may sit in a cold chain that breaks, and a new protocol may be taught once and then forgotten. Implementation science studies these breakdowns systematically rather than blaming the frontline worker for them, and it asks about barriers and enablers at the level of the patient, the family, the clinician, the team, the clinic, the supply system and the policy environment. For the advanced practice nurse the practical implication is that you should evaluate the delivery of a program and not only its outcome, because an outcome that was never delivered is not evidence of a failed idea.

Operational research is the kind that a nurse can actually run in her own setting, and it is best kept small, specific and answerable. The question should come from a problem you can see, such as whether a checklist reduces missed doses on a ward, whether a short message to a phone improves return for a follow-up appointment, whether a different dressing lowers infection, or whether the time from arrival to treatment changes when the triage nurse is given a new role. The design should be one that your clinic can sustain, which usually means a before-and-after comparison, a comparison between two similar clinics, or a simple survey rather than a randomized trial. Collect as few variables as will answer the question, and decide in advance how the data will be recorded and analyzed, because a study that begins collecting and then asks what to do with the numbers usually produces a drawer of paper rather than a finding. Sample size does matter, and small numbers produce uncertain answers, so a study of 20 patients can suggest a difference that a study of 200 would erase. The nurse should also decide in advance what she will do with each possible result, and she should ask early whether the project needs ethical review, because work that tests a change in local care with aggregate data may be quality improvement, while collecting information from people to produce generalizable knowledge is research with human participants.

Research ethics in tropical settings begins from a history that a nurse should know and should not flinch from, because the syphilis study in Tuskegee, the deliberate infection experiments in Guatemala and the trials of the colonial era have left a legitimate suspicion that has to be earned back rather than dismissed. The populations that tropical research most often approaches are precisely the ones whose vulnerability makes ethical protection necessary, because they are ill, poor, dependent on a health system they cannot easily challenge, and often unable to read the consent document placed in front of them. They may be children, or women in households where a husband or an elder speaks for them, or people whose language the consent form does not use well. Vulnerability of that kind does not mean that research should not happen, because the diseases in question will not be solved without it, but it does mean that participation must be genuinely free and genuinely informed, and that the burden of making it so falls on the investigator rather than the participant.

Consent is the center of that work, and it is a process rather than a signature. Explaining the purpose, the procedures, the risks, the possible benefits, the alternatives and the right to withdraw at any time without losing care is not a formality to be hurried through at the end of a clinic day. In a low-literacy setting the conversation may need to be read aloud, translated, witnessed and documented with a thumbprint, and the nurse should be sure the participant understood rather than merely agreed. Free consent also has to be free in a practical sense, which means that an offer of care withheld from those who decline is not a choice but a coercion, and a token payment large enough to change a household's decisions is a pressure rather than a thank you. Community permission is a separate matter and does not replace individual consent, because a chief or a committee can open the door, but the person who takes part still has to decide for themselves. Children require the permission of a parent or guardian together with the child's own agreement as far as the child can give it, and consent requirements are revised between countries, so the current national guideline must be consulted before enrolling anyone.

Community engagement and benefit sharing are the parts of ethics that determine whether research leaves anything behind. Engagement means meeting the community before recruitment begins, listening to its leaders, its health workers, its teachers and its women's groups, and asking what questions they would want answered rather than announcing what will be studied. It means explaining the study in the language people actually use, answering suspicion directly, and being present in the community for the whole duration rather than only during enrollment. Benefit sharing means that the community receives something real and predictable, whether that is training for its health workers, medicine where it is ethical to provide it, equipment that will outlast the project, or results that are reported back honestly and in time to matter. Ancillary care is part of this, because research inevitably uncovers problems it did not set out to find, and a plan for what happens to a participant found to have severe anemia, or high blood pressure, or tuberculosis should be written before enrollment rather than improvised when the result arrives.

Ethics committees are the formal expression of this responsibility, and they exist at the institutional, the national and sometimes the regional level, and any research involving human participants is expected to pass review, including studies run by students, studies that use records rather than people, and studies that a nurse considers obviously harmless. The committee exists to be a check on the enthusiasm of the investigator, which is exactly the quality that makes good research possible and that also makes it easy to overlook the interests of the people being studied. One of the hardest questions such a committee has to answer is what the control group receives, because if you are testing a new treatment in a country where the internationally recommended standard of care is not available, the comparison group might receive what the local standard is, or what the global standard recommends, and the two answers are ethically very far apart. That question has no comfortable resolution in every case, and its difficulty is the reason the discussion belongs at the design stage, in public, with people who are not invested in the answer.

The nurse's place in research is more central than the typical description admits, and it begins with recruitment. The person who explains the study and approaches the family is usually a nurse, and that position carries a specific hazard, because a nurse who also provides care can make a refusal feel like a rejection of that care. The nurse is also the person who notices when enrollment is drifting toward the easiest patients and away from the ones the study was meant to help, which is a form of selection bias created in the clinic rather than in the protocol. Protecting participants means protecting their privacy as well, which in a small community may mean being careful about what is said aloud, how names are stored and who has access to the completed forms, and it means monitoring, because recognizing an adverse effect, recording it properly and reporting it within the required time is an obligation rather than a decision.

Data quality is a clinical responsibility, and this chapter would be dishonest if it treated it as clerical. A study is only as good as its forms, and the errors that ruin data are ordinary and recognizable: a missing weight, a date written in the wrong format, a value recorded without its unit, an identifier copied incorrectly from one page to another. Consistency matters as much as accuracy, because if three nurses measure a mid-upper arm circumference in three slightly different positions, the study will report a difference between nurses as though it were a difference between children. Good practice is unglamorous and takes only a little time: training the team together on the measurements before the study begins, checking the equipment against a known standard, recording the unit every time, filling the form completely before the participant leaves, and reviewing a sample of completed forms early enough to correct a systematic mistake while it can still be corrected. The nurse is usually the only person positioned to notice that a form is being filled in wrongly in real time, which makes her the last line of defense for the integrity of the whole study.

Data also carry duties beyond their accuracy. Confidentiality means that a completed form is a person, and it must live in a locked place, with coded identifiers where possible, and with access limited to those who need it. It means that a dataset shared with a collaborator abroad should not carry names, and that a photograph or a voice recording requires its own explicit agreement, because these are not the same as a signature on a clinical consent form. The nurse should also know what her country requires her to report, because some findings, such as a diagnosis of a notifiable infection, must go to the surveillance system regardless of what the study protocol says, and a researcher cannot promise more confidentiality than the law allows. These are the details that make a study trustworthy to the people who take part in it, and they also determine whether that community will consider taking part in the next study, when a different disease needs an answer.

To summarize, evidence appraisal is the ordinary clinical skill of asking whether a comparison was fair, whether the measurement was trustworthy, and whether the result applies to the patient in front of you, which means matching the study design to the question rather than to its reputation. Bias tilts a result and cannot be averaged away, confounding creates a false link that must be measured to be removed, and effect modification is a finding rather than a nuisance because it tells you for whom the intervention works. Sensitivity and specificity describe a test, while predictive value describes a patient, and predictive value changes as prevalence changes, so the same positive result can mean very different things in two clinics on the same day. Evidence generated elsewhere travels for mechanisms and for harms but only conditionally for benefits, so borrowing a result means stating your assumptions out loud. A guideline is evidence plus judgment, and reading it critically means finding out which is which and what the recommendation actually promises. Ethics is the framework that makes the work worth doing, and it lives in the consent conversation, in the accuracy of a form and in the honest return of a result. Regimens are revised, guidance differs between countries, and the current national guideline must be checked before prescribing, and the same discipline that makes you check a dose is the discipline that makes you ask where it came from. Hold all of it together and you will not merely follow the evidence; you will finish it, for the patient in front of you.

# Chapter 40 — Global Health Ethics, Humanitarian Work, and Field Practice

The chapters before this one taught you what to do. This chapter asks a harder question, which is who you are while you do it. Tropical medicine is practiced in places where the health system is thin, where government may be absent or predatory, and where the people you treat have often been failed by institutions several times before they ever meet you. Ethics in that space is not a decorative set of rules appended to clinical work. It is the structure that decides who receives the last available bed, who is told the truth about a diagnosis, and who is quietly left out. The advanced practice nurse who works in humanitarian and field settings needs a working moral framework rather than a slogan. This chapter builds that framework and then follows it into the unglamorous reality of logistics, security, teamwork, exhaustion, and the discipline of leaving behind something that survives your departure.

Begin with the 4 classical principles, because they remain the shared vocabulary of clinical ethics and they are the terms in which your decisions will be defended or attacked. Beneficence is the obligation to act for the patient's good, to choose the intervention that offers real benefit rather than the one that merely looks busy. In a field clinic, beneficence is tested by limits, because you may be able to help 1 person greatly or 20 people modestly with the same 6 hours. Non-maleficence is the obligation to avoid harm, and it reaches further than most nurses expect. It covers the harm of a drug given without a clear indication, the harm of a needle reused because supplies ran out, and the harm of a promise made to a family that the program cannot keep. Autonomy is the obligation to respect the person's own decision, which in practice means consent that is informed, voluntary, and understood. Justice is the obligation to distribute benefit and burden fairly, and in global health it is almost always the principle under the greatest strain.

Beneficence and non-maleficence pull in opposite directions more often than textbooks admit. A child with severe malnutrition may benefit from a therapeutic feeding program that requires the family to walk 3 hours each way, and the harm of that journey to a household with other children is real. The nurse who weighs only the biological benefit has not finished the ethical analysis. You also have to ask who bears the cost of the good you are doing, and whether that cost was ever consented to. A useful habit is to state the benefit and the harm in the same sentence, aloud, before you decide. If the two cannot both be said plainly, the decision is not yet clear.

Autonomy requires more than a signature. Many of the people you serve have had little experience of a clinician asking what they want, and some have good reason to distrust the question. Consent depends on language, on literacy, on whether the patient is speaking for themselves or for a household, and on whether saying no is genuinely possible without losing access to care. In many settings the family is the decision-making unit, and the skilled nurse works with that reality without using it as an excuse to bypass the patient. Where a patient cannot consent, document who consented on their behalf and why. The test is whether the patient, hearing the story afterward, would recognize the decision as their own.

Justice is the principle that governs the queue, the allocation, and the boundaries of the program. It asks why a child in this district dies of a disease that is treatable 200 kilometers away, and it asks the harder question of what you, with the resources in front of you, owe to the person you cannot reach. Distributive justice in a field setting is not an abstraction, because it is the set of rules that determines who is enrolled, who is transferred, and who is sent home with symptomatic treatment because the diagnostic capacity has run out. Those rules must be written down, applied consistently, and open to challenge. A rule that cannot be explained to the people it excludes is not a rule but a preference.

Scarcity makes the principles concrete. Imagine 1 functioning oxygen concentrator and 2 patients who both need it, a young woman with pneumonia and an older man with advanced heart failure and a life expectancy measured in weeks. Beneficence points toward each of them. Justice forces a comparison. The defensible answer rests on likelihood of benefit, urgency, and the ethical priority of saving life over prolonging an expected death, and it should not rest on age, wealth, tribe, language, or the persuasion of the family. Write the criteria down before the crisis, because criteria invented during a crisis are usually criteria that protect the powerful. The nurse who participates in that allocation is doing clinical work, not administrative work, and should be supported rather than blamed.

The most corrosive effect of scarcity is not the rationing itself but the secrecy that grows around it. When staff cannot name the limits, they start to ration by avoidance, by not asking, and by not looking at the patient who cannot be helped. That pattern protects the clinician from grief and abandons the patient. Naming the constraint in a team meeting, writing the criteria where they can be seen, and rotating the hardest decisions among several people all reduce the damage. Moral distress is the name for the pain of knowing the right thing and being unable to do it, and it is an occupational hazard that a good team can share and a bad team will hide.

Now consider the 4 humanitarian principles, which came from the experience of relief work in war and have been carried into peacetime practice. Humanity means that human suffering is recognized and answered wherever it is found, without a prior judgment about whether the sufferer deserves it. Neutrality means that assistance does not take sides in hostilities or in a political or ideological dispute, and it does not mean that the nurse has no opinions, only that aid is not a weapon. Impartiality means that assistance is guided by need alone, with no priority given to nationality, race, religion, gender, or political affiliation. Independence means that humanitarian action is autonomous from the political, economic, military, or other objectives that any actor may hold in the area. Together they form a working doctrine, and each of them is easier to state than to live.

The tensions appear as soon as real actors arrive. Neutrality is tested when one party to a conflict controls the road you must use, or when an armed group demands a share of the medicines you brought. Impartiality is tested when the population you can reach is not the population most in need, because the most needy are behind a front line. Independence is tested when the money for your program comes from a government with a stake in the outcome. Humanity is tested when a casualty arrives from one side of the fight and someone in your team has a reason to feel nothing. The principles do not resolve these cases, but they make the case visible, which is the necessary first step.

Dual loyalty is the everyday version of that problem. It describes the situation in which the clinician owes an obligation to an institution, an employer, a state, or a commander, and a simultaneous obligation to the patient, and the two obligations point in different directions. A prison nurse is asked to certify fitness for an interrogation. A company nurse is asked to declare a worker fit for a task the worker cannot safely perform. A ministry nurse is asked to record a case as something other than what it is, because a certain diagnosis triggers reporting obligations and bad publicity. The nurse is caught in the middle, and the middle is where professional identity is either built or quietly surrendered.

There is no formula that dissolves dual loyalty, but there are habits that protect you. Know before you sign what your contract obliges you to report and to whom. Know which professional codes and licensing bodies hold jurisdiction over you and can be appealed to when the employer is not the final authority. Document clinical findings in your own record, in your own words, at the time, so that a later dispute has a factual base. Tell the patient what you are obliged to disclose before you disclose it. Find at least 1 colleague who can hear the situation without punishing you for naming it.

A serious nurse must also hold the critique of humanitarianism, because the movement's own literature raises it. Relief can create dependency when it substitutes for local systems rather than strengthening them. It can distort a local economy when international staff are paid salaries that a national health worker cannot match, drawing the best clinicians out of the public system and into the project. It can concentrate decision-making in distant capitals, so that a district's priorities are set by a funding cycle rather than by a district's patients. None of these failures makes relief illegitimate. They make it accountable, and an accountable program measures its footprint on the local system, not only its outputs.

The critique also concerns the image of the helper. The nurse who arrives believing that they are the solution, rather than a temporary and narrow contribution to work that locals have been doing all along, will make predictable mistakes. Parachute practice, in which a clinician works outside their competence because no one is watching, harms patients and discredits the profession. Practicing beyond your scope in a remote clinic is not courage, because it is a risk you have transferred to someone who did not consent to it. The dignified position is to name your limits out loud and to build the referral, the supervision, and the second opinion around them.

The argument for local capacity is therefore not a slogan but a design requirement. The people who will still be there in 10 years are the national staff, the community health workers, the district officers, and the families. A program that treats them as the delivery mechanism rather than the owners of the work has misunderstood its own purpose. Localization means sharing authority over budgets, protocols, and priorities, not only sharing the labor. It means paying national colleagues fairly for their skill rather than thanking them for their sacrifice. It also means accepting that a locally set priority may not be the one your organization finds most attractive, and supporting it anyway.

What a humanitarian nurse actually does is worth stating plainly, because the popular image is wrong. The work is logistics, security, teamwork, and cultural navigation at least as much as clinical care, and often more. You will count, order, transport, unpack, and protect supplies. You will sit in coordination meetings where the schedule of a mobile clinic depends on whether a road is passable and whether a militia has moved a checkpoint. You will negotiate with a village leader for a place to hold the clinic and with a driver about a route that avoids an ambush. The clinical hour is the visible part of a day that was mostly spent making that hour possible.

Logistics is clinical care in disguise. A vaccine that has lost its cold chain protects no one, so the temperature log matters as much as the injection technique. Quantification, which is the arithmetic of how much of each drug and supply a population will need over a stated period, prevents both stock-outs and expired stock. A stock-out of an antimalarial in the middle of a transmission season is an ethical failure with a supply chain, and it is often foreseeable. Keep a simple paper register of what goes out and what comes in, reconcile it weekly, and report shortages early, because early reporting is the only kind that can still change an order. The nurse who manages the store well has treated every patient in the queue.

Where clinical management enters the field, give the same attention to the dose that you would give at home. Severe dehydration is treated with oral rehydration salts, 1 sachet dissolved in 1 liter of clean water and given by mouth in small, frequent sips, with a plan to reassess the patient within 4 hours. Severe malaria in an adult may be treated with artesunate, 2.4 milligrams per kilogram intravenously at the start, again at 12 hours, and again at 24 hours, followed by a full course of an artemisinin-based combination therapy when the patient can swallow. A common field antibiotic regimen is ceftriaxone, 1 gram intravenously every 24 hours in an adult, with pediatric dosing calculated by weight, and simple analgesia such as acetaminophen, 1 gram by mouth every 6 hours, with a lower ceiling in liver disease. The World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention both publish current regimens, and you should read that guidance directly rather than rely on a remembered number. Regimens are revised, guidance differs between countries, and the current guideline must be checked before prescribing. Verify the drug, the concentration, the dose, the route, and the interval with a second person whenever the calculation is unusual.

Monitoring and adverse effects are the part of field practice that quietly decides outcomes. Every patient who receives fluid needs a plan for urine output, mental status, and respiratory rate, observed and recorded at stated intervals rather than estimated at the end of a shift. Every patient on a long course of doxycycline needs to know about photosensitivity so that a sunburn is not mistaken for a drug allergy, and anyone started on mefloquine should be warned about and asked about sleep disturbance, vivid dreams, anxiety, and mood change, because the neuropsychiatric effects are the reason that drug is avoided in some patients. Ivermectin is generally well tolerated, but the fever and itching that follow treatment of a heavy filarial or onchocercal burden are expected reactions that should be explained in advance so that they are not read as treatment failure. Write the adverse event down, report it through the channel that exists, and tell the next clinician, because a side effect that is never recorded cannot inform anyone else's prescribing.

Documentation and data belong in the same breath. A field program runs on paper registers, tally sheets, and clinic ledgers long before it runs on a database, and those sheets are the evidence for the next order, the next grant, and the next outbreak investigation. Record the patient identifier, the date, the diagnosis as you understand it, the treatment given, and the outcome, using the same definitions every day so that the numbers mean something. Data quality is a nursing responsibility and not an administrative imposition, because a duplicate entry undercounts coverage and an unchecked tally can hide a cluster of cases. Protect the register as carefully as the medicines, because a lost register is a lost patient history and, in some contexts, a danger to the people named in it.

Security awareness is a professional skill and not a personality trait. It begins with context analysis, which means understanding who controls the area, what recent incidents have occurred, and what the local rules of behavior are. It continues with acceptance, which is the patient and gradual building of consent for your presence among the community, the authorities, and the armed actors who are not the same people. Practical habits include a curfew that you actually observe, travel in a marked vehicle with a driver who knows the route, a communication plan with a check-in time and a missed check-in procedure, and a rule that no one moves alone. Know the difference between a checkpoint that is routine and one that is not, and know that the safest response is usually calm, slow, and unremarkable.

Security also means understanding the boundaries of your own role. You are not a combatant, and you should not be used as one, which means refusing to carry weapons, to transport fighters, or to let your vehicle or your radio be used for military purposes. Coordination between civilian and military actors is sometimes necessary for access and always delicate, because proximity to one armed actor costs you access to another. Accept the security advice of people who know the context, including national staff, even when it conflicts with the plan you brought. Report incidents factually and without embellishment, because exaggeration destroys the credibility the next team will depend on.

Teamwork in the field is cross-cultural by default, and cultural navigation is a core competency rather than a courtesy. Learn how decisions are actually made, who speaks first, how disagreement is expressed, and what a direct question may cost the person answering it. Work with interpreters as professionals by briefing them before the consultation, speaking in short units, addressing the patient rather than the interpreter, and never using a family member as an interpreter for a sensitive disclosure. Gender norms may determine who can examine whom, and ignoring that does not make you progressive, it makes you ineffective. When you are unsure, ask, and ask the person with the least power in the room as well as the most.

Working with national staff as colleagues rather than assistants is the single most important professional decision you will make. Your national colleagues know the language, the geography, the politics, and the clinical reality of the place, and they are the ones who will remain when you leave. Pay them equitably, include them in decisions that affect them, name them in reports, and support their progression into the roles you currently occupy. Do not create a two-tier team in which international staff hold authority and national staff hold risk, because in an evacuation that arrangement becomes lethal. Ask what they need, believe the answer, and be prepared to be told that your presence is itself the problem.

The psychological cost of this work deserves the same seriousness as the clinical content. Moral injury is the injury that comes from witnessing or participating in something that violates your own moral commitments, and it is different from exhaustion. You may be required to follow a policy you believe is wrong, to leave a patient you cannot help, or to choose between 2 people who both deserve the bed. The damage accumulates quietly, and it does not disappear when the contract ends. Noticing it early, in yourself and in your team, is a clinical skill that you should practice deliberately.

Burnout is the later stage, marked by detachment, cynicism, irritability, sleep disturbance, and a loss of the sense that the work means anything. What genuinely helps is unglamorous, and it includes protected sleep, days off that are actually off, a supervisor who listens without turning the conversation into an evaluation, peer support from people who have seen the same things, and a rotation out of the highest-exposure role before the breaking point. What helps less than organizations hope is a single debrief after a critical incident, a poster about resilience, or an expectation that staff will manage it alone. Ask directly about suicide risk, intrusive memories, and alcohol use, and know where to refer someone who needs more than a conversation.

Practical preparation is part of ethics, because an unprepared nurse becomes a burden and a risk. Build the skills your context demands, which may include obstetric emergency care, wound care, triage, basic fracture management, and the use of the ultrasound machine that will be the only imaging available. Confirm your vaccinations and check what the destination requires, since some countries require proof of yellow fever vaccination for entry and some require prophylaxis documentation for certain visas. Arrange medical evacuation insurance that actually covers the country you are going to and not merely the region, and know the policy number and the evacuation trigger. Clarify your registration and licensure status, because practicing under a license that does not cover the setting can leave you and your patient unprotected.

Preparation also covers the life you are leaving behind. Set up your finances, your medications, and a way for family to reach you, and write down the decisions you want made if something happens to you. Discuss the separation with the people who depend on you honestly, including its length and its uncertainty, rather than promising a date you cannot guarantee. Decide in advance how you will communicate and how often, because silence during a security incident is its own kind of harm to the people at home. Anxieties that are anticipated and planned for consume far less of your attention in the field than anxieties that ambush you there.

Plan the exit from the first week and not the last. Sustainability means that a service, a skill, or a system continues after your contract ends, and it has to be designed deliberately. Identify who will take over each task, write the protocols in the language and the format the successor can use, and train toward competence rather than attendance. Plan the supply transition early, and do not let a program end by simply running out of the drug that patients have come to depend on. Handing over authority is harder than handing over a task, and it is the test of whether the work was ever about the patients or only about the organization.

The professional duty to advocate is the last obligation and the one most easily dropped. You will see things that are not medical problems at all, such as a market with no latrines, a school fee that keeps a child out of care, or a road that closes in the rainy season and takes the referral with it. Your witness has value, and it has limits, because speaking out can endanger the people who remain. Advocate with the consent of those affected, with accurate documentation, and through channels that protect them, whether that is a professional association, a national health authority, or a humanitarian organization's policy office. Bearing witness is part of nursing, and it is done most safely as a collective rather than as an individual act of conscience.

Community engagement is the practical mechanism by which those principles reach the ground. A program that arrives without explanation, selects its beneficiaries by a list no one has seen, and leaves without a farewell will be understood as an extraction rather than a service. Engagement means meeting community leaders and women's groups before the first clinic day, explaining what the program can and cannot do, and asking what the community itself sees as the priority. It means managing rumors early, because a false belief about what a vaccine or a drug does spreads faster than any health education poster. It also means accepting that some communities will decline, and that a refusal honestly given is a legitimate answer rather than an obstacle to be worked around.

Monitoring, supervision, and quality review are part of the ethical obligation and not a bureaucratic layer above it. A nurse who supervises others should visit the peripheral site, watch the work, check the register against the stock, and give feedback that is specific and private. Clinical audits, simple case reviews, and a running log of complications and deaths turn individual experience into shared learning rather than repeated error. Adverse-event surveillance is the same discipline applied to medicines, and it depends on staff believing that reporting will not be punished. Where a death is reviewed openly and without blame, the next patient is safer, and where it is hidden, nothing is learned.

To summarize, global health ethics is the practice of applying beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy, and justice when resources are short and institutions are weak. The humanitarian principles of humanity, neutrality, impartiality, and independence give you a shared language, and the tensions between them must be named rather than smoothed over. Dual loyalty is a daily reality, and it is survived by knowing your obligations, documenting clearly, and finding colleagues who will hear the truth. The field nurse works through logistics, security, teamwork, and cultural navigation as much as through clinical skill, and the dose, the cold chain, and the register are all ethical instruments. National colleagues are the owners of the work and the future of the system, so authority and pay must reflect that. Prepare your skills, your vaccinations, your insurance, your registration, and your family before you go, protect your mind and the minds of your team while you are there, and plan the exit so that the work outlives your presence. Finally, carry the duty to advocate carefully, accurately, and with the consent of the people you serve.

# Chapter 41 — Emergency Obstetrics and Newborn Care

This chapter is about births that go well and births that do not, because across much of the tropical world the only skilled person at a delivery is a nurse. Around a quarter of a million women still die each year from causes connected to childbirth, and more than 2 million babies die within their first month of life. Those deaths concentrate in the poorest places, and most follow complications that a nurse with knowledge, drugs, and steady hands can prevent or survive. The World Health Organization counts the direct killers of birthing women as severe bleeding, pre-eclampsia and eclampsia, obstructed labor, infection, and the complications of unsafe abortion. Hear the warning before anything else: regimens are revised, guidance differs between countries, and every dose in this chapter reflects current World Health Organization recommendations, so verify the current guideline for your setting before you prescribe or act.

Preparation is a clinical skill, and it lives on the shelf. Keep the delivery pack complete in one place: clean gloves, soap and water or alcohol rub, a sterile blade, cord ties or clamps, gauze, and two warm cloths for drying the baby. Count weekly the drugs this chapter names, oxytocin, ergometrine, misoprostol, magnesium sulfate, calcium gluconate, tranexamic acid, dexamethasone, and intravenous antibiotics, and remember that oxytocin and ergometrine weaken in heat, so store them in the coolest corner of the drug room and replace stock that has survived a hot season. Check daily what cannot be improvised: a newborn bag and mask in two sizes, suction, a blood pressure cuff, a thermometer, a scale, a watch, a fetoscope, and a light that works when the power does not. Keep partographs, the delivery register, and the referral plan within reach of the bed, and know your blood situation before nightfall, who could donate, where the nearest screened blood waits, and what you will do if there is none.

Every emergency here is easier to see if you know normal labor first, because normal is the pattern that emergencies break. True labor is contractions that grow stronger, longer, and closer together, that do not settle with rest, and that steadily open the cervix. The first stage runs from those contractions to full dilation at ten centimeters, its active phase counted from about four to six centimeters, the second runs from full dilation to the birth, the third ends when the placenta is out, and the fourth covers the first two hours afterward, when most bleeding happens. When a woman arrives, take her story, her age, her earlier births, any past bleeding, fits, or operations, her antenatal visits and test results, and her tetanus immunization. Then examine her: feel the abdomen for the baby's position and whether the head has settled into the pelvis, listen to the fetal heart, time the contractions, record temperature, pulse, and blood pressure, and do a vaginal examination only when it will change what you do, making it answer how open the cervix is, how low the head lies, whether the waters have gone, and whether the scalp is swelling or the skull bones are overriding.

The partograph is the most useful piece of paper in this chapter: a graph of labor drawn against time. On it you plot the opening of the cervix in centimeters against the clock, alongside the fetal heart, the strength and frequency of contractions, and the mother's pulse, blood pressure, temperature, and urine. An alert line marks the progress a healthy labor should make, about one centimeter per hour, and an action line sits two to four hours behind it. If the plot crosses the alert line your vigilance rises, and if it reaches the action line labor is failing and you act, usually by referring, hours before instinct would tell you. In active labor, listen to the fetal heart at least every 30 minutes, count contractions over ten minutes at the same interval, and record the pulse each round, because the discipline of the partograph is that it makes you look, write what you saw, and then see what you wrote.

Through most of the first stage your work is presence, not intervention. Encourage her to drink by mouth, to pass urine every two hours, because a full bladder blocks descent and tires the uterine muscle, and to change position freely. Welcome a companion of her choosing, which measurably shortens labor, and watch for the warnings: bleeding before the birth, a fetal heart below 100 or above 180 beats per minute, meconium in the waters with an abnormal heart, fever of 38 degrees Celsius or more, and the plot drifting toward the action line. Waiting is right when observations stay normal and the plot keeps moving forward. Acting is right the moment a warning appears, and the action may be as simple as repositioning the woman and calling the referral center while there is still daylight and fuel.

The second stage announces itself: the cervix is fully open, the woman feels an involuntary urge to push, and the contractions are long and strong. Support her to push with the contractions in whatever position she finds strongest, to breathe and rest between them, while you check the fetal heart between contractions every five minutes or so. Do not hurry a normal second stage, and do not ignore a stalled one, because an hour of strong pushing with no visible descent means labor is failing, usually from a mismatch between the head and the pelvis. The signs of a baby in trouble are a heart rate that stays slow after the contraction ends, thick meconium, or a mother whose strength suddenly collapses. Decide the plan before you need it, who calls for help, who stays at the mother, and who receives the baby.

The birth of the head rewards gentle hands. Wash and glove, and let the head emerge slowly, ideally between contractions, one hand controlling the crown so it does not spring out and tear the perineum, the other supporting the tissue beneath. As the head is born, feel quickly for a cord around the neck: if it is loose, slip it over the head or under the body, and if it is tight, clamp it with two ties and cut between them before the shoulders come. The head then rests and turns to one side, telling you the shoulders are rotating to fit, so with the next contraction guide a gentle downward pull to free the anterior shoulder, then an upward one for the posterior, and the body follows easily. Routine episiotomy is not recommended by the World Health Organization, because a controlled natural birth tears less than fear suggests, and a cut is right only when the baby is distressed or a tear is heading toward the rectum.

The first minute after birth is shared work, because drying the baby and watching the mother happen at once. Dry the baby head to toe with a warm cloth, swap the wet cloth for a dry one, and lay the baby skin to skin on the chest with a hat and a cover, the rubbing itself enough stimulation for most babies to cry. Delay clamping the cord for one to three minutes, until it stops pulsating, unless the baby needs resuscitation, in which case clamp, cut, and move to the warm surface without delay. Cut with a clean instrument, leave the stump dry and open to the air, and put the baby to the breast within the first hour, because suckling releases the mother's own oxytocin and helps the uterus clamp down. Meanwhile someone is watching her: the color of her face, her blood pressure, and the trickle of blood that means the third stage is moving.

Manage the third stage actively, because that is where hemorrhage is prevented, and the physiology explains the steps. The placenta separates as the uterus shrinks, and the signs are a small gush of blood, a sudden lengthening of the cord, and a firm, globular uterus. Within one minute of the birth give 10 units of oxytocin by intramuscular injection, the uterotonic the World Health Organization lists first for this purpose, then wait for the signs of separation before touching the cord. Perform controlled cord traction only with trained hands: clamp the cord and hold it in one hand, rest the other just above the pubic bone to support the uterus, and pull the cord steadily downward and outward with a contraction, because traction without that counter support can turn the uterus inside out. Twist the membranes as the placenta comes so they trail out whole, then massage the top of the uterus firmly every 15 minutes for two hours, and if you have never been supervised in cord traction, your guideline permits oxytocin and massage alone, done honestly and on time.

Examine the placenta every time, as though a life hangs on it, because one does. Lay it flat, fit the cotyledons together like a jigsaw, look for a missing piece or torn vessels, and confirm the cord carries two arteries and one vein. Measure the blood loss deliberately: collect pads and swabs and weigh them if you have a scale, since one gram of added weight is about one milliliter of blood, and train your eye with measured amounts, because the distance between 500 and 1000 milliliters is the distance between watching and fighting. Then run the fourth stage as a schedule, not a feeling: every 15 minutes for two hours, feel the uterus, count the pulse, take the blood pressure, look at the bleeding, and check that she has passed urine. Most fatal hemorrhage occurs within the first one to four hours, so the quiet hour after a birth is a watch, not a rest, and the baby at the breast is doing pharmacology for you.

Postpartum hemorrhage means bleeding of more than 500 milliliters within 24 hours of a vaginal birth, and more than 1000 milliliters is severe; it is the leading direct cause of maternal death, responsible for roughly a quarter of such deaths worldwide. The mechanism dictates the response. At term, blood crosses the placenta at nearly 500 milliliters per minute, and when the placenta peels away, the flow is stopped not by clot but by muscle, interlacing uterine fibers strangling the vessels like living ligatures. If the uterus stays soft, a raw surface the size of a dinner plate bleeds into the vagina and the cavity, and a mother can lose a fatal liter of blood in fifteen minutes. Hold the causes as one sentence: the uterus is soft, the birth canal is torn, placental tissue is left inside, or the blood will not clot, and the soft uterus, called atony, causes about seven of every ten cases, which is why your first move is always the same.

Run the response as a sequence you could drill blindfolded. Shout for help, set a clock, rub the top of the uterus with your knuckles until it feels firm, empty the bladder with a catheter because no uterus contracts well against a full one, and put the baby to the breast. Give 10 units of oxytocin intramuscularly and run an intravenous infusion of 20 units in one liter of fluid at 60 drops per minute, doubling the rate until the uterus tightens, and never push oxytocin straight into a vein, because a bolus drops the blood pressure. If bleeding continues, add ergometrine 0.2 milligrams intramuscularly, never in a woman with high blood pressure or pre-eclampsia, and never while the placenta is still inside, because it can seal the uterus around it. Where no oxytocin exists, misoprostol 800 micrograms under the tongue is the substitute, and the shivering and fever of the first hour are expected effects, not allergy. Tranexamic acid, 1 gram intravenously over ten minutes, is part of World Health Organization guidance when bleeding is heavy: give it as early as possible within three hours of the birth, repeated once after 30 minutes if the bleeding has not stopped. Meanwhile run two wide cannulas with fluids, warm her, elevate her legs, and write the times as you work.

If the uterus is firm and bleeding still runs, the cause is not atony, and your hands must find it. With good light and a second pair of gloves, inspect in order the labia, the vaginal walls, and the cervix in a full circle, and repair what you see with absorbable sutures. If the uterus stays soft despite the drugs, hold bimanual compression: make a fist inside the vagina against the front of the uterus, press the other hand on the abdomen behind the fundus, and squeeze the uterus between them until the drugs catch up. The improvised balloon tamponade, described many times in humanitarian practice, fills the uterus from inside: push a urinary catheter into a condom, tie the base watertight with thread, insert it sterile into the uterus, inflate it with 250 to 500 milliliters of clean water, and leave it 12 to 24 hours with antibiotic cover. Built from two cheap items, that balloon has saved more lives in remote hospitals than any machine you are still waiting for.

A placenta that has not come within 30 minutes of active management is retained, and the clock is now against her. Give another dose of oxytocin, empty the bladder, encourage suckling, and repeat controlled cord traction only when the signs of separation appear, because dragging on a placenta that is partly stuck snaps the cord and can invert the uterus. If an hour has passed since the birth she needs manual removal, which asks a trained hand, sterile technique, pain relief, and usually antibiotic prophylaxis, and for most rural posts that means referral. An incomplete placenta is its own emergency, because a fragment left behind keeps the uterus soft and bleeding and can infect her days later. Whenever a woman leaves after a difficult third stage, send her intravenous line running, her notes in her hand, and her escort briefed on the sentence that matters at the other end.

Pre-eclampsia is the disease that kills quietly before it kills loudly. It is new blood pressure at or above 140 over 90 millimeters of mercury after twenty weeks of pregnancy, with protein in the urine, and it is severe at 160 over 110, or at lower pressures with the danger signs. The mechanism in plain words: the placenta implants too shallowly, its arteries stay narrow, and distress signals from it make the mother's vessels clamp down everywhere, so pressure climbs, the kidneys leak protein, the brain grows irritable, the liver swells and aches, and the lungs can flood. That is why the questions at every antenatal contact never change: severe headache, blurred vision or flashing lights, pain under the right ribs, swelling of face and hands, sudden weight gain, and the baby moving less. Take the blood pressure of every pregnant woman at every visit, even the quick ones, and dipstick the urine, because the headache she calls nothing at term may be her last words before a convulsion.

The drug that changed this disease is magnesium sulfate, and most low-resource programs use the intramuscular regimen carried in World Health Organization guidance. Give 4 grams intravenously, diluted in fluid, over five to ten minutes, and at the same time 10 grams deep intramuscularly, 5 grams into each buttock, mixed with a little lidocaine in the same syringe to make it bearable. Continue with 5 grams intramuscularly every four hours, alternating buttocks, for 24 hours after the birth or the last fit, and give each dose only if three checks pass: her knee reflexes are present, her breathing is at least 16 per minute, and her urine flows at least 30 milliliters per hour, which is why she needs a catheter and an hourly chart. Toxicity arrives in order, the reflexes go, the breathing slows below 16, and then come the flush, the drowsiness, and the arrest, and the antidote is calcium gluconate, 10 milliliters of a 10 per cent solution intravenously over five to ten minutes. If she fits again give 2 grams intravenously over five to ten minutes, because the wonder of magnesium is that it prevents fits in most of the women who would otherwise have them, and the discipline of magnesium is the counting, since the distance between cure and poison is a rate.

Blood pressure control is gentler than instinct suggests. Severe pressures, at or above 160 over 110 millimeters of mercury, come down with drugs the World Health Organization lists: hydralazine 5 milligrams intravenously, repeated every 20 minutes up to a total of 20 milligrams, or labetalol 20 milligrams intravenously over ten minutes followed by 40 and then 80 if needed, or, where no intravenous drug exists, nifedipine 10 milligrams by mouth repeated after half an hour. The aim is to leave the danger zone, not to normalize the number, because a sudden fall starves the placenta and distresses the fetus. Between emergencies, methyldopa 250 milligrams by mouth three times a day, or labetalol by mouth, holds the pressure as your guideline directs, and fluids are given with an open eye, because these women flood easily and a patient with wet lungs and scant urine has a failing kidney, not thirst. Hold the whole picture in view, because the only cure for pre-eclampsia is delivery of the placenta, so once she is stable plan the birth, and if it is likely to be preterm, between 24 and 34 weeks, give dexamethasone 6 milligrams intramuscularly every 12 hours, four doses, to mature the baby's lungs.

If she fits, your first acts are the airway and the drug: roll her onto her side, restrain nothing, force nothing into her mouth, suction only what blocks the throat, and start the magnesium. Eclampsia does not respect the delivery, because fits come before labor, during it, and up to 48 hours after birth, so a headache after delivery is still an emergency. Once she is conscious and stable she is delivered, and the magnesium continues for a full day after. Her dangers in the following hours are cerebral hemorrhage from unchecked pressure, lung edema from enthusiastic fluids, kidney failure, and placental abruption, the placenta tearing loose with the baby's blood loss hidden inside her, and the fetal heart is your window onto that last one. The women who die of this disease mostly die of delay, a headache minimized at one post and a fit arriving on the road.

Obstructed labor is labor that cannot succeed, and the partograph is how you meet it early. The head is too big for the pelvis, lies in a bad position, or a shoulder blocks the way, and the picture is strong contractions with a cervix that has stopped opening and a baby that has stopped descending. The clues gather one by one: the plot crosses the alert line and then the action line, the scalp swells into a soft bump, the skull bones override with molding you can feel growing hour by hour, the bladder will not empty by itself, the mother turns exhausted, dehydrated, and feverish, and the fetal heart slows again and again as the head is crushed. The last warning is a groove rising between the upper and lower parts of the uterus, a band you can see and feel, which means the wall is stretched toward tearing, and when you can put a hand on that groove, waiting is over.

Now the honest part: what to do when the operation that fixes obstruction is a day away by road. The delay changes the plan but not the nursing, because she still needs an intravenous line running, a catheter to watch her urine, nothing by mouth, position changes, and antibiotics if her waters have been open for many hours or she has fever, since sepsis travels with obstruction. The delay forbids the temptation: never give oxytocin to augment an obstructed labor, because the drug can rupture the uterus, and a rupture on a road turns a rescue into a funeral. If the head is low and the failure is in the second stage, an operator trained in the vacuum may finish the birth, but a vacuum pulled by an untrained hand tears the baby's scalp, so know your level and say it aloud. Arrange transport at the first crossing of the action line, with an escort who knows the story, a referral letter in her hand, a call made ahead, and the road driven in daylight where possible. Sometimes the baby has already died by the time the decision is made, and then every step serves the mother's survival, because the birth must still happen somewhere, and the grief needs a plan too.

Turn now to the newborn, and hold resuscitation as a drill, because its steps are few enough to practice until they happen by themselves. The first minute after birth decides more than the next hour, and the World Health Organization's basic newborn resuscitation course, like programs called Helping Babies Breathe, builds everything around that minute. Before every birth lay out a warm dry surface, two warm cloths, a bag and mask in newborn size, suction, and a working light, and squeeze the bag against your palm to prove it works. The sequence: dry the baby at once and thoroughly, swap the wet cloth for a dry one, position the head neutral with the neck slightly extended, clear the mouth first and then the nose only if they are blocked, and rub the back and soles to stimulate breathing, never probing deep in the throat of a baby who is breathing, because the reflex it triggers can stop breathing altogether. A baby who is crying, breathing easily, and holding good tone goes to the mother and needs nothing more, while a baby who is not breathing, or who is gasping, those slow seagull sighs, needs ventilation now.

Ventilation is the skill that saves, and oxygen is the afterthought. Take a mask that covers the mouth, chin, and nose without pressing the eyes, seal it with your fingers in a ring around the edges, lift the jaw toward it, and squeeze the bag about 40 times a minute, even and unhurried, watching for the chest to rise. If the chest does not move, reposition the head before blaming the bag, because a bad seal and a bad position explain almost every failure, and after a minute of good ventilation you reassess aloud: heart rate, breathing, color. If the heart rate stays below 60 beats per minute despite a moving chest, add chest compressions, three pushes to one breath at about 120 events a minute with two thumbs on the breastbone, done only by a person trained in them. Room air is the first choice for nearly all babies, and oxygen is added only if a baby stays blue in the center despite a rising chest, and only where oxygen exists. Reassess every minute and let the team hear the numbers, because the hardest honest sentence in this drill is that if after 20 minutes of good ventilation the heart has never started, the baby will not come back, and what follows is care for the parents.

Survival of a newborn in a cold clinic is a chain, and every link is free: a warm room, a hat, skin to skin, bathing delayed to at least the second day, and kangaroo positioning for the small one. Weigh every baby before its first long sleep, because a baby below 2500 grams is the one who dies on a mild night with a temperature of 35.5 degrees Celsius. The danger signs of the first days are fast breathing over 60 per minute, grunting, the chest sucking inward, a blue face, floppiness, refusal to feed, cold skin, and convulsions, and each is a referral sign. Give every baby vitamin K, 1 milligram intramuscularly once, as the World Health Organization's newborn guidance directs, keep the cord clean, dry, and uncovered, and feed within the first hour and often after, because a newborn's sugar is measured in hours.

Kangaroo mother care is the low-resource answer to the incubator. A baby born early or small cannot hold its temperature, because the skin is thin, the fat is absent, and the body surface is vast for the weight, and an incubator solves that with electricity, spare parts, and a technician, all of which a remote post lacks. The mother's chest solves it with biology, because her chest warms and cools with the baby's needs, a synchrony found in every study that has looked for it. The method is strict but simple: a stable baby below 2000 grams is placed upright between the breasts, head turned to one side, held by a wide cloth wrapped around both chests, wearing a hat, in continuous skin contact day and night, freed only for washing and the toilet, and fed breast milk alone while the family shares the holding so the mother sleeps. Done this way deaths fall, breastfeeding rises, infection drops, and discharge comes sooner, and the effect travels home, because the incubator is a person: this is the most beautiful economy in tropical medicine.

Documentation is the least glamorous part of this chapter and the part that makes the next birth safer, because notes are how a place learns. Write every delivery up during or immediately after it, never reconstructed later from memory. The record holds the woman's story and antenatal facts, the times of labor onset, arrival, rupture of the membranes, full dilation, the birth, and the placenta, the completed partograph, every drug with its dose, route, and clock time, the weighed or estimated blood loss, the state of the perineum, and for the baby the weight, temperature, condition at one and five minutes, resuscitation steps in order, vitamin K, and the first feed. The delivery register, kept in sequence, is both the district's data and your program's memory, and the counts of hemorrhages, fits, and resuscitations, read over months, tell you what to drill next, while referral letters travel with the woman, a copy stays behind, and a phone call follows the letter, because papers get lost on roads. Review the emergencies as a team, reading near misses aloud and asking not who erred but what the system needed, and write in ink, write legibly, and never write what you did not do.

Your role in this work is wider than your hands. You are the person who trains the traditional birth attendant to recognize danger signs and to come early rather than late, and who drills the cleaner and the midwife in the same sequence until it is muscle, and even a two-person team assigns its roles out loud before the emergency, one at the mother's head, one for the baby, with the phone numbers on the wall. Consent and dignity travel with the medicine: explain what you will do, welcome the companion she chooses, and honor the modesty her culture and faith expect, because a woman who trusts the post comes before the emergency, not after it. When a birth goes wrong the debrief is for you too, because a traumatic delivery lodges in the person who held the mask, and saying it aloud to a colleague, sleeping, and asking for supervision are clinical skills, not indulgences. Knowing your limits is the last tool in this chapter, and saying that this is beyond me while calling for help is the act that makes it safe for you to practice alone.

To summarize, a safe birth at a remote post is prepared long before the contractions start: a checked shelf, a partograph plotted honestly, and a team that has drilled hemorrhage, eclampsia, and the newborn minute until they happen by reflex. Recognize normal labor so you can recognize its failure, and act when the graph, the heart rate, or the mother herself tells you to. Manage the third stage actively with oxytocin, controlled cord traction in trained hands, and massage, and answer hemorrhage with the drilled order: rub the uterus, empty the bladder, give the uterotonics in their right sequence, tranexamic acid, compression, and the condom balloon, calling early for help and blood. Treat pre-eclampsia as the quiet emergency it is, run magnesium sulfate with its hourly checks of reflexes, breathing, and urine, lower only the dangerously high pressures, and remember that delivery is the cure. Read obstruction from the partograph before the uterus warns you with a groove, refer at the action line, and never augment an obstructed labor. Give the newborn the golden minute of drying, warmth, airway, and ventilation with room air, then keep the small baby warm on the mother's chest, the incubator that never fails. Every dose in this chapter reflects current World Health Organization guidance, but regimens are revised and guidance differs between countries, so verify the current guideline before you act, and write every birth down so that the next one is safer.

# Chapter 42 — Trauma, Wound Care, and Minor Surgery

Trauma reaches the remote clinic before any other emergency does. Road traffic injuries, falls from heights, burns from open cooking fires, and machete or animal wounds arrive together, and the nearest surgeon may be a full day of travel away. In that geography, the advanced practice nurse is not the assistant to a trauma team; you are the trauma team, and the decisions usually fall to whoever holds the dressing tray. This chapter walks through the skills that save the most: the primary survey, the control of bleeding, the judgment of which wound to close and which to leave open, abscess drainage, debridement, burns, splints, chest drains, and the prevention of tetanus and rabies. Where a dose or a schedule appears, it reflects current published guidance, and you must verify the current version before you act.

The primary survey exists to prevent one specific error: letting a dramatic wound distract you while the patient quietly dies of something you never checked. The order never changes, and it is worth saying aloud until it is automatic: airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure. Before any of it, stop at the edge of the scene and look for what creates second victims, which means moving traffic, leaking fuel, unstable structures, a live wire, or an angry crowd. Once the scene is safe, work in the fixed order, because a blocked airway kills in minutes and a crushed leg, however terrible, does not. Talk as you work, since a patient who answers in clear sentences has, at that moment, a working airway and a working brain, and that single observation is the fastest triage tool you own. If helpers are present, assign one to hold the head still, because any blow violent enough to cause visible injuries is violent enough to break the cervical spine.

The airway comes first, and the maneuver matters more than any equipment. If the voice is hoarse, the breathing gurgles, or the patient is unconscious, open the airway with a jaw thrust, which lifts the tongue forward without tilting the neck, and keep the head held still with hands while you check breathing. Look at the chest, listen at the mouth, and feel air on your cheek, spending seconds, not minutes. A hole in the chest that sucks air with every breath is sealed first with an occlusive dressing taped on three sides, so that air can escape but not return. An unconscious patient who is breathing goes onto the side, rolled as one unit with the spine protected, because a relaxed airway left flat will flood. Simple positioning, the recovery position, and clearing debris save more airways in remote settings than any device that is not on the shelf.

Breathing assessed, move to circulation, and in trauma that word means bleeding. Let your eyes lead your hands: scan the scalp, the chest, the abdomen, both flanks, the thighs, and the ground beneath, because a patient lying in a spreading pool has already lost more than a liter. A fast, thin pulse with cold, pale, anxious skin means shock until proven otherwise, and the bleeding that causes it is usually on the outside, which is the good news, because you can reach it. Disability is a rapid check of consciousness, pupil size, and one-sided weakness, telling you whether the brain is injured along with the body. Exposure means undressing enough to find every wound, then covering the patient again at once, because a cold trauma patient bleeds worse. Only after these five steps comes the secondary survey, a head-to-toe examination with the mechanism, the allergies, the medications, the last meal, and the events, taken from witnesses when the patient cannot speak.

Hemorrhage control deserves its own minutes, because bleeding is the most preventable cause of trauma death. Direct pressure stops most external bleeding by pressing the vessel walls together so a clot can form, and it works only when it is truly direct. Lay a thick pad of clean cloth on the wound, press hard with the heel of your hand, and do not lift the pad to peek, because every peek destroys the clot that is forming. If the pad soaks through, add layers on top rather than removing them. Hold real pressure for a full ten minutes when the situation allows, since impatience, not technique, is the usual reason for failure.

Some wounds cannot be pressed against a bone, and these are the ones that need packing: the groin, the armpit, the neck, the buttock, and the deep thigh. Packing fills the cavity with gauze or clean cloth firmly enough to create pressure from inside, squeezing the bleeding vessel's walls shut. Fill from the depth upward, layer by layer, pressing each layer down before adding the next, so that the cavity is filled rather than plugged at its mouth. If hemostatic gauze, the kind carrying a clotting agent, is on the shelf, it goes against the deepest bleeding point first, held with pressure for the time stated on the package, usually about three minutes. Plain gauze works too, but a deep thigh wound can swallow several meters of bandage before the bleeding slows. Leave the pack in place for at least a day before opening and cleaning the wound again, and that delay is a deliberate part of the treatment, not neglect.

The tourniquet is for the limb wound that floods despite pressure, meaning amputations, mangling injuries, and major vessel wounds, and for the trapped patient who must be freed or carried. Place it 5 to 7 centimeters above the wound, never over a joint, and tighten until the bleeding stops and the pulse beyond it disappears, which takes real force and hurts. A commercial tourniquet is best, but a folded cloth about 5 centimeters wide, twisted tight with a stick as a windlass, works, while wire, string, or a narrow cord cuts skin without stopping the flow. Write the time on the forehead or on the tourniquet, and once bleeding is controlled, do not loosen it in the field without training, since each loosening restarts the bleeding and wastes the clot. The complications are real, with pain, nerve injury, and limb loss after two hours or more, so a tourniquet is a bridge to repair, never the repair. Tell the receiving clinician about it and its time, and teach the technique widely in your community, because most rural bleeding deaths happen before any clinic is reached.

Once the patient is stable, every wound gets the same four questions before anything is cleaned. How did it happen, because glass on clean skin, a machete through mud, and a tooth over a knuckle carry different risks. How long ago, because bacterial counts in a wound double every hour or so in a warm climate, and time is the wound's worst enemy. How dirty, meaning soil, saliva, river water, dead tissue, or a foreign body left inside, remembering that a puncture drives contamination deep where you cannot reach. And what lies beneath the skin at that spot, which you test by asking the patient to move everything the wound could cross and by checking pulses, sensation, and strength beyond it. A wound crossing a joint, opening a tendon sheath, exposing bone, made by a bite, or sitting over a fracture belongs to surgical hands, and it is better to transfer a stable patient with an open tendon than to close over one.

The decision to close a wound is a decision about bacteria. A freshly cut, clean wound closed within the first hours heals quietly, because living tissue can defend the small numbers present. A contaminated wound closed tightly seals bacteria inside a warm, airless space with no drainage and no defense, which is the exact recipe for a closed abscess, and in a tropical climate the recipe succeeds with terrible reliability. That is why not closing is often the correct answer in remote practice, and it is a mark of experience rather than defeat. Classic teaching allows primary closure within about 6 hours for clean wounds, and up to 24 hours on the face, but the clock matters less than the wound itself. A wound that looks clean and freshly made can usually be closed, and a wound that looks angry never should be, whatever the clock says.

Delayed primary closure works like this: clean the wound thoroughly, leave it open under a loose dressing, and look again after 48 to 72 hours. If it is clean then, with no fever, spreading redness, or pus, bring the edges together with a few sutures, and it will heal as though it had been closed on the first day. If it is not clean, it declares itself while still open, and you have lost nothing but a short wait. Healing by secondary intention means letting the wound fill with new tissue from its floor, contracting slowly over weeks, and it is the natural path for punctures, bites, and heavily contaminated wounds. Keep such wounds clean and dressed, protect them from flies, and tell the patient honestly that healing will take weeks and leave a scar, which is a fair price for avoiding an infection under a closed skin. The face, with its rich blood supply, forgives closure more readily, while the lower leg, where swelling and poor venous return slow everything, forgives almost nothing dirty.

Whatever you decide about closing, irrigation comes first, and its lesson is that the volume of clean fluid removes bacteria and debris mechanically, so that nothing you pour into a wound adds as much as it removes. Irrigate with normal saline where it exists, or with boiled and cooled water, or with any water fit for drinking, since studies have found no meaningful difference in infection rates among them, and a liter flushed through a wound beats any antiseptic. Use a 20 to 60 milliliter syringe with a cannula, aiming a stream at moderate pressure across the wound and out again, letting the dirty fluid run off the lowest edge into a basin. Avoid jet-like pressure, which can drive contamination deeper and splash blood toward your eyes. Antiseptics belong on the intact skin around the wound, not in it: alcohol and hydrogen peroxide damage the living tissue you are trying to save, and povidone-iodine inside the wound should be dilute and brief if used at all. Wear gloves and eye protection, wash hands between patients, and remember that the wound must be protected from your bacteria as much as from the patient's.

Debridement is the removal of what cannot live: crushed fat, gray muscle that does not bleed when cut, fragments detached from any blood supply, and tissue already decayed. Dead tissue is not a bystander but food for bacteria, a barrier to antibiotics, and the reason small wounds become large infections. Under good local anesthesia, lift the dead material with forceps and cut it away in small increments, working until bright bleeding appears from every edge, which is the reliable sign of living tissue. Color is a weaker guide than bleeding and contractility, since viable muscle is red and twitches when touched, while dead muscle is dull and still. Stop when the wound is clean, not when it is pretty, and be conservative over tendons, joints, and nerves, which deserve the chance to recover if they have any attachment at all. Wounds needing repeated formal debridement, or debridement that would open a joint or expose major vessels, belong to surgical hands, and your work is to clean, dress, stabilize, and arrange the transfer.
