Nothing in wound care justifies skipping anesthesia, because the pain of repair is itself a reason patients stay away. Lidocaine 1 per cent, which is 10 milligrams per milliliter, infiltrated through a fine needle just under the skin at the wound edges, blocks the sodium channels that carry pain, with a maximum safe dose of 3 milligrams per kilogram of body weight without epinephrine and 5 milligrams per kilogram with it. Injecting slowly through the wound edge rather than through intact skin hurts less, and warming the solution helps too. Inflamed tissue defeats lidocaine because infection makes tissue acidic and the drug cannot reach the nerve, which is why anesthesia around an abscess is so unrewarding. Watch for systemic toxicity as you infiltrate, with numbness of the tongue and lips, ringing in the ears, slurred speech, confusion, and at worst a seizure, and stop injecting at the first sign. For fingers and toes, a ring of plain lidocaine at the base anesthetizes the whole digit and keeps you out of a painful wound bed. The limits given here follow widely published guidance, but verify the current one before you infiltrate, since recommendations are revised from time to time.

Suturing by voice begins with materials. Nonabsorbable sutures, most commonly nylon or polypropylene, are for skin: they hold until the wound has healed, and are then removed. Absorbable sutures, such as polyglactin, are for the layers beneath the skin, for fascia, muscle, and the inside of the mouth, dissolving over weeks so that nothing must be fished out later. Silk handles pleasantly but provokes tissue reaction and is a poor choice in contaminated wounds. Sizes are spoken by number, with 3-0 or 4-0 for skin on trunk and limbs, 5-0 for the face and hands where scars should be fine, and 2-0 for the scalp and for repairs under tension. The needle is curved: skin takes a cutting needle, whose sharp edges pass through tough hide cleanly, while deeper layers take a round-bodied tapered needle that spreads rather than slices. Sutures come packaged sterile with the needle already attached, and a stocked, resterilized instrument set, autoclaved where power allows or boiled for a full 15 minutes where it does not, is worth more to your patients than any antiseptic on the shelf.

The simple interrupted suture is the stitch to master, and it is best spoken as a cycle. Grip the needle a third of the way back from its point, enter the skin about 5 millimeters from the wound edge, and drive the point downward and forward through the full thickness, letting the needle travel its own curve rather than forcing it. Emerge on the cut surface at the depth where you will enter the other side, because matched depth is what makes the edges meet level. Cross the wound, take the matching bite, and roll the needle out through the skin 5 millimeters beyond, so that the two bites and the wound floor form one symmetric loop. Tie with the instrument in your hand, placing the first throw double, flattening the knot to the side of the wound rather than on the line, and cinch until the edges just touch, never tighter, because strangled skin swells and dies. Cut the tails to about half a centimeter, place the next stitch 5 to 10 millimeters along, and keep checking your work, since the edges should sit slightly raised and meeting at the surface.

Two mattress techniques solve what the simple stitch cannot. The vertical mattress takes a deep bite far from the edge and a shallow bite close to it on the same side before crossing, closing dead space underneath and everting stubborn edges, and it is the stitch for wounds that keep springing apart. The horizontal mattress spreads tension across two bites on each side, useful over a joint or on a shin where skin cannot be brought together without help, and both mattress stitches are spaced more widely and released earlier if the skin blanches, because their tension is their purpose and their danger. Not every wound needs a needle at all: shallow, clean, low-tension wounds do well with wound adhesive or with adhesive strips anchored across the cleaned edges, and every stitch you avoid is pain spared and a supply preserved. Removal timing follows the skin's healing rate, with face sutures out at 5 to 7 days, scalp and trunk at 10 to 12, limbs at 12 to 14, and over joints up to 14. Cut the stitch at the skin and pull the clean end, never the knotted end, through the track, so that surface bacteria are not dragged into the wound.

An abscess is a walled-off collection of pus, most often seeded by Staphylococcus aureus, the common skin bacterium, entering through a hair follicle or a break in the skin. The signs are heat, tenderness, and swelling, but the sign that matters is fluctuance, the soft give of fluid under your fingers when one presses and another rests on the far side of the mass. The overlying skin becomes shiny and thin, sometimes with a pointing white head, and the patient guards the part and walks differently depending on where it sits. Antibiotics alone fail for a mechanical reason: the cavity has no blood supply, so no drug reaches the pus, and the pressure inside is what makes the pain throb in time with the pulse. Fever and spreading redness mean containment is failing. A superficial abscess that is clearly fluctuant and away from major structures is yours to drain, and drainage is the treatment, complete in itself.

There are times the knife is the wrong instrument. An abscess still in its early hot, hard, red stage, with no give under the fingers, is in the cellulitis phase, and cutting it releases no pus while opening clean tissue to infection, so warm compresses, rest, an antibiotic active against skin bacteria, and patience until fluctuance appears are the correct care. A swelling you cannot confidently feel, a deep or multiloculated abscess, or one in the palm, the neck, the breast, or the groin, where a blind cut can open a vessel, a nerve, or a duct, belongs to imaging and surgical hands, and the rural move is antibiotics and transfer. When you drain, anesthetize the skin over the dome or field-block around it, because injecting into the cavity both hurts and fails. Incise with a number 11 blade along the natural creases, make the opening wide at its base, express the pus gently, sweep a hemostat once through the cavity to break the inner walls, and irrigate. Pack loosely with gauze for 24 to 48 hours, then begin warm soaks twice a day, and leave the wound open, because an abscess heals by secondary intention, and closing it over is how it comes back.

Burns are assessed by depth and extent, and depth decides everything. A superficial burn, like most sunburn or a brief flash, is red, painful, blanches under pressure, and heals within a week because only the outer layer of skin is hurt. A superficial partial-thickness burn reaches into the dermis: it is blistered, moist, pink, extremely painful, still blanches, and heals in two to three weeks with good care. A deep partial-thickness burn is mottled red and white, less painful because the nerve endings themselves are injured, no longer blanches, and takes more than three weeks or needs grafting. A full-thickness burn destroys the whole skin, leaving a leathery, waxy, or charred surface that is dry, painless, and unable to heal from within. The trap is the deep burn that looks survivable, so treat any burn of uncertain depth as the deeper one and reassess at 48 hours, since depth declares itself over two days.

Extent is measured as per cent of total body surface area, counting only partial and full-thickness burns, because superficial burns lose no meaningful fluid. The rule of nines gives the adult: 9 per cent for the head, 9 for each arm, 18 for the front of the trunk, 18 for the back, 18 for each leg, and about 1 per cent for the groin. The patient's own palm, fingers included, is a portable 1 per cent measure for scattered burns. Children carry proportionally more of their surface on the head and less on the legs, so their numbers differ, and if children are common in your clinic, learn the pediatric version. Suspect a burned airway with any facial burn, singed nasal hair, hoarseness, or a fire in an enclosed space, and treat it as an urgent transfer even when breathing is still comfortable, because the airway narrows over hours. First aid is cooling with clean running water for 10 to 20 minutes if within three hours of the burn, never ice, keeping the rest of the patient warm, and gently explaining that ash, egg, and toothpaste belong on the table, not in the wound.

Fluid needs in the first hours are calculated, not guessed, because both under-resuscitation and over-resuscitation kill. The Parkland formula, in its classic form, gives 4 milliliters of Ringer's lactate per kilogram of body weight for each per cent of body surface area burned, with half of that volume in the first 8 hours counted from the moment of the burn, and the remainder over the following 16 hours. The formula is only a starting point, and the patient then tells you the truth: pass a catheter for any large burn, and keep the urine at half a milliliter per kilogram per hour in adults and 1 milliliter per kilogram per hour in children. Concentrated dark urine means more fluid, and a clear flood with puffy eyelids means less. Refer burns over 10 per cent of the surface in adults and over 5 per cent in children, burns of face, hands, feet, genitals, or joints, any full-thickness burn, any airway burn, and every chemical or electrical burn, after cooling, fluid, analgesia, and tetanus care have begun. Give morphine for a significant burn in small titrated doses without hesitation, because the pain is severe and its memory lasts. The volumes above follow standard trauma teaching, but verify the current guidance your program uses before writing a fluid plan.

Fracture care in the field is splinting, and the reasons are worth hearing: immobilizing the bone ends stops the fragments sawing into muscle and nerve, quiets pain dramatically, slows the hidden bleeding a broken femur can hold, and keeps a closed fracture closed. A splint must cross the joint above and the joint below the break, and it must be padded, because a hard splint on prominent bone makes wounds of its own. Improvised splints are everywhere: sticks or poles laid along the limb and wrapped with cloth, cardboard folded into a gutter, a folded blanket for padding, a sling for arms and collarbones, sandbags to hold a leg at rest. A femur may need traction, and traction without training has caused real harm, so if you have not been taught it, splint, give analgesia, and transfer. Gentle longitudinal traction to straighten a grossly deformed limb is reasonable when the distal pulses are absent, since restoring circulation outranks skin, and the alignment is then held while the splint goes on. Before and after every splint, perform the same neurovascular check: feel the pulse beyond the injury, press the nail bed and watch the color return in under two seconds, and ask the patient to move the fingers or toes and report any change in sensation, comparing with the other side whenever unsure.

An open fracture is an orthopedic emergency with an infection clock running, because the broken bone has been in contact with the dirt of the road. Do not push the bone end back under the skin unless it threatens to pierce the skin or the limb beyond it is pulseless, since reducing it in the field drags contamination inward; cover the bone with a clean, preferably sterile moist dressing, splint in the position found, and give antibiotics early. Current surgical guidance favors a first-generation cephalosporin such as cefazolin 1 gram intravenously, with added coverage for soil organisms, such as metronidazole, for heavily soiled wounds, and the exact regimen must be verified against the current guideline before you give it. Assess tetanus prophylaxis on every open fracture without exception, and keep the patient nil by mouth from the start, because early surgery is likely. Your documentation should state the time of injury, the antibiotic time, the wound's appearance, and the distal findings, because the receiving surgeon will build decisions on your notes. A suspected pelvic fracture after a crush or a high fall, with pain on pressing the hips or blood at the urethral opening, is stabilized by binding the pelvis snugly with a folded sheet at the hip level, since the binder reduces the space available to bleed into.

The chest drain is the one invasive procedure in this chapter that demands supervised training before you attempt it alone, and what follows is written to make you a safer decision-maker and monitor, not a self-taught operator. The situations demanding a drain are tension pneumothorax, a large pneumothorax with breathlessness, and a hemothorax filling the chest with blood. A tension pneumothorax is a one-way tear in the lung: air enters the chest with each breath and cannot leave, pressure collapses the lung and then pushes the heart and the great veins aside, and the patient dies because the veins are squeezed shut and no blood returns. The signs are severe breathlessness, distended neck veins, absent breath sounds with a drum-like chest on one side, and shock, with the windpipe pushed away from the affected side appearing late. Treat it first with a needle, not a tube: a large-bore needle thrust into the second intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line, or the fifth space just in front of the armpit, with the hiss of escaping air confirming the diagnosis and buying time. After the needle, a drain always follows, because the needle is a bridge, not a treatment. A small pneumothorax in a comfortable patient is watched with rest and oxygen if available, not drained.

Placing a drain, when you are trained and equipped, follows a fixed anatomical path. The safe entry is the fourth or fifth intercostal space in front of the mid-axillary line, roughly level with the nipple or just below, and the tube passes just above the upper border of the rib below the space, because each rib carries its nerve, artery, and vein in a groove along its underside. Clean widely, drape with whatever clean barrier exists, and infiltrate generous local anesthesia into skin, rib edge, and pleura, since the pleura is exquisitely sensitive. Make a 2 to 3 centimeter incision, spread the muscles bluntly with a hemostat down to the pleura, and avoid stabbing through with the trocar, which is how lungs and vessels get injured. Pass a drain of fitting size, commonly 28 to 32 French in adults for blood and smaller for air, direct it upward and forward, secure it to the skin with a stout suture, and dress the site airtight. Where any imaging exists, a chest radiograph confirms the position, and where none exists the clinical signs do: breath sounds returning, neck veins settling, the patient speaking in longer sentences. Never let a chest drain be your first unsupervised procedure, and never let anyone talk you into it before you have been proctored through several.

The underwater seal is not a ritual but a one-way valve made of water. The tube from the chest runs down to a bottle kept below chest level, its end sitting 2 to 3 centimeters under the surface of sterile water or clean saline: when the patient breathes in, the water column inside the tube rises, and when air or blood leaves the chest, it bubbles out below the surface. Water allows air out and blocks its return, whatever the patient does, which is the whole point. Keep the bottle below the chest always, because lifting it above floods tube water back into the chest, and laying it flat empties the seal. The improvised version, long described in humanitarian surgical manuals, is a clean bottle with a tight lid pierced by two holes, a long tube reaching 2 to 3 centimeters under the water, and a short tube open to the air as a vent, taped at every joint, with a one-way flutter valve as the substitute when movement cannot be avoided. Monitor by looking and listening: the water column should swing with each breath, steady bubbling means a continuing air leak, and the rule that saves lives is never to clamp a bubbling drain, because clamping turns the leak back into a tension pneumothorax. Record the drainage volume and character every hour early on, and more than 1500 milliliters of blood immediately, or more than 200 milliliters per hour for several hours, means surgical bleeding and an urgent conversation about transfer. Remove the drain when the lung is re-expanded, the leak has stopped for a day, and drainage is minimal, asking the patient to hold the breath and bear down while you pull the tube and close the pre-placed purse-string suture.

Every wound, burn, and puncture gets two questions in the same breath: tetanus and rabies. Tetanus is caused by the bacterium Clostridium tetani, whose spores sit in soil and dust in every village and enter through wounds so small they are forgotten, germinating in dead tissue and releasing a toxin that travels to the nerves and produces the terrible spasms of lockjaw. Once the spasms begin, the patient needs intensive care that most of the world does not have, which makes prevention the entire strategy. The scheme taught by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, whose current version you must verify before acting, is this: for a clean minor wound, a patient with a complete series needs a booster only if more than 10 years have passed; for a dirty wound, meaning soil, saliva, feces, puncture, dead tissue, or burn, a booster is needed if more than 5 years have passed; and a patient whose series is unknown or incomplete needs both tetanus toxoid and passive protection with human tetanus immunoglobulin, commonly 250 international units into the muscle, a portion infiltrated around the wound. Guidance differs between countries and is revised from time to time, so check the current national schedule rather than trusting memory. Record exactly what was given, on which date, and into which site. Where vaccination coverage is thin, assume nothing, because adults may have no childhood series at all, and a woman who recalls being vaccinated long ago may mean she once received a single dose.

Rabies is untreatable once symptoms begin and entirely preventable before them, which makes any mammal bite an emergency of the same rank as a hemorrhage. The wound care is the first treatment: wash with soap and running water for a full 15 minutes, then apply a virucidal agent such as povidone-iodine if available, and washing alone removes a large share of the risk. The World Health Organization grades exposures into categories: category one, touching or feeding an animal or a lick on intact skin, needs only washing and reassurance; category two, a nibble on uncovered skin or a scratch without blood, needs washing and vaccine; category three, any bite or scratch that breaks skin, a lick on broken skin, or saliva on mucous membranes, needs washing, vaccine, and rabies immunoglobulin. The vaccine is given into the deltoid muscle on day 0, day 3, day 7, and once between days 14 and 21 by the schedules in common use, and regimens differ between countries and products, so the first dose is never delayed while the animal is being sought. Immunoglobulin, when the category demands it, is infiltrated into and around the wound as far as volume allows, with the remainder injected at a site distant from the vaccine, never in the same syringe and never in the same limb. Human rabies immunoglobulin is dosed at 20 international units per kilogram of body weight, and the product you stock dictates the schedule, so verify the current protocol of the World Health Organization and of your national program before giving the series. Take the animal's story seriously, since an animal that behaved strangely, that cannot be observed, or that has died raises your urgency rather than lowering it.

Consent and pain control are not the wrapping around these procedures; they are part of the procedures, and they run through every step. Before you touch a wound, tell the patient what you found, what you plan to do, what it will feel like, and how long it will take, and obtain agreement, through an interpreter when languages differ, and document that you did. An unconscious patient is covered by the emergency exception, a child by the caregiver's agreement in simple honest words, and a patient who refuses a reasonable procedure receives your explanation, the risks stated plainly, and a documented refusal with a witness. For pain, climb a simple ladder: ibuprofen 400 milligrams by mouth every eight hours with food for mild wounds, and morphine 5 to 10 milligrams by mouth every four hours, or in smaller intravenous doses where you are trained and equipped, for burns, fractures, and chest drains. Local anesthesia is the analgesic of the procedures themselves, and a patient who does not flinch under your needle gets better repairs than one who is fighting you. Watch the adverse effects you can cause: ibuprofen can injure the kidneys of a dehydrated patient, and morphine slows breathing, so check the respiratory rate and depth after every opioid dose and keep the reversal agent on the shelf if you can stock one. Pain that returns after you leave is a reason patients never come back, so send every wound home with a spoken and written plan for the next two days of analgesia, and verify these doses against current guidance before prescribing.

The unglamorous work decides whether any of this is possible. A trauma kit you can carry contains what you cannot improvise: sterile gloves in several sizes, gauze and elastic bandages, a suture set with needle holder, forceps, scissors, and scalpel, local anesthesia, syringes and needles, adhesive tape, a tourniquet, a blood pressure cuff, a light you can aim, and a marker for writing times. Stock deep what you use daily and single what you rarely use, rotate everything by expiry date, and audit the kit on a fixed weekday, because midnight on the roadside is the wrong moment to learn the needle holder is missing. Sterilization is a quiet discipline: autoclave when power allows, and otherwise boil instruments at a rolling boil for 15 minutes, then store them dry in closed containers, and never call an instrument sterile if it has been lying loose in a drawer. Irrigation alone can consume liters, so plan water like a drug, in covered containers refilled on a schedule, with a basin beneath the wound and a safe way to dispose of the dirty fluid. Lighting, waste, and sharps handling belong to the trauma response, because a needle that pierces a colleague after a night procedure opens a wound chapter of its own. Keep the checklist inside the bag and let any team member audit against it without asking permission.

Monitoring is what turns procedures into care. After a tourniquet, the time is recorded and the limb reassessed on arrival; after packing, the wound is reassessed at 24 hours by a planned revisit, not when the pain returns; after splinting, pulses and sensation are rechecked at one hour and again the next day, since swelling under a splint is silent until it is dangerous; after a chest drain, bottle height, swinging, drainage, and breathing are charted every hour early on; after a burn, hourly urine output is your gauge of whether the fluid plan is right. Every closed wound is inspected at 48 hours, and every wound left open gets its first dressing change at the same interval, because the second day is when infection declares itself. Teach the family the signs that mean immediate return: spreading redness, throbbing pain, fever, pus, a bad smell, red streaks running toward the armpit or groin, and new numbness beyond the wound. Watch also for the harms of your own treatments, such as the numb tongue after too much lidocaine, the pale skin under a too-tight mattress stitch, the patient who cannot pass urine after morphine, or the diarrhea that follows a careless antibiotic course. Then set the follow-up date in writing, with the day and the place, because a plan that lives only in your head does not reach a patient walking three hours home.

Documentation is clinical work and legal work at once. In the record, write the mechanism and time of injury, the findings with a simple sketch of the wound, the care given with times, the tetanus and rabies status and what was given for each, the analgesia and its effect, the consent conversation, the instructions spoken aloud, and the follow-up plan, then sign and date it. In road traffic injuries and assaults your notes may become evidence, so record facts and measurements, not opinions about fault. Registers serve surveillance, because a rise in dog bites feeds the rabies program and a cluster of burns from one stove design informs prevention, and the numbers you keep are the numbers the district can act on. Your role as an advanced practice nurse is to hold all of this at once, and it extends outward: teach bleeding control and tourniquet use to teachers and drivers, teach families dressing changes and the danger signs, and train community health workers to clean simple wounds and to recognize what must travel. Knowing what to refer is a greater skill than knowing how to cut, and the honesty to say so protects patients more than any procedure.

To summarize, trauma care in a remote setting begins with looking before touching, and the primary survey of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, and exposure protects the patient from the dramatic wound while they die of a quiet one. Bleeding is stopped with direct pressure first, then packing, then a tourniquet with its time written down, and every wound is judged by its mechanism, its age, its contamination, and what lies beneath it. Clean wounds close, contaminated wounds wait or heal open, liters of clean irrigation beat any antiseptic, dead tissue must be cut away, and the simple interrupted suture, placed with matched bites and removed on time, is the spine of repair, with mattress stitches for the wounds that spring apart. Abscesses are drained only when they fluctuate, burns are sized by depth and surface and resuscitated by formula then titrated to urine, fractures are splinted above and below with neurovascular checks before and after, and the chest drain, when truly needed, works through a water seal you can improvise and must never clamp while it bubbles. Every wound asks about tetanus and rabies in the same breath, with schedules verified against the current guidance of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization before you act. Consent, analgesia, monitoring, honest records, and teaching carry the same weight as the procedures, and the nurse who holds the whole of this, not only the cutting, is the reason patients in remote places survive their injuries.

# Chapter 43 — Anesthesia, Sedation, and Pain Management

Anesthesia clears a room in a remote clinic, because it names the part of medicine most nurses are taught never to do alone. Where an anesthetist exists, the surgeon cuts while somebody else owns the airway and the depth of unconsciousness. Far from that hospital, the nurse who holds the needle must also hold the airway, and the only monitor may be your own eyes and a hand on a pulse. This chapter is not a license to give general anesthesia; it is an account of the sedation, local anesthesia, and pain relief an advanced practice nurse can deliver safely with training. Where doses appear, they reflect the guidance of the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and you must verify the current version and your national protocol before acting, because protocols are revised.

Everything that makes sedation safe is repetitive and a little dull, and the dullness is the point. The same checks and the same chart, performed the same way every time, prevent the catastrophic errors that no amount of talent can rescue. Four rules carry most of the weight: assess the airway before you sedate anyone, respect fasting, monitor continuously with one person whose only task is watching, and have oxygen, suction, and a rescue plan ready before the first drug. That observer is not a luxury, because in a small clinic the observer may be an assistant you taught to count breaths aloud, to call your name when the breathing changes, and to hold a mask on a face. The moment the observer also passes instruments, the monitoring has stopped and the patient becomes the least watched person in the room.

Before the procedure, walk the room and ask the questions aloud. Is the suction working and within one second of my hand, is oxygen flowing, is the mask the right size for this face, are the drugs drawn and labeled, and is the light good enough to see color? The surgical safety checklist of the World Health Organization is the most widely used version of this discipline, with a briefing before and a debriefing after, and adopting it in a one room clinic makes forgetting harder. Name the rescue drugs on the shelf before you need them: naloxone for opioids, flumazenil where a benzodiazepine was used, and glucose for the child whose sedation is really low blood sugar.

Airway assessment is a two minute conversation and examination that can save a life. Ask whether the patient has ever had trouble with anesthesia, whether a previous procedure was difficult, whether there is snoring at night, a hoarse voice, or a swelling in the neck. Then look at how far the mouth opens, whether the jaw slides forward, whether the neck bends and extends, whether the teeth are loose or missing, and whether a large tongue sits in a small mouth. A patient whose open mouth shows mostly the soft palate, whose chin is short, whose neck is stiff, or whose breathing is already noisy is a patient you do not sedate alone. Stridor, a changed voice, drooling, and a swollen tongue or floor of the mouth are absolute stop signs, and the right action is to sit the patient up, give oxygen, and arrange urgent transfer.

Fasting exists because a full stomach and a depressed cough reflex make a predictable disaster. Stomach contents reach the back of the throat, the reflex that would close the airway is asleep, and the lungs receive what the stomach held, which is called aspiration and can kill within minutes or cause a pneumonia that kills in days. Guidance for planned sedation in healthy adults commonly asks for two hours without clear fluids, four hours without breast milk, and six hours without light food, and the numbers differ for children and between national protocols, so check the guideline you work under. The fasting rule is never a reason to delay care for a patient who is bleeding, obstructed, or dying, and there the plan shifts to a rapid controlled technique with suction ready. If the airway is uncertain and the stomach is full, ask whether the procedure can wait or be done under local anesthesia.

Monitoring is a set of questions you ask the patient's body again and again, and the trend matters more than any single number. Keep a hand on the pulse, count the breathing for a full minute rather than estimating, watch the chest rise and the color of the lips, and measure the blood pressure every few minutes. If a pulse oximeter is available, a falling oxygen saturation warns you before the patient looks blue; without one, your eyes and ears do the same work, because noisy breathing and a rising pulse are the oldest monitors in medicine. An electrocardiogram, called ECG after this, is useful when the heart is at risk or the drug disturbs the rhythm, but it means nothing unless somebody watches the screen.

Local anesthesia is the safest anesthesia there is, and it works by blocking the channels in the nerve membrane so the impulse never travels. It produces numbness without unconsciousness, so the patient keeps their own airway, breathing, and protective reflexes, and that is why it sits at the top of the ladder. Lidocaine begins within two to five minutes and lasts one to two hours depending on the tissue and the dose, which makes it the workhorse of infiltration and field blocks. Longer acting drugs exist, but the longer they act the more toxic they can be to the heart, and bupivacaine has caused deaths after small accidental injections into a vein. Choose the shortest acting drug that will finish the procedure, and never keep topping up a block simply because the patient is still awake.

The maximum safe dose of lidocaine is the number that turns local anesthesia from safe into lethal, and it is worth knowing in milligrams and in milliliters. With plain lidocaine the ceiling in common guidance is about 4.5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight, and with epinephrine added the ceiling rises to about 7 milligrams per kilogram, because the blood vessels narrow and the drug leaves the tissue more slowly. Many protocols also cap the total at 300 milligrams plain and 500 milligrams with epinephrine, whatever the weight would allow. A 1 per cent solution holds 10 milligrams in each milliliter, so 300 milligrams equals 30 milliliters, and this arithmetic is the one most often done wrong at the bedside. For a patient weighing 60 kilograms, plain lidocaine allows about 270 milligrams, which equals 27 milliliters of 1 per cent, so write the running total on the packaging as you inject.

Local anesthetic systemic toxicity follows an order worth memorizing, because the earliest signs are easy to dismiss as anxiety. The patient reports a metallic taste, numbness around the mouth, or ringing in the ears, and may feel light headed or see shimmering lights. Next comes agitation, confusion, muscle twitching, and a rising pulse, and at that stage the level in the blood is high enough to cause a seizure. After the seizure the depression deepens, the breathing slows, the blood pressure falls, and the rhythm of the heart can deteriorate into a wide and slow arrest that is very hard to reverse. The early signs are subjective and a child may not describe them, so ask directly about taste in the mouth and tingling lips, and stop the injection the moment any of these signs appear.

Treatment begins with stopping the injection and calling for help, then securing the airway and giving oxygen, because low oxygen and acid in the blood make the drug more toxic to the heart. A seizure is treated with a benzodiazepine, such as diazepam 5 to 10 milligrams intravenously in an adult or midazolam in small titrated doses, and every pediatric dose must be calculated by weight from the current protocol before use. If the patient arrests or the rhythm becomes unstable, the antidote is an intravenous lipid emulsion, usually a 20 per cent preparation, given as a weight based bolus and then an infusion, and the exact regimen must be read from the current guideline because it is easy to get wrong. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation continues with prolonged effort, because recovery from local anesthetic arrest is sometimes delayed. Give no more local anesthetic, avoid lidocaine as an antiarrhythmic, and record the drug and dose before transfer.

Epinephrine added to lidocaine prolongs the block, reduces bleeding, and raises the safe dose, and it carries its own cautions. It narrows the vessels and can in theory reduce blood flow to a fingertip, a toe, or the nose, and although modern evidence suggests the danger has been overstated, many remote protocols still avoid it in digits and in skin that is already short of blood. Good technique matters as much as the drug: use the smallest needle that will do the job, inject slowly while withdrawing the needle, aspirate before each injection to be sure you are not in a vein, and warm the solution toward body temperature. Avoid injecting into infected tissue when you can, because the acid environment weakens the drug, and never inject against resistance in a closed space such as a finger.

The digital block is one of the most useful procedures in a remote clinic, and it is also where careless technique does permanent harm. Each finger has two nerves running along its sides, one toward the palm and one toward the back, and each is blocked by a small injection at the base, entering just above the web space, advancing toward the bone, aspirating, and injecting 1 to 2 milliliters of plain lidocaine before repeating on the other side. A ring block carries the same idea around a digit, with the anesthetic deposited as the needle is withdrawn until a complete ring of numbness surrounds the base. Use plain lidocaine without epinephrine, keep the total under the weight based limit, and avoid a tight bandage around the base of the finger. Test the block before you cut, wait five minutes if sharp pain remains, and treat a finger that turns pale, cold, and painful as a surgical emergency.

The fascia iliaca block changes the experience of a broken hip in a place where nobody can give a spinal. The target is the femoral nerve and the other nerves passing beneath the strong sheet of fascia over the front of the thigh, and the aim is to fill that space with local anesthetic. The landmark is the line from the front of the hip bone to the pulse in the groin, divided into thirds, with the needle entering at the junction of the outer and middle thirds and a distinct give as it passes through two layers of fascia. A common regimen is 0.3 to 0.5 milliliters per kilogram of 0.25 per cent bupivacaine, or an equivalent volume of lidocaine, up to the maximum safe dose, checked against the current protocol. Weakness of the front of the thigh is expected, but puncture of the femoral artery and nerve injury are the risks, so aspiration and slow injection are not optional.

Ketamine is the drug that makes remote sedation possible. It produces a dissociative state in which the patient is unaware of the world while the airway reflexes, the breathing, and the blood pressure are largely preserved, and it also produces deep analgesia, which is why it suits reducing a fracture or cleaning a burn. The usual intravenous dose for procedural sedation is 1 to 2 milligrams per kilogram given slowly, with the effect beginning in about a minute, while the intramuscular dose is 4 to 5 milligrams per kilogram with onset in about five minutes. It raises the heart rate, the blood pressure, and the secretions, and it can cause vomiting and, rarely, spasm of the vocal cords, so oxygen and suction must be ready. These doses follow widespread guidance, and the current protocol of the World Health Organization and of your national service must be checked before use, because pediatric and adult regimens differ.

The vivid dreams and hallucinations of ketamine are what patients remember and the reason some clinics refuse to stock it. They are more common in adults than in young children and are reduced by a quiet, dimly lit room, by keeping stimulation to a minimum, and by a calm voice explaining what is happening. A small dose of a benzodiazepine before the ketamine, such as midazolam 0.05 to 0.1 milligrams per kilogram intravenously, reduces the reactions, though it also deepens the sedation. Ketamine is not for everyone, and a patient with an uncontrolled rise in blood pressure, a recent heart attack, an unstable rhythm, or a severely narrowed aortic valve may not tolerate the surge in heart rate and pressure. A patient with a known psychotic illness may have a frightening emergence, and a patient with a full stomach, a bowel obstruction, or an airway already compromised risks vomiting and aspiration.

Once ketamine is given, the work becomes watching. Stay at the head, keep the airway in view, and watch the chest and the color without interruption, because the reflexes are preserved but not perfect and the tongue can still fall back. Record the pulse, the breathing, the blood pressure, and the oxygen saturation every five minutes, and describe the level of consciousness simply, as whether the patient responds to voice, to touch, or not at all. Vomiting is common, so keep suction ready and turn the patient onto the side as the effect wears off. Do not leave the patient alone until they can hold a conversation, sit up steadily, and drink without choking, and never send someone home alone to walk after a procedure that altered consciousness.

Pain control is not a separate subject from anesthesia; it is the same subject, and the analgesic ladder of the World Health Organization remains the clearest way to organize it. The first step is the non-opioid drugs, and in most remote clinics that means paracetamol, also called acetaminophen, and ibuprofen. Paracetamol for an adult is usually 1 gram by mouth every six hours, with no more than 4 grams in a day, and that ceiling falls in liver disease, severe malnutrition, and heavy alcohol use. For a child the usual dose is 15 milligrams per kilogram by mouth every six hours, measured with a syringe rather than a spoon, because the margin between a safe and a dangerous dose is small. Ibuprofen for an adult is 400 milligrams by mouth every eight hours with food, and it can injure the kidneys of a dehydrated or elderly patient and irritate the stomach, so verify these doses in the current guidance before prescribing.

The second step adds a weak opioid when the first is not enough, and tramadol is the drug most often available. An adult dose is 50 to 100 milligrams by mouth every six hours, up to 400 milligrams in a day, and the dose must be reduced in the elderly and in anyone with kidney or liver disease. Tramadol lowers the seizure threshold, so it is a poor choice for a patient with epilepsy, and it can cause a dangerous reaction with some antidepressants and other drugs that raise serotonin. Constipation, nausea, dizziness, and drowsiness are common, and the nausea is often worse on an empty stomach.

The third step is morphine, the drug most feared and most needed in a place with no surgeon. The fear comes from a story about addiction that does not fit the patient in acute pain, because dependence after a short course is not the disease of addiction, and untreated severe pain is the far commoner harm. The starting dose for an opioid naive adult is 5 to 10 milligrams by mouth every four hours, or 2.5 to 5 milligrams intravenously, with intramuscular and subcutaneous doses in the same range, and for a child about 0.1 to 0.2 milligrams per kilogram intravenously. Watch the breathing rather than the pain score, because respiratory depression is the effect that kills, and it appears as a slowing rate, deep sleep, and small pupils. Naloxone, 0.4 milligrams intravenously in an adult or 0.01 milligrams per kilogram in a child, reverses the breathing depression but also the analgesia, so it is given only when breathing is failing. Verify every dose against the current guidance of the World Health Organization and your national protocol, because opioid regimens are revised and differ between countries.

Morphine is a controlled drug, and the paperwork is part of the treatment. Keep it in a locked cupboard within a locked room, record every ampoule and tablet in a register that shows the balance and the signature, and have a second person witness the discarding of any unused portion, so that no one can be accused and no one can divert. Because supply is fragile, calculate a week of expected use and order ahead, and keep the stock where the temperature will not ruin it. The side effects are predictable: constipation is universal and needs a stimulant laxative, nausea usually passes, sedation settles as the dose is adjusted, and itching responds to an antihistamine. The myth of respiratory depression at correct doses frightens clinicians into giving too little, and the patient in agony who is then given a large rescue dose out of desperation is exactly the situation that causes harm.

There are analgesics that come from a person rather than a pharmacy, and they are not placebos when they are honest. Immobilizing a fracture, elevating a swollen limb, applying cold in the first day and warmth afterward, and positioning the patient so the injured part is supported can remove a surprising share of the pain. Slow breathing guided by your own counting reduces the panic that amplifies pain, and it costs nothing. Explain what will happen, when it will happen, and how long it will last, and never tell a patient that a treatment will not hurt when it will, since the lie destroys the trust the next reassurance needs.

Procedural sedation makes a patient comfortable enough for a painful procedure, and it sits on a continuum that nobody can control precisely. At one end is minimal sedation, in which the patient is calm and awake, and at the other is general anesthesia, in which the patient is unrousable and the airway may need support, and a patient can slip from one to the other with one extra milliliter. That is why the same standards apply to sedation as to anesthesia, with fasting, an airway plan, continuous monitoring, and a dedicated observer. Midazolam is a short-acting benzodiazepine, given intravenously in small increments of 0.05 to 0.1 milligrams per kilogram in an adult, and it produces calm and amnesia with a real risk of oversedation when combined with an opioid. The combination of a benzodiazepine with an opioid is the commonest cause of sedation disasters, so reduce each dose and increase the monitoring when both are needed. Every sedated patient needs defined discharge criteria, usually steady vital signs, a return to the baseline level of consciousness, and a responsible adult to stay with them.

Nitrous oxide is a gas that produces analgesia and light sedation, and where a cylinder and a mixing device exist it is one of the kindest tools in the clinic. A mixture of 50 per cent nitrous oxide and 50 per cent oxygen is safe to breathe for a conscious patient, it begins to work within a minute, and it wears off within minutes after the mask is removed, which suits a dressing change, a suture, or a joint reduction. It is not a general anesthetic at that concentration, but it must never be used without oxygen because the gas alone causes hypoxia. Avoid it in a patient with a collapsed lung, a bowel obstruction, a blocked middle ear, or a head injury with raised pressure, because it expands gas filled spaces, and repeated heavy exposure harms the staff and the patient's vitamin B12. Scavenging, a well sealed mask, and adequate ventilation protect the nurses who use it every day.

The most important skill in this chapter is knowing what not to attempt. Spinal anesthesia, epidural anesthesia, general anesthesia with a breathing tube, deep sedation of a child with a difficult airway, major abdominal surgery, and any procedure that requires paralysis are beyond the scope of an untrained clinician, however confident the moment feels. Regional blocks that approach the spine, the brachial plexus, the neck, or the eye belong to providers with supervised training, and a single weekend course does not create that competence. Saying no is itself a clinical skill: begin with what you can do, because a refusal that offers nothing sounds like indifference, and you can give pain relief, splint the limb, clean the wound, and organize transport. Then say plainly what you cannot do and why, such as the anesthesia for this operation is not available here, so we are sending you where it can be done safely. If the patient refuses transfer, document the conversation, the risks explained, and the refusal, with a witness.

The logistics are what make all of this possible or impossible, and they deserve the same attention as the pharmacology. A sedation kit should hold oxygen with a delivery device that fits an adult and a child, a working suction with a rigid and a soft tip, a bag and mask in several sizes, airways in several sizes, intravenous cannulas and fluids, and a means of keeping the patient warm. The emergency drug box should hold epinephrine, atropine, naloxone, flumazenil, diazepam or midazolam, dextrose, hydrocortisone, and an antihistamine, with the doses written on a card taped inside the lid. Check the cylinder pressure, the suction, and the expiry dates on a fixed day every week and record the check, because the equipment that fails is almost always the equipment nobody looked at.

Complications follow the drugs and the procedures, and each has a first move you should know without thinking. Anaphylaxis appears as sudden low pressure, wheeze, swelling, and a rash, and the treatment is epinephrine 0.5 milligrams of the 1 in 1,000 solution intramuscularly in the outer thigh for an adult, or 0.01 milligrams per kilogram for a child, repeated every five minutes as needed. Spasm of the vocal cords appears as a high pitched sound and then silence after a stimulus, and it is broken by stopping the stimulus, removing the debris, and applying positive pressure with a mask. Aspiration appears as coughing, a falling oxygen saturation, and a wet chest during or after sedation, and it is managed with oxygen, suction, positioning, and transfer. Cardiac arrest here is usually preceded by hypoxia or a drug error, so the first response to a falling saturation is always to stop, look at the airway, and give oxygen. Document every complication, and hold a short debrief with the team, because hidden complications repeat.

Some patients need the plan changed before the first drug is drawn. A child is not a small adult: the doses are per kilogram, the airway is smaller and more easily obstructed, the tongue is proportionally larger, the breathing is easier to depress, and a child loses heat quickly, so warmth and a parent's arms are part of the anesthesia. A pregnant woman in the second half of pregnancy has a full stomach, a compressed vein when she lies flat, and a greater sensitivity to opioid sedation, so she is positioned tilted and monitored closely. An elderly patient with a thin body and a slow liver needs smaller doses given more slowly, and a patient who is severely malnourished has little protein to bind the drug and little reserve to survive its side effects. A patient with human immunodeficiency virus, liver disease, kidney disease, or sickle cell disease may have altered drug handling and a lower tolerance for hypoxia, so check the interactions in the current reference rather than guessing.

Documentation is the memory of the procedure, and in a remote clinic it is also the supervision you do not have. Before the procedure, record the indication, the consent conversation and who gave it, the airway assessment, the fasting time, the baseline vital signs, the weight used for the dose calculation, and the allergies. During it, record every drug with its dose, its route, and its time, and the observations with the same time, so that the chart reads as a story rather than a set of disconnected numbers. After it, record the recovery, the discharge criteria that were met, the analgesia given and its effect, the instructions spoken to the family, and the follow up date, and write the complications in plain words, including the ones that resolved. The nursing role is broader than any technique, because you are also the system that teaches others to count a respiratory rate, to hold a mask, and to call for help without hesitation.

Put the pieces together in a composite patient. A woman of about 70 years arrives after a fall, with a shortened and externally rotated leg and pain that makes every movement a scream, and the nearest hospital with an anesthetist is a five hour drive over a rough road. You assess the airway, confirm she has not eaten for eight hours, place a cannula, and give a fascia iliaca block with the dose calculated from her weight after checking the local anesthetic limit and the current protocol. You splint the leg, give paracetamol and a small dose of morphine with a laxative and an antiemetic, monitor the breathing and blood pressure every fifteen minutes, and write down the times and doses. She sleeps on the journey, arrives stable, and the anesthetist at the hospital knows exactly what she received because your note travels with her. The procedure you did not do, the open reduction, was never yours, and the analgesia you did give made the transfer survivable.

To summarize, anesthesia in a remote setting is a discipline of limits, preparation, and watching rather than a set of heroic improvisations. Assess the airway before you sedate anyone, respect fasting, keep one person whose only job is monitoring, and have oxygen, suction, and a rescue plan ready before the first drug is drawn. Local anesthetics are safest when the maximum dose of lidocaine, about 4.5 milligrams per kilogram plain and about 7 milligrams per kilogram with epinephrine, is calculated with care, and toxicity is recognized by the metallic taste, the tingling lips, and the ringing ears and treated by stopping, oxygenating, controlling the seizure, and using lipid emulsion where it exists. Digital, ring, and fascia iliaca blocks extend safe analgesia to the finger, the toe, and the broken hip, while spinal, epidural, and general anesthesia remain the work of trained providers. Ketamine is the workhorse of remote sedation, with its preserved reflexes, its doses by weight, its emergence reactions that quiet and darkness reduce, and its short list of patients who should not receive it. The analgesic ladder of paracetamol, ibuprofen, tramadol, and morphine gives effective relief when the doses are calculated and the fear of morphine replaced by careful monitoring. Know what you can do, learn it thoroughly, and say no clearly and kindly to what you cannot, because honesty about limits is the foundation of safe sedation.

# Chapter 44 — Pediatrics and Severe Acute Malnutrition in Remote Practice

Every chapter in this book meets a clinician somewhere, but this one meets you in the hardest place, a health post where you are the only person able to assess a sick child. More than five million children die each year before their fifth birthday, most from pneumonia, diarrhea, malaria, measles, and the malnutrition underneath them all. Severe acute malnutrition contributes to roughly one in every ten deaths in children under five and multiplies the danger of every infection beside it. This chapter follows the systematic assessment of the sick child, the treatment of dehydration, the staged care of severe acute malnutrition, and the outpatient program for the child who can still eat. Every dose and volume here reflects current World Health Organization guidance, but guidance is revised and differs between countries, so verify the current national guideline before you prescribe or act.

The integrated management of childhood illness is a systematic way of examining a sick child, built for a setting where a laboratory may not exist and one visit may be the only chance. It asks you to follow the same order every time rather than chase the complaint the mother offers first, because the complaint that brings a child in is often not the condition that will kill that child tonight. For each child you check the danger signs, then cough or difficult breathing, diarrhea, fever, and ear problem, then nutrition, immunization, and any other concern. You classify rather than merely diagnose, placing the child in a category that carries an action, such as severe pneumonia, some dehydration, or severe acute malnutrition with complications, and then you treat, counsel, and write the follow-up date where the next nurse can find it.

The general danger signs mean immediate action, before any other question is answered. A child who cannot drink or breastfeed, who vomits everything, who has had convulsions, or who is lethargic or unconscious is in danger now. For the young infant the list is equally urgent: not feeding well, convulsions, fast breathing of 60 breaths or more per minute, severe chest indrawing, fever of 37.5 degrees Celsius or more, a temperature below 35.5 degrees Celsius, and movement only when stimulated. Any one of these signs means urgent treatment and usually referral, so in a remote post you begin treatment while you arrange the journey. Stridor in a calm child, and a child too weak to cry, are equally alarming, and in pediatrics the sickest child is often the stillest.

The examination is quick, ordered, and almost entirely done with your hands and eyes. Count the respiratory rate for a full minute while the child is calm, because crying doubles it, and know your thresholds: 60 or more per minute under 2 months, 50 or more from 2 months to 12 months, and 40 or more from 12 months to 5 years. Look for lower chest wall indrawing, listen for stridor, and note whether the child can feed. Weigh the child, measure length or height, measure the mid-upper arm circumference on the left arm midway between the shoulder and the elbow, and check the immunization card. Press both feet for a few seconds and look for pitting edema, because bilateral pitting edema is itself a form of severe acute malnutrition, and write every number down as you go.

Nutritional status is judged in three ways, and each catches children the others miss. The weight-for-height measure compares the child with a reference child of the same height, and a value below minus 3 standard deviations from the median defines severe wasting. The mid-upper arm circumference is the fastest field measure, and a value below 115 millimeters in a child from 6 to 59 months defines severe acute malnutrition, while 115 to 125 millimeters defines moderate acute malnutrition. Bilateral pitting edema of both feet defines severe acute malnutrition regardless of weight, and it is the sign most often missed. A child can be severely malnourished with a normal-looking weight if the child is stunted, so trust the numbers over your impression and record each measurement on the growth card.

Dehydration kills through shock, and the signs that predict it are physical and behavioural rather than historical. Ask the mother about diarrhea and vomiting, but base your classification on what you see: the child's general state, whether the eyes are sunken, whether the child drinks eagerly or poorly, and how fast a skin pinch returns. A child who is restless and irritable, with sunken eyes, who drinks eagerly, and whose skin pinch returns slowly has some dehydration. A child who is lethargic or unconscious, with sunken eyes, who cannot drink or drinks poorly, and whose skin pinch returns very slowly has severe dehydration. The number of stools matters less than these signs, so let the mother's report raise suspicion without settling it, and weigh the child at admission.

Rehydration follows the degree you have just classified, and the plan is chosen for the child rather than the disease. A child with no dehydration goes home on the first plan: extra fluids after every loose stool, continued feeding, and clear instructions on when to return. A child with some dehydration stays for the second plan, which gives oral rehydration salts at 75 milliliters per kilogram over 4 hours, offered by cup or spoon while breastfeeding continues. Reassess after 4 hours: if the signs have gone, switch to the first plan, and if some dehydration persists, repeat the second, while a child who vomits waits about ten minutes and then continues slowly. Give zinc, 20 milligrams by mouth once a day for 10 to 14 days, or 10 milligrams for an infant under 6 months, to shorten the diarrhea.

Severe dehydration is treated as shock and demands the third plan, and the pace is measured in minutes. For a child under 12 months give 30 milliliters per kilogram of Ringer's lactate solution intravenously in the first hour, then 70 milliliters per kilogram over the next 5 hours. For a child from 12 months to 5 years give the same 30 milliliters per kilogram in the first 30 minutes, then 70 milliliters per kilogram over the next 2 and a half hours. If you cannot place an intravenous line, or if the child is not in shock, a nasogastric tube is a legitimate route and far safer than delay. Start oral rehydration salts as soon as the child can drink, usually after 3 or 4 hours, reassess the pulse, breathing, and skin pinch at least every hour, and never leave a child on intravenous fluids without a nurse watching.

A severely malnourished child with diarrhea is a different patient, and the ordinary rehydration plan can kill that child. The malnourished body holds sodium and leaks potassium, its heart is fragile, and a rapid infusion of fluid can flood the lungs and stop the heart. For this reason the World Health Organization uses a special rehydration solution for malnutrition, known as ReSoMal, which contains less sodium and more potassium and magnesium. Give it slowly, 5 milliliters per kilogram every 30 minutes for the first 2 hours, then 5 to 10 milliliters per kilogram per hour for up to 10 hours, alternating with the starter formula. The goal is to replace the deficit gradually, and you stop when the child is rehydrated, when weight begins to rise, or when the edema begins to fall. Intravenous fluid is reserved for the child in shock, given slowly and in small volumes.

Severe acute malnutrition is not simply hunger, and treating it as hunger is one of the ways a child dies in your care. The malnourished child has adapted to scarcity: the metabolism slows, the sodium and potassium pumps in every cell begin to fail, fluid shifts out of the vessels, and the body burns its own tissue to stay alive. The heart muscle is thin and weak, the liver is fatty, the kidneys conserve water poorly, the immune system is badly impaired, and the gut lets bacteria cross into the blood. A severely malnourished child can die from an infection a well-nourished child would shrug off, and from food given too quickly, which is why the first feed is deliberately weak.

The child in front of you may show none of the noisy signs you were taught to fear. A severely malnourished child often has no fever with a serious infection, because the body cannot mount the response, and the child may be hypothermic instead. The child may be quiet, still, and seemingly content, with cold hands and feet and a weak cry. Bilateral pitting edema can hide the wasting, so a child who looks plump may be severely malnourished, and puffiness of the eyes and feet is not good nutrition. Assume that every severely malnourished child has an infection even when nothing points to one, and look for the hidden sites in the mouth, ears, skin folds, lungs, and perineum.

Hypoglycemia is the first killer of the first hours, and it is silent. A severely malnourished child has small glycogen stores and a high demand, so blood glucose can fall below 3 millimoles per liter without convulsions or sweating. Check the blood glucose on admission in every child, and treat immediately if it is low. A conscious child takes 50 milliliters of dextrose at 10 per cent by mouth or by nasogastric tube, and an unconscious child takes 5 milliliters per kilogram of dextrose at 10 per cent intravenously, followed by the same oral dose. Then start the starter formula at once and feed every 2 to 3 hours, day and night, because the treatment of hypoglycemia is a rhythm of feeding rather than one dose of sugar. Hypothermia travels with it, and an axillary temperature below 35.5 degrees Celsius means the child must be warmed actively and gently, skin to skin against the mother, with a hat, dry blankets, and a warm room.

The World Health Organization organizes the care of severe acute malnutrition into ten steps, and the order of the steps is the treatment. During stabilization you treat and prevent hypoglycemia and hypothermia, treat and prevent dehydration, correct electrolyte imbalance, treat and prevent infection, and correct micronutrient deficiencies, and only then do you begin cautious feeding. The course then runs through three phases: stabilization in the first week, transition in the second week, and rehabilitation from about the third week until discharge. In stabilization the child receives the starter milk known as F-75, which is low in energy and protein, given often and in small volumes, and in transition the child moves to a higher-energy milk known as F-100 or to ready-to-use therapeutic food, so that each phase keeps its own food, its own volume, and its own dangers.

The starter formula is deliberately weak, and understanding why makes its slowness easier to accept. F-75 provides about 75 kilocalories in every 100 milliliters, with modest protein and added potassium, magnesium, and micronutrients. It is given at about 130 milliliters per kilogram per day divided into feeds every 2 to 3 hours, which is 8 feeds in 24 hours. The sodium is kept low and the potassium high because the malnourished cell holds too much sodium and too little potassium, so the formula treats that imbalance as much as it feeds. Give the feed by cup, spoon, or syringe, use a nasogastric tube only when the child cannot take enough by mouth, and stop to reassess if the child vomits repeatedly, becomes more lethargic, or shows a rising pulse and breathing rate.

Feeding too fast kills through a mechanism called refeeding syndrome, and the mechanism is worth hearing in plain words. When a starved cell suddenly receives glucose, insulin rises, and the cell pulls phosphate, potassium, and magnesium out of the blood and into the cell. The blood is left dangerously low in all three, the thin heart muscle cannot contract properly, the rhythm can become unstable, and the child can die suddenly in the night. Fluid can also overload the lungs and circulation, especially if too much sodium and water are given while the child is being fed. This is why the first formula is weak, why the volumes are calculated by weight, and why feeds are frequent and small, and refusing to feed a child faster is not neglect but the protection that saves the first week.

Transition begins when the child is stable, has a good appetite, and is losing edema, usually in the second week, and the formula then becomes stronger. F-100 provides about 100 kilocalories in every 100 milliliters, given at 150 to 220 milliliters per kilogram per day, or the child moves to ready-to-use therapeutic food, a peanut-based paste needing no cooking and no clean water. In rehabilitation the target is catch-up growth of at least 5 grams per kilogram per day, and good programs aim for 10 grams per kilogram per day or more. Weigh the child every morning before the first feed and watch the curve, and remember that emotional and sensory stimulation belongs here too, because a child who is played with, talked to, and held gains weight faster than a child left alone in a cot.

Every child with severe acute malnutrition receives antibiotics, whether or not there is an obvious infection, because the immune system cannot be trusted to announce one. For the child admitted with complications, the World Health Organization recommends ampicillin, 50 milligrams per kilogram intravenously every 6 hours, with gentamicin, 7.5 milligrams per kilogram intramuscularly or intravenously once a day, for at least 7 days. For the child treated at home without complications, the recommendation is amoxicillin, 15 milligrams per kilogram by mouth every 8 hours for 5 days, with metronidazole, 7.5 milligrams per kilogram every 8 hours for 7 days, added when there is severe diarrhea or infected skin. Check the doses against the current World Health Organization guideline and your national formulary, because national regimens differ.

Vitamin A deficiency is both a cause and a consequence of severe acute malnutrition, and it can blind a child within days, so every malnourished child receives it. The dose depends on age: 50,000 international units for an infant under 6 months, 100,000 international units from 6 to 11 months, and 200,000 international units for a child 12 months and older, given by mouth on the first day and repeated on the second. Measles is a catastrophe for a malnourished child, so vaccinate at admission if the child is 6 months or older and not already vaccinated, and give a second dose at 9 months as the routine schedule requires, while in an outbreak the World Health Organization recommends vaccination from 6 months of age. Vitamin A is safe at these doses but toxic in excess, so record each dose and do not repeat it within a month without a clear reason.

Beyond vitamin A, several micronutrients are given from the first day, and iron is deliberately not one of them. Give folic acid, 5 milligrams on the first day and then 1 milligram a day, potassium at 3 to 4 millimoles per kilogram per day, magnesium at 0.4 to 0.6 millimoles per kilogram per day, zinc at 2 milligrams per kilogram per day, and a multivitamin supplement. Iron is withheld until the child is in rehabilitation, has a good appetite, and is gaining weight, and then it is given at about 3 milligrams of elemental iron per kilogram per day. The reason is that free iron feeds bacteria and can worsen infection during the acute phase, and early iron has been associated with higher mortality.

The first day has a rhythm, and a nurse who runs it the same way every time will not forget a step. On admission, weigh and measure the child, check the temperature and blood glucose, classify dehydration, screen for danger signs, and take the history for feeding, diarrhea, fever, cough, and the household. Put the child in a warm place, start antibiotics, and give vitamin A and the other micronutrients as the guideline directs, but if the child is hypoglycemic or hypothermic, treat that first, before any feed. Feed every 2 to 3 hours, day and night, record the volume taken at every feed rather than the volume offered, and write the baseline weight on the chart so that tomorrow's weight can be compared with it.

Most children with severe acute malnutrition can be treated at home, and that is the great advance of recent decades. The World Health Organization recommends outpatient care for a child with severe wasting or nutritional edema who passes the appetite test, has no complication, and is clinically well and alert. The complications that force admission include any general danger sign, persistent vomiting, convulsions, severe dehydration, severe pneumonia, high fever, hypothermia, severe anemia, and any condition needing intravenous treatment or a transfusion. A child who is not eating, or whose mother cannot bring the child back weekly, also belongs in inpatient care, and the decision is never permanent, because a child who fails the appetite test at the next visit moves to the ward and a child in the ward moves home as soon as the criteria are met.

The appetite test is the single most useful bedside decision in the outpatient program, and it takes half an hour. Wash your hands, sit the child on the mother's lap, and offer a known amount of ready-to-use therapeutic food, about one quarter to one third of a sachet for a small child. Let the child eat without force or distraction for up to 30 minutes, and watch how eagerly the paste is taken. The child passes if the offered amount is eaten, and fails if it is not, or if the child is too weak, too breathless, or too ill to eat, and a failed test is a clinical finding rather than a judgment about the mother. Repeat the test at every weekly visit, because appetite can return or disappear, and the result is what moves the child between care settings.

The weekly outpatient visit is short but it must be complete, because it is the only contact the program has with the child. Weigh the child, measure the mid-upper arm circumference, check both feet for edema, and ask about feeding, appetite, diarrhea, vomiting, fever, cough, and any danger sign. Do the appetite test, give the ready-to-use therapeutic food ration for the coming week, give the daily amoxicillin if the child is in the first days of treatment, provide vitamin A when it is due, and check the immunization card. Praise what the mother is doing well, because the program depends on her, and make the next appointment explicit in day, hour, and place. A child who is not gaining weight after two weeks, or who is losing weight, needs a careful examination and probably admission.

Recognize the child who must move from home to hospital before the child is in extremis. Any danger sign, a failed appetite test, new or worsening edema, refusal to eat, persistent vomiting, or diarrhea that does not settle means admission. A child who has not gained weight after 2 weeks of outpatient treatment, or who has lost weight at any visit, needs a full reassessment for infection, tuberculosis, human immunodeficiency virus, and inadequate feeding at home. A child who deteriorates during inpatient care, with a rising pulse or respiratory rate, a falling temperature, or increasing lethargy, needs escalation and probably referral to a facility with oxygen, transfusion, and a physician. In a remote post, arrange referral while the child is still stable enough to travel, in daylight, with a referral note, a supply of feed, and an escort who knows the destination.

Record the weight every morning before the first feed, the temperature and pulse every 4 hours in the ward, the respiratory rate at the same interval, the volume of every feed, and every stool, vomit, and dose. Watch for the early signs of fluid overload and heart failure: a pulse that rises by 25 beats per minute and a respiratory rate that rises by 5 breaths per minute above the previous readings, with increasing breathlessness, a new cough, or puffiness of the eyelids. If those signs appear, reduce the feed, return to the starter formula, and reassess, because catching overload early prevents a death from too much food or fluid. Weigh daily in the ward and weekly at home, plot the weights so the curve speaks before the child does.

Some things must never be done to a severely malnourished child, and naming them protects the child when you are tired. Never give a diuretic for nutritional edema, because the edema is a shift of fluid rather than excess fluid, and a diuretic will only dehydrate the child and disturb the electrolytes. Never give iron during stabilization, and never give a high-protein or high-energy diet in the first week, because both increase a metabolic load the child cannot carry. Never rehydrate a severely malnourished child with standard oral rehydration salts or rapid intravenous fluid, except for shock, and then only with the slow regimen. Never force-feed a child or leave a feed unfinished without writing it down, and never send a child home without a follow-up appointment and a clear explanation of the danger signs.

The things that save children in a remote clinic are ordinary supplies, and their absence is a clinical emergency. Keep ready-to-use therapeutic food in a cool, dry, dark place, off the floor, protected from rodents, and rotate stock so the oldest sachet is used first, because the paste is heat sensitive. The powdered therapeutic milks must be mixed with clean water in a clean container, used within 24 hours, and never boiled after mixing, because heat destroys the vitamins. Keep a stock of vitamin A capsules, amoxicillin suspension, the rehydration solutions, zinc, folic acid, potassium, and magnesium, and count them weekly so a stock-out is seen before it becomes a death. Protect the cold chain for measles vaccine, with a cold box and ice packs ready for the day the refrigerator fails. The equipment list is short: a scale accurate to 100 grams, a length board and a height board, color-banded mid-upper arm circumference tapes, thermometers, a blood glucose meter with unexpired strips, feeding cups, nasogastric tubes, soap, and warm blankets. Check the scale against a known weight every week, because a drifting scale makes the program blind.

Documentation is not administration; it is the memory of the clinic and the safety net for the child. Record every admission in the nutrition register with the name, age, sex, weight, height, mid-upper arm circumference, edema, appetite test result, immunization status, and date. Keep an individual card at the bedside or with the mother, on which every feed, dose, temperature, and weight is written, and use the same card at every weekly visit so the curve is continuous. Record discharges, transfers, deaths, and defaulters, and keep a defaulter list with a name and a way to reach the family, because a child who stops coming is at high risk and invisible unless someone writes the child down. Report the tallies to the district each week or month as your system requires, since the numbers drive the supply of therapeutic food and the staffing of the ward.

The nurse is the clinician in this chapter, and the role carries more autonomy than in any hospital. You assess, classify, prescribe according to a protocol, feed, monitor, teach, and decide when to refer, often without a physician within a day's travel. Work with community health workers, who can screen with a mid-upper arm circumference tape, refer, and follow children in their villages, and supervise them with regular visits and simple feedback. Task-sharing saves lives only when the tasks are taught, supervised, and supported with supplies and referral, so treat the community health worker as a colleague and give that worker the tools the work requires. Teach the mother from the first day, because she will feed the child at 2 in the morning, and teach the grandmother and the father too, because they decide what happens in the house.

Counseling is the difference between a child who finishes treatment and a child who relapses, so it belongs in the clinical encounter and not in a leaflet. Explain the diagnosis in plain words: the child is severely malnourished, the body has adapted to too little food, and recovery takes weeks. Show the mother how much ready-to-use therapeutic food to give, how to store it, and how to feed the child little and often, and explain that breastfeeding must continue and energy-dense family food must be added. Teach the danger signs that mean return immediately: inability to drink or breastfeed, vomiting everything, convulsions, unusual sleepiness, fast or difficult breathing, fever, diarrhea, swelling of the feet, or refusal to eat. Agree on the follow-up date, ask the mother to repeat the plan back to you, and write it on the card, because the mother is the most important member of the team.

Discharge is a milestone, not an ending, and the criteria should be clear before the child reaches them. A child may go home when the weight-for-height is at or above minus 2 standard deviations, or the mid-upper arm circumference is 125 millimeters or more, with no edema, sustained over at least 2 consecutive measurements, and when immunization is up to date and the mother can describe the feeding plan and the danger signs. After discharge, keep the child in growth monitoring and supplementary feeding if the program offers it, and see the child again at 1 month, 3 months, and 6 months, because relapse is common in the first months. Prevention is the long game: exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months, timely and adequate complementary feeding, vaccination, deworming, vitamin A supplementation, insecticide-treated bed nets, and water, sanitation and hygiene in the household. Treat a child who recovers and then returns with edema as a signal that something at home has not changed.

To summarize, the child who arrives at your remote clinic is assessed in the same systematic order every time, with the general danger signs sought first and the whole child examined rather than the loudest complaint.
