Dehydration is classified by the signs that predict it and rehydrated by degree, with the severely malnourished child treated differently, more slowly, and with a solution made for that child. Severe acute malnutrition is a physiological emergency, not hunger, and its first hours belong to warmth, glucose, antibiotics, micronutrients, and small frequent feeds of starter formula, because feeding too fast can kill through refeeding syndrome. The child who passes the appetite test and has no complication can be treated at home with ready-to-use therapeutic food and weekly follow-up, while the child who fails the test or deteriorates belongs in a bed with close monitoring. The unglamorous work carries the outcome, the accurate scale, the full stock, the honest chart, the taught mother, and the nurse who checks the current guidance. Most of these children live when the ordinary steps are done in the right order.

# Chapter 45 — Chronic Disease Care at a Distance

The diseases that fill this book are infectious, and that is exactly why the chronic diseases of the same communities are so easily missed. A clinic organized around fever and the next outbreak records a blood pressure only when somebody complains, while a person whose arteries are quietly narrowing feels nothing at all. Hypertension, diabetes, epilepsy, asthma and heart failure now cause a large and growing share of illness and death in low-income and middle-income countries, alongside malaria and tuberculosis rather than instead of them. The World Health Organization has described this double burden for years, and the trend continues as populations age, as people move into cities and as diets shift toward processed food and added salt. The work does not end when the fever breaks, because the treatment begun today will still matter in ten years, and its success will be invisible for most of that time.

Hypertension is called the silent epidemic because it produces no dependable symptom until it has damaged something that cannot be repaired. Headache, dizziness and nosebleeds are common in everyone and therefore useless as a screening question, so the only reliable approach is to measure the blood pressure of adults who did not ask for it. The World Health Organization and most national protocols advise measuring every adult seen at a health facility, with particular attention to people over the age of forty, people with diabetes, people with a body mass index above 25, tobacco users, people with a family history of early heart attack or stroke, and women whose pregnancy was complicated by high blood pressure. Where human immunodeficiency virus is common, some treatment regimens themselves raise blood pressure and add a further reason to measure at every refill visit. Waiting for the patient to raise the subject means the diagnosis will be made in an emergency room.

The technique decides whether the number you write is real. The cuff must fit the arm, because one that is too small inflates the reading and one that is too large lowers it, and the arm should be bare, supported and level with the heart. Let the patient rest quietly for five minutes without talking, then take two readings a minute apart and average them. A single high reading is not a diagnosis and a single normal one does not exclude it, so where possible the diagnosis rests on repeated measurements on separate days. The threshold for treatment is usually a systolic pressure at or above 140 millimeters of mercury or a diastolic pressure at or above 90 millimeters of mercury, confirmed on separate occasions, while many protocols treat at 130 over 80 for people with diabetes, chronic kidney disease or established heart disease.

The World Health Organization package of essential noncommunicable disease interventions sets out these thresholds and the accompanying drug choices, but national protocols differ and the version in force where you work is the one that governs your practice. You must verify the current guideline before you label anyone hypertensive or begin a medicine, because thresholds for older adults, for pregnant women and for people with other illnesses are revised as evidence accumulates. Nothing in this chapter should be applied from memory, and the same caution applies to every dose named in it. Where your national protocol and this chapter disagree, the protocol wins.

For nearly everyone the first prescription is not a tablet. Reducing salt is the single most effective dietary change, and it means less salt in cooking, fewer bouillon cubes and less processed food rather than a vague instruction to eat less salt. Modest weight loss, regular walking, less alcohol and stopping tobacco all lower pressure and, more importantly, lower the risk of the stroke and heart attack that hypertension is really about. Because food insecurity and the price of vegetables make this advice harder to follow than the prescriber assumes, the plan must be built from what is available and affordable. The usual target is a pressure below 140 over 90 and below 130 over 80 for people with diabetes or kidney disease, with a gentler target in the very old to avoid falls and dizziness.

When a medicine is needed, the World Health Organization recommends starting with one of four classes, and the choice depends on what is on the shelf, what the patient can afford and what other conditions are present. A thiazide-type diuretic such as hydrochlorothiazide at 25 milligrams once a day is cheap and effective. A calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine at 5 to 10 milligrams once a day works equally well, is well tolerated and needs no laboratory monitoring. An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor such as enalapril at 5 to 20 milligrams twice a day or lisinopril at 10 milligrams once a day is preferred when diabetes or protein in the urine is present, but it must be avoided in pregnancy. If the first drug does not reach the target after a month, add a second class rather than push the first to its maximum. One tablet containing two classes and taken once a day is the simplest regimen of all.

The schedule a nurse can keep alone is the schedule that fits how people actually live. A common approach is to review the patient every month until the pressure is at target and every three months afterward, with an annual check of kidney function, electrolytes, urine protein and cardiovascular risk where the laboratory allows it. Each visit should be short and standardized: measure, compare with the target, ask about side effects and missed doses, and refill enough to last until the next appointment plus a small margin. Give the patient a card bearing the diagnosis, the medicines, the doses and the next date, because that card survives a fire, a flood or a move. If the patient cannot come, a community health worker can carry the refill and take a measurement, and that visit is worth more than a perfect one that never happens.

Some pressures cannot wait for next month. A systolic pressure above 180 millimeters of mercury together with chest pain, breathlessness, severe headache, visual disturbance, confusion, weakness on one side or a seizure suggests that an organ is being damaged now, and that patient needs urgent referral rather than an extra tablet in the clinic. The distinction between a very high pressure causing no harm and one injuring the brain, heart or kidneys depends on symptoms and examination rather than on the number alone. Where transfer is impossible, treat what you can, document the reasoning and the discussion with the family, and remember that lowering a pressure too quickly can itself cause harm.

Diabetes arrives in the same clinics and is recognized far later than it should be, because thirst, frequent urination and weight loss are blamed on heat, work or age until the disease is advanced. Diagnosis rests on a fasting plasma glucose at or above 126 milligrams per deciliter, or a random glucose at or above 200 milligrams per deciliter with typical symptoms, or a glycated hemoglobin at or above 6.5 per cent, each confirmed where possible by a second test. In a remote clinic the glucose meter and the urine dipstick are often the only tools, and a dipstick showing glucose and ketones in a thin, thirsty patient is a warning of imminent danger rather than a curiosity. Every person with diabetes needs a plan for the day when tablets no longer control the glucose, decided calmly in advance instead of improvised during a crisis. These criteria come from the World Health Organization and widely used national guidance and are revised periodically, so verify the current version before you diagnose.

The complications of diabetes are what make it lethal, and each has a screening test a nurse can perform. The eyes should be examined at least once a year, and any sudden change in vision is an emergency. The kidneys are followed with urine protein and, where available, a creatinine measurement, because early kidney disease is silent. The nerves are tested with a fine filament at several points on each foot or, where no filament exists, with light touch and vibration sense, since loss of protective sensation is the finding that predicts ulceration. Tuberculosis is more common and more severe in people with diabetes, so a cough lasting more than two weeks deserves investigation rather than reassurance.

Metformin remains the first medicine in most protocols, started at 500 milligrams once or twice a day with food and increased slowly to as much as 1,000 milligrams twice a day as tolerated, because the gradual increase prevents the nausea and diarrhea that make patients abandon it. It is cheap, it rarely causes low blood sugar when used alone, and it is safe in most people, though it is avoided in advanced kidney disease, in severe liver disease and during acute illness with dehydration. A sulfonylurea such as glibenclamide at 2.5 to 5 milligrams once or twice a day or gliclazide at 40 to 80 milligrams once a day can be added, but these medicines do cause low blood sugar, especially in older people and in those who eat irregularly. When tablets no longer hold the glucose down, or when the patient is losing weight and ketones are present, insulin is required and should be started rather than delayed. These doses come from the World Health Organization and national protocols and are revised from time to time, so confirm them against the guideline currently in force.

Insulin frightens nurses and patients alike, and much of that fear is about storage rather than the injection. The common preparations are a rapid-acting analog used at meals, a short-acting soluble insulin, an intermediate-acting isophane insulin that is cloudy and usually given once or twice a day, and a long-acting analog given once a day. An unopened vial or pen must be kept cold between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius, but the vial in use may be kept at room temperature for about four weeks and must never be frozen. Where there is no refrigerator, an evaporative cooler made from two clay pots with wet sand between them keeps insulin usefully cool, and a shaded hole in damp ground or a box wrapped in wet cloth can serve the same purpose. Teach the patient to look at the vial before every dose and to discard one that has been frozen, has turned cloudy or contains particles, because that glance protects more doses than any rule in a book.

The foot examination is the piece of nursing work in this chapter that prevents the most amputations. At every visit, and at least once a year for everyone, look at both feet with the shoes and socks off, in good light, and compare them. Ask about numbness, burning and cramps, test sensation, feel the pulses, and inspect the skin between the toes, on the heels and across the soles for cracks, calluses, blisters and ulcers. Cut the nails straight across rather than into the corners, treat fungal infection because broken skin is the doorway, and examine the shoes, since a tight shoe or a foreign object inside it produces an ulcer faster than any other cause. Give the patient a mirror and teach a daily self-examination, because a small ulcer seen this week is a saved leg next year.

Education matters more than the prescription, and it has to be concrete. Teach the patient to recognize low blood sugar, the sweating, trembling, hunger and confusion that come when glucose falls, and to treat it at once with sugar, honey or a sweet drink followed by a meal. Teach the sick day rules, that illness raises glucose, that fluids must continue, that some medicines are paused and insulin often is not, and that vomiting or drowsiness means urgent travel to the clinic. Teach the family to give the injection, to rotate sites so that lumps do not form and to dispose of the needle safely, and write the whole plan on a card to rehearse at least once a year.

Epilepsy is among the most treatable conditions in this book and among the most neglected, largely because of what people believe about it. In many communities a seizure is read as possession, contagion, a curse or a punishment, and the consequences fall on the whole family as well as on the person, so that children are withdrawn from school and adults are barred from work and marriage. The treatment gap is enormous, and its main cause is not the absence of effective medicine but the distance between the diagnosis and a clinic that stocks it. Your first clinical act is often not a prescription but a sentence spoken to the family that separates the illness from the meaning they have attached to it. That sentence, repeated by a trusted nurse, changes what happens to the patient more than any tablet.

For most people with repeated seizures, a single medicine controls the attacks, and the first-line options are old, cheap and well understood. Phenobarbital at 60 to 100 milligrams taken at night is the least expensive and is widely used, though it causes sedation and can affect behavior and learning in children. Phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate and levetiracetam are alternatives, and the choice depends on the seizure type, the age, the possibility of pregnancy and what the shelf contains, while valproate must not be given to a woman who may become pregnant because it damages the developing fetus. The principle that matters most is to start low, increase slowly to the lowest dose that controls the seizures, and stay with one effective medicine rather than adding a second because the first was never pushed to an adequate dose. Doses vary with age and weight, come from the World Health Organization and national protocols, and are revised from time to time, so check the current guidance before you prescribe.

A person who has been free of seizures for years will eventually ask whether the medicine can stop, and the answer must be careful. Most protocols suggest considering withdrawal only after a seizure-free interval of at least two years, and often five in adults, weighing the seizure type, the cause, the electroencephalogram and the consequences of a recurrence. Withdrawal is never abrupt, because stopping suddenly can provoke a seizure, so the dose is reduced in steps over weeks or months under supervision. The person who drives, works at heights, swims or operates machinery carries a different risk from the person whose seizures were nocturnal and infrequent. Give the patient a specific plan and a date to return, and never let a request to stop become an unplanned stopping.

The emergencies of epilepsy are few but they must be recognized within minutes. A seizure lasting more than five minutes, or repeated seizures without recovery between them, is status epilepticus and threatens the brain, so protect the airway, place the person on the side, give oxygen if it exists, and give a benzodiazepine by whatever route you have, such as diazepam rectally or midazolam into the cheek, then arrange urgent transfer. Never put anything into the mouth of a seizing person and never restrain the limbs. Between attacks, counsel on the ordinary dangers that kill people with epilepsy, which are burns from cooking fires, drowning in rivers and wells, falls from roofs and trees, and injury on the road.

Asthma is often missing from registers in tropical clinics because the diagnosis is recorded as recurrent bronchitis, pneumonia or a cough that never quite resolves. The pattern that should raise suspicion is wheeze, cough and breathlessness that come in attacks, worse at night or early morning and provoked by dust, smoke, cold air, exercise or infection. Many people living with untreated asthma receive repeated courses of antibiotics that do nothing, while the inflammation in the airway is never addressed. The inhaled route is what makes asthma treatment both effective and safe, because the medicine reaches the airway directly at a dose far too small to cause the side effects of the same drug taken by mouth. Where no inhaler can be found, that is a supply failure to be solved rather than a reason to give oral medicines indefinitely.

Treatment rests on two kinds of inhaler. A reliever, usually albuterol, known in many countries as salbutamol, is taken when symptoms occur, one or two puffs through a spacer, and repeated during an attack. A preventer, an inhaled corticosteroid such as beclomethasone or budesonide, is taken every day, often twice a day, whether or not the person feels unwell, and it is the medicine that reduces attacks, hospital admissions and deaths. The most common reason preventer treatment fails is not the drug but the technique, so every visit is a chance to watch the patient use the device and correct it, and if a spacer is unavailable, a clean plastic bottle with a hole cut in the base for the inhaler works as a holding chamber and is far better than an inhaler used badly. Where inhaled steroids are genuinely unavailable, a low dose of oral prednisolone on the worst days may be used under a written plan, but this is a compromise, because long-term oral steroids cause diabetes, thin bones and infection.

Every patient with asthma should leave the clinic with a written plan that says what to do when control is good, when it is worsening and in an emergency. In an acute attack, give the reliever repeatedly, one or two puffs through a spacer every twenty minutes during the first hour if needed, give oxygen where available, and add oral prednisolone at about 40 milligrams once a day for five days for a moderate or severe attack, checking the current guideline for the dose appropriate to age and weight. Signs of a life-threatening attack are a silent chest, exhaustion, drowsiness, difficulty speaking and low oxygen, and these require immediate transfer. A peak flow meter, where one exists, turns the plan into numbers, but the clinical picture remains the final authority. After the attack settles, review the preventer dose, because an attack is evidence that the maintenance treatment was not enough.

Heart failure in tropical practice has a different set of causes from the ones taught in wealthy countries. Untreated hypertension, rheumatic heart disease, cardiomyopathy after pregnancy, severe anemia, Chagas disease, tuberculosis of the pericardium and the late effects of other infections all produce a heart that cannot keep up, and the patient presents with breathlessness on effort and when lying flat, swollen ankles, an enlarged tender liver, a raised neck vein and weight gain from fluid. An electrocardiogram, the electrical recording of the heart, shows the rhythm, the rate and evidence of previous injury, and it is one of the few investigations worth carrying to a remote post, after which the short form ECG may be used. Point-of-care ultrasound, where it is available, answers the questions that matter most, which are whether the heart is beating well, whether the left side is full or empty and whether there is fluid around the heart. Without these tools the diagnosis rests on the history and the examination, and the response to treatment becomes the test.

Treatment begins with a diuretic, usually furosemide at 20 to 40 milligrams by mouth once or twice a day, adjusted to symptoms, weight and urine output, with potassium watched where it can be measured. An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker are added once the patient is stable, because they change the course of the disease rather than only the fluid, and spironolactone is added in selected cases. Digoxin at 0.125 to 0.25 milligrams once a day remains useful for rate control in atrial fibrillation and for symptom relief, but its margin between the therapeutic and the toxic dose is narrow, so toxicity must be suspected when nausea, vomiting, visual disturbance, confusion or a new slow rhythm appears. Salt restriction and daily weighing are as important as any drug, and a weight gain of two kilograms in three days is a signal for action. The trap that kills is the breathless patient with pulmonary edema who is given fluid into a vein, so in heart failure the needle stays out.

A chronic clinic is not mainly a series of diagnoses but a relationship maintained across years, and the advanced practice nurse carries it alone in most remote posts. You are the pharmacist who explains the tablets and counts them, the counselor who hears that the medicine was shared with a relative or stopped after a dream, the clinician who adjusts the dose under protocol and the record keeper who notices that somebody has not come back. These roles are performed in the same ten minutes, often in a language that is not your first, and each demands a different kind of attention. The strain is not dramatic but cumulative, and it shows up as a register that has not been updated, an angry exchange about a wait or a decision made too fast because the queue is long. Recognizing that strain for what it is, and building small routines that protect the quality of the visit, is part of competent practice rather than a luxury.

Documentation is what turns individual visits into continuity. A chronic disease register, kept on paper where there is no computer, lists each patient, the diagnosis, the current medicines, the last measurement, the next appointment and the outcome, and it is the only way to see who has been lost. A patient-held card duplicates the essentials so that another clinic, another country or a hospital at the end of a long journey can understand what has been tried, and a stock card records what came in, what went out and what remains. Follow-up reminders, delivered by a community health worker on a bicycle or by a telephone message, are what convert a register from a list into a system, and tracing those who default is one of the highest-value tasks in the clinic. Write the date, the dose and the reason for every change, because the note you write today is the only history the next clinician will have.

Monitoring for adverse effects is a scheduled activity, not a reaction to complaints. Thiazide diuretics and furosemide can lower potassium and sodium, so cramps, weakness and confusion deserve a measurement where a laboratory exists. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors cause a dry cough that is harmless but intolerable, and they can raise creatinine and potassium and cause swelling of the lips and face, which is a reason to stop the drug at once. Metformin can cause stomach upset and, in severe illness or kidney failure, a dangerous build-up of lactic acid, while insulin and the sulfonylureas cause low blood sugar, with older people and those who eat little at the greatest risk. Phenobarbital sedates, phenytoin can cause gum overgrowth, unsteadiness and blood disorders, and long-term steroids cause weight gain, high glucose, thin bones and infection. Review the whole list at every visit and ask specifically about the effects that people do not volunteer.

Interrupted supply is the defining problem of chronic disease care in remote settings, and it deserves to be treated as a clinical fact rather than an administrative nuisance. A person who takes a blood pressure medicine for eight months and then cannot obtain it for two faces a risk that is not the same as never having started, because the vessels have adapted and the pressure may rebound. An interrupted antiepileptic can precipitate a seizure that costs a job, a driving license or a life, and stopping a beta blocker abruptly can provoke a heart attack. The cause is usually a broken link along a long chain, a delayed order, a currency shortage, an expired batch, a flooded road or a warehouse that sent the wrong strength. The clinical consequence is always the same, and it lands on the patient and the nurse rather than on the supply system.

Several practical strategies stretch a fragile supply, and they begin with knowing your own numbers. Keep a simple consumption record and calculate what a month of treatment actually uses, so that orders rest on data rather than on impressions when the shelves look empty. Hold a buffer stock of the medicines that prevent death, and protect it by rotating older batches to the front and checking expiry dates every month. Choose simple regimens precisely because they survive interruption: one tablet once a day rather than three tablets three times daily, a fixed-dose combination rather than two separate tablets, and a refill that covers the interval to the next visit with a small margin. Where the law permits, let community health workers hold and distribute refills for stable patients, which reduces both travel and the risk of default. Share information with neighboring clinics, because one site's surplus is another site's emergency.

Because interruption will happen, the plan for it must exist before it does, and the patient must be told what the plan is. Discuss at the first visit and again at intervals which medicine matters most, what to do if it runs out, whether a substitute is acceptable and when to return. Some protocols allow a temporary switch within the same class, such as replacing one calcium channel blocker with another or one thiazide with another, and some conditions tolerate a gap far better than others, so the priority list reflects that. Do not silently substitute a different drug, because the patient may later receive the old one from another source and take both. Give the patient a written explanation of any substitution, including the old name, the new name and the reason. Honesty here is not a confession of failure but the clinical intervention that prevents the harm of an unplanned stop.

When the stock truly cannot cover everyone, the nurse faces a rationing decision that no guideline fully resolves. The usual principle is to protect the medicines that prevent immediate death or irreversible injury, to keep the treatment that is longest established and hardest to restart, and to avoid starting a new long-term medicine that cannot be continued. It is fairer and safer to tell the patient the truth, that the medicine is finished and that the next delivery is expected but not guaranteed, and to say what to watch for in the meantime. Document what you did and why, because the record protects the patient and it protects you. Where a decision is genuinely beyond your authority, refer it rather than absorbing it alone, even if the referral is only a telephone call to a supervisor. The moral weight of scarcity belongs to the system, but the responsibility for how you communicate it belongs to you.

Systems matter even when you are working alone, and the World Health Organization has published a package of essential noncommunicable disease interventions designed for primary care in low-resource settings, with protocols for screening, treatment and follow-up that a nurse can carry out. The same organization maintains a model list of essential medicines, and national programs adapt both to local realities, including the specific drugs they will actually procure. Decentralizing refills, training mid-level providers and integrating chronic care into clinics that already see mothers and children are the measures that most reliably improve long-term outcomes. Even a small clinic contributes by reporting its register data upward, because the numbers that show rising hypertension and diabetes are what justify the next order and the next post. Your scope of practice determines what you can do alone, and it varies by country, by employer and by the standing orders you work under, so write your protocols down, agree them with your supervisor and review them when the national guideline changes, because supervision is the mechanism that makes a lone nurse safe to be alone.

To summarize, chronic disease is now a large part of the work of every tropical clinic, and it demands a different discipline from the one that treats infections. Hypertension is found by measuring rather than by asking, its treatment follows the World Health Organization package of essential noncommunicable disease interventions and your national protocol, and its success depends on a follow-up schedule that a lone nurse can keep. Diabetes requires the foot examination that prevents amputation, an insulin supply kept cool without a refrigerator and education the patient carries in hand. Epilepsy and asthma are treatable with inexpensive medicines whose real obstacles are stigma, technique and supply, and heart failure demands that you treat the fluid without adding to it. The nurse is at once pharmacist, counselor and clinician, and the register, the patient card and the stock book are clinical instruments rather than paperwork. The one intervention that must never be left to chance is the honest conversation about what happens when the medicines run out, held early, in advance and in plain language, because a plan shared before the shortage is worth more than a promise made during it. Verify the current guideline before you prescribe, and let every patient leave knowing exactly what comes next.

# Chapter 46 — Mental Health and Psychosocial Support

In most of the places this course is meant for, specialist mental health care is not merely stretched, it is largely absent. The World Health Organization estimates that in low and middle income countries, between 76 and 85 per cent of people with a severe mental disorder receive no treatment at all in the course of a year. Many of those countries spend less than 2 per cent of their health budgets on mental health, and in some of them a single psychiatrist serves a population of 1 million or more. The nearest psychiatric bed may lie 2 days of travel away, and the nearest counselor may not exist. Understand what this means for your practice: for most of the people you will ever care for, you are the only mental health worker they will ever meet.

The World Health Organization has answered this gap with a program built to be delivered by people like you rather than by specialists, and its name organizes this chapter. It is called the mental health gap action program of the World Health Organization, and its companion volume, the intervention guide, converts what specialists know into step by step instructions for nonspecialist clinicians. It covers depression, psychosis, epilepsy, dementia, substance use, self-harm and suicide, and the psychological problems of children. Its central principle is task sharing: care moves from the psychiatrist to the nurse, and from the nurse to the community health worker, through protocols tested for exactly that purpose. When you manage a disturbed mind with a nurse's license and a thin formulary, you are not improvising; you are following a tested protocol, and that changes both your confidence and your duty of care. The regimens inside it are revised as evidence grows and guidance differs between countries, so check the current edition before you prescribe anything you hear here.

Emergency medicine worked out long ago that survival after cardiac arrest depends less on the brilliance of the hospital than on a chain of survival: early recognition, early resuscitation by whoever is standing there, early defibrillation, and only then transfer to advanced care, each link failing if the one before it fails. Mental health care in a remote setting obeys the same logic, and chain of survival thinking will organize everything you do. The first link is recognition, because a depression nobody names is a depression nobody treats. The second is early action with what exists, a conversation, a tablet, a family conference, started today rather than after a referral that may never come. The third is keeping the person safe and connected while time does its work, and the fourth is follow-up, the long, unglamorous carrying of the case. Your hospital training pulls you toward the heroic end of the chain, the transfer and the specialist, but the outcomes are decided earlier, in the village, by you.

Depression is the condition you will see most, and it hides. The textbook picture of low mood, loss of pleasure, broken sleep, poor appetite, fatigue, guilt, and slowed thinking is real, but in many cultures the doorway complaint is physical: heaviness in the body, burning in the chest, generalized aches, headache, or the phrase you will hear across three continents, thinking too much. Two questions screen for it as well as longer instruments in most hands: over the past weeks, has your mood been low, and are you still able to enjoy anything. Ask them while you take the blood pressure, and ask them of everyone with a chronic disease, because depression travels with tuberculosis, HIV, diabetes, and the social wreckage of displacement. A person can be sad about an illness and also have an illness of sadness, and the second is treatable.

Before the management, the mechanism, because it explains every step that follows. Depression behaves like a self-reinforcing cycle: bereavement, poverty, illness, or violence drains the capacity for pleasure and action, the person withdraws, withdrawal removes the activities that once gave reward and connection, and the empty life deepens the mood, which deepens the withdrawal. Meanwhile the stress response stays switched on, with the poor sleep and constant vigilance that implies. This is why moralizing fails, and why treatment works on the cycle rather than on character. The interventions ahead all do one of two things: they put action back before the mood is ready, or they rebuild the ability to solve the problems that keep the state low. Medication shifts the biology just enough for the psychology to take hold.

Do not diagnose depression in a vacuum, because several conditions wear its costume. Anemia, hypothyroidism, chronic malaria, advanced HIV infection, and malnutrition all flatten a person, and so do drugs: mefloquine given for malaria can produce depression, anxiety, and nightmares, efavirenz given in antiretroviral therapy does the same in a minority, and steroids, alcohol, and cannabis belong on the list. Check the hemoglobin if you can, look for fever and parasites, review every medicine the person takes, and ask the alcohol questions before you settle on the label. Ten minutes of exclusion at the start prevents 3 months of treating the wrong thing.

For mild and moderate depression the first line treatment is not a drug, and this is the most liberating fact in the chapter: the psychological interventions that work can be delivered by a trained nonspecialist, which in your setting means you. The intervention guide names problem-solving treatment, behavioral activation, and interpersonal therapy, individually or in groups, over roughly 6 to 8 sessions. These are structured skills, learned in days and refined with supervision, not mysterious arts, and the evidence for them in low and middle income settings is strong. Group interpersonal therapy has been delivered by trained lay workers to mothers in rural Africa with results that rival specialist care. Say it plainly: the best depression treatment available to your community is a conversation you can be trained to have.

Behavioral activation is the easiest to learn, so take it as the model. You help the person list the small actions that once gave pleasure or mastery, walking to the market, tending a goat, greeting a neighbor, and then schedule them back into the week before motivation returns, because action leads mood rather than the reverse. The plan starts absurdly small, one walk, one shared meal, and grows each week. Attendance matters more than brilliance, and a missed session is resumed, never punished. Mechanically you are re-coupling the person to the sources of reward the illness cut off, and the mood follows over weeks. If the person cannot reach you, teach the same structure to a community health worker and supervise it by telephone or radio.

Problem-solving treatment does the same work from the other direction. The person brings the 2 or 3 problems that grind them down, debt, a hostile in-law, an unmanageable illness, and you teach a fixed sequence: define the problem concretely, list every possible response without judging any, choose one, plan it, carry it out, and review the result the next week. The sequence matters because rumination, the circular helpless thinking that maintains depression, is replaced by defined steps, and agency returns with each step that ends in anything at all. It travels well across cultures, because people everywhere know how to make a list and make a choice. A typical course is 6 sessions and needs no materials the clinic does not already own.

Add medication when depression is moderate to severe, when there is hopelessness or suicidal thinking, when functioning has collapsed, or when sessions cannot be delivered. The 2 drugs most likely to be on your shelf, both named in the intervention guide, are fluoxetine and amitriptyline. Fluoxetine usually starts at 20 milligrams by mouth once daily, in the morning because it can disturb sleep, and is later raised to 40 or 60 milligrams in some people. Amitriptyline starts low, 25 to 50 milligrams by mouth at night, using its sedative effect to restore sleep, and climbs over 1 to 2 weeks toward a usual range of 75 to 150 milligrams at night. In older adults, start at one half of these doses and climb more slowly. Confirm every figure against the current national guideline and the current edition of the guide before prescribing, because regimens are revised and formulations differ.

Tell the person 3 things before the first tablet, because the telling itself improves adherence. Benefit takes time: 2 to 4 weeks before improvement, and a fair trial is 6 to 8 weeks at an adequate dose. The first days can bring nausea, jitteriness, headache, or insomnia with fluoxetine, and drowsiness, dry mouth, constipation, and dizziness on standing with amitriptyline; most of these fade. And stopping must be discussed before starting, because treatment continues for at least 6 to 9 months after the person feels well, longer after repeated episodes, and abrupt cessation causes a withdrawal that families mistake for relapse. Amitriptyline is dangerous in overdose, acting on the heart, so for any suicidal person dispense a limited quantity and let the family hold the bottle. Review the other drugs the person takes, because fluoxetine adds its serotonergic effect to medicines such as tramadol. Write the start date, the dose, and the review date in the register the day you prescribe.

Anxiety in most of the world speaks through the body before it speaks through the mind, and if you are unprepared you will chase it with the wrong tools. Palpitations, chest tightness, dizziness, breathlessness, burning in the epigastrium, numbness of the hands, heat rising in the head, and the conviction of physical disease: these are the ordinary presentations, and the mechanism is the threat response, the fight or flight system firing without a threat, with all the adrenaline of a stampede and nowhere to run. The symptoms are real physiology, misattributed. Your first task is exclusion, and it is quick: anemia, malaria, hyperthyroidism, heart failure, asthma, hypoglycemia, and alcohol withdrawal all masquerade as anxiety, and each can be suspected in a remote clinic. Once the physical causes are set aside, name the condition, explain the adrenaline, and say plainly that the racing heart will not injure them. That explanation is not a preamble to treatment; in anxiety it often is the treatment.

Then teach the skills. Slow breathing, about 6 breaths a minute with a longer exhale, reliably douses the threat response; teach it with your hands, count with the person, and set it as homework 3 times a day regardless of symptoms. Add progressive muscle relaxation, problem-solving treatment when the worries circle a solvable problem, and a graded return to the situations the person has begun to avoid, since avoidance feeds anxiety the way withdrawal feeds depression. For a panic attack in front of you, stay unhurried, breathe with the person, ground them in what can be seen and touched, and let the attack finish, which it will, in minutes. Benzodiazepines such as diazepam have a narrow role, the first days of overwhelming distress, alcohol withdrawal, or catastrophe, in short tapering courses of roughly 2 weeks, because dependence arrives quickly where refill decisions are made by whoever is present.

Psychosis arrives loudly in a village, and the volume matters, because the crowd that gathers can turn an emergency into a catastrophe. You will meet agitation, fear, disorganized speech, answering voices or unseen presences, fixed false beliefs, refusal of food, and sometimes a person roped by exhausted relatives. Before anything else, calm the situation, and understand that this step precedes medication the way clearing the airway precedes ventilation. Speak slowly and simply, let a single person speak at a time, and move the person if possible to a quiet, dim corner, offering water and removing anything that could become a weapon. Bring in the relative the person trusts most, who may persuade where you cannot. Many agitated people settle with this alone, and every patient you calm with your voice is one saved from a struggle, an injury, or a forced injection given in front of the entire village.

Before you diagnose acute psychosis, exclude the brain insults that mimic it, because in the tropics an acute psychiatric presentation is often a medical emergency in costume. Cerebral malaria, hypoglycemia, meningitis, sepsis, urinary infection in an older person, head injury, alcohol withdrawal, intoxication with cannabis, solvents, or khat, and drugs such as mefloquine and steroids can all produce agitation, hallucination, and disorganization. Check the temperature, the glucose, the pupils, the neck, the hydration, and any fever in the preceding days, and look for a seizure that was missed. A person acutely confused for the first time, with fever or fluctuating awareness, is delirious until proven otherwise, and the cause is usually found with your hands, a thermometer, and a rapid test. Treating the malaria is then the treatment of the psychosis, while haloperidol given by reflex, before the examination, can mask the very signs you need.

When medication is needed after de-escalation, the drug most likely to be on your shelf, and the one the intervention guide builds around, is haloperidol. For severe agitation, 5 milligrams intramuscularly, repeated if needed after 30 to 60 minutes until the person is calm, is the usual course, starting lower in small or older people; by mouth, 2 to 5 milligrams 2 or 3 times a day is a common range. Alternatives, where they exist, are chlorpromazine, 25 to 50 milligrams by mouth twice a day, and risperidone, 2 milligrams twice a day, often better tolerated, especially in the old. If the person can swallow, the oral route is always preferable to an injection, in dignity and in safety alike. Pair the first haloperidol doses, as many protocols direct, with an anticholinergic to prevent dystonia, and keep that pairing when you order supplies. As with every dose in this chapter, verify against the current guideline before prescribing.

The adverse effects of antipsychotics are not footnotes; they are the reason families abandon treatment. Acute dystonia, a sudden spasm of the neck, jaw, or eyes within days of the first doses, terrifies relatives, who read it as the drug poisoning the person; it is reversed with biperiden, 2.5 to 5 milligrams intramuscularly, repeatable. Akathisia is subtler and more dangerous, an inner restlessness that looks exactly like the agitation you were treating, so giving more drug makes the person worse while you believe you are helping; the correct move is a lower dose. Parkinsonism, the slowed, stiff, shuffling state, arrives over weeks, and tardive dyskinesia, the writhing movements of face and tongue, over months and years, and neither is quickly reversible. Haloperidol also prolongs a segment of the heart's electrical cycle, the interval seen on the electrocardiogram, and in heat it impairs sweating and temperature control, so in the hot season insist on water and shade for every patient on antipsychotics. Chlorpromazine adds sedation, low blood pressure on standing, and marked sun sensitivity; risperidone adds weight gain and, in the old, falls. Examine for movement effects at every visit, keep the dose at the lowest that works, and record what you find, because that examination is the safety net.

Long term care of psychosis is family care, because the family, not you, provides the daily treatment. Teach them that the person has an illness of the brain, not a curse, not a contagion, and that it usually responds to medication taken daily and for a long time. Ask them to learn the early signature of relapse, poor sleep, withdrawal, suspiciousness, because early action at home can prevent the crisis entirely. Never stop an antipsychotic abruptly, because rebound psychosis punishes the person for the health system's failure, and when you rotate posts, write the story of the case in the register so the next nurse continues rather than restarts.

Suicide hides best of all the risks, and the core skill is to ask about it directly, in plain words, because the fear that asking plants the idea has been tested repeatedly and is wrong. Ask: have you felt so low that you wished you were dead. Have you thought of ending your life. Have you thought about how you would do it. Do you have the means at home, tablets, a pesticide, a rope, a weapon. Have you tried before, and what has stopped you so far. The answers place the person on a ladder, from passive wishes, to active thoughts, to a plan, to preparation, and each rung raises the urgency of your response. Do not promise secrecy you cannot keep, and do not flinch; your steadiness is part of the treatment.

What you do with the answers is mostly practical, not medical, and it is where a nurse outperforms an entire specialist system. Remove the means, and in a rural community the decisive one is the pesticide, because organophosphate self-poisoning fills district hospitals and kills more surely than almost any method available at home, so work with the family to lock away chemicals, tablets, and tools. Dispense sub-lethal quantities, days of amitriptyline rather than months, held by a relative. For a person with a plan, arrange continuous company, a family roster day and night if needed, and review the situation yourself every few days. For passive wishes alone, a scheduled review within the week, plus treatment of the underlying depression, is usually the right intensity. Say directly that these precautions are how you keep the person alive while the treatment starts working, and remember that alcohol dissolves restraint, so a low mood plus a drinking habit multiplies the risk. Where the community will listen, village level means restriction, locked pesticide stores and controlled sales, saves lives year after year, and it is legitimate nursing advocacy. Self-harm in adolescents, cutting or burning without intent to die, gets the same direct questions, because the behaviors overlap more than they differ, and the underlying distress is the treatable thing; balance the young person's confidentiality against their safety, share what must be shared with a caregiver, and say exactly what you are sharing and why.

Substance use belongs here because it is the most common mental health problem in most of your communities, and because a nurse can do more about it in 5 minutes than a specialist ever will. Screen routinely: how many days in the past month did you drink, and how much on a typical day. The brief intervention, tested by the World Health Organization across cultures, has a fixed shape: give feedback on what the screening showed, place responsibility with the person, give clear advice, offer a menu of options, listen with empathy, and end by strengthening their confidence in their own ability to change. A single conversation in that shape measurably reduces drinking at 6 months, a claim most drugs in this book cannot make. For khat in the Horn of Africa, cannabis everywhere, and solvents among street youth, the same structure holds in a different language, and harm reduction beats a lecture that changes nothing.

Dependence is a different matter, because stopping suddenly is where drinking kills. Untreated alcohol withdrawal escalates from tremor and sweating to seizures and then to delirium, with confusion, fever, and terror, and the last stage carries real mortality, so a dependent drinker who must stop needs cover. The usual agent is diazepam, a common regimen being 10 milligrams by mouth 4 times on the first day, tapering over 5 to 7 days and adjusted to sedation, and before any sugar or feeding, give thiamine, 100 milligrams by mouth or intramuscularly, because thiamine deficiency is why withdrawn drinkers lose their memory and collapse. Liver disease travels with alcohol, which matters because tuberculosis and HIV treatment also stress the liver, and the combination is the routine problem of district medicine rather than the exception. These regimens vary between programs, so check your current national protocol before managing a withdrawal at home.

Grief fills your clinic in communities carrying war, famine, epidemic, and displacement, and your first duty is to stop treating it as an illness. Normal grief comes in waves, triggered by reminders and mixed with moments of ease and even laughter, and it does not flatten a person permanently. Communities hold grief with ritual, the wake, the prayer, the mourning period, the shared meal, and one of the cruelest wounds of displacement and of epidemic control is that these rituals get severed, the burial no one could attend in the viral hemorrhagic fever outbreak, the mourning cut short in a camp. Where you can, protect and enable the ritual rather than replacing it with counseling, because the ritual is the therapy the community already owns, and your psychological vocabulary is a poor substitute. Grief becomes an illness worth treating when, after weeks, the waves stop and the flatness stays, unrelenting guilt, self-loathing, no relief at all, and thoughts of death, and that is depression, and it responds to the depression treatments of this chapter. The famous stages of grief are one observer's description, not a schedule, and a person who does not follow them is not failing.

Trauma is where untrained helpers do the most damage, because the instinct, to have the person tell the story, to relive it in detail, to ventilate, feels helpful and is often harmful. The tested framework for the first days and weeks is psychological first aid, described by the World Health Organization and embedded in the emergency guidelines of the Inter-Agency Standing Committee: promote safety, a place to sleep, food, protection from further harm; promote calm, your unhurried voice and clear information; promote connectedness, finding the family, the children, the neighbors; promote self-efficacy, asking what the person needs and letting them do it; and promote hope, with concrete plans rather than promises. Notice that none of this requires describing the event at all. Offer to listen, never force the telling, and never signal that the distress is a disorder in the making, because the great majority recover from terrible events with support and time and never need a diagnosis.

Now the trap, named plainly because whole programs have fallen into it: do not run single-session debriefing after an incident, the structured session in which everyone exposed recounts the event once, in sequence, in the days afterward. Trials have been run on this intervention; it does not prevent post-traumatic stress disorder, and in several studies it made outcomes worse, plausibly by forcing processing before the mind is ready and by labeling normal reactions pathological. It persists because it feels humane and gives an agency something visible to do. What works instead is watchful support: psychological first aid in the first days, problem-solving treatment for those still struggling after a few weeks, and, for the minority who, a month or 2 on, still carry nightmares, avoidance, and a body that startles at everything, a trauma-focused therapy from someone trained in it, or a referral if one exists. Keep a list of who was exposed, follow them up, and let time do most of the work under your supervision.

Epilepsy is not a mental illness, but in many communities you will be its only defender, and the two travel together in stigma. The seizure, and the confusion, fear, or aggression that follow, get read as madness or possession, children are barred from school, adults from marriage and work, and burns from falling into the cooking fire are a signature you will meet. Your tasks are concrete: teach first aid, do not restrain, force nothing into the mouth, roll the person to the side, protect the head, time the seizure, and stay until alertness returns; treat with anticonvulsants and keep the supply continuous, because interrupted treatment produces seizures; and think through the tropical causes, neurocysticercosis, cerebral malaria, birth injury, covered elsewhere in this course. Common drugs are carbamazepine, started at 200 milligrams by mouth twice a day and often increased, and phenobarbital, typically 60 to 180 milligrams at night, with the choice set by what your program stocks and by the current national guideline, which you should verify before prescribing. Ask about adherence at every visit, because half of seizure relapses in remote settings are supply failures, not drug failures.

Intellectual disability is the other condition routinely mistaken for madness, and it usually reaches you through an exhausted family, a child who does not speak, an adult labeled violent. Your first act is to look for pain and discomfort, because behavior is communication in a person who cannot explain: a bad tooth, an ear infection, constipation, an untreated fracture, abuse no one has asked about, and the behavior often changes when the pain is treated. Only then consider medication, and reluctantly, because antipsychotics given for the behavior of intellectual disability sedate without helping and carry exactly the long term harms described earlier. Give the family what they most need, which is a plan rather than a drug: how to communicate, how to structure the day, what the person can still learn, which school will take them. Speak to the person and not about them, and correct the village's labels when you have the standing to do it. None of this requires a specialist, and all of it is nursing.

Here is the hard sentence this chapter owes you: the referral you requested will almost never come. There is no bed, or no money for transport, or the family refuses, because the distant hospital is, in their experience, where people go to die. The psychosis, the epilepsy, the depression is yours, and the real question of remote mental health work is how a single nurse carries a chronic caseload without being crushed by it. The answer is not stamina; it is structure, and the rest of this chapter is that structure.

Begin with the register, because the case that is not written down is remembered until you are transferred and then lost. Every person under active mental health care gets a line: diagnosis, treatment, dose and start date, risk status, who watches them at home, and the next review date, and you sweep the register weekly for dates falling due. Follow-up is scheduled and brief, not an open door into chaos. Trained community health workers visit between your sessions, watch for relapse signatures, count tablets, and report back, extending the chain of survival beyond your physical reach. Groups multiply you, because one nurse can serve 20 people in a morning of group interpersonal therapy, and the members carry each other for the rest of the week, which in a village outweighs your clinic. Meet the traditional and faith healers the families actually consult, learn what they do, agree on who they send to you, and never mock them, because a war between you and them ends with the patient losing in the middle. And find supervision wherever it lives, by radio, telephone, or telemedicine, because a nurse who carries psychoses alone and unreviewed for a year is practicing without a net.

Documentation deserves its own paragraph, because in remote settings the chart is the continuity, and the continuity is the treatment. Write what you found, what you excluded, what you gave, and what you decided not to do and why. Record risk in full, the suicide questions asked, the answers, the plan, and the family instruction, because if a death follows, your note is the care. Record the movement examination after antipsychotics, the mood questions and their answers, the doses and the dates, so the next nurse continues rather than restarts. And write carefully in a small community, where registers are read by clerks, relatives, and the curious: keep it factual, spare the humiliating detail, and store the book in a locked box, because confidentiality broken once ends trust for the whole village.

Monitoring is the discipline that separates treatment from dispensing, and it needs rhythm rather than heroics. Every visit asks the same 4 things: sleep, appetite, function, and the 2 mood questions from earlier. A person started on an antidepressant is reviewed at about 2 weeks, mainly for adverse effects and early agitation, and at 4 to 6 weeks for benefit; if nothing has moved by 8 weeks at an adequate dose, reconsider the diagnosis, check adherence, address alcohol, and raise or switch rather than drift. A person on an antipsychotic is examined for movement effects at every visit, with the dose kept at the lowest that holds them settled. A person who has been suicidal is asked about suicide again at every visit until the risk has clearly passed, because risk moves. Weigh people when you can, ask the old about falls, and stop the treatments that are not working rather than accumulating them. The unglamorous habit that makes all of this happen is a fixed review day with the register in front of you.

Logistics is the least romantic paragraph here and the one that decides whether the rest survives reality. Psychotropic medicines need no cold chain, but they need forecasting, because in mental health a stockout is not an inconvenience: abrupt haloperidol interruption tips a person into relapse, abrupt diazepam interruption causes seizures, abrupt amitriptyline stoppage produces a withdrawal the family reads as relapse. Order against the register, against the actual caseload, not against a vague idea, and keep a buffer for the stable long term patients who depend on you alone. A sensible remote formulary mirrors the intervention guide: fluoxetine or amitriptyline, haloperidol with its biperiden, chlorpromazine or risperidone, diazepam under lock with a running count, thiamine, and an anticonvulsant or 2, carbamazepine or phenobarbital. Guard the diazepam and log it, because it is the drug most likely to walk away. Check expiry on a set day each quarter and dispose of outdated stock by the rules you apply to any medicine, because a clinic that hands out expired psychotropics forfeits the trust its tablets depend on. Where you can, stock the supplies that make psychological treatment real: a quiet room, a bench in the shade, and time on your schedule with a door that closes.

The last duty in this chapter is to yourself, and it is the point the syllabus insists on: how to carry the case alone without carrying it home. You will carry the woman who drank the pesticide while you were away, the man who hanged himself the week after a good visit, the child tied to a post by a family you had nothing to offer, and they will follow you to bed if you let them. What protects you is not detachment, it is ritual and structure: a deliberate end to the working day, a handover of worry to a colleague or a notebook, a walk, a run, a prayer, whatever reliably closes the door. Peer support, other clinicians who do this work, is the strongest single protection known in humanitarian practice, and you should build it before you need it, the way you build the drug buffer. Supervision is where the moral injury of impossible choices gets processed before it calcifies into cynicism. And watch yourself for the markers you now know so well, sleep, mood, alcohol, enjoyment; ask yourself the 2 questions as if you were the patient, because in a posting with no replacement nurse, your own untreated depression is a clinical risk to an entire district.

To summarize, mental health care in remote tropical settings is not a referral problem, it is a chain of survival problem in which you are the recognizer, the therapist, the prescriber, and the follow-up system at once. Recognize depression behind its somatic mask and treat it with behavioral activation and problem-solving treatment, before or alongside fluoxetine or amitriptyline, with the review dates kept. De-escalate psychosis with your voice and your arrangements before reaching for haloperidol, exclude the medical emergencies that mimic it, and guard against the movement effects that make families stop treatment. Ask about suicide directly, act on the answers by restricting the means and scheduling review, remember that alcohol and pesticides kill more than despair alone, offer psychological first aid and time, and refuse the single-session debriefing. Treat grief as a process the community already knows how to do, and defend epilepsy and intellectual disability against the label of madness. Build the structure that carries chronic cases alone: the register, the review day, community health workers, groups, and supervision, and write everything down so the care survives your rotation. Every regimen named here comes from the intervention guide of the mental health gap action program of the World Health Organization, and each is revised periodically and differs between countries, so verify the current guideline before you prescribe. And when the day ends, close the door deliberately, because the people you serve need you back tomorrow, and the only way to be back tomorrow, year after year, is to refuse to carry into the night what belongs to the daylight.

# Chapter 47 — Point-of-Care Ultrasound and Basic Laboratory Skills

Ultrasound has become the stethoscope of the modern remote clinician, and this chapter teaches you to carry it as one. A machine the size of a thick book now answers questions that once demanded a hospital: is there blood in the abdomen, is there fluid around the heart, is the lung wet, is the fetus alive. It uses no radiation, it costs nothing per scan, it can be repeated as often as the patient's condition changes, and it brings the answer to the bedside rather than the patient to the machine. Used well, it shortens the distance between suspicion and decision; used carelessly, it replaces a good clinical judgment with a bad picture. The same chapter then turns to the second craft the remote nurse carries alone, the basic laboratory, because a clinic that can confirm malaria, measure hemoglobin and glucose, read a urine dipstick, test for the human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis, and match blood safely is a different clinical place from one that cannot. The recommendations here follow the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the clinical and laboratory guidance of Doctors Without Borders, and every figure and regimen in what follows is current guidance rather than settled truth, so verify the current guideline before you act on any of it.

Point-of-care ultrasound is not a smaller version of the radiologist's complete study, and the difference matters more than the machine. The radiologist surveys an organ system and describes everything seen; you ask a single question with a yes or no answer and stop once it is answered. Is there free fluid, is the right ventricle collapsing, does the lung slide. This focus is what makes the skill learnable in weeks rather than years, and it keeps the scan honest, because the moment an untrained hand goes looking beyond the question, mistakes multiply. The method never changes: decide the question first, choose the probe and view that answer it, hold still, interpret, record. The scan never replaces the history and the examination, because the question you bring to the probe was chosen by everything else you already know about the patient.

The three probes that matter in remote practice each trade depth for detail, and the trade is physics rather than preference. Sound at a higher frequency paints a finer picture but tires quickly and cannot reach far, while sound at a lower frequency travels deep but paints coarsely. The curvilinear probe, working around 2 to 5 megahertz, is the abdominal and obstetric workhorse, reaching the liver, the aorta, the kidneys and the pregnant uterus through a wide curved window. The phased array probe, with a small flat face, slips between the ribs and is the cardiac probe, though it also reaches the abdomen in a pinch. The linear probe, working around 6 to 13 megahertz, lives near the surface, with the neck vessels, the arm veins, the lung surface, abscesses and foreign bodies. Gel or clean water must stand between probe and skin, because sound does not cross air, and a dry probe sees nothing at all.

The machine's controls are few, and the three that matter are depth, gain and the freeze button. Depth sets how much tissue fills the screen, and the structure you are asking about belongs in the middle third, because anything pressed against the very top or bottom of the display is hard to interpret and easy to misjudge. Gain is brightness, and it is the control that misleads beginners most: turned too high, a dark fluid collection fills with gray noise until free fluid looks like tissue, and turned too low, faint real findings vanish. The freeze button stops the moving picture so you can study it, measure it and save it, and saving is a habit to form early, because a stored image can be reviewed by a distant mentor tomorrow while a live glance cannot. Orientation comes from the marker embossed on the probe and the dot on the edge of the screen: hold the probe marker toward the patient's head or the patient's right, and the screen dot tells you which side of the image is which. Every modern machine carries presets named for abdomen, heart or vessel, and starting from the right preset saves a minute of fumbling at the bedside.

Artifacts are the shadows and echoes that mislead a beginner, and learning them early prevents most early errors. Bone and stones stop sound cleanly and throw a dark shadow behind them, while gas scatters it into a dirty, noisy shadow that flickers when the patient moves or belches. A mirror artifact can duplicate the liver across the diaphragm and invent a structure that does not exist, and an edge shadow drops a dark stripe off the rounded side of a cyst or vessel. True fluid, by contrast, is black, homogeneous and quietly bordered, and its edges come to sharp points where it wedges between organs, which is how free blood announces itself. When an image makes no sense, do not turn the gain and hope; move the probe, ask the patient to breathe deeply or roll to one side, and compare with the other flank, because a real finding stays and an artifact dissolves.

The focused abdominal scan for free fluid in trauma is the classic remote application, and it is built on anatomy rather than dexterity. The examination, the focused assessment with sonography in trauma, looks at the places where blood pools in a patient lying on their back: the right upper quadrant where the liver meets the right kidney, in the space named Morrison's pouch, the left upper quadrant around the spleen, the pelvis behind the bladder or uterus, and the sac around the heart. Slide the curvilinear probe through each window, hold still through several breaths, and look for black, sharply pointed collections where none should be. The reasoning is simple, because the peritoneum is a basin with dependent pockets and free fluid obeys gravity, so a negative scan in every window makes significant intraperitoneal bleeding unlikely. The interpretation belongs to the whole patient, because this scan sees peritoneal blood and says nothing about the retroperitoneum, the bowel or the solid organs themselves, and a battered patient with a negative scan still needs observation and often transfer. In the unstable patient a positive scan is not a reason to keep scanning but a reason to call the surgeon, activate the transfusion plan and prepare the road, which is how the trauma guidance of the World Health Organization and Doctors Without Borders intends it to be used.

The cardiac scan answers three questions, and each can change a resuscitation, and all three can be learned from two or three views. The easiest window in a breathless supine patient is the subcostal view, with the probe held flat under the rib cage looking up at the heart, while the parasternal long axis view between the ribs of the left chest shows the left ventricle in profile. The first question is whether there is fluid in the pericardium: an anechoic stripe circling the heart means an effusion, and when that fluid presses hard enough the right ventricle squeezes inward as it relaxes, the sign of tamponade, because the inelastic sac stops the heart from filling. The second is whether the heart is beating at all, a question that matters in arrest, because a still heart despite an organized rhythm on the electrocardiogram changes the prognosis and the conversation with the family. The third is whether the left side is full or empty: a small, thick-walled ventricle slamming almost shut with each beat suggests a circulation that is empty and needs volume, while a dilated, sluggishly contracting one suggests failure or overload rather than dehydration. The inferior vena cava adds a slow measure of the tank, since a flat vein that collapses with each breath supports the empty side of the answer and a wide, motionless vein supports the full or obstructed side.

The lung scan is the most elegant example of turning a limitation into a tool, because ultrasound cannot pass through air, and the lung is air. What the probe watches instead is the pleural line, the bright shimmering ribbon where the lung surface meets the chest wall, and how it behaves with each breath. In the normal lung the line slides sideways with respiration, the sliding sign, and where the lung slides there is no pneumothorax at that spot, because a collapsed lung no longer rubs against the chest wall. Absent sliding after chest trauma, a procedure or unexplained hypoxia means pneumothorax until proved otherwise, and if the probe finds a point on the chest wall where the sliding returns, the lung point, the diagnosis is as close to certain as bedside medicine allows. Vertical comet-tail artifacts called B-lines, when more than three fan out from one patch of pleura, mean the lung substance is wet, the profile of pulmonary edema or pneumonitis, while a patch of lung that looks like liver with bright branching specks inside is a consolidated pneumonia. Fluid above the diaphragm, black and curving with the breath, is a pleural effusion, and unlike computed tomography, or CT, the scan can be repeated every hour to watch a fluid plan succeed or fail.

The obstetric scan earns its place in remote practice through four questions: is the pregnancy in the uterus, is the fetus alive, how does it lie, and how grown is it. A heartbeat is visible from about six weeks of pregnancy, a little later through the abdominal wall, and the flicker in the chest is the single most reassuring and most devastating finding the machine delivers; count it over time and expect 110 to 160 beats per minute in mid and late pregnancy. The lie and position answer themselves once you find the head: a head down over the pelvis is cephalic, a head under the ribs is breech, and a shoulder or back over the pelvis is transverse, which means this delivery needs planning and probably referral. Gestational age comes from measurement, since before about 13 weeks the crown-rump length on one careful view is the most accurate measure in all of obstetrics, and later the width of the head and the length of the femur are compared with tables the machine carries. The estimated weight follows, and the value of knowing it shows in the decisions it drives, because a baby much smaller than dates raises intrauterine growth restriction and a pregnancy beyond any date the mother knows raises questions the scan alone cannot settle. Be honest about the limits of your training: an intrauterine pregnancy makes an ectopic pregnancy far less likely but does not fully exclude one, and a claim about the placenta's position is not yours to make until you have been trained to make it, because false comfort is worse than no scan at all.

The aorta and the kidneys complete the abdominal panel, and both scans take minutes. With the curvilinear probe held transversely from the rib margin to the navel, the aorta lies in front of the spine as a pulsating circle, and a side-to-side width less than 3 centimeters is normal, while 3 centimeters or more is an aneurysm whose risk of rupture rises steeply with every centimeter of growth. The patient who makes this scan matter is the older man with sudden abdominal or back pain and a falling blood pressure, and here is the trap the scan must be taught with: a ruptured aneurysm bleeds into the retroperitoneum, where this scan cannot see it, so a normal-looking aorta in a collapsed patient does not exclude rupture and must not slow the transfer. Each kidney is found on its flank as a bean of gray tissue with a black collecting system at its core, and when that core splits into ballooned black cones the outflow is obstructed, most often by a stone, which throws its own clean shadow. Follow the tract to the bladder and measure the residual after the patient passes water, because a bladder that never empties explains a fever, a sepsis and a wet bed. Repeated over days, the kidney scan becomes a monitor that tells you whether an obstruction is settling or a drainage plan is working, which is the quiet way this machine earns its electricity.

Vascular access is the scan that most quickly turns the machine from a diagnostic instrument into a lifesaver, and it is where the linear probe earns its keep. When veins collapse in shock, edema, obesity or a squirming child, the landmark method fails, and the probe shows the vein before the needle ever touches the skin. Vein and artery identify themselves on the screen, because a vein flattens when you press with the probe while an artery resists and pulses, and the internal jugular vein in the neck sits just beside the carotid artery, a relationship the scan must respect every single time. Watch the needle enter in the plane of the probe, follow its tip as a bright dot sliding toward the dark lumen, and never advance a tip you cannot see, because the tip you have lost is the one that perforates the far wall or the artery. Once you believe you are in, confirm it: blood flashes back, saline flushes without swelling, and bubbles swirl in the vein on the screen, while a flush into an artery brightens and streams the wrong way. Practice on the easy patient with the good veins while nothing is at stake, because the scan you have done twenty times is the one that behaves when it matters.

Knowing what ultrasound cannot do protects patients more than any new view, so finish the training with the limits. Ultrasound does not pass through gas or bone, so bowel and skull keep their secrets, and the retroperitoneum hides behind gas-filled loops. It is operator dependent to a degree no other bedside skill is, and a normal scan from an untrained hand is worth little, because the machine documents nothing unless you save, and a saved image reviewed by a mentor is the only way your learning becomes visible to anyone but you. A negative scan never overrides the clinical picture, since the angry abdomen with a negative focused assessment with sonography in trauma still needs observation, the patient whose lung slides can still be desperately sick, and the fetus can hide anomalies beyond any untrained eye. It cannot measure organ function, it cannot diagnose bowel injury, and it cannot turn a nurse into a radiologist, and pretending otherwise is how a good tool causes bad care. The scan is a question asked of the body, and when the answer is beyond your training, the correct act is to ask a distant mentor by saved image, or to refer, or both.

The second half of this chapter moves from the screen to the bench, because the basic laboratory of a remote clinic is usually a nurse working alone with a box of reagents and an unreliable fridge. The tests you can run are few, and each earns its place by changing a decision today rather than by decorating a chart: the malaria film and the rapid diagnostic test, hemoglobin, blood glucose, the urine dipstick, the tests for the human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis, and the grouping and crossmatching that make transfusion survivable. Running them well has less to do with chemistry than with discipline, because the errors of a small laboratory are almost never subtle failures of science; they are expired strips, warm reagents, unlabeled tubes, mislabeled patients and results nobody wrote down. The nurse who runs these tests is also their quality officer, their stock clerk and their auditor, and the rest of this chapter walks through each test and then through the system that keeps them honest. Keep one habit above all: a test whose result cannot be trusted is worse than no test, because it manufactures false certainty, and false certainty in a remote clinic kills with a straight face.

The malaria film remains the reference standard, and it is the one test in this chapter where your technique changes the answer directly. The thick film smears a larger volume of blood in one spot, dries unstained, and concentrates parasites so that a light infection can still be found; its cost is that the red cells are destroyed in staining, so species and density are hard to judge from the thick film alone. The thin film spreads blood in a single layer of intact red cells, fixed with a quick dip in methanol before staining, and it shows the parasite inside the red cell, where its shape and its dots name the species, above all the difference between the parasite Plasmodium falciparum, the species that causes severe and cerebral malaria, and the milder species that relapse.
