Staining is typically Giemsa diluted in buffered water, roughly one part stain to nine parts water for around ten minutes, but follow the local laboratory protocol and verify it, because timing and dilution differ between programs. Read the thick film for the yes or no, counting parasites against a fixed number of white blood cells, commonly 200, and read the thin film for the species and the percentage of red cells infected, which together give the parasite density per microliter that treatment response is judged by. A clean slide, an even smear, a stain at the right acidity and a patient correctly labeled are the whole of the science, and the rest of the skill is patience at the microscope.

The malaria rapid diagnostic test exists because microscopy needs a microscope, a stain, electricity and a practiced eye, and none of these are guaranteed at two in the morning. The strip carries antibodies against parasite antigens, commonly histidine-rich protein 2 for Plasmodium falciparum or parasite lactate dehydrogenase, and a colored line forms when antigen is present; the workflow is a drop of blood, a fixed number of buffer drops, and a strict reading window, usually at 15 to 20 minutes, because a line read too early understates and a line read too late invents. Store the kits dry and cool, never freeze them, and treat the expiry date as law, because heat and humidity quietly destroy the antibodies months before the date passes. A positive test in a fever is a diagnosis, but a negative test deserves more respect than it usually gets, since light infections, and parasites whose histidine-rich protein gene has been deleted, which is increasingly reported in several regions, can produce a false negative. The World Health Organization therefore asks that treatment follow a confirmed test wherever testing exists, and that a negative result in a severely ill patient never be allowed to close the case, because severe malaria kills between one clinic visit and the next. The right sequence is the test, the treatment of whatever it shows, the film for species and density when the patient is sick, and the retest when the story and the strip disagree.

Hemoglobin measurement at a distance works through four methods, each a compromise you should understand rather than merely perform. The direct-reading hemoglobinometer takes one drop of blood into a small cuvette and converts its color to a number on the spot, and it is the most accurate portable option provided the cuvettes are dry, unscratched and within date. The microhematocrit gives the packed cell volume instead: spin a heparinized capillary tube of blood in a small centrifuge for about five minutes, read the column of packed red cells against the scale, and treat a packed cell volume of roughly 33 per cent as equivalent to about 11 grams per deciliter of hemoglobin, remembering that the relationship drifts in pregnancy and in iron deficiency. The copper sulfate method is pure physics, because a drop of blood either sinks or floats in a solution calibrated to a chosen threshold, so it does not measure hemoglobin but sorts donors and patients into above and below, and it keeps working with no electricity at all. The hemoglobin color scale of the World Health Organization compares a drop of blood on filter paper against printed standards and reads to within about one gram per deciliter, which is enough to find the severe anemia that matters. Whatever the method, agree the thresholds with your protocol before the emergency, because numbers around 7 grams per deciliter in pregnancy and 4 grams per deciliter in a stable child are where transfusion decisions turn in current guidance, and the current national guideline, not this paragraph, must be checked before blood is ordered.

Blood glucose is the cheapest piece of information per test in this chapter, and the glucometer strip is also the most commonly ruined test in remote clinics. The machine reads a drop of capillary blood on an enzyme strip, and the strips die fast in heat, humidity and open air, so keep the container closed with its desiccant, write the date each vial is opened, and discard within the window the manufacturer prints, usually a few months. Wash the finger or discard the first drop when hands are unwashed, never squeeze the fingertip hard, because tissue fluid dilutes the drop and falsely lowers the reading, and run the control solution with each new vial and whenever a reading makes no clinical sense. The thresholds to carry in your head are simple: below 70 milligrams per deciliter is hypoglycemia and needs feeding or sugar now, and below 40 milligrams per deciliter is severe and needs intravenous dextrose immediately, with the exact doses and concentrations taken from the current severe illness guideline before you need them. In severe malaria, severe dengue, severe malnutrition, sepsis and any convulsing or depressed patient, glucose belongs in the first minutes of assessment and then on a schedule, commonly every four to six hours, because hypoglycemia recurs and announces itself as a worsening of every other symptom. Write the numbers down with the time, because a glucose trend is a story while a single glucose is a snapshot, and the trend is what tells you whether the patient is drifting toward a crisis or away from one.

The urine dipstick is a battery of chemical tests on one plastic strip, and it earns a paragraph of warnings because its errors are quiet ones. Dip a fresh midstream sample, drain the excess against the container rim, and read each pad at its stated time against the chart on the bottle in good light, because a pad read too early or too late returns a confident wrong answer. The nitrite pad needs bacteria to have dwelt in the bladder for hours, so a negative nitrite does not exclude infection in a pregnant woman or small child who voids often, and the leukocyte esterase pad can be falsely quiet in a patient with very few white cells. The blood pad detects intact red cells, but it also detects free hemoglobin and myoglobin, so it turns positive in malaria with hemolysis and in snakebite with muscle injury, which is not bleeding from the kidney but is easily misread as such. Protein matters most in pregnancy, because two plus or more in a woman with high blood pressure or symptoms is pre-eclampsia until excluded, and the quantitative confirmation is 300 milligrams or more in a full day of urine, so the dipstick is the trigger rather than the verdict. Glucose on the dipstick is common in later pregnancy from the normal lowering of the kidney's threshold and does not by itself mean diabetes, while a very dilute sample makes everything less sensitive, so read the specific gravity pad first and judge the rest accordingly. Strips expire, heat ruins them months before the printed date, and a bottle stored loose in a dusty bag should be treated as suspect, so date every bottle when opened and keep it lidded.

The tests for the human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis arrive as rapid kits, and the counseling around them is as much the intervention as the chemistry. Test with informed consent, in privacy, and with a plan for whatever the result is, because a test whose positive result leads nowhere is a harm rather than a service. The algorithm for the human immunodeficiency virus in most national guidelines is a sequence of rapid tests: a sensitive screening test first and, if positive, a confirmatory rapid test based on a different antigen, read exactly at the stated minute and never from a line you half see. Respect the window period, which is why an exposed patient with a negative test is told when to return rather than told they are safe forever, and the same principle governs the exposed infant, whose early tests reflect the mother's antibodies rather than the infant's own. A positive result is delivered in the same unhurried voice as a negative one, with immediate linkage to antiretroviral therapy, which current World Health Organization guidance starts on the day of diagnosis, and with partner notification raised gently and only with the patient's consent. The register where results are recorded is confidential, and so is the conversation, because in many communities the wrong person learning a result causes more harm than the virus itself, and the nurse holds that boundary.

Syphilis pairs with it in pregnancy because congenital syphilis is entirely preventable with one injection, and the rapid treponemal test detects antibody that lasts for years or for life, so a positive line may mean active syphilis or an infection treated a decade ago. Where a confirmatory non-treponemal test such as the rapid plasma reagin exists, it is used to show active disease and to follow the response to treatment; where it does not, the national protocol decides whether to treat on the single positive, and in pregnancy the answer is usually to treat. Current World Health Organization guidance treats early syphilis with benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units intramuscularly as a single dose, and late or unknown-duration syphilis with the same dose once weekly for three weeks, with alternatives for the penicillin-allergic patient set by the national guideline, and these regimens are revised and must be verified before you inject. Expect the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction within the first hours after treatment, a fever with chills, headache and transient worsening as the dying spirochetes provoke inflammation, which is common, usually brief and occasionally dangerous in pregnancy, so watch the fetal heart and the contractions and keep the patient near for those hours. The counseling follows the same discipline as for the human immunodeficiency virus: consent, privacy, the meaning of the result in plain language, treatment of the partner, and the return visit confirmed rather than assumed.

Crossmatching where no blood bank exists is the most serious test in this chapter, and it should be done rarely, deliberately and inside a written protocol, because it is the one place where a laboratory error kills within minutes. Select donors with the standard criteria: healthy, commonly between 18 and 60 years of age, weighing at least 50 kilograms, with a hemoglobin above the national threshold, usually 12.5 grams per deciliter, and defer anyone with anemia, current infection, a risk behavior for a transmissible virus, recent illness or surgery, or a pregnancy. Screen the unit with rapid tests for the human immunodeficiency virus, hepatitis B, hepatitis C and syphilis, and in a malaria-endemic area for malaria as well, because transfusing parasites into a sick recipient is a real and avoidable harm. Group the blood on a tile with antisera, where cells that clump in anti-A serum or anti-B serum name the group and the rhesus antiserum names the rhesus, and repeat the grouping on the recipient with the same care. The major crossmatch mixes donor cells with recipient serum and looks for clumping, and the minor crossmatch mixes donor plasma with recipient cells, and clumping in either means the unit is refused, while in an emergency uncrossmatched group O rhesus negative blood is the fallback chosen knowingly, with consent, never the shortcut of assumed compatibility. The whole act, from donor interview to bedside identity check, belongs to the nurse, and the check of names, groups and expiry between two people at the bedside is the last and most important test of all.

Transfusion itself is a monitored procedure, and the nurse is the monitor. Take the temperature, pulse, blood pressure and respiratory rate before the unit starts, fifteen minutes into it and hourly after, because most severe reactions announce themselves in the first minutes, and the first signs are fever, restlessness, a racing pulse, a rising respiratory rate or a falling blood pressure. A hemolytic reaction from mismatched blood shows fever with back or flank pain, dark urine, falling blood pressure and bleeding from puncture sites, and the response is the same for any serious reaction: stop the unit, keep the line open with saline, reassess the patient, send the unit and a fresh sample back to the bench, and document everything with times. Milder fever and rash reactions are managed by slowing or stopping and reviewing according to the national guideline, and the difference between a minor reaction and a fatal one is decided at the bedside, so a reaction is never treated as background noise. The blood itself lives between 2 and 6 degrees Celsius in a monitored fridge, leaves the fridge for one patient only, and once out should start within the usual 30 minutes and finish within about 4 hours, because warm blood breeds bacteria and a unit hanging too long becomes a sepsis. These rules are blood service standards, and the current national standard and the local blood service guideline, not memory, are what govern your fridge log, your discard times and your paperwork.

Quality control without a quality department is a set of small habits performed daily rather than a department, and the habits are what make results trustworthy. The refrigerator temperature is read morning and evening with a maximum and minimum thermometer and written in a log, with an agreed alarm threshold so that a failing fridge at night is a discovered problem rather than a morning surprise. Reagents are dated the day they are opened, stored at the temperature their label demands, and used first expiry first out, and a monthly count of stock, matched against the register of tests performed, tells you what to order before the shortage instead of after it. Cold chain is verified rather than assumed, because a cool box with conditioned ice packs and a thermometer travels with every reagent, and the receiving nurse records what arrived and at what temperature. Controls are run whenever a new lot of anything is opened: the positive and negative control in the kit box, the control solution for the glucometer, the known-positive serum kept for the rapid tests, and a known sample through the hemoglobin method, and a failed control takes that test out of service until the failure is explained. Competence is audited the same way, through a logbook of who performed which test, periodic slides sent to a reference laboratory to be read blind against your own reading, and honest removal of yourself from a test you have not performed recently enough to trust your hands.

The discipline of writing results down is the quiet spine of the whole chapter, because in a clinic with rotating staff and no server, the register is the chart, the audit and the memory of the facility. Every result is written with the date, the time, the patient's name and identifier, the method, the result with its units, and the initials of the person who performed it, in a book that never leaves the facility and is reviewed at handover. Trends matter more than snapshots, and they exist only if the numbers sit in one place: the parasite density at diagnosis and again at 24 and 48 hours to show the treatment working, the glucose series, the hemoglobin before and after transfusion, the dipstick protein across the antenatal visits. An image saved or a simple sketch of a positive finding, with the date, extends the register to the ultrasound, and an image that can be sent to a mentor doubles as teaching and documentation at once. A result recorded and not acted upon is paperwork, and a result acted upon and not recorded is a rumor, so the entry in the book and the entry in the patient's chart close the loop together. The register is also the record that survives you, and in a referral, a mass campaign or an outbreak investigation it becomes the evidence on which others decide, so write it for the stranger who will read it next year.

Training and logistics keep both crafts alive, and both are nursing responsibilities rather than footnotes. Ultrasound skill is built by supervised repetition, not by watching, and a common pathway is dozens of supervised normal scans per application, a logbook of images reviewed by a mentor who can be reached by phone or saved image, and a standing rule against interpreting alone what you have not been signed off to interpret. The machine needs care the way a microscope does: probes are never dropped, cables are never wound tightly, the screen is shielded from dust and direct heat, and the unit is charged and stored in its case between uses. Gel is a consumable that runs out far from resupply, so ration it, keep the bottle capped against drying, and know that clean water works for a quick look though it demands a firmer hand, while improvised covers of clean plastic sheeting let the probe travel between patients without carrying their skin flora. Power is a clinical issue here as everywhere, so know how many hours the battery holds, which solar or generator arrangement recharges it, and which examinations to ration when the sky is overcast for a week. The same logic governs the bench, with a microscope under its dust cover, reagents off the floor and away from the fridge's exhaust, and a named person for every inventory, because equipment without an owner decays into scenery.

Safety around ultrasound deserves its own words, because the question is asked often and deserves an honest answer. At the low outputs used for diagnostic imaging, no harm has been demonstrated across decades of obstetric use, but prudence stands as a principle: use the lowest power that answers the question, spend the least time that answers it, and never scan out of curiosity what you can learn by hand. The real harms of this tool are indirect, and they are the false reassurance of a scan read wrongly, the delay while an untrained operator searches an abdomen while the patient needed the road, and the privacy taken from a patient examined without explanation, cover or a chaperone when culture asks for one. Explain the scan in plain language before you start, say what the picture can and cannot tell, and share the finding honestly, because the machine in your hand changes what the patient believes is happening to them. The same consent, privacy and honest explanation govern the rapid tests, and a patient who understands what is being tested and why cooperates better, returns sooner and tells the neighbors the truth rather than the rumor.

To summarize, point-of-care ultrasound extends the physical examination with questions a handheld machine answers in minutes, and the method is always the same: a focused question, the right probe, a steady hand and an honest record. Learn the probes and the three controls, respect the artifacts, and let the focused assessment with sonography in trauma, the cardiac and lung scans, the obstetric scan, the aorta and kidney scans and the vascular access scan each answer only what they are able to answer, remembering always what ultrasound cannot see. The laboratory the nurse runs alone earns trust through the malaria film and rapid diagnostic test, the hemoglobin methods that work without mains power, the glucose meter with its fragile strips, the urine dipstick read at its stated times, the rapid tests for the human immunodeficiency virus and syphilis delivered with consent and linkage to care, and the rarely performed, carefully protocolized crossmatch followed by a monitored transfusion. Quality is a set of daily habits rather than a department, with the temperature log, the expiry discipline, the cold chain, the controls run on every new lot and the register in which every result is written with time, name and initials. The nurse in these settings is the operator, the analyst, the quality officer and the person who writes it all down, and every figure and regimen in this chapter is current guidance rather than settled truth, so verify the current guideline before you act.

# Chapter 48 — Dental, Eye, and Ear, Nose and Throat Basics

Teeth, eyes, ears, noses and throats fill more clinic days than any textbook admits, and the word basics in this title is a trap. These small structures crowd the face around the airway and the brain, and their diseases can blind, choke, or descend into the deep spaces of the neck. The woman who has chewed on one side for two years comes to you because you are the only person who will look. The discipline is constant: understand the mechanism before the maneuver, do only what you can do safely, and refer what deserves a specialist while the patient can still travel.

Dental pain is one of the commonest reasons an adult walks hours to a rural facility. Caries, or tooth decay, begins when bacteria in plaque ferment sugar and produce acid that dissolves the enamel; once it is breached the decay spreads toward the pulp, the living core of nerve and blood vessel. Inflammation of that pulp, called pulpitis, is the throbbing pain that keeps people awake, and when the pulp dies the infection escapes at the root tip into the bone, forming the periapical abscess. Fluoride strengthens enamel and the frequency of sugar drives the acid attacks, so the most useful dental act in a village is teaching families to brush twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste.

To examine the painful tooth you need light, a dry field, and time, in that order. Have the patient point with one finger, then inspect each surface: the biting surface, the two neighboring sides, the cheek side, and the tongue side. Tap each tooth with a metal handle, because tenderness to percussion means the inflammation has reached the ligament that suspends the tooth in bone. Press the gum over each root, looking for a tender bulge, the gumboil, which drains a chronic abscess, and rock the crown between two instruments to test mobility. Finish with the questions that localize the pain: triggered by cold and gone in seconds, spontaneous and worse at night, or sharp only on biting?

The answers sort pulpitis into its two forms, and the distinction decides what you can offer. Pain only with cold, sweet, or biting, fading within seconds and pointing to an obvious cavity, is likely reversible pulpitis: the pulp is inflamed but alive, and cleaning the decay and sealing the tooth relieves it. Pain that arrives unprovoked, wakes the patient at night, and is hard to localize is likely irreversible pulpitis: the pulp is dying, and no dressing from outside will quiet it for long. A periapical abscess adds percussion tenderness, a tooth that feels high on closing, a gumboil, facial swelling, and sometimes fever. Without radiographs you make this distinction at the chair and record which tooth and what you found.

Dental triage comes down to one question: has the infection left the tooth? Caries with mild reversible pulpitis or a painless gumboil can wait for the visiting dentist for days. Mark these findings as urgent: facial swelling crossing the midline or below the jaw line, fever above 38 degrees Celsius, trismus, meaning the mouth opens less than two fingerbreadths, difficulty swallowing, drooling, or a muffled voice. Swelling in the floor of the mouth spreading from a lower molar is Ludwig angina until proved otherwise, an airway emergency: keep the patient sitting upright and refer now. Acute necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis presents with sudden painful bleeding gums, craters punched out between the teeth, a foul metallic taste, and breath that fills the room, and it responds to metronidazole, 400 milligrams by mouth three times a day in an adult, plus cleaning, fluids, and food. When the same destruction invades the cheek of a malnourished child, it is noma, a gangrene that can perforate the face within days; give penicillin and metronidazole, feed the child, and refer.

A temporary filling is one of the small procedures that genuinely saves discomfort, and it suits a clean cavity with reversible pulpitis, a lost filling without deep decay, or a tooth awaiting the dentist. Clean out debris and soft decay with a spoon shaped excavator, rinse with clean water, and dry the cavity with gauze, because moisture is the reason most dressings fall out. Press in a zinc oxide temporary restorative material and adapt it to the walls with the flat end of an instrument. Have the patient bite on a strip of gauze, because a filling that sits high hurts within hours, and the patient feels it first, so trim it. Send the patient away with one instruction: nothing hard on that tooth, and return if the pain worsens rather than settles.

Dental anesthesia makes all of this possible. For upper teeth the jawbone is thin, so a supraperiosteal infiltration works: inject one to two milliliters of 2 per cent lidocaine with epinephrine into the gum beside the root tip, aspirating first. For lower molars the bone is dense, and you need an inferior alveolar nerve block: with the mouth wide open, insert the needle into the hollow just behind the last lower molar at the height of the chewing surface, advance one to two centimeters until gentle bone contact, then withdraw, aspirate, and deposit about 1.5 milliliters slowly. A 1.8 milliliter cartridge of 2 per cent lidocaine contains 36 milligrams, and the ceiling is about 7 milligrams per kilogram with epinephrine and 4.5 without it, so count your cartridges. Do not inject into visibly infected tissue, because acidic pus inactivates the anesthetic and the needle carries infection deeper. Watch for tingling lips and a metallic taste, the first warnings of lidocaine toxicity.

Extraction is the definitive treatment for most teeth you will meet, and the safe rule is to extract only teeth loose enough for the forceps to do most of the work. Teeth firmly fixed in healthy bone, upper molars whose roots sit near the maxillary sinus, and any tooth in a hot, swollen field belong to a dentist, because a fractured root or a hole into the sinus turns a simple extraction into a complicated one. Wait until the lip or tongue is truly numb before you begin. Luxate the tooth with an elevator worked between root and socket wall, then grasp the crown as far down the root as possible and deliver with slow rocking rather than a straight pull. Inspect the tooth for broken roots, leave the clot undisturbed, and have the patient bite on folded gauze for 15 to 20 minutes before checking the socket again.

Aftercare is a short list the patient can repeat back to you. Bite on the gauze for half an hour, with no rinsing, no straws, and no spitting for the first 24 hours, because suction can pull the clot out. Eat soft, cool food on the other side, expect saliva streaked with blood for a day, and return for frank bleeding. From the day after, rinse gently with warm salt water, half a teaspoon of salt in a cup of boiled and cooled water, three times a day after meals. Give paracetamol, 15 milligrams per kilogram up to 1 gram every six hours by mouth, adding ibuprofen, 10 milligrams per kilogram every eight hours, when the stomach and kidneys are sound. Tell the patient when to return: uncontrolled bleeding, swelling that increases after the second day, fever, difficulty opening the mouth, or pain that worsens after three days.

The commonest complication after extraction is not infection but dry socket, and recognizing it spares the patient pointless antibiotics. The story is a return two to four days after extraction, often of a lower molar, with severe throbbing pain, a bad taste, and an odor, but no fever, no swelling, and a socket whose white bone lies exposed where the clot should be. The mechanism is loss of the clot with a bare, inflamed bone surface, and the risk rises after difficult extractions, in smokers, and in patients who rinsed too early. Treatment is mechanical: irrigate the socket with warm saline and pack it with ribbon gauze carrying a eugenol dressing, changed every one to two days until the bone is covered. Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is spreading swelling, fever, or trismus.

Antibiotics have a narrow place in dental care, and prescribing them for every toothache is how a clinic manufactures resistance. They do not relieve the pressure pain of pulpitis or cure an abscess pocket, which is why drainage is the treatment and the antibiotic is only the escort. Give them when there is fever or spreading cellulitis, when the patient is malnourished, diabetic, or immunosuppressed, and when extraction must wait: amoxicillin, 500 milligrams by mouth three times a day for three to five days in an adult, or 40 to 50 milligrams per kilogram per day in a child, with metronidazole, 400 milligrams three times a day, added for anaerobic spread. For penicillin allergy, clindamycin is the classic alternative. The World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention both teach that the antibiotic is an adjunct to removing the cause, never a substitute for it. Regimens are revised regularly and guidance differs between countries, so check the current national protocol before you prescribe.

Keep a register of extractions, the reasons, and the complications, because a clinic that can say it removed 400 teeth last year can argue for a visiting dentist and a fluoride program in a way a clinic with no data cannot. Everything that enters a mouth is sterilized between patients, and a pressure cooker at full steam for 20 minutes is a legitimate field method where an autoclave is absent. Ask about oral pain in every antenatal and well child visit, and teach the link between sugary drinks and night pain. Remember that recurrent oral thrush in an adult raises the question of human immunodeficiency virus infection or uncontrolled diabetes, and deserves testing.

Turn now to the eye, and begin every eye encounter by measuring what the patient can see, because vision is the vital sign of the eye and the number that decides urgency. Test each eye separately with the other covered, using a chart at 6 meters, a reduced chart at 3 meters, an illiterate E chart, or the ability to count fingers, see hand movements, or perceive light. Write the number down, because a red eye with normal vision is almost never an emergency, while a red eye with reduced vision always is. After vision comes the flash examination with a torch: the pupil, the pattern of redness, the clarity of the cornea, and the red glow from the depths of the eye. Fluorescein strips, moistened with clean water and swept across the lower lid, stain raw epithelium green.

The foreign body in the eye is the commonest ocular procedure a remote clinic performs, and the history sets the risk. Grinding or hammering metal throws fragments that can penetrate the globe with little external evidence, so that history obliges you to exclude a penetrating injury first. Evert the upper lid by folding it over a probe while the patient looks down, because the speck that moves with every blink often hides there. After a drop of topical anesthetic, irrigate with clean water, since many specks float away, then lift what remains with a moistened cotton swab; a rust ring can be teased off with a flat sterile needle. If the eye may be penetrated, shown by an irregular or teardrop pupil, blood in the front chamber, or a visible tear, place a rigid shield resting on the orbital bones, give nothing by mouth, check tetanus cover, start systemic antibiotics, and refer urgently. Never press on a globe that may be open, and never give topical anesthetic for home use, because the eye feels fine while an ulcer eats.

A corneal abrasion, a scratch through the surface epithelium, presents with sudden pain, foreign body sensation, tearing, and photophobia, and fluorescein shows the raw patch glowing green. Management rests on two facts: the epithelium usually heals within 24 to 72 hours, and the raw surface is open to bacteria, above all Pseudomonas, which can destroy an eye in a day or two. Once no foreign body remains under the lid, give antibiotic ointment, chloramphenicol 1 per cent three times a day or tetracycline twice a day for three to five days, and control pain with oral paracetamol and ibuprofen. Review at 48 hours: worsening pain, a cloudy cornea, or a white level of cells in the front chamber means an infected ulcer, not an abrasion. The old custom of a tight eye patch has been settled against: patching does not speed healing, it hides the eye that most needs watching, and a contact lens wearer, whose particular danger is a Pseudomonas ulcer, must never be patched.

Conjunctivitis, inflammation of the membrane over the white of the eye and the inner lids, is usually a nuisance, but sorting bacterial from viral decides what you do and what you teach. Bacterial infection gives a thick discharge that glues the lashes shut overnight and often crosses to the other eye; it settles with lid hygiene and a topical antibiotic such as tetracycline ointment twice a day for five to seven days. Viral infection gives a watery discharge, grittiness, a tender gland in front of the ear, and often a cold; no antibiotic shortens it, and your treatment is hygiene education: hand washing, separate towels, and keeping the child home. Purulent discharge in a newborn is gonococcal until proved otherwise and can melt the cornea within days, so it is an emergency. Severe pain, reduced vision, or a cloudy cornea is never simple conjunctivitis, and the label mild must follow the findings.

One form of conjunctivitis stands above all others in the tropics, because trachoma, caused by the bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis, is the commonest infectious cause of blindness on earth. Repeated childhood infections scar the inner surface of the upper lid, and years later the scar contracts and rolls the lashes inward, so that every blink drags hair across the cornea; that stage, trichiasis, is what finally blinds, and it is prevented by nothing more exotic than a washed face. Look for foamy follicles like grains of rice on the inner upper lid in children, and in adults for inturned lashes the patient plucks out with tweezers, which puts the patient on a surgical list. The World Health Organization recommends community treatment with a single dose of azithromycin by mouth, 20 milligrams per kilogram, erythromycin for 14 days in pregnancy, surgery for trichiasis by outreach teams, and sustained face washing and sanitation. The surgery takes minutes and saves the eye, so your job is case finding.

Learn the red flags of the painful eye by heart, because each is a sight threatening emergency wearing the mask of a routine red eye. Severe pain with a hard globe, a half dilated fixed pupil, halos around lights, nausea, and vision loss in an older patient is acute angle closure glaucoma: the drainage angle has shut and the pressure has climbed, so refer immediately. Deep aching with photophobia, a small sluggish pupil, and a ring of redness around the cornea, called ciliary flush, suggests anterior uveitis, often linked to tuberculosis, leprosy, or an arthritis syndrome. A cloudy cornea with a white or yellow level of cells in the front chamber, called a hypopyon, indicates a bacterial or fungal ulcer, and the same sign after surgery or trauma means endophthalmitis, which counts in hours. The rule is simple: a red eye with vision loss, ciliary flush, a cloudy cornea, or a hypopyon goes to the eye unit today.

The flash examination of the pupil is your neurology and your pressure gauge at once. Shine a torch into one eye and watch both pupils, which should be round, equal, and briskly reactive. A pupil fixed in the middle position, in a red eye with a hard globe, belongs to angle closure. A small, irregular pupil with ciliary flush belongs to uveitis, and a teardrop pupil drawn to one corner means a ruptured globe. For pressure sense, rest two fingers gently on the closed upper lids and compare the two eyes, because an eye in angle closure feels like a stone, and an eye that may be open must never be pressed. Check the red reflex last: a clear red glow means the media are clear, while a white reflex in a child, called leukocoria, means cataract or a tumor, and the child must reach a surgeon.

Vitamin A deficiency is the leading cause of preventable childhood blindness, and it lives where diet is poor and measles, diarrhea, and severe acute malnutrition are common. The vitamin maintains the epithelia of the body, including the conjunctiva and cornea, and it is the raw material of the retinal pigment; deficiency first steals night vision, then dries the conjunctiva, then softens and perforates the cornea, a stage called keratomalacia that blinds. Your screening signs are the child who stumbles after dusk, a foamy gray patch on the white of the eye, called a Bitot spot, and any cornea that looks dry or hazy in a child with measles or malnutrition. Treatment is high dose vitamin A by mouth on the World Health Organization schedule: 200,000 international units on the day of diagnosis and the next day, plus a third dose two to four weeks later, for a child over 12 months, with one half that dose between 6 and 11 months and one quarter under 6 months. In pregnancy high doses can harm the fetus, so the doses for women of reproductive age are lower and weekly; verify the exact regimen in the current World Health Organization guidance.

Cataract, the clouded lens, is the leading cause of blindness worldwide, and most of it is cured by an operation that takes about 20 minutes, which makes your referral pad a tool for restoring sight. The mechanism is lens protein losing its transparency under age, ultraviolet light, diabetes, trauma, or congenital infection; the story is painless progressive blurring with glare, and the finding is a dim red reflex or a white pupil. The rule that separates it from urgent causes is that cataract is painless and quiet: slow loss over months is cataract, while a cloudy eye with pain or rapid loss is something else. What the distant service can do is what you cannot: a small incision, removal of the lens, and implantation of a plastic lens, delivered at a base hospital or by a surgical team that sets up for a week in a district center. Your part needs no surgeon: record the acuity of each eye, keep a list of candidates with name, age, and village, counsel that the operation works, arrange transport, and review the eye on the first day, because new pain and worsening vision then is endophthalmitis.

Eye injuries follow a few patterns. The chemical burn leads the list, because alkali from cement, lime, or bleach penetrates deeper than acid and keeps dissolving tissue from within; treatment is immediate, copious irrigation with clean water for at least 20 to 30 minutes, prying the lids open while the water runs across the eye. Blunt trauma gives its spectrum: blood layered in the front chamber, called hyphema, needs rest, an upright position, a shield, and daily review, with extra vigilance in sickle cell disease. A sunken eye with double vision on looking up is an orbital floor fracture, referred in days, while a tense eye bulging forward with falling vision after trauma is a retrobulbar hemorrhage, one of the few minute counted emergencies in this field. The suspected open globe is handled like a cast: no drops, no ointment, no pressure, a rigid shield on the orbital bones, systemic antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis, nothing by mouth, and urgent referral with the vision you measured written on the slip.

The ear examination rewards slow discipline. Choose the largest speculum the canal accepts, brace your hand against the head, and pull the pinna upward and backward in adults and downward and backward in small children. Inspect the canal skin, then the eardrum: its color, its position, its translucency, and the light reflex. A normal drum is pearly gray and moves when you puff air against it, while a bulging red drum that does not move is acute otitis media, and a clean hole with hearing loss defines chronic perforation. Screen hearing with a whispered voice, and if you carry a 512 hertz tuning fork, compare bone and air conduction and note which side the sound favors when the fork rests on the skull. Those tests tell you, without any audiometer, whether the loss sits in the middle ear or in the nerve.

Acute otitis media begins with a blocked eustachian tube, usually after a viral cold, so fluid pools in the middle ear and bacteria grow in it; the pressure on the drum causes the pain, and the drum bulges, reddens, and loses its light reflex. In a small child the signs may be only night crying, ear tugging, and fever, which is why the integrated management of childhood illness approach tells you to look at the drum in every unexplained fever. Treatment is analgesia first, because most of what the child needs is relief for two days while the tube drains: paracetamol, 15 milligrams per kilogram every six hours by mouth, and ibuprofen, 10 milligrams per kilogram every eight hours with food. Antibiotics belong to the bulging, painful drum in a child under two years, in a toxic child, or when pain persists past 48 hours; the World Health Organization pocket book of hospital care for children gives amoxicillin at 40 to 50 milligrams per kilogram per day for five days, while several national guidelines use twice that dose for ten days, so check the current guideline rather than memory. Treat the complications as emergencies: a boggy, tender swelling behind the ear is mastoiditis, and a lopsided smile is a facial nerve palsy.

Otitis media with a perforated drum announces itself by discharge: the drum bursts under pressure, the pain eases suddenly, and pus wells from the canal. The treatment then is dry mopping: twist a strip of clean absorbent cloth into the canal, remove it, and repeat until it comes out dry, three or more times a day, because drops swimming on top of pus never reach the middle ear. Then give topical quinolone drops, such as ciprofloxacin 0.3 per cent, four drops twice a day for one to two weeks; quinolones are chosen because they do not deafen, whereas aminoglycoside drops, the gentamicin and neomycin family, can deafen through an open drum and must never be used. Discharge through a drum for more than two weeks defines chronic suppurative otitis media; such a child needs the same treatment, a hearing check, and a place on the list for an ear surgeon. The finding that ends patience is a perforation at the margin with a pearly mass or a long foul smell, which suggests cholesteatoma, an expanding skin cyst that erodes bone and needs surgery.

Otitis externa is inflammation of the ear canal skin rather than the middle ear, and the tragus test separates them: pressing the tragus or pulling the pinna causes sharp pain in otitis externa and little in a simple middle ear infection. The canal is swollen, its skin red and moist, and itching is often as prominent as pain. In the tropics the fungal form is common, with wet debris that looks like soggy newspaper, often caused by Aspergillus species, and it follows water, sweating, and cotton buds. Treatment is aural toilet and dryness: clean the canal with dry wicks, then apply acetic acid 2 per cent drops or quinolone drops for the bacterial form and antifungal drops for the fungal one, according to what you see. Forbid cotton buds, explain that the canal cleans itself from the inside out, and keep the ear dry. The severe end is necrotizing otitis externa: an older diabetic with deep unrelenting pain, granulation tissue on the canal floor, or a sagging face has infection penetrating bone and needs intravenous antibiotics and referral.

Foreign bodies in the ear and nose are a pediatric classic, and the technique is chosen by the object, not by habit. A living insect in the ear is the one emergency of the set, because the drumming of wings against the drum is agony; drown it first with lidocaine or clean oil, then extract the immobilized body with forceps. Irrigate a smooth object with warm water only if the eardrum is intact, never irrigate a bean, which swells and wedges, and treat a button battery as a burn that must come out within hours. In the nose, look for a one sided, foul discharge and a child who was playing with seeds or foam. Have the child occlude the clear nostril and blow hard, or make a seal over the open mouth, occlude the clear nostril, and give a short puff, which drives the object out without any instrument. An object you can see may be grasped with forceps or hooked with a right angle hook, always passed behind it and pulled forward, never pushed back toward the throat. If two attempts fail, stop and refer rather than traumatize the child.

Epistaxis is controlled almost always by pressure and posture, and the technique deserves to be taught to every staff member. Sit the patient up, leaning slightly forward over a basin, pinch the soft cartilage of the nose tip, not the bony bridge, firmly for a full 10 to 15 minutes without letting go to peek. Tell the patient to spit blood out rather than swallow it, because swallowed blood causes nausea and vomiting, which restart the bleed. More than 90 per cent of nosebleeds come from a tangle of vessels at the front of the septum, so pressure on the tip is pressure on the source. If bleeding continues after two rounds of pressure, inspect the septum with a light and a speculum, and either touch a visible vessel with a silver nitrate stick or pack the nose with petroleum jelly ribbon gauze, layered from the floor upward, removed at 24 to 48 hours. Blood trickling steadily down the throat and failure of a good anterior pack mean a posterior bleed, which needs hospital with the airway watched. Always ask which anticoagulant or traditional medicine the patient takes, and whether malaria or dengue has lowered the platelets, because the nosebleed is sometimes the first sign of the disease you must actually treat.

Sore throat is nearly always viral, and the discipline is to find the minority that needs penicillin, because in the tropics that minority carries lifelong consequences. Bacterial infection with Streptococcus pyogenes, the group A streptococcus, is suggested by fever, tonsils swollen with white exudate, tender lumps at the front of the neck, and no cough, whereas viral sore throat arrives with a runny nose, hoarse voice, and mouth ulcers. The reason to treat is the aftermath, because untreated streptococcal pharyngitis can trigger acute rheumatic fever, which scars the heart valves for life, and it can inflame the kidneys. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommend penicillin V by mouth, 500 milligrams twice a day for ten days for adults and 250 milligrams twice a day for small children, or a single intramuscular dose of benzathine benzylpenicillin, 1.2 million units, with a cephalosporin or azithromycin as the alternative in penicillin allergy. Insist on the full ten days even when the throat is quiet by day two, because the course is for the immune system, not the symptoms. These are the doses of current guidance at the time of writing; regimens are revised, national protocols differ, and you must verify the current guideline before you prescribe.

The sore throat that is more than a sore throat announces itself through the airway, and four swellings must be recognized on sight. A peritonsillar abscess, or quinsy, shows one tonsil bulging toward the middle with the uvula pushed aside, a muffled, hot potato voice, and difficulty opening the mouth; it needs drainage and intravenous antibiotics, which means referral unless you are trained and equipped for aspiration. A retropharyngeal abscess, usually in a child under five, shows a neck held stiffly still, refusal to swallow, drooling, and sometimes a bulge of the back wall of the throat; computed tomography in hospital maps it, but the diagnosis is made at the door, and it needs drainage under anesthesia. Epiglottitis, now rare where the Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccine reaches children but still seen where it does not, is the fastest of all: a child sitting still, leaning forward, drooling, with a muffled voice and labored breathing. For that child the rule is absolute: do not examine the throat, do not lay the child down, sit the child up, give oxygen if you have it, and escort to hospital. Diphtheria completes the set: a gray membrane over the tonsils that bleeds when scraped, and a swollen bull neck; the priority is antitoxin early, while it can still neutralize the toxin, and urgent referral with respiratory precautions.

The neck abscess must never be missed, because it is the deep infection that hides behind an ordinary fever and a stiff neck. A patient with fever, tenderness and fullness on one side, torticollis, a swelling that pushes the tonsil or the throat wall inward, or the danger signs of drooling, hoarseness, or stridor has a deep space infection until proved otherwise, and the treatment is intravenous antibiotics and drainage in hospital, never incision in your procedure room. The urgency is anatomy: the fascial spaces of the neck run down into the chest, so an untreated infection can descend into the mediastinum, clot the internal jugular vein, and erode the great vessels. The jugular clot is the syndrome called Lemierre, in which Fusobacterium necrophorum, a normal mouth bacterium, seeds septic clots to the lungs of a young adult days after a sore throat. Look inside the mouth of every fever with a stiff neck, feel both sides for warmth and lost contours, and remember that a deep abscess in its first days is hard and tender rather than soft.

Across these three systems run the same small procedures that save discomfort, and the same cautions about the drugs they use. Lidocaine toxicity announces itself with tingling lips, a metallic taste, and ringing ears before it progresses to seizures, so count your cartridges and aspirate always. Metronidazole causes nausea and reacts severely with alcohol, quinolone drops sting, the ibuprofen family strains the kidneys of the dehydrated patient, and high dose vitamin A can raise the pressure inside an infant's head for a day, with vomiting and a bulging fontanelle. Monitoring is the quiet half of care: check the extraction socket before discharge and again at half an hour, review the corneal abrasion and the otitis media at 48 hours, the nasal pack at 24 to 48 hours, the hyphema daily, and the eye operated for cataract on the first day. Put every review date in a register with the patient's village, because a patient who cannot be found cannot be reviewed, and the defaulters list is a clinical tool.

Documentation carries the same weight as the procedure itself. Record which tooth, which eye, which ear, the vision or hearing before treatment, the anesthetic and cartridges, the complications, the drugs and doses, the instructions, and the follow up date; your note is the patient's next consultation, and in referral it is the letter that travels. Logistics decides whether any of it happens, so build three trays deliberately: the dental tray with the light, mirrors, excavators, elevators, forceps, cartridges and syringe, gauze and suture; the eye tray with fluorescein strips, topical anesthetic, antibiotic ointment, a torch, a shield, and an acuity chart; and the ear, nose and throat tray with an otoscope and spare batteries, alligator forceps, a right angle hook, ribbon gauze, silver nitrate sticks, and a 512 hertz tuning fork. Everything that enters a mouth, an ear, or a nose is sterilized between patients, single use needles stay single use, and expiry dates are checked monthly. If a dental or surgical eye team passes through twice a year, your lists, your register, and your ready trays are half of their productivity.

The discipline of referring what deserves a specialist is a skill, not a defeat, and it starts with knowing your own hands. Write down before you need it what you can do confidently, what you can do with coaching, and what you will never attempt, and let that list change only with training, not with the pressure of a bad night. Photographs have changed the calculus of referral: a phone picture of an eardrum, a cornea, or a facial swelling, taken with consent and sent to a distant colleague, can turn a risky transfer into a plan. Build the relationship with the receiving facility before you need it, and agree on what your letters should contain. You are the examiner who finds the inturned lashes, the teacher who explains the salt water rinse, the coordinator who puts the malnourished child on vitamin A, and the trusted person whose advice decides whether a family travels at all.

To summarize, dental pain, eye complaints, and ear, nose and throat problems are the daily work of a remote clinic, and in each a few findings separate the routine from the emergencies that threaten sight or airway. Examine with light and time, treat pain first, drain what needs draining, and use antibiotics only as the escort to a procedure that removes the cause. Measure vision before and after, look behind the upper lid, keep the ear dry, pinch the soft part of the nose for 15 minutes, and look inside the mouth of every fever with a stiff neck. Know the doses you give, name the guideline they come from, and verify the current edition before you prescribe, because regimens are revised and guidance differs between countries. Do gently and well what your hands and your trays can do safely, document it clearly, and refer what deserves a specialist while the road is still open.

# Chapter 49 — Triage and Referral

Triage is the discipline of ranking, not the ceremony of sorting that the word sometimes suggests. The triage question is never whether a patient is sick, because in a remote clinic nearly everyone in front of you is sick in some way. The question is narrower: who needs help in the next five minutes, who can wait an hour, and who can safely wait a day. Ask it in those words and the room stops being a crowd and becomes an order.

Triage is not a doorway ritual that ends once the patient sits down. It is a continuous state of attention, repeated at every handover and after every intervention, because the patient who could wait an hour at eight in the morning may not be able to wait an hour at ten. The nurse is almost always the person who performs it and repeats it, since the clinician may be in the operating room, on the radio, or asleep after a night of call. When triage fails, it usually fails not because knowledge was absent but because nobody was assigned to keep looking.

The rapid assessment begins before you touch anyone, from the doorway of the room. Look at the patient's color, posture, and work of breathing, and listen for the sounds that carry, such as stridor, grunting, or the wet gurgle of an airway filling with vomit. Airway danger is announced by drooling, a muffled voice, gurgling, or a hand held to the throat, and burns around the mouth warn that swelling will worsen over hours. Never lie a patient with airway obstruction flat, and never force a look with a tongue depressor in a child who is drooling.

Breathing failure is more often a matter of effort than of rate, and the nurse who counts only the respiratory rate will miss it. Look for the muscles between the ribs and above the collarbone pulling inward, for the child whose head bobs with every breath, and for the patient who has stopped speaking in full sentences. Circulation declares itself through cold hands, a mottled knee, capillary refill longer than three seconds, and a fast thready pulse, and the blood pressure falls only after all of these. Severe distress, blue lips, exhaustion, or a falling level of consciousness means oxygen, positioning, and immediate referral.

Consciousness is the fourth pillar, and any change in it is a red flag until proved otherwise. Assess it with a simple ladder: alert, responding to voice, responding only to pain, and unresponsive. Check the pupils, check the blood sugar when a meter is available, and look for a stiff neck, because a first seizure or a seizure lasting more than five minutes requires treatment now and referral afterward. Children compensate beautifully and then fail within minutes, and the integrated management of childhood illness of the World Health Organization teaches danger signs any trained worker can find: inability to drink, vomiting everything, convulsions, and lethargy.

Obstetric triage puts the mother first and the baby second, and it is the one setting where two patients share a single decision. Heavy vaginal bleeding, a blood pressure of 160 over 110 or higher, severe headache with blurred vision, convulsions, and absent fetal movement are all red flags, as is a presenting part that is not the head. The woman who has bled and is now cold, restless, and thirsty needs treatment for shock before she needs a diagnosis, so place her on her left side, secure an intravenous line, and move. Trauma triage marches through the primary survey, so splint the fractures, cover the wounds, keep the patient warm, and move, because the interval from injury to definitive care is the strongest predictor of survival.

The focused assessment with sonography in trauma looks for free fluid in the abdomen and around the heart, but its absence changes nothing about the order of your actions. Fever is not a category by itself, but fever with a danger sign is one of the loudest alarms in tropical practice. In a malaria endemic area, a positive rapid diagnostic test confirms infection but does not tell you how sick the patient is, and a negative test does not exclude malaria in a severely ill patient whose blood film has not been examined. Treat the sickest patient for the most likely lethal cause without waiting for perfect proof, and verify the current national guideline before prescribing, because the criteria for severe malaria are revised.

Many facilities translate the ranking into colors, because a color can be seen across a room and understood by a family. Red means attention now, usually within minutes; yellow means attention soon, within an hour, and a patient who must be watched; green means a patient who can walk, wait, and be sent home with advice. Write the category, the time it was assigned, and the time of the next review beside every patient, and treat a missing category as a red one. Labels are often improvised, and that is acceptable if the meaning is shared, such as colored cards or a seating order along a bench.

When more than one patient arrives at once, triage changes from a queue into an allocation of scarce hands, and the arithmetic becomes brutal. Assign the first trained person to stand at the door and do nothing but ranking, because the greatest error in a surge is that everyone begins treating the first patient they meet. Sort by the likelihood of survival with the resources available: the patient who needs one intervention you can give goes first, the patient who needs an operation you cannot perform may have to wait, and the patient who is already dying may receive comfort only. Vital signs are the backbone of both triage and monitoring, and their value comes from repetition rather than from any single reading. Record the respiratory rate, the pulse, the level of consciousness, the oxygen saturation when a meter exists, and the last urine passed, with the time beside each value. One set of numbers is a snapshot, while a set taken every 15 minutes is a trajectory, and the trajectory tells you whether treatment is working. The patient who is waiting is still a patient, so name a watcher for every shift and tell that person to look at the breathing, the color, and the alertness of everyone in the waiting area at least every 15 to 30 minutes.

There are times when waiting is the correct clinical decision, and the skill is to know which waits are safe. A child with diarrhea who is drinking and playing, an adult with a mild fever and no danger sign, and a woman in early labor with a normal examination can all be observed, provided the observation has a schedule and a person attached to it. A safe wait always has a defined interval for reassessment, a defined set of findings that would end it, and a plan for what happens if the patient worsens at night. Referral is the central clinical act of remote practice, and it deserves the same seriousness as prescribing. Three questions organize it: does this patient need care that only a higher level can provide, can this patient survive the journey, and is there anything at the destination that will change the outcome. A referral that answers yes to the first question and no to the second is a decision to kill the patient politely, and one that answers yes to the first two and no to the third spends a family's savings for nothing. Ask all three every time, and write down how you answered them.

Certain conditions oblige you to evacuate, and the list is short enough to memorize. It includes an airway that is threatened or already blocked, respiratory failure that does not improve with first treatment, shock that persists after intravenous fluid, a surgical abdomen, an open fracture, a head injury with a falling level of consciousness, a seizure that will not stop, severe malaria with any danger sign, meningitis, severe pneumonia in a child with danger signs, a woman with severe pre-eclampsia or hemorrhage in pregnancy, and a newborn who is not feeding or is breathing fast. The purpose of the list is speed, because when the diagnosis is on it you stop deliberating and start preparing the journey. Just as important is the discipline of treating in place, because every unnecessary transfer consumes a vehicle, a driver, a nurse, and a family's money, and it exposes the patient to real risk. A patient can usually be treated where you are when the diagnosis is one you manage with confidence, when treatment is adequate by mouth or by injection, when monitoring is available, and when a deterioration would still leave time to travel. Uncomplicated malaria, simple diarrhea with mild dehydration, an uncomplicated urinary infection, and a closed fracture that can be splinted all fit this description. The test is not whether you would prefer the patient to be seen by a doctor, since you would always prefer that; the test is whether the journey adds more benefit than risk.

There is a small but real group of patients for whom the journey is the greater danger. A patient whose airway is obstructed and unprotected, a patient in profound shock who is still bleeding, a woman in advanced labor with an imminent delivery, and a patient actively convulsing should not be loaded into a vehicle until the immediate threat is controlled. A patient with severe shortness of breath who desaturates when moved, and a patient with severe anemia whose heart is already failing, may die in the first minutes of travel rather than at the destination. Sometimes the honest conclusion is that moving the patient will kill them before the operating room does, and that care must be delivered where they lie, with the family present and the reasoning recorded.

There is another group for whom transfer changes nothing because the destination has no treatment that will alter the course. Advanced cancer with no available chemotherapy, end stage organ failure with no dialysis, and a catastrophic brain injury with no ventilator all belong here, and sending such a patient on a painful journey to a place that will confirm what you already know transfers distress rather than treating disease. Honest palliative care in place, with pain relief and symptom control, is a legitimate and often superior plan. The World Health Organization is explicit that comfort is a treatment and not a surrender, and its guidance on pain relief and opioid dosing is revised and differs between countries, so verify the current national guideline before you prescribe.

Palliative transfer is a distinct plan with its own logic, and it is chosen when the patient cannot be made comfortable where they are but will not receive curative treatment at the destination. Whatever the reason, the transfer is made for comfort, so the preparations differ: a plan for pain and breathlessness, an escort who understands that the goal is not resuscitation, and a letter stating clearly that the patient is for comfort only. The most important sentence in that letter tells the receiving clinician not to begin an aggressive search you have already completed. Palliative transfer is not a lesser referral, it is a referral with a correctly stated objective.

The referral decision is a comparison of two risks, the risk of staying and the risk of going. The risk of staying is the probability that the untreated condition deteriorates, multiplied by the harm that deterioration would cause. The risk of going is the probability that the journey itself produces harm, multiplied by the severity of that harm. Assessing transport risk begins with the question of who will actually drive, so ask how long the journey takes in the worst case, whether a river or a ferry must be crossed, and whether the receiving facility will still be receiving when the patient arrives.

Stabilization before transport rests on a single observation: the first hour of the journey is the most dangerous hour, because in that hour the patient leaves the monitoring and the hands that were keeping them alive. Everything you can do in the clinic should be done before the wheels turn, not attempted on a rough road. Secure the airway or position the patient so that it stays open, obtain intravenous access and start fluids if shock is present, give the first dose of the definitive drug, stop the seizure, splint the fracture, warm the patient, and treat the pain. The measure of a good stabilization is that every line is taped, the next dose is drawn up, and nothing essential remains to be done during the first hour.

Some specific actions repay the time they take. In a convulsing patient, stop the seizure before loading the vehicle, because a seizure in transit is how patients die on the road. In a child with severe dehydration, begin the rehydration plan of the World Health Organization and, when shock is present, give the fluid that the current guideline specifies for that child's weight, remembering that a malnourished child needs slower and smaller volumes. In severe malaria give the first parenteral dose before departure, in suspected bacterial meningitis give the first antibiotic, and in severe pre-eclampsia give magnesium sulfate according to the current national guideline, because every regimen named here is revised and differs between countries.

Doses deserve to be spoken carefully, with the source named and the instruction to verify. For an adult with severe malaria, current World Health Organization guidance uses intravenous artesunate at a weight based dose given at zero, 12, and 24 hours and then once a day. For a seizure that will not stop, an intravenous benzodiazepine such as diazepam or lorazepam is given at a weight based dose, and for severe pre-eclampsia magnesium sulfate is given by the regimen in the national guideline. Every one of these numbers has been changed by a guideline revision at some point, so verify the current edition and confirm the weight before you calculate.

Fluid resuscitation is where good intentions and physiology sometimes part company, so the remote nurse needs a defensible plan. In a child with shock and no severe malnutrition, current guidance calls for a bolus of an isotonic crystalloid at a weight based volume, repeated and reassessed, with attention to the signs of overload that may follow. In a child with severe acute malnutrition, fluids are given more slowly and in smaller volumes, because the malnourished heart tolerates a rapid load poorly. In an adult with hemorrhage, the goal is to stop the bleeding and to keep the circulation sufficient to preserve consciousness and urine output rather than to fill the patient to a normal blood pressure, so record the volume given and the response.

The documentation that travels with the patient is often the only voice the patient has at the destination, and it should be written for a stranger who is tired and busy. Include who the patient is, with age, sex, and a contact for the next of kin; what happened, in a short narrative; what you found, including the vital signs and the important negative findings; what you have already given, with drug names, doses, routes, and times; and what you are asking for. Add the allergies, the weight, and the pregnancy status, and keep a duplicate or photograph the sheet with consent. Sign it, date it, and print your name and the facility, because an unsigned note is only a rumor.

Communication with the receiving facility before departure is one of the highest yield actions in the whole process, and it is frequently skipped. A call that says who is coming, what the problem is, what the patient needs, and when the patient will arrive allows the receiving team to prepare a bed, hold blood, alert a surgeon, and keep oxygen ready. Use a structured order of speech so the critical facts survive a bad connection: identify yourself and the patient, state the problem in one sentence, give the vital signs, say what you have done, state what you need, and confirm the estimated time of arrival. Ask a direct question and wait for a direct answer, namely whether the facility will accept this patient and whether the service needed is available now.

Communication fails in predictable ways, and the remote nurse should plan for each one. The network may be down, the only phone may have no credit, the receiving clinician may be in the operating room, and the family may have no way to call ahead. Build redundancy before you need it: know the alternate number, keep a written card with the referral criteria and the direct line of the destination, and agree on a fallback plan for a patient who arrives unannounced. Use whatever channel exists, including a community radio, a passing driver, or a health worker traveling the same way, and always send the written letter with the patient even when the telephone call succeeded.

The escort is part of the treatment, and choosing the escort is a clinical decision rather than an administrative one. A patient who needs oxygen, an intravenous infusion, or repeated doses of a drug needs an escort who can deliver those things, while a patient who needs only comfort may travel with a family member who has been taught what to watch for at the gate. Give the escort a written summary of the diagnosis, the treatment already given, the doses due during the journey, and the signs that require a stop. The transport kit holds a bag and mask, suction, oxygen if the facility has it, intravenous cannulas and fluid, the drugs the patient is likely to need, an anticonvulsant, a source of glucose, dressings, a splint, and a torch, and it is checked at the start of every shift and restocked after every use.

Monitoring during the journey is a matter of position, warmth, and repeated observation. Keep the airway open, keep the patient warm, and keep the injured part still, and check the breathing, the color, and the level of alertness at intervals written on the referral sheet. A patient carried on the back of a motorcycle or in the bed of a truck is exposed to cold, dust, and vibration, so wrap the patient and pad the stretcher, and check any intravenous line for patency and for swelling at every stop. If the patient deteriorates, the general rule is to stop, treat what is treatable, and then decide whether to continue or turn back.

Death on the road is a known event in remote practice, and it is often preventable, which is why it deserves to be named rather than avoided. The common mechanisms are an airway lost in a patient who was laid flat, aspiration of vomit, respiratory failure that progressed without oxygen, hemorrhage that continued because the source was never controlled, and a drug dose that was miscalculated. Review every death in transit as a case, without blame but with honesty, and ask whether the referral was necessary, whether the patient was stable enough, whether the escort was equipped, and whether the destination was right. Transfer carries its own adverse effects, and the nurse should anticipate them the way she anticipates the side effects of a drug. Immobility produces pressure injury, and a long journey on an empty stomach produces nausea and aspiration. Drug reactions travel too, and an allergic reaction that begins in transit is far harder to treat than one that begins in a room with a tray of drugs. Give an antiemetic when nausea is likely, check the pulses beyond every plaster before departure, and send the drugs that treat the complications you can foresee, because a referral is not complete until the risk of the journey itself has been reduced.

Sometimes the family refuses the journey, and the response is neither to bully nor to abandon. Ask what the refusal means, because a father may be unable to leave the harvest, a mother may have no one to keep the other children, and a family may believe that a person who dies away from home cannot be buried properly. Explain what you believe will happen without treatment, offer whatever you can offer in place, and write down that the offer was made, the reason given, and the plan for follow up. If the patient is a child or cannot decide, the ethical weight shifts, so involve a supervisor, a community leader, or the local authority, and keep the door open, because a family treated with respect often returns.

Referral is not a single step but a ladder of levels, and the remote nurse should know every rung. The health post refers to the health center, the health center to the district hospital, and the district hospital to the regional hospital, and each rung has different capabilities in surgery, blood banking, imaging, and intensive care. When travel is impossible, a consultation by telephone or a stored photograph sent to a distant colleague can change management without moving the patient, so ask for it early and record the advice and the name of the person who gave it. A referral that never closes is a loose end in the patient's care and in the clinic's records. Ask the receiving facility to send back a short note with the diagnosis, the treatment given, and the plan, and give the family a written request for that note to carry. When the patient returns, enter the outcome in a register, because the register is how a clinic learns whether its triage decisions were right, and follow up the patients who were sent away and never returned. Count the patients seen, the number assigned to each category, the number referred, the number who arrived, and the number who died, and review the trend monthly with the team.

The logistics of movement decide more referrals than any clinical judgment, and the nurse who manages them is doing clinical work. Know in advance where the vehicle is, who can drive it, whether it is fueled, and who authorizes its use at night, because a referral that waits three hours for a signature is a referral that waited too long. Keep a written agreement with the district office and the ambulance service that sets out how a vehicle is requested, how fuel is reimbursed, and what happens when the ambulance is already out. Identify the alternatives before you need them, such as a motorcycle with a trailer, a boat, or a stretcher carried by four people, and establish a hard rule about night travel on unsafe roads.

The supplies that make referral possible must be kept for referral and not consumed by routine work. Reserve a small stock of the drugs used in stabilization, a cylinder of oxygen if you have one, intravenous fluids, and the dressings and splints for the journey, and label them for that purpose. If the district hospital needs blood, ask in advance how a donor is found and how long cross matching takes, since a patient with severe anemia may need to wait for a relative to arrive. Check the oxygen supply and the delivery device before the emergency, keep the referral kit at the point of departure rather than in a locked store, and tell your supervisor when the reserve is running low rather than after it is gone.

The nursing role in triage and referral is one of the few places in medicine where the nurse holds the whole decision and must own it. In many remote facilities the nurse is the most senior person present at night, and the triage category, the decision to travel, and the letter are hers to make and to sign. That authority is legitimate only when it is supported by training, by standing orders that a medical officer has approved, and by a clear channel to a senior clinician by telephone. Escalate early, document the advice you received and the name of the person who gave it, and never let a fear of looking foolish delay a call for help.

The moral weight of these choices should be acknowledged honestly rather than papered over. The nurse who chooses which of two patients receives the last unit of blood, who tells a family that the journey is futile, or who watches a patient die on the road after deciding to travel carries something that no protocol can relieve. It helps to name the feeling accurately, because this is moral distress and not incompetence, and it arises when the right action is unavailable rather than when you have failed to find it. Talk about the difficult decisions with a colleague, a supervisor, or a mentor, and write the reasoning down at the time, because a documented decision can be defended and learned from while an undocumented one is remembered as a private failure. Telling the truth to the patient and the family is part of the referral, not a separate courtesy. Explain what you think is wrong, what you can and cannot do, why you are recommending the journey, what it will cost in money and time, and what you expect to happen at the other end. Consent for transfer should be explicit, but the signature is worthless unless the conversation was real, so record what was said and give the family a copy of the transfer note.

To summarize, triage is the discipline of ranking patients by the urgency of their need, and it is repeated rather than performed once, so that the patient who could wait an hour is examined again before that hour ends. Look for the red flags by system, the airway that is narrowing, the breathing that costs effort, the circulation that fails before the blood pressure does, and the consciousness that is fading, and remember that children compensate and then collapse. Use color categories, improvised labels, and a deliberately generous threshold for urgency, accepting that over-triage is the safer error. The referral decision weighs the risk of staying against the risk of travel, and it separates those who must go, those who can be treated in place, those for whom the journey is the greater danger, and those for whom comfort is the honest goal. Stabilize before the wheels turn, because the first hour is the most dangerous, name the drug and the dose and the guideline they came from, and verify the current national or World Health Organization regimen before you prescribe.

# Chapter 50 — Protocol-Based Practice

Imagine the hour that decides a great many remote cases. It is 2 in the morning, the generator has been silent for 3 hours, a small child has been convulsing for 4 minutes, and the nearest physician is 200 kilometers away and asleep. In that room, the difference between a good outcome and a preventable death is rarely a machine. It is a remembered sequence of steps, performed in the right order, at the right moment. A protocol is that sequence written down, argued over, tested on thousands of patients, and carried into the room ahead of you.
