The nurse who has done this once will find that most legal questions in remote practice reduce to looking something up rather than guessing.

To summarize, the law in the places where this book is used is mostly far away, and it arrives only when something has already gone wrong. What protects you in the long interval is not the statute you have never read but three things you can control. The first is competence, which means knowing your scope, prescribing only from the current national guideline and the current essential medicines list, and recognizing the edge of your ability before you cross it. The second is documentation, which means writing the reasoning, the consent, the refusal, the instruction, the referral, and the error in a record that a stranger can read and trust. The third is the respect of the community, which is earned by showing up, telling the truth, and treating every patient as a person whose story was borrowed rather than owned. Keep your registration, your permission, and your insurance in a folder you can carry, ask in writing for the supervision the law requires, and verify the current guidance before you act on any regimen you learned years ago. Do these things and you will rarely need the law, and when you do need it, it will find a nurse who did the ordinary work well.

# Chapter 61 — Funding and Negotiation

The clinic where you work lives on money as surely as a patient lives on oxygen, and the money fails long before the medicine runs out. You will notice this in a particular way, because the nurse is usually the person who discovers that the fuel for the generator has not been paid, that the cleaner has not been paid, that the guard has not been paid, and that the last box of amoxicillin was signed for by someone who is no longer answering the telephone. Every one of those failures is a clinical event waiting to happen, even though none of them appears in a clinical guideline. This chapter is about the money that keeps a small clinic alive, the people who control it, the systems that move it, and the negotiation that decides how much of it arrives and on what terms. It is unglamorous and it is not optional, because in remote practice the budget is part of the treatment plan.

A useful way to hold this subject is to stop treating finance as an administrative nuisance and start treating it as a second set of vital signs. When the cash flow is healthy, the shelves are full, the staff are present, the cold chain holds, and the referral vehicle starts on the first attempt. When the cash flow is sick, you will see the earliest signs in exactly the same places you would look for shock in a patient: the peripheries go cold first. The guard misses a shift, the fuel drum empties, the transport money for the referral runs out, and the nurse covers the gap out of her own pocket. By the time the clinic cannot buy drugs, the illness has been progressing for months, and someone will try to treat the symptom with a single donation instead of the cause. Learning to read those early signs is a professional skill, and it belongs to you as much as the ability to read a fever.

The money that runs a clinic in a remote district comes from a small number of sources, and each source has its own appetite. The ministry of health is the sovereign authority and the eventual owner of the service, and it generally wants coverage, equity, data, and alignment with national policy, not the survival of your particular building. The district health office is the ministry in its most immediate form, and it wants its reports on time, its supervision visits accommodated, and its targets met by a clinic that does not embarrass it. Nongovernmental organizations bring flexible money, technical support, and a mandate that is often narrower than your patient load. Private donors, faith communities, diaspora associations, and international foundations bring money with a story attached, and the story usually determines what the money may be spent on. Finally, the community itself is a funder, in cash, in labor, in land, in food for staff, and in the legitimacy without which no clinic in a remote place survives.

Because these actors want different things, your first practical task is to map them before you need them. Write down, in one page of plain sentences, who controls which resource, what each one measures, who signs, who disburses, and how long each one takes to pay. The ministry may control salaries and essential drugs while a nongovernmental organization controls the vehicle and the outreach budget, while the community controls the land and the security. Knowing this map prevents the most common error in small-clinic finance, which is asking the wrong actor for the wrong thing and concluding that nobody will help. It also tells you where a delay will hurt first and where a single signature can release an entire quarter of supplies. Update the map when people change postings, because in district health systems a single transfer can orphan an agreement for six months.

It helps to be honest about what each actor is actually rewarded for, because negotiation is easier when you can offer the other side something it already wants. The district officer is rewarded for complete reports, for immunization coverage, for outbreak detection, and for staying within a budget that was set in a capital city far away. A nongovernmental organization is rewarded for measurable results inside a defined project period, and it must justify its spending to its own headquarters. A donor is rewarded for a visible, verifiable outcome and for the absence of scandal. The community is rewarded when its members survive childbirth, when its children grow, and when the clinic treats its people as constituents rather than as beneficiaries. When you frame a request in the currency each actor values, you stop begging and start trading.

The formal instrument that moves money is the grant or the service agreement, and its cycle has a rhythm you can learn in a single year. It begins with identification, when a donor announces a call or a ministry invites a proposal. It continues with the proposal, which describes the problem, the plan, the people, and the price. It then moves to award, when a contract or a letter of agreement converts intention into obligation. Implementation follows, and it lasts far longer than the excitement of the award. Reporting and audit follow implementation, and they are where a careless clinic loses its next grant. Close-out ends the cycle, and its purpose is to confirm that what was promised was delivered and that nothing was diverted. A nurse who internalizes this rhythm stops being surprised by deadlines and stops treating reporting as an interruption of clinical work.

The proposal is where a clinic's future is either won or quietly lost, and its logic must be visible in plain language. State the problem in the terms your listener already cares about, such as how many women in the catchment area deliver without a skilled attendant or how many children arrive with severe dehydration after a long journey. Then state what you will do, who will do it, what it will cost, and how anyone will know it happened. Avoid promising what your team cannot deliver in a rainy season, because an unmet target damages your credibility more than a modest target does. A proposal written from the clinic's own register is stronger than a proposal written from a template, because the numbers are yours and they can survive questioning. Name the source guideline for any clinical activity you propose, and check the current edition before you commit your program to it.

The budget is a clinical document in disguise, and it rewards a nurse who has actually counted things. Every line should be built from a unit cost multiplied by a realistic quantity, so that 1,200 consultations in a year becomes the drug, the glove, the test, the register, and the transport that each consultation truly consumes. Under-budget the invisible items and the clinic will fail clinically: transport for referrals, fuel for the cold chain, per diem for outreach, batteries, maintenance, printing, and the modest but essential allowance for the person who cleans and the person who guards. Add a contingency of 5 to 10 per cent, and be prepared to explain it, because a budget with no slack will be broken by the first price rise or the first flood. Remember that a budget is a promise with numbers attached, and every number you cannot defend becomes a number someone else will cut.

The budget narrative matters as much as the arithmetic, because it explains causation to a reader who has never been to your district. Write sentences that answer why this quantity and not another, why this vehicle and not a motorcycle, why the storage is rented and not built. Explain the exchange rate you used, the inflation you assumed, and the month in which you expect prices to rise. If you are paying a community health worker a stipend, say what the stipend is meant to cover and why a volunteer would otherwise be unable to continue. A reviewer who understands your reasoning is far more likely to defend your budget than a reviewer who sees only a large number with no explanation.

Reporting has two faces, narrative and financial, and the two must tell the same story. The narrative report says what was done, for whom, with what result, and what went wrong, and it should be written from registers and not from memory. The financial report says what was spent against each line, and it must reconcile with the accounting records to the last cent. Submit both on the day they are due, even if one is imperfect, because a late report invites suspicion while a candid early report invites help. When you cannot spend a line, say so early and ask for a reallocation, since unspent money discovered at the close is treated very differently from unspent money explained in advance. A donor who trusts your reporting will forgive a bad quarter; a donor who cannot find your report will not.

The audit is not an accusation, though it will feel like one the first time. It is a methodical test of whether money moved the way the records say it moved, and its basic instruments are the receipt, the signature, the bank statement, the stock card, and the comparison between them. Your best preparation is a habit rather than a scramble: every payment leaves a trace the same day, every purchase has a requisition, and every item that enters the store appears in the stock card before it appears in a patient's hand. Segregate duties wherever staffing allows, so that the person who orders is not the person who receives and not the person who pays. When the same nurse does all three because there is no one else, document that reality openly and add a monthly counter-signature by a colleague or a community representative. A finding explained by a real staffing constraint is survivable; a finding discovered by the auditor alone is not.

Accounting for every cent is a discipline of small habits, and it begins with the daily close. At the end of each day, the cash box is counted, the day's receipts are numbered and clipped together, and the running balance is written in a single ledger that never leaves the clinic. Petty cash is the easiest place to lose control and the easiest place to keep control, provided that every withdrawal is written before the money leaves the box and every voucher carries a purpose, a date, and two signatures. Never allow the practice of borrowing from one line to cover another, even for a genuinely urgent purchase, because a temporary loan that is not written down becomes a permanent unexplained gap. When you travel, leave the ledger with a named person and a written handover, so that the account continues while you are away. The purpose of all this is not tidiness; it is the protection of the clinic, of your colleagues, and of your own name.

Every clinic should know what one patient costs, because that number governs every negotiation you will ever have. To calculate it, add the fixed costs that exist whether or not a patient arrives, such as rent, salaries, security, and maintenance, to the variable costs that rise with each visit, such as drugs, tests, dressings, and transport. Divide the total by the number of patients actually seen in the same period, and you have the average cost per patient, which is a blunt instrument but an honest one. Then calculate the cost of specific services, such as one uncomplicated malaria treatment, one normal delivery, or one child treated for severe acute malnutrition, because these figures are what a ministry or a donor can compare with its own. If your average cost rises while your patient numbers are stable, investigate before you conclude that care has become wasteful, since the rise may reflect a sicker population, a longer rainy season, or a price increase. Knowing your number also protects you from accepting a grant that pays for only a fraction of what it asks you to do.

Money must be triaged exactly as patients are triaged, and the categories are just as unforgiving. First comes the money that keeps people alive today: drugs that treat anaphylaxis, severe malaria, and bacterial sepsis, plus the fuel and the driver who make referral possible. Second comes the money that prevents tomorrow's catastrophe: vaccines, the cold chain, insecticide-treated bed nets, water treatment, and the salaries that keep trained staff from leaving. Third comes the money that maintains the capacity to deliver any of it: maintenance, calibration, registers, supervision, and the training that keeps skills current. Fourth, and last, comes the money that improves how the work feels: paint, furniture, signage, and the small comforts that raise morale. A clinic that spends its maintenance money on paint will look better and function worse, and a clinic that spends its prevention money on rescue will spend everything on rescue within a year.

Negotiation with the ministry is the longest relationship of your professional life, and it is not a single conversation but a patient campaign. The ministry controls the salary bill and the essential drug supply, and it releases both through a chain of offices, each of which can delay without ever refusing. Your leverage is rarely money; it is data, credibility, and the quiet evidence that your clinic reduces the burden on the district hospital. Bring the register, bring the referral numbers, bring the outbreaks you detected first, and ask for specific things with specific quantities and dates. Ask early, ask in writing, and record what was promised and when, because institutional memory in a district office is short and a written record is a form of memory. Do not frame your request as a complaint about the past; frame it as the resource required for a result the ministry itself has promised.

The memorandum of understanding is the document that converts goodwill into an obligation, and every clinic dependent on outside support should have one. It should name the parties, the purpose, the duration, the resources each side will provide, the reporting each side will receive, and the way the arrangement ends. It should state who owns the building, the vehicle, and the equipment if the partnership dissolves, because the answer will otherwise be decided by whoever is standing in the compound on the day. It should include a process for dispute, a schedule for review, and a clause protecting clinical independence, so that no funder can direct who is treated or which drug is used. Have it read by someone with legal training if any is available, and keep a signed copy in the clinic, not only in a distant office. A memorandum of understanding that is clear about endings is what allows a partnership to last.

Patience is the actual technique of this negotiation, because the ministry moves on an annual budget cycle that you do not control. A request submitted in the wrong month may sit for a year, not because it was refused but because the envelope for that period was already closed. Learn the calendar of planning, budgeting, procurement, and disbursement, and insert your request at the point where it can still be included. Build a relationship with the district officer as a colleague rather than as a gatekeeper, and remember that this person is also constrained by a capital city. Repeat your request at each review without hostility, and let your records show that you asked consistently and reasonably. When something finally arrives, thank the office publicly, because a ministry that is seen to deliver to your clinic will deliver again.

Salaries deserve their own negotiation, and they carry a specific trap for the nurse leader. If you recruit staff onto a donor-funded salary, you must plan for the month the donor leaves, or you will create a clinic that cannot survive its own success. Ask early whether the ministry will absorb the posts, and write the transition into the agreement rather than hoping for it. Pay people on time, because a late salary in a remote setting becomes an absent nurse, and an absent nurse becomes a clinical risk that no amount of goodwill repairs. If you must choose between a modest team paid reliably and a larger team paid erratically, choose the smaller team, and say so plainly to whoever is pressing you to expand. Staff who trust the payroll will stay through hard seasons, and continuity of staff is the single most valuable clinical asset a remote clinic owns.

Negotiation with the community is where the clinic either becomes an institution or remains a project. The community's contribution is seldom cash in the amounts that a donor imagines, but it is real: land, a building, a guard, a cleaner, firewood, food for staff, labor for a fence, and the social permission to work. Ask for a contribution that is genuinely within reach, and never construct a fee that excludes the poorest household from care, because a clinic that only serves those who can pay has abandoned its purpose. Involve the existing structures, the village council, the women's group, the religious leaders, the teachers, and the traditional birth attendants, and let them help decide what the contribution should be. When the community gives, it acquires a stake, and a clinic with a stake is defended, repaired, and defended again. Write the arrangement down, even when it is customary, so that a new committee does not reopen an old agreement from a position of ignorance.

The stake that makes a clinic theirs is built through small decisions as much as through large ones. Let the community committee see the budget summary, not to audit every line but to understand what the clinic can and cannot do. Consult them before you introduce a fee, a schedule change, or a new service that will alter how people travel to reach you. When a donation arrives, announce it and explain its conditions, so that nobody believes the clinic is hiding resources. Invite the committee to help resolve the difficult cases, such as the family that refuses referral or the patient who demands a drug that will not help, because a shared decision is harder to resent. Ownership is not a slogan; it is the accumulated experience of being asked.

Donors arrive with money and with conditions, and the conditions can be more consequential than the amount. A vertical program that funds only one disease will pull your staff toward that disease and away from the patients who do not fit its definition. A donation of equipment may require a specific brand of consumable that you cannot buy locally, converting a gift into a permanent supply problem. A reporting requirement may demand data that your register does not collect, so your team spends its evenings transcribing instead of resting. Read the conditions before you accept, and calculate the true cost of compliance, including staff time, storage, and transport. It is legitimate, and often wise, to decline a donation whose ongoing cost exceeds its benefit, and to explain that refusal in writing. A clinic that accepts everything will eventually be owned by its donors rather than by its community.

The equipment that arrives with strings deserves its own caution, because the true cost of a machine is not its purchase price. An ultrasound device requires a trained operator, a probe that someone will eventually break, a power supply that does not spike, and a maintenance contract that someone must fund after the donor has gone. A refrigerator for vaccines requires fuel or solar capacity, spare parts, and a person whose job includes logging the temperature twice a day. A vehicle requires tyres, insurance, a licensed driver, and a budget line for the breakdown that will happen on the worst road in the district. Before you accept any equipment, ask who will repair it, who will supply it, and who will pay when the warranty ends. If no one can answer, the equipment is not an asset; it is a future monument to a good intention.

Sustainability is the question nobody likes, and it must be asked at the moment of acceptance rather than at the moment of crisis. The honest version of the question is this: when this grant ends, what part of this work will continue, who will pay for it, and what will we stop doing? Plan the handover from the beginning, train local staff rather than relying on an expatriate, and shift recurring costs onto the ministry and the community wherever possible. Keep the services that are cheap and highly effective and be willing to close the ones that only a donor will fund. Write the exit strategy into the proposal, because a funder who sees a plausible ending trusts the project more, not less. Sustainability does not mean that everything continues; it means that what is essential survives the loss of any single payer.

Corruption will find you, and it usually arrives politely, framed as a cost of doing business. It may be a request to inflate an invoice, a demand for a payment to release a shipment, a relative inserted onto a payroll, or a box of drugs that leaves the store without a patient. It may also be offered as a favor, a discount, or an acceleration, which is the same transaction wearing better clothes. The first defense is structure: competitive quotations, written specifications, delivery verification by a second person, and payment by transfer rather than cash wherever the system permits. The second defense is transparency, because money recorded publicly in a ledger that several people can see is much harder to divert than money that only one person understands. The third defense is the habit of refusing early, clearly, and without a lecture, because a refusal that arrives at the moment of the request is far safer than a refusal that arrives after the goods have been accepted.

The strategies that work against corruption are unglamorous and repeatable. Never pay a bribe from clinic funds, because the payment creates a record that will eventually be discovered, and the discovery will be used against the clinic and not against the person who asked. Say no to the specific request and yes to the legitimate process, offering the correct form, the correct office, and the correct fee. Bring a witness to negotiations that you expect to be difficult, and note the date and the substance of the conversation afterward. Use the community committee as a shield as well as a partner, since a decision made openly in front of representatives is difficult to corrupt in private. Report serious diversion through the proper channel, and understand that in some settings the proper channel is itself compromised, which is a limit you must recognize rather than pretend away.

When a refusal is dangerous, your obligation shifts from the money to the person. If a demand is accompanied by a threat, do not negotiate alone, do not travel alone, and do not allow a confrontation to develop in a place with only one exit. Involve your organization's leadership, the district authorities, and where appropriate the community elders, and let the request be answered by a body rather than by an individual. Document what was asked and by whom, keep the record somewhere other than the clinic, and agree on a plan with your team about what each person will say if the request is repeated. There are settings in which the correct answer is to relocate the activity rather than to resist in place, and there is no shame in that decision. Your safety is not a lesser value than the money, and a ruined clinic helps no one.

The moral position of the clinician who must ask for money is uncomfortable, and it deserves to be named rather than suppressed. You will sit across from someone who controls resources and explain why children in your catchment area should not die, and you will feel that you are selling something that should not need selling. The discomfort is real, but it is not a reason to avoid the work, because the alternative is a clinic that cannot act on the knowledge it possesses. Reframe the request as evidence rather than appeal: you are not asking for charity, you are presenting data about preventable death and proposing a costed remedy. Ask with dignity, ask repeatedly, and do not allow the asking to become flattery or performance, because the person across the table can recognize both. The medicine remains yours; the money is only the means by which it reaches the patient.

The greater danger is that the asking quietly corrupts the medicine, and this happens more often than outright theft. It happens when a service is delivered because it is funded rather than because it is needed, and when a patient is enrolled in a program to satisfy an indicator rather than to receive a benefit. It happens when the clinic's priorities drift toward whatever the current donor finds photogenic, while the unglamorous work of tuberculosis follow-up or mental health support is left undone. It happens when a nurse begins to see patients as units of output, and when the register is completed more carefully than the patient is examined. The safeguard is to keep a clinical decision-making forum, however small, that reviews what is being done and why, and to keep the guideline rather than the grant at the center of each decision. Write down the moments when you declined money because it would have distorted care, because that record is your conscience in documentary form.

Clinical work that depends on funding still depends on clinical evidence, and the two must be kept in the right order. When you propose a treatment protocol to a funder, name the source in the text, whether that is the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, or the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. Regimens and recommendations are revised, guidance differs between countries, and the current national guideline must be checked before you commit money or prescribe a drug. The World Health Organization Model List of Essential Medicines is a reasonable anchor for what a small clinic should be able to obtain, but it is revised regularly, so verify the current edition before ordering. If a donor pushes a treatment that no current guideline supports, the correct answer is a documented refusal, not a compromise at the bedside.

The unglamorous logistics of procurement and storage are where a budget is either realized or wasted. Order early, because the interval between a requisition and a delivery in a remote district is measured in months, and a stockout of one drug can force a referral that costs more than the drug would have. Protect the cold chain with a temperature log, a backup power source, and a named person responsible for it every day, including weekends. Rotate stock so that the oldest usable batch leaves first, and keep a bin card that any auditor can reconcile with the physical count. Plan transport for the rainy season, because the road that is passable in February may be impassable in July, and a shipment that arrives late may arrive spoiled. These tasks are administrative in name and clinical in consequence, and they are the most common place where a well-funded clinic still fails its patients.

Monitoring and evaluation are not a donor ritual; they are the instruments by which a clinic learns whether its money is doing anything. Choose a small number of indicators that reflect real outcomes, such as the proportion of children with severe acute malnutrition who recover, the proportion of pregnant women who deliver with a skilled attendant, or the time from a positive malaria test to the first dose of treatment. Collect them from the registers you are already keeping, so that measurement does not compete with care for the same hours. Review them monthly with the team, and act on what the numbers reveal, even when the revealed problem is a staffing pattern rather than a supply. Report the failures as well as the successes, because a monitoring system that only produces good news has stopped monitoring anything. The best use of an indicator is to change a decision, and if no decision ever changes, the indicator is decoration.

The adverse effects of funding deserve the same vigilance you give to the adverse effects of a drug. A delayed disbursement produces a stockout, a stockout produces a dangerous substitution, and a dangerous substitution produces a patient who does not improve. An interrupted salary produces an absent nurse, and an absent nurse produces a delayed diagnosis. A sudden influx of money produces a sudden expansion of activity that the team cannot sustain, followed by a contraction that destroys community trust. Track these cause-and-effect chains as deliberately as you track a fever curve, and build contingency into the plan: a buffer of essential drugs, a reserve of transport money, and a small emergency fund that only two people can release. When an adverse financial event occurs, name it in the report, because a hidden interruption becomes an unexplained failure and then a lost grant.

Documentation is the thread that holds the whole system together, and the nurse is usually the person who keeps it. Keep the proposal, the award letter, the budget, the memorandum of understanding, the procurement file, the stock cards, the payroll record, the bank statements, and every report in one place that a successor can find. Number your receipts, file them by month, and keep the retention period the funder requires, which is often several years after the final report. Photograph or scan the key documents and store a copy away from the clinic, because fire, flood, and theft do not respect filing cabinets. Record decisions as well as transactions, including who approved a reallocation and why, since an auditor's hardest question is usually about a decision rather than a payment. A complete file turns a suspicious question into a short conversation.

The nursing role in all of this is larger than most training programs admit, and it is worth stating plainly. The nurse is typically the person who knows what was actually consumed, what actually broke, what the patients actually needed, and what the register actually says, which means the nurse holds the evidence that makes any budget honest. Bring that evidence to the negotiation, speak in costs and outcomes rather than in complaints, and insist on being present when the clinic's resources are discussed. Train a colleague to keep the ledger, so that the clinic is not dependent on one person's memory or one person's honesty. Insist on the segregation of duties even when staffing is thin, and put the counter-signature in place before it is needed. When you eventually leave, the quality of the handover will be judged by whether the next nurse can reconstruct the entire financial story from the file.

A single month in a well-run clinic shows how these pieces fit together. In the first week you reconcile the previous month, file the receipts, and pay the guard, the cleaner, and the outreach staff on time. In the second week you review the stock cards, order what is running low, and check the cold chain log for gaps. In the third week you hold the community committee meeting, present the budget summary, and discuss the one decision that needs their consent. In the fourth week you write the report, compare the spending against the plan, and send the honest narrative with the honest figures. Overlaying all of it are the negotiations that have no fixed date, the telephone call to the district office, the visit from a donor, and the quiet conversation in which a request for an improper payment is refused. None of this appears in a clinical guideline, and all of it determines whether the guideline can be followed.

It is worth returning, finally, to the reason the money matters at all. A budget is not a moral achievement and a deficit is not a sin; both are simply the conditions under which you will or will not be able to act. What matters is that the resources you control are converted into care, that the conversion is visible, and that no patient is turned away because a form was late. The clinician who can account for every cent, who negotiates without bitterness, and who refuses corruption without theatrics has done something that is rarely celebrated. That person has made the clinic trustworthy, and trust is the resource that attracts every other resource. Ask for what your patients need, spend it as if they were watching, and let your records be the argument you make on their behalf.

To summarize, the money that keeps a remote clinic alive is a clinical matter, and the nurse is its most reliable steward. Learn the actors, the ministry of health, the district office, the nongovernmental organizations, the donors, and the community, and learn what each one measures and controls. Work the grant cycle deliberately, from proposal to budget to report to audit to close-out, and keep records that can answer any question years later. Negotiate with the ministry for supplies and salaries through a clear memorandum of understanding, and negotiate with the community for the contribution that turns a project into an institution. Read the conditions attached to donations, count the true cost of equipment, and answer the sustainability question at the beginning rather than at the end. Triage money as you triage patients, know your cost per patient, and resist corruption early, openly, and with the protection of structure and witnesses. Ask for what your patients need without letting the asking distort the medicine, name your source guideline in the text, and verify the current one before you act. In the end, the purpose of every ledger, every report, and every difficult conversation is the same, which is that the patient in front of you receives the care that the evidence says is due.

# Chapter 62 — Security and Field Safety

A clinic is useful only for as long as it is open, staffed, and trusted, and those three conditions are exactly what insecurity destroys. Security in this chapter does not mean fortification or armed response. It means the ordinary discipline that keeps a nurse, a patient, and a vehicle out of the situations where harm becomes likely. A clinic that is secure is not a clinic with high walls; it is a clinic whose team has thought carefully about where the risks lie and has arranged the day so that most of them never arrive. The guidance that follows draws on the security management system of the United Nations, the World Health Organization, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and the field manuals of Doctors Without Borders. Security guidance is revised as conflicts change, and practice differs between countries and between agencies, so verify the current guidance and your own organization's security plan before you rely on any threshold or route named here.

Begin with the recognition that the most senior clinician on site is usually the person responsible for security, whether or not the job title says so. In a remote post the nurse often decides whether a journey happens, whether a patient is transferred, whether the gate is opened after dark, and whether the team stays or leaves. Each of those is a clinical decision wearing the clothes of an administrative one, because the answer determines who receives care and who does not. This is why security belongs to the same professional competence as triage or drug dosing rather than to a separate department far away. A nurse who understands the mechanism of risk can argue for the safer plan with evidence instead of fear. And the person who can explain the risk is usually the person who is listened to.

Assessment begins before arrival, and it begins with a map of actors. You need to know who holds authority, who holds influence, and who holds weapons in the district where you will work. That map includes the ministry of health and its district officer, the local government administrator, the traditional authority and the religious leaders, the police, the army, any armed group that controls the roads, the market association, the teachers, the youth association, and the women's groups that organize much of daily life. Each of these actors can protect your work or obstruct it, and each has a different reason for doing either. Ask who has been helpful to previous clinics and who has not, and ask why. Write the map down, name a contact for each entry, and revise it every few months, because the actors change faster than the buildings do.

The physical geography decides what is possible, and it must be read season by season. Learn which roads are passable in the dry months and which become rivers in the rains, where the bridges are weight-limited, where the culverts wash out, and where the tarmac ends. Learn the distance and the driving time to the referral hospital in the best conditions and in the worst, because the difference is often a factor of three rather than a fraction. Find the alternate routes and check them with your own eyes rather than on a screen, since a route that exists on a map may pass through a checkpoint that will not let you continue. Identify the airstrip, its length, its surface, and who controls access to it. Note the hours of daylight across the year, because that number sets the boundary of every journey you will plan.

The history of the place is the part of the assessment that documents never contain. Ask what happened here in the last election, during the last epidemic, and after the last dispute over land or cattle or water. Ask when the last attack on a clinic or a health worker occurred, what preceded it, and whether anyone was ever held responsible. Ask about the grievance that people still mention in the market, because that grievance is the soil in which a future incident grows. Ask about the previous organization that worked here and why it left, since the answer is often instructive rather than flattering. Listen especially to the driver, the cleaner, the translator, and the community health workers, who move through places that outsiders never see. What they know is operational intelligence, and it costs nothing but respect to collect it.

The assessment is never finished, and treating it as a form completed at the start is one of the commonest mistakes in field practice. Security is a moving picture, so you monitor it the way you monitor a patient: at a defined interval, against defined signs, with a named person responsible for noticing change. The signs that matter include a new checkpoint, a new weapon in the market, a change in the tone of a conversation with an official, a rumor that repeats, a staff member who reports being followed, and a sudden silence from a source who usually speaks. Record the signs in one place, with dates, and review them at the weekly team meeting rather than in a crisis. A pattern is visible in a written record and invisible in memory. Monitoring is therefore the bridge between the assessment you made and the decision you must make tomorrow.

Road travel is where most field teams meet harm, and vehicle discipline is the cheapest protection available. Before every departure, walk around the vehicle and look at it rather than trusting the driver's reassurance, because the driver may be tired or eager to leave. Check the fuel level against the distance and add a reserve of at least a quarter of a tank beyond what the journey requires. Check the engine oil, the coolant, the brake fluid, the tire pressures including the spare, the jack and the wrench, the lights, the horn, the wipers, and the first aid kit. Confirm that the communication device works, that its battery is charged, and that the credit or subscription is current. Confirm that every occupant has a seat belt that fastens and that the load, including any patient, is secured so that it cannot become a missile. Initial the log, because a check that leaves no trace is a check that will quietly stop happening.

Speed is the variable that converts a mistake into a fatality, and the arithmetic deserves to be understood before it is legislated. The energy of a moving vehicle rises with the square of its speed, so doubling the speed does not double the harm; it multiplies it roughly fourfold. A loaded four-wheel drive with a high center of gravity rolls over at a lower speed than the same vehicle empty, and a roof rack loaded with supplies raises that center further. Set a ceiling for your own team that is slower than the legal limit and slower again on gravel, in the rain, and at night if night travel is unavoidable. Brief the driver before departure on the ceiling and on the reason for it. Nobody in the vehicle, including the most senior clinician, should ever ask the driver to go faster, because the request transfers the risk to everyone without transferring the responsibility.

The rule against driving at night saves more field lives than any other single rule, and it should be treated as close to absolute. Darkness removes the pedestrian, the animal, the unlit truck, the washed-out culvert, and the unmarked checkpoint from your view until they are inside your stopping distance. Darkness also changes the behavior of people at checkpoints and on the road, and it makes a breakdown far harder to see and to avoid. Plan the day backward from the journey so that you arrive well before dusk, and build in a margin for the delay that a flat tire or a broken bridge will certainly cause. If the journey cannot be completed in daylight, the correct decision is usually to leave earlier, to travel in two stages with a night stop, or not to travel at all. The nurse who cancels a journey because of the clock is practicing medicine, not avoiding it.

Every journey needs a breakdown plan, because a mechanical failure is a certainty and a surprise only if you have not planned for it. Decide in advance who will be called first, what information they will need, and how the message will reach them if the radio or the telephone has no signal. Carry water, food, a shade, a spare container of fuel, a basic tool kit, and a means of repairing the tire yourself, because the recovery vehicle may be a day away. Decide whether the team stays with the vehicle or walks out, and make that decision in advance, when it can still be made calmly, rather than at the roadside in the heat. Never split the group in a way that leaves one person alone, and never abandon the vehicle on a main road where it can be looted or where it becomes a hazard. Tell the receiving post the make, the color, the plate number, and the last known position before departure. A plan that exists only in the head of the driver is not a plan.

The checkpoint is the ordinary interface between your team and armed authority, and preparation removes most of its danger. Keep a single folder, in the vehicle and never in the luggage, containing the identity documents of every occupant, the vehicle registration and insurance, the driving permit, the travel authorization, the passenger manifest, the cargo list, and the documentation for any medicines or samples being carried. Medicines and controlled substances need a written justification and the correct permits, because an unexplained box of ampoules invites a suspicion that no explanation at the barrier can dispel. Keep the documents clean, current, and legible, and keep photocopies in a second place in case the original folder is confiscated. Know which documents each kind of checkpoint is entitled to see, and know the difference between a demand that is lawful and one that is not. A folder in order is not a formality; it is the difference between a two-minute stop and an hour of negotiation.

Demeanor at the barrier matters as much as the paperwork. Slow the vehicle, switch off the radio or the music, keep both hands visible on the wheel, and greet the person in charge before offering any document. Nominate one person, usually the driver or the team leader, to speak, and let that person do all of the speaking so that two voices never contradict each other. Stay calm, stay polite, and do not argue about the law at the barrier, because the argument will be lost there and won in writing later. Do not offer a bribe where your organization forbids it, and do not carry anything, for anyone, that you have not inspected yourself, because a favor asked at a checkpoint is often a trap. Learn the shape of the refusal that keeps everyone alive: the order to take a road you have been told is unsafe, the demand to carry a passenger or a package of unknown contents, the instruction to hand over a patient or a sample, and the pressure to drive after dark. A refusal delivered calmly, without moralizing, with an alternative offered in its place, is among the most valuable sentences a field nurse can learn.

A crowd behaves as a fluid rather than as a collection of individuals, and it must be handled with the respect you would give to water. Never drive a vehicle into a crowd, because the vehicle stops being a vehicle and becomes the thing the crowd is against. If you meet a demonstration, stop at a distance, turn the vehicle so that you can leave, keep the engine running, and wait rather than negotiate or push through. Do not photograph, do not shout, and do not single out anyone in the crowd, because attention is what turns curiosity into hostility. If the clinic is near a demonstration, close the gate early, keep patients inside, and wait for the crowd to disperse on its own, since most crowds are temporary and most confrontations are created by the attempt to end them quickly. The demonstration is almost never about you, and the sooner you behave as though it is not, the sooner it will pass.

Firearms in a community change the meaning of every dispute, and the clinic must define itself as a place apart from them. Negotiate and publish a simple rule that no weapon enters the patient area, whether carried by a soldier, a police officer, a hunter, or a neighbor. Enforce it consistently, because an exception granted once becomes the rule thereafter. Provide a place at the gate where weapons can be left, and be realistic about who has the authority to enforce the rule, since a nurse cannot disarm an armed man and should not try. Where an armed actor insists on entering, your objective is to protect the patients and the staff and to document what happened, not to win the argument at the door. Make the neutrality of the clinic visible through its practice: treat the wounded from every side, keep political symbols off the wall, and never use the clinic as a platform. A clinic known to be even-handed is a clinic less often attacked, and that reputation is built in ordinary weeks rather than in crises.

Every journey must exist on paper before it exists on the road. Leave a journey plan with a colleague who is staying behind, and include the names of everyone traveling, the vehicle and its plate number, the destination, the route, the purpose, the departure time, the expected arrival time, and the check-in times along the way. The person staying behind is not a clerk but a named monitor whose job during your absence is to watch the clock and to act on what it says. Agree the check-in interval before departure, and keep it short enough that a missed check-in is meaningful rather than routine. Keep a board in the office that shows who is out, where they are, and when they are due back, and update it by hand if the power and the network are unreliable. A journey that is invisible to the rest of the team is a journey that cannot be rescued.

The missed check-in is the signal that converts concern into action, and the response must be written before it is needed. Define the margin, so that a check-in is late by fifteen minutes in one setting and by two hours in another, depending on the terrain and the network. When the margin passes, the monitor starts a fixed ladder: try the radio, try the telephone, try the satellite device, call the destination post to see whether the team arrived, call the driver's alternate number, and then alert the designated security contact and the organization's office. Give the monitor the authority to climb that ladder without seeking permission from someone who is asleep, and name a deputy for the days the monitor is away. Do not wait for reassurance, and do not accept a rumor as a check-in. Record every attempt with its time and its result, because that record is what a search or an investigation will use, and because it is the only way the plan can be improved afterward.

Neutrality is a working tool rather than a moral position, and it must be understood precisely if it is to protect anyone. In humanitarian practice neutrality means that you do not take sides in a hostilities, impartiality means that you treat according to need, humanity means that you relieve suffering wherever you find it, and independence means that your decisions follow need rather than the instruction of any party. These four principles are the reason an armed group may allow a clinic to treat both its own wounded and the wounded of its opponent. Neutrality does not require silence about what you witness, and it does not require you to pretend that all parties behave identically. It does require that the clinic's actions, and not only its statements, are even-handed. The credibility of that even-handedness is the clinic's actual armor, and it is built slowly and lost quickly.

Neutrality has limits, and the field worker should know them before the day they matter. A party to a conflict may decide that a clinic is aligned, whether because of where it is, whom it has treated, or what it has said, and no amount of correct practice can guarantee otherwise. When a threat becomes targeted rather than incidental, the options narrow to negotiation through a trusted intermediary, temporary suspension of activities, relocation of staff, or withdrawal. Each of those decisions belongs to the organization's designated security authority rather than to the individual nurse, and the point of naming that authority in advance is so that the decision can be made quickly and defended later. Prepare the handover while you still have room to negotiate: brief the ministry, the district officer, and the community leaders on what will stop and what will continue. Write the decision, its reasoning, and its date, because memory is unreliable in a crisis and the record is the institution's protection. Leaving is not a failure of courage when the alternative is a clinic that has become a target endangering patients and staff alike.

The evacuation of staff is a different problem from the evacuation of a patient, and the two plans should never be confused. A medical evacuation moves a sick patient toward a higher level of care, while a security evacuation moves staff away from a threat, sometimes leaving the clinic standing and sometimes leaving the country. Field practice usually distinguishes three postures: hibernation, in which the team stays in place behind a locked gate until the situation clears; relocation, in which the team moves to a safer part of the country; and evacuation, in which the team leaves entirely. Each posture has a defined trigger, a defined authority who calls it, an assembly point, and a route, and none of those should be improvised on the day. Everyone must know the trigger and the assembly point without consulting a document. The plan must also say who remains responsible for the patients and the medicines when the team leaves, because a clinic abandoned without a handover becomes a supply depot for whoever arrives first.

The grab bag is the physical form of the evacuation plan, and it should be packed for the realistic scenario rather than the dramatic one. It holds identity documents and copies, local currency in small notes, a printed contact list, a charged communication device with its charger, water and food for the first day, a headlamp and spare batteries, a change of clothes, a light rain shell, basic toiletries, and any personal medicine that cannot be bought locally. The medical component typically includes a small wound kit, an analgesic, an antimalarial for treatment and for prophylaxis, an antibiotic for common infections, oral rehydration salts, and a small supply of any drug that a chronic condition requires. In current World Health Organization and national guidance, adult malaria prophylaxis with doxycycline is commonly 100 milligrams by mouth once a day, and an antibiotic such as ciprofloxacin for a simple infection is commonly 500 milligrams by mouth every twelve hours, while an antimalarial treatment course follows the national first-line combination. Doxycycline commonly causes nausea and makes the skin burn more easily in strong sun, and ciprofloxacin can cause tendon pain and uncommon disturbances of the heart rhythm, so each must be monitored and stopped if an adverse effect appears. These regimens are revised and differ between countries, so verify the current guideline before you pack or take any of them.

Documents deserve their own paragraph because their absence causes more delay and more danger at a barrier than any other single failure. Keep the passport, the visa, the work permit, the professional license, the vaccination record, and any authorization to carry medicines current, and begin the renewal process months before the expiry rather than weeks. Carry a paper copy of every essential document in a second bag, and store an electronic copy with a trusted colleague abroad as well as on your own device. Carry a small card in your wallet with your blood group, your allergies, your chronic conditions, your regular medicines, and two emergency contacts who can be reached from the country where you work. Write the contact details in a form that works without a charged telephone, because a number stored only in a dead device is not a contact. The nurse who carries the team's documents should check them at the same monthly interval as the grab bag, since a permit that expired quietly is indistinguishable at a barrier from a permit that never existed.

A plan that has never been rehearsed is a document rather than a capability. Rehearse the security plan as you would rehearse a resuscitation: with a short scenario, a time limit, and a person assigned to watch what actually happens. A tabletop exercise in which the team talks through a checkpoint, a road closure, a medical evacuation, and a relocation costs an hour and reveals every unspoken assumption in the plan. A physical drill in which everyone walks to the assembly point in the dark with the grab bag teaches things that no discussion can, including how long it takes, who cannot find the key, and which gate is locked. After each rehearsal, write down the failures and assign each one to a named person with a date, then rehearse the corrected plan at the next interval. The rehearsal is uncomfortable, and that discomfort is the entire point, because it is cheaper to be embarrassed in an exercise than surprised in an incident.

The most likely threat to a field nurse is not a gunman but an accident, and the mundane causes deserve more of your attention than the dramatic ones. Road traffic crashes dominate the statistics of field injury, followed by falls, burns, electrical injuries, and animal bites. Fatigue is the great multiplier in all of them, so protect sleep on the nights before a long drive and refuse to drive when you have not slept. The same discipline applies to the ordinary equipment of the post: the ladder used as a bench, the exposed wiring, the generator with its hot exhaust, the fuel stored beside the kitchen fire, the cooking gas cylinder that is never leak-tested, and the oxygen cylinder that is not chained upright. Keep a fire extinguisher where it can be reached, check it on a schedule, and keep every exit unlocked from the inside at all times. A clinic can lose a staff member to a preventable fall in exactly the week it is preparing for an armed attack, and the fall is far more probable.

Some of those accidents carry a clinical consequence that must be managed at the moment it happens. A dog bite or a scratch from a suspect animal requires immediate and thorough washing of the wound with soap and clean running water for at least 15 minutes, because washing removes virus before it can enter the nerve. After washing, apply an antiseptic, do not suture the wound tightly, and arrange rabies post-exposure vaccination without delay, together with rabies immunoglobulin for a category of exposure that requires it, following the current World Health Organization and national regimens. A deep puncture, a wound contaminated with soil or manure, or a fracture sustained in the field also needs tetanus assessment and the appropriate vaccine or immunoglobulin, again according to the current guideline. A needle-stick or a splash to the eye or the mouth starts a clock for human immunodeficiency virus post-exposure prophylaxis and for hepatitis B, and that clock is best carried in writing inside the grab bag. Every one of these regimens is revised and differs between countries, so confirm the current protocol before you act, and record the exposure, the time, the treatment given, and the follow-up date in the register.

The security guard is the first person a patient meets and the first line of the clinic's defense, and the post deserves to be designed rather than improvised. Select the guard in consultation with the community, so that the person at the gate is known, accountable, and unlikely to be coerced by a neighbor. Give the guard a written contract, a clear job description, an identifying badge, and a wage that is paid on time, because an unpaid guard is a guard who leaves or who supplements the income in ways the clinic cannot see. Train the guard in what the role actually requires: how to greet and register visitors, when to refuse entry, when to call for help, how to use the radio, how to write the night log, and what not to do, which includes not making arrests and not carrying a weapon the organization has not authorized. Visit the gate at night yourself, at irregular intervals, because a supervisor who never comes at night will never know what happens at night. Respect the guard as a colleague, since a person treated as furniture will behave accordingly, and the gate is the beginning of every clinical story that ends well.

Security is ultimately a relationship with the community rather than a set of barriers, and the community usually knows about a threat before the clinic does. Build the channels through which that knowledge can travel in both directions: the community health workers, the traditional birth attendants, the women's groups, the market leaders, the teachers, and the religious congregations. Make it easy and safe for a neighbor to warn you, and make it clear what you will and will not do with the information, because a clinic believed to report names to the police may lose the very warnings that keep it safe. Reciprocate by sharing what you can: the vaccination dates, the outbreak news, the reason a road is closed, and the honest explanation when the clinic cannot help. A community that has a stake in the clinic will defend it more effectively than any wall, and that stake is built by years of consistent, respectful presence. Where the community helped to write the rules at the gate, the community also helps to enforce them.

Every security measure has adverse effects, and a serious team monitors them as carefully as it monitors a drug. A gate that closes too early, a journey cancelled too readily, or a curfew applied too broadly leaves patients without care, and the harm falls hardest on the people who can least afford to travel. The staff carry their own adverse effects: the fatigue of permanent vigilance, the guilt of leaving a patient behind, the irritability that follows months of restraint, and the numbness that follows an incident never discussed. Monitor these signs the way you would monitor a fever, and record them in a security log that includes incidents, near misses, threats, and the decisions taken in response. Review the log at a fixed interval with the whole team, look for trends rather than isolated events, and act on the pattern before it produces an injury. Documentation in this domain is not bureaucracy; it is the memory that a frightened team does not have, and the evidence a distant office needs in order to send help.

The nurse's role in field security is partly clinical and partly moral, and the two cannot be separated. You are the person most likely to notice that a colleague has stopped sleeping, that a driver has been drinking, that a patient's relative has made a threat, or that a journey is being planned for reasons of pride rather than need. You are also the person who must sometimes say out loud that the clinic is beyond its limit and that a specific plan is unsafe, and that sentence is a professional act rather than an act of disloyalty. Support the colleague who is sent home, the family of a staff member who was hurt, and the whole team after an incident, because the days that follow an event are when people most need a structured debrief and are least likely to ask for one. Protect your own sleep, your own food, and your own contact with the people who remind you why the work matters. And remember that refusing an unsafe journey is not abandoning a patient, because a nurse who is dead or captured treats no one.

To summarize, security is not a wall around the medicine but the condition that lets the medicine happen at all, and it belongs to the nurse's competence rather than to a distant office. The work begins with an assessment made before arrival and continued forever afterward: the map of actors, the roads and the seasons, the history of the place, and the signs that are monitored, written down, and reviewed. The journey is protected by a vehicle check, a sane speed, a rule against driving at night, a breakdown plan, and a journey plan left with a named colleague who acts when the check-in is missed. The checkpoint is passed with papers in order, one calm voice, and the practiced refusal that keeps everyone alive, while crowds are met with distance and the clinic is kept as a place apart from weapons and from politics. Neutrality, impartiality, humanity, and independence protect the clinic until they fail, at which point the designated authority calls hibernation, relocation, or evacuation, and the grab bag, the documents, and the rehearsal make that call survivable. The most likely harm remains the ordinary accident, which is why the seat belt, the ladder, the wiring, the fire extinguisher, and the sleep before a long drive matter more than the dramatic scenario, and the same mundane care covers the animal bite, the deep wound, and the needle-stick, whose vaccination and drug regimens must be checked against the current World Health Organization and national guidance, which are revised and differ between countries. The security guard, trained, paid, respected, and supervised, together with the community that helped to write the rules, will protect the clinic better than any fortification. And the nurse who plans for the worst, monitors honestly, documents carefully, and says out loud when a plan is unsafe is the person who keeps the clinic open, staffed, and trusted for the patients who need it.

# Chapter 63 — Your Own Health

The clinician is the most valuable piece of equipment in any remote clinic, and the only one that cannot be replaced by a donation. A funder can ship a refrigerator, an ultrasound machine, or a crate of antibiotics, and all of those things will arrive eventually and be installed by someone. Nobody can ship a replacement for you. When you are the person who runs the antenatal clinic, sets the fracture, reads the malaria film, and knows which child is failing to thrive, your absence is not a staffing inconvenience. It is a hole in the middle of the service, and the patients who fall into that hole are the ones you were there to protect. This chapter is about keeping the equipment in working order, which means treating your own body and mind as a clinical responsibility rather than as a private matter.

There is a particular trap in this work, which is that caring for other people is a legitimate reason to postpone caring for yourself, and a very persuasive one. The clinic is always open, the queue is always long, the motorbike is always broken, and there is always a reason why your own dental abscess, your own cough, or your own missed vaccination can wait until the next rotation. The principle to hold instead is that your health is one of the systems the clinic depends on, exactly like the cold chain or the generator. When it fails, everything downstream fails with it, and the failure is sudden. So the same seriousness you would apply to a patient's fever must be applied to your own, and the same documentation must exist, because a health problem that is not written down is a health problem that will be forgotten.

Preparation begins before departure, and the vaccines are the first item because they are cheap, durable, and almost completely protective. The World Health Organization publishes the vaccines recommended for health workers and for travel to specific regions, and the national schedule of your destination country may add requirements that your home country does not. The practical rule is to start at least 6 weeks before departure, because several of these vaccines need more than one dose and because the immune response takes time to develop. That timeline is frequently ignored, and the nurse who receives a posting with 10 days of notice ends up taking whatever can still be given and accepting the gaps. Write the plan down, with the dates for each dose, and treat those dates like a drug regimen rather than like a suggestion. Records must be kept in two places, a paper card you carry and a photograph or a scan stored where you can reach it.

Several vaccines deserve specific attention for the nurse going to tropical practice. Hepatitis A and hepatitis B can be given together as a combined vaccine, and the hepatitis B series of three doses is the one that matters most, because it protects against a blood-borne virus you will meet through needle-stick injuries and through contact with blood in a clinic where gloves run short. Typhoid vaccine is available as an injectable dose or as a course of oral capsules, and neither is fully protective, so it joins hand hygiene rather than replacing it. Yellow fever vaccine is a single dose that is required for entry to some countries and whose certificate becomes valid 10 days after administration. Rabies pre-exposure vaccination simplifies the response to a bite or a scratch, but it does not remove the need for post-exposure treatment, and a tetanus booster every 10 years keeps a mundane wound from becoming a fatal one. These schedules are revised, they differ between countries, and the current World Health Organization or Centers for Disease Control and Prevention guidance must be checked before your appointment, because the edition that was current when your colleague trained may already have changed.

The record of your vaccination matters more than most people expect, and losing it is a real operational problem. Keep the international certificate with your passport, keep a copy in your personal file, and keep a photograph of both on a device that travels with you. If you work for an organization, ensure that your occupational health record names every vaccine, its date, and its batch number where known, because a needle-stick injury will send you looking for that information in a hurry. When you arrive at a new post, give the medical officer a written summary of your immunizations, your chronic conditions, your allergies, and the drugs you take, and keep a copy for yourself. Update it after every vaccination and after every change of medication, because a stale summary can mislead the person treating you.

Malaria prophylaxis is where good intentions most often collapse, and the collapse is understandable. The tablets are taken for months, they can cause unpleasant effects, the risk feels abstract on a quiet week, and nobody is checking. Then the nurse who has been advising patients about adherence for a year quietly stops taking her own tablets, and 6 weeks later she is the patient with fever and a positive blood film. The principle is to choose the drug deliberately, in advance, with a clinician who knows your history, and then to take it on a fixed schedule that does not depend on how you feel. The main options include atovaquone with proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine, and tafenoquine, and the choice depends on the resistance pattern where you are going, on your pregnancy status, on your psychiatric history, and on whether you have glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency. Guidance on which drug suits which destination is published by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and by the World Health Organization, and it changes as resistance spreads, so verify the current recommendation for your exact area before you commit to a drug for a long deployment.

Each option carries its own adverse effects, and knowing them in advance is what turns a nuisance into a manageable plan. Doxycycline commonly causes stomach upset, sun sensitivity that can be severe in equatorial light, and vaginal candidiasis in women, and it must be taken every day without gaps because it has a short duration of action. Mefloquine can produce vivid dreams, anxiety, insomnia, and in a small proportion of people serious neuropsychiatric effects, which is why a personal or family history of depression, anxiety, or seizures makes it a poor choice. Atovaquone with proguanil is generally well tolerated but is costly and must be taken with food at the same time each day. Tafenoquine is taken less often but requires testing for glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency first, because it can destroy red cells in people who lack the enzyme.

The discipline of continuing is mostly arithmetic, and the arithmetic is easy to get wrong. You must begin before arrival, continue through the whole stay without gaps, and continue for the period of time the chosen drug requires after you leave the malarious area, which is 4 weeks for doxycycline and 1 week for atovaquone with proguanil. Count the tablets you will need, add a margin for loss and for delays, and carry the prescription with the drug so that a customs officer or a pharmacy can see what it is. If you travel to a different region, the correct drug may change, and a visit to a travel medicine clinic between postings is worth the time. Some clinicians also carry a course of standby emergency treatment for malaria, to be used only when fever appears and no reliable testing or care is within reach, and the current World Health Organization guidance describes when that approach is appropriate. Both the prophylaxis and the standby treatment must be verified against the current edition of the guidance before you rely on them, because regimens and patterns of resistance are revised continuously.

Even with perfect prevention, exposures happen, and the needle-stick is the one that will find you. The risk depends on the size of the needle, the depth of the injury, the amount of blood involved, and the prevalence of blood-borne viruses in the population you serve, which in many tropical settings is high. The immediate response is not complicated and it must be automatic: wash the wound with soap and water, let it bleed briefly under running water, do not scrub it or squeeze it hard, and if blood or body fluid has reached an eye or the mouth, irrigate that area with clean water or saline for several minutes. Do not apply bleach, do not cauterize, and do not delay to finish the procedure you were doing. Then report it the same day, because everything that follows depends on the clock. This is the moment when the habit of writing things down protects you, because the time of injury, the source, and the action taken are the facts that determine your treatment.

The most time-critical element of a needle-stick is the post-exposure drugs for human immunodeficiency virus, and the reason is biological. The virus establishes itself in the body over hours to days, and antiretroviral drugs given early can interrupt that process before it becomes permanent infection. Current guidance from the World Health Organization and from national programs recommends starting a combination of antiretroviral drugs as soon as possible, ideally within 2 hours and certainly within 72 hours of the exposure, and continuing for 28 days. A commonly used regimen is tenofovir disoproxil fumarate 300 milligrams once daily, plus lamivudine 300 milligrams once daily, plus dolutegravir 50 milligrams once daily, though the exact combination depends on local resistance patterns and on whether the source person is already on treatment. The drugs have their own adverse effects, including nausea, headache, kidney effects, and liver effects, so monitoring is part of the course. This is a situation where the protocol must be known before the injury happens, because there is no time to research it afterward, and where the current guideline must be checked rather than remembered, because these recommendations are revised.

The needle is not the only exposure, and the same protocol must cover the others. Blood splashed onto broken skin or a mucous membrane, a bite that breaks the skin, a splash of cerebrospinal fluid or amniotic fluid, and unprotected sexual contact in the field all require assessment. Testing the source person, with consent and confidentiality, is what determines whether the full drug course is needed, and the process must be organized in advance so that a frightened patient is not approached clumsily at the moment of crisis. Hepatitis B exposure in a vaccinated clinician with documented protective antibody is handled differently from exposure in someone who was never vaccinated, and unvaccinated staff may need immunoglobulin and a vaccine course, while tetanus cover should be confirmed at the same time. The exposure must be written in an incident register, not because anyone wants to blame you, but because patterns of injury reveal faults in equipment and procedure that can be fixed.

Fever in yourself must be treated with exactly the seriousness you would apply to a patient, and this is harder than it sounds. The clinician who has malaria is a patient, not a colleague with a mild illness, and the temptation to take a couple of tablets and stay on duty is the precise mechanism by which severe malaria develops in health workers. Fever in a tropical setting demands a malaria test, preferably both a rapid diagnostic test and a thick and thin blood film, and a single negative test does not end the assessment if the clinical picture is convincing. It also demands the same differential thinking you would apply to anyone else, including dengue, typhoid, a rickettsial infection, leptospirosis, a urinary tract infection, or an ordinary respiratory illness. Do not prescribe for yourself from memory, and do not use your own professional knowledge to talk yourself out of a diagnosis. Ask a colleague to examine you, tell them the whole history, and accept the plan they make.

There is a specific danger in being both the prescriber and the patient, and it is that you will choose the diagnosis that lets you keep working. The nurse who treats her own fever with an antimalarial and continues the clinic may be treating the right disease with the wrong dose, or the wrong disease entirely, and the second possibility is the one that kills. If you test positive for malaria, take the full course of artemisinin-based combination therapy at the correct dose, record it, and arrange cover for the clinic before you need it. If you develop any danger sign, such as confusion, difficulty breathing, dark urine, inability to keep fluids down, or a fever that does not settle, you need treatment given intravenously and referral, and the referral decision must be made by someone who is not you. A named colleague should know where you keep your medical information and should be authorized to act if you become unable to decide. The clinic plan for your own illness is a document worth writing on a calm day and worth rehearsing.

Water and food are the exposures you can control most easily, which makes the failures less forgivable. Drinking water should be boiled, filtered, or treated with chlorine, and the treatment must be done correctly rather than symbolically, because a single untreated container can undo a month of care. Ice is water you did not treat, raw vegetables may have been washed in water you did not treat, and salads, unpasteurized milk, and undercooked meat carry the same lesson. The nurse who teaches a village about boiling water and then accepts a glass of untreated water to avoid giving offense has traded a small social discomfort for a bout of hepatitis A, typhoid, or a parasitic infection. You can accept hospitality without drinking the water by taking the glass, holding it, and drinking from your own bottle, and the maneuver is worth practicing before you need it. Food that is freshly cooked and still hot is safer than food that has been sitting, and street food is safer when you can see the heat and the clean hands that produced it. Insecticide-treated bed nets, repellent, and long sleeves belong to the same list, because vector-borne infection is also a personal exposure you can reduce.

Sleep is a clinical variable rather than a luxury, and its loss degrades the exact skills a remote nurse depends on. Decision-making, the recognition of a deteriorating patient, arithmetic for drug doses, and the ability to stay calm in a crisis all fall away with accumulated sleep debt, and the person who is most affected is often the last to notice. The clinic schedule is usually built around the patients rather than around the staff, and the on-call rota often means that one person is available for everything at every hour. That structure must be interrupted deliberately, with protected sleep after a night call, a rota that rotates the night burden, and a rule that nobody drives a long road after a night without sleep. Naps of 20 to 30 minutes can restore alertness for a few hours, and they are far better than a third cup of coffee. Caffeine taken late in the day buys an hour and costs the following night, so its timing matters as much as its quantity, and so does the alcohol that is offered at the end of a hard day.
