The body's limits also include heat, food, and movement, and remote practice punishes all three. Working in equatorial heat without shade or without enough salt and water leads to heat exhaustion and occasionally to heat stroke, and the warning signs are headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion, and the paradoxical stopping of sweat. Drink before you are thirsty, take the salt your body needs if you are sweating heavily for hours, and schedule heavy physical work for the early morning. Eating irregularly in a place where meals depend on the market and the season produces the same hypoglycemia and poor judgment you would look for in a patient, and it is easy to skip lunch and call it dedication. Movement is also part of maintenance, whether it is a daily walk, the stairs instead of the lift, or a routine that keeps strength and balance. The clinician who is physically depleted makes worse decisions and recovers more slowly from every illness, which is a clinical risk to the patients as much as a personal cost.

A chronic condition does not pause because you have taken a posting, and managing one at a distance is the same problem your patients face, only with more knowledge and less excuse. Diabetes, hypertension, asthma, epilepsy, thyroid disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and a history of mental illness all require a supply of medicine, a way to monitor, and a plan for what happens when the supply is interrupted. Before departure, calculate the quantity you need for the whole assignment, add a margin of at least one quarter, and find out whether the drug is on the national formulary of the country you are entering. If it is not, you must carry your own, with the prescription, the generic name written clearly, and enough to cover a delay in your return. Insulin needs reliable cold storage, which in a place with unreliable power means planning a backup source and monitoring the temperature of whatever container you use. Ask yourself what you would do if the supply ran out, write the answer down, and identify the nearest facility that could help.

Monitoring a chronic condition without a laboratory requires equipment you can trust and reagents you can keep valid. A blood pressure cuff can be checked against a colleague's and recalibrated, a glucose meter needs strips that have not expired and that have been stored away from heat and moisture, and a peak flow meter or a simple thermometer needs no calibration at all. Record your own readings in the same way you record a patient's, with the date and the value, because a pattern over 3 months is far more informative than a single number. If you take a drug with a narrow margin, such as an anticoagulant or an antiepileptic, arrange for the blood tests it requires to be done at a referral laboratory, and plan the journey rather than hoping the test will come to you. Tell at least one colleague at the post what you have and what you take, because a medical emergency is the wrong time to reveal a history that could have been known. The same principle that makes you ask a patient about adherence applies to you, and self-deception about your own adherence is common and dangerous.

A small personal medical kit is the practical expression of everything in this chapter, and it should be assembled before departure and checked at every rotation. It should contain your own prescription medicines with a written list, a course of treatment for malaria suited to the area, a broad spectrum antibiotic for common infections, oral rehydration salts, a thermometer, a blood pressure cuff if you have a chronic condition, wound dressings, and the supplies for a needle-stick or a minor injury. Include a copy of your vaccination record, your prescriptions, your allergies, and the telephone numbers of a clinician at home who knows your history. Include a small supply of the drugs you would not want to be without if the clinic pharmacy were empty, such as an asthma inhaler or an epinephrine auto-injector. Check the expiry dates every 6 months and replace what has gone, because a kit full of expired medicine is a false reassurance. Keep the kit where you can reach it in the dark, and tell one colleague where it is.

The mental load of this work belongs in the same paragraph as the physical, because it produces physical consequences and it is treated as an afterthought. You will see deaths that were preventable, suffering you cannot relieve, and choices that no training prepared you for, and each of those leaves a residue. The residue appears in poor sleep, irritability, a shortening fuse with colleagues and patients, a sense that nothing you do matters, and a growing distance from the people at home who cannot understand what you have seen. None of that is weakness, and naming it early is a clinical act rather than a confession. The chapter on burnout and moral injury takes this subject further, and it is worth listening to next, but the essential point here is that protection belongs to you and to your team, not only to the organization. The colleague who notices and asks the direct question is often the most effective intervention available in the field, and you are that colleague for someone else.

Several practical measures reduce the load, and they are worth building into the routine rather than the crisis. Regular contact with home, at a fixed time and in a form you can keep, sustains the relationships that hold you together when the work is hard. A boundary around the clinic, whether it is a walk at the end of the day or a rule that the radio is switched off during one meal, keeps the work from filling every hour. Supervision, whether by telephone, radio, or a visit from a senior colleague, gives the difficult cases somewhere to go other than your own head, and the habit of writing them down helps in the same way. Watch your use of alcohol, because a drink that helps you sleep on a hard day becomes the thing that is doing the sleeping for you. Recognize your own warning signs and tell someone when they appear, because insight fades exactly when it is most needed.

The check-up during home leave is easy to postpone and expensive to skip, and it should be scheduled before the leave begins. Book the appointments early, because a 4 week leave disappears quickly, and put the ones that require fasting or a second visit at the start rather than at the end. The list includes a general medical review, blood pressure and blood glucose, a dental examination, an eye examination, cervical or prostate screening as appropriate, and the laboratory tests that your age and history require. It also includes the vaccines that have expired or that your posting has made relevant, and a review of every medicine you take, including the ones you buy yourself. Mental health deserves a real appointment, not a five minute conversation at the end of a consultation about something else. Bring the written summary of your field records, because the clinician at home will otherwise have to reconstruct 2 years of your life from memory.

The clinician seeing you at home needs a specific kind of information, and the tropical exposure history is what most of them will not think to take. Tell them where you have served, for how long, whether you lived in a rural or an urban area, what water you drank, whether you walked barefoot, and whether you had any episode of fever, diarrhea, or skin problem that resolved without a diagnosis. That history determines which screening tests are worth doing, which may include a blood count for eosinophilia, a stool examination, a urine examination for schistosomiasis, and a test for tuberculosis infection, because exposure in a clinic or a community can be significant. Some infections are silent for years, and the point of the screen is to find them while they are still treatable rather than when they present as disease. No screening list is universal, and the correct tests depend on your exact exposure and on national guidance, so ask what the current recommendation is for a returning health worker and verify it before the appointment. Take the answer in writing and file it with the rest of your record.

The team's duty to each of its members is the part that no individual can carry alone, and it works in both directions. You owe your colleagues an honest answer when they ask how you are, and you owe them the same question asked without an agenda. A small team in a remote place should know each other's chronic conditions, allergies, and the person to call in an emergency, and that information should be kept where the whole team can reach it without awkwardness. When a colleague is unwell, the clinical response is the same as for a patient: assess, treat, and remove that person from duty if the illness makes their work unsafe. If a colleague withdraws, drinks more, or stops laughing at things that used to be funny, that is a finding to act on rather than a mood to tolerate.

The organization employing you has obligations that a nurse should know before signing, and a refusal to ask about them is a common mistake. Ask about medical evacuation cover for staff, about health insurance that works in the country of posting, about the supply of personal protective equipment and its fit, about rest days and leave, and about what happens to your post if you become ill. Ask whether there is a staff medical kit with the drugs and supplies that the team itself might need, and whether anyone is responsible for checking its expiry dates. Ask who covers the clinic when a staff member is sick, because the answer reveals whether the duty of care is real or rhetorical. Ask about the policy for reporting an exposure, and about confidentiality when a staff member is diagnosed with a blood-borne infection.

To summarize, your health is the equipment the clinic cannot replace, and it deserves the same assessment, documentation, and follow-up you give a patient. Prepare before departure with the vaccines recommended by the World Health Organization and with the malaria prophylaxis chosen for your exact destination, take it without gaps, and continue it for the full period after you leave. Know the exposure protocol before the needle-stick happens, start post-exposure drugs for human immunodeficiency virus within hours, and report every injury the same day. Treat your own fever as seriously as anyone else's, test for malaria, and arrange cover and referral in advance rather than improvising while ill. Control the water and the food, protect your sleep, and manage any chronic condition with a surplus of medicine and a written plan for interruption. Carry the mental load openly, keep the check-up on home leave, and accept that your colleagues are part of your safety system and you are part of theirs. Keep every regimen in this chapter framed as what current guidance says, and verify the current guideline before you act on it, because recommendations change and your situation is specific.

# Chapter 64 — Burnout and Moral Injury

Burnout is not a synonym for being tired, and it is not a character flaw. It is a syndrome that arises from prolonged exposure to a demanding working environment, and it has three recognizable faces. The first is exhaustion so deep that a night of sleep does not touch it, a tiredness that lives in the bones and is waiting before the first patient arrives. The second is cynicism, a hardening toward the people you are there to serve, which arrives quietly and often feels like protection. The third is a fading sense that any of it matters, a slow leak of meaning from work that once felt like a calling. When all three are present together, and when they persist for weeks rather than days, burnout is the honest word.

Most clinicians know ordinary fatigue, and it is important to separate it from what is described here. Ordinary fatigue yields to sleep, to a weekend, to a few days away from the clinic. The exhaustion of burnout does not behave that way. You sleep and wake unrefreshed, you take a day off and spend it dreading the return, and you notice that your shoulders have begun to rise before you have thought about the day at all. When rest stops working, the problem is no longer a matter of hours, and one more long weekend will not solve it.

Cynicism deserves an honest hearing, because it usually begins as a defense rather than a defect. In a clinic that never stops, a certain emotional distance lets you keep moving, since a person who feels every death at full volume will not last the month. So the mind builds armor. You begin to refer to patients by their disease rather than their name, you make a joke you would not have made 2 years ago, and you stop asking the question whose answer you cannot act on. The armor works, and that is the trouble, because it protects you from the pain while closing the channel through which the work used to give something back.

The third face is the quietest and the most dangerous. It is not sadness, although sadness may accompany it. It is the erosion of the belief that what you do changes anything. You still perform every task, and you perform it competently, but the internal sentence has changed from this child will live to another one will come tomorrow with the same illness. Some clinicians describe watching themselves work from a slight distance, no longer certain why they chose this life. This is the dimension that most strongly predicts a person leaving the profession, and it is the least visible to everyone else.

It helps to understand burnout as a response to working conditions rather than as a personal weakness. The research that defined the modern understanding of this syndrome, built through the second half of the twentieth century, treated it as an occupational phenomenon with measurable parts. If the cause is a person's fragility, the remedy is the person's resilience. If the cause is an unstaffed clinic, an impossible caseload, and no relief in sight, then the remedy has to include those things as well. The World Health Organization addresses the mental health of health workers through its mental health gap action program and its guidance for humanitarian settings, and those documents should be read in their current form, because thresholds and recommendations in this field are revised often and differ between countries.

Remote practice adds its own pressures, and isolation is the first of them. In a district clinic a day from the referral hospital, the clinician may be the only person within many kilometers who thinks in medical terms. There is no corridor conversation in which a difficult decision is casually tested, and no colleague who has seen the same rash and can say what it turned out to be. Uncertainty therefore has nowhere to go except inward, where it accumulates. The isolation is not only professional but social, linguistic, and often spiritual, and it compounds every other stressor because none of them can be worked through in company.

Responsibility without backup is the second pressure, and it changes the shape of a decision. When the physician is 5 hours away, the nurse does not merely carry out a plan but makes the plan, owns it, and lives with its outcome. The weight is not only the work but the authorship of it. A single clinician may hold the delivery room, the tuberculosis register, the medication refills, and the security of the compound in mind at the same moment, with no one to hand any of it to. Over months the nervous system treats this as a permanent state of alert, and a body that cannot stand down stops recovering between shifts.

Role diffusion makes the load heavier still. In a small team the nurse is often also the pharmacist, the laboratory, the logistics officer, the translator, and the person who negotiates with the local authorities. Each of these is a legitimate task, and each carries its own small cognitive tax. When the same person holds all of them, the day fragments into so many pieces that none receives full attention, and the quiet satisfaction of doing one thing well disappears. Any plan for preventing burnout in such a setting must begin by counting these roles aloud and asking which can be shared, delegated, or dropped.

Then there are the moral choices that no training prepared anyone for. Who receives the last unit of blood when 2 patients need it? Which child is admitted when there is one bed and 3 children who qualify? How much morphine is set aside for the dying when the supply has to last another 6 weeks? These are not clinical questions with a correct answer waiting in a guideline but allocation decisions made under scarcity. The person who makes them is often the person with the least power to change the scarcity. Training programs teach pathophysiology and protocols, and almost none of them teach a clinician how to carry the memory of choosing.

Moral injury is the name for the wound that forms when those choices, or the circumstances around them, violate a person's own moral code. It is not the same as burnout, although the two travel together and are easily confused. Burnout is a depletion of energy and meaning that comes from overload, while moral injury is a wound to identity and conscience that comes from what a person did, saw, or could not prevent. It can arise from an act you performed, an act you witnessed, or a failure you believe was yours. The betrayal may be personal or institutional, and that distinction matters, because the injury often deepens when the institution that should have protected you denies what happened.

Picture a child with severe malaria who arrives at dusk, convulsing and pale. The referral hospital is a day away on a road that floods, the ambulance is a motorcycle with a trailer, and there is no fuel. The child dies at 4 in the morning while you hold the mother's hand. Nothing you did was wrong, and nothing within reach would have changed the outcome, and yet something in you has shifted. That is the shape of moral injury in remote practice. It is not a failure of competence but the wound of standing at the edge of what is possible and being asked to accept it as normal.

Guilt and grief are often entangled here, and separating them is not an academic exercise. Grief is the sorrow of loss, it asks to be witnessed, and it softens slowly with time and company. Guilt is a verdict on the self, it asks for punishment, and it does not soften with rest. In moral injury the guilt is frequently misplaced, because the clinician is holding responsibility for an outcome that belonged to a broken system, a missing road, a national budget, or a war. A useful question, asked gently, is what exactly you believe you should have done differently, and whether that thing was truly available to you. When the honest answer is nothing, the work is to move the guilt back to its rightful owner, who is often no one in the room.

Moral injury also carries a betrayal dimension that is easy to miss. The wound is not only about the patient but about what the clinician believed the institution stood for and what the institution proved to be. Promises of evacuation that never came, a supervisor who dismissed a report, a supply chain that failed for the fourth month, a salary unpaid while the clinic was praised abroad. A person who once said I work for this organization begins to say I work despite it, and that shift drains motivation more thoroughly than any long shift. Naming the betrayal is part of treatment rather than an act of disloyalty, because a wound that cannot be described cannot be dressed.

Recognition begins with honest monitoring of yourself, which is difficult because the instrument and the subject are the same person. Certain signals are reliable. Sleep that has changed in pattern or quality, irritability toward people who do not deserve it, a growing reluctance to answer the radio, drinking that has moved from occasional to routine, charting at 2 in the morning because the day will not let you sit still, and a loss of interest in the patients you used to find interesting. None of these alone proves anything. A cluster of them sustained over a month, however, deserves the same seriousness as a physical symptom you would not ignore in a patient.

Recognizing it in a colleague requires the attentiveness you would give a deteriorating patient, with the difference that there is no monitor. The change is usually qualitative rather than dramatic. The person who always ate with the team now eats alone, the one who laughed at everything has gone flat, and someone who was reliably warm has become abrupt with patients and then disproportionately apologetic about it. Sometimes the clearest sign is what has stopped: the questions, the jokes, the ordinary grumbling that used to release pressure.

When you see it, ask, and ask plainly. The most effective question is not how are you, which invites a reflexive fine, but something specific, such as saying that you have noticed the person is not sleeping much and seems to be carrying something, and that you would like to know how they are. Then be quiet long enough for the answer to arrive. What you can promise is that you will stay, that you will help find the right support, and that the conversation will not be repeated as gossip. Often the most useful thing a colleague provides is the knowledge that someone has noticed.

Documentation in this area is unglamorous and genuinely protective. An organized record of critical incidents, near misses, and the conditions that produced them does 3 things at once. It gives the individual a written account that can be revisited with a counselor without having to rebuild the event from memory, and it turns private distress into evidence that a manager can use to argue for staffing, fuel, or evacuation capacity. It also protects the clinician if an outcome is later questioned, because it shows what was known and what was attempted at the time. Keep it factual, keep dates and times, and keep it in a clinical or operational file separate from the personnel file, with a stated rule about who may read it.

The processing that helps begins with other people, though not in the way crisis response often imagines it. A structured operational debrief, held within a few days of a serious event, walks through the facts first, then the decisions, then the feelings, then what will change, and it is voluntary and confidential. Its purpose is to close gaps in understanding and to let people hear that others carry the same weight. The difference between a debrief that is structured and one that is forced is the whole difference between repair and harm. When attendance is mandatory and disclosure is expected in front of a supervisor, the room will produce performance rather than truth.

Peer support is the backbone of what works, and it does not require a psychologist on site. It requires a named colleague, agreed in advance, whom you can call at an unreasonable hour. It requires a regular check-in that happens whether or not there is a crisis, so that the habit exists before it is needed. Much of the most useful conversation happens while walking, while washing instruments, or on the drive back from an outreach visit, because side by side is easier than face to face for many people. Build the practice in a calm month so that it is already there in a bad one.

Writing it down is a quiet intervention with a long history of use. Some clinicians keep an incident journal in which the event, the decision, and the feeling are recorded separately, which forces the mind to distinguish what happened from what it concluded. Others write a letter to the patient or the family that will never be sent, and find that finishing the sentences releases something. Expressive writing of this kind has been studied for decades and appears to help people organize difficult experience into a coherent narrative, which is part of how meaning is rebuilt. Whatever form it takes, the point is to move the material out of the loop in the head and onto something that can be read.

There is also a set of responses that reliably makes things worse, and the first is alcohol. In isolated postings drinking is often the shared social ritual, which makes the early warning signs easy to miss. The pattern that matters is not the quantity on any one evening but the function it has taken on, such as drinking to sleep, drinking to stop replaying the day, drinking alone, or drinking before noon. A short questionnaire, of the kind the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends for screening, asks how often in the past year you have had 6 or more drinks on one occasion and whether you have ever felt you should cut down, and it identifies most people who need a second look. Monitoring your own intake honestly, in the same way you would monitor a patient's, is not self indulgence but basic surveillance of a known occupational hazard.

Silence is the second harmful response, and it is usually driven by stigma rather than stoicism. Many health professionals still believe that admitting distress will be read as incompetence, and where your post, your housing, and your visa depend on the same employer, that fear is rational. So the clinician says nothing, and the silence compounds the injury, because an experience that cannot be spoken becomes a private conviction that one is uniquely broken. The remedy is not to demand disclosure but to change what disclosure costs. When senior staff describe their own difficult cases without losing standing, and when support is clearly separated from appraisal, the calculation changes and people begin to talk.

The third harmful response is the single session pressure to talk. Well meaning teams sometimes require everyone involved in an event to sit in a circle and recount it in detail, once, immediately, and then consider the matter closed. For some people this helps, but for many it reopens the wound without providing the followup that healing requires, and the evidence for single session psychological debriefing as a preventive measure is weak to negative. The guidance of the World Health Organization on psychological first aid makes the same point in practice, that the aim in the first days is safety, calm, connection, and practical help rather than the reconstruction of traumatic detail. Structured support should be offered, scheduled, and repeated, and it should allow a person to decline without penalty and to return when ready.

Prevention that actually works begins with the workload, because much of what is called burnout is simply too much work for too few people. Concrete limits are possible even in small clinics: a maximum number of patients seen per clinician each day, a maximum number of consecutive night duties, a protected rest day after a night on call, and a standing rule that no single person covers 2 critical areas at once. These numbers should be written down and negotiated rather than left to goodwill, because goodwill is exactly what gets consumed first. They should also be monitored, which means that someone records the actual figures each week and compares them with the agreed ceiling. A limit that is never measured is a wish rather than a limit.

Leave is the second pillar, and it has to be scheduled, defended, and taken. In many remote posts leave is technically available and practically impossible, because there is no one to cover the clinic in your absence, and that is an organizational failure which the individual is then invited to absorb. The fix is to plan coverage in advance, to train a second person for the essential tasks, and to treat a broken leave plan as an operational risk rather than a personal inconvenience. The supervisor should track leave the way the clinic tracks vaccine stock, with a simple register that shows who is due, who is overdue, and what is blocking it. A clinician who has not left the compound in 8 months is not a hero but a predictable emergency.

Relationships are the third pillar and the most protective of all. The strongest predictor of whether a person survives a hard posting is not personality or prior experience but whether they have at least one relationship in which they can be honest. That relationship may be a peer in the same clinic, a mentor at a distance who can be reached by telephone, or a partner at home who is willing to hear the parts that are not presentable. It should be deliberately cultivated before it is needed, because the middle of a crisis is a poor time to build trust. Teams that eat together, that discuss the difficult case together, and that keep their humor kind tend to keep their people.

The supervisor who asks is a specific and learnable role. A good supervisor does not wait for a request for help but asks, on a schedule, in private, and with enough specificity that the answer cannot be a reflex. Such a supervisor asks about sleep, about the last difficult case, about what the person is dreading this week, and about what would make the next month easier. The supervisor knows the referral pathway for mental health support, including how to reach it by telephone or radio when the person is hundreds of kilometers away, and then follows up, which is the part that proves the asking was real.

The duty to prevent this belongs to the organization first and to the individual second, and reversing that order is a common and damaging mistake. It is the organization that must ensure mental health care is available and confidential, that psychological injury is treated as a legitimate reason for medical evacuation, and that a person who reports distress is not quietly moved to the end of the contract list. The individual's duty is real but narrower: to notice, to report, to use the leave provided, to show up for colleagues, and to seek help before the choice is taken away by collapse. Resilience training cannot substitute for adequate staffing, and offering it as a substitute converts a system failure into a personal one.

When the injury is severe enough that support and rest are not sufficient, treatment should be sought with the same seriousness as for any other condition. Structured psychological therapies have good evidence for trauma related and grief related distress. Where medication is indicated, an antidepressant such as sertraline may be started at 25 to 50 milligrams by mouth once a day and adjusted slowly, with attention to sleep, agitation, and adverse effects in the first weeks. Those thresholds follow current guidance from the World Health Organization and national formularies, and that guidance is revised periodically and differs between countries, so the current version must be checked before anything is prescribed.

Building this support into a small clinic is a logistics problem, and treating it as one makes it more likely to happen. Write down who the peer contacts are and post the list where it can be found at 3 in the morning. Agree how a person reaches help by radio or telephone when the network is down, and identify the nearest facility able to provide psychological care. Keep mental health records in a locked file separate from the personnel file, with a stated rule about who may open it. Ensure that any medication needed for mental health is on the same resupply list as antimalarials and antibiotics, so that a course is not interrupted halfway. Decide in advance what the organization will do about transport, accommodation, and pay if a clinician must leave for care.

Monitoring applies to the helpers exactly as it applies to patients. If medication is started, the clinician needs a followup appointment, a way to report adverse effects, and someone who will notice if the supply runs out. Agitation, worsening sleep, or new thoughts of self harm in the first weeks require prompt review rather than reassurance. If alcohol has become the main coping strategy, withdrawal can be dangerous, and management may include thiamine, often 100 milligrams by mouth or intramuscularly, and a benzodiazepine under supervision, with doses and regimens taken from current national guidance and from the World Health Organization, which are revised and vary between countries and must be verified before use. The principle is simple: the same standards of assessment, treatment, and followup that you would apply to a patient apply to you.

The nursing role in all of this is larger than it is usually acknowledged to be, and it runs in 2 directions. Nurses are the people most likely to notice a colleague's change early, because they work side by side at the bedside and share the same small kitchen. Nurses are also frequently the ones holding the team together, which places them at high risk themselves. A lead nurse can make the difference by protecting breaks, rotating the hardest duties, naming a peer support contact for each shift, and asking the direct question when someone is not themselves. That work is not an addition to clinical care, because in a remote setting it is the maintenance that keeps clinical care possible.

Most people who reach this point do return to work, and that fact deserves to be said clearly, because the fear of permanent damage is itself part of the burden. Return is safer when it is planned rather than abrupt. A graded return, with reduced duties or shorter shifts for the first weeks, allows confidence to rebuild without another overload. A named mentor who checks in weekly gives the returning clinician a place to say that it is still hard. A review of the event, conducted without blame and focused on what the system will change, closes the loop that the mind keeps trying to close on its own, and a clear statement from the supervisor that the person's standing is intact removes the anxiety that often accompanies the first shift back.

The team has a role in that return, and it is mostly a matter of restraint. Welcome the person back without interrogation, without the raised eyebrow, and without treating them as fragile. Do not assume that a good week means the matter is finished or that a bad week means the return has failed. If the returning colleague wants to talk about what happened, listen; if they do not, let ordinary work be the therapy of reentry. The person who comes back is usually watching for evidence of having been diminished, and the surest way to prevent that is to treat them as the competent colleague they still are.

There is an institutional argument for doing this well that goes beyond kindness. Replacing a clinician in a remote posting is slow, expensive, and often impossible, and the institutional memory that leaves with them cannot be purchased. Teams that lose people to preventable burnout often lose their programs soon afterward, and the community pays the price in the services that disappear. Measuring turnover, holding honest exit conversations, and reviewing every departure for what the organization could have changed are not sentimental exercises but the same quality monitoring a clinic applies to any other outcome it cares about. What is counted is what gets managed, and this deserves counting.

None of this is an argument for cynicism about the work itself. The reason burnout and moral injury matter so much in tropical medicine is precisely that the work matters and that the people doing it are the scarcest resource the system has. A clinician who is exhausted, injured, and unsupported cannot remain compassionate for long, and a system that relies on individual heroism is a system quietly planning to consume its staff. The honest position is neither that distress is weakness nor that suffering is the price of service. It is that the work is worth doing by people who are also worth keeping, and that both claims have to be built into the roster, the budget, and the weekly conversation.

To summarize, burnout is a syndrome with 3 parts, exhaustion that rest does not repair, cynicism that hardens as armor, and a fading sense that the work matters, and it grows from working conditions rather than from personal defect. Remote practice intensifies it through isolation, responsibility without backup, and the moral choices that no training prepares anyone for, which can leave the deeper wound of moral injury, the violation of one's own moral code by what was done, witnessed, or not prevented. The patient who died for want of a hospital a day away is the emblem of that wound, and separating guilt from grief is the first step in dressing it. What helps is honest recognition in yourself and in your colleague, a structured and voluntary debrief, sustained peer support, and writing the experience down, while what harms is alcohol, silence, and the single forced session of talk. What prevents it is mostly organizational, with workload limits that are measured, leave that is scheduled and taken, relationships built in advance, and a supervisor who asks on a schedule and follows up. Most people do return, and a graded, blameless, well supported return is what makes that possible, so the last word belongs as much to the institution as to the individual, because keeping the clinician is part of treating the patient.

# Chapter 65 — Knowing Your Limits

A thermometer is trusted because it converts a bodily change into a number that anyone can read, and the recognition of your own limit deserves the same status. A limit is a reading you take before you act rather than after, and it tells you where your training, your experience and your equipment stop being sufficient for the patient in front of you. Like the thermometer, it is a clinical instrument, and like the thermometer it is only useful when it is used honestly. The strange thing is that most clinicians reach for the thermometer before every consultation and almost never reach for the limit until something has gone wrong. The reasons are understandable, because training rewards action, patients arrive whether or not you are ready, and in a remote post there may be no senior colleague to impose the pause that a hospital would impose. A limit is also harder to see than a fever, since nothing on the outside marks a clinician who is about to attempt something beyond their reach. This chapter is about learning to take that reading, and about what to do with the answer.

Begin with the competence boundary, and accept that it is a real line rather than a feeling of nervousness. Everything that a nurse can do clinically falls into three zones. In the first zone are the skills you were trained in, have performed many times, and could now perform while tired, at night, with a frightened family watching. In the second zone are the skills you were trained in but have practiced rarely, or practiced long ago, or practiced only on a model. In the third zone are the skills you were never trained in at all, however well you understand the theory. The second zone is the dangerous one, because it feels like competence from the inside and looks like competence from the outside. A nurse who knows intellectually how to reduce a dislocated shoulder, deliver a breech baby, or place a chest drain may be convinced of their ability and still lack the repetition that makes the hands reliable. The boundary is not a judgement of character; it is a description of the evidence.

The distinction that matters most is between knowledge and volume. A manual can teach you the sequence of a procedure in an afternoon, and a workshop can let you perform it once on a model, and neither of those converts into the ability to manage the same procedure when it bleeds, when the anatomy is unusual, or when the patient stops breathing. Competence is built by repetition with feedback, because hands learn through correction rather than through explanation. A skill practiced twenty times under the eye of someone more experienced is a different thing from a skill practiced twice without anyone watching. This is why the honest question is not whether you know how to do something but how many times you have done it, how recently, with what outcomes, and with whom available should it go wrong. The answer to that question is the boundary, stated plainly.

A practical way to take the reading is to ask three questions before any significant act. Have I been trained and supervised in this, and can I name the person who trained me? Have I performed it often enough and recently enough that my hands know it without my having to reconstruct the steps? If it goes wrong, do I have the drugs, the blood, the oxygen, the equipment and the second pair of hands needed to rescue the patient? If any answer is no, the plan changes, and it changes before the first incision, the first dose, or the first attempt. These questions take perhaps thirty seconds, and they cost nothing when the answer is yes. Their whole value lies in being asked before the act rather than being remembered after it. The nurse who asks them habitually is not timid; the nurse who asks them habitually is the one who is safe to work with.

Beware the single good outcome, because it teaches a false lesson more effectively than failure does. A difficult delivery that ended well, a wound that healed after a closure you improvised, or an airway that opened after an attempt you were not trained for will all feel like proof of ability. Yet one survival may reflect the patient's youth, a generous anatomy, or simple luck, and none of those can be scheduled for the next patient. The right question after such an event is not whether you succeeded but whether you would be willing to repeat the same decision in the same conditions with the same resources. If the answer is that you would not, then the first outcome was not a competence, it was an exception. Recording the exception honestly is how a clinician keeps a boundary from drifting outward on the strength of a coincidence.

The boundary is not supposed to stay where it is, and a clinician who never expands it is not being careful but stagnant. Growth, however, must be deliberate and documented rather than accidental. The pattern that works begins with naming the specific skill, then obtaining training from someone qualified to give it, then performing it repeatedly under direct supervision, then having that supervision attest to the number and the quality of the performances, and only then beginning independent practice. Each stage has a gate, and the gate is passed by evidence rather than by enthusiasm. The supervisor should be named in advance, and their willingness to supervise should be confirmed rather than assumed. An expansion that happens because nobody was watching is not growth; it is drift, and drift is the mechanism by which most overreach occurs.

Keep a written log, because memory is generous and records are not. A log for clinical procedures needs only a few columns: the date, the procedure, the indication, whether it was performed under supervision, the immediate outcome, any complication, and the name of the supervisor or the person consulted. The log serves three purposes at once. It tells you honestly how much of a skill you actually have, it shows a supervisor or a licensing body what you have done, and it reveals the pattern of your complications before that pattern becomes a reputation. Review it at fixed intervals, perhaps every three months, and look for the skills that are decaying as well as the skills that are growing. A log kept only when a procedure goes well is a marketing document rather than a record.

Where case volume is low, the boundary shrinks unless something is done about it, and simulation and drills are how a remote team fights that decay. A skill used twice a year will not be available on the night it is needed, however well it was learned. Run drills for the emergencies that would otherwise be performed by someone out of practice, including the postpartum hemorrhage, the neonatal resuscitation, the anaphylaxis, the convulsing child, and the blocked airway. Run them with the actual equipment, in the actual room, with the actual team, and rotate the roles so that everyone has held each one. The organization employing you has a duty to fund refresher training, and the nurse has a duty to ask for it in writing rather than to hope it appears. Maintenance of competence is not a personal hobby; it is part of the job description that nobody writes down.

There is a well described trap in which the least experienced clinician is the most confident, because confidence is built from the inside while competence is visible only from the outside. This is why self-assessment alone can never be the whole answer, and why a colleague who watches you work is worth more than any amount of private reflection. Invite direct observation and ask for specific feedback rather than general reassurance, asking not whether the procedure went well but whether the steps were in the right order, what was slow, and what would have been done differently. Where video or a checklist is available, use it, because a recording shows what memory edits out. The clinician who can hear criticism without defending against it is the clinician who keeps learning after the formal training ends. Defensiveness is the enemy of the boundary, because it blinds the one person who most needs to see.

The boundary is also written into law and into institutional rules, and a nurse working remotely needs to know both. Scope of practice, standing orders, delegation arrangements and the protocols of a task-sharing program together define what you may do and under whose authority. The World Health Organization has published guidance on task sharing for maternal and newborn health and for other services, and many ministries of health have adapted that guidance into national documents, but the arrangements differ substantially between countries and are revised as policy changes. Before you rely on any authorization to perform a procedure, verify the current national scope of practice and the current program protocol rather than trusting what you were told at orientation. A skill you possess but are not authorized to use is still beyond your limit, and the fact that you could do something is never a legal or ethical justification for doing it.

The situation that exceeds the individual may exceed the clinic as well, and the two are not the same problem. A patient may present with a condition you personally cannot manage but that the clinic is equipped and staffed to manage, in which case the answer is to find or call the right colleague. Alternatively, the patient may present with a condition that is beyond the post itself, such as an obstructed labor requiring cesarean section, a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, a penetrating abdominal wound, a child needing ventilation, a patient needing dialysis, or a hemorrhage requiring blood that does not exist within a day's drive. In that second situation there is no internal answer, and the clinical task becomes stabilization, honest communication, and transfer or palliation. Confusing the two situations produces two opposite errors, which are abandoning a patient the clinic could have treated and attempting a rescue the clinic was never able to provide.

Saying that something is beyond you is a clinical act, and it must be said out loud at the time rather than explained afterward. The sentence is short and it needs to be practiced: I am not able to do this safely here, and we need to arrange the next step together. Say it to the team first, so that the plan can change while there is still time to change it, and then say it to the patient and the family in the language they use. What makes that sentence possible is not courage alone but a team culture in which the person who names the limit is respected rather than overruled. If the culture punishes the acknowledgement, the limit will be discovered later by a complication instead. The nurse who speaks early protects the patient and also protects the colleague who would otherwise be pulled into an attempt they did not choose.

Overreach is the failure mode this chapter exists to prevent, and its first error is almost never technical. The hands fail second; the decision fails first. The classic scene is a clinician alone, confronted by a patient who will certainly die without an operation or a procedure, deciding that the only humane choice is to attempt it even though the training, the assistants, the anesthesia, the blood and the postoperative care are all absent. That decision feels like courage in the moment, and it is usually described as courage afterward, especially if the patient survives. But the reasoning is flawed, because the alternative to an attempt is not always death; it is often transfer, temporizing, or a dignified death in the company of family rather than an agonizing death on an improvised table. The overreach that kills is not a single reckless act but a habit of mind that treats willingness as a substitute for capability.

The line between brave and reckless can be stated fairly precisely. Bravery accepts a risk that is known, proportionate to the benefit sought, and mitigated as far as the circumstance allows. Recklessness accepts a risk that is unknown, disproportionate to the likely benefit, or unmitigated because nobody paused to count what was missing. A nurse who performs a procedure within their competence to save a bleeding patient in a clinic with the right drugs at hand is brave, while a nurse who performs the same procedure for the first time, alone, at night, without the drugs to manage the complications, is reckless, even though the two look similar from the doorway. The distinguishing test is not the intensity of the desire to help but the quality of the preparation and the honesty of the assessment. Courage without an inventory is simply a wager with someone else's life.

Certain procedures have such a narrow margin that partial training is more dangerous than none, and they deserve to be named so that the boundary becomes concrete. Cesarean section, laparotomy for a ruptured viscus, craniotomy, open reduction of a fracture, spinal anesthesia, and definitive airway management in a child all require a team, and they require resources that a remote post rarely has, including oxygen, suction, blood, a functioning anesthesia supply, sterile instruments, and a person whose only task is to watch the patient. Being able to start such a procedure is not the same as being able to finish it, and the hardest part of most of them is not the first minutes but the recognition and management of what follows. Where these procedures are genuinely required, the correct intervention is usually pre-referral stabilization and urgent transport rather than improvisation. The nurse who declines to open an abdomen in a clinic with no blood bank has not failed the patient; the nurse has understood the patient's actual chances.

Competence decays with time and with the conditions of practice, which means the boundary must be re-read rather than remembered. A skill performed regularly in a well-lit clinic with help available is not the same skill when performed at night after a long shift with one assistant and a torch. Fatigue, hunger, illness and distraction all lower the ceiling, and the honest clinician adjusts the limit for the day rather than pretending that a stable limit exists. Illness in the clinician deserves the same seriousness as illness in the patient, because a nurse with a fever and a headache is not making good decisions. These are not excuses offered in advance; they are variables that belong in the assessment. The boundary is therefore not a fixed property of a person but a reading that changes with the day, the patient and the support available.

The limit is also a logistics problem, and this is the part of the assessment that clinicians most often neglect. A drug you can prescribe but cannot monitor is a drug you cannot safely give, because the adverse effects that require a blood count, an electrocardiogram, a potassium measurement or a glucose measurement may be undetectable where no laboratory exists. A procedure you can perform but cannot rescue is a procedure whose complications will become the patient's cause of death, including the pneumothorax you cannot drain, the hemorrhage you cannot replace, the respiratory depression you cannot reverse, and the anaphylaxis whose second dose of epinephrine has expired. Oxygen, blood, suture, sterile gloves, local anesthetic, reversal agents and a functioning light source are all part of the definition of what you are able to do. Before adding a capability, count the consumables that capability consumes, and count them honestly rather than by memory. A limit is often set not by skill but by the shelf.

When you decide that a patient must stay because transfer is impossible, monitoring becomes the substitute for capability, and it must be planned with the same care as a treatment. Write down what will be measured, how often it will be measured, who will measure it, and what number triggers the next action. For a patient receiving magnesium sulfate for eclampsia, for example, World Health Organization guidance describes a loading dose of 4 grams given intravenously over five to twenty minutes followed by an infusion of 1 gram every hour, with monitoring of the deep tendon reflexes, the respiratory rate and the urine output, because magnesium toxicity announces itself first through lost reflexes and then through respiratory depression. Regimens for eclampsia and for every other condition are revised as evidence accumulates, guidance differs between countries, and the current national or World Health Organization guideline must be checked before you prescribe or infuse anything named in this chapter. Monitoring is not a lesser form of treatment; in a remote setting it is the form of treatment that keeps the patient alive until help can come.

Every intervention you decide to perform carries adverse effects, and the duty to anticipate them belongs to the person performing the intervention. Before the act, say aloud what the three most likely complications are and what you will do when each appears. Lay out the rescue equipment before you start rather than after the patient deteriorates, because a search for a syringe in a crisis is a delay measured in brain tissue. Name the person responsible for watching the patient while your hands are busy, since a clinician whose eyes are inside a wound cannot also be watching the chest rise. Know your stop rules in advance, meaning the number of attempts after which you will stop, the amount of blood loss after which you will stop, and the degree of agitation after which you will stop. A complication recognized in its first minute is a clinical problem; the same complication recognized in its fifth minute is often a death.

Some rescue knowledge is specific enough that it should be present before the procedure that might require it. Local anesthetic systemic toxicity, for instance, presents with agitation, ringing in the ears, a metallic taste, seizures and then cardiac arrest, and its treatment includes stopping the injection, supporting the airway, giving oxygen, controlling seizures, and administering an intravenous lipid emulsion when it is available. Procedural sedation with ketamine can produce emergence reactions and, less commonly, apnea, which means that the drug should not be given by a nurse who has no way to support ventilation. Opioids given for pain can cause respiratory depression, and naloxone must be at hand if morphine is being used. Each of these is a concrete example of a general rule: the drug and its antidote, and the procedure and its rescue, belong together or not at all. Verify the current dosing and monitoring recommendations for any of these drugs before you use them, because both change.

You are also an object of monitoring, and this is the part of knowing your limits that nurses most often skip. Watch your own sleep, your own appetite, your own alcohol use, your own irritability, and your own physical symptoms, because each of them changes the ceiling on what you can safely do. A nurse who has not slept for two nights should not be the person making an operative decision, and a nurse with a fever in a malarial area should be a patient before being a clinician. Write down your own limits for the day at the start of the day, for example no procedures after eighteen consecutive hours awake, no independent sedation when alone in the building, and no long journeys after a night call. These rules sound rigid until the first time they prevent a catastrophe. Asking a colleague to cover, or to stand beside you, is a clinical intervention with a measurable benefit.

Backup is a component of the plan rather than a hope, and it must be built before it is needed. Identify by name the colleague you will call when a case exceeds you, and the second name for when the first is unreachable, and the third for when the telephone network is down. Write the numbers on the wall of the clinic and in the front of the register, not only in your own telephone, because the person who needs them may be the one on duty after you. Agree in advance what information you will transmit, in what order, and what you will have prepared before the call begins. Test the chain at intervals by making a call that is not an emergency, so that you learn the delays, the wrong numbers and the times of day when nobody answers. A backup that has never been tested is a story the team tells itself.

The chain needs redundancy, because a single contact is a single point of failure. The ladder usually runs from the nearest experienced colleague, to the district or referral hospital, to the regional specialist center, to a national or international telemedicine service that accepts images and messages. Each rung answers a different question, since the first may know the patient and the context, the second may accept a transfer, the third may advise on a rare diagnosis, and the fourth may provide an opinion when no one closer is available. Learn the hours of each service, the language in which it works, and the format its clinicians need, because advice arrives faster when the request is well formed. Where the internet is intermittent, use store-and-forward messaging with a clear photograph, a short history and a specific question, and expect the answer to come hours later rather than immediately. The purpose of the chain is not to make you omniscient; it is to make sure that being at your limit never means being alone.

A protocol is a limit made portable, which is why protocol-based practice and knowing your limits are the same discipline seen from two angles. A protocol carries the accumulated experience of people who saw many more cases than you will, and it tells you where to stop, what to check and when to escalate. But a protocol can only help if you follow it, and it can only be followed if it exists in the language and the format your team actually uses. When you deviate, and there are legitimate reasons to deviate, write down the reason, the alternative you chose, and who was consulted, because an undocumented deviation is indistinguishable from an error. When a protocol is wrong for your setting, adapt it openly with a named person accountable for the adaptation rather than ignoring it quietly. The protocol is not a substitute for judgement, but it is a far better base for judgement than memory under pressure.

Peer support is the mechanism by which limits are shared rather than carried alone, and it works best when it is routine rather than exceptional. Establish a regular case discussion in which difficult cases are presented, including the ones that went badly, and protect the time for it even when the clinic is busy. A mistake reviewed without blame is not a mistake excused; it is a mistake converted into knowledge that the whole team can use. The person presenting should be the person involved, and the discussion should move from what happened, to what the system allowed, to what will change. Confidential incident reporting that carries no punishment for honesty catches the near misses that never reached a patient, and near misses are the cheapest lessons available. If the only time a complication is discussed is when someone is being disciplined, nobody will ever report the next one.

When you have crossed your own limit, the response has a sequence, and the order matters. First, secure the patient, because the immediate clinical problem outranks your own discomfort. Then disclose to the patient and the family what happened, in plain language and without excuses, and answer their questions as fully as you can. Then write the record while it is fresh, including the times, the observations, the actions, the consultations and the outcome, because a record written a week later is worth much less. Then report the event to your supervisor and, where required, to the organization and the authorities, even when the patient came to no harm. Then take part in the review and accept the changes it produces, because the point of the exercise is to protect the next patient. Concealment is the one response that converts a single clinical event into a permanent professional one.

Humility is not a mood but a daily practice, and it consists largely of asking one question before acting. What am I missing, and who would know? The question is short enough to ask before every significant decision and specific enough to change the answer. Build pauses into the work where the question can actually be asked, including a brief before a procedure, a moment before a discharge, and a check before a transfer. Ask it of the least senior person in the room as well as the most senior, because the person holding the torch or mixing the drug often sees what the operator does not. The clinician who asks the question out loud teaches everyone present to ask it too, and that teaching may matter more than the answer received. Humility is not the absence of confidence; it is confidence that can tolerate being corrected.

Your limits should be written down where the whole team and the community can see them, because an unspoken limit gets tested by every emergency that arrives. Post the list of services the clinic provides, the services it does not provide, the days and hours it can provide them, and the arrangements for what it cannot. Then explain the same list to the community leaders, the traditional healers and the community health workers, so that the expectation matches the reality before a crisis rather than during one. Saying no is only acceptable when it is accompanied by an alternative, and the alternative is usually a plan describing what will be done here, what will be done there, who will decide, and how the patient will travel. Refusing to attempt something beyond the clinic is not the same as abandoning the patient, and the difference is visible in whether a plan exists. A clinic that says no clearly and stays involved keeps the community's trust; a clinic that says yes and fails loses it.

The transfer itself has a logistics and a documentation that determine whether the limit became a death. Stabilize before departure, because the most dangerous hour of any journey is the first, and a patient who is deteriorating in the clinic will almost certainly deteriorate faster on the road. Treat the reversible threats first, including the hypoglycemia, the dehydration, the seizures, the fever, the pain, and the hemorrhage that can be controlled with pressure. In severe malaria in a child, for example, the World Health Organization recommends a pre-referral dose of rectal artesunate to buy time for the journey, and the exact formulation, dose and eligibility differ between guidance versions, so verify the current recommendation before you give it. Send a written summary with the patient, containing the history, the examination findings, the treatment given with times, the results that exist and the question you are asking. Send an escort who knows the patient, and make sure the receiving facility knows the patient is coming.

Documentation is the nurse's memory, the patient's continuity and the clinician's protection, and it deserves to be treated as clinical work rather than as clerical residue. A good record of a case that exceeded you contains what you observed, what you decided, what you did, what you declined to do and why, whom you consulted and when, what you advised the patient, and where the patient went next. Write the reasoning as well as the action, because a record that shows only the intervention cannot explain a decision that was correct for the setting. Sign it, time it, and keep it legible, since an illegible record protects nobody. When a patient is transferred, a copy travels with them and a copy stays in the register, so that the next clinician can reconstruct the story without guessing. The record of a limit honestly documented is what allows the system to learn; the same limit undocumented is what allows it to repeat.

The team around you has its own limits, and recognizing them is part of the same discipline. A community health worker, a traditional birth attendant, a cleaner who has become an assistant and a junior colleague all have boundaries that deserve the same honesty you ask of yourself, and none of them benefit from being flattered into a procedure they cannot perform. Teach by naming the boundary rather than by testing it, which means saying what a person may do, what they must call you for, and what nobody in this clinic does. Delegate with the same care you would want if the roles were reversed, which means the training, the supervision, the log and the escalation path. Respect the experience of staff who have worked in the community for years, because their knowledge of the place and its people is a clinical resource that no course provides. The team that shares an accurate map of its own limits is far safer than the team that assumes everyone can do everything.

The system employing you carries a duty that no individual can discharge alone, and it is fair to name that duty out loud. An organization that posts a single nurse in a remote clinic without supervision, without refresher training, without a functional referral pathway and without the authority to refuse an unsafe task has not shared the limit; it has transferred the risk to the least powerful person in the chain. Supervision should be scheduled rather than occasional, and it should include a review of the log, the complications and the difficult decisions. Continuing education should be funded and counted as working time, because competence belongs to the service rather than to the individual's spare hours. Most importantly, the organization should publicly support a clinician who declines to perform a procedure beyond their training, so that the refusal is understood as policy rather than as personal failure. A nurse who must choose between professional safety and continued employment will eventually make the wrong choice.

Across a career, the boundary moves many times, and the task is to keep the record of it honest. Early practice expands quickly, then plateaus, then partially decays, and it may contract further with age, illness or a long period away from procedures. Each of those changes should be acknowledged rather than resisted, because a limit that is denied does not disappear; it simply becomes invisible to the person who most needs to see it. The most experienced nurse in a district is not the one who can do everything but the one who knows precisely what they can do, what they cannot, and who to call for the difference. This is the promise with which this book ends: knowing your limit is not weakness but the highest form of competence, because the clinician who says this is beyond me and then stays with the patient has protected that patient twice, once by not harming them and once by not leaving them. The limit, honestly read and openly spoken, is not the edge of your usefulness but the shape of your safety.

To summarize, the recognition of your own limit is a clinical instrument as real as the thermometer, and it must be read before you act rather than after. Know the three zones of your competence, beware the second one, and distinguish the number of times you have performed a skill from your knowledge of its steps. Expand the boundary deliberately under supervision, keep a log, review it honestly, and maintain your skills with drills when the case volume is low. When a case exceeds you or the clinic, say so out loud at the time, arrange the backup you have already built, and choose transfer, temporizing or palliation over the improvisation that kills. Monitor the patient you keep, anticipate the adverse effects of what you do, and document the decisions, the consultations and the limits so that the next clinician and the next patient are safer. Humility, practiced as a question before every act, is what keeps competence honest, and honesty about the limit is the form of courage that this work actually requires. The patient is best protected by the clinician who knows what they cannot do, says it plainly, and does not walk away.

# Appendix A — Drug Formulary and Dosing: How to Read It, and What to Verify

This appendix gathers the medicines used throughout this book and speaks their doses aloud, class by class. It is a formulary in narrative form rather than a table, because a table invites copying while a sentence invites thought. For each drug it names what the drug treats, the adult and pediatric doses, the route, the frequency, the adverse effects that matter and the monitoring that keeps the patient safe. Every dose is offered as what current guidance says and not as settled truth, because regimens are revised, guidance differs between countries, and the guideline in force where you practice must be checked before anything is prescribed. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control publish the guidance this appendix follows.

Dose is never a single number that travels unchanged from one patient to the next. Weight, age, pregnancy, breastfeeding, kidney and liver function, co-infection and the indication all move the number, and the same drug may treat at one dose and prevent at another. Because a child is not a small adult and many drugs are dosed by weight bands, an accurate scale and a current weight chart are clinical instruments rather than clerical ones. Formulation matters too, because a tablet that cannot be crushed, a capsule taken with fat and a syrup measured in milliliters each demand a different instruction. Resistance redraws the map continuously, so the local guideline always outranks a remembered dose.

The antimalarials come first, and the artemisinin-based combination therapies are the backbone of treatment for uncomplicated falciparum malaria nearly everywhere. Each pairs a fast-acting artemisinin derivative with a slower partner drug that removes the residue and guards against resistance. Artemether with lumefantrine is the most widely used, and the adult dose is 4 tablets by mouth at the start, again 8 hours later, then twice a day for 2 more days, taken with food that contains fat. The pediatric dose rises from 1 tablet at 5 to less than 15 kilograms to 4 tablets above 35 kilograms. The common effects are headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting and sleep disturbance, and any dose vomited within 30 minutes is repeated.

Severe malaria is treated with artesunate given intravenously, and here a drug changes the risk of death by a measurable margin. The adult dose is 2.4 milligrams per kilogram intravenously at the start, again at 12 hours, again at 24 hours, and then once a day until the patient can swallow tablets. Children under 20 kilograms receive 3 milligrams per kilogram per dose because they clear the drug faster. The powder is dissolved in its supplied solvent and given as a slow injection over 1 to 2 minutes, because a rapid push can drop the blood pressure. Destruction of red cells after recovery can cause anemia 1 to 3 weeks later, so a blood count is repeated in follow-up and a full course of oral combination therapy always follows.

Chloroquine still has a narrow place, defined by geography rather than habit. It remains effective against Plasmodium vivax in most of the world outside Oceania and parts of Southeast Asia, and it clears the blood but never touches the dormant liver forms. The adult treatment dose is 25 milligrams of chloroquine base per kilogram over 3 days, usually 10 milligrams per kilogram on the first day, 10 on the second and 5 on the third, all by mouth. Its effects include itching, nausea, headache and blurred vision, and prolonged high doses can damage the retina permanently. Overdose causes profound low blood pressure, rhythm disturbance and cardiac arrest, so the nurse confirms the species and the local resistance pattern before the first tablet.

The dormant liver forms of Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale need a drug that reaches where the other antimalarials cannot. Primaquine is given by mouth at 0.25 to 0.5 milligrams per kilogram once a day for 14 days for radical cure, and a single low dose of 0.25 milligrams per kilogram kills the gametocytes of falciparum malaria. Tafenoquine is given as a single 300 milligram dose by mouth in adults, and one dose removes the adherence problem of 14 days of tablets. Both can destroy red cells dangerously in people with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency, so testing is required first, and both are avoided in pregnancy and in infants under 6 months. Both also cause nausea, abdominal pain and headache, so the nurse confirms the enzyme result and warns that the drug must not be restarted without a new test.

Three further drugs serve both treatment and prevention. Atovaquone with proguanil is taken by mouth with food as 4 adult tablets once a day for 3 days to treat uncomplicated malaria, with weight bands from 1 tablet at 11 kilograms to 4 tablets above 40 kilograms, while prevention uses 1 tablet daily from 1 to 2 days before exposure until 7 days after leaving. Mefloquine is taken at 250 milligrams once a week for prevention, starting 1 to 2 weeks before travel, and it is not used to treat an established infection. It can cause vivid dreams, insomnia, anxiety, depression and rarely psychosis, and it is avoided in people with epilepsy or psychiatric illness. Doxycycline is taken at 100 milligrams once a day by mouth for prevention, continuing for 4 weeks after leaving, and it causes sensitivity to sunlight and irritation of the esophagus, so it is taken with a full glass of water.

The antileishmanial drugs treat a parasite that hides inside the cells of the immune system, and the choice depends on the form of the disease, the country and what is in stock. Liposomal amphotericin B is preferred for visceral leishmaniasis in many programs, given at 3 milligrams per kilogram intravenously on days 1, 3, 5 and 7, while some national guidelines use a single 10 milligram per kilogram dose. The conventional deoxycholate form is given at 0.5 to 1 milligram per kilogram once a day intravenously over several hours, and it is much more likely to damage the kidneys and to cause fever, chills and muscle pain. The nurse follows the creatinine, the potassium and the magnesium and watches the fluid balance closely. Amphotericin B also treats severe histoplasmosis and cryptococcal disease, so the same monitoring discipline serves several chapters.

Miltefosine is the only oral antileishmanial in common use, given at 2.5 milligrams per kilogram per day by mouth in 2 or 3 divided doses for 28 days, with a maximum of 150 milligrams per day. It is teratogenic, so it is never given in pregnancy, and women of childbearing age must use effective contraception. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and a rise in creatinine are common, and the drug is taken with food to reduce the stomach upset. Sodium stibogluconate is given at 20 milligrams of antimony per kilogram per day intravenously or intramuscularly for 20 to 28 days, and it can disturb the heart rhythm, inflame the pancreas and injure the liver and kidneys. Paromomycin is given at 15 milligrams per kilogram per day intramuscularly for 21 days in some regions, and the electrocardiogram, the pancreatic enzymes, the liver enzymes, the renal function and the hearing are checked before and during treatment.

The trypanocides are few, old and difficult. Benznidazole is the first choice for Chagas disease in most settings and is given by mouth at 5 to 7 milligrams per kilogram per day in 2 divided doses for 60 days, with food. The effects that stop treatment most often are a skin rash, which may involve the mucous membranes, and a peripheral neuropathy that begins as tingling in the hands and feet and can become permanent if the drug is continued. Nifurtimox is the alternative, given by mouth at 8 to 10 milligrams per kilogram per day in 3 or 4 divided doses for 60 to 90 days, and it more often causes loss of appetite, weight loss, nausea, insomnia and neuropathy. Blood counts fall with both drugs, so a count is checked during the course, and the nurse warns about the rash in advance because a patient who expects it reports it early.

Human African trypanosomiasis is treated according to the species and the stage, and that distinction matters more than any other decision. Pentamidine is used for the early stage of the West African form at 4 milligrams per kilogram once a day intramuscularly or intravenously for 7 to 10 days, and it can make the blood sugar fall and then rise, drop the blood pressure and injure the kidney. Suramin treats the early stage of the East African form, beginning with a test dose of 100 to 200 milligrams intravenously, followed by 1 gram on days 1, 3, 5 and 7 and then once a week for 5 weeks. Eflornithine crosses into the brain and is given at 100 milligrams per kilogram intravenously every 6 hours for 14 days alone, or at 200 milligrams per kilogram every 12 hours for 7 days with nifurtimox, and it can suppress the bone marrow and cause seizures. Fexinidazole is an oral drug for the late stage of the West African form, given at 1.8 grams once a day for 10 days in adults above 35 kilograms and at lower weight-based doses in children. Confirming the stage, the species and the weight before the first dose prevents the most serious error in this family, which is treating a brain-stage infection with a drug that never reaches the brain.

The antifilarial drugs are given to whole communities as well as to individuals. Ivermectin is given by mouth as a single dose of 150 to 200 micrograms per kilogram, repeated once a year or every 6 to 12 months for lymphatic filariasis and onchocerciasis. It must not be given to a person heavily infected with Loa loa, because the rapid death of those parasites can inflame the brain and sometimes kill, and it is avoided in pregnancy and in children under 5 years or under 15 kilograms in most programs. Albendazole is given at 400 milligrams by mouth as a single dose alongside ivermectin or diethylcarbamazine in elimination programs, and diethylcarbamazine is given at 6 milligrams per kilogram per day by mouth in divided doses for 12 days. All three can produce the reaction that follows the death of the worms, with fever, itching, rash, headache, dizziness and joint pain, and this is expected, so the patient is warned and supported with fluids, rest and a simple analgesic.

The anthelmintics are among the safest medicines in this appendix, and the main risk is not the drug but the missed diagnosis.
