Albendazole is given as a single 400 milligram dose by mouth for roundworm, hookworm and whipworm infection, with 200 milligrams for children between 12 and 24 months, and mebendazole is given as 100 milligrams twice a day for 3 days, or as a single 500 milligram dose for hookworm and roundworm. Praziquantel is given at 40 milligrams per kilogram by mouth in 1 or 2 doses for schistosomiasis, at 60 milligrams per kilogram per day in 3 divided doses for 3 days for neurocysticercosis, and at 25 milligrams per kilogram 3 times a day for 2 days for food-borne trematode infections. Praziquantel can cause abdominal pain, nausea, headache, dizziness and drowsiness, so patients are advised not to drive on the day of treatment. Triclabendazole is the drug of choice for fascioliasis at 10 milligrams per kilogram by mouth once or twice, and niclosamide treats the adult tapeworms at 2 grams by mouth for adults and 50 milligrams per kilogram for children. Prolonged high-dose albendazole requires blood count and liver monitoring, and the nurse weighs the patient, checks for pregnancy and treats the whole household when the infection is a household problem.

The antiprotozoal drugs treat the intestinal and genital protozoa, and metronidazole carries the widest range of uses. Metronidazole is given by mouth at 500 milligrams 3 times a day for 7 to 10 days for giardiasis, at 750 milligrams 3 times a day for 7 to 10 days for intestinal amebiasis, at 500 milligrams every 8 hours intravenously for severe amebic colitis or liver abscess, and as a single 2 gram dose for trichomoniasis. The pediatric dose is usually 15 to 30 milligrams per kilogram per day in divided doses, depending on the indication. It causes a metallic taste, nausea and headache, and it produces a severe reaction with alcohol that includes flushing, vomiting, palpitations and low blood pressure, so alcohol must be avoided during treatment and for 3 days afterward. Tinidazole is given as a single 2 gram dose for giardiasis and trichomoniasis, or 2 grams once a day for 3 to 5 days for amebiasis, and nitazoxanide is given at 500 milligrams by mouth every 12 hours for 3 days in adults, with 100 milligrams for children 1 to 3 years old and 200 milligrams for children 4 to 11 years old.

The antibiotics recur across this book in roles far beyond their usual hospital uses, and two of them deserve special attention. Doxycycline is the treatment of choice for rickettsial disease at 100 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 7 to 14 days, for leptospirosis at 100 milligrams twice a day for 7 days and as a single 300 milligram dose for cholera, and it is also used for plague. It is generally avoided in young children, but when a serious rickettsial infection is the alternative, the risk of the infection outweighs the risk to the teeth. Azithromycin is given as a single 1 gram dose by mouth for cholera, at 500 milligrams once a day for 3 days for shigellosis and as a single dose of 20 to 30 milligrams per kilogram for yaws in children. Its main effects are nausea, abdominal pain and diarrhea, it is one of the safer antibiotics in pregnancy, and for both drugs the nurse checks the weight, the pregnancy status and the interval before the next dose.

Three more antibiotics complete the recurring set, and each has a specific niche in tropical practice. Ceftriaxone is given at 1 to 2 grams intravenously once a day in adults for severe bacterial infection, at 2 grams once a day for 7 to 14 days for typhoid fever when the organism is susceptible, and at 50 to 75 milligrams per kilogram per day in children, while a single 500 milligram intramuscular dose treats gonorrhea. Ciprofloxacin is given at 500 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 3 days for cholera and for 7 to 14 days for typhoid fever where the organism remains susceptible, and it can cause tendon pain and rupture, especially in older patients and those taking corticosteroids. Cotrimoxazole, the combination of trimethoprim and sulfamethoxazole, is given at 960 milligrams twice a day by mouth for common bacterial infections, at weight-based doses for childhood pneumonia and at 960 milligrams once a day to prevent opportunistic infection in people with HIV infection. It can cause rash, bone marrow suppression and a dangerous rise in potassium, so the patient is taught to report a rash at once. For all three the nurse confirms the indication, the weight, the renal function and the local resistance pattern before the first dose.

The antituberculous drugs are always used in combination, because a single drug selects resistance within weeks, and the standard regimen for drug-susceptible tuberculosis begins with 2 months of isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol, followed by 4 months of isoniazid and rifampicin. Isoniazid is given at 5 milligrams per kilogram per day in adults, usually 300 milligrams, and at 10 to 15 milligrams per kilogram per day in children, and it can cause a peripheral neuropathy that is prevented with pyridoxine, as well as liver injury. Rifampicin is given at 10 milligrams per kilogram per day in adults, usually 600 milligrams, and at 15 milligrams per kilogram in children, and it turns urine, sweat and tears orange, injures the liver and interferes with many other drugs, including antiretroviral therapy for HIV infection. Pyrazinamide is given at 20 to 25 milligrams per kilogram per day in adults and 30 to 40 milligrams per kilogram in children, and it causes liver injury, joint pain and a rise in uric acid, while ethambutol at 15 to 20 milligrams per kilogram per day can damage the optic nerve, so vision is checked before treatment. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis requires a longer regimen with second-line drugs such as bedaquiline, linezolid and clofazimine, and the nurse who watches adherence and side effects is as important to the outcome as the prescription itself.

The antifungals in this book treat the deep mycoses that follow inhalation or implantation of a fungus, and the three that recur are itraconazole, ketoconazole and amphotericin B. Itraconazole is given by mouth at 200 milligrams once or twice a day for 3 months or longer for mild to moderate histoplasmosis and paracoccidioidomycosis, and the capsule is taken with food while the liquid preparation is taken on an empty stomach. It can injure the liver and the heart and it interacts with a long list of medicines, and where the laboratory can measure the level of the drug in the blood, that level guides the dose. Ketoconazole is given at 200 to 400 milligrams by mouth once a day for prolonged periods in some settings, but it can injure the liver, suppress the adrenal glands and disturb the hormones, so it has largely been replaced. Amphotericin B is given intravenously at 0.5 to 1.5 milligrams per kilogram once a day, or as a liposomal preparation at 3 to 5 milligrams per kilogram once a day, and it causes fever, chills, kidney injury and losses of potassium and magnesium. The nurse checks the liver enzymes, the renal function, the electrolytes and the drug interactions, and teaches the patient how and when to take each formulation.

Antivenom is unlike every other medicine here, because the dose is not calculated from the weight of the patient but from the amount of venom that must be neutralized. The dose is the same for a child and an adult, the drug is given intravenously for systemic envenomation and never intramuscularly, and the number of vials depends on the product, the species and the severity of the poisoning. Because antivenoms differ between regions and manufacturers, the nurse reads the label of the product in hand, and the national protocol and the poison center are consulted whenever there is doubt. The most feared reactions are immediate anaphylaxis and a delayed serum sickness with fever, rash and joint pain, so the patient is watched closely during the infusion, with adrenaline, oxygen and resuscitation equipment at the bedside. The antivenom is only one part of care, because the airway, the breathing, the circulation, the coagulation and the wound all need attention at the same time, and the nurse records the time of the bite, the product and lot and every reaction.

The unglamorous parts of a formulary decide whether a drug ever reaches the patient. Most of these medicines need protection from heat, light and moisture, and some need a cold chain verified daily with a thermometer rather than assumed from the presence of a refrigerator. Stock is rotated so that the earliest expiry is used first, and a drug that is expired, discolored or unlabeled is not a drug, whatever the box says. Counterfeit and substandard medicines are a real danger in many settings, and the nurse protects patients by ordering through the national supply system, checking packaging and batch numbers and reporting anything that seems wrong. The formulation matters in the field as much as in the prescription, because a tablet that cannot be divided accurately, a syrup without a measuring cup and an injectable without the correct diluent each turn a correct dose into an incorrect one. A stock-out is a clinical event rather than an administrative one, and it must be anticipated, reported and planned for with an alternative regimen in advance.

Monitoring is where the nurse turns a prescription into safe care, and it begins before the first dose with the weight, the allergies, the pregnancy and breastfeeding status, the renal and liver function and the exact indication. The baseline tests differ by drug, but the common set includes the blood count, the glucose, the creatinine, the liver enzymes and the electrolytes, and for some drugs an electrocardiogram or a vision check. During treatment the nurse watches for the specific adverse effect each drug is known to cause, such as the rash of benznidazole, the neuropathy of the trypanocides, the low blood sugar of pentamidine, the visual change of ethambutol, the hearing loss of the aminoglycosides and the kidney injury of amphotericin B. Every dose is verified against the current national guideline and the product label, and high-risk doses are calculated independently by two people, with the units written out in full before the arithmetic is done. The nurse documents the dose, the route, the time, the lot number and any reaction, teaches the patient what to expect and what to report, and arranges the follow-up test before the patient leaves. Where treatment is observed directly, the person who observes the dose records it honestly, because a signature that does not reflect a swallowed tablet is worse than no record at all.

To summarize, this appendix is meant to be used with your ears and your judgment rather than with your memory alone, because a dose recalled without its guideline is a dose that can harm. Every figure spoken here is what the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control have published as current guidance, and every one is subject to revision as resistance shifts and new evidence arrives. The habit that keeps patients safe is to confirm the indication, weigh the patient, check the allergy, pregnancy and organ function, read the current national guideline, write the units in full and verify the calculation before the drug is given. The nurse who does that, who monitors the effect each drug is known to cause, who warns the patient about the rash or the dizziness or the orange urine and who documents the lot and the reaction is doing the work that turns a formulary into medicine. Guidance differs between countries and is revised without announcement, so a dose that was correct last year may be wrong today.

# Appendix B — Incubation Periods and Clinical Decision Points

An incubation period is the time between the moment a pathogen enters the body and the moment the first symptom appears. In tropical medicine it is the most useful piece of arithmetic you have, because it turns a vague travel history into a probability statement. Fever 3 days after leaving a malarious region argues against malaria and toward dengue, chikungunya, influenza, cholera, shigellosis, or a rickettsial infection. Fever 12 days after leaving moves malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, acute HIV infection, and the hepatitis viruses to the front. This appendix walks through the windows by length, then sets out the decision points where that arithmetic changes practice.

Two clocks run at once in every fever, and confusing them is the commonest error in this reasoning. The first measures days since exposure, which is what an incubation period describes; the second measures days of illness, which is what the chart records. When a patient arrives on the fifth day of fever, work backward to an exposure window before comparing that illness with any range. Incubation periods are ranges, not appointments, and they shift with inoculum size, route of entry, immune status, prior vaccination, and chemoprophylaxis. Treat every number here as a distribution with a long tail.

The first group is the very short, less than 7 days, and it dominates when illness begins soon after exposure. Dengue appears 4 to 10 days after the bite, usually 5 to 7, and chikungunya appears after 3 to 7 days, with a range of 1 to 12. Both are carried by Aedes mosquitoes, which bite in daylight, so ask about daytime biting in towns and cities. Dengue opens with abrupt fever, headache, eye pain, muscle and joint pain, and often a rash as the fever falls. Chikungunya is set apart by disabling joint pain that can persist for months, and neither disease has a rapid cure, so the value of this window lies in the monitoring it triggers.

Influenza appears 1 to 4 days after exposure, usually 2 days, and in the tropics it is easily mistaken for dengue. Cholera is faster, appearing a few hours to 5 days later, usually 1 to 2 days, with profuse painless watery diarrhea and rapid dehydration rather than fever. Shigellosis follows 1 to 3 days after exposure and causes fever, cramps, tenesmus, and bloody diarrhea. Rickettsial infections appear 2 to 14 days later, usually about 5 to 7 days, with fever, headache, and muscle aches, and the clue is an eschar at the site of a tick, mite, or flea bite. These illnesses can become critical before any laboratory result returns, so rehydration begins on the clinical picture.

What the short windows mean diagnostically is that they serve as an exclusion tool as much as a diagnostic one. A fever beginning within 7 days of exposure cannot be explained by the long-incubation diseases unless an older second exposure exists. The examination then turns to specific findings: the rash and falling platelet count of dengue, the dehydration of cholera, the blood in the stool of shigellosis, and the eschar of rickettsial disease. A single negative test is least reassuring here, because organism counts rise and fall across the first days and a specimen taken too early is often falsely negative. Repeat sampling and paired serology are the answers, so record every date and time precisely.

The second group covers 1 to 3 weeks, and it is the busiest window in tropical medicine. Malaria sits at its center, and the incubation period of Plasmodium falciparum, the species responsible for the most severe form of malaria, is 7 to 30 days, usually 10 to 15. Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale can relapse weeks or months after a bite, because dormant liver forms reactivate, which is why malaria can appear long after a patient leaves an endemic area. No clinical feature reliably separates malaria from the other causes of fever in this window. The World Health Organization therefore advises parasitological testing for every febrile patient with a compatible exposure, and repeat testing when the first result is negative.

Typhoid fever appears 6 to 30 days after exposure, usually 7 to 14, and it unfolds in steps. Fever climbs through the first week, abdominal pain and a faint rash follow in the second, and untreated cases may bleed or perforate the bowel in the third. Leptospirosis appears after 5 to 14 days, with a range of 2 to 30, and often begins with sudden fever, severe headache, calf muscle pain, and red eyes, progressing in severe cases to jaundice, kidney injury, and bleeding. Both diseases are diagnosed by tests that perform poorly early in the illness, so ask about flooded streets, rodent contact, freshwater swimming, and unpasteurized dairy. When leptospirosis is suspected with jaundice and kidney injury, treatment should not wait for confirmation.

Hepatitis A has an incubation period of 15 to 50 days, averaging about 28, and hepatitis E runs 15 to 60 days, averaging about 40. Both spread by the fecal-oral route and can cause jaundice, dark urine, and fatigue, and though both are usually self-limited, hepatitis E is dangerous in pregnancy. Acute HIV infection appears 10 to 28 days after exposure and often looks like a mononucleosis-like illness with fever, sore throat, rash, and enlarged lymph nodes, so test for HIV whenever the window and the syndrome fit. Brucellosis appears 5 days to 6 months later, usually 2 to 4 weeks, with undulant fever and joint pain after livestock contact or unpasteurized milk. Q fever appears after 9 to 39 days, and yaws appears after 9 to 90 days as a painless skin lesion.

The middle window is where most diagnostic confusion lives, because many diseases share the same 1 to 3 week interval and the same nonspecific fever. The answer is not to test everything at once but to let the exposure history and the pace of illness order the possibilities. A patient with a slow pulse and abdominal symptoms after travel differs from one with jaundice, red eyes, and muscle pain after a flood. Serology depends on the immune response rather than the organism, so testing too early produces false negatives. This is the group where a repeat sample 2 to 4 weeks later is most valuable.

The third group is measured in months, and it shifts the work from acute resuscitation to chronic assessment and public health action. Active pulmonary tuberculosis usually emerges within the first 2 years of infection, yet latent infection can reactivate decades later when immunity falls, so age, HIV infection, diabetes, and steroid use dominate the risk assessment. Cough for more than 2 weeks, fever, night sweats, and weight loss suggest tuberculosis, but their absence does not exclude it. Because transmission is airborne, the diagnosis triggers isolation and notification before it triggers treatment. Screening household contacts and offering preventive therapy belong to the same decision, and the regimen depends on current World Health Organization guidance.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis appears weeks to months after the bite of an infected sand fly, while visceral leishmaniasis emerges after 2 to 8 months with prolonged fever, weight loss, an enlarged spleen and liver, and suppression of the bone marrow. Lymphatic filariasis may produce no swelling for many months or years, so the parasite can be present long before the limb changes, and onchocerciasis takes 1 to 3 years before skin and eye changes appear. Once symptoms begin, rabies is almost universally fatal, so its incubation period of 1 to 3 months, sometimes longer, is a window for prophylaxis rather than a waiting game. Any bite from a suspect animal needs wound washing and immediate assessment for vaccination and, for high-risk exposures, immune globulin.

Schistosomiasis causes an acute illness 2 to 8 weeks after exposure to contaminated freshwater, with fever, cough, abdominal pain, and an enlarged liver and spleen, and the chronic form develops over months to years as eggs lodge in the bladder, bowel, or liver. Amoebic liver abscess usually appears weeks to months after infection, with fever and right upper quadrant pain, and it may occur without preceding diarrhea. Hepatitis B appears 45 to 180 days after exposure, averaging about 90 days, and may pass unnoticed into chronic infection. Chagas disease begins 1 to 2 weeks after the bite of an infected triatomine bug and then persists silently for decades before causing heart failure or digestive dilation. Echinococcosis develops over years, with cysts found incidentally or when they cause pain, so a migrant who has not traveled for 20 years can still carry these infections.

The fourth group is the very long, meaning conditions that can appear decades after exposure. Leprosy has an incubation period commonly given as 2 to 20 years, averaging about 5 to 8 years, and it begins insidiously with a skin patch that has lost sensation. Strongyloidiasis can persist for decades through autoinfection, in which larvae mature within the same host without leaving, and it may cause only intermittent symptoms until immunity is suppressed. Corticosteroids, cancer chemotherapy, or transplantation can then convert a quiet infection into disseminated strongyloidiasis with overwhelming sepsis, which is why screening before starting corticosteroids is a standard safety step for patients who have lived in endemic areas. A negative recent travel history is never a reason to stop asking where a patient was born and raised.

The diagnostic meaning of the long windows is that today's illness may be the first evidence of an infection acquired years ago, so the search widens rather than stops. Serology is strongest here, because the immune response has had time to develop, but a positive result may reflect past exposure rather than active disease. Imaging carries more weight: chest radiography for tuberculosis, ultrasound for liver abscess and echinococcosis, and echocardiography for Chagas heart disease. Public health follow-up becomes part of the clinical plan, because tuberculosis, leprosy, and hepatitis B require notification and contact investigation. The nurse often reconstructs the timeline from old documents and migration records, so write down the country, the years of residence, and the date of arrival.

The first decision point is when to treat empirically, before a diagnosis is confirmed. Empirical treatment is justified when the likely disease is dangerous and the available test is slow, insensitive, or absent, and when waiting carries more risk than the drug. Familiar examples include suspected severe malaria, cholera with severe dehydration, suspected bacterial meningitis, and suspected rickettsial infection with an eschar. Obtain the specimens you can obtain quickly, then start treatment without letting sampling delay the first dose. The agent must follow current World Health Organization guidance or the equivalent national guidance, and every dose must be verified against the patient's weight, kidney and liver function, allergies, and pregnancy status before it is given.

The second decision point is when to refer urgently, and in tropical medicine the answer is often sooner than expected. Severe malaria with impaired consciousness, convulsions, difficulty breathing, dark urine, or low blood glucose needs immediate parenteral treatment and monitoring. Dengue with warning signs needs admission even when the patient looks stable. Suspected rabies, suspected viral hemorrhagic fever, tetanus, meningococcal infection, snakebite with coagulopathy, and any patient in shock or respiratory failure also belong here. Referral is not a transfer of responsibility but a clinical intervention, so stabilize the patient, document what has been given, and speak directly to the receiving team before the journey begins.

The third decision point is when to isolate, which protects the patient and the health workers alike. Airborne precautions are required for suspected pulmonary tuberculosis, measles, and varicella, and for some viral hemorrhagic fevers. Contact precautions, with gowns, gloves, and careful hand hygiene, are required for cholera, shigellosis, and other enteric infections, and for infected wounds that shed organisms. Suspected viral hemorrhagic fever usually requires contact and droplet precautions together, and personal protective equipment must be put on and removed with a trained observer watching every step. Clean water, safe waste disposal, and hand hygiene stop most transmission in a ward, and suspected notifiable disease is reported early rather than after confirmation.

The fourth decision point is the timing of repeated malaria films, and it is the most contested arithmetic in tropical fever. A single negative blood film does not exclude malaria, because parasite density fluctuates and can fall below detection for hours at a time. Guidance from the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention advises repeating thick and thin films every 12 to 24 hours for a total of 48 to 72 hours, usually three sets. A rapid diagnostic test can be used alongside microscopy, but it may remain positive for weeks after a treated infection, and a polymerase chain reaction test is more sensitive but is not available everywhere. The nursing contribution is decisive: label every specimen with the exact time, make sure the second and third films are actually drawn, and alert the clinician if the patient deteriorates before the series is complete.

The fifth decision point is the day of illness at which dengue turns critical. The critical phase begins as the fever falls, usually between day 3 and day 7 of illness and most often around day 4 to day 6, and it lasts about 24 to 48 hours. This is when plasma leakage raises the hematocrit, lowers the blood pressure, and, without careful fluid management, causes shock. The paradox is that the patient often feels better as the temperature drops, so watch for persistent vomiting, severe abdominal pain, bleeding, black stools, restlessness, and cold clammy skin. The nursing plan is serial monitoring of vital signs, urine output, hematocrit, and platelet count, with fluids adjusted to the leakage and verified for each patient against current World Health Organization guidance.

The logistics of this appendix matter as much as its biology, because a window is useful only if the specimen is collected and delivered correctly. Draw blood films for malaria before treatment begins and send them without delay, and draw blood cultures before antibiotics whenever that does not delay treatment. Serology usually needs paired samples, an acute specimen in the first week and a convalescent specimen 2 to 4 weeks later, and both must be stored so that the pair can be tested together. Cold chain failures, mislabeled tubes, and specimens left overnight in a hot vehicle commonly make a result uninterpretable, and the nurse who checks the label and the timing prevents most of them. Some diseases must be reported to a public health authority at the moment of suspicion, and when a result is delayed the clinical plan still moves forward.

Monitoring is where these windows become concrete nursing work. For any febrile illness in the short group, record temperature, pulse, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and level of consciousness at a defined interval, and record urine output, because urine is the most honest measure of perfusion. In dengue, track the hematocrit and the platelet count and watch the trend rather than a single value, since a rising hematocrit with a falling platelet count signals leakage. In severe malaria, check the blood glucose at least every 4 to 6 hours, because hypoglycemia is common and rapidly reversible, and watch for convulsions, anemia, and difficulty breathing. In cholera and other severe diarrheal disease, count the stools or weigh them, replace the losses, and reassess continuously, and write every observation down with its time.

Adverse effects deserve the same attention as the diseases, because treatment can harm a patient who is already fragile. Doxycycline causes nausea and photosensitivity and is generally avoided in pregnancy and in young children for most indications, though the balance changes in serious rickettsial disease. Isoniazid can injure the liver and cause peripheral neuropathy, which is why pyridoxine is often given alongside it, and rifampin turns urine orange and interacts with many other drugs, including antiretroviral therapy and hormonal contraception. Ethambutol can damage the optic nerve, so vision is assessed before treatment and monitored during it. Praziquantel and the drugs used against filarial infections can provoke fever, rash, and swelling as the parasites die, so every one of these effects is a reason to warn the patient and schedule follow-up.

The nursing role across all of these windows is one of construction, surveillance, and translation. The nurse builds the timeline by asking about travel, residence, freshwater contact, animal exposure, sexual history, injections, and blood transfusion, and by writing every date down. The nurse watches for the change that the window predicts, whether that is the fall in temperature that opens the dengue critical phase or the third negative film that lets malaria be set aside. The nurse translates the plan for the patient and the family, explaining why a second blood test is needed next week and why a medicine that turns urine orange is still the right one. The nurse also holds the safety net by verifying the dose before it is given, and often is the only person who recognizes that a former resident of an endemic area with eosinophilia and steroid exposure needs screening for strongyloidiasis.

The regimens described in this appendix are drawn from current guidance of the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control, and that guidance is revised as resistance patterns and evidence change. A dose that is correct in one country may be wrong in another, and drug names, formulations, and pediatric schedules differ between national programs. Before you prescribe or administer anything described here, read the current guideline for your setting and confirm the dose, the route, the frequency, and the duration against the patient in front of you. Check the weight, kidney and liver function, allergies, and pregnancy status, and when two clinicians independently calculate the same dose, the chance of arithmetic error falls sharply. The responsibility for the dose you give rests with the person who gives it.

To summarize, the incubation period is a filter and not a verdict, because it tells you which diseases are possible in the time you have measured. Illness within 7 days of exposure points to dengue, chikungunya, influenza, cholera, shigellosis, and rickettsial disease, and it demands rapid assessment of hydration, bleeding, and shock. Illness at 1 to 3 weeks points to malaria, typhoid, leptospirosis, hepatitis A and E, acute HIV infection, brucellosis, Q fever, and yaws, and it requires that malaria be excluded with repeated films over 48 to 72 hours. Illness measured in months points to tuberculosis, leishmaniasis, filarial infection, rabies, schistosomiasis, amoebic liver abscess, hepatitis B, Chagas disease, and echinococcosis, and it shifts the work toward serology, imaging, notification, and contact investigation. Decades later, leprosy and strongyloidiasis can still appear, so the residence history matters as much as the travel history. Know the window, verify the dose against current guidance, monitor the trend rather than the single number, and let the timeline choose the next test.

# Appendix C — Case Studies with Nursing Management Plans

This appendix turns the substance of the earlier chapters into ten composite cases, each built from patterns that advanced practice nurses meet in tropical settings rather than from any single person's record. Every case here is a composite, no case describes a real patient, and no identifying detail belongs to anyone living or dead. Each case follows the same shape, moving from a short narrative to the nursing management, then to the priority nursing problem, the monitoring that matters, and the point at which the nurse must escalate. Doses appear throughout, because a tropical medicine course without them is useless, but every dose is spoken as current guidance and never as settled truth. Regimens are revised, national programs adapt them differently, and the current guideline must be checked before anything is prescribed, so treat each number as a prompt to verify rather than as a substitute for the source.

Before the first case, fix the habits that govern all of them. Confirm the patient's weight in kilograms, because most pediatric doses are calculated per kilogram and a weight guessed from age is a weight guessed wrong. Write the calculation down, have a second nurse repeat it independently, and compare the result with the current guideline rather than with memory. Check that the unit on the label matches the unit you intended, because a concentrated solution can turn a correct number into a tenfold error. Recheck kidney and liver function when it is available, since failing organs change the interval as much as the dose. Logistics belong to the plan as much as the drug does, so each case names what the clinic must actually stock, who can transport a deteriorating patient, whether screened blood is available, and whether the family can return for follow up. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control publish revisions on different schedules, and the national program where you work usually has the last word.

A 3 year old child arrives at a district clinic with 3 days of fever, repeated vomiting, and a convulsion seen at home. The child is drowsy, does not localize pain, breathes deeply, and has cool hands with slow capillary refill. The family returned 2 weeks ago from a region where malaria is transmitted all year, and the blood film shows Plasmodium falciparum, the species responsible for the most severe form of malaria, at high density. The bedside glucose is dangerously low, so this is severe malaria with hypoglycemia and acidosis, and the risk is greatest in the first hour.

Give 5 milliliters per kilogram of 10 per cent dextrose intravenously at once, then run a continuous infusion and recheck the glucose after 30 minutes, because one bolus is often not enough in a child whose parasites consume glucose. Current guidance from the World Health Organization lists intravenous artesunate as the treatment of choice, at 3 milligrams per kilogram per dose below 20 kilograms and 2.4 milligrams per kilogram per dose above that weight, given at the start, at 12 hours, at 24 hours, and then daily. Verify that dose against the national guideline and have a second nurse repeat the calculation independently, because a reconstituted powder invites a dilution error. Intramuscular artemether and intravenous quinine are the listed alternatives, and their regimens must be read at the time rather than recalled. Continue the drug intravenously until the child can swallow, then finish a full course of artemisinin-based combination therapy.

The priority nursing problem is impaired glucose regulation with impaired consciousness, and the monitoring that matters is glucose, breathing pattern, urine output, and level of consciousness. Measure glucose every 30 minutes until it is stable and then every hour, and record deep breathing as a sign of acidosis rather than as anxiety. Inspect the intravenous site often, because extravasation is easy to miss on a dark limb. Escalate at once for another convulsion, a glucose that falls again after a bolus, deepening breathing, or no urine within 6 hours, and arrange referral for transfusion if pallor deepens or the hemoglobin falls below the threshold in the national guideline.

A 34 year old man attends a travel clinic 10 days after returning from 3 weeks in West Africa with fever, headache, and muscle aches and no localizing symptom. He took no chemoprophylaxis and recalls mosquito bites despite using repellent. His temperature is 38.9 degrees Celsius and his pulse is 104 beats per minute, and the examination is unremarkable apart from mild dehydration. Two thick and thin blood films and a rapid diagnostic test are reported as negative for malaria parasites. He asks whether he can go home with paracetamol and return if he feels worse.

A single negative film does not exclude malaria, because the parasite density can be low, the reading can fail, and some parasites no longer make the protein that a rapid diagnostic test detects. Current guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention asks that films be repeated every 12 to 24 hours for a total of 3 sets over 48 to 72 hours before malaria is set aside, and that severe illness still be examined by microscopy after a negative rapid test. The differential includes dengue, typhoid, leptospirosis, rickettsial infection, acute HIV, and hepatitis, and blood cultures should be drawn before any antibiotic is given. Avoid empirical antibiotics in a well patient with fever, because they blur the diagnosis and select for resistance. Give fluids by mouth, treat the fever with paracetamol, and record the full exposure and sexual history.

The priority nursing problem is risk of missed or delayed diagnosis, and the monitoring that matters is the temperature curve, the pulse pressure, the urine output, and any new rash, bleeding, confusion, or breathlessness. Explain the plan in plain words and give it in writing, because a traveler who feels well may not return. Make the appointment for the second film before he leaves and record a telephone number for the family. Escalate immediately for confusion, bleeding gums, dark urine, a falling platelet count, or shock, and arrange admission rather than another outpatient visit. Fever in a returning traveler is malaria until repeated films prove otherwise.

A 27 year old woman presents on the fifth day of illness with fever that has just broken, severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, and a rash over the trunk and limbs. Her platelet count has fallen from 140,000 to 60,000 per microliter over 2 days, and her hematocrit has risen by 18 per cent above her baseline. She is restless, her hands and feet are cool, and her pulse pressure has narrowed. There is no bleeding and no breathlessness yet. This is dengue entering the critical phase, which usually begins as the temperature falls and lasts 24 to 48 hours.

The critical phase is a problem of leaky capillaries, so plasma escapes into the chest, the abdomen, and the tissues while the blood cells stay behind, and a rising hematocrit with a falling platelet count is the signature. Current guidance from the World Health Organization uses crystalloid at 5 to 10 milliliters per kilogram per hour for the first 24 to 48 hours in a patient who can still drink, adjusted by the hematocrit and the urine output rather than by the platelet count alone. Give paracetamol for pain, never give nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or aspirin, and never give an intramuscular injection when the platelets are low. Monitor the hematocrit, the vital signs, the pulse pressure, the urine output, and the signs of fluid overload every hour. Fluid algorithms differ between the World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and national programs, so verify the volume and the rate against the guideline in use.

The priority nursing problem is risk of shock from plasma leakage with possible bleeding, and the narrowest monitoring is the pulse pressure, the hematocrit, and the urine output. Measure the hematocrit every 4 to 6 hours during the critical phase and keep an accurate fluid balance. Watch for restlessness, cold extremities, and a falling pulse pressure, which are the earliest signs of compensated shock. Escalate at once for shock, for a hematocrit that falls with bleeding, for a hematocrit that stays high with a fast pulse, or for breathlessness with a rising fluid level. Recovery begins with reabsorption, so expect a falling hematocrit with a good urine output and reduce the fluid rather than continue it.

A 41 year old farmer is brought to a rural health center 2 hours after a bite on the ankle from a snake he describes as brown with a triangular head. The ankle is swollen and bleeding from the fang marks, and he has vomited twice. A bedside whole blood clotting test shows that the blood has not clotted after 20 minutes. His blood pressure is 96 over 60 millimeters of mercury and his pulse is 118 beats per minute. This is a viper bite with coagulopathy, and the systemic effects may worsen over the next several hours.

The coagulopathy comes from venom that consumes clotting factors, so the blood cannot clot and the patient bleeds from the wound, the gums, the gut, and the intravenous sites. Current guidance from the World Health Organization describes antivenom as the only treatment that reverses this, and the initial dose varies by region and by species, so it must be read from the national guideline and never recalled from memory. Give the antivenom intravenously over about 1 hour, diluted as the product directs, with epinephrine and airway equipment at the bedside, because anaphylaxis is common and a skin test does not predict it. Verify the product and the dose against the guideline with a second nurse, and record the batch number and the time. Avoid incision, suction, tourniquets, and ice, and never give the antivenom intramuscularly.

The priority nursing problem is risk of hemorrhage and of anaphylaxis, and the monitoring that matters is the wound, the gums and venipuncture sites, the vital signs, the urine output, and the clotting test repeated every 6 hours. Keep the limb still and at the level of the heart, and avoid intramuscular injections for tetanus prevention and for analgesia. Treat pain with paracetamol, because nonsteroidal drugs add to the bleeding risk. Escalate for continued bleeding, a clotting time that stays prolonged, a falling blood pressure, breathlessness, or swelling that spreads up the limb within hours, and arrange transfer to a facility that stocks antivenom and screened blood.

A 24 year old woman who is 22 weeks pregnant presents with 3 days of fever, chills, and headache, and a blood film shows Plasmodium falciparum, the parasite of severe malaria, at a moderate density with no criterion of severity. She is alert, she is not vomiting, and her fetus is moving normally. She is anemic, with a hemoglobin of 8.4 grams per deciliter, and she has had no antenatal care until now. She lives in a district where malaria is transmitted throughout the year. This is uncomplicated falciparum malaria in the second trimester, and the risk is that placental infection will cause anemia, poor fetal growth, and preterm delivery.

Current guidance from the World Health Organization treats uncomplicated falciparum malaria in the second trimester with an artemisinin-based combination therapy given by mouth for 3 days, and artemether with lumefantrine is the combination most widely used, taken twice a day with food that contains fat. Verify the exact product and the weight band against the national guideline, have a second nurse check the tablet count, and observe the first dose so that vomiting is recognized and the dose repeated. Add folic acid and iron for the anemia, treat the fever with paracetamol, and recheck the hemoglobin after treatment. If any criterion of severity appears, change to intravenous artesunate at once, because parenteral artesunate is recommended in every trimester of severe disease. Never give primaquine or tafenoquine during pregnancy.

The priority nursing problem is risk of maternal anemia and fetal compromise, and the monitoring that matters is the temperature, the hemoglobin, the fetal heart rate, and the signs of preterm labor. Count fetal movements and listen to the fetal heart at every visit, and record any uterine activity. Escalate for vomiting that prevents oral treatment, a falling hemoglobin, vaginal bleeding, contractions, reduced fetal movement, or any criterion of severe malaria, and involve the maternity team early. Arrange follow up films and a repeat hemoglobin, and give an insecticide-treated bed net with instruction on its use.

A 36 year old man with HIV and a helper T cell count of 60 cells per microliter begins treatment for pulmonary tuberculosis, and antiretroviral therapy is added 2 weeks later. He improves at first, then in the third week he develops high fever, painful swollen lymph nodes in the neck, and increasing breathlessness. His chest radiograph shows worsening shadowing, and his sputum is again negative for acid-fast bacilli. He is alert and his blood pressure is stable. This deterioration during immune recovery is the pattern of the immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome rather than of treatment failure.

The syndrome arises when recovering immunity recognizes a heavy load of mycobacterial antigen and mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response, so the patient worsens as the immune system improves. Current guidance from the World Health Organization and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is to continue both treatments and to treat the inflammation rather than to stop the drugs, and corticosteroids are used for severe paradoxical reactions under a defined regimen and taper. Verify the dose and the taper against the current guideline, and exclude an alternative explanation such as drug resistance, a new infection, or a drug reaction before accepting the diagnosis. Monitor the liver enzymes, because tuberculosis drugs and antiretroviral drugs both stress the liver, and watch for a rash from the antiretroviral drug. Never stop antiretroviral therapy without senior advice.

The priority nursing problem is impaired gas exchange with risk of airway obstruction from the swollen nodes, and the monitoring that matters is the respiratory rate, the oxygen saturation, the temperature, the size of the nodes, and the liver enzymes. Position the patient upright, give oxygen, and record the exact time of every dose so that adherence can be assessed. Watch for stridor, difficulty swallowing, or a rapidly enlarging node, because these signal compression of the airway. Escalate for worsening breathlessness, a falling oxygen saturation, confusion, jaundice, or a rash with fever, and involve the tuberculosis program and the HIV team together rather than separately.

A 58 year old man who grew up in a rural area of Southeast Asia is about to start high dose corticosteroids for an autoimmune condition. He has had intermittent abdominal bloating and episodic itchy skin for years but feels well otherwise. Screening before treatment includes a stool examination and a blood test for Strongyloides stercoralis, the threadworm that can persist for decades, and the blood test is positive. He has no fever, no diarrhea, and no breathlessness at present. This is chronic strongyloidiasis, and the danger is that corticosteroids will trigger overwhelming infection.

The worm has a cycle that reinfects the same host, so a person can carry it silently for decades, and corticosteroids suppress the immune control that keeps the cycle contained, which allows massive multiplication and dissemination to the gut, the lungs, and the bloodstream. Treat before the corticosteroids begin, and if those drugs are already under way, treat at the same time rather than waiting. Current guidance from the World Health Organization lists ivermectin at 200 micrograms per kilogram by mouth once a day for 1 to 2 days for uncomplicated infection, with a longer course for disseminated disease, and albendazole at 400 milligrams by mouth twice a day for 7 days as an alternative. Verify the weight, the dose, and the duration against the national guideline and have a second nurse check the calculation. Confirm cure by repeated stool tests, because a single negative test does not prove that the infection has cleared.

The priority nursing problem is risk of disseminated infection once immunosuppression begins, and the monitoring that matters is the temperature, the respiratory rate, the stool pattern, the skin, and the white cell count. Teach the patient to report fever, cough, breathlessness, abdominal pain, or a new rash at once rather than at the next appointment. Record the date that treatment started and the date that corticosteroids are due to start, and tell the prescribing clinician if the order is reversed. Escalate for fever with breathlessness, a rash spreading over the trunk, abdominal pain with distension, or confusion, because disseminated strongyloidiasis is a medical emergency with a high death rate when it is missed.

A 45 year old woman who migrated 12 years ago from a rural region of Bolivia is told that her blood donation tested positive for Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite that causes Chagas disease. She feels well, works full time, and has no chest pain, palpitations, or difficulty swallowing. On examination she has a normal pulse and no edema. She is frightened by the result and asks whether she is infectious to her family. This is chronic Chagas disease detected in the indeterminate phase, and the priority is confirmation and a cardiac assessment.

The infection is transmitted by triatomine bugs in the Americas, and it can also pass from mother to child, in blood products, and in an organ transplant, but it is not spread by casual contact, so sharing a home does not put her family at risk. Confirm the result with a second and different test, because a single positive donation test is not a diagnosis. Current guidance from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization lists benznidazole at 5 to 7 milligrams per kilogram per day by mouth in 2 divided doses for 60 days, and nifurtimox at 8 to 10 milligrams per kilogram per day in 3 or 4 divided doses for 60 days, and the choice depends on availability, age, and pregnancy. Verify the dose and the duration against the current national guideline and have a second nurse check the calculation, because the course is long and side effects are common. Warn her that treatment often causes rash, nausea, and tingling in the hands and feet, and that it is not given during pregnancy.

The priority nursing problem is lack of knowledge about a chronic infection that carries a cardiac risk, and the monitoring that matters is the heart rhythm, the symptoms of heart failure, and the swallowing pattern. Obtain an electrocardiogram and arrange a cardiac evaluation, because a conduction abnormality may appear years after infection. Screen her children for the infection, since mother to child transmission is possible, and arrange testing for anyone in the family who may donate blood. Escalate for fainting, palpitations, chest pain, breathlessness on exertion, or difficulty swallowing, and refer to a cardiologist or a gastroenterologist as the local service allows.

A 30 year old man presents with a large pale patch on his forearm that has been numb for 6 months, and his ulnar nerve is thickened and tender. He has begun to lose strength in his hand and cannot grip a cup firmly. This is leprosy, also called Hansen disease, and the tender nerve indicates a type 1 reaction, in which the immune system attacks the nerve itself. The reaction is an emergency for the nerve, because the damage can become permanent within days. He has no other illness and takes no regular medication.

The nerve is the organ at risk, so treatment aims to stop the immune attack while continuing the antibacterial drugs. Current guidance from the World Health Organization treats multibacillary leprosy with rifampicin, dapsone, and clofazimine, and treats a nerve reaction with prednisolone at 40 to 60 milligrams by mouth each day, tapered slowly over 12 to 20 weeks. Verify the dose and the taper against the national guideline and have a second nurse check the tablet count, because the taper is long and a missed step causes relapse. Teach the patient that the antibacterial drugs may darken the skin, that urine and sweat may turn red, and that clofazimine causes a harmless change in skin color. Give analgesia for nerve pain, avoid drugs that are toxic to nerves when an alternative exists, and report the case to the national leprosy program.

The priority nursing problem is risk of permanent nerve damage and disability, and the monitoring that matters is the strength of the hand, the sensation in the patch, the size and tenderness of the nerve, and the closure of the eye. Test grip strength and sensation at every visit and record the findings on a simple drawing that the next nurse can read. Teach the patient to protect the numb hand from burns and cuts and to inspect the feet every day. Escalate for worsening weakness, a new patch, increased nerve pain, or a foot ulcer, because these signal an uncontrolled reaction that needs a change in treatment. Address the stigma directly, because fear of the diagnosis delays care more than the drugs do.

A 4 year old child is brought to a treatment center during an outbreak with profuse watery diarrhea and vomiting for 12 hours. The child is lethargic, the eyes are sunken, the skin pinch returns slowly, and there has been no urine output. The pulse is fast and weak and the extremities are cold. A stool specimen is sent for culture, but the picture is severe dehydration from cholera, caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae, and treatment must begin before the result returns. The outbreak has already affected several households that share the same water source.

Severe dehydration is corrected with fluid given intravenously, and current guidance from the World Health Organization gives 100 milliliters per kilogram over 3 hours for a child, with the first 30 milliliters per kilogram given in the first hour and the remainder over the following 2 hours. Verify the volume and the rate against the national guideline and against the child's weight, and check the calculation with a second nurse, because both the total and the speed matter. Give oral rehydration salts as soon as the child can drink, and continue breastfeeding if the child is still nursing. Add zinc at 20 milligrams by mouth each day for 10 days, or 10 milligrams each day for an infant below 6 months, and give a single dose of azithromycin at 20 milligrams per kilogram by mouth where the guideline recommends an antibiotic. Record every stool and every vomit, and note the time of each.

The priority nursing problem is deficient fluid volume with risk of shock, and the monitoring that matters is the pulse, the capillary refill, the skin pinch, the urine output, and the number of stools. Weigh the child on arrival and again after rehydration, and use the change as a measure of the fluid given. Watch for overhydration as well, because a fast infusion in a small child can cause breathlessness. Escalate for a weak pulse, no urine after the first hour, continuing profuse diarrhea, drowsiness, or difficulty drinking, and notify the outbreak team so that the water source can be investigated. Teach the family to prepare oral rehydration salts with clean water and to bring the child back at once if the diarrhea returns.

To summarize, these ten composite cases repeat the same lessons in different bodies, and the repetition is deliberate. A negative test never replaces a clinical assessment, a dose is never given from memory, and the nurse who measures the glucose, the urine output, the pulse pressure, or the skin pinch is often the one who sees the turn before anyone else. Each case named a priority nursing problem, the monitoring that mattered, and the threshold for escalation, and each one showed that logistics, adverse effects, and the family's ability to return are part of the clinical plan rather than an afterthought. The World Health Organization, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control revise their guidance, national programs adapt it, and the current version must be checked before any regimen described here is prescribed. Every case in this appendix is a composite, and none of them describes a real person. Carry the pattern rather than the number, verify the number every time, and the patient in front of you will be safer for it.

# Appendix D — Glossary, Key Guidelines, and Reading List

This appendix is not a list to be scanned but a set of definitions to be heard aloud. Each term is given as a sentence, because a fragment cannot be repeated back to a colleague or reasoned with. These words appear again and again in the chapters before this one. A listener who has them settled will hear every later sentence more accurately. Listen once for shape, then return whenever a word in a guideline stops making sense. The reading list at the end describes each title by what it contains.

A vector is a living carrier that moves a pathogen from one host to another. A reservoir is the population or environment where a pathogen normally lives and multiplies. A host is any organism that harbors the pathogen. The definitive host is where the parasite reaches sexual maturity, and the intermediate host is where it passes through an immature stage. An accidental host is one the pathogen can infect but does not need in order to persist. A zoonosis is an infection that passes naturally from an animal to a human being. Spillover is the moment when a pathogen crosses from its usual animal reservoir into a person.

Incidence is the number of new cases in a defined population over a defined period. It shows how fast transmission is happening now. Prevalence is the total number of existing cases in a population at a given moment. It includes people who have been ill for a long time as well as those just infected. A disease can have a low incidence and a high prevalence when it is acquired slowly and cannot be cured. The opposite pattern occurs when a disease kills quickly or resolves quickly. Incidence answers the question of risk, and prevalence answers the question of burden.

Endemic means that a disease is constantly present at a predictable and expected level. It does not mean harmless, because malaria and tuberculosis are endemic across large regions and still kill enormous numbers. Epidemic means that cases have risen above what is expected for that place and season. An outbreak is the same event on a smaller or more localized scale. Pandemic means an epidemic that has spread across several countries or continents with sustained transmission in each. Hyperendemic and holoendemic describe how intense malaria transmission is in an area. A single case of an eliminated disease is an outbreak.

Control means reducing a disease burden to a manageable level, and it accepts that transmission may continue. Elimination means interrupting transmission in a defined geographic area, so that no new locally acquired cases occur there. Surveillance and the tools must be maintained, because the pathogen can return. Elimination as a public health problem is weaker than elimination of transmission, because it allows cases to continue below an agreed threshold. Eradication means the permanent global reduction of cases to zero, so that intervention can stop. It has been achieved only for smallpox. A nurse who uses these four words precisely will be understood by a program officer.

Surveillance is the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, and use of health data, and it exists to drive action. Indicator-based surveillance counts cases of named conditions through clinics and laboratories. Event-based surveillance listens for rumors, unusual clusters, and signals that fit no form. A case definition is the standard set of clinical, laboratory, and epidemiological criteria that decides whether a person counts as a case. It usually provides categories of suspected, probable, and confirmed. The same patient can be a suspected case in one country and a confirmed case in another. Case definitions are revised during outbreaks, so a nurse working from a version from the previous week may classify patients incorrectly.

Sensitivity is the proportion of people with a disease whom a test correctly identifies as having it. Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease whom a test correctly identifies as not having it. A highly sensitive test rarely misses a case but often raises a false alarm. A highly specific test rarely raises a false alarm but often misses a case. Predictive value depends on how common the disease is in the population being tested. The same test therefore performs differently in a referral hospital and in a village screening program. This is why a negative rapid malaria test may be repeated after 2 to 3 days when the story is convincing.

The incubation period is the time from infection to the first symptom or sign of illness, and it shapes quarantine and contact tracing. The prepatent period is the time from infection to the point at which the pathogen can be detected. The two periods are not the same, which explains why a test can be negative while a person is already infected. Parasitemia is the amount of parasite present in the blood, and it changes a malaria decision at the bedside. Viremia is the amount of virus present in the blood, and it governs the chance that a mosquito will be infected from that patient. Neither measurement is fixed, because both rise and fall with the days of the illness.

Chemoprophylaxis is the use of a medicine before or during exposure to prevent disease rather than to treat it. It is most familiar in malaria, where it suppresses the parasite instead of sterilizing the infection. Suppression holds the parasite below the level that causes symptoms, so illness can follow after the drug is stopped. This is why a course is sometimes finished after departure, and the schedule belongs to current national guidance. Chemoprophylaxis differs from presumptive treatment, which is a full course given on the suspicion of infection. It also differs from terminal prophylaxis, which clears dormant liver forms at the end of exposure.

Mass drug administration is the treatment of an entire at-risk population at intervals, without testing each person first. It is the engine of programs against lymphatic filariasis, onchocerciasis, soil-transmitted helminths, schistosomiasis, and trachoma. The medicines are safe enough at population scale, and repeated rounds reduce the reservoir until transmission falls. Coverage, meaning the proportion of eligible people who swallow the medicine, decides whether the program succeeds. Mass drug administration also requires community consent and a system for recording adverse effects. Directly observed therapy means that a named person watches the patient swallow each dose, and the observer may be a health worker, a trained community member, or a family member. It was developed for tuberculosis, where irregular treatment breeds resistance.

Task-shifting is the deliberate redistribution of clinical tasks from more highly trained workers to workers with shorter training. It is supported by protocols, supervision, and a clear scope of practice. It allows a clinic with a single physician and 12 nurses to function, and it is why an advanced practice nurse may prescribe in a district hospital. Task-shifting is safe when the protocols are current, the supervision is real, the referral path is agreed, and the law authorizes the worker. It is unsafe when it is used as a substitute for staffing. The nurse who accepts a shifted task also accepts the duty to escalate when a case falls outside the protocol.

The World Health Organization is the agency of the United Nations responsible for international public health. Its role is to synthesize evidence across countries and issue guidance that a ministry of health can adapt. Its malaria guidelines, its tuberculosis guidance, and its model list of essential medicines are the documents a program officer hands to a new nurse. The organization also maintains international standards for surveillance and outbreak reporting. Its guidance carries grades that describe how strong each recommendation is and how confident the evidence is. Because it speaks to a global audience, its advice is often broader than the national guidance that follows it.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is the national public health agency of the United States, best known in tropical medicine for its travel health guidance and its surveillance reports. Its travel medicine handbook, known as the Yellow Book, gathers pretravel advice, country risks, and vaccine and chemoprophylaxis recommendations. Its weekly report on morbidity and mortality is one of the fastest ways to read about an outbreak while it is still unfolding. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control monitors communicable disease across the European Union. Its value lies in its surveillance bulletins and its short, dated rapid risk assessments. Those assessments assume European laboratory capacity, so they must be read alongside a national protocol.

Beneath the international agencies sit the national programs, and it is the national program that a nurse must obey. It has adapted the global evidence to the local drug supply, the local laboratory, and the local law. Ministries of health issue their own treatment guidelines, essential medicine lists, and reporting forms, and these carry legal weight in a clinic. The adaptation matters because drug availability, resistance patterns, and diagnostic capacity differ. This is what the nurse must hear clearly before prescribing. Treatment regimens are revised as evidence accumulates, national recommendations differ from one country to another, and they change from year to year. The current national guideline and the product label must be checked immediately before any medicine is prescribed or administered.

A guideline is only as good as its date and its method. The first two things to look for are when it was published and how its evidence was graded. A document that states its search strategy, its conflicts of interest, and the strength of each recommendation deserves more trust than a page of assertions with no author. When a new guideline appears, read the summary of changes first, because that is where the revisions affecting practice are concentrated. In a setting with intermittent electricity and expensive data, keep one authoritative copy per clinic, dated on its cover. Refresh it through the district health office or the national program, and give one named person that task, because an unowned document becomes an old document.

Logistics are unglamorous and decisive, and the shelves a nurse uses are shaped by weight, batteries, and weather. A textbook in the clinic and a printed protocol in a plastic sleeve are consulted more often than a perfect file on a laptop. The danger is the well-thumbed outdated printout, which is trusted precisely because it is familiar. Every printed page should carry its date and be replaced as a unit rather than page by page. Expired medicines, cold chain failures, and stock-outs also belong to logistics. The nurse who checks the vaccine carrier temperature is doing clinical work. When a drug is unavailable, substitution is not casual, because the alternatives differ in dose, safety, and monitoring.

Monitoring after a medicine is started is where attention converts into safety, and the parameters depend on the drug. Some medicines require a blood count, some require liver or kidney tests, and some require a glucose measurement. A baseline value taken before the first dose turns a later abnormality into a comparison instead of a puzzle. The practical instrument is a flow sheet that records the date, the dose given, the observation, and the person who gave it. Monitoring also includes the patient's report of sleep, appetite, vision, hearing, skin, and mood, because some harm is felt before it is measured. The nurse who asks the same short set of questions at every visit will detect toxicity early.

An adverse effect is a harmful and unintended response to a medicine at a normal dose, and reporting it is a professional duty. The four things worth writing down are what was given, when it was given, what else the patient was taking, and what happened next. National pharmacovigilance centers collect these reports, and the World Health Organization coordinates them internationally. That is how a rare harm becomes visible when it would be lost in one clinic. Serious reactions and reactions to a newly introduced medicine deserve a report even when the link is uncertain, because suspicion is the raw material of signal detection. Causality is assessed later and formally, so the nurse should never withhold a report for fear of being wrong.

The nursing role in all of this is to be the last check between a recommendation and a patient. Weight is recorded in kilograms, the dose is calculated in milligrams per kilogram, and a second person verifies the decimal point. Look-alike names, confused units, and a tired night shift are the conditions in which a tenfold error happens. The second check exists because competence is not the same as infallibility. Beyond the arithmetic, the nurse translates the guideline into the household's language, explains why the full course matters, arranges the follow-up, and recognizes the deterioration that means referral now. The nurse also holds the ethical duty to say aloud when a protocol cannot be followed safely.

A reading list is useful only if each title is described by what it contains. Manson's Tropical Diseases is the large reference that covers the field in depth and serves mechanism, differential diagnosis, and the unusual presentation. Hunter's Tropical Medicine and Emerging Infectious Diseases is its closest companion, strong on clinical management and on the infections of returning travelers. The Oxford Handbook of Tropical Medicine is the compact field handbook that answers the common question quickly. Markell and Voge's Medical Parasitology teaches life cycles and laboratory identification, and Diagnostic Medical Parasitology by Garcia is the bench reference for the microscope. Where There Is No Doctor remains the plain-language guide for practice far from a hospital, and Travel Medicine covers the pretravel consultation.

The journals divide into those that publish primary research, those that publish reviews, and those that publish surveillance. The American Journal of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene and the Transactions of the Royal Society of Tropical Medicine and Hygiene are the two general journals of the field. The Lancet Infectious Diseases and Clinical Infectious Diseases publish the trials and reviews that change practice. The open access journal of the Public Library of Science devoted to neglected tropical diseases is rich in program and field research. Emerging Infectious Diseases and the weekly report on morbidity and mortality are the fastest routes to outbreak information. The Bulletin of the World Health Organization serves policy evidence, and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews appraises treatment questions. Reference documents age at different speeds, so an anatomy lesson may outlive a dose.

To summarize, this appendix is a small vocabulary and a small library rather than a set of rules. The definitions of vector, reservoir, host, and zoonosis explain how an infection travels, while incidence, prevalence, endemic, epidemic, and pandemic explain how much of it there is. Control, elimination, and eradication describe what a program tries to achieve, and surveillance and case definitions describe how a program knows what is happening. Chemoprophylaxis, mass drug administration, directly observed therapy, and task-shifting are the arrangements by which prevention and treatment are delivered at scale. The guideline bodies supply the source, the national program supplies the authority, and the reading list supplies the depth. None of the three replaces the habit of checking the current document before a medicine is given.
